It can mean accompaniment/association ("with"), involvement (working with someone), or having something in your possession (leaving with the diamonds). Compare: con la (feminine singular), con las (feminine plural), con el (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Ten cuidado con los coches cuando cruces la calle.
native_language_example: Be careful with the cars when you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ayudar (to help), estar (to be), quedarse (to stay), or terminar (to finish) to say someone is dealing with homework. Also common as "con mis/tus/sus deberes" (with my/your/his/her homework). In some countries you may also hear "la tarea" for homework.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes ayudar con los deberes de matemáticas?
native_language_example: Can you help me with my math homework?

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your fingers rather than a tool (like a fork, brush, or comb). It often implies doing it by hand: eating finger food (comer con los dedos), combing hair (peinarse con los dedos), counting on your fingers (contar con los dedos), or finger-painting (pintar con los dedos).
target_language_example: No toques la pantalla con los dedos, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t touch the screen with your fingers, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone behaves in relation to other people in general. It often follows adjectives or verbs like ser amable, ser considerado/a, tener paciencia, or tratar a alguien (e.g., “Sé amable con los demás”).
target_language_example: No seas tan duro con los demás; todos cometemos errores.
native_language_example: Don’t be so hard on others; we all make mistakes.

meaning: with the children; with the kids.
additional_notes: Uses "con" (with) + "los niños" (the children). It can mean being together/doing an activity together ("salir con los niños"), or being good at dealing with children ("ser genial/paciente con los niños"). "Niños" can refer to boys specifically or to children in general; "los" makes it "the" (specific children, often your/their kids).
target_language_example: Voy al parque con los niños después de la escuela.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with the kids after school.

additional_notes: Used with "con" to say you do something using your eyes (i.e., by watching/looking). Often appears in set phrases like "con los ojos abiertos" (with eyes open) and "con los ojos vendados" (blindfolded), and in contrasts like "con el oído... con los ojos" (by ear… by eye).
target_language_example: Reconocí el edificio con los ojos, no con el nombre.
native_language_example: I recognized the building by sight, not by its name.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: having your eyes open. Used literally (e.g., “sleep with your eyes open”) and figuratively to mean staying alert/cautious and paying close attention (similar to “with your eyes open” / “with your eyes wide open”). Often follows an action: “dormir/besar/estar con los ojos abiertos”.
target_language_example: Tienes que caminar con los ojos abiertos en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: You have to walk with your eyes open in this city.

additional_notes: Literally “with the eyes closed.” Used to describe someone doing something while their eyes are shut (resting, listening, sitting). It can also be used figuratively to mean “easily / without thinking,” but in your examples it’s physical.
target_language_example: Respira hondo con los ojos cerrados.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath with your eyes closed.

additional_notes: Describes someone who is about to cry or is already crying a little (from sadness, emotion, or even joy). Used as an adverbial phrase to describe how someone looks, speaks, or does something: "mirar/hablar/estar" con lágrimas en los ojos.
target_language_example: Me despedí con lágrimas en los ojos.
native_language_example: I said goodbye with tears in my eyes.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with or using something that belongs to you. It’s followed by a singular noun: con mi teléfono (with my phone), con mi hermano (with my brother). For plural, use con mis (with my + plural noun).
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo con mi computadora.
native_language_example: I go to work with my computer.

additional_notes: Use it to say you are accompanied by your family or doing something together with them. It often answers “Who are you with?” (¿Con quién estás?) or adds context to an activity (hablar con mi familia = to talk with my family). You can swap in other possessives: con tu familia (with your family), con su familia (with his/her/their family).
target_language_example: Voy al parque con mi familia.
native_language_example: I’m going to the park with my family.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "con" (with) + "mi hermana" (my sister). It can mean being together/working alongside someone ("trabaja con mi hermana") or being involved with someone ("tuvo una relación ... con mi hermana").
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi hermana esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your brother (going somewhere, being with him, doing an activity). It can describe companionship (“I went with my brother”) or who someone is currently with (“He’s with my brother”).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi hermano esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my brother tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your daughter, spending time with her, or doing an activity involving her. "Con" can mean "with" in the sense of accompaniment (being together) or involvement (doing something with/for someone).
target_language_example: Estoy en el parque con mi hija.
native_language_example: I’m at the park with my daughter.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with your mother (doing an activity together) or that something happens in her company. It can also mean “with” in the sense of living together (e.g., Vivo con mi madre = I live with my mother). The preposition con usually becomes conmigo only with the pronoun mí (“with me”), not with nouns like mi madre.
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi madre.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my mother.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your father or doing an activity alongside him. "Con" usually means "with" (in the sense of accompaniment): con mi madre (with my mother), con mi amigo (with my friend).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mi padre esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my father tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your father or doing an activity alongside him. "Con" means "with" and "mi papá" means "my dad" (common and informal for "my father"; "mi padre" is more neutral/formal).
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con mi papá esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my dad tonight.

meaning: 'with my' (with things that belong to me).
additional_notes: Used to say you are doing something using/along with your own things (plural): con + mis + plural noun. It agrees with what you own: con mi (singular), con mis (plural). Common with family members, body parts, belongings, grades, problems, etc.
target_language_example: Voy a viajar con mis amigos este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to travel with my friends this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an activity together with your friends. You can swap the possessive or the noun: con tus amigos (with your friends), con sus amigos (with his/her/their friends), con mi amiga (with my (female) friend).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con mis amigos.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your parents, or that you live in the same home as your parents ("Vivo con mis padres"). Often follows verbs like vivir (to live), estar (to be), hablar (to speak), etc.
target_language_example: Ahora vivo con mis padres porque estoy estudiando.
native_language_example: Now I live with my parents because I'm studying.

meaning: “with my own eyes” (I saw it myself).
additional_notes: Used to stress that you personally witnessed something and aren’t just repeating what you heard. Often appears with verbs like ver (to see) or creer (to believe): “Lo vi con mis propios ojos.” Can be adjusted for person/number: con tus/sus/nuestros propios ojos.
target_language_example: No lo puedo creer, pero lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it, but I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to emphasize that an action should be done cautiously, attentively, or thoughtfully (physically: walking/handling; mentally: choosing words/friends, reading, listening). It’s a common intensifier of cuidado (“care”).
target_language_example: Abre la caja con mucho cuidado; es frágil.
native_language_example: Open the box very carefully; it’s fragile.

meaning: "with more" (used to intensify how you do something).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun to describe doing an action in a stronger or greater way: con más atención (more attention), con más ganas (more motivation/effort), con más calma (more calm), con más fuerza (more force), con más entusiasmo (more enthusiasm), con más expresión (more expression). It often appears with verbs like escuchar, intentar, tomar(se) algo, trabajar, tocar, darle.
target_language_example: Habla con más claridad, por favor.
native_language_example: Speak more clearly, please.

additional_notes: Used to compare how often something happens or how often you do something. Often appears with verbs like ir (to go), ayudar (to help), ocurrir (to happen), comer (to eat). You can also use it in comparisons: «Voy con más frecuencia a X que a Y» = “I go to X more often than to Y.”
target_language_example: Deberíamos vernos con más frecuencia.
native_language_example: We should see each other more often.

additional_notes: Used when “us” refers to a group of females, or a mixed group speaking from a female perspective. It often appears with verbs of coming/going/staying (Ven/Vengan/Quédate/Quédese con nosotras) and can also mean “toward us / with us” in how someone behaves: “Él es muy amable con nosotras” = “He is very kind to us.” Contrast: “con nosotros” for a male or mixed group speaking from a male/mixed perspective.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir con nosotras al cine?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with your group or accompanies you. With verbs of movement it often means “come/go with us” (Puedes venir con nosotros). With estar/venir/quedarse/vivir it can mean being with you, staying with you, or living with you (Está con nosotros; Se va a quedar con nosotros; Vivirá con nosotros). It can also mark who someone feels something toward: enfadado con nosotros = “mad at us.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres cenar con nosotros esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to have dinner with us tonight?

meaning: with whom; with the person who.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person you do something with, often in a relative clause after a noun: “alguien con quien hablar” (someone to talk with). No accent here because it’s not a question. In questions/exclamations it’s “con quién” (accent): “¿Con quién hablas?”
target_language_example: Busco a alguien con quien practicar español.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone to practice Spanish with.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with a person or thing that belongs to them: con + su (singular possessive adjective). The owner can be “his,” “her,” “your (usted),” or “its,” so the meaning depends on context. For plural, use con sus (“with his/her/your/their …”).
target_language_example: Voy al cine con su hermano.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her brother.

meaning: with his/her duty; with what he/she is supposed to do.
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb phrase "cumplir con" ("to fulfill"), as in "cumplir con su deber" = "to do/fulfill your duty". "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context; you can also say "con mi deber" (my duty), "con tu deber" (your duty, informal), "con nuestro deber" (our duty).
target_language_example: Como médico, tengo que cumplir con mi deber.
native_language_example: As a doctor, I have to do my duty.

additional_notes: Means someone is together/doing something in the company of their family (not alone). "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their," but in this phrase it often translates as "his/her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con su familia esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with his/her family tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **con** (“with”) plus **su** (“his/her/your/their”) and **hermana** (“sister”). **Su** is ambiguous, so it can mean *his sister, her sister, your sister,* or *their sister* depending on context. Often appears after verbs like **confundir** (to confuse/mix up): **confundir a X con su hermana** = “to confuse X with his/her sister.”
target_language_example: A veces la gente me confunde con su hermana.
native_language_example: Sometimes people confuse me with her sister.

additional_notes: Means someone is accompanied by their brother ("con" = with; "su" can mean his or her). Used after verbs like "llegar" (to arrive), "venir" (to come), "ir" (to go). In comparisons and identifications, "con" can also mean "compared with" ("Comparado con su hermano...") or "mistaken for" ("Lo confundí con su hermano").
target_language_example: Marta fue al cine con su hermano.
native_language_example: Marta went to the movies with her brother.

additional_notes: Means someone is together/accompanied by their son. "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their," so context tells you whose son it is. For a clear gender distinction, Spanish can also use "con su hija" (with his/her daughter).
target_language_example: Voy al médico con su hijo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the doctor with his/her son.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing something together with their mother. "Su" is a possessive that can mean his, her, their, or your (formal), so the exact meaning depends on context. With family members you often use "con" + possessive + noun: "con su padre", "con su hermana", etc.
target_language_example: Hoy voy al mercado con su madre.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the market with his/her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their father, lives with their father, goes/returns with their father, or does something in the company of their father (e.g., talking, meeting). “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” depending on context. Also used in expressions like “parecido con su padre” (“a resemblance to his/her father”).
target_language_example: Hoy voy al médico con su padre.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to the doctor with his/her father.

meaning: with his/her/your (formal) work; regarding his/her/your work.
additional_notes: “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or “your” (formal “you”), so the exact meaning depends on context. Common with verbs like ayudar (to help) and continuar/seguir (to continue/keep going): “Ayudarle con su trabajo” = “help him/her with his/her work,” “Siga con su trabajo” = “Keep working / Continue with your work.” It can also express attitude: “serio con su trabajo” = “serious about his/her work.”
target_language_example: No puedo salir ahora; estoy ocupado con su trabajo.
native_language_example: I can’t go out now; I’m busy with your work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is together with or connected to something that belongs to them (plural): con sus abuelos (with his grandparents), con sus ahorros (with his savings), con sus juguetes (with his toys). Also used in set phrases like "tener problemas con sus..." (to have problems with your...), and "mantenerse al día con sus..." (to keep up with your...). "Sus" can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context tells you whose it is.
target_language_example: Siempre sale con sus amigos los viernes.
native_language_example: He always goes out with his friends on Fridays.

additional_notes: Uses "con" (with) + "sus" (his/her/their) + "amigos" (friends). "Sus" can mean "his," "her," "your (formal)," or "their"—context tells you whose friends. You can change number/gender: "con su amigo" (with his/her friend), "con sus amigas" (with his/her/their (female) friends).
target_language_example: Hoy voy al cine con sus amigos.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to the movies with his/her friends.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ayudar (to help), hacer (to do), and terminar (to finish) to say someone is dealing with their homework. The owner is shown by sus, which can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context makes it clear.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ayudarme con mis deberes esta tarde?
native_language_example: Can you help me with my homework this afternoon?

meaning: with his/her children; at his/her children (after an emotion like 'angry').
additional_notes: Literally means “with his/her children.” It can show who someone is together with (Vive con sus hijos. = He/She lives with his/her children). After feelings like estar enfadado/enojado or verbs like enfadarse, "con" marks the person you’re upset/angry with: Estaba enfadada con sus hijos. = She was angry at her children. "Sus" can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Está cansada porque viaja con sus hijos todo el día.
native_language_example: She’s tired because she travels with her children all day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their parents or does something in their parents’ presence (e.g., live with them, talk with them, argue with them). "Sus" can mean "his," "her," "their," or the formal "your" (usted/ustedes), depending on context.
target_language_example: Los fines de semana cena con sus padres.
native_language_example: On weekends, he/she/they have dinner with their parents.

meaning: with their own eyes; personally (as a direct witness).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ver/mirar to emphasize that someone saw something directly, not through someone else’s account. It can change person/number to match the subject: con mis/tu/sus/nuestros propios ojos.
target_language_example: No lo creí hasta que lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: I didn’t believe it until I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize totality or intensity: "con todo mi corazón" = "with all my heart." It also appears in common patterns like "con todo gusto" (gladly) and "con todo tipo de..." (with all kinds of...). With "con todo lo que..." it means "with everything that..." / "with all that...".
target_language_example: Te apoyaré con todo lo que tengo.
native_language_example: I’ll support you with everything I have.

additional_notes: Used before a verb clause (often with the relative pronoun “que”) to refer to the totality of things in a situation: con todo lo que contiene/está pasando/hacía (“with everything that it contains/is happening/he did”). It can also mean “using everything (that someone had)” in contexts like attacks or effort: “Nos atacaron con todo lo que tenían” = “They attacked us with everything they had.”
target_language_example: Con todo lo que tengo que hacer hoy, no puedo salir.
native_language_example: With everything I have to do today, I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Use **con tu** before a **singular** noun: *con tu vecino* (with your neighbor), *con tu batería* (with your drum). For plural, use **con tus** (*con tus amigos* = with your friends). If the noun is feminine, it’s still **tu**: *con tu hermana* (with your sister).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hablar con tu profesor un momento?
native_language_example: Can I talk with your teacher for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses **con** (“with”) + **tu hermano** (“your brother”). It can mean being together/alongside someone ("Viniste con tu hermano") or how you treat someone ("Sé bueno con tu hermano"). With verbs like **confundir** (“to confuse”), **con** can mean “for/as” someone else: **Te confundí con tu hermano** = “I mistook you for your brother.”
target_language_example: ¿Vas al cine con tu hermano?
native_language_example: Are you going to the movies with your brother?

additional_notes: Uses "con" (with) + "tu madre" (your mother). Common after verbs like ir/ve (to go), quedarse (to stay), and casarse (to marry): "casarme con tu madre" = "to marry your mother". Often said as an instruction or command: "Ve/Vete con tu madre" = "Go with your mother" ("vete" is the more direct/colloquial imperative of ir: "go away/leave").
target_language_example: No quiero ir solo; voy con tu madre.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go alone; I’m going with your mother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/in the company of the person you’re speaking to’s dad. Also used with verbs like "hablar" (to talk) or "quedarse" (to stay) to mean doing that with him. Word-by-word: con (with) + tu (your) + padre (father).
target_language_example: Voy a ir con tu padre al supermercado.
native_language_example: I’m going to go to the supermarket with your father.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "con" (with) + the possessive "tus" (your, for "tú"). It’s followed by a plural noun: "con tus problemas" (with your problems), "con tus clientes" (with your clients). Often used to show what you use, what you have, or who you’re dealing/talking with; can also appear in emphasis phrases like "con tus propios ojos" (with your own eyes).
target_language_example: No puedo ir con tus amigos hoy.
native_language_example: I can’t go with your friends today.

additional_notes: Emphasizes direct, firsthand observation (not just hearing about it). Often used with verbs like ver (“to see”) and in imperatives: “Velo con tus propios ojos.” You can change the possessive to match the person: con mis propios ojos (with my own eyes), con sus propios ojos (with his/her/their own eyes), con nuestros propios ojos (with our own eyes).
target_language_example: No me lo creí hasta que lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: I didn’t believe it until I saw it with my own eyes.

meaning: “with a” (with one + a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is together with, accompanied by, or using something: con un tenedor (with a fork), con un hablante nativo (with a native speaker). The noun after it is usually masculine singular; for feminine singular, use “con una” (e.g., con una amiga).
target_language_example: Voy a la fiesta con un amigo.
native_language_example: I'm going to the party with a friend.

additional_notes: Used with "con" to say you are with someone (company/along with them) or living/doing an activity together. "Un amigo" is masculine; for a female friend you can say "con una amiga."
target_language_example: Voy al cine con un amigo esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with a friend tonight.

additional_notes: Common after verbs like "topar con" (to run into/come upon) when a boat hits or gets stuck on a shallow pile of sand in the water. "Banco de arena" = a sandbar; "con" here means "with" in the sense of encountering something.
target_language_example: El barco topó con un banco de arena y se quedó atascado.
native_language_example: The boat hit a sandbar and got stuck.

additional_notes: Used to say the instrument/tool used to do an action. You can swap in another object after con (e.g., con una cuchara, con un tenedor). It can describe neutral actions (cutting an apple) or violent actions (stabbing).
target_language_example: Corté el pan con un cuchillo.
native_language_example: I cut the bread with a knife.

meaning: with a bit of; with some (of).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a small amount of something (often a noun): con un poco de calor (a bit of heat), con un poco de presión (a bit of pressure). It’s also very common in the expression “con un poco de suerte” = “with a bit of luck / hopefully.”
target_language_example: Con un poco de ayuda, terminamos más rápido.
native_language_example: With a bit of help, we finished faster.

additional_notes: Used to say that adding a bit more of something (effort, time, patience, money, etc.) would make success possible. Often appears with a conditional idea: “could/would have.” You can use it alone as an encouragement: “Con un poco más de esfuerzo.”
target_language_example: Con un poco más de tiempo, terminamos el proyecto hoy.
native_language_example: With a little more time, we can finish the project today.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una + noun). Often indicates accompaniment ("with a friend"), an instrument/tool ("with a knife"), or a means/cause ("burned himself with a hot pan"). For masculine nouns, use "con un"; for plurals, "con unas" / "con unos".
target_language_example: Corté la cebolla con una cuchilla.
native_language_example: I cut the onion with a blade.

additional_notes: Basic phrase meaning someone is accompanied by a woman, or is in a relationship/has sexual experience with a woman depending on context. Common with verbs like estar (estar con una mujer = to be with a woman / to have been with a woman), casarse (casarse con una mujer = to marry a woman), and tener un romance (un romance con una mujer = an affair/romance with a woman).
target_language_example: Se fue a la fiesta con una mujer que conoció en el trabajo.
native_language_example: He went to the party with a woman he met at work.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing/saying something while smiling, often to show friendliness, confidence, or to hide feelings (e.g., worry). It can also modify a noun: “una sonrisa inocente/enorme” = “an innocent/huge smile.”
target_language_example: Me saludó con una sonrisa y me ofreció ayuda.
native_language_example: He greeted me with a smile and offered to help.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to one person (usted). Common with verbs like pasarla bien (to have a good time), hablar (to talk), vivir (to live), compartir (to share). In informal situations with friends/family, you usually say con tú/contigo instead.
target_language_example: Me gustaría hablar con usted un momento.
native_language_example: I would like to speak with you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say you are together with a group of people you address as ustedes (common in Latin America; in Spain it’s the formal plural). Often follows verbs like hablar (talk), estar de acuerdo (agree), trabajar (work), ir (go), reunirse (meet), discutir (discuss). For 'with us' use con nosotros / con nosotras.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo ir con ustedes al restaurante?
native_language_example: Can I go with you (all) to the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used in regions where people use voseo (vos instead of tú), especially in Argentina, Uruguay, and parts of Central America. It’s the standard preposition + pronoun combination: con + vos. In other varieties you’ll often hear con tú (less common) or contigo (“with you”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hablar con vos un momento?
native_language_example: Can I talk with you for a moment?

additional_notes: “Vosotros” is the informal plural form of “you” used mainly in Spain (Latin America usually uses “ustedes”). Use “con vosotros” to say you are with a group, going with them, or doing something together. The formal version is “con ustedes”.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo ir con vosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Can I go with you all to the movies?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "con" (with) + the stressed pronoun "él" (him). "Él" (he) has an accent to distinguish it from "el" (the). Used after a preposition like "con" to say you are together with a male person.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con él hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk with him today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with a male person (él = “him”) in a specific location introduced by en (“in/at”). Note the accent: él (he/him) vs el (“the”). Very common in phrases like vivir con él en…, estar con él en…, encontrarse con él en….
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme con él en Madrid unos días.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay with him in Madrid for a few days.

meaning: 'with him because of…' / 'with him for…' (gives the reason or purpose).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **con él** (“with him”) + **por** (“because of/for”) + a noun or verb phrase. Use **por** to explain the reason (anger, gratitude, a motive like money) or the purpose (e.g., going out *for* drinks): *Estoy enojado con él por eso* = “I’m mad at him because of that”; *Salir con él por unos tragos* = “go out with him for a few drinks.”
target_language_example: Estoy agradecida con él por ayudarme tanto.
native_language_example: I’m grateful to him for helping me so much.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the ability, permission, or learning process of driving a car. In many places you’ll also hear “conducir un coche” (especially in Spain) or “manejar un auto” (common in Latin America).
target_language_example: ¿Sabes conducir un auto?
native_language_example: Do you know how to drive a car?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "conducir" (to drive) + "un coche" (a car). Often appears with "saber" or "poder" to talk about ability: "Sé/Puedo conducir un coche". You can also say "conducir" without "un coche" when it’s clear what you mean (e.g., "No sé conducir").
target_language_example: No puedo conducir un coche porque no tengo carnet de conducir.
native_language_example: I can’t drive a car because I don’t have a driver’s license.

additional_notes: Used with a person, yourself, or an ability: confianza en mí (trust me), confianza en sí mismo/a (self-confidence), confianza en mis capacidades (confidence in my abilities). Common with tener (“to have”) and verbs like confirmar (“to confirm/reaffirm”).
target_language_example: No tengo mucha confianza en mi español todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t have much confidence in my Spanish yet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s confidence in their own abilities or worth. With people, you commonly say tener confianza en sí mismo/a (“to have self-confidence”) or faltar confianza en sí mismo/a (“to lack self-confidence”). Change “mismo” to “misma” when referring to a woman: confianza en sí misma.
target_language_example: Necesito más confianza en mí mismo para hablar en público.
native_language_example: I need more self-confidence to speak in public.

confiar el uno en el otro

target_language_multi_word_term: confiar el uno en el otro
additional_notes: Used to talk about mutual trust between two people or groups. You’ll also see variations like “confiar el uno en la otra” (male + female) or “confiar los unos en los otros” for more than two people. Very similar in meaning to “confiar el uno en el otro / confiar el uno en la otra”.
target_language_example: Si queremos que esto funcione, tenemos que confiar el uno en el otro.
native_language_example: If we want this to work, we have to trust each other.

additional_notes: Used with a person, group, or thing you trust: confiar en alguien/algo. You can also use it with a clause using que: confiar en que + verb ("to trust that...").
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en mí.
native_language_example: You can trust me.

meaning: to trust me; to have confidence in me.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "confiar" with the preposition "en" ("confiar en + person/thing"). Often appears with "tener que" or "deber" to mean "(you) have to trust me" (e.g., "Tienes que confiar en mí"). "Mí" is the stressed form of "me" used after prepositions like "en".
target_language_example: Si quieres que te ayude, tienes que confiar en mí.
native_language_example: If you want me to help you, you have to trust me.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase “confiar en” (“to trust in”) with “ti” after the preposition “en.” Often used when saying someone is reliable or when you decide to place trust in them. For formal “you,” use “confiar en usted.” For plural “you,” “confiar en ustedes” (Latin America) or “confiar en vosotros” (Spain).
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en ti mismo/a; lo estás haciendo bien.
native_language_example: You can trust yourself; you’re doing well.

meaning: to trust him; to rely on him.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition “en” after confiar: “confiar en + person/thing” (to trust/rely on). “Él” is the stressed form of “he/him” and is used here after a preposition. Common in phrases like “tener que” (have to) or “no tener más remedio que” (have no choice but) + confiar en él.
target_language_example: Si quieres terminar a tiempo, tienes que confiar en él.
native_language_example: If you want to finish on time, you have to trust him.

additional_notes: "Confía" is the tú (informal singular) command form of "confiar" (to trust). Use "confía en" to tell one person to trust in someone/something: "Confía en mí" (Trust me), "Confía en tu instinto" (Trust your instinct). It can be about people, advice, feelings, or plans. (Formal: "Confíe en".)
target_language_example: Confía en mí; todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Trust me; everything is going to turn out fine.

additional_notes: An informal second-person singular command (tú) from confiar: “(you) trust.” Use it to ask someone to believe you or rely on you. For “you” formal (usted), say: Confíe en mí. With friends you may also hear: Confía en mí, por favor.
target_language_example: Confía en mí: todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Trust me: everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: Used with a person/thing: "Confío en ti / en él / en ello" = “I trust you/him/it.” Also used with "en que + verb" to mean “I’m confident that…” (often followed by the subjunctive in Spanish): "Confío en que todo salga bien" = “I’m confident everything will go well.”
target_language_example: Confío en ti y en que lo vas a lograr.
native_language_example: I trust you, and I’m confident you’ll do it.

additional_notes: From the verb "confiar" (to trust) + "en" (in/on) + "ti" (you). Used to express trust in a person. The opposite is "no confío en ti" (I don’t trust you). You can swap the person: "confío en usted" (formal you), "confío en él/ella" (him/her), "confío en ustedes" (you all).
target_language_example: No te conozco bien, pero confío en ti.
native_language_example: I don’t know you well, but I trust you.

additional_notes: From the verb conocer (“to know/meet”). Use the personal "a" before a direct object that is a specific person or people: conoce a Mary, conoce a sus hermanos. If the object is a thing/place, you don’t use "a": conoce Madrid, conoce la historia.
target_language_example: ¿Conoces a mi profesora?
native_language_example: Do you know my teacher?

meaning: to meet; to get to know (a person).
additional_notes: Used with people (or pets/personified things). Spanish uses the “personal a” before a direct object that is a specific person: Conozco a Ana. Often means “to meet (for the first time)” in context, and can also mean “to know (someone)” more generally (as opposed to saber, which is for knowing facts/information).
target_language_example: ¿Cuándo vas a conocer a mis padres?
native_language_example: When are you going to meet my parents?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "conocer" to talk about knowing/being acquainted with people. The "a" is the personal "a" used before a specific person (or sometimes a specific group): "¿Conoces a mi hermana?". "Conoces" is the "tú" (you) form; other common forms: "conoce a" (he/she/you-formal knows), "conocen a" (they/you all know), "conozco a" (I know). Contrast: "conocer" (people/places) vs. "saber" (facts/how to).
target_language_example: ¿Conoces a mi profesor de español?
native_language_example: Do you know my Spanish teacher?

additional_notes: Preterite (past) form of **conocer** used for first meeting someone: **conocer a + person**. The **a** is the personal **a** used before a specific person (e.g., *conoció a Tom*). For places/things you usually use **conocer** without **a** (e.g., *conoció Boston* = he visited/got to know Boston).
target_language_example: Ayer conoció a mi hermana en la fiesta.
native_language_example: Yesterday he met my sister at the party.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of conocer used for meeting a person for the first time. Use "a" before a specific person (the personal "a"): conocí a Tom / conocí a mi esposa. Not used for knowing facts or places (there you’d usually use "conocí" without "a").
target_language_example: Conocí a tus padres en la fiesta.
native_language_example: I met your parents at the party.

additional_notes: Use **conozco** (from *conocer*) to say you know/are familiar with a person or have met them. The **a** is the *personal a*: it goes before a direct object that is a specific person (or a pet), e.g., **Conozco a María**. With things/places, you usually drop **a**: **Conozco Madrid / Conozco este libro**. Contrast with **saber**, which is for knowing facts or how to do something (**Sé la respuesta**, **Sé nadar**).
target_language_example: No conozco a tu profesor, pero conozco a tu hermana.
native_language_example: I don’t know your teacher, but I know your sister.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a person you know (or know of) and then describe what they can do or what they’re like. The verb is conjugated for the speaker: yo conozco (“I know”), and it’s followed by a relative clause with que (“who/that”). For other people: Conoces a alguien que… (“Do you know someone who…?”), Conozco a alguien que podría… (“I know someone who could…”).
target_language_example: Conozco a alguien que puede arreglar tu coche.
native_language_example: I know someone who can fix your car.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression (mucho, poco, diez años, tiempo, etc.) to say how long you have known someone. Structure: (Yo) lo/la/los/las conozco desde hace + duration. Note: "desde hace" is like "for" in English here (not literally "since ago").
target_language_example: La conozco desde hace tres meses.
native_language_example: I've known her for three months.

additional_notes: Used with a person who knows/realizes something: most commonly **ser consciente de + noun/que-clause** (e.g., *Soy consciente de que es difícil*). You may also hear **estar consciente de** in some regions; note that **estar consciente** can also mean “to be conscious/awake” (not unconscious).
target_language_example: No soy consciente de lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I'm not aware of what happened.

additional_notes: Used with estar/ser (most often estar) to say someone realizes/knows there is danger. It agrees in gender/number: consciente (m./f. sing.), conscientes (plural). Common negatives: no estar consciente del peligro (“not aware of the danger”).
target_language_example: No estaba consciente del peligro hasta que escuché la alarma.
native_language_example: I wasn’t aware of the danger until I heard the alarm.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "construir" (to build) + "una casa" (a house). You can change the article to be specific: "construir la casa" = "to build the house". Common patterns: "quiero construir una casa" (I want to build a house), "para construir una casa" (in order to build a house).
target_language_example: Queremos construir una casa cerca del mar.
native_language_example: We want to build a house near the sea.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/encontrarse (to be in contact), tener (to have contact), and perder (to lose contact). It can refer to communication with a person/group (calls, messages, etc.) or close connection/exposure to something (e.g., nature, a language). Often appears as "en contacto con" (in contact with).
target_language_example: Sigo en contacto con mis amigos de la universidad.
native_language_example: I’m still in contact with my friends from college.

additional_notes: Most common with money: "en efectivo contante y sonante" = cash you can count (not a check, not a transfer). It’s also used to emphasize that something/someone is the real thing (often in insults): "la X contante y sonante" = "the X itself" / "the very embodiment of X."
target_language_example: Me pagaron en efectivo contante y sonante.
native_language_example: They paid me in cash.

additional_notes: Used with an ending number after al: contar del uno al diez/cien/mil. Also remember contar can mean “to tell” (a story), but in this pattern it clearly means “to count”.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes contar del uno al veinte?
native_language_example: Can you count from one to twenty?

additional_notes: Used to express opposition, fighting/competing, being protected from something, or being “against” an idea or proposal. It’s the contraction of "contra" + "el" (not *contra él*, which means “against him”). In plural: "contra los"; feminine: "contra la/las".
target_language_example: Voté contra el plan porque era demasiado caro.
native_language_example: I voted against the plan because it was too expensive.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to show opposition or resistance (often after verbs like luchar, pelear, ir). Use "contra el" for masculine singular nouns.
target_language_example: Estamos en contra de la violencia.
native_language_example: We are against violence.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like estrellarse (to crash), poner (to put), and apoyarse/estar apoyado (to lean/be leaning) to show contact with the wall. It implies being right up against it, not just near it.
target_language_example: Apoya la bicicleta contra la pared, por favor.
native_language_example: Lean the bike against the wall, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not allowed because it breaks the rules. Common patterns: "Es contra las reglas" (It’s against the rules) and "(Algo) va contra las reglas" (Something goes against the rules).
target_language_example: No puedes entrar aquí; es contra las reglas.
native_language_example: You can’t come in here; it’s against the rules.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something because they were forced or pressured, not because they wanted to. Often appears with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "obligar" (to force), "casarse" (to get married), or "quedarse" (to stay). You can change the possessive: contra mi/tu/su/nuestra/vuestra voluntad (against my/your/his-her/our/your will).
target_language_example: Firmó el contrato contra su voluntad.
native_language_example: He signed the contract against his will.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "contar" (to tell) in the preterite tense ("contó" = he/she told). The indirect object pronoun often appears before the verb: "me" (to me), "nos" (to us), "te" (to you). Word order is flexible: "Me contó una historia interesante" = "Ella me contó una historia interesante."
target_language_example: El guía nos contó una historia interesante sobre la ciudad.
native_language_example: The guide told us an interesting story about the city.

additional_notes: Used with a person after "a": convencer a alguien = to convince someone. It’s often followed by "de" + infinitive or noun (convince someone to do something / of something), or by "para que" + subjunctive (convince someone so that they do something): "Convencí a María de ir" / "Convencí a Tomás para que volviera". The "a" is the personal "a" used with direct objects that are people.
target_language_example: No puedo convencer a mi hermano de venir conmigo.
native_language_example: I can’t convince my brother to come with me.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong belief or certainty about a statement: (estar) convencido/a/os/as de que + clause. It agrees with the person (convencido/convencida/convencidos/convencidas) and is often used with estar: “Estoy convencido de que…”.
target_language_example: Estoy convencida de que va a salir bien.
native_language_example: I’m convinced that it’s going to turn out well.

additional_notes: Preterite (past) form of "convencer": "[Someone] convenció a [person]" = "[Someone] convinced [person]". Very commonly followed by: (1) "para" or "a" + infinitive (action): "convenció a Rima para quedarse"; or (2) "de que" + verb phrase (often in subjunctive): "convenció a Tom de que le prestara…".
target_language_example: Ella convenció a su hermano para estudiar más.
native_language_example: She convinced her brother to study more.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "convertir" to say that someone/something changes form or becomes something else. Often appears in the passive: "ser convertido en" (was turned into). You’ll also see the reflexive form "convertirse en" meaning "to become/turn into" (e.g., "Me he convertido en...").
target_language_example: La fábrica fue convertida en un museo.
native_language_example: The factory was turned into a museum.

additional_notes: "Convertirme" is the reflexive verb "convertirse" (to become), conjugated for "yo" (I). It’s followed by "en" + a noun/role: "convertirme en escritor" (become a writer). Often used for goals, destiny, or change; in other persons: "convertirte en" (you), "convertirse en" (to become).
target_language_example: De niño, quería convertirme en médico.
native_language_example: As a kid, I wanted to become a doctor.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (or role/status) after en: convertirse en médico, convertirse en ciudadano. It often implies a change over time or a transformation, and is commonly used with a purpose clause: para convertirse en…. Conjugate convertir(se) and keep the reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se): me convierto en…, se convirtió en….
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un gran líder.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great leader.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **convertir en** (“to turn/transform into”). It’s used to say that one thing causes another to become something different. **Convierte** is 3rd person singular present (he/she/it/you-formal “turns”), and the object pronouns often come before it: **lo/la/los/las/nos** (e.g., *la convierte en...*, *nos convierte en...*).
target_language_example: El estrés lo convierte en una persona impaciente.
native_language_example: Stress turns him into an impatient person.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of **convertirse en** (“to become”) and **convertir (a alguien/algo) en** (“to turn someone/something into”). Used to talk about a completed change in status, role, or identity. Often appears as **se convirtió en** (became) or **(alguien) convirtió a X en Y** (made/turned X into Y).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un gran líder.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great leader.

additional_notes: From the verb "convertir" (to turn/convert). "Convirtió" is the past tense (he/she/it/you-form did it), and it’s usually used with a direct object: "X lo/la convirtió en un(a) Y" = "X turned him/her into a Y". For talking about someone becoming something by themselves, Spanish often uses "se convirtió en..." (e.g., "Él se convirtió en un cantante famoso"). Use "en un" with masculine nouns; with feminine nouns use "en una".
target_language_example: La magia lo convirtió en un gato.
native_language_example: The magic turned him into a cat.

additional_notes: From the verb **latir** (to beat, like a heart). **Late** is the present tense: *El corazón late* = “The heart beats/is beating.” It’s also used in expressions like **me late el corazón** (“my heart is beating”) and **el corazón late en la garganta** (“your heart feels like it’s beating in your throat”) to talk about being nervous, excited, or scared. Note: Spanish **late** is not related to English “late” (tardy).
target_language_example: Cuando escuché la noticia, mi corazón late muy rápido.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, my heart beats very fast.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed. Pattern: [subject] corre más rápido que + (yo/tú/él/ella/nosotros/ustedes/ellos) or + a noun (e.g., un perro). The verb changes with the subject (corro/corres/corre/corremos/corren).
target_language_example: Mi hermano corre más rápido que yo.
native_language_example: My brother runs faster than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare running speed. Structure: (subject) + puede/puedo + correr más rápido que + (person/thing). You can replace the subject after que with a pronoun (yo, él, ella) or a noun (un hombre, Ken).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes correr más rápido que tu hermano?
native_language_example: Can you run faster than your brother?

meaning: 'ran toward' (he/she/it ran in the direction of).
additional_notes: "Corrió" is the past tense (preterite) of "correr" for él/ella/usted. "Hacia" means "toward" and is used with a destination or person: "corrió hacia la puerta" (toward the door), "corrió hacia él" (toward him).
target_language_example: Cuando vio el autobús, corrió hacia la parada.
native_language_example: When he saw the bus, he ran toward the stop.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito): corrió = “ran.” The pattern “tan + adverb/adjective + como pudo” means “as [adverb/adjective] as (he/she) could,” expressing doing something to the maximum possible. You can swap in other verbs and adjectives/adverbs: “hizo tanto como pudo” (did as much as he could), “habló tan claro como pudo” (spoke as clearly as she could). You can also change the subject: “corrí…/corriste…/corrimos…”.
target_language_example: Corrí tan rápido como pude para no perder el autobús.
native_language_example: I ran as fast as I could so I wouldn’t miss the bus.

additional_notes: Used after una/otra/alguna/ninguna + cosa to add an extra item or point: una cosa más (one more thing), otra cosa más (one more/another thing). Common when wrapping up a conversation: «Sólo una cosa más» / «Tengo una cosa más que decir».
target_language_example: Antes de irnos, sólo una cosa más: ¿tienes las llaves?
native_language_example: Before we leave, just one more thing: do you have the keys?

additional_notes: Most literally it means “the thing that/which,” used to introduce a clause describing something: "la cosa que vi" = “the thing that I saw.” It can also be used parenthetically after a statement to add a comment, often with a slightly skeptical tone: "..., cosa que dudo" = “..., which I doubt."
target_language_example: No encuentro la llave, cosa que me preocupa.
native_language_example: I can’t find the key, which worries me.

additional_notes: A general phrase for positive things (benefits, nice experiences, good-quality items). Often used with verbs like "merecer" (to deserve), "tocar" (to happen to someone / to get), and "venir" (to come), or in the pattern "una de las cosas buenas de..." (one of the good things about...).
target_language_example: Me han pasado muchas cosas buenas este año.
native_language_example: A lot of good things have happened to me this year.

meaning: things on my mind; a lot to think about.
additional_notes: Used with tener (tengo/tiene) to say you're mentally busy or preoccupied with worries, tasks, or thoughts. Often appears with muchas/demasiadas to emphasize feeling overwhelmed.
target_language_example: No puedo concentrarme; tengo demasiadas cosas en la cabeza hoy.
native_language_example: I can’t focus; I have too many things on my mind today.

additional_notes: Used to say other matters have higher priority than what you’re talking about. Very common in the pattern "tener cosas más importantes que + infinitive" (e.g., que hacer / que pensar / de que preocuparse). You can also use "pasar" with it to mean "more important things are happening."
target_language_example: Lo siento, tengo cosas más importantes que hacer ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have more important things to do right now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or specifies “cosas” (things). Very common after phrases like “hay cosas que…”, “cosas que ver”, “cosas que explicar”, “una de las cosas que…”. You can often translate it as “things that…”, and sometimes just “things…” in natural English.
target_language_example: Tengo cosas que hacer esta tarde.
native_language_example: I have things to do this afternoon.

meaning: things to do; tasks/errands to take care of.
additional_notes: Very common way to talk about your to-do list or responsibilities. Often used with verbs like tener (to have): "Tengo cosas que hacer" = "I have things to do." You can add quantity words: "un par de cosas que hacer" (a couple of things to do), "muchas cosas que hacer" (many things to do).
target_language_example: No puedo salir ahora; tengo cosas que hacer en casa.
native_language_example: I can’t go out right now; I have things to do at home.

meaning: “things that … not / didn’t / shouldn’t …” (introduces a negative relative clause).
additional_notes: Used when you want to say “things that” followed by a verb in the negative. The exact meaning depends on the verb that comes next: cosas que no hiciste (“things you didn’t do”), cosas que no debe decir (“things one shouldn’t say”), cosas que no diría (“things I wouldn’t say”). Often implies denial, refusal, or something inappropriate.
target_language_example: No me culpes por cosas que no hice.
native_language_example: Don’t blame me for things I didn’t do.

meaning: “believes in” (has faith in; thinks something is real/true; supports an idea).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **creer en** (“to believe in”). It’s used for believing in the existence of something (**creer en fantasmas / en Dios**) and for believing in or supporting an idea or principle (**creer en el socialismo**, **creer en convertir la basura en combustible**). Pattern: **[person] cree en + noun/idea**.
target_language_example: Mi hermana cree en la medicina natural.
native_language_example: My sister believes in natural medicine.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or belief followed by a clause. "Cree" is the present tense of "creer" for usted (formal you) and for él/ella (he/she); context (or punctuation like a question mark) tells you which one it is. Often used in questions: "¿Cree que…?" = "Do you think…?"
target_language_example: ¿Cree que va a llover mañana?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used when someone is too trusting and accepts whatever another person says. Structure: (él/ella/usted) cree + todo lo que + [person] + dice / [clause]. You can change the verb to match the subject: creo / crees / cree / creemos / creen.
target_language_example: No creas todo lo que lees en internet.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything you read on the internet.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what “we” (the speaker + others) think, believe, or assume. It’s the 1st person plural (nosotros) present tense of creer + que, and it’s followed by a clause (often with indicativo for beliefs/opinions: “Creemos que es…”, “Creemos que vendrá…”).
target_language_example: Creemos que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: We think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present tense of "creer" (to think/believe) in the "they" form: "(ellos/ellas/ustedes) creen". Often the subject is omitted in Spanish, so "creen que..." can mean "they think that..." or "you (plural) think that..." depending on context. Commonly followed by an idea or statement introduced by "que".
target_language_example: Creen que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: They think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb *creer* (to think/believe) in the tú form: *tú crees*. Very common before a full clause: *¿Crees que…?* (question) or *Crees que…* (statement). Often *que* can be omitted in English: *¿Crees que soy…?* = “Do you think I’m…?”
target_language_example: ¿Crees que va a llover mañana?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain tomorrow?

meaning: "I think we should / I believe we need to."
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion about what the group ("we") should do. "Creo que" = "I think" and "debemos" = "we must/should" (from "deber"). Often followed by an infinitive: "creo que debemos esperar" (I think we should wait).
target_language_example: Creo que debemos irnos ya porque es tarde.
native_language_example: I think we should leave now because it’s late.

additional_notes: Used to give a mild opinion or suggestion about what’s best to do. After “creo que”, the verb “debería” (conditional of deber) expresses “should/ought to” in a polite, less forceful way. The subject can change: “Creo que debería irme” = I should leave; “Creo que debería irse” = he/she/you (formal) should leave.
target_language_example: Creo que debería hablar con ella primero.
native_language_example: I think I should talk to her first.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion about what a group ("we") ought to do. "Creo que" = "I think (that)", and "deberíamos" is the conditional form of "deber" ("we should/ought to"), which sounds a bit softer and more polite than "debemos" ("we must"). Often followed by an infinitive: "...deberíamos ir / decir / hacer".
target_language_example: Creo que deberíamos irnos a casa ya.
native_language_example: I think we should go home now.

additional_notes: Used to offer a recommendation in a polite, not-too-direct way. Literally “I believe that you ought to…”. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., hablar, ver, saber). You can change the verb ending for other people: “creo que deberías” (you, informal singular), “creo que debería” (he/she/you formal), “creo que deberían” (you all/they).
target_language_example: Creo que deberías descansar un poco.
native_language_example: I think you should rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a strong suggestion that someone leave. In context it can sound polite (softening with "creo que") or like a firm warning/order, especially with words like "ahora", "ya mismo", or "de inmediato". "Deberías" is the conditional of "deber" (should/ought to) and "irte" is "ir" + "te" (to leave/go away).
target_language_example: Creo que deberías irte antes de que empiece la reunión.
native_language_example: I think you should leave before the meeting starts.

meaning: “I think that the…” / “I believe that the…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or guess: **Creo que + clause** (“I think that…”). Here **el** is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), so this pattern is often followed by a masculine noun (e.g., *el campeón*) or a masculine person/thing referred to indirectly (e.g., *el de mantenimiento* = “the maintenance guy”). For feminine/plural, you’d use **creo que la / los / las**.
target_language_example: Creo que el profesor no viene hoy.
native_language_example: I think the teacher isn’t coming today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or assumption about what a woman/girl did, knows, feels, etc. In Spanish you normally keep que after creo; in English we often drop “that” (“I think she…”). Ella can be omitted if it’s already clear who you mean: Creo que sabe la verdad (“I think she knows the truth”).
target_language_example: Creo que ella no viene hoy.
native_language_example: I think she’s not coming today.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or guess. Often followed by an adjective ("creo que es hermoso"), a noun ("creo que es un avión"), or a longer clause ("creo que es lo que debo hacer"). In everyday speech you may also hear "creo que" without "es" when what comes next isn’t "it is."
target_language_example: Creo que es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you believe the moment has come to do something, often as a gentle suggestion or decision. It’s followed by an infinitive (ir, volver, levantarse, etc.). You can also hear it without “creo” as “Es hora de…” (“It’s time to…”), which sounds more direct.
target_language_example: Creo que es hora de hablar con el jefe.
native_language_example: I think it’s time to talk to the boss.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or best guess. It’s most common before a verb phrase: “Creo que eso es…” (I think that’s…), “Creo que eso va a…” (I think that’s going to…). In negatives, “No creo que eso…” means “I don’t think that…”.
target_language_example: Creo que eso es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I think that’s a good idea.

meaning: "I think that that is..." / "I believe that that is..."
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or guess about something. Often followed by an adjective (correcto) or a noun phrase (para mí, su mano, algo bueno). In conversation it can sound a bit repetitive; you may also hear "creo que es..." when "eso" is understood.
target_language_example: Creo que eso es mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I think that that is my phone.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or guess about something close to you or just mentioned. After **este** you normally add a masculine singular noun (e.g., *este caballero*, *este suéter*) or you can use **este** as a pronoun when the noun is clear from context. Variations: **creo que esta** (feminine), **creo que estos/estas** (plural).
target_language_example: Creo que este lugar es perfecto para cenar.
native_language_example: I think this place is perfect for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or belief about something in the present. It’s often followed by a noun ("...tuvo"), an adjective ("...importante"), or a full idea. In conversation you may also hear "Creo que es..." (dropping "esto") when the thing is clear from context.
target_language_example: Creo que esto es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I think this is a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you believe (but aren’t 100% sure) that you’re in love. Often followed by **de + person/thing**: **Creo que estoy enamorado de ella/de esta chica** (“I think I’m in love with her/this girl”). You can change for gender/number: **enamorado** (male speaker), **enamorada** (female speaker).
target_language_example: Creo que estoy enamorado de ti.
native_language_example: I think I’m in love with you.

additional_notes:
Used to express an opinion or guess about someone’s state, condition, or what they’re doing. 
- Creo que = “I think/I believe” 
- está = “is” (temporary state/location; from estar). 
Often followed by an adjective (cerca, enferma, enamorada) or a verb in the -ando/-iendo form (está diciendo/viendo). You can also say “Creo que está…” without “que” in casual speech, but “Creo que está…” is very common.
target_language_example: Creo que está cansado hoy.
native_language_example: I think he’s tired today.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or guess about something that already happened. It’s often followed by an adjective or phrase describing how it was (e.g., bien, malo, lo mejor). You can also hear “creo que era” when talking about a past ongoing situation or description.
target_language_example: Creo que fue una buena idea.
native_language_example: I think it was a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief: "Creo que..." = "I think/believe that...". The "la" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it comes before a feminine noun (la elección, la entrevista, la gramática, la marea). With a masculine noun, you’d use "creo que el...".
target_language_example: Creo que la respuesta es correcta.
native_language_example: I think the answer is correct.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion/guess (creo que = “I think/believe that”). The pronoun **le** is an **indirect object pronoun** meaning “to him/to her/to you (formal)” (and in some regions, sometimes “to him” instead of **lo**). It often appears with verbs like **gustar** (Creo que le gustas = “I think he/she likes you”), and also before many verbs to show who is affected/receives something (Creo que le puse demasiado azúcar = “I think I put too much sugar in it/for him/her”).
target_language_example: Creo que le falta un poco de sal.
native_language_example: I think it needs a little more salt.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion: "Creo que..." = "I think...". The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (e.g., "Creo que lo encontré" = "I think I found it"). With "ser" or "estar", "lo" often means "so/that way": "Creo que lo está" = "I think he/she is (like that / so)"; "Creo que lo soy" = "I think I am".
target_language_example: Creo que lo entiendes.
native_language_example: I think you understand it.

meaning: “I think that the …” (talking about a plural masculine noun: “the …”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion: **creo que + (clause)**. Here **los** is the masculine plural definite article (“the”), used with masculine plural nouns (e.g., *los policías, los idiomas, los cumpleaños*). For feminine plural use **las**, and for singular use **el/la**.
target_language_example: Creo que los perros son muy inteligentes.
native_language_example: I think that dogs are very intelligent.

meaning: "I think that I…" (starting a sentence where "me" is "me/to me/myself").
additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion/guess: "Creo que…" + a verb. The "me" is an object/reflexive pronoun whose meaning depends on the next verb: e.g., "me debes" = "you owe me", "me lo he dejado" = "I left it (behind)" (to myself), "me pondré" = "I'll put on". Often followed by present, past, or future forms depending on what you're talking about.
target_language_example: Creo que me equivoqué.
native_language_example: I think I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, make a suggestion, or express an opinion about what someone should do. "Creo que" softens the statement (less direct than "necesitas..."). You can follow it with an infinitive ("comer", "dormir") or a noun ("algo").
target_language_example: Creo que necesitas hablar con el profesor.
native_language_example: I think you need to talk to the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to politely express your opinion that something isn’t true or won’t happen. Often followed by more information: “Creo que no + (verb...)” (e.g., “Creo que no entiende”). You can also use it alone as a short answer: “—¿Vienes? —Creo que no.”
target_language_example: —¿Va a llover hoy? —Creo que no.
native_language_example: —Is it going to rain today? —I don't think so.

meaning: “I think (that) we…” / “I think (that) us…” (introduces an opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Used to start a sentence giving your opinion: creo que = “I think/I believe.” The word nos is a pronoun meaning “us,” “to us,” or part of “we/each other” depending on the verb that follows (e.g., Creo que nos está enviando un mensaje = “I think he/she is sending us a message”; No creo que nos hayamos conocido = “I don’t think we’ve met”). Often used with no creo que… to disagree or express doubt.
target_language_example: Creo que nos van a ayudar mañana.
native_language_example: I think they’re going to help us tomorrow.

meaning: "I think I can" / "I believe I can."
additional_notes: Used to express that you believe you’re able to do something, often as a polite/soft way to say you can do it. It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "Creo que puedo + infinitivo" (e.g., "creo que puedo hacerlo"). In conversation it can also show modest confidence or uncertainty (similar to “I think I can…”).
target_language_example: Creo que puedo hacerlo yo solo.
native_language_example: I think I can do it by myself.

meaning: “I think you know…” / “I believe you know…”
additional_notes: Used to say you assume the other person already knows something, often as a polite or indirect way to introduce a point. Commonly followed by: “a lo que me refiero” (what I mean), “la respuesta” (the answer), “lo que quiero decir” (what I’m trying to say). In Spanish, “creo que…” often softens the statement (it sounds less blunt than stating it as a fact).
target_language_example: Creo que sabes por qué estoy aquí.
native_language_example: I think you know why I’m here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion: "Creo que..." = "I think/I believe...". The "se" usually belongs to the verb that follows (often reflexive or a pronoun meaning something like "himself/herself/itself," or an impersonal/passive "se"). It can combine with other pronouns: "se te cayó" = "you dropped / it fell from you" (literally, "it fell to you").
target_language_example: Creo que se va a olvidar de llamarte.
native_language_example: I think he/she is going to forget to call you.

meaning: “(I) think/believe that … is” (with subjunctive, often after doubt/negation).
additional_notes: This appears most often as **(no) creo que sea + noun/adjective** (“I (don’t) think it’s …”). After **no creo que…** and other expressions of doubt/uncertainty, Spanish commonly uses the **subjunctive**: **sea** (from *ser*). In contrast, an affirmative certainty often uses the indicative: **Creo que es verdad** (“I think it’s true”).
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

meaning: "I think it would be better if…" (a suggestion/advice).
additional_notes: Used to recommend an action or say what you think is the best idea. It’s often followed by the present subjunctive (e.g., “entremos”, “salgamos”, “se vaya”, “venga”). Common in polite but firm advice: “Creo que será mejor que + [action].”
target_language_example: Creo que será mejor que hablemos mañana.
native_language_example: I think it would be better if we talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you probably know something, but with some uncertainty (softer than "sé..."). Often followed by an indirect question ("cuál es...", "dónde...", "por qué...", "lo que...") or a noun ("la respuesta").
target_language_example: Creo que sé cómo llegar a tu casa.
native_language_example: I think I know how to get to your house.

additional_notes: Used to agree or confirm something, often with a bit of uncertainty or politeness. It can stand alone as an answer (“—¿Vienes? —Creo que sí.”) or be followed by a full clause (“Creo que sí está en casa” = “I think he/she is at home.”). The “sí” emphasizes a positive answer.
target_language_example: —¿Tienes tiempo mañana? —Creo que sí.
native_language_example: —Do you have time tomorrow? —I think so.

meaning: "I think (that) you…" / "I think (that) …to you" (with te = you).
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or guess: creo que = “I think/I believe.” The word te is the object pronoun “you” (informal singular), so what follows is usually something happening to you (e.g., “I think it scared you”), someone doing something to you (“I think he/she is calling you”), or your situation (“I think I can help you”). It’s very common to drop “that” in English, but Spanish keeps que: “Creo que te…”.
target_language_example: Creo que te entiendo mejor ahora.
native_language_example: I think I understand you better now.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or tentative conclusion about what you and others have (something, time, a deal, work to do, etc.). Often followed by a noun phrase ("Creo que tenemos un problema") or something like "que + verb" to continue the idea.
target_language_example: Creo que tenemos suficiente tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: I think we have enough time to finish.

meaning: "I think we have to" / "I believe we need to".
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion about what the group ("we") should do. "Creo que" softens the statement (it’s your view, not a certainty). It’s followed by "tenemos que" + infinitive (e.g., dejar, parar, ser, usar) to express obligation/necessity.
target_language_example: Creo que tenemos que irnos ahora.
native_language_example: I think we have to leave now.

meaning: "I think I have" / "I believe I have."
additional_notes: Used to express that you probably have something, but you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by a noun ("creo que tengo una") or by "que" + a full idea ("creo que tengo algo de pizza sobrante"). In polite contexts you might hear "Ud." (usted) after it.
target_language_example: Creo que tengo tu libro en mi mochila.
native_language_example: I think I have your book in my backpack.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion/belief about what someone has (a thing, a quality, a reason, etc.). Very common in conversation. Often followed by a noun or phrase: creo que tienes razón (I think you’re right), creo que tienes tiempo (I think you have time).
target_language_example: Creo que tienes razón, pero necesitamos más información.
native_language_example: I think you’re right, but we need more information.

meaning: “I think I’m going to…” (said before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to express what you believe you will do soon or what seems likely: Creo que voy a + infinitive (e.g., irme, intentarlo). It can also be used humorously/exaggeratedly to react to something (e.g., “That’s so sweet, I think I’m going to throw up.”).
target_language_example: Creo que voy a pedir otra bebida.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to order another drink.

meaning: “I think we/I already…” or “I think I’ll go now.”
additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying (“I think…”). The word “ya” often means “already” (with a past action) or “now / at this point” (when you’re about to do something, like leaving).
target_language_example: Creo que ya es hora de irnos.
native_language_example: I think it’s time for us to go now.

additional_notes: A common sentence starter used before a verb to say you think something has already been done or obtained. "creo que" = "I think (that)", "ya" = "already", and "lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (referring to something understood from context). Often followed by a verb phrase like "hecho" (done) or "tengo" (I have it).
target_language_example: Creo que ya lo encontramos; gracias de todos modos.
native_language_example: I think we already found it; thanks anyway.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion about what he does, is, or will do. In Spanish, after *creo que* you typically use the indicative (e.g., *creo que él conoce…*). After *no creo que* you often use the subjunctive (e.g., *no creo que él logre…*). Often *él* can be omitted if it’s clear who you mean: *Creo que conoce bien a Roma.*
target_language_example: Creo que él viene mañana.
native_language_example: I think he’s coming tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed or assumed in the past, often when it turned out to be wrong or surprising. It’s the preterite of creer (to believe/think) + que (that). Commonly followed by a full clause: “Creí que + [subject] + [verb]…”.
target_language_example: Creí que la tienda estaba cerrada, pero estaba abierta.
native_language_example: I thought the store was closed, but it was open.

meaning: "I thought you were…" / "I believed you were…" (talking about what you believed in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say you had a belief/assumption in the past (creí = preterite of creer, “I thought/believed”). Often it implies that belief turned out to be wrong or changed later. "Eras" is the imperfect of ser for "tú" (“you were”), describing what someone was like.
target_language_example: Creí que eras mi profesor, no mi vecino.
native_language_example: I thought you were my teacher, not my neighbor.

meaning: "I thought that you..." (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed about the other person in the past. "Creí" is the preterite of "creer" (I thought/believed), "que" = that, and "te" is the object pronoun for "you" (informal singular: you / to you). Often followed by a verb: "Creí que te gustaría..." = I thought you’d like...
target_language_example: Creí que te interesaría este libro.
native_language_example: I thought you’d be interested in this book.

meaning: "I thought you had..." (talking about something that happened before another past moment).
additional_notes: Used to say you believed something in the past: creí = “I thought” (simple past). te = “you” (informal singular). habías + past participle (ido, marchado, olvidado, ahogado, etc.) is the past perfect/pluperfect: “you had (done something)”. Often introduces a misunderstanding: “I thought you had left / forgotten me.”
target_language_example: Creí que te habías perdido.
native_language_example: I thought you had gotten lost.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone believed or assumed in the past, often when it turns out to be wrong or is being corrected. "Creía" is the imperfect tense of "creer" (to believe/think), and "que" introduces the clause that follows (often optional in English: "I thought (that)...").
target_language_example: Creía que hoy era lunes, pero es martes.
native_language_example: I thought today was Monday, but it’s Tuesday.

meaning: "I thought it was" / "I believed it was" (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (creía, era) to describe a past belief or assumption, often something you later found out was wrong. Common pattern: "Creía que era..." + noun/adjective/clause. For a more sudden, finished thought, Spanish often uses "creí que era" (preterite).
target_language_example: Creía que era tu teléfono, pero era el mío.
native_language_example: I thought it was your phone, but it was mine.

meaning: crossing the street; across the street.
additional_notes: "Cruzando" is the gerund of "cruzar" (to cross). It can describe an action in progress ("está cruzando la calle ahora" = he is crossing now) or be used to mean location ("cruzando la calle" = across the street). Similar to "al cruzar la calle" (when crossing the street) in some contexts.
target_language_example: La farmacia está cruzando la calle.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across the street.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase using **cruzar** (to cross) + a direct object. You can replace **el río** with other things you cross: **cruzar la calle** (cross the street), **cruzar la frontera** (cross the border). You’ll often hear it with ways of crossing: **en barco** (by boat) or **por el puente** (via the bridge).
target_language_example: Vamos a cruzar el río por el puente.
native_language_example: We’re going to cross the river via the bridge.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "cruzar" (to cross) + "el río" (the river) + "a nado" (by swimming). You can swap in other places: "cruzar la piscina/el lago a nado" = to swim across the pool/lake. "A nado" describes the method (swimming), not direction.
target_language_example: No es buena idea cruzar el río a nado si hay mucha corriente.
native_language_example: It’s not a good idea to swim across the river if the current is strong.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going from one side of a street/road to the other. Often appears with a person who helps someone (e.g., llevar de la mano, ayudar a) or with warnings about danger (Es peligroso cruzar la calle aquí).
target_language_example: Mira a ambos lados antes de cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: Look both ways before crossing the street.
