additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of cruzar (“to cross”) + la calle (“the street”). Used for a completed action in the past; the subject can be a person or an animal and is often understood from context.
target_language_example: María cruzó la calle cuando el semáforo se puso en verde.
native_language_example: María crossed the street when the light turned green.

additional_notes: Used to express optimism or to say that many outcomes could happen (sometimes with a tone of “you never know”). It can stand alone as a full sentence. Commonly appears with “creer que…” (to believe that…) or “pensar que…”.
target_language_example: Si trabajas duro, cualquier cosa es posible.
native_language_example: If you work hard, anything is possible.

additional_notes: Used to exclude one specific thing from a very broad set. It’s often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause: “cualquier cosa excepto eso” (anything except that). In statements like “Es cualquier cosa excepto un caballero,” it means “he’s anything but a gentleman” (emphatic: definitely not).
target_language_example: Puedo comer cualquier cosa excepto mariscos.
native_language_example: I can eat anything except seafood.

additional_notes: Used to exclude something strongly or to emphasize that something is definitely not true. Common patterns: (1) statement: “Es cualquier cosa menos X” = “He/It is anything but X.” (2) with actions: “Haría cualquier cosa menos X” or “Hace cualquier cosa menos X” = “He would do anything except X.”
target_language_example: Este lugar es cualquier cosa menos tranquilo.
native_language_example: This place is anything but quiet.

meaning: "anything for" (willing to do/give anything in order to get or help someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to show strong willingness or readiness to sacrifice. Common with conditional verbs like "haría/daría cualquier cosa por..." (= "I’d do/give anything for..."). Depending on context, it can mean doing something to achieve a goal ("for" = "in order to get") or doing it out of loyalty/affection ("for" = "for someone").
target_language_example: Haría cualquier cosa por verte feliz.
native_language_example: I’d do anything to see you happy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with the subjunctive (e.g., cualquier cosa que digas, que vaya a pasar). It means there is no limitation: any thing/event that happens, is found, or is said. Often appears after verbs like decir, pasar, encontrar, escuchar.
target_language_example: Puedes pedirme cualquier cosa que necesites.
native_language_example: You can ask me for anything you need.

additional_notes: Used to say it doesn’t matter which place (no specific location). Often appears after prepositions like “en” or “desde”: “en cualquier lugar” = “anywhere.” It’s singular in Spanish (lugar), but in English it can be “any place” or “anywhere.”
target_language_example: Puedes encontrar un cajero en cualquier lugar.
native_language_example: You can find an ATM anywhere.

additional_notes: Used to compare priorities or preferences, often with words like "más que" (more than) or "sobre" (above): "más que cualquier otra cosa" = "more than anything else"; "sobre cualquier otra cosa" = "above anything else." It can also mean giving up/choosing one thing instead of everything else.
target_language_example: Ahora mismo necesito descansar más que cualquier otra cosa.
native_language_example: Right now I need to rest more than anything else.

additional_notes: Used to compare with the rest of a group or to mean “any different alternative.” It agrees in gender and number with the noun: cualquier otra persona (any other person), cualquier otros problemas (any other problems), cualquier otras opciones (any other options). Often appears after a noun (cualquier otro árbol) or before a noun (cualquier otra cosa).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con cualquier otra persona; quiero hablar contigo.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to any other person; I want to talk to you.

additional_notes:
Common in comparisons to mean “any other student” in a group. Often appears with: 
- **tan/tanto... como**: *tan duro como cualquier otro estudiante* (“as hard as any other student”) 
- **más/menos... que**: *más inteligente que cualquier otro estudiante* (“more intelligent than any other student”).
**Cualquier** agrees in number: *cualquier otro estudiante* (singular), *cualesquiera otros estudiantes* (formal/plural; often people just say *cualquier otro estudiante* or rephrase).
target_language_example: No soy mejor que cualquier otro estudiante; solo practico todos los días.
native_language_example: I'm not better than any other student; I just practice every day.

additional_notes: Used to compare with the rest of a group or to mean “any different alternative.” It agrees in gender and number with the noun: cualquier otra persona (any other person), cualquier otros problemas (any other problems), cualquier otras opciones (any other options). Often appears after a noun (cualquier otro árbol) or before a noun (cualquier otra cosa).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar con cualquier otra persona; quiero hablar contigo.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk to any other person; I want to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to say that any person is able to do something (in general). It’s often followed by an infinitive: “Cualquiera puede hacerlo” (“Anyone can do it”). With “no” it changes meaning to “not just anyone can…” (i.e., it’s not easy or not everyone is able): “No cualquiera puede ser maestro.”
target_language_example: Cualquiera puede aprender español con práctica.
native_language_example: Anyone can learn Spanish with practice.

meaning: “When I grow up, I want to be …”
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you want to become in the future (often said by children). You can follow it with a job ("médico"), a description ("feliz"), or “like” someone: "igual a/que ti" (like you) / "como tú" (like you). "Crezca" is the present subjunctive of "crecer" used with "cuando" to refer to a future time.
target_language_example: Cuando crezca, quiero ser doctora.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a doctor.

additional_notes: Uses **cuando** (“when”) + **empezó** (past of *empezar*, “started”) + **a** + infinitive (**llover**, “to rain”). Common in stories to describe one past event happening right after another, often with **apenas** (“barely/hardly”) or **no… cuando** (“we hadn’t… when…”).
target_language_example: Estábamos caminando cuando empezó a llover.
native_language_example: We were walking when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to set the time for another action/event in the past. Commonly followed by an imperfect (was doing / were doing) to describe what was already happening: “Cuando entré..., ella estaba...”. It uses the preterite entré (a completed action: “I entered”). You’ll also see “entré en la habitación” (more literal), but “entré a la habitación” is very common.
target_language_example: Cuando entré a la habitación, todos se quedaron en silencio.
native_language_example: When I entered the room, everyone went silent.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a past time or situation, often describing background states/habits with the imperfect tense: era = “was.” The subject (“I/he/she”) is usually understood from context: cuando era pequeño/a = “when I was little,” cuando era más joven = “when he/she was younger.” Note: Spanish era can look like English “era” (a historical period), but here it’s the verb ser (“to be”) in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando era estudiante, vivía cerca de la escuela.
native_language_example: When I was a student, I lived near the school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the past (yourself or someone else) at a younger age. It uses the imperfect tense (era) to describe an ongoing state in the past. You can change the person: cuando era joven (I/he/she was young), cuando eras joven (you were young), cuando éramos jóvenes (we were young).
target_language_example: Cuando era joven, quería ser médico.
native_language_example: When I was young, I wanted to be a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was true or happened in the past, during an earlier period of your life. The verb is usually in the imperfect: era (I/he/she was). You can change the subject: cuando eras más joven (when you were younger), cuando éramos más jóvenes (when we were younger), cuando era más joven (when he/she was younger).
target_language_example: Cuando era más joven, quería vivir en otro país.
native_language_example: When I was younger, I wanted to live in another country.

meaning: when I was a child / as a kid.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened or was true during your childhood. It often introduces a memory or past habit and is followed by the imperfect tense (e.g., tenía, vivía). You can change the gender/number: cuando era niña (female speaker), cuando era niño/niña (singular), cuando éramos niños/niñas (we), cuando eran niños/niñas (they).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, jugaba en el parque todos los días.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I played in the park every day.

meaning: "when I was little" / "when I was a child" (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened regularly or over a period of time in your childhood. It uses the imperfect tense (era) for background/past situations. Change the adjective to match the speaker: cuando era pequeño (male speaker). You can also say cuando era niña (female) / cuando era niño (male).
target_language_example: Cuando era pequeña, me encantaba leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: When I was little, I loved reading before going to sleep.

meaning: when I was little / when I was a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in your childhood. It uses the imperfect tense (era) to describe an ongoing past state (“I was”). You can change the ending to match the speaker: cuando era pequeña (female speaker), cuando éramos pequeños (we), cuando eras pequeño/a (you).
target_language_example: Cuando era pequeño, jugaba afuera todos los días.
native_language_example: When I was little, I played outside every day.

meaning: when I was a child (a boy).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened repeatedly or at some point in the past during your childhood. For a girl, say “cuando era una niña.” You’ll also hear “cuando era niño/niña” without “un/una.”
target_language_example: Cuando era un niño, jugaba en este parque todos los días.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played in this park every day.

meaning: “when I/he/she was in …” (in a place, situation, or time in life).
additional_notes: Used to set background time in the past. "Estaba" is the imperfect of "estar" (describes an ongoing state). Often followed by a location (en Japón), a life stage/school grade (en primer grado, en la escuela), an organization (en las Fuerzas Especiales), or a situation/condition (en problemas, en el suelo). Changes with the subject: cuando yo estaba en…, cuando él estaba en…, etc.
target_language_example: Conocí a mi mejor amigo cuando estaba en la universidad.
native_language_example: I met my best friend when I was in college.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen at the moment the other person is ready. It’s addressed to “tú” (informal singular): estés is the present subjunctive of estar, commonly used after cuando to refer to a future/unknown time (not a fixed past event). You can follow it with a command or request: “Llámame cuando estés listo.”
target_language_example: Avísame cuando estés listo para salir.
native_language_example: Let me know when you’re ready to leave.

additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive of llegar (llegue) after cuando to talk about a future or not-yet-known moment: Cuando llegue..., te llamo / hablaremos. If it’s a habitual or past event, Spanish typically uses the indicative instead: Cuando llego a casa, ceno. / Cuando llegué, te llamé. Often the subject is understood from context (e.g., Te llamaré cuando llegue = “when I arrive”).
target_language_example: Te escribo cuando llegue al hotel.
native_language_example: I’ll text you when I get to the hotel.

meaning: when the time comes; when the moment arrives.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen later, at the right/appropriate time—often implying “not yet” or that the timing isn’t decided. Uses the present subjunctive (llegue) after cuando to refer to a future moment. Can be said on its own (“Cuando llegue el momento.”) to mean “When the time comes.”
target_language_example: Te lo diré cuando llegue el momento.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you when the time comes.

meaning: “when we arrive” (referring to a future moment).
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive (lleguemos) after cuando because it talks about something that will happen in the future. Often followed by a plan or instruction: “Cuando lleguemos, (we will/should) …”. If it’s a habitual/past meaning, you use the indicative instead (cuando llegamos = when we arrive/arrived, as a general fact).
target_language_example: Cuando lleguemos al hotel, te llamo.
native_language_example: When we get to the hotel, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive (llegues) after cuando to talk about a future event: Cuando llegues, llámame. If it’s not about the future (habitual/past), Spanish uses the indicative: Cuando llegas, siempre me llamas (when you arrive, you always call me). Often followed by a destination: cuando llegues a casa / al final de la calle / ahí.
target_language_example: Cuando llegues a casa, mándame un mensaje.
native_language_example: When you get home, send me a message.

additional_notes: Used to set the time of another action or situation in the past. Often followed by an imperfect description of what was happening or what things were like at that moment (e.g., "estaba lloviendo", "había..."). In "para cuando llegué", it means "by the time I arrived" (something had already happened before you arrived).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, la tienda ya estaba cerrada.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the store was already closed.

additional_notes: Used to say what was happening or what you did at the moment you arrived somewhere. Common in storytelling, often followed by a place (cuando llegué a la escuela) and can appear at the beginning or middle of the sentence. Verb is past (pretérito) of llegar: llegué = I arrived.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a casa, ya estaban cenando.
native_language_example: When I arrived home, they were already having dinner.

meaning: “when I got home” / “when I arrived home.”
additional_notes: Used to set the time for another action or situation. Often pairs with the imperfect (tenía, estaba + -ando, había + past participle) to describe what was happening or had already happened at that moment.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a casa, mi hermana ya había cenado.
native_language_example: When I got home, my sister had already eaten dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite "llegué" to mark a completed action in the past. Often used to set the time for another past event (e.g., something was happening, was about to happen, or had already happened when you arrived). Word order can change: "Cuando llegué a la estación, ..." or "... cuando llegué a la estación."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a la estación, ya habían cerrado las puertas.
native_language_example: When I arrived at the station, they had already closed the doors.

additional_notes: Used to set the time of another past action or state (often in the imperfect: estaba/era/parecía...) at the moment someone arrived home. "Llegó" is the preterite (completed action) of "llegar". The subject (he/she/you formal) is often understood from context; you can also say "cuando llegué a casa" (when I got home) or "cuando llegaron a casa" (when they got home).
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a casa, se dio cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: When he got home, he realized he had forgotten his keys.

meaning: "when I" (followed by a verb), often with "me" as an object/reflexive pronoun.
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause. After "cuando" you can use "me" before the verb when the verb takes "me" (object or reflexive), e.g. "cuando me vaya" = "when I leave" (with "irse"). It’s usually followed immediately by a conjugated verb: "cuando me llames" (when you call me), "cuando me levante" (when I get up).
target_language_example: Te llamo cuando me levante.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I get up.

additional_notes: Used to set the time for another action or situation in the past. It’s often followed by an imperfect tense (estaba, había) to describe what was happening or what the situation was at that moment. You can place it at the start of the sentence or at the end.
target_language_example: Cuando me desperté, ya era de noche.
native_language_example: When I woke up, it was already nighttime.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something that happened at the moment someone saw you. “Vio” is the simple past (preterite) of “ver” (to see) for él/ella/usted. You can swap “me” for another object pronoun: “cuando te vio” (when he/she saw you), “cuando nos vio” (when he/she saw us).
target_language_example: Cuando me vio, me saludó con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: When he/she saw me, he/she greeted me with a smile.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the time in the past when two people first met. Often appears in comparisons with "que" (e.g., "mejor/peor que cuando nos conocimos" = "better/worse than when we met") or with expressions like "parece que fue ayer" ("it feels like it was yesterday").
target_language_example: Aún recuerdo lo nervioso que estaba cuando nos conocimos.
native_language_example: I still remember how nervous I was when we met.

additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose the time (permission or an open invitation). It can sound friendly (“Come back anytime”) or, depending on tone/context (especially “Vete cuando quieras”), a bit dismissive like “leave whenever you want.”
target_language_example: Pasa por mi casa cuando quieras.
native_language_example: Stop by my house anytime you like.

meaning: "when" + "se" (used for reflexive actions or impersonal/passive sentences).
additional_notes: You’ll see "cuando se" before a verb when the action is reflexive (someone does it to themselves: "cuando se viste" = "when she gets dressed") or when "se" makes the sentence impersonal/passive (no specific subject: "cuando se publicó" = "when it was published" / "when it got published"). The verb after "se" is conjugated normally.
target_language_example: Cuando se habla en voz baja, es difícil entender.
native_language_example: When people speak quietly, it’s hard to understand.

meaning: "when it comes to" / "as for" (a particular topic or person).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject you’re talking about (a skill, situation, person, etc.). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive: "Cuando se trata de matemáticas..." / "Cuando se trata de ti...". Very common in advice, comparisons, and opinions.
target_language_example: Cuando se trata de cocinar, prefiero recetas simples.
native_language_example: When it comes to cooking, I prefer simple recipes.

additional_notes: A time clause used to say something happened at the moment the phone rang. Often appears with another past action that was in progress or about to happen (commonly with the imperfect or with ir a + infinitive): “Estaba/iba a…” + cuando sonó el teléfono.
target_language_example: Estaba estudiando cuando sonó el teléfono.
native_language_example: I was studying when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to start a time clause with tú (informal “you”), often followed by a verb: cuando te pones… (“when you put on…”), cuando te veo… (“when I see you…”). After cuando, Spanish often uses the indicative for habitual/past events (cuando te llamo…) and the subjunctive for future or uncertain events (cuando te vea…, cuando te lo encuentres…, cuando te venga bien…).
target_language_example: Cuando te sientas mejor, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: When you feel better, we'll go for a walk.

meaning: “when I/he/she had” (used to say someone’s age at the time).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an age (e.g., "cuando tenía ocho años") to mean "when (someone) was eight years old." It sets the time in the past by giving the person’s age. The verb agrees with the person (yo tenía, él/ella tenía, nosotros teníamos, etc.).
target_language_example: Aprendí a nadar cuando tenía seis años.
native_language_example: I learned to swim when I was six years old.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s age at the time something happened in the past. The verb is in the imperfect (tenía) because it describes a past state/background. You can change the number or person: cuando tenía cinco años, cuando tenías tres años, cuando teníamos tres años.
target_language_example: Aprendí a montar en bici cuando tenía tres años.
native_language_example: I learned to ride a bike when I was three years old.

additional_notes: Used to compare the speaker’s past with the listener’s present, often to share an experience, give advice, or show understanding. The tense is imperfect (tenía) because it refers to an ongoing state in the past (“I was … years old”). You can change the possessive to fit the person: cuando tenía mi/su edad (“when I was my/his/her/their age”).
target_language_example: Cuando tenía tu edad, también me daba miedo hablar en público.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I was also afraid of speaking in public.

additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive form "vuelva" (from "volver") after "cuando" to talk about something that hasn’t happened yet (a future return). If the return is habitual or already happened, Spanish often uses the indicative (e.g., "cuando vuelve" / "cuando volvió"). Who is returning is shown by context or by adding a subject: "cuando vuelva él/ella", "cuando vuelva mi mamá".
target_language_example: Te llamaré cuando vuelva a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I get back home.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens in relation to you: "cuando yo tenía siete años" (when I was seven), "cuando yo lo diga" (when I say so). In Spanish the subject pronoun is often optional, so you’ll also hear just "cuando diga..."; "yo" is added for emphasis or contrast. After "cuando" + a future event, Spanish typically uses the present subjunctive (e.g., "cuando yo lo diga", "cuando yo quiera").
target_language_example: Te llamaré cuando yo llegue a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I get home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time in the past when you were in a certain state/age. It’s commonly followed by the imperfect tense (era, tenía, vivía) and then a description of a repeated action or ongoing situation in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando yo era adolescente, vivía con mis abuelos.
native_language_example: When I was a teenager, I lived with my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about habits, routines, or situations from your childhood or earlier years. It’s commonly followed by the imperfect tense (e.g., era, tenía, iba, vivía) to describe ongoing states or repeated actions in the past. You can also drop the subject for a more natural sound: «Cuando era joven…».
target_language_example: Cuando yo era joven, no teníamos internet en casa.
native_language_example: When I was young, we didn’t have internet at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened or was true during your childhood. It typically uses the imperfect past tense (era) because it describes a past time period/background, habits, or ongoing states. You’ll also hear it with gender/number changes: cuando yo era niña (if the speaker is female), cuando yo era niño/niña (neutral/mixed), cuando yo era joven (when I was young).
target_language_example: Cuando yo era niño, íbamos a la playa todos los veranos.
native_language_example: When I was a child, we went to the beach every summer.

meaning: as much as you want; as long as you want.
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose the amount or duration of an action. Often follows a verb as an invitation/permission: "Bebe cuanto quieras" (drink as much as you want), "Quédate cuanto quieras" (stay as long as you want).
target_language_example: Puedes comer cuanto quieras, pero no tires comida.
native_language_example: You can eat as much as you want, but don’t waste food.

meaning: “the more” (used in comparisons: the more…, the more…).
additional_notes: Used to show a linked increase or decrease between two things: “Cuanto más + verb/adjective…, más/menos + verb/adjective…”. Often paired with “más” (the more) or “menos” (the less) in the second part.
target_language_example: Cuanto más estudias, más fácil es el examen.
native_language_example: The more you study, the easier the exam is.

meaning: "the older (someone) gets" / "the more old" (used in comparisons).
additional_notes: Used in the common comparison pattern: «Cuanto más + adjective/verb..., más/menos + result...», meaning “the more…, the more/less…”. Here «viejo» = “old,” usually about a person; you can add the verb: «Cuanto más viejo me hago/te vuelves…». Often followed by «más…» or «menos…» in the second part.
target_language_example: Cuanto más viejo me hago, más valoro el tiempo.
native_language_example: The older I get, the more I value time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (La guerra duró cuatro años), a period up to the present (Estos cuatro años...), or someone’s age (Tengo/Cumplo cuatro años; Mi hijo tiene cuatro años). You’ll often see it with verbs like durar (to last), vivir (to live), estudiar (to study), tener (to be [age]), and cumplir (to turn [an age]).
target_language_example: Viví en Madrid cuatro años.
native_language_example: I lived in Madrid for four years.

additional_notes: Used to describe animals and also objects like tables/chairs that have four supporting legs. Usually you’ll see it with the verb tener: "tener cuatro patas" (to have four legs).
target_language_example: Ese perro tiene cuatro patas.
native_language_example: That dog has four legs.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a layer of something on top of it (snow, mud, gold, cheese, etc.). It agrees with the noun: cubierto (masc. singular), cubierta (fem. singular), cubiertos (masc. plural), cubiertas (fem. plural). Often used with estar: "Está cubierto de barro".
target_language_example: Mis zapatos están cubiertos de nieve.
native_language_example: My shoes are covered in snow.

meaning: 'account/bill for' or (in darse cuenta de) 'of' in 'to realize'.
additional_notes: 1) With services or expenses, cuenta de + noun often means a bill or account: la cuenta de teléfono (phone bill), la cuenta de luz (electric bill). 2) In the very common verb phrase darse cuenta de, it means “to realize/notice (something)”: Me di cuenta de mi error. The meaning here isn’t a literal “account of.”
target_language_example: Todavía no he pagado la cuenta de internet.
native_language_example: I still haven't paid the internet bill.

meaning: “(to) realize that” (used in expressions like darse cuenta de que / caer en la cuenta de que).
additional_notes: Almost always appears as part of a larger phrase: **darse cuenta de que + clause** (“to realize that”) or **caer en la cuenta de que** (“to suddenly realize that”). It’s followed by a verb clause: *Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.* Common past forms: **me di cuenta**, **se dio cuenta**, **nos dimos cuenta**, **se dieron cuenta**.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había dejado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I realized that I had left the keys at home.

additional_notes: Literally “stories/tales of fairies.” Used for traditional children’s stories (princesses, witches, magic). It’s also common in the negative (No creo en…) to mean “I don’t believe in unrealistic/fantasy ideas.”
target_language_example: Esto no es un cuento de hadas; hay que trabajar duro.
native_language_example: This isn’t a fairy tale; you have to work hard.

meaning: no matter what; whatever it takes.
additional_notes: Used to express strong determination to do something despite difficulties or consequences. It’s a fixed expression built from the subjunctive of "costar" ("cueste") and is often placed after the action: "Voy a hacerlo, cueste lo que cueste."
target_language_example: Voy a terminar este proyecto, cueste lo que cueste.
native_language_example: I’m going to finish this project, no matter what.

additional_notes: From the verb cuidar + de. Used as an affirmative tú command (imperative): “Cuida de…” = “Take care of…”. Often means to look after someone for a period of time, or to care for/protect them.
target_language_example: Por favor, cuida de los niños esta noche.
native_language_example: Please take care of the kids tonight.

meaning: Watch out for / be careful with.
additional_notes: Used as a warning about a possible danger or problem. Common in signs and spoken warnings: "¡Cuidado con...!" + noun (el tren, la escalera, las abejas). It can also be advice to take care with something: "Cuidado con tu espalda" = be careful not to hurt your back.
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado con el coche que viene!
native_language_example: Watch out for the car coming!

meaning: "Watch out for the..." / "Be careful with the..."
additional_notes: Used as a warning before a masculine singular noun (el). Often said on its own (“¡Cuidado!”). You can change the article to match the noun: cuidado con la, cuidado con los, cuidado con las. Common for hazards (edges, fire, animals) or to warn someone not to damage/ruin something.
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado con el escalón, que está roto!
native_language_example: Watch out for the step—it’s broken!

meaning: "watch out for the..." / "be careful with the..." (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone about a specific thing (danger, obstacle, or something you might damage). It’s often said as a quick warning: “¡Cuidado con la puerta!” = “Watch out for the door!” (For masculine nouns: “cuidado con el…”.)
target_language_example: Cuidado con la puerta, está cerrándose.
native_language_example: Watch out for the door, it’s closing.

meaning: “Watch out for the…” / “Be careful with the…” (plural masculine nouns).
additional_notes: Used as a warning before a plural noun: *Cuidado con los + [plural noun]*. Often translated as “watch out for” (danger) or “be careful with” (handle cautiously). For plural feminine nouns, use **cuidado con las**.
target_language_example: Cuidado con los escalones; están mojados.
native_language_example: Watch out for the steps; they’re wet.

meaning: 'be careful not to' / 'take care not to'.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb tener: "tener cuidado de no + infinitive". It introduces an action you want to avoid (often as advice, a warning, or describing what you did to avoid a problem). In everyday speech you’ll also hear "tener cuidado de no" or simply "cuidado con" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Ten cuidado de no olvidarte el pasaporte.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your passport.

meaning: to take care of; to look after.
additional_notes: Used to mean you are responsible for someone’s care or well-being (often a person, but also pets or tasks). You can also hear it without “de” (e.g., “cuidar a los niños” / “cuidar a mi madre”), especially when the direct object is a person.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes cuidar de mi perro este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Can you look after my dog this weekend?

meaning: to take care of me; to look after me.
additional_notes: Used when someone provides care, protection, or help for you. You can also use it reflexively to mean being independent: "cuidar de mí mismo/a" = "take care of myself" (mismo = male speaker, misma = female speaker). Often used with obligations: "debes/tienes que cuidar de mí" (you must/you have to take care of me).
target_language_example: Cuando estoy enfermo, necesito que alguien cuide de mí.
native_language_example: When I’m sick, I need someone to take care of me.

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility or blame. Often appears as a short apology (“Culpa mía.”) or in the structure “Es culpa mía” = “It’s my fault.” You can intensify it with words like “todo” (all) or “esto” (this): “Todo esto es culpa mía.”
target_language_example: Perdón, fue culpa mía.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was my fault.

meaning: (he/she) keeps his/her promises; fulfills his/her promises.
additional_notes: Used with a subject to say someone does what they said they would do. The verb is "cumplir" (to fulfill/keep), and "sus" changes depending on who the promises belong to: "cumplo mis promesas" (I keep my promises), "cumples tus promesas" (you keep your promises), "cumplimos nuestras promesas" (we keep our promises). Often appears with "siempre" (always) or "nunca" (never).
target_language_example: No confío en él porque nunca cumple sus promesas.
native_language_example: I don’t trust him because he never keeps his promises.

meaning: to fulfill; to comply with; to meet (a duty/obligation/requirement).
additional_notes: Used with duties, obligations, rules, promises, requirements, or responsibilities: cumplir con mi deber/una obligación/las normas/los requisitos. Often implies doing what is expected or required.
target_language_example: Tenemos que cumplir con los requisitos para solicitar la beca.
native_language_example: We have to meet the requirements to apply for the scholarship.

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions (embedded questions) after verbs like saber (to know), preguntar (to ask), decir (to say), etc. Spanish keeps normal word order (cuál era...), where English usually flips it: 'what the problem was' (not 'what was the problem') in an indirect question. 'Era' is imperfect past, often used for background/ongoing situations in the past.
target_language_example: No entendía cuál era el problema.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what the problem was.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (era) to refer to a name you’re trying to recall or that was mentioned before. "Su" can mean “your” (formal usted) or “his/her,” depending on context. It can be used as a direct question (¿Cuál era su nombre?) or in an indirect question after verbs like preguntar: "Le pregunté cuál era su nombre."
target_language_example: Perdón, se me olvidó: ¿cuál era su nombre?
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot—what was your name?

meaning: 'which is...?' / 'what is...?' (asking for a specific choice or identification).
additional_notes: Used in questions with ser (to be). Choose cuál when you’re selecting/identifying one thing among options or possibilities: ¿Cuál es tu plan? (your specific plan). It’s often followed by a noun: ¿Cuál es tu nombre/dirección/número de teléfono? With plural nouns use cuáles son: ¿Cuáles son tus planes?
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu dirección?
native_language_example: What’s your address?

meaning: “what is the …?” (asking which one/which thing it is).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity/definition of a specific masculine singular thing: “¿Cuál es el punto?”, “¿Cuál es el significado…?”. For feminine nouns use “cuál es la”, and for plurals use “cuáles son los/las”. Often used in indirect questions too: “No sé cuál es el…”.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el problema?
native_language_example: What is the problem?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is wrong or what the main issue is. Also appears inside longer sentences after verbs like saber (to know) or descubrir (to find out): "Sé cuál es el problema" = "I know what the problem is." Often written with an accent when it’s an indirect question: "cuál es..."
target_language_example: No entiendo: ¿cuál es el problema?
native_language_example: I don’t understand—what’s the problem?

additional_notes: Used to ask for information about something that belongs to or is associated with the person you’re addressing (su = your, formal singular, or sometimes “your” plural). Often followed by a noun: “¿Cuál es su nombre?” = “What is your name?” In questions it’s commonly written as “¿Cuál es su …?”
target_language_example: Disculpe, ¿cuál es su nombre completo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your full name?

meaning: "what is your" (asking about someone’s specific thing: your source/idea/weakness, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific piece of information about the other person. It’s the combination of: ¿Cuál…? (“Which/What…?”) + es (“is”) + tu (“your”, informal singular). Often followed by a noun: ¿Cuál es tu nombre? (What’s your name?). For formal “your,” use cuál es su.
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿cuál es tu apellido?
native_language_example: Sorry, what’s your last name?

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions (Dime cuáles son tus intenciones) and direct questions (¿Cuáles son…?) to ask for a list or to identify specific items in a group. It’s the plural form: cuál = which/what; son = are (they). Often followed by a plural noun: cuáles son las razones/ventajas/medicinas.
target_language_example: ¿Cuáles son tus planes para mañana?
native_language_example: What are your plans for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say someone’s age. Common in questions like “¿Cuántos años tienes?” (informal you) and “¿Cuántos años tiene usted?” (formal you). In reported speech it often appears without the question marks: “Me preguntó cuántos años tenía.”
target_language_example: ¿Cuántos años tienes?
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: A very common greeting used to ask about someone’s well-being. Use it with friends and in many everyday situations. You can add a name or a term of address (e.g., “Amigo, ¿cómo estás?”). With “tú” (“¿cómo estás tú?”) it adds emphasis, like “How about you?”
target_language_example: Hola, Marta, ¿cómo estás?
native_language_example: Hi, Marta, how are you?

additional_notes: Used in questions and statements to ask or explain the way a thing/system/process works. Often appears after verbs like entender (to understand), saber (to know), enseñar (to teach), and phrases like no tengo idea de… (I have no idea about…). In questions it’s common to write: ¿Cómo funciona?
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes explicar cómo funciona esta app?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how this app works?

meaning: how to do it; how to do something.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the way to perform a task or action. Often follows verbs like saber (to know), enseñar/mostrar (to teach/show), decir (to tell), preguntar (to ask), and olvidar (to forget): “Sé cómo hacerlo” = “I know how to do it.” It can refer to a specific task already mentioned (it = lo) or more generally “how to do it.”
target_language_example: Si no sabes cómo hacerlo, te lo explico paso a paso.
native_language_example: If you don’t know how to do it, I’ll explain it to you step by step.

meaning: how to get to the beach.
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions. Often appears after verbs like "decir" (tell) in requests: "Dígame/Decidme/Díganme...". You can swap "la playa" for another destination (p. ej., "cómo llegar al hotel"). In questions, you can also say: "¿Cómo llego a la playa?"
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿me puede decir cómo llegar a la playa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the beach?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question or explanation about the way a process happens, typically with the impersonal/passive "se" ("se pesca" = "people fish" / "fishing is done"). It’s common before verbs like "hace" (is done), "dice" (is said), "traduce" (is translated), "convierte" (becomes/is converted), "siente" (feels), etc. Often translates as “how to …” or “how …” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes cómo se dice "thank you" en español?
native_language_example: Do you know how you say "thank you" in Spanish?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the method/process for doing something. Often appears after verbs like enseñar (to teach), mostrar (to show), or preguntar (to ask): “enséñame/muéstrame/pregúntale cómo se hace.” Literally “how it is done,” with se making it impersonal/passive (“it’s done”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes explicarme cómo se hace este ejercicio?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how to do this exercise?

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions (after verbs like preguntar, saber, recordar) and in direct questions. It’s the imperfect past (llamaba), so it often implies you’re asking about a name you knew before, a name at that time, or a name you can’t remember now. The person/object is shown by context or pronouns (e.g., no recuerdo cómo se llamaba = I don’t remember what his/her name was).
target_language_example: No me acuerdo cómo se llamaba el profesor de matemáticas.
native_language_example: I don’t remember what the math teacher’s name was.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sentirse" (to feel). It can refer to a third person ("how he/she feels") or be part of a question to someone you address as "usted" ("¿Cómo se siente?" = "How do you feel?").
target_language_example: Después del viaje, le pregunté cómo se siente.
native_language_example: After the trip, I asked him/her how he/she feels.

meaning: "how you" (used to ask or say how something happens to you / how you do something).
additional_notes: Very common in questions, indirect questions, and exclamations: ¿Cómo te fue? (How did it go for you?), Mira cómo te comportas (Look at how you behave). The pronoun "te" is the informal singular "you" used as an object or reflexive (e.g., "te comportas" = you behave). Often followed by a verb: cómo te queda (how it fits/looks on you), cómo te trata (how they treat you).
target_language_example: No entiendo cómo te sientes hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how you feel today.

meaning: “how you feel” / “how are you feeling?” (informal, to one person).
additional_notes: Uses the verb *sentirse* (“to feel”). It can be an indirect phrase after verbs like *decir*/*entender* (“tell/understand how you feel”), or a direct question: *¿Cómo te sientes?* Use *te* with someone you address as *tú* (informal singular). For formal singular, say *¿Cómo se siente?*
target_language_example: ¿Cómo te sientes hoy?
native_language_example: How are you feeling today?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is enjoyable, comforting, or makes you happy. Common patterns: “Da gusto + infinitive” (Da gusto estar aquí. = It’s nice to be here), “Da gusto que + subjunctive” (Da gusto que hayas regresado. = I’m glad you’re back), and “A uno le da gusto…” (It makes you happy/pleased…). It can also describe something that feels good physically (El sol da gusto. = The sun feels nice).
target_language_example: Da gusto verte otra vez.
native_language_example: It’s nice to see you again.

additional_notes: Used to say that a choice, difference, or condition is unimportant. Often appears as "Me da igual..." = "I don't care..." / "It’s all the same to me," followed by "que" + verb (Me da igual que seas...) or "si" + clause (Me da igual si vienes...). It can also stand alone: "Da igual."
target_language_example: Da igual si llegamos tarde; la tienda está cerrada.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter if we arrive late; the store is closed.

meaning: “feel like it / want (to),” often with a sense of “whatever (someone) pleases.”
additional_notes: Used almost always in the pattern "hacer lo que (me/te/le/nos/les) da la gana" or "ir a donde (me/te/le…) da la gana" to emphasize freedom to do what you want, sometimes with an annoyed or defiant tone (similar to "do whatever you want"). The pronoun changes with the person: me, te, le, nos, les.
target_language_example: No me digas qué hacer: haré lo que me dé la gana.
native_language_example: Don’t tell me what to do: I’ll do whatever I want.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say something scares someone: me/te/le/nos/les da miedo + noun or infinitive. Example: Me da miedo el fuego (Fire scares me). With an infinitive, it means being afraid to do something: Te da miedo decirlo (You’re afraid to say it).
target_language_example: Me da miedo hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say who feels embarrassed: me da vergüenza, te da vergüenza, le da vergüenza, nos da vergüenza, les da vergüenza + (to do something). Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., preguntar, decirlo) or by “eso/esto” to refer to something previously mentioned. Similar to “tener vergüenza,” but phrased as something that "gives" you embarrassment.
target_language_example: Me da vergüenza hablar en público.
native_language_example: I’m embarrassed to speak in public.

additional_notes: This is the past participle form used in the very common phrase **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/notice”). It’s normally used with reflexive pronouns and often in perfect tenses: **me he dado cuenta de...** (I’ve realized...), **no se ha dado cuenta de...** (he/she hasn’t noticed...). It can be followed by a noun (**de mi presencia**) or by **de que + clause** (**de que hallamos el núcleo**).
target_language_example: Me he dado cuenta de que hoy es lunes.
native_language_example: I just realized that today is Monday.

additional_notes: Imperative phrase using **dar** (“to give”): **dale** = “give (him/her/you formal)”. Often used when asking someone to pass on affection/greetings to another person: **Dale un beso a X (de mi parte)** = “Give X a kiss (from me/on my behalf).” You can also hear **Dale un beso** with no **a + person** when the person is understood.
target_language_example: Dale un beso a tu mamá de mi parte.
native_language_example: Give your mom a kiss from me.

additional_notes: Command form: da (tú) + me (“to me”) → dame. Used to ask/order someone to hand you something. Use with feminine singular nouns that take la (e.g., la linterna, la cámara). For masculine singular, use “dame el”.
target_language_example: Por favor, dame la llave.
native_language_example: Please give me the key.

additional_notes: Command form using the informal "tú": "da" (give) + "me" (to me) → "dame". "Las llaves" means "the keys" (usually a set). Common with "de/del" to specify what the keys are for: "las llaves del coche" (the car keys). Can also be used urgently with words like "ahora" (now).
target_language_example: Dame las llaves, por favor; necesito entrar.
native_language_example: Give me the keys, please; I need to get in.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone you address as tú to hand you something. Structure: dame (give me) + tu (your) + noun: “Dame tu abrigo.” If you use a formal tone (usted), say “Déme su …”.
target_language_example: Dame tu pasaporte, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me your passport, please.

meaning: “Give me a …” (informal command/request to one person).
additional_notes: From the verb dar (“to give”): da (tú command) + me (“to me”) + un (“a” masculine). It’s commonly used to ask for something or for time: “Dame un minuto.” If the noun is feminine, use “dame una …” (e.g., “Dame una idea.”). You can soften it with “por favor.”
target_language_example: Dame un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a moment, please.

additional_notes: An informal, affectionate way to ask someone (often a partner, family member, or child) for a kiss. "Dame" is the command form of "dar" (to give) for "tú". You can add details like "de despedida" (goodbye/farewell) or terms of endearment like "mi amor".
target_language_example: Antes de irte, dame un beso.
native_language_example: Before you go, give me a kiss.

additional_notes: A direct request using the tú imperative of **dar** (“to give”): **dame** = “give me.” Often followed by **de + noun** (e.g., *dame un poco de agua* = “give me a little water”) or **de eso** (“of that”). Add **por favor** to make it more polite: *dame un poco, por favor*.
target_language_example: Dame un poco de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a little water, please.

additional_notes: From the verb "dar" (to give): "dame" = "give me" (tú command). "Una" is feminine singular and is usually followed by a feminine noun (una botella, una lista, una moneda, una propina, una razón). It can also appear in expressions like "dame una mano" meaning "give me a hand/help me." Use "deme" for a more formal/polite version (usted).
target_language_example: Dame una botella de agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object to say something scares someone: "Me dan miedo las arañas" (Spiders scare me). The thing that scares you is usually plural with "dan" ("Las montañas rusas dan miedo"), but you can also use singular: "da miedo" ("Eso da miedo" = That’s scary). Often interchangeable with "dar miedo" vs. "asustar" ("Las arañas me asustan").
target_language_example: Esa película da miedo, pero la quiero ver.
native_language_example: That movie is scary, but I want to watch it.

meaning: going around; wandering around; turning in circles (also: pacing).
additional_notes: Present participle of "dar vueltas" (literally "to give turns"). Used for movement with no fixed destination (wandering around) or repetitive circular movement (going around something / turning in circles). Common with places or "alrededor de" (around): "dar vueltas alrededor de la mesa". Can also imply you’ve been walking/driving around for a while, often without finding what you want.
target_language_example: Estoy dando vueltas por el centro buscando un cajero.
native_language_example: I’m wandering around downtown looking for an ATM.

dar con una frase de quince sílabas

target_language_multi_word_term: dar con una frase de quince sílabas
meaning: to find/come up with a fifteen-syllable sentence.
additional_notes: Core expression: “dar con (algo)” = “to find (something)” / “to manage to find,” often after searching or trying. It’s similar to “encontrar,” but can suggest effort or difficulty. You can use it with any object: “dar con la solución” (find the solution), “dar con la dirección” (find the address).
target_language_example: No logro dar con una frase de quince sílabas.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to come up with a fifteen-syllable sentence.

meaning: "to give" + "a/an" (often used in set phrases like giving advice, taking a step, or having an attack/shock).
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common pattern: **dar un + noun**. Sometimes it’s literal (**dar un consejo** = “give advice”), and sometimes it’s part of an idiom where English uses a different verb (**dar un infarto** ≈ “to have a heart attack”; **dar un paso** = “take a step”). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un minuto?
native_language_example: Can you give me a minute?

meaning: to thank (someone); to say thank you to (someone).
additional_notes: Uses the verb dar (“to give”) + le (“to him/her/you-formal”) + las gracias (“thanks”). It’s a polite way to thank someone: Quiero darle las gracias… (“I want to thank you…”). You can add por + reason: darle las gracias por su ayuda (“thank you for your help”). Change le depending on who you’re thanking: darte las gracias (to you, informal), darle las gracias (to you formal / to him/her), darles las gracias (to you all / to them).
target_language_example: Quería darle las gracias por venir hoy.
native_language_example: I wanted to thank you for coming today.

additional_notes: Used when you decide to try someone or something and see if it works out. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: darle (to him/it), darle (to you—formal), darles (to them/you all), darme (to me), darte (to you—informal). You can add what the chance is for with “de + infinitive”: “Dame una oportunidad de explicarlo.”
target_language_example: Deberías darle una oportunidad al nuevo restaurante.
native_language_example: You should give the new restaurant a chance.

additional_notes: Literally “to give myself a shower,” but the natural English meaning is “to take a shower.” It uses a reflexive pronoun (me). You can change it depending on who is showering: darme (I), darte (you), darse (he/she/you formal), darnos (we), daros (you all), darse (they/you all). Often used with tener que / necesitar / querer: “Tengo que darme una ducha.”
target_language_example: Después del gimnasio, voy a darme una ducha.
native_language_example: After the gym, I'm going to take a shower.

additional_notes: Literally “to give you the thanks.” Used to express gratitude directly to someone you address as tú. Often followed by por + noun/clause (“darte las gracias por…” = “to thank you for…”). For usted, use “darle las gracias”; for more than one person, “darles las gracias.”
target_language_example: Sólo quería darte las gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: I just wanted to thank you for your help.

additional_notes: This is the tú (informal singular) form of the idiom **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/to notice”). It’s reflexive (with **te**) and is commonly followed by **que + clause** (*Te das cuenta de que…*) or by a noun/phrase (*Te das cuenta de su valor*).
target_language_example: ¿Te das cuenta de que ya es muy tarde?
native_language_example: Do you realize it’s already very late?

additional_notes: Informal command used to tell one person to hurry. It’s the tú (informal) imperative of the reflexive phrase darse prisa (“to hurry”). You can soften it with por favor, or use the formal version: dese prisa (usted).
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa, que vamos a llegar tarde!
native_language_example: Hurry up, we're going to be late!

additional_notes:
Common meanings depend on context:
1) As a response: “De acuerdo.” = “Okay/All right.” (Agreeing to do something).
2) Agreement: “estar de acuerdo (con…)” = “to agree (with…).” Example: “Mi tío estaba de acuerdo.”
3) Tag at the end of a request: “…, ¿de acuerdo?” = “…, okay?/all right?” (asking for confirmation).
4) In more formal writing you may see “de acuerdo con” or “de acuerdo a” meaning “according to…”.
target_language_example: De acuerdo, lo haré mañana.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it tomorrow.

meaning: (to be) in agreement with him; to agree with him.
additional_notes: Used with estar (and its past forms like estuve/estaba) to say you agree with a man or male person (“él”). Often followed by sobre + topic: “estar de acuerdo con él sobre el plan” = “to agree with him about the plan.” For a woman, use “de acuerdo con ella.”
target_language_example: No estoy de acuerdo con él en esto.
native_language_example: I don't agree with him about this.

meaning: (to be) in agreement with me; agree with me.
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb estar: “estar de acuerdo con + person/pronoun” = “to agree with + someone.” Here, “conmigo” means “with me.” You can also use it in questions: “¿Estás de acuerdo conmigo?”
target_language_example: ¿Estás de acuerdo conmigo en que debemos irnos ya?
native_language_example: Do you agree with me that we should leave now?

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with the person you’re speaking to. Often follows estar: “(Estoy) de acuerdo contigo.” You can add emphasis with words like “totalmente” (totally) or “completamente” (completely). You can also switch the pronoun depending on who you agree with: de acuerdo con él/ella/ellos/ustedes.
target_language_example: Estoy de acuerdo contigo: es una buena idea.
native_language_example: I agree with you: it’s a good idea.

meaning: to agree on / be in agreement about.
additional_notes: Used to say people share the same opinion about a topic: "estar de acuerdo en eso" (agree on that). With a clause, it often appears as "estar de acuerdo en que + verb" (agree that...): "Estoy de acuerdo en que es importante." You’ll also see "quedar de acuerdo en + infinitive/noun" meaning "to agree to / arrange to" do something: "Quedamos de acuerdo en salir temprano."
target_language_example: Estamos de acuerdo en que debemos salir temprano.
native_language_example: We agree that we should leave early.

meaning: "of water" (used to say something contains water, is made of water, or is a quantity of water).
additional_notes: Often used after a noun to specify what it contains or is about: botella de agua (bottle of water), vasos de agua (glasses of water), presión de agua (water pressure). Also used after quantity words: un litro de agua (a liter of water), un poco más de agua (a little more water).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer una botella de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a bottle of water, please?

meaning: 'next door' / 'next to (it)' / 'nearby (the one next to it)'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean the one next to it: "la habitación de al lado" (the next room), "la puerta de al lado" (the next door), "el perro de al lado" (the dog next door). It can refer to an adjacent place (next room/apartment/house) or the neighboring people/thing. Often implies immediate proximity (right next to), but in some contexts it can be more generally 'nearby' (e.g., "el hotel de al lado del río" = the hotel next to the river).
target_language_example: Voy a preguntarle al vecino de al lado si ha visto mi paquete.
native_language_example: I'm going to ask the next-door neighbor if they've seen my package.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often an emotional or physical reaction) to show the reason/cause: you do something because you’re very happy. Common with verbs like gritar (to shout), llorar (to cry), saltar (to jump), bailar (to dance).
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la noticia, salté de alegría.
native_language_example: When they gave me the news, I jumped for joy.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or will happen, but you’re not sure exactly how or in what way. Often expresses uncertainty, approximation, or that the details aren’t important. Commonly placed at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence as a softener (like “well, somehow…”).
target_language_example: De alguna forma, vamos a encontrar una solución.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’re going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to point to a place you’re in or near. With people, it often means they’re local ("Soy de aquí" = "I’m from here / I’m from around here"). With movement verbs like "salir" it means leaving this place ("salir de aquí" = "get out of here / leave here").
target_language_example: ¿Eres de aquí o estás de visita?
native_language_example: Are you from around here, or are you visiting?

meaning: "of art" / "art" (used to describe something related to art).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify its type or focus: "clase de arte" (art class), "museo de arte" (art museum). It’s a common pattern in Spanish: noun + "de" + subject area.
target_language_example: Mañana tengo clase de arte.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have art class.

additional_notes: Most commonly appears after the verb phrase “dejar de + infinitive” (“to stop doing something”). With “beber,” it can mean stopping drinking alcohol in general, or stopping drinking a specific drink if it’s stated (e.g., “dejar de beber café”).
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de dejar de beber alcohol.
native_language_example: I’m trying to stop drinking alcohol.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe someone’s temporary mood or attitude at a particular moment (e.g., "Estoy/Estás/Está/Estaba de buen humor"). The opposite is "de mal humor" (in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy de buen humor porque dormí bien.
native_language_example: Today I'm in a good mood because I slept well.

meaning: 'baseball' / 'of baseball' (used to describe something related to baseball).
additional_notes: Uses "de + [sport]" to mean something is associated with that sport: "jugadores de béisbol" (baseball players), "partidos de béisbol" (baseball games), "campo de béisbol" (baseball field). Often functions like an adjective in English ("baseball" as a modifier).
target_language_example: Me compré una gorra de béisbol.
native_language_example: I bought myself a baseball cap.

additional_notes: Uses **de + noun** to describe what something is made of, contains, or is flavored with: **licor de café** (coffee liqueur), **helado de café** (coffee ice cream). With quantities it means “some (of)” that thing: **algo de café** = “some coffee.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes algo de café?
native_language_example: Do you have some coffee?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while you are traveling toward your home. Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Me encontré con él de camino a casa". You can add more details after it: "de camino a casa desde la escuela" (on the way home from school).
target_language_example: Compré pan de camino a casa.
native_language_example: I bought bread on the way home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened while traveling toward school. Often used with things that happen unexpectedly (meeting someone, losing something, getting caught in rain). You can swap in another destination: de camino a casa / al trabajo.
target_language_example: Me encontré con mi profesor de camino a la escuela.
native_language_example: I ran into my teacher on the way to school.

meaning: 'to have dinner' (used after verbs like acabar/terminar/hora/olvidarse).
additional_notes: Often appears in structures like: terminar/acabar de cenar (to finish having dinner), (es) la hora de cenar / hora de cenar (it’s time for dinner), olvidarse de cenar (to forget to have dinner), esperar a que acabe de cenar (wait until they finish dinner). It uses the preposition "de" because Spanish commonly says "acabar/terminar de + infinitive" and "olvidarse de + infinitive."
target_language_example: No salgas todavía; estoy a punto de acabar de cenar.
native_language_example: Don’t go out yet; I’m about to finish dinner.

meaning: to feed; to give (someone/animal) food to eat.
additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase “dar de comer (a alguien/algo)” = “to feed (someone/animal)”. You can add the person/animal with “a”: “dar de comer a los niños / al perro”. Also appears in the proverb “No muerdas la mano que te da de comer” (“Don’t bite the hand that feeds you”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes dar de comer al gato mientras estoy fuera?
native_language_example: Can you feed the cat while I’m out?

meaning: (to) feed my dog; (to) give food to my dog.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase "dar de comer (a/al) + [person/animal]" = "to feed". Often you’ll see the indirect object pronoun too: "le doy de comer a mi perro" (I feed my dog) / "me olvidé de darle de comer" (I forgot to feed him). In everyday Spanish, "darle de comer a mi perro" is more natural than saying "de comer a mi perro" by itself.
target_language_example: Antes de salir, tengo que darle de comer a mi perro.
native_language_example: Before I leave, I have to feed my dog.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ir/estar/salir/venir to say someone is out shopping (e.g., ir de compras = to go shopping). It often implies shopping for clothes, groceries, or general purchases.
target_language_example: Vamos de compras después del trabajo.
native_language_example: We’re going shopping after work.

meaning: made of leather; leather (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe the material something is made from: "zapatos de cuero" (leather shoes), "cinturón de cuero" (leather belt). It can also stand alone when the item is understood from context: "Éstos son de cuero" = "These are leather."
target_language_example: Quiero una chaqueta de cuero negra.
native_language_example: I want a black leather jacket.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “birthday” or “for someone’s birthday”: fiesta de cumpleaños (birthday party), cena de cumpleaños (birthday dinner). With age: pastel/tarta de cumpleaños (birthday cake). Often used with possessives: mi fiesta de cumpleaños (my birthday party).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a venir a mi fiesta de cumpleaños?
native_language_example: Are you going to come to my birthday party?

additional_notes: Uses "de" to link something to money: "problemas de dinero" (money problems/financial problems), "hablar de dinero" (to talk about money), "escaso de dinero" (short on money). Often translates naturally as "financial" depending on the noun (e.g., "dificultades de dinero" = financial difficulties).
target_language_example: Estoy corto de dinero este mes.
native_language_example: I'm short on money this month.

meaning: 'of it' / 'about it' (referring to something previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Used with verbs/adjectives that take the preposition de, especially: estar seguro de ello (“to be sure of it”) and hablar de ello (“to talk about it”). Ello is a neutral pronoun meaning “it/that” (often for an idea, situation, or topic). In everyday Spanish, people also often use de eso instead of de ello.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de ello ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about it right now.

meaning: “of them” / “their” (referring to a group of males or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to show possession or association: el trabajo de ellos = “their work.” Also used in partitive expressions with quantities: la mitad de ellos = “half of them.” For an all-female group, use de ellas.
target_language_example: No sé nada de ellos desde el verano pasado.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about them since last summer.

meaning: “of that” / “from that” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition **de** (“of/from”) + **esa** (“that”, feminine singular). It refers back to a specific thing already known in context, usually followed by a feminine noun (explicit or implied): **de esa conclusión** (“of that conclusion”), **de esa distancia** (“from/of that distance”), **de esa suma** (“of that amount”). For masculine, use **de ese**; for plural, **de esas/de esos**.
target_language_example: No me acuerdo del nombre de esa calle, pero está cerca.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the name of that street, but it’s close.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or way something is done, often referring back to something already mentioned or visible in the situation. Common with negatives for correction or disapproval: "No de esa forma" = "Not like that."
target_language_example: No lo hagas de esa forma; hazlo con más cuidado.
native_language_example: Don’t do it like that; do it more carefully.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take "de" (like hablar de, dudar de, saber de, ocuparse de) to refer vaguely to certain matters/things already known from context. Often implies you don’t want to be specific ("that sort of thing").
target_language_example: No quiero saber de esas cosas.
native_language_example: I don’t want to know about that kind of stuff.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner or way something is done or thought. Often appears after verbs like pensar (to think), hacerlo (to do it), decirlo (to say it), or irse (to leave). Can be used in corrections or prohibitions: «No de ese modo» = “Not like that.”
target_language_example: No lo hagas de ese modo; hazlo más despacio.
native_language_example: Don’t do it like that; do it more slowly.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a type of thing already mentioned: "cosas de ese tipo" = "things like that." With "tipo" meaning "type," it’s fairly literal ("of that type"). Note: in some contexts, "ese tipo" can also mean "that guy" (colloquial), so "librarme de ese tipo" can mean "get rid of that guy."
target_language_example: No me gustan las películas de ese tipo.
native_language_example: I don’t like movies like that.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like hablar (to talk), saber (to know), etc., to refer back to a specific thing already mentioned or understood from context: hablar de eso = to talk about that; no sé nada de eso = I don't know anything about that. Very common in conversation.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about that right now.

de eso es de lo que

target_language_multi_word_term: de eso es de lo que
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the topic or thing being referred to, often before verbs like hablar (to talk) or tratarse (to be about): "De eso es de lo que estoy hablando" = "That's what I'm talking about." It’s a focus/cleft structure ("It’s X that..."), common in spoken and written Spanish. Variations you may hear: "Eso es de lo que..." or "De eso es de lo que se trata" ("That’s what it’s about").
target_language_example: De eso es de lo que te quería preguntar.
native_language_example: That's what I wanted to ask you about.

additional_notes: Used to say what the real meaning, purpose, or main idea is. Very common when concluding or clarifying something: “Así que de eso se trata” = “So that’s what it’s about.” You can also add a noun/topic: “De eso se trata la vida” (That’s what life is about) or “De eso se trata esto” (That’s what this is about).
target_language_example: Ahora lo entiendo: de eso se trata.
native_language_example: Now I get it: that’s what it’s about.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to link it to something: possession or relation ("of this...") or origin ("from this..."). It’s the contraction of "de" + "esta". Examples: "el agua de esta fuente" (the water of this fountain), "productos de esta región" (products of this region).
target_language_example: No me acuerdo del nombre de esta calle.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the name of this street.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner something happens or to invite someone to see/understand something from a particular perspective. Often followed by “como” (e.g., “De esta forma es como…” = “This is how…”).
target_language_example: Hazlo de esta forma para que sea más fácil.
native_language_example: Do it this way so it’s easier.

additional_notes: Used when **estar** is put in the infinitive after **de** to link to a state or situation: **feliz de estar...** (“happy to be...”), **la impresión de estar...** (“the impression of being...”). It can also express a cause or reason, especially with physical feelings: **me duelen... de estar + participle/adjective** (“...from being/sitting/standing so long”).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado de estar de pie todo el día.
native_language_example: I’m tired of standing all day.

meaning: "to be here" / "being here" (often after a feeling like happy or glad).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives or expressions of emotion to give the reason/cause: "Estoy contento/feliz de…" = "I’m happy/glad to…" or "about…". Here, "estar" is used for being in a place (location).
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de estar aquí con ustedes.
native_language_example: I’m really glad to be here with you all.

additional_notes: Used to indicate belonging/origin related to something close/identified: de + este + masculine singular noun (e.g., de este club = “of this club”). For feminine nouns, use “de esta”; for plural, “de estos/de estas”. Note: “de + el” contracts to “del”, but “de + este” does not contract.
target_language_example: ¿Eres miembro de este club?
native_language_example: Are you a member of this club?

additional_notes: Uses de + este lugar (“this place”). Meaning depends on context: (1) origin or leaving: irse/salir/vámonos de este lugar (“leave this place”); (2) belonging/connection: el dueño de este lugar (“the owner of this place”). Often used to point to a specific place you’re in or talking about.
target_language_example: No me gusta la energía de este lugar.
native_language_example: I don’t like the vibe of this place.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to link something to the country you’re currently talking about. Often expresses belonging or connection ("the politics of this country"), or origin in some contexts ("people from this country"). "Este" agrees with "país" (masculine singular).
target_language_example: La comida de este país es muy variada.
native_language_example: The food of this country is very varied.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take "de" to refer to something previously mentioned, happening now, or understood from context. Common patterns: "un poco de esto" (some of this), "disfrutar de esto" (enjoy this), "deshacerse de esto" (get rid of this), "escapar de esto" (escape from this), "hablar de esto" (talk about this). "Esto" is for something close in time/space or the current situation; compare with "de eso" (of/about that).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de esto ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about this right now.

meaning: '(from) popping those balloons' (used after *dejar de* = 'to stop').
additional_notes: This phrase is typically part of the structure **dejar de + infinitive** (“to stop doing something”): *Deja de explotar esos globos* = “Stop popping those balloons.” **Explotar** here means “to pop” (like a balloon).
target_language_example: Deja de explotar esos globos, por favor.
native_language_example: Stop popping those balloons, please.

meaning: 'from smoking' / 'to smoke' (used after certain verbs and expressions, especially about quitting or being against smoking).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears after verbs like "dejar de" (to stop/quit doing something): "dejar de fumar" = "to quit smoking." It can also follow expressions like "estar en contra de" (to be against): "estar en contra de fumar" = "to be against smoking." Here, "de" introduces an infinitive (fumar).
target_language_example: Quiero dejar de fumar este mes.
native_language_example: I want to quit smoking this month.

meaning: “smoking and drinking” (usually after verbs like “dejar”/“parar”: “to quit smoking and drinking”).
additional_notes: This phrase is most commonly used after **dejar de** or **parar de** to say you stopped doing an activity: **dejar de fumar y de beber** = “to quit smoking and drinking.” The **de** comes from the verb pattern (**dejar/parar + de + infinitive**).
target_language_example: Este año decidí dejar de fumar y de beber.
native_language_example: This year I decided to quit smoking and drinking.

meaning: soccer (used to say something is related to soccer).
additional_notes: “De” often means “of” or “for.” You use “de fútbol” after a noun to describe it: equipo de fútbol (soccer team), zapatos de fútbol (soccer shoes/cleats), torneo de fútbol (soccer tournament). It’s neutral and very common. In many countries “fútbol” means soccer; in the US you may also see “fútbol americano” for American football.
target_language_example: Necesito una camiseta de fútbol para el entrenamiento.
native_language_example: I need a soccer shirt/jersey for practice.

additional_notes: Used with the perfect infinitive: **de haber + past participle** (de haber hecho / dicho / robado...). It often comes after expressions that require **de** (e.g., *acusaron a alguien de...*, *estar feliz de...*, *tener suerte de...*, *presumir de...*) to mean that something happened earlier: *feliz de haber salido* = “happy to have graduated/left.” In more formal writing, **De haber + participle, ...** can start a conditional meaning **“if it had...” / “had it...”** (*De haber ocurrido..., hubiera...*).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de haber terminado el proyecto a tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m proud to have finished the project on time.

additional_notes:
Used in a few common patterns:
- After verbs/adjectives that take **de** (e.g., *estar avergonzado de*, *estar arrepentido de*): **de haber sido + adjective/noun** = “of having been …” (*Estoy avergonzado de haber sido grosero*).
- At the start of a sentence (more formal): **De haber sido + …, habría + participle** = “If … had been …, (it) would have …”
- In the structure **ha de haber sido** (as in *El papá ha de haber sido enorme*), it expresses deduction: “must have been …”.
target_language_example: Me arrepiento de haber sido tan impaciente contigo.
native_language_example: I regret having been so impatient with you.

additional_notes: Spanish often uses "de" before an infinitive after certain verbs, nouns, and set expressions. Common patterns include: "turno de hablar" (turn to speak), "basta de hablar" (enough talking), "dejar/parar de hablar" (to stop talking), "tratar de hablar" (to try to speak), and "encargarse de hablar" (to take charge of speaking). In English, this is often translated without "of" (e.g., "my turn to speak").
target_language_example: Es tu turno de hablar ahora.
native_language_example: It’s your turn to speak now.

meaning: 'to do that' (literally, 'of doing that'), used before an infinitive after certain verbs.
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs and expressions that require **de + infinitive**, such as **tratar de** (to try to), **arrepentirse de** (to regret), **convencer a alguien de** (to convince someone to), **tener la oportunidad de** (to have the chance to), **ser incapaz de** (to be unable to), and sometimes **deber de** (should/probably should, depending on context). In these cases, **de** is required before **hacer**.
target_language_example: Me alegro de hacer eso contigo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to do that with you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "morir"/"morirse" or "estar muriéndose" to say someone dies or is dying because of hunger. Very common as an exaggeration in everyday speech: "Me muero de hambre" = "I’m starving."
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, me muero de hambre.
native_language_example: After work, I’m starving.

meaning: of English; English (as a school subject).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to specify the language is English, especially in education or language-related contexts: examen de inglés (English test), maestro/profesor de inglés (English teacher), clase/curso de inglés (English class/course).
target_language_example: Tengo clase de inglés los martes.
native_language_example: I have English class on Tuesdays.

meaning: 'of going to' (used before a destination or an activity).
additional_notes: Used when an infinitive phrase with ir a (“to go to”) is linked to something else, often after nouns or expressions like deseo de... (desire to...), momento de... (time to...), planes de... (plans to...). It’s also common after verb phrases that take de + infinitive, e.g., deber de ir a... (“should probably go to...”).
target_language_example: Tengo ganas de ir a la playa este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I feel like going to the beach this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with "de" + "la" to show origin (from the library) or relationship/possession (the library's...). "De" can mean "of" or "from" depending on context.
target_language_example: Saqué este libro de la biblioteca.
native_language_example: I took this book from the library.

meaning: "of the wedding" / "from the wedding" (related to the wedding).
