additional_notes: Used after many nouns/adjectives to show a relationship or source. Here, **su** means “your / his / her / their” (it’s ambiguous—context tells you which). Common patterns: **orgulloso/a de su hija** = “proud of your/his/her/their daughter”; **la boda de su hija** = “your/his/her/their daughter’s wedding”; **una llamada de su hija** = “a call from your/his/her/their daughter.”
target_language_example: Estoy muy orgullosa de su hija.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of your/his/her/their daughter.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or to specify who/what something is related to. Spanish “su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your” (formal/usted), or “their,” so the context tells you whose son it is. Often used after nouns like: la muerte de su hijo (the death of his/her son), el casamiento de su hijo (his/her son’s wedding), orgulloso de su hijo (proud of his/her son), hablar de su hijo (talk about his/her son).
target_language_example: Me habló de su hijo y de lo bien que le va en la escuela.
native_language_example: He/she talked to me about his/her son and how well he’s doing at school.

additional_notes: Used after verbs or phrases like estar convencido/a de, dudar de, or convencer a alguien de to say what someone is convinced/doubtful about. In Spanish, su can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero creo que la evidencia muestra de su inocencia.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but I think the evidence shows his/her innocence.

additional_notes: Used to show relationship or origin connected to someone's mother. In Spanish, "su" can mean "his", "her", "your (formal)", or "their", so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Aprendió a cocinar de su madre.
native_language_example: He/She learned to cook from his/her mother.

meaning: of her husband / about her husband; from her husband.
additional_notes: Means “of her husband” (possession/relationship) or “about her husband” when talking about him (e.g., quejarse de su marido = complain about her husband). With verbs like divorciarse de, it means “from” (divorced from her husband). Note: su can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so de su marido can also be “of his/your/their husband” depending on context.
target_language_example: Siempre habla de su marido en el trabajo.
native_language_example: She always talks about her husband at work.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific person’s death. Common after nouns like el misterio/la causa/el aniversario/el porqué de su muerte. "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their," depending on context.
target_language_example: Todavía no sabemos la causa de su muerte.
native_language_example: We still don’t know the cause of his/her death.

meaning: 'of his/her father' (belonging to, from, or about his/her father).
additional_notes: Uses de + possessive + noun. It can show possession/connection (El carácter de su padre = her/his father's personality), origin/traits (Tiene los ojos de su padre = he/she has his/her father's eyes), or topic (habla mal de su padre = speaks badly about his/her father). Su can mean 'his', 'her', 'your (formal)', or 'their'—context tells you whose father it is. Often interchangeable with the possessive adjective: el carácter de su padre = su carácter (but 'de su padre' is clearer about who it refers to).
target_language_example: Aprendió a conducir en el coche de su padre.
native_language_example: He/She learned to drive in his/her father's car.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives or nouns to say that a behavior, comment, or decision is attributed to someone: Es muy amable de su parte ("That’s very kind of you"); Fue un error de su parte ("It was a mistake on his/her part"). It can also mean "on someone’s side" in contexts like La ley está de su parte ("The law is on your/his/her side"). You can change the possessive: de mi parte, de tu parte, de nuestra parte, etc.
target_language_example: Fue muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con la tarea.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you to help me with the homework.

meaning: (so afraid that they're) afraid of their own shadow; very timid/easily scared.
additional_notes: Used with "tener miedo" or "estar asustado" to emphasize that someone is extremely fearful or skittish, even when there’s no real danger. The possessive changes with the person: de mi propia sombra, de tu propia sombra, de su propia sombra.
target_language_example: No es peligroso, pero está asustado de su propia sombra.
native_language_example: It’s not dangerous, but he’s afraid of his own shadow.

meaning: about his/her work; from his/her job.
additional_notes: Uses de + su + trabajo. With verbs like quejarse de / hablar de / ser admirador de, it means “about his/her work.” With verbs like echar (a alguien) de, it means “from/out of his/her job” (to be fired). “Su” can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Lo despidieron de su trabajo el mes pasado.
native_language_example: They fired him from his job last month.

meaning: of his/her life; (with «qué será de…») what will become of him/her.
additional_notes: Usually refers to someone’s life or situation. Common in the expression «¿Qué será de su vida?» meaning you wonder what happened to someone or how they’re doing now. «Su» can mean “his,” “her,” or “your (formal)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hace años que no lo veo; me pregunto qué será de su vida.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him in years; I wonder what became of him.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun (sus + plural), after de. The possessor can be él/ella/usted/ellos/ellas depending on context (e.g., de sus pacientes = of their/his/her patients).
target_language_example: Siempre habla de sus hermanos.
native_language_example: He/She always talks about his/her/their brothers.

meaning: of his/her/their friends; from his/her/their friends.
additional_notes: Uses **de** + **sus** (his/her/their) + **amigos** (friends). It can indicate belonging/relationship (**of**) or source/origin (**from**), depending on the verb: e.g., *recordar los nombres de sus amigos* = “remember the names of his friends”; *pedir prestado... de sus amigos* = “borrow... from their friends.”
target_language_example: Ella recibió ayuda de sus amigos.
native_language_example: She got help from her friends.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like aprender (to learn), arrepentirse (to regret), or hablar/culpar (to blame) to say you learn from, regret, or talk about someone’s mistakes. “Sus” can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Todos podemos aprender de sus errores.
native_language_example: We can all learn from their mistakes.

additional_notes: Uses **de** (“of”) + **sus** (“his/her/their”) + **hijos** (“children/sons”). **Sus** can mean *his*, *her*, *their*, or *your (formal)* depending on context, so you often rely on the sentence to know whose children. Common after another noun to show what it’s about: **el cuidado de sus hijos** (“the care of his/her/their children”), **la custodia de sus hijos** (“custody of his/her/their children”).
target_language_example: Ella habla mucho del futuro de sus hijos.
native_language_example: She talks a lot about the future of her children.

meaning: 'of his/her/their parents' (or 'from his/her/their parents,' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s parents with the possessive "sus" (can mean "his," "her," "their," or formal "your"). Often appears after expressions like "independiente de" (independent of/from) or in phrases like "los deseos de sus padres" (their parents’ wishes).
target_language_example: No depende de sus padres para pagar la renta.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t depend on his/her parents to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sus" (= his, her, their, or formal your) to describe an ideal or perfect version of something: "la casa de sus sueños" (their dream house), "el hombre de sus sueños" (the man of her dreams). It can also be used more literally about actual dreams or a dreamlike state, depending on context.
target_language_example: Encontró el trabajo de sus sueños.
native_language_example: He/She found the job of their dreams.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used after the preposition “de” to refer back to the subject (“herself”). Common with verbs like hablar de (talk about), reírse de (laugh at), avergonzarse de (be ashamed of). The pronoun changes: de mí (about me), de ti, de sí mismo (himself), de sí misma (herself), de sí mismos/mismas (themselves). Note the accent: “sí” (reflexive) ≠ “si” (if).
target_language_example: Ella siempre habla de sí misma en las reuniones.
native_language_example: She always talks about herself in meetings.

additional_notes: Used with verbs or expressions that take "de" (like "dudar de...") to refer back to the same male person ("himself"). For a female person, use "de sí misma"; for plural, "de sí mismos / de sí mismas". Often used for self-reflection or self-doubt.
target_language_example: A veces duda de sí mismo, pero sigue adelante.
native_language_example: Sometimes he doubts himself, but he keeps going.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective or phrase like "ser afortunado/a" (to be lucky) to say what you’re lucky about: "Eres muy afortunada de tener tales amigos" = “You’re very lucky to have such friends.” "Tales" means “such” (like these / of that kind).
target_language_example: Me siento muy afortunado de tener tales amigos.
native_language_example: I feel very lucky to have such friends.

meaning: text; (used in set phrases like “text message,” “textbook,” “word processor”).
additional_notes: Means “of text / for text” and is most commonly used in fixed combinations: "mensaje(s) de texto" (text message(s)), "libro(s) de texto" (textbook(s)), and "procesador de texto" (word processor). It’s neutral and literal: "de" + "texto".
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes mandar un mensaje de texto cuando llegues?
native_language_example: Can you send me a text message when you arrive?

meaning: 'about you' / 'of you' (sometimes 'from you,' depending on the verb).
additional_notes:
Very common after verbs like hablar (to talk), saber (to know), oír/escuchar (to hear), and pensar (to think):
- hablar de ti = to talk about you
- saber/no saber nada de ti = to know/not know anything about you; also 'not to have news from you'
- he oído/escuché de ti = I’ve heard about you
- pensar lo mismo de ti = to think the same of you (have the same opinion about you)
Literal word-for-word is often 'of you,' but English usually uses 'about you.'
target_language_example: No he sabido nada de ti últimamente.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard anything about you lately.

meaning: "of all" (refers to a feminine plural group).
additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns to mean “of all the …” or “out of all the …,” often to show something is part of or connected to the whole group. It can be followed directly by a noun (de todas las ciudades) or used without the noun when it’s understood (de todas, la mejor).
target_language_example: De todas las opciones, prefiero la primera.
native_language_example: Of all the options, I prefer the first.

additional_notes: Used to compare or refer to something within a whole group of feminine plural nouns (e.g., "la mejor de todas las joyas" = "the best of all the jewels"). Also used to mean "from/against all the..." depending on the verb: "defender a alguien de todas las críticas" = "defend someone from all criticism." It’s the feminine plural form; with masculine plural you use "de todos los."
target_language_example: Este es el más caro de todas las opciones.
native_language_example: This is the most expensive of all the options.

meaning: in the whole world; from all over the world; everyone.
additional_notes: Often used for emphasis with superlatives: el/la más + adjective + de todo el mundo (“the ...est in the whole world”). With nouns like gente/turistas, it usually means “from all over the world.” With verbs like burlarse/acordarse, it can mean “everyone” (i.e., everybody).
target_language_example: Es el mejor chocolate de todo el mundo.
native_language_example: It’s the best chocolate in the whole world.

additional_notes: Often follows a noun to mean “of everything” (el precio de todo = the price of everything; el final de todo = the end of everything). With verbs like acordarse, olvidar, hablar, informarse, etc., it means “about everything” or “of everything” (Me acuerdo de todo = I remember everything; informado de todo = informed about everything). In the phrase “tener/hay de todo,” it means “to have all kinds of things / a bit of everything.”
target_language_example: En esa tienda hay de todo: comida, ropa y libros.
native_language_example: That store has everything: food, clothes, and books.

meaning: "of all" (out of everyone/everything in a group).
additional_notes: Used to single out one person/thing from a larger group, very often with superlatives: "De todos..., es el/la más..." (= "Of all..., he/she/it is the most..."). Common patterns: "de todos los/las + plural noun" (of all the ...) and "de todos mis + plural noun" (of all my ...).
target_language_example: De todos los restaurantes de la ciudad, este es el más barato.
native_language_example: Of all the restaurants in the city, this one is the cheapest.

meaning: "of all the" (refers to the whole group).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to, applies to, or includes every member of a plural masculine/mixed group. You’ll also see it in set patterns like "la ubicación de todos los..." (the location of all the...) or with verbs like "hacerse de" to mean "to get/obtain" something: "se hizo de todos los..." = he got all the.... For feminine plural, use "de todas las"; for plural without a noun, "de todos" / "de todas".
target_language_example: No me acuerdo de todos los nombres.
native_language_example: I don’t remember all the names.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative (el/la mejor, el/la peor, el/la más + adjective) to mean “ever” or “in history.” It’s a very common way to emphasize that someone/something is the greatest, cutest, biggest, etc., compared to all others in the past and present.
target_language_example: Este es el mejor concierto de todos los tiempos.
native_language_example: This is the best concert of all time.

meaning: three years old; three years (in length).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify either (1) someone’s age (especially with niño/niña, hijo/hija: “un niño de tres años” = “a three-year-old child”), or (2) the duration/length of something (“una sentencia de tres años” = “a three-year sentence”). You can also set it off with commas as extra information: “Mi hija, de tres años, …”.
target_language_example: Adoptaron un perro de tres años.
native_language_example: They adopted a three-year-old dog.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it’s related to road traffic, driving, or transportation on streets. Common collocations: leyes de tráfico (traffic laws), reglas de tráfico (traffic rules), accidentes de tráfico (traffic accidents), atasco de tráfico (traffic jam). Often interchangeable with "de tránsito" in many regions.
target_language_example: Hay muchas señales de tráfico en esta avenida.
native_language_example: There are many traffic signs on this avenue.

additional_notes: It’s the preposition **de** + the possessive **tu** (“your”). Use it with verbs like **hablar de** (“to talk about”) and **contar de** (“to tell about”), or with nouns to mean “of/from your” (e.g., **de tu tamaño** = “of your size”). Before a noun, Spanish often prefers **de + possessive** instead of English “your + noun” in some set phrases: **los de tu especie** = “those of your species/type” (i.e., people/creatures like you).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablarme de tu familia?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about your family?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s age relative to the person you’re speaking to. Often follows “ser” (Es de tu edad.) or a noun (un hijo/una hija de tu edad). You’ll also hear “como de tu edad” to mean “around your age.”
target_language_example: Creo que ella es de tu edad.
native_language_example: I think she’s your age.

meaning: on your side; by your side.
additional_notes: Used literally for physical position (e.g., sleeping on your left/right side) and figuratively to show support (“I’m on your side”). It can also mean that facts/circumstances favor you (“The statistics are on your side”). With verbs like estar/quedarse/no moverse, it often means staying close to someone (“by your side”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: estoy de tu lado.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m on your side.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or connection with someone’s mother: *casa de tu madre* (your mom’s house), *un amigo de tu madre* (a friend of your mom). In some vulgar insults it can appear after a swear word (e.g., *… de tu madre*), but by itself it’s neutral.
target_language_example: Tengo que pasar por la casa de tu madre esta tarde.
native_language_example: I have to stop by your mom’s house this afternoon.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to show possession or relationship ("your father's"), or origin/source ("from your father"). Often follows a noun: "la casa de tu padre" = "your father's house". "Padre" is "father" (more formal/neutral); "papá" is more common for "dad".
target_language_example: Este reloj es de tu padre.
native_language_example: This watch is your father's.

meaning: “on your part” / “from you” (your doing; your responsibility).
additional_notes: Used to comment on someone’s action or behavior, often after an adjective: Es muy amable/considerado/generoso de tu parte (“That’s very kind/thoughtful/generous of you”). It can also express responsibility or blame: Fue descuidado de tu parte… (“It was careless of you to…”). Not the same as “parte” meaning “part” in a physical/object sense.
target_language_example: Es muy amable de tu parte ayudarme con esto.
native_language_example: It’s very kind of you to help me with this.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to, happens in, or is the most important/best/worst within your life. Very common with superlatives: “el mejor día de tu vida” (the best day of your life), “la decisión más importante de tu vida” (the most important decision of your life).
target_language_example: Hoy es el mejor día de tu vida.
native_language_example: Today is the best day of your life.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association: de + tus + plural noun (masculine or feminine), e.g., de tus actos / de tus ideas. Common in set phrases like “ser responsable de tus…” (“to be responsible for your…”). Not used before singular nouns (use “de tu…”).
target_language_example: Estoy orgulloso de tus logros.
native_language_example: I'm proud of your achievements.

additional_notes: Uses de to show what something is made of or the type/category. Very common in partitive expressions like algo de té (“some tea”) and quantities like una libra de té (“a pound of tea”).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres algo de té con limón?
native_language_example: Do you want some tea with lemon?

additional_notes: Uses "de" to show (1) possession/connection: "la casa de un amigo" (a friend’s house), "el auto de un amigo" (a friend’s car); or (2) origin/source: "tomó prestado... de un amigo" (borrowed ... from a friend), "recibí ayuda de un amigo" (got help from a friend). Often appears after a noun (to say who it belongs to) or after a verb (to say who something comes from).
target_language_example: Tengo un consejo de un amigo.
native_language_example: I have some advice from a friend.

meaning: of one year; for a year.
additional_notes: Used to express a time span or point of comparison involving one year. Common in phrases like “de un año a otro” (from one year to another), “de un año al siguiente” (from one year to the next), and in duration expressions like “menos de un año” (less than a year).
target_language_example: Viví allí durante más de un año.
native_language_example: I lived there for more than a year.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to show that something belongs to, comes from, or describes a man (possession/association): la reputación de un hombre (a man’s reputation), el sueño de un hombre viejo (an old man’s dream). Contrast: de un hombre = “of a man” (one/any man), de el hombre (del hombre) = “of the man” (a specific man).
target_language_example: La voz de un hombre se oía en la calle.
native_language_example: A man’s voice could be heard in the street.

meaning: back and forth; from one side to the other.
additional_notes: Used for repeated movement between two places/sides (often pacing). With verbs like caminar, ir, pasar, pasear. You can also say “de un lado al otro” in some contexts, but “de un lado a otro” is very common.
target_language_example: Estoy nervioso y camino de un lado a otro en la sala.
native_language_example: I'm nervous and I pace back and forth in the living room.

meaning: at any moment; suddenly; from one moment to the next.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen very soon/any time now, or that something can change suddenly. Often with future tense (llegará/llegarán) for “any moment now.” In negatives it can mean “not overnight” (not quickly): “no se aprende de un momento a otro.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: el médico puede llegar de un momento a otro.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: the doctor could arrive any moment now.

additional_notes: Uses de to link something to a tree: possession/part (“a branch of a tree”), origin/source (“rescue a cat from a tree”), or as part of a location phrase like a la sombra de un árbol (“in the shade of a tree”).
target_language_example: Tomó una hoja de un árbol y la guardó.
native_language_example: He took a leaf from a tree and kept it.

meaning: from a (certain) family; belonging to a family.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s family background or social origin (e.g., "de una familia rica/noble/respetable" = from a rich/noble/respectable family). Also common with verbs like "venir" or "ser" ("Viene/Es de una familia...").
target_language_example: Ella viene de una familia humilde.
native_language_example: She comes from a humble family.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to link something to a woman (possession, description, origin, or association). Very common in titles and descriptions: "el retrato de una mujer" (the portrait of a woman), "la atracción de una mujer" (a woman’s attraction).
target_language_example: Escuché la voz de una mujer en la calle.
native_language_example: I heard a woman's voice in the street.

meaning: (with quedarse/quedar) stunned; frozen in shock; speechless.
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the expression “quedarse/se quedó de una pieza” or “quedé de una pieza” to describe someone who is so surprised or shocked that they can’t react for a moment. It can also be used literally to mean “in one piece” (e.g., moving from one piece of a puzzle to the next, or taking/keeping something in one piece), but the “stunned” meaning is the common idiomatic one.
target_language_example: Cuando me dijo la noticia, me quedé de una pieza.
native_language_example: When she told me the news, I was stunned.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (or similar) to say someone is taking time off: "Estoy de vacaciones". You can also use it with ir to talk about going on vacation somewhere: "Quiero ir de vacaciones a...".
target_language_example: Mis padres están de vacaciones esta semana.
native_language_example: My parents are on vacation this week.

meaning: summer (used to describe something related to summer).
additional_notes: Often follows a noun to say it’s a “summer” thing: casa de verano (summer house), tarde de verano (summer afternoon), noches de verano (summer nights), nubes de verano (summer clouds). It can describe time (a summer evening) or something meant for/typical of summer.
target_language_example: Me encantan las noches de verano en la playa.
native_language_example: I love summer nights at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true or sincere. It often goes next to what it emphasizes: before the verb/adjective ("De veras necesito...") or after it ("me gusta de veras..."). As a question ("¿De veras?"), it means "Really?" / "Is that so?".
target_language_example: ¿De veras vas a mudarte mañana?
native_language_example: Are you really going to move tomorrow?

meaning: “to see you” (used after certain verbs/adjectives/nouns that take **de**).
additional_notes: **De verte** = **de** + **ver** (to see) + **te** (you). It commonly appears after expressions like **estar feliz de verte** (to be happy to see you), **alegrarse de verte** (to be glad to see you), **qué gusto de verte** (what a pleasure to see you), and **con la esperanza de verte** (in hopes of seeing you). In **dejar de verte**, it means “to stop seeing you.”
target_language_example: Me alegro mucho de verte otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you again.

meaning: life-or-death; extremely serious/urgent (where survival is at stake).
additional_notes: Used after nouns like "cuestión" (matter/issue), "problema" (problem), or "lucha" (fight/struggle): "una cuestión/problema/lucha de vida o muerte." Often emphasizes that something is critical and cannot be taken lightly; sometimes used a bit figuratively for strong emphasis.
target_language_example: Para él, conseguir ese medicamento era una cuestión de vida o muerte.
native_language_example: For him, getting that medicine was a matter of life or death.

meaning: “of wine” / “(made) of wine” (used to specify the drink).
additional_notes: Most often follows a quantity container or measure to say what it contains: "un vaso de vino" (a glass of wine), "dos copas de vino" (two glasses of wine), "un poco de vino" (a little wine). It’s the same pattern as "de agua" (of water), "de café" (of coffee).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres una copa de vino o prefieres agua?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of wine or do you prefer water?

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like perder de vista (to lose sight of), no perder de vista (to keep an eye on / not lose sight of), and conocer de vista (to recognize someone by sight, without really knowing them). Also appears in the phrase punto(s) de vista (“point(s) of view”).
target_language_example: Lo conozco de vista, pero nunca hemos hablado.
native_language_example: I recognize him by sight, but we’ve never talked.

additional_notes: Used to indicate returning to a destination: "Volver/ir/correr de vuelta a + lugar". It can also be used to return to a subject in conversation or media: "De vuelta a + tema" (like “Back to the news”). You’ll also see it with tickets/trips: "billete de vuelta a + ciudad" = “return ticket to + city.”
target_language_example: Después de cenar, volvimos de vuelta al hotel.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went back to the hotel.

meaning: 'back in/into/on' (returned to a place), or 'back in' (after a period of time).
additional_notes: Uses "de vuelta" (= back/again, returned) plus "en" to say someone/something is back in a place ("de vuelta en el carro", "de vuelta en el escritorio") or back after a time period ("de vuelta en un día o dos"). Very common with verbs like volver/estar/poner/traer: "estar de vuelta en..." (to be back in...), "poner ... de vuelta en..." (to put ... back in/on...), "traer ... de vuelta en..." (to bring ... back in...).
target_language_example: Estaré de vuelta en la oficina mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: I'll be back in the office tomorrow morning.

meaning: “of these are mine” (used after a quantity: “some/many/most of these are mine”).
additional_notes: This is a sentence chunk that usually comes after a quantifier: "Algunas/Bastantes/La mayoría/La mitad/Un montón de éstas son mías." Here, "de éstas" = “of these (feminine plural items)”. If the items are masculine, use "de éstos". The possessive agrees with what is owned: "son mías" (feminine plural), "son míos" (masculine plural), "es mía/mío" (singular).
target_language_example: La mayoría de éstas son mías.
native_language_example: Most of these are mine.

additional_notes: Used to say that a certain number/portion of the items you’re pointing to belong to you, usually after a quantity word: “algunos / muchos / tres / la mayor parte de éstos son míos.” You can also use “estos” (without accent) when it’s not after a preposition: “Estos son míos.”
target_language_example: Dos de éstos son míos, y los demás son de Ana.
native_language_example: Two of these are mine, and the rest are Ana’s.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically lower than something else or placed beneath it. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la alfombra, la mesa). With masculine singular it’s "debajo del" (de + el). You’ll also see it with plurals: "debajo de las/los".
target_language_example: El gato está debajo de la mesa.
native_language_example: The cat is under the table.

additional_notes: A location phrase used to say something is beneath the bed. Uses the preposition "debajo de" (under/beneath) + a noun with an article ("la cama"). You can swap the noun: "debajo de la mesa" (under the table), "debajo del sofá" (under the couch).
target_language_example: Hay polvo debajo de la cama.
native_language_example: There is dust under the bed.

additional_notes: A location phrase used to say something (or someone) is in the space beneath a table. Often used with estar (to be located) or with verbs like esconderse (to hide): "Está debajo de la mesa" / "Me escondí debajo de la mesa".
target_language_example: Los niños están debajo de la mesa.
native_language_example: The children are under the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically under something else. It’s the contraction of "debajo de" + "el" → "debajo del" (use "debajo de la" with feminine nouns, e.g., "debajo de la mesa"). Common in fixed phrases like "debajo del brazo" (“under the arm”, meaning tucked under the arm).
target_language_example: Las llaves están debajo del libro.
native_language_example: The keys are under the book.

additional_notes: A location phrase: "debajo de" + noun = "under/beneath" something. It’s also common to say "bajo el árbol" with the same meaning. Use "del" because it’s the contraction of "de + el" (debajo de + el árbol).
target_language_example: Dejé la mochila debajo del árbol.
native_language_example: I left the backpack under the tree.

meaning: “must be / probably” (a guess or strong likelihood).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express supposition or probability: debe de + infinitive (e.g., debe de estar, debe de haber llegado). This is different from debe + infinitive, which more often expresses obligation (“has to / must”). In everyday speech, many speakers don’t strictly keep this distinction, but it’s a helpful rule for learners.
target_language_example: Debe de estar cansada después del viaje.
native_language_example: She must be tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used to make a deduction about someone’s location or state. In everyday speech, many speakers also say "debe estar" with the same meaning. The idea is probability/inference (not an order).
target_language_example: Tu teléfono debe de estar en tu mochila.
native_language_example: Your phone must be / is probably in your backpack.

additional_notes: Used to make a guess or deduction (supposition), often based on evidence: "Debe de haber llovido" = "It must have rained." In many places, people also say "debe haber" without "de" with the same meaning. It’s commonly followed by a past participle (debe de haber + participle) to talk about something that probably happened.
target_language_example: Debe de haber salido ya; no contesta el teléfono.
native_language_example: He must have left already; he isn’t answering the phone.

meaning: "must have been" / "it must have been" (a strong guess).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong assumption about the past: present tense of "deber de" + "haber" + past participle. Often followed by a noun or adjective: "Debe de haber sido el oxígeno" (must have been the oxygen), "Debe de haber sido muy hermosa" (must have been very beautiful). In everyday speech you may also hear "debe haber sido" without "de".
target_language_example: Debe de haber sido un malentendido.
native_language_example: It must have been a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to make a guess or deduction (supposition), often based on evidence: "Debe de haber llovido" = "It must have rained." In many places, people also say "debe haber" without "de" with the same meaning. It’s commonly followed by a past participle (debe de haber + participle) to talk about something that probably happened.
target_language_example: Debe de haber salido ya; no contesta el teléfono.
native_language_example: He must have left already; he isn’t answering the phone.

additional_notes: Used to make an assumption/inference based on clues, not to give an order. Very common with time (“Ya debe de ser tarde.” = “It must be late already.”). In everyday speech, many speakers also say “debe ser” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: No contesta; debe de ser que está ocupado.
native_language_example: He’s not answering; he must be busy.

additional_notes: Used to make an assumption/inference based on clues, not to give an order. Very common with time (“Ya debe de ser tarde.” = “It must be late already.”). In everyday speech, many speakers also say “debe ser” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: No contesta; debe de ser que está ocupado.
native_language_example: He’s not answering; he must be busy.

meaning: “must be” / “is probably” (about someone’s state or condition).
additional_notes: Uses deber (must/probably) + estar (to be, for temporary states/emotions) to make a strong guess about how someone feels or is at the moment. Often followed by an adjective (orgulloso, enfadado, cansado) or a phrase like “de + alguien” (orgulloso de ti).
target_language_example: Debe estar cansada después del viaje.
native_language_example: She must be tired after the trip.

meaning: “must be” / “is probably” (about someone’s state or condition).
additional_notes: Uses deber (must/probably) + estar (to be, for temporary states/emotions) to make a strong guess about how someone feels or is at the moment. Often followed by an adjective (orgulloso, enfadado, cansado) or a phrase like “de + alguien” (orgulloso de ti).
target_language_example: Debe estar cansada después del viaje.
native_language_example: She must be tired after the trip.

meaning: “must have” / “should have” (strong guess that something happened).
additional_notes: Used to make a deduction about the past. Structure: debe + haber + past participle (debe haber estudiado = must have studied). With "ya" it often means “must have already…”. With reflexive/indirect pronouns: "Se me debe haber olvidado" = I must have forgotten (it). In negative form: "No debe haber…" = can’t have / must not have.
target_language_example: Debe haber llegado tarde porque había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: He must have arrived late because there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: "must have been" (a strong guess about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express a deduction or strong probability about a past situation, not a confirmed fact. Structure: deber (present) + haber + past participle (sido). You can change the verb at the end: Debe haber estado / Debe haber tenido / Debe haber dicho, etc.
target_language_example: Debe haber sido un día largo para ti.
native_language_example: It must have been a long day for you.

meaning: "must have been" (a strong guess about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express a deduction or strong probability about a past situation, not a confirmed fact. Structure: deber (present) + haber + past participle (sido). You can change the verb at the end: Debe haber estado / Debe haber tenido / Debe haber dicho, etc.
target_language_example: Debe haber sido un día largo para ti.
native_language_example: It must have been a long day for you.

meaning: “must have” / “should have” (strong guess that something happened).
additional_notes: Used to make a deduction about the past. Structure: debe + haber + past participle (debe haber estudiado = must have studied). With "ya" it often means “must have already…”. With reflexive/indirect pronouns: "Se me debe haber olvidado" = I must have forgotten (it). In negative form: "No debe haber…" = can’t have / must not have.
target_language_example: Debe haber llegado tarde porque había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: He must have arrived late because there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: “There must be something.” / “There has to be something.”
additional_notes: Used to express a strong guess or conclusion (probability), not just obligation: "debe" + infinitive often means "must" in the sense of "it must be (true)". "haber" is impersonal here (like "there is/are"), so you don’t name a subject: "Debe haber algo en la nave" = "There must be something in the ship." It’s also common before a relative clause: "Debe haber algo que podamos hacer" (There must be something we can do).
target_language_example: Debe haber algo que no estamos viendo.
native_language_example: There must be something we’re not seeing.

meaning: 'There must be a…' / 'There’s probably a…' (singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to make a logical guess or assumption about something that exists or is happening. It’s built from "deber" (must/should) + "haber" (there is/are). Change the article to match the noun: "debe haber una" (feminine), and plural: "debe haber unos/unas".
target_language_example: Debe haber un error en la factura.
native_language_example: There must be a mistake on the bill.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong assumption or logical conclusion that something exists. It’s the expression: deber + haber (“must be/there must be”) + una, so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (una forma, una manera, una razón, una salida). For a masculine noun, use “debe haber un” (e.g., “un problema”).
target_language_example: Debe haber una solución para esto.
native_language_example: There must be a solution for this.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or a requirement. Very common in instructions and rules, often followed by a past participle to form the passive: "debe ser + participle" (e.g., "debe ser tomado" = "must be taken"). It can also express a logical conclusion in other contexts ("Debe ser tarde" = "It must be late").
target_language_example: Este formulario debe ser firmado por un adulto.
native_language_example: This form must be signed by an adult.

additional_notes: Used to identify something or someone when you’re not 100% sure, but you think it’s very likely. It’s based on deber + ser: Debe ser el profesor. / Debe ser la estación. You can change el to la/los/las depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Debe ser el restaurante del que me hablaste.
native_language_example: It must be the restaurant you told me about.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or a requirement. Very common in instructions and rules, often followed by a past participle to form the passive: "debe ser + participle" (e.g., "debe ser tomado" = "must be taken"). It can also express a logical conclusion in other contexts ("Debe ser tarde" = "It must be late").
target_language_example: Este formulario debe ser firmado por un adulto.
native_language_example: This form must be signed by an adult.

additional_notes: From the verb "deber" + infinitive ("tener"). It expresses obligation/requirement ("He must have his own land...") and can also express a logical guess or deduction depending on context ("He must have some information" = you assume it’s true). The subject can be understood (yo/tú/él/ella/usted) and is often omitted in Spanish.
target_language_example: Para entrar, debe tener un pasaporte válido.
native_language_example: To enter, you must have a valid passport.

additional_notes: Formed from the verb phrase **deber** (“must/should/ought to”) + **ser** (“to be”). It’s used to say what is necessary, expected, or recommended about a person or thing. **Deben** is 3rd person plural (they/you all). Often followed by an adjective or past participle: *Deben ser fuertes* (“They must be strong”), *Deben ser considerados* (“They must be considered”).
target_language_example: Para entrar, deben ser mayores de 18 años.
native_language_example: To enter, they must be over 18.

meaning: “should be” (it ought to be / is expected to be).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (debería) + infinitive estar to express expectation or what is the right thing regarding a state, condition, or location. Often followed by an adjective, past participle, or a place phrase: “debería estar listo” (should be ready), “debería estar en casa” (should be at home).
target_language_example: Ya debería estar en casa.
native_language_example: He/She should already be at home.

additional_notes: Used to express expectation or what is considered normal/right: someone or something is supposed to be here, but may not be. You can change the person/place: “Deberías estar aquí” (you should be here), “debería estar allí” (should be there).
target_language_example: El paquete debería estar aquí mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: The package should be here tomorrow afternoon.

meaning: "should be in / should be at" (expected to be in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is expected to be in a certain location now (based on logic, plans, rules, or what’s normal). It’s the conditional of deber + infinitive (debería) and often implies uncertainty: you think that’s where it is, but you’re not 100% sure. Common with places: en la cama, en casa, en el trabajo, en la India.
target_language_example: A esta hora, mi hermano debería estar en casa.
native_language_example: At this time, my brother should be at home.

additional_notes: Used to say that something was the right thing to do in the past but didn’t happen, often expressing regret or criticism. It’s the conditional of deber (debería) + haber + past participle: debería haber llamado = should have called. Negative: no debería haber dicho eso = shouldn’t have said that.
target_language_example: Debería haber estudiado más para el examen.
native_language_example: I should have studied more for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to express regret, criticism, or that the right action wasn’t done earlier. It’s the conditional of deber (debería) + haber + past participle (hecho). You can change the verb: debería haber ido (should have gone), debería haber dicho (should have said).
target_language_example: Debería haber hecho la tarea ayer.
native_language_example: I should have done the homework yesterday.

meaning: "should have arrived" / "was supposed to have arrived."
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (debería) + perfect infinitive (haber llegado). It can express (1) expectation about timing (often with ya = "by now") or (2) regret/criticism about being late (often with antes = "earlier"). The subject can be included (Él/Mi amigo...) or omitted if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Ya debería haber llegado a casa.
native_language_example: He/She should have arrived home by now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past action that would have been better or more correct (often expressing regret). It’s the conditional of deber (“should”) + haber + past participle hecho (“done”), with lo = “it.” With no (“No debería haberlo hecho”), it means “I/you shouldn’t have done it.”
target_language_example: Debería haberlo hecho antes, pero se me olvidó.
native_language_example: I should have done it earlier, but I forgot.

additional_notes: "Debería" is the conditional form of "deber" (to have to / should) and is used to give advice or say what would be a good idea. It can be used with different subjects: (yo) debería, (tú) deberías, (él/ella/usted) debería, etc. Follow it with the infinitive "ir" and then "a" + a destination/place (e.g., "a casa", "a Boston").
target_language_example: Deberías ir a casa ahora.
native_language_example: You should go home now.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (debería) + ser to talk about what is expected, advisable, or likely. Often expresses a recommendation or a mild obligation (softer than “tiene que ser”). It can also mean something is probably the case: “Eso debería ser fácil” = “That should be easy.”
target_language_example: Debería ser más barato si lo compras en línea.
native_language_example: It should be cheaper if you buy it online.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or express what the speaker thinks is appropriate/expected. It’s formed with the conditional of deber (deberías) + estar + an adjective (agradecida, orgulloso) or a place/state (con tu familia, en la cama, en silencio). Often implies gentle pressure or criticism depending on tone.
target_language_example: Deberías estar más atento en clase.
native_language_example: You should be more attentive in class.

meaning: “you should have …” (you were expected to do it in the past, but you didn’t).
additional_notes: Used to criticize, regret, or give advice about a past action that didn’t happen. Structure: deberías (tú conditional of deber) + haber + past participle (intentado, hablado, mantenido, realizado, tratado, etc.). Often implies the speaker thinks it would have been better if you had done it.
target_language_example: Deberías haberme llamado antes de venir.
native_language_example: You should have called me before coming.

meaning: “you should have seen” (you missed it; it would’ve been worth seeing).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (deberías) + haber + past participle (visto) to talk about something in the past that someone didn’t see/do. Often used as a comment expressing regret, surprise, or emphasis: “You should’ve seen his/her/their face!” You can add an object right after: deberías haber visto la película / lo que pasó / su cara.
target_language_example: Deberías haber visto su reacción cuando se lo dije.
native_language_example: You should have seen his reaction when I told him.

meaning: "You should have done it." (you didn’t, and now you regret it / it was a mistake not to)
additional_notes: Used to criticize or give advice about a past action that didn’t happen. Grammar: deberías ("you should") + haber + hecho (past participle) forms the perfect infinitive, meaning "should have done". The -lo is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (haberlo = "to have it"). You can change -lo to -la/-los/-las depending on what "it" refers to (e.g., deberías haberla hecho).
target_language_example: Deberías haberlo hecho ayer, ahora es demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: You should have done it yesterday; now it’s too late.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. It’s the conditional form of deber ("should/ought to") + hablar con ("to talk to"). Often followed by a person (name, él/ella/ellos) or a role (tu jefe, el médico). You can make it softer or stronger with words like quizá (maybe) or realmente (really).
target_language_example: Deberías hablar con tu profesor después de clase.
native_language_example: You should talk to your teacher after class.

meaning: 'you should go to' / 'you should go and (do something)'.
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. It’s the conditional form of deber (“should/ought to”): deberías = “you should” (to one person, informal or formal depending on context). Ir a is followed by a place (a casa, a la peluquería) or by an infinitive to suggest an action (ir a hablar, ir a ver, ir a pasar el rato).
target_language_example: Deberías ir a hablar con tu jefe mañana.
native_language_example: You should go talk to your boss tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. "Deberías" is the conditional of "deber" and often sounds a bit softer/more polite than "debes". "Irte" = "to leave/go away" ("ir" + reflexive "te"), so the idea is 'you should leave and go home'. You can add reasons or timing: "a descansar" (to rest), "ahora" (now), "mientras puedas" (while you can).
target_language_example: Te ves cansado; deberías irte a casa.
native_language_example: You look tired; you should go home.

meaning: you should ask/request (something) from him/her; you should tell him/her (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. "Deberías" = "you should" (from deber). "Pedirle" = "to ask/request from him/her"; "le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him" or "to her" (context tells which). Common patterns: pedirle + noun ("Deberías pedirle permiso." = you should ask him/her for permission) and pedirle que + subjunctive ("Deberías pedirle que te ayude." = you should ask him/her to help you).
target_language_example: Deberías pedirle ayuda a tu profesora.
native_language_example: You should ask your teacher for help.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of deber (deberías) to give advice or a recommendation, often about staying somewhere or remaining in a certain state. Quedarte is the informal 'you' (tú) form of quedarse; it refers to you staying/remaining. Can be followed by a place (aquí, en casa, en la cama) or by an adjective/participle (despierto). For 'you all should stay,' use deberíais quedaros (Spain) or deberían quedarse (Latin America).
target_language_example: Si estás cansado, deberías quedarte en casa.
native_language_example: If you're tired, you should stay at home.

meaning: you should be able to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is expected to have the ability to do something, often because of their skills, situation, or circumstances. It’s made of deberías (you should) + ser capaz de (to be able to), and it’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., hacerlo, encontrar, caminar).
target_language_example: Con un poco de práctica, deberías ser capaz de hablar más rápido.
native_language_example: With a little practice, you should be able to speak faster.

additional_notes: A warning or advice. Uses the conditional of deber (“deberías” = “you should”), often followed by con (“with/about”) or a la hora de + infinitive (“when it comes to…”). Can also be said on its own as a general warning.
target_language_example: Deberías tener cuidado al cruzar la calle de noche.
native_language_example: You should be careful when crossing the street at night.

additional_notes: A common way to give advice or a mild warning. Uses the conditional of "deber" (deberías) to sound less direct than an order. Often followed by "con" + noun (deberías tener más cuidado con tu dinero) or "en" + place/situation (en un cruce).
target_language_example: Deberías tener más cuidado al conducir de noche.
native_language_example: You should be more careful when driving at night.

meaning: "you must be" / "you should be" (obligation, expectation, or strong guess).
additional_notes: From deber (you must/should) + estar (to be, often temporary state or location). It can express: (1) an obligation/requirement: "Debes estar aquí a las nueve" = you have to be here at nine; (2) an expectation of where someone belongs: "donde debes estar" = where you’re supposed to be; (3) a strong assumption about someone’s state: "Debes estar muerta de hambre" = you must be starving. Often followed by a place (aquí, cerca, de vuelta, fuera) or an adjective (asustada, cansado/a).
target_language_example: Debes estar en casa antes de las diez.
native_language_example: You must/should be home before ten.

meaning: "you must/should do" (you’re required/expected to do something).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone what they are obligated to do. It’s made of deber (to have to/must) in the tú form debes + hacer (to do/make). Often followed by an infinitive or a thing to do: debes hacer algo / debes hacer tus tareas. You’ll also see the command form haz (do!) in similar phrases: Haz lo que debes hacer.
target_language_example: Debes hacer la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: You must do your homework before going out.

meaning: "You should/must do what you…" (followed by another verb).
additional_notes:
This is a common sentence frame used to give advice or instructions. 
- "Debes" = "you should" or "you must" (depending on context).
- "hacer" = "to do".
- "lo que" = "what/that which".
- "te" is an object pronoun that usually goes with the next verb (e.g., "te dicen" = "they tell you", "te parezca" = "seems to you").
Often used as: "Debes hacer lo que te dicen" (do what they tell you) or "Debes hacer lo que te parezca correcto" (do what seems right to you).
target_language_example: Debes hacer lo que te diga el médico.
native_language_example: You should do what the doctor tells you.

meaning: you must leave / you have to go.
additional_notes: Uses the tú form of deber to express obligation or strong necessity. Irte = ir + te (“to go” + “yourself”), commonly meaning “to leave” (go away from here). Often followed by a time phrase (ahora, ya, ahora mismo) or a destination (a casa).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero debes irte ya.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you have to leave now.

meaning: "you must be" / "you should be" (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun to say what someone is required or expected to be: Debes ser paciente/responsable. It’s the verb deber (tú form: debes) + infinitive ser. Often translates as “must” for strong obligation and “should” for advice, depending on context.
target_language_example: Debes ser honesto conmigo.
native_language_example: You should be honest with me.

additional_notes: Formed by deber (tú) + infinitive tener. Used to express obligation/advice (“You should be more careful”) or a strong guess about someone’s condition (“You must be hungry”). Often followed by a noun (hambre, cuidado) or an object (tus asuntos) + a complement (en orden).
target_language_example: Debes tener paciencia con los niños.
native_language_example: You should have patience with children.

additional_notes:
Used to warn or advise someone to be cautious. Often followed by:
- "al" + infinitive: "Debes tener cuidado al conducir" (be careful when driving)
- "con" + noun: "Debes tener cuidado con el cuchillo" (be careful with the knife)
You can also say it alone as a general warning: "Debes tener cuidado."
target_language_example: Debes tener cuidado cuando cruces la calle.
native_language_example: You should be careful when you cross the street.

meaning: due to the / because of the (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something. It’s a formal/neutral equivalent of “por” in many contexts. Use "debido a" + noun (or "debido a que" + clause). Change "la" to match the noun: "debido al" (masc. sing.), "debido a los/las" (plural).
target_language_example: Debido a la lluvia, cancelaron el partido.
native_language_example: Because of the rain, they canceled the game.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something (a delay, cancellation, etc.). It’s common at the start of a sentence followed by a comma ("Debido al mal tiempo, ..."), or at the end without a comma ("... debido al mal tiempo"). Similar to "por el mal tiempo" or "a causa del mal tiempo".
target_language_example: Debido al mal tiempo, la excursión se canceló.
native_language_example: Due to the bad weather, the trip was canceled.

meaning: “you should have” (you were supposed to do something, but didn’t).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past action that didn’t happen and to criticize or express regret. It’s the tú (informal singular) form: debiste + haber + past participle (aceptado, dicho, pagado, etc.). It often implies “and it would have been better if you had.”
target_language_example: Debiste haberme llamado antes de venir.
native_language_example: You should have called me before coming.

meaning: “you should have come” (you didn’t, and it’s a regret/criticism).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional perfect idea in Spanish: **deber** (should/ought to) + **haber** + past participle (**venido**). It talks about a past action that didn’t happen (or the speaker assumes it didn’t) and expresses that it was the right thing to do. Often sounds like a reproach: *Debiste haber venido a la fiesta.* You can add time words like *ayer, antes, más pronto*.
target_language_example: Debiste haber venido conmigo; te habría gustado.
native_language_example: You should have come with me; you would have liked it.

additional_notes: Formed from the past tense of *deber* + *haber* + past participle: **debió haber + participle** (e.g., *debió haber comprado*). It’s used either to (1) make a strong guess/inference about what probably happened (*He must have heard*), or (2) say what was the right thing to do but didn’t happen (*He should have bought pencils*). Context usually makes clear which meaning fits.
target_language_example: Debió haber olvidado la cita.
native_language_example: He must have forgotten the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest (sometimes reluctant) admission. Very common for acknowledging a mistake, a weakness, or that someone else is right. You can change the tense/person: "debes admitir que" (you have to admit), "tuve que admitir que" (I had to admit), "debería admitir que" (I should admit).
target_language_example: Debo admitir que estaba nervioso antes de la entrevista.
native_language_example: I have to admit that I was nervous before the interview.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or comment (often a little emphatic or polite), sometimes expressing surprise or giving a compliment/criticism. You can change the verb for other people: "debes decir que" (you must say), "debo decir que" (I must say). In speech it can sound like “I have to say…”.
target_language_example: Debo decir que me encanta tu idea.
native_language_example: I must say that I love your idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation or need to speak with a person. "Debo" is from "deber" (to have to/ought to), and it’s stronger than "tengo que" in some contexts. Add the person after "con": "debo hablar con él/ella/usted/ellos". You can also add a topic: "debo hablar con ella al respecto" (about it).
target_language_example: Debo hablar con mi jefe antes de irme.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my boss before I leave.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or duty. "Debo" is the present tense of "deber" (to have to / must), and it’s usually followed by an infinitive like "hacer" (to do/make): "debo hacer + [something]". It can also appear inside a longer phrase: "lo que debo hacer" (“what I must do”).
target_language_example: Debo hacer la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework before going out.

meaning: 'I must/should go to' (or 'I have to go to').
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation or need to go somewhere or go do an action. After "ir a" you can use an infinitive to mean "go to do something" (e.g., "debo ir a buscar...") or a place to mean "go to [place]" (e.g., "debo ir a casa / a la oficina"). In conversation, "tengo que ir a" is also very common.
target_language_example: Lo siento, debo ir a trabajar ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go to work now.

meaning: I have to leave / I must go.
additional_notes: "Debo" (from deber) expresses obligation: "I have to" or "I must." "Irme" means "to leave" (literally "to go myself"), and it’s commonly used to say you need to go. Often followed by a time word like "ahora" (now) or a reason: "Debo irme, tengo una reunión" (I have to leave, I have a meeting).
target_language_example: Lo siento, debo irme ya.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to leave now.

meaning: “I have to go back to …” / “I must return to …” (and then do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation/need to return to a place (“debo volver a casa/la oficina”) or to do an action again (“debo volver a dormir”). If the next word is a verb, use the infinitive: “volver a + infinitive” (go back to doing something). If it’s a place, use “volver a + noun/place.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, debo volver a trabajar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to get back to work.

meaning: 'I should have' (regret about a past action).
additional_notes: Used to say you regret not doing something (or regret doing it) in the past. Structure: debí haber + past participle (hecho, tomado, dicho, gastado). With no: No debí haber + past participle = 'I shouldn’t have…'.
target_language_example: Debí haber estudiado más para el examen.
native_language_example: I should have studied more for the exam.

meaning: to say goodbye; to bid farewell.
additional_notes: Used for leaving or ending a visit/relationship. Often appears with verbs like pasar/vinir: “pasé/vine a decir adiós” = “I just stopped by/came to say goodbye.” You can also use it with “sin” to mean not doing it: “sin (siquiera) decir adiós” = “without (even) saying goodbye.”
target_language_example: Antes de irme, quiero decir adiós a todos.
native_language_example: Before I leave, I want to say goodbye to everyone.

additional_notes: Used when you want to speak up or express a comment. Very common after verbs like necesitar/querer/poder/deber (e.g., “necesito decir algo”). Often implies “make a remark” or “speak” rather than giving lots of details.
target_language_example: Antes de irnos, tengo que decir algo.
native_language_example: Before we leave, I have to say something.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something someone just said or is about to say. Very common in reactions: “No vuelvas a decir eso” = “Don’t say that again,” and “No acabas de decir eso” = “You didn’t just say that.” In “Puedes decir eso de nuevo,” it’s often an enthusiastic response meaning you strongly agree or you like what was said (“You can say that again!”).
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas venido a decir eso.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you came to say that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the specific thing you’re saying, usually followed by a clause (often with a verb): “decir lo que piensas” (say what you think), “decir lo que pasó” (say what happened). It can also appear with emphasis like “déjame decir lo que…” (let me say what…).
target_language_example: Tengo que decir lo que pienso.
native_language_example: I have to say what I think.

meaning: to say nothing / not say anything; (with "con" + noun) to mean anything.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with negation: "no decir nada" = "to say nothing / not say anything" (often to stay quiet or avoid causing trouble). With "con" it means "to mean" or "to imply": "No quise decir nada con eso" = "I didn’t mean anything by that." Often followed by a clause: "no decir nada que..." = "not say anything that...".
target_language_example: Mejor no decir nada y esperar a que se calme.
native_language_example: It’s better not to say anything and wait for him/her to calm down.

meaning: to say that; to state that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or an opinion/fact: "dijo que..." (he/she said that), "he oído decir que..." (I’ve heard it said that). It can also be used in set phrases like "Debo decir que..." (I must say...) and "Está de más decir que..." (Needless to say...).
target_language_example: Tengo que decir que no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I have to say that I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun + "a" to mark who you’re telling: "decirle a Tom" = "tell Tom" (literally, "tell to him, to Tom"). The "le" refers to the person receiving the information (him/her/you-formal), and the "a + name" clarifies who that is. For plural, use "decirles a".
target_language_example: Tengo que decirle a mi profesora la verdad.
native_language_example: I have to tell my teacher the truth.

additional_notes: Used when you’re going to be honest with someone. The "-le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (formal). You can change it: decirte la verdad (tell you), decirles la verdad (tell them/you all), decirme la verdad (tell me). Often used with "tener que" (have to) or "voy a" (I’m going to).
target_language_example: Tengo que decirle la verdad a mi mamá.
native_language_example: I have to tell my mom the truth.

additional_notes: Used when you want to be honest with a specific person. Structure: decir + indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) + la verdad + a + person/name. For example: decirle la verdad a María = “tell María the truth.” You can also say “decir la verdad” without specifying who you’re telling it to.
target_language_example: Tengo que decirle la verdad a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I have to tell my boss the truth.

additional_notes: Uses the verb decir (“to tell/say”) plus an indirect object pronoun me (“to me”) and la verdad (“the truth”). You can change the pronoun depending on who is being told: decirte la verdad (tell you), decirle la verdad (tell him/her/you formal), decirnos la verdad (tell us). Often used with tener que (“to have to”) or poder (“can”) to ask or insist someone be honest.
target_language_example: Tienes que decirme la verdad.
native_language_example: You have to tell me the truth.

meaning: 'to tell you something' (to say something to you).
additional_notes: Uses the informal singular object pronoun te (“to you”). Often introduces news, a confession, or an important point: Debería/Quería/Voy a decirte algo. For a formal or plural “you,” use decirle algo (to you, formal) or decirles algo (to you all).
target_language_example: Tengo que decirte algo importante.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you’re about to say to the listener. It often sounds a bit serious or like “I need/want to tell you something.” You’ll commonly see it with verbs like necesito/quiero/tengo que: “Necesito decirte una cosa…”. (Literally: “to tell you a thing,” but in English it’s usually “something.”)
target_language_example: Oye, necesito decirte una cosa importante.
native_language_example: Hey, I need to tell you something important.

meaning: “I now pronounce you husband and wife.”
additional_notes: Fixed phrase said by an officiant at the end of a wedding ceremony to officially declare two people married. The verb is usually first person present: (Yo) os/les declaro marido y mujer. “Os” is used in Spain for “you (plural)”; “les” is common in Latin America (and also used formally).
target_language_example: Por el poder que me confiere la ley, os declaro marido y mujer.
native_language_example: By the power vested in me by law, I now pronounce you husband and wife.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or what something stated (e.g., a message, a letter). The imperfect tense (decía) often sets background, repeats what someone used to say, or describes an ongoing statement in the past. Person changes: yo decía que, tú decías que, él/ella decía que, etc.
target_language_example: Ella decía que no tenía tiempo para venir.
native_language_example: She said that she didn’t have time to come.

meaning: “they said they want to talk” / “they were saying they want to talk.”
additional_notes: Used to report what other people said (indirect speech). "Decían" is the imperfect past of "decir" (“they said/they were saying”), and it’s often used when you’re relaying information you heard. You can add who they want to talk to with "con" + a person/pronoun (con usted/ustedes/contigo, etc.).
target_language_example: Decían que quieren hablar contigo esta tarde.
native_language_example: They said they want to talk to you this afternoon.

meaning: 'he/she dedicated his/her life to' (spent their life focused on).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s lifelong commitment to a cause, field, or activity. The verb is in the past tense (dedicó). Change the possessive depending on the person: dedicó mi vida a (I dedicated my life to), dedicó tu vida a (you), dedicó su vida a (he/she/you formal). After a can come a noun (a la ciencia, a la paz) or an infinitive verb (a ayudar, a estudiar).
target_language_example: Ella dedicó su vida a cuidar a su familia.
native_language_example: She dedicated her life to taking care of her family.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the toes on your foot. Usually appears with a number or possessive: “los dedos del pie” (the toes), “mis dedos del pie” (my toes), “entre los dedos del pie” (between the toes). You can also say “dedos de los pies” when talking about toes on both feet.
target_language_example: Me duele un dedo del pie.
native_language_example: One of my toes hurts.

additional_notes: Command form (tú) of **dejar de + infinitive**. Used to tell someone to stop an action: *Deja de + verbo* (e.g., *Deja de hablar* = “Stop talking”). You’ll also see it in other forms: *dejo de, dejas de, deja de, dejamos de, dejaron de…* It can be used literally (“stop doing”) or with weather/ongoing situations: *si deja de llover* = “if it stops raining.”
target_language_example: Deja de preocuparte por eso.
native_language_example: Stop worrying about that.

additional_notes: An (often firm) command using the tú form of "dejar de" + infinitive ("to stop doing something"). You can add "ya" to sound more impatient: "Ya deja de hablar" = "Stop talking already." For a more formal version (usted): "Deje de hablar."
target_language_example: Deja de hablar, por favor; estoy en una llamada.
native_language_example: Stop talking, please; I'm on a call.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or to ask someone not to interfere: Deja que + verb (present subjunctive): “Let him/her/them…”. Often implies “don’t stop it; allow it to happen.” With pronouns you’ll often hear: Deja que me/te/le/nos/los/las + verb.
target_language_example: Deja que te ayude con eso.
native_language_example: Let me help you with that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or to offer to do something for the other person: "Deja" (let/allow) + "que" + a verb in the present subjunctive. The "te" is the object pronoun meaning "you" (informal singular). Common with verbs like ayudar (help), llevar (take/carry), enseñar (show/teach), mirar (look at), preguntar (ask), abrazar (hug).
target_language_example: Deja que te ayude con eso.
native_language_example: Let me help you with that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information, a story, an explanation, or a secret. Literally it’s “allow that I tell you,” but in natural English it’s usually “let me tell you.” Common follow-ups: "deja que te cuente un secreto/una historia/lo que pasó".
target_language_example: Deja que te cuente lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: Let me tell you what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Commonly used as a request/instruction when you can’t answer the phone (voicemail) or when someone is trying to contact you. It’s the informal tú command form of "dejar"; the formal version is "deje un mensaje" (usted).
target_language_example: No puedo contestar ahora; deja un mensaje después del tono.
native_language_example: I can’t answer right now; leave a message after the tone.

additional_notes: From the verb pattern "dejar de + infinitive" = “to stop doing something.” Here it’s the past participle phrase used with "haber" (present perfect or past perfect): "He/has dejado de fumar" = “I have stopped smoking,” "Había dejado de fumar" = “I had stopped smoking.”
target_language_example: Mi padre ha dejado de fumar este año.
native_language_example: My dad has quit smoking this year.

meaning: to quit smoking; to stop smoking.
additional_notes: "Dejar de" + infinitive means "to stop (doing something)". So "dejar de fumar" is a common way to say you’re quitting cigarettes. It often appears with advice or goals: "deberías dejar de fumar" (you should quit smoking), "quiero dejar de fumar" (I want to quit).
target_language_example: Quiero dejar de fumar este año.
native_language_example: I want to quit smoking this year.

meaning: “Let me…” / “Allow me to…” (polite, addressing you formally).
additional_notes: Used with the formal command form (usted) of dejar: “Deje…” + “que” + verb. The pronoun “le” refers to the person being addressed (you, formal) and is often used with verbs like explicar, mostrar, llevar: “Deje que le explique…” = “Let me explain (it) to you.” In practice it’s a very polite way to offer help or ask permission to do something for someone.
target_language_example: Deje que le ayude con las maletas.
native_language_example: Let me help you with the bags.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (completed past) form of the common pattern "dejar de + infinitive" = “to stop doing something.” Here, "dejé" = “I stopped,” and "fumar" = “to smoke.” It can mean you quit permanently or that you stopped for a period (often clarified with something like "por un año").
target_language_example: El año pasado dejé de fumar.
native_language_example: Last year I quit smoking.

additional_notes: Used to say you stopped doing something in the past and how long ago it happened. Pattern: **Dejé de + infinitive + hace + time period** (e.g., *hace dos años* = two years ago, *hace seis meses* = six months ago, *hace poco* = not long ago). You can swap *fumar* for another verb: *Dejé de comer carne hace un año* (I stopped eating meat a year ago).
target_language_example: Dejé de fumar hace seis meses.
native_language_example: I quit smoking six months ago.

additional_notes: Past tense of the phrase “dejar de + infinitive” (to stop doing something). Use it to say someone/something stopped an action: “dejó de funcionar” (stopped working), “dejó de sonar” (stopped ringing). For other subjects: “dejé de” (I stopped), “dejaste de” (you stopped), “dejó de” (he/she/it stopped), “dejaron de” (they stopped).
target_language_example: Dejó de llover de repente.
native_language_example: It stopped raining suddenly.

additional_notes: Past tense: dejó (from dejar) + de + infinitive. Use it to say someone stopped doing an activity; with “fumar” it means quitting smoking. You can add a time expression: “Dejó de fumar el año pasado.” (If you’re talking about yourself: “Dejé de fumar.”)
target_language_example: Después de la operación, dejó de fumar.
native_language_example: After the operation, he/she quit smoking.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “dejar” (to leave) in the past tense: “dejó” = “(he/she) left.” Often said when someone forgot to close a door. You may also hear the reflexive version “se dejó la puerta abierta,” which suggests it happened by mistake/accident (“ended up leaving the door open”).
target_language_example: Perdón, dejé la puerta abierta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I left the door open.

additional_notes: Del is the contraction of de + el (“of/from the”). So del accidente literally means “of the accident,” and it’s used to refer to the accident as the cause or topic (e.g., por culpa del accidente = “because of the accident”). You may also see lo del accidente, where lo del means “the thing about / what happened with,” referring to the accident as a topic already known in context.
target_language_example: No puedo ir hoy por culpa del accidente.
native_language_example: I can’t go today because of the accident.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (meaning “of/from the”). It’s used before a masculine singular noun (el). Note: “agua” is feminine, but it uses “el” in the singular (el agua) for pronunciation; it still takes feminine adjectives (el agua fría). “Del agua” can talk about origin/material (sal del agua), a quality (sabor del agua), or movement/source (salir del agua).
target_language_example: Saqué el vaso del agua y lo sequé.
native_language_example: I took the glass out of the water and dried it.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” and is used before a masculine singular noun like “almuerzo” (lunch). It commonly appears in phrases like “antes del almuerzo” (before lunch), “después del almuerzo” (after lunch), “bufé del almuerzo” (lunch buffet), or “restos del almuerzo” (lunch leftovers). In natural English, this is often just translated with “lunch” (e.g., “lunch buffet,” “lunch leftovers”).
target_language_example: Voy a terminar esto antes del almuerzo.
native_language_example: I’m going to finish this before lunch.

additional_notes: Contraction of “de + el” before the masculine singular noun “amor” (“de” never combines with “la”). Used to show possession/association (“the language of love”) or origin (“from love”), and is common in poetic or figurative phrases like “Dios del amor” (God of love) or “la casa del amor” (the house of love).
target_language_example: Hablamos del amor toda la noche.
native_language_example: We talked about love all night.

meaning: “of the car” or “from/out of the car” (de + el auto).
additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el.” With “auto” it can mean possession/relationship (el precio del auto = the car’s price) or movement/source when used with verbs like “bajar/salir” (bajar/salir del auto = get out of the car). Also appears in location phrases: “abajo del auto” (under the car), “abajo del asiento del auto” (under the car seat).
target_language_example: Saca las maletas del auto, por favor.
native_language_example: Please take the suitcases out of the car.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“from/of + the”). Use “del avión” to say you got off the plane (bajar del avión) or to describe something that belongs to or is part of the plane (la cola del avión = the plane’s tail). Sometimes it’s used with “la/el” to mean “the one from the plane” (e.g., “la del avión” = “the plane one,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Cuando bajamos del avión, buscamos nuestras maletas.
native_language_example: When we got off the plane, we looked for our bags.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it in relation to the year (time within the year). Common with time words like día, mes, estación/temporada: el último día del año (the last day of the year), las estaciones del año (the seasons of the year).
target_language_example: Enero es el mes más frío del año aquí.
native_language_example: January is the coldest month of the year here.

meaning: “from the bank” or “of the bank” (the bank’s).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + el** → **del** (used before a masculine singular noun like **banco**). Use it for origin/source (**sacar dinero del banco** = withdraw money from the bank) or to show something belongs to/comes from the bank (**un préstamo del banco** = a loan from the bank).
target_language_example: Voy a sacar dinero del banco esta tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to withdraw money from the bank this afternoon.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + el** → **del**. Used to link something to the forest (possession/association: *el grito del bosque* = “the forest’s cry”) or to indicate origin (*viene del bosque* = “it comes from the forest”).
target_language_example: Escuchamos ruidos extraños del bosque por la noche.
