native_language_example: We heard strange noises from the forest at night.

meaning: “of/from the road/way”; often “out of the way.”
additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el”. With places it often means “from/off” (e.g., “quítate del camino” = move out of the way). You’ll also see it in descriptions like “en la mitad del camino” (in the middle of the road/path) or “a ambos lados del camino” (on both sides of the road/path).
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿me dejas pasar? Estás en medio del camino.
native_language_example: Sorry, can you let me through? You’re in the middle of the way.

additional_notes: Del is the contraction of de + el (“from/of the”). Use del cielo to describe something coming from above (from the sky) or belonging to the sky/heavens: cayó del cielo (“fell from the sky”), un hombre del cielo (“a man from the sky”), la gente del cielo (“people from the heavens/sky,” sometimes poetic or mythical).
target_language_example: Parecía que la luz venía del cielo.
native_language_example: It seemed like the light was coming from the sky.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (never *de el*). Use it to talk about someone/something belonging to a club (e.g., “el presidente del club” = “the club’s president”) or coming/being removed from a club (e.g., “sacar a alguien del club” = “take someone out of the club”).
target_language_example: ¿Eres miembro del club?
native_language_example: Are you a member of the club?

meaning: “of the car” / “from the car” (also like “the car’s”).
additional_notes: Del = de + el (a required contraction), used before a masculine singular noun. Common for possession/parts: las llaves del coche (“the car keys”), el volante del coche (“the car’s steering wheel”), el neumático del coche (“the car’s tire”). With some verbs it can mean “from the car”: Baja del coche (“Get out of the car”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes sacar las bolsas del coche?
native_language_example: Can you take the bags out of the car?

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (so you use it before a masculine singular noun like “colegio”). It can mean origin/movement (“vienen del colegio” = they come from school) or belonging/connection (“una carta del colegio” = a letter from the school; “los chicos del colegio” = the kids at/of the school). In time expressions, “después del colegio” means “after school.”
target_language_example: Salgo del colegio a las tres.
native_language_example: I leave school at three.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“of/from the”). You’ll often see “del crimen” in police/legal contexts: el arma del crimen (the murder weapon), la escena/escenario del crimen (the crime scene), las pruebas del crimen (evidence of the crime). It can also follow adjectives like “culpable del crimen” (guilty of the crime) and “inocente del crimen” (innocent of the crime).
target_language_example: Encontraron huellas en la escena del crimen.
native_language_example: They found fingerprints at the crime scene.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“from the”). “Cuarto” here means “room” (often a bedroom). You’ll commonly see it after verbs of leaving or escaping: “salir del cuarto” (to leave the room), “escapar del cuarto” (to escape from the room).
target_language_example: Salí del cuarto en silencio.
native_language_example: I left the room quietly.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + el" → "del". Used to talk about something that belongs to breakfast (food left over from breakfast) or happens relative to breakfast time (before/after breakfast: "antes/después del desayuno").
target_language_example: Me tomé un café después del desayuno.
native_language_example: I had a coffee after breakfast.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + el". Used to talk about a part of the day or something associated with that day: "la mayor parte del día" (most of the day), "el resto del día" (the rest of the day), "la comida más importante del día" (the most important meal of the day).
target_language_example: Me quedo en casa el resto del día.
native_language_example: I’m staying home for the rest of the day.

meaning: “of the day when” (referring to a specific day on which something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause (“en que…”) that describes what happened on that day. It commonly follows verbs of remembering/forgetting (me acuerdo…, nunca me olvidaré…) or a noun phrase like “la noche del día en que…”. Often interchangeable with “el día cuando…”, but “el día en que…” is more common in standard Spanish.
target_language_example: Siempre hablaré del día en que me mudé a España.
native_language_example: I’ll always talk about the day when I moved to Spain.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (used with masculine singular nouns like “el edificio”). Use it for origin/movement away from a place (salir/correr del edificio = to leave/run out of the building) and for relationships like possession or description (las puertas del edificio = the building’s doors; la parte norte del edificio = the north part of the building).
target_language_example: El ascensor está al final del edificio.
native_language_example: The elevator is at the end of the building.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + el** → **del**. Used to say someone/something belongs to a team (**del equipo**) or comes from that team (**uno del equipo** = “one of the team members”). Often followed by a type of team: **del equipo de fútbol** (“of the soccer team”).
target_language_example: Necesitamos a alguien del equipo para ayudar con el proyecto.
native_language_example: We need someone from the team to help with the project.

meaning: of the government; government (as an adjective).
additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de + el". Use "del gobierno" to say something belongs to, comes from, or is related to the government: "un agente del gobierno" (a government agent), "lo del gobierno" (the stuff/thing about the government). Often you can translate it as "government" before a noun in English.
target_language_example: Necesito un documento del gobierno para el trámite.
native_language_example: I need a government document for the procedure.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“of/from the”). Use it to talk about coming from the hospital (volver/salir/marcharse del hospital) or receiving something from there (noticias del hospital). Common phrase: “dar de alta del hospital” = “to discharge (someone) from the hospital.”
target_language_example: Acabo de salir del hospital.
native_language_example: I just got out of the hospital.

additional_notes: “Del” is a contraction of “de + el” and is used before a masculine singular noun like “hotel.” It often marks possession or association (e.g., “el baño del hotel” = “the hotel’s bathroom”) and is also used in location phrases (e.g., “al oeste del hotel” = “west of the hotel,” “cerca/lejos del hotel” = “near/far from the hotel”).
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en la recepción del hotel.
native_language_example: I left the keys at the hotel reception desk.

meaning: of the lake; from the lake.
additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de + el". With "lago" it often means (1) "of the lake" to describe something related to the lake (e.g., "el agua del lago" = the lake water), or (2) "from the lake" to indicate origin/location (context decides). It can also be used in fixed phrases like "cerca del lago" (near the lake), "vista del lago" (view of the lake), and "del otro lado del lago" (from/on the other side of the lake).
target_language_example: Sacaron un pez del lago.
native_language_example: They took a fish out of the lake.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "el" ("del"). Used with "mar" to indicate origin/source (sacado del mar = taken out of the sea) or description/association (rugido del mar = roar of the sea).
target_language_example: Encontramos conchas del mar en la playa.
native_language_example: We found seashells from the sea on the beach.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to say two or more people/things are connected to the same person/thing: del mismo país (from the same country), del mismo sujeto (in love with the same guy/person). It changes for gender/number: de la misma (fem. sing.), de los mismos (masc. pl.), de las mismas (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Somos del mismo equipo.
native_language_example: We’re on the same team.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + el" → "del" (so it’s always followed by a masculine singular noun, often implied: "el otro" = "the other one/person"). Common in set phrases like "uno al lado del otro" (next to each other). With verbs like "saber" or "hablar", "del otro" can mean "about the other (person)" (e.g., "sabemos del otro" = we know about each other).
target_language_example: No sé mucho del otro candidato.
native_language_example: I don't know much about the other candidate.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de + el". It’s used to link something to the park (possession/association: "el banco del parque" = the park bench) or to show origin: "vengo del parque" = I’m coming from the park.
target_language_example: Salimos del parque a las seis.
native_language_example: We left the park at six.

meaning: from the past; of the past.
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that belongs to earlier times or is no longer relevant. Common in phrases like “cosa del pasado” (a thing of the past) and “hablar del pasado” (to talk about the past). It’s the contraction of “de + el” → “del” before the masculine singular noun “pasado”.
target_language_example: Eso quedó en el pasado; ya no me preocupa.
native_language_example: That stayed in the past; it doesn’t worry me anymore.

meaning: “of the hallway/corridor” or “(on/at) the aisle side.”
additional_notes: “Del” = “de + el” (“of/from the”). “Pasillo” is a hallway/corridor in a building, and also an aisle (e.g., on a plane). Used in location phrases like “al fondo del pasillo” (at the end of the hallway) or to describe seats: “del lado del pasillo” (aisle seat/aisle side).
target_language_example: Mi oficina está al final del pasillo, a la derecha.
native_language_example: My office is at the end of the hallway, on the right.

meaning: “of the country” / “in the country” (sometimes “from the country”).
additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” ("of/from the"). With superlatives or rankings it often means “in the country” (e.g., “una de las mejores escuelas del país” = “one of the best schools in the country”). With verbs of movement/separation (like “exiliar”, “salir”, “expulsar”), it can mean “from the country.”
target_language_example: Es el mejor restaurante del país.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the country.

additional_notes: "Del" = "de + el" (“from the”). Used after verbs like escapar(se), salvar(se) to say someone got away from danger or is no longer in danger. Also used with estar + adjective (e.g., estar informado del peligro) to mean “about the danger.”
target_language_example: Los niños se alejaron del peligro rápidamente.
native_language_example: The kids quickly moved away from danger.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“of/from the”). “Pueblo” can mean (1) a town/village (physical place) or (2) the people/the common people (a community). Context tells you which meaning fits: “en el centro del pueblo” = in the town center; “hijo del pueblo” = from the people / of humble origins.
target_language_example: Compramos pan en la panadería del pueblo.
native_language_example: We bought bread at the town bakery.

meaning: “that I told you about” / “that I spoke to you about” (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to refer back to something already mentioned: “the … that I told you about.” It’s a relative clause with de + el que. It changes with gender/number: del que (m. sg.), de la que (f. sg.), de los que (m. pl.), de las que (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ésta es la película de la que te hablé.
native_language_example: This is the movie I told you about.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“of/from the”). You’ll often see it in place expressions like “cerca del río” (near the river), “en el fondo del río” (at the bottom of the river), and “al lado del río” (next to the river).
target_language_example: Nos sentamos a comer cerca del río.
native_language_example: We sat down to eat near the river.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is from, belongs to, or is characteristic of a particular century. You’ll often see it after a noun (e.g., "una máquina del siglo XX"). The century is written with Roman numerals in Spanish: "siglo XX" = 20th century (years 1901–2000).
target_language_example: Es una novela famosa del siglo XX.
native_language_example: It’s a famous novel from the 20th century.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + el** → **del**. With **protegerse/proteger (a alguien) del sol**, it means “to protect (yourself/someone) from the sun.” With nouns like **la salida del sol** (“sunrise”) or **las quemaduras del sol** (“sunburn”), it often means “of the sun.”
target_language_example: Ponte protector solar para cuidarte del sol.
native_language_example: Put on sunscreen to protect yourself from the sun.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as an adverb meaning "completely/entirely," especially in negative sentences: "no... del todo" = "not completely" / "not entirely." Less commonly, in more literal contexts it can mean "of the whole" (e.g., "parte del todo" = "part of the whole").
target_language_example: No entiendo del todo lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: I don’t completely understand what you said.

additional_notes: Del = de + el. With "orgulloso del trabajo," it means “proud of the job/work” (de = “of/about”). With time expressions like "luego del trabajo," it means “after work” (de = “from/after,” referring to the time when work ends).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres tomar un café después del trabajo?
native_language_example: Do you want to have a coffee after work?

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to the universe. "Del" is a contraction of "de + el" ("of/from the"). You’ll often see it after nouns: "la lengua del universo" (the language of the universe).
target_language_example: La historia del universo es fascinante.
native_language_example: The history of the universe is fascinating.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "de + el". With "árbol" it can mean (1) origin/movement away: "bajó/saltó del árbol" = came down/jumped from the tree; or (2) possession/relationship: "las hojas/ramas del árbol" = the tree's leaves/branches (the leaves/branches of the tree).
target_language_example: El gato no quiere bajar del árbol.
native_language_example: The cat doesn’t want to come down from the tree.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is positioned ahead of you or happens where you can directly see it. Often with verbs like estar (to be), sentarse (to sit), pasar (to pass), and hacer (to do).
target_language_example: No hables de eso delante de mí, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about that in front of me, please.

additional_notes: Used to express suspicion that something that sounds very good is probably not real or not as good as it seems. Often appears after verbs like parecer (to seem) or sonar (to sound): "Parece/Suena demasiado bueno para ser cierto". You can use it alone as a reaction: "Demasiado bueno para ser cierto."
target_language_example: La oferta parece demasiado buena para ser cierta.
native_language_example: The deal seems too good to be true.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to + verb” form): “demasiado cansado para + infinitivo”. It expresses that someone’s tiredness prevents them from doing the action. Agree “cansado” with the person: cansado (male), cansada (female), cansados/cansadas (plural).
target_language_example: Estoy demasiado cansado para salir esta noche.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old enough to do something (often followed by an infinitive: "para + verb"). You can add emphasis with "aún" or "todavía" (“still”): "todavía demasiado joven para...". It can also be used with "para mí" to mean someone is too young for you as a partner.
target_language_example: Soy demasiado joven para conducir.
native_language_example: I’m too young to drive.

additional_notes: Use it for physical distance ("not too far from here") or to say something has gone past an acceptable limit (a joke, a situation, behavior). Often used with verbs like "ir" ("ha ido demasiado lejos") or "llevar" ("llevó la broma demasiado lejos").
target_language_example: Perdón, me pasé; fui demasiado lejos con lo que dije.
native_language_example: Sorry, I went too far with what I said.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something isn’t big/old/strong enough to do something or to be suitable for something. Common patterns: "Es/era demasiado pequeño para + infinitive" (too young/small to do something) and "Es/era demasiado pequeño para + noun" (too small for a person/thing/purpose). You can change the adjective for gender/number: "demasiado pequeña", "demasiados pequeños", etc.
target_language_example: El sofá es demasiado pequeño para cuatro personas.
native_language_example: The sofa is too small for four people.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at an excessive speed. It can describe actions (conducir/manejar, comer, olvidar) or events (Todo pasó demasiado rápido). The form changes for gender/number: demasiado rápido (masc. sing.), demasiado rápida (fem. sing.), demasiado rápidos/rápidas (plural).
target_language_example: Estás hablando demasiado rápido; no te entiendo.
native_language_example: You’re speaking too fast; I don’t understand you.

additional_notes: Used to say an action happens after the right time, so it’s no longer possible or is harder to fix. Often appears with "ya" ("ya es demasiado tarde" = "it’s already too late") and in future warnings ("será demasiado tarde" = "it will be too late"). Also used in the encouraging phrase "nunca es demasiado tarde" ("it’s never too late").
target_language_example: Lo siento, llegamos demasiado tarde para ver el show.
native_language_example: Sorry, we arrived too late to see the show.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): demasiado tarde para + infinitive. It expresses that the time has already passed to do an action (often because someone arrived, woke up, or decided after the right moment).
target_language_example: Salimos demasiado tarde para llegar a tiempo al cine.
native_language_example: We left too late to get to the movie theater on time.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount or duration of time is excessive. Common with verbs like pasar (to spend) and esperar (to wait): “pasar demasiado tiempo (haciendo algo)” = “to spend too much time (doing something)”, “esperar demasiado tiempo” = “to wait too long”. Also appears with “ha pasado demasiado tiempo” = “too much time has passed / it’s been too long.”
target_language_example: No quiero perder demasiado tiempo en esto.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste too much time on this.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being inside a place/limit (“dentro de la casa”, “dentro de unos límites”) and also for time deadlines or time frames (“dentro de cinco días” = within/in five days). Often followed by a noun or time expression.
target_language_example: La reunión empieza dentro de una hora.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in an hour.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time in the future measured from the present moment. You can swap the number/time unit: dentro de una semana (in a week), dentro de tres días (in three days), dentro de un mes (in a month).
target_language_example: Te llamo dentro de dos semanas para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in two weeks to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically inside a place/thing (dentro de la cerradura, dentro de la cabina) or figuratively within a group or category (dentro de la OCDE). It’s “de la” because the noun is feminine singular; with a masculine singular noun it becomes “dentro del” (de + el).
target_language_example: Deja el paraguas dentro de la casa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the umbrella inside the house, please.

additional_notes: Used for something physically inside your body (literal) or for emotions, thoughts, or something personal that you feel "within" yourself (figurative). Often used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "vivir" (to live).
target_language_example: Siento que hay algo dentro de mí que no puedo explicar.
native_language_example: I feel like there is something within me that I can’t explain.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. It often goes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Te veré dentro de poco"), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis. Similar in meaning to "pronto" or "en poco tiempo".
target_language_example: Voy a llamarte dentro de poco.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you soon.

meaning: in a month (one month from now).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen one month later, counted from now or from a reference point in the conversation. Common with future plans and reminders: "Te llamaré dentro de un mes" (I'll call you in a month). With "hasta", it means "not until a month has passed": "No me llames hasta dentro de un mes" (Don’t call me for a month / until a month from now).
target_language_example: La reunión es dentro de un mes.
native_language_example: The meeting is in a month.

meaning: in an hour (one hour from now).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after one hour has passed from the present moment (a future time relative to now). Often used with future tense or near-future expressions: “sale dentro de una hora”, “volveré dentro de una hora”. Contrast: “en una hora” can also mean “in one hour,” but it can sometimes mean “within an hour” (time limit) depending on context.
target_language_example: Te llamo dentro de una hora.
native_language_example: I'll call you in an hour.

meaning: in a week; one week from now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a future time measured from now (about seven days later). Often used for deadlines and plans (e.g., entregarlo, vernos).
target_language_example: Te llamo dentro de una semana para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in a week to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is within an enclosed space or interior of something. It’s the contraction of “dentro de + el” → “dentro del”. With feminine nouns, use “dentro de la” (e.g., dentro de la casa).
target_language_example: Dejé el móvil dentro del bolso.
native_language_example: I left my phone inside the bag.

additional_notes: Used to say that something changes based on a condition or factor. It’s the verb depender (to depend) in the 3rd person (depende = it depends) + de (on). Often followed by a noun (Depende de tu decisión) or a clause introduced by qué/si (Depende de qué tan fuerte sea).
target_language_example: Depende del clima si vamos a la playa.
native_language_example: It depends on the weather whether we go to the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is determined by a particular factor. It’s the verb phrase "depender de" (to depend on) + the feminine singular article "la" (the). Use "depende de" + noun; choose the article that matches the noun: "depende del" (de + el) for masculine, "depende de la" for feminine, and no article with some pronouns/clauses ("depende de ti", "depende de lo que pase").
target_language_example: El resultado depende de la preparación.
native_language_example: The result depends on the preparation.

meaning: "it depends on you" / "it's up to you."
additional_notes: Used to say that the decision or outcome is in the other person’s hands. Often comes after words like ahora (now), todo (everything), or eso (that): "Ahora depende de ti" (Now it’s up to you), "Eso depende de ti" (That depends on you). You can swap ti for another person/pronoun: "depende de mí" (on me), "depende de nosotros" (on us).
target_language_example: ¿Salimos hoy o mañana? Depende de ti.
native_language_example: Are we going out today or tomorrow? It’s up to you.

meaning: "it depends on the" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something changes based on a condition or factor. It’s the 3rd-person singular of depender + de + el (= del). Use "depende de la" with feminine singular nouns (Depende de la hora), and "depende de los/las" for plurals (Depende de los precios / de las reglas). Often followed by a clause: "Depende de si..." or "Depende de lo que...".
target_language_example: Podemos ir mañana, pero depende del clima.
native_language_example: We can go tomorrow, but it depends on the weather.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: tener derecho a + infinitive (“to have the right to do…”). Often appears in phrases like no tienes/no tenéis derecho a… (“you have no right to…”), stressing that something is not allowed or not fair/justified.
target_language_example: Tienes derecho a pedir una explicación.
native_language_example: You have the right to ask for an explanation.

additional_notes: Used to claim that you are entitled to information (often the truth or details about a situation). Common with "Tengo/Tenemos derecho a saber..." followed by what you want to know: "la verdad", "dónde están...", "en dónde estuvo...".
target_language_example: Tengo derecho a saber qué pasó anoche.
native_language_example: I have the right to know what happened last night.

additional_notes: A formal/legal phrase meaning the basic rights and freedoms every person should have. Often used in politics, law, and social-justice contexts. Usually plural: "los derechos humanos".
target_language_example: Todos merecemos respeto y derechos humanos.
native_language_example: We all deserve respect and human rights.

meaning: to rest a little; to take a short break.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or say you need a brief rest (physically or mentally). Very common with verbs like "necesitar" and "deberías": "Necesito/deberías descansar un poco." You can also use it as a group plan: "Vamos a descansar un poco" (Let’s take a short break).
target_language_example: Estoy cansado; voy a descansar un poco.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point of an action, distance, or viewpoint: distance (desde aquí hasta…), perspective (la vista desde aquí), or what you’ll handle/continue doing from your current position (Me encargaré desde aquí). Often pairs with “hasta” to show a range: “desde aquí hasta allí”.
target_language_example: Desde aquí puedo ver toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: From here I can see the whole city.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (el) after desde to mark a starting point in time (desde el día…, desde el año pasado) or a place/direction (desde el teléfono…, desde el sudeste). For feminine nouns, use desde la; for plural, desde los/las. Often pairs with hasta (“from… to…”): desde el lunes hasta el viernes.
target_language_example: Desde el lunes estoy trabajando mucho.
native_language_example: Since Monday I’ve been working a lot.

additional_notes: Used to say that something started last year and has continued up to now. Often used with the present tense in Spanish: "Vivo aquí desde el año pasado" = "I’ve lived here since last year."
target_language_example: Trabajo en esta empresa desde el año pasado.
native_language_example: I’ve worked at this company since last year.

desde el fondo de mi corazón

target_language_multi_word_term: desde el fondo de mi corazón
meaning: “from the bottom of my heart”; very sincerely and deeply.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong, genuine feelings (often gratitude or love, but it can also intensify negative feelings like hate). It commonly goes with verbs like agradecer/decir/querer/odiar. You can change the possessive to match the speaker: desde el fondo de tu/su/nuestro corazón.
target_language_example: Gracias desde el fondo de mi corazón por estar aquí hoy.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for being here today.

additional_notes: Introduces the exact point in time when something started being true. Very common with the past tense: Desde el momento en que + (past event), (result/feeling) empezó en ese instante. Also works with present/future when talking about when something will start: Desde el momento en que llegues, empezamos.
target_language_example: Desde el momento en que lo escuché, supe que era mentira.
native_language_example: From the moment I heard it, I knew it was a lie.

meaning: from the beginning; from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true or happening starting at the very beginning. Also common when restarting something: “Otra vez desde el principio” = “Again from the beginning / Let’s start over.”
target_language_example: Si no entiendes, podemos empezar desde el principio.
native_language_example: If you don’t understand, we can start from the beginning.

meaning: from the point of view (of); from the perspective (of).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or evaluation based on a particular area or criterion (e.g., legal, cultural, health). It’s often followed by “de” + noun: “desde el punto de vista de la salud / legal / cultural”.
target_language_example: Desde el punto de vista del profesor, el examen fue demasiado fácil.
native_language_example: From the teacher’s point of view, the exam was too easy.

meaning: since this morning (from this morning until now).
additional_notes: Used with actions or situations that started this morning and are still continuing or relevant now. It often appears with the present perfect (he/ha estado + gerundio) or with "llevar" to emphasize duration ("Llevo desde esta mañana...").
target_language_example: Estoy cansado porque trabajo desde esta mañana.
native_language_example: I’m tired because I’ve been working since this morning.

meaning: for years; for many years (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say something started years ago and has continued until the present (or up to the time being talked about). Often goes with the present tense (La conozco desde hace años) or present perfect (No la he visto desde hace años). Similar idea: "since years ago."
target_language_example: No hablamos desde hace años.
native_language_example: We haven’t talked for years.

meaning: for a long time; for a long time now.
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past and has continued up to now, or that a long time has passed since something happened. Often appears with present perfect (he + participle) or the present tense in Spanish (which can translate as “have been …” in English).
target_language_example: No te veo desde hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in a long time.

meaning: for three years; since three years ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an action/state that started in the past and continues up to now. Common with the present tense (e.g., "Vivo...") or with the present perfect/progressive ("He estado...", "He vivido..."). Structure: "desde hace + time period" (desde hace un mes / dos semanas / cinco años).
target_language_example: Trabajo aquí desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for three years.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns after **desde**. It can mark a starting point in place (**desde la azotea** = from the rooftop) or time (**desde la infancia** = since childhood). It can also introduce a relative clause with **la que** (**desde la que...** = from which...).
target_language_example: Desde la estación, puedes ver el centro de la ciudad.
native_language_example: From the station, you can see the city center.

meaning: from the window; out of the window.
additional_notes: Used to say where you are seeing something from (your viewpoint) or where something is thrown from. With verbs like ver (“to see”), it means you’re looking from inside/by the window: Lo vi desde la ventana. With verbs like arrojar/tirar (“to throw”), it can mean “out of the window.” You can also specify which window: desde la ventana de mi habitación (“from my bedroom window”).
target_language_example: Se oían los pájaros desde la ventana.
native_language_example: You could hear the birds from the window.

additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point in time from which something has been true or has changed. Often follows phrases like "Ha pasado mucho tiempo..." (A lot of time has passed...) or statements about change: "cambió mucho...". The verb after "que" is typically in the past (e.g., "te escribí", "lo vi").
target_language_example: He aprendido mucho español desde la última vez que hablamos.
native_language_example: I’ve learned a lot of Spanish since the last time we talked.

meaning: 'from my point of view' / 'in my opinion'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal perspective or opinion (often at the start of a sentence). You can also use it after a statement: "..., desde mi punto de vista." With "mirar/verte" it means "see it from my point of view" (try to understand my perspective). You can swap the possessive: "desde tu/su/nuestro punto de vista".
target_language_example: Desde mi punto de vista, deberíamos salir más temprano.
native_language_example: From my point of view, we should leave earlier.

meaning: “since I/he/she was…” (from the time when someone was…).
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past at a certain life stage/age and continued afterward. It’s often followed by a noun phrase like un niño/una niña/un bebé/muy joven. You can change the verb for person/number: desde que era (I/he/she was), desde que éramos (we were), desde que eran (they were).
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde que era adolescente.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here since I was a teenager.

meaning: since I was a child (ever since childhood).
additional_notes: "Desde que" marks the starting point of an action or situation that has continued up to the present (or up to another point in the past). The verb after "desde que" is commonly in the imperfect (era) to describe an ongoing past time. You can change the person/gender: "desde que era una niña", "desde que éramos niños", etc.
target_language_example: He vivido aquí desde que era un niño.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here since I was a child.

additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point of a period of time: from the moment “you left” up to now (or up to another reference point). It often introduces a clause with a verb ("desde que + [verb]") and can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: No he dormido bien desde que te fuiste.
native_language_example: I haven’t slept well since you left.

meaning: since we were children (ever since we were kids).
additional_notes: Used to say something started in the past (when you were kids) and has continued up to now. Often follows a main clause: “Nos conocemos desde que éramos niños” (We’ve known each other since we were children).
target_language_example: Somos amigos desde que éramos niños.
native_language_example: We’ve been friends since we were kids.

meaning: “always” / “for as long as I can remember.”
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time, basically all your life or since the earliest time you can remember. Often used with verbs like conocer (to know), querer (to love/like), or vivir (to live): “Lo conozco desde siempre” = “I’ve known him forever.”
target_language_example: He vivido en este barrio desde siempre.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this neighborhood for as long as I can remember.

meaning: from a (certain) point of view; from the perspective of.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the perspective/angle you’re considering (e.g., practical, educational, political). Often followed by an adjective or noun: “desde un punto de vista práctico/educativo/político”. It can appear at the start of a sentence as a framing phrase.
target_language_example: Desde un punto de vista económico, esta decisión tiene sentido.
native_language_example: From an economic point of view, this decision makes sense.

meaning: “I wish I could…” / “I would like to be able to…”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense of "desear" (desearía) to express a wish or regret about something you can’t do (often because it’s not possible right now). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "Desearía poder + infinitive" (e.g., desearía poder ir, ayudar, quedarme).
target_language_example: Desearía poder ayudarte, pero no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I wish I could help you, but I don’t have time today.

meaning: "I wish that..." / "I would like it if..."
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about a situation, often something unreal, unlikely, or not true right now. It’s the conditional of "desear" + "que", and it typically triggers the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "desearía que vinieras", "desearía que hubiera"). You can also use it politely to express what you’d like someone to do.
target_language_example: Desearía que pudiéramos hablar en privado.
native_language_example: I wish we could talk in private.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down, especially when speaking. Often said alone ("Despacio, por favor.") or with a verb like "Habla" (you, informal), "Hable" (you, formal), "Hablad" (you all, informal Spain), or "Hablen" (you all, formal/Latin America). You can add "más" or "un poco más" for "more" / "a bit more": "Habla un poco más despacio, por favor."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes repetirlo más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "despertar" (to wake up) with a direct object ("al bebé" = "the baby"). Often appears with phrases like "por temor a" (for fear of), "para evitar" (to avoid), or "va a" (is going to), especially when talking about noise or being quiet so the baby stays asleep.
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta despacio para no despertar al bebé.
native_language_example: Close the door softly so you don't wake the baby up.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" or "quedarse" to say someone doesn’t sleep during the night (often: "quedarse despierta toda la noche" = "to stay awake all night"). "Despierta" agrees with a female subject; for a male subject use "despierto toda la noche". You can also use "despierto/a" after "estar" ("estuve despierta toda la noche").
target_language_example: Me quedé despierto toda la noche estudiando.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying.

additional_notes: Used to talk about staying awake late into the night. Often appears with the verb “quedarse” (to stay/remain): “quedarse despierto hasta tarde” = “to stay up late.” You can adjust for gender/number: despierto (m.), despierta (f.), despiertos/despiertas (plural).
target_language_example: Los fines de semana me quedo despierto hasta tarde.
native_language_example: On weekends I stay up late.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does not sleep during the whole night. Often appears with the verb phrase “quedarse” (to stay): “quedarse despierto toda la noche” = to stay awake all night. “Despierto” changes for gender/number: despierta, despiertos, despiertas.
target_language_example: Me quedé despierto toda la noche estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to give a routine instruction that should be done every time you eat (common in health advice and medication directions). "Después de" = "after" + "cada" = "each" + "comida" = "meal/food."
target_language_example: Recuerda lavarte las manos después de cada comida.
native_language_example: Remember to wash your hands after each meal.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the action of having dinner. It’s a time expression: después de + infinitive (después de comer, después de estudiar, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos a dar un paseo después de cenar.
native_language_example: We’re going to go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once the school day or a class period is finished. Common in school-related plans and routines: "después de clases, voy a…" (after class, I’m going to…). You can also hear "después de la clase" (after the class) for one specific class.
target_language_example: Nos vemos después de clases para estudiar.
native_language_example: See you after class to study.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than eating. It can be followed by nothing (after eating/after the meal) or by an object: «después de comer mi comida» (after eating my food). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence, with a comma when it starts the sentence.
target_language_example: Después de comer, vamos a dar un paseo.
native_language_example: After eating, we're going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens once 10 minutes have passed from a starting point (often from the beginning of an action or situation). You can replace the number/time: después de cinco minutos (after five minutes), después de una hora (after an hour).
target_language_example: Después de diez minutos, empezó a llover.
native_language_example: After ten minutes, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens next in time, referring back to an action or event already mentioned. It’s common in storytelling and giving instructions: Primero..., y después de eso.... Also often shortened to "después" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Terminamos de comer y después de eso fuimos al cine.
native_language_example: We finished eating and after that we went to the movies.

additional_notes: Used to say one action happened after a completed earlier action. It’s followed by a past participle: después de haber + participio (haber encontrado, haber leído, haber terminado). In everyday speech you can often also say: después de + infinitivo (Después de leer la carta...).
target_language_example: Después de haber cenado, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: After having dinner, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say that one event happens later in time than another. It’s the feminine form of “después de” + the article “la”; use it before a singular feminine noun (e.g., “después de la clase”). Before a masculine noun, use “después del” (de + el).
target_language_example: Después de la cena, vamos a dar un paseo.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the meal (cena = dinner). Often placed at the start or end of the sentence: “Después de la cena, …” / “… después de la cena.”
target_language_example: Después de la cena, hago la tarea.
native_language_example: After dinner, I do my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens following the end of the school day. It can be followed by a verb phrase (e.g., "después de la escuela + jugamos/estudio/trabajo").
target_language_example: Después de la escuela, hago mi tarea y luego salgo con mis amigos.
native_language_example: After school, I do my homework and then hang out with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once it has rained. It commonly introduces a time clause at the beginning of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also appear later in the sentence. You can swap in other events: después de la clase (after class), después de cenar (after dinner).
target_language_example: Después de la lluvia, salimos a caminar.
native_language_example: After the rain, we went out for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once a person has died (often in discussions about the afterlife: "la vida después de la muerte" = "life after death"). It can describe a time period (“after death”) or beliefs (“after death there is nothing”).
target_language_example: Muchas religiones hablan de lo que pasa después de la muerte.
native_language_example: Many religions talk about what happens after death.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens later than an event or time period that belongs to someone/something. It’s "después de" + the possessive adjective "su" (his/her/its/your formal). With plural possessions use "después de sus" (after his/her/their...).
target_language_example: Después de su cena, se fue a casa.
native_language_example: After his/her dinner, he/she went home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing events, words, or actions that happened before, often implying contrast, surprise, or a complaint (like “considering everything that…”). It’s commonly followed by a verb: “después de todo lo que + ha pasado / habíamos dicho / he hecho…”.
target_language_example: Después de todo lo que hiciste por mí, no puedo decir que no.
native_language_example: After everything you did for me, I can’t say no.

additional_notes: Used to say that one event happens later than another: después de + noun. Here, "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article; with feminine nouns use "después de una" (e.g., después de una pausa). With plural nouns: "después de unos/unas". Often followed by an event or period of time (e.g., un descanso, un golpe).
target_language_example: Después de un buen desayuno, salimos de casa.
native_language_example: After a good breakfast, we left the house.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time period: "después de una lluvia" (after a rain), "después de una década" (after a decade). It must be followed by a feminine singular noun; with a masculine singular noun you usually say "después de un". With "el" it becomes "después del" (after the).
target_language_example: Después de una reunión larga, me fui a casa.
native_language_example: After a long meeting, I went home.

meaning: “after a long …” (often followed by a noun like wait/absence).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens following a long period of time. It’s typically completed with a feminine noun because of “una” (e.g., una espera = a wait, una ausencia = an absence). Common pattern: “Después de una larga + [noun], …” or “… después de una larga + [noun].”
target_language_example: Después de una larga espera, por fin nos atendieron.
native_language_example: After a long wait, they finally helped us.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than an event or time. It’s the contraction of “después de + el” (de + el = del). With feminine nouns, use “después de la” (no contraction): “después de la clase”. With plural nouns: “después de los / de las”.
target_language_example: Después del almuerzo, voy a llamar a mi mamá.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to call my mom.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens later than (and usually as a consequence of) a specific accident. Often followed by a result or change: "Después del accidente, ..." or used with a time expression: "tres horas después del accidente".
target_language_example: Después del accidente, tuvo que ir al hospital.
native_language_example: After the accident, he had to go to the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunchtime. Often followed by an action or a time (e.g., “después del almuerzo, …”). In Spanish, “después de” becomes “después del” before a masculine singular noun like “almuerzo” (de + el = del).
target_language_example: Nos vemos después del almuerzo.
native_language_example: See you after lunch.

meaning: after work; after getting off work.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you do once your workday ends. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence or set off with commas, and can be emphasized with words like "inmediatamente" (immediately) or "directo" (straight).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, vamos a cenar.
native_language_example: After work, we're going to have dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically located behind something else (place/position), or figuratively hidden “behind” an appearance or explanation (e.g., detrás de la fachada = behind the facade). Use it before a feminine singular noun: detrás de la puerta, detrás de la cómoda. With a masculine noun, use detrás del (de + el).
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la silla.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the chair.

additional_notes: A location phrase using detrás de (“behind”) + la cortina (“the curtain”). Used literally for something physically hidden or positioned behind a curtain; it can also suggest something happening secretly/out of sight (like “the men behind the curtain”). You can also say de detrás de la cortina (“from behind the curtain”).
target_language_example: El gato está detrás de la cortina.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the curtain.

additional_notes: Used to say something (the sun, moon, etc.) is hidden/covered by clouds and not visible. Often appears with verbs like "desaparecer" (to disappear) and "ser" (to be): "desapareció detrás de las nubes", "está/es invisible detrás de las nubes". You can also say "desde detrás de las nubes" = "from behind the clouds".
target_language_example: El sol salió de detrás de las nubes.
native_language_example: The sun came out from behind the clouds.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something/someone is located or moves behind the speaker. Often with verbs like estar (to be), ponerse (to stand/get), ir/venir (to go/come): "Está detrás de mí" = "He/She is behind me."
target_language_example: No te pongas detrás de mí; no puedo verte.
native_language_example: Don’t stand behind me; I can’t see you.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position/movement at your back (often as a warning: “Behind you!”). It can also mean “following you” (walking/driving after you): “Iremos detrás de ti.” In some contexts, “estar detrás de alguien” can imply support or pursuit (“backing you” / “after you”), but the basic meaning is physical location. Also note: “ti” is used after prepositions (de, a, para, etc.).
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado, hay un perro detrás de ti!
native_language_example: Careful, there's a dog behind you!

meaning: behind him; (also) after him / pursuing him.
additional_notes: Most literally it means physical position (“behind him”). In some contexts, especially with verbs like andar/ir/estar detrás de, it can mean someone is “after him” (chasing, following, or trying to get him). In phrases like “cerró la puerta detrás de él,” it describes an action done as he passes (he closed the door behind him).
target_language_example: Había alguien detrás de él, pero no se dio la vuelta.
native_language_example: There was someone behind him, but he didn’t turn around.

additional_notes: "Detrás de" means "behind" in a physical sense. "Del" is the contraction of "de + el" (used with masculine singular nouns: detrás del sofá, detrás del arbusto). It can also mean "after" in the sense of pursuing or looking for someone/something: La policía va/anda detrás del asesino = The police are after the killer.
target_language_example: El gato está escondido detrás del coche.
native_language_example: The cat is hiding behind the car.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the phrase "darse cuenta" (to realize/notice), most often with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/se/nos/os di(o) cuenta". It commonly takes "de" + noun ("me di cuenta de eso") or "de que" + clause ("me di cuenta de que..."), and can be emphasized with "ya" ("Ya me di cuenta" = "I already realized").
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten the keys.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (past) form of the reflexive verb phrase **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/notice”). It’s commonly followed by **de** + a noun (**Me di cuenta de su ausencia**) or **de** + a clause (**Me di cuenta de que la amaba**). In negative, **No me di cuenta de...** means “I didn’t realize/notice...”.
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que olvidé las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized I forgot the keys.

meaning: "I assumed" / "I took it for granted that".
additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular preterite of the expression "dar por sentado que" (literally "to give for seated," but meaning to assume something is true without checking). You can change the verb to match the subject and tense: "doy por sentado que..." (I assume), "dio por sentado que..." (he/she assumed), "dimos por sentado que..." (we assumed). It’s commonly followed by a clause with "que".
target_language_example: Di por sentado que la reunión era a las seis.
native_language_example: I assumed the meeting was at six.

meaning: “the doctor says that…” / “the doctor tells me to…”
additional_notes: Used to report a doctor’s advice or instructions. It’s often followed by the present subjunctive (camine, coma, deje, etc.) because it expresses what the doctor recommends or tells someone to do.
target_language_example: Dice el médico que descanse más y que beba agua.
native_language_example: The doctor says I should rest more and drink water.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or claims. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., “Mamá dice que…”, “Tom dice que…”), and it’s followed by a full clause (usually with a verb): “dice que + [sentence]”.
target_language_example: Mi hermano dice que mañana no trabaja.
native_language_example: My brother says that he isn’t working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says about a woman/girl. "Dice" is the 3rd-person singular of *decir* (he/she/you-formal says). "Que" introduces the reported clause. "Ella" (she) is often optional in Spanish unless you want emphasis or clarity: *Dice que sabe dónde están* is more common than *Dice que ella sabe…*. Related: *Se dice que ella…* = “It’s said that she…” (impersonal/rumor).
target_language_example: Dice que ella no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: He/She says that she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or says. The subject of dice is often implied (él/ella/usted). What follows after que is a statement with es (“is”). You can change the verb to match the person/tense: digo que es (I say it’s), dicen que es (they say it’s), dijo que era (he said it was).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dice que es urgente.
native_language_example: My boss says it’s urgent.

meaning: "(he/she) says no" or "(he/she) says that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with a subject understood from context (often él/ella/usted). "Decir que no" can mean refusing (saying no) or denying something (saying it didn’t happen): e.g., "Dice que no" = "He/She says no"; "Dice que no lo hizo" = "He/She says he didn’t do it."
target_language_example: Le ofrecí ayuda, pero dice que no.
native_language_example: I offered him/her help, but he/she says no.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want. The subject is usually implied from context (él/ella/usted), and the verb that follows is in the present tense: "dice que quiere + infinitive" (e.g., quiere ser/ir/hacer). Note that Spanish "dice" means "says" (it’s not related to English "dice").
target_language_example: María dice que quiere viajar a México este verano.
native_language_example: María says she wants to travel to Mexico this summer.

meaning: "(He/She) says that…" (introduces what someone claims; the clause uses "se").
additional_notes: Used to report what someone says. After "dice que", the "se" belongs to the following verb and can be: (1) reflexive ("se iba" = he left, "se recuperará" = he’ll recover), or (2) impersonal/passive "se" ("se venden" = they are sold). In speech you often add a subject: "Él/Ella dice que…"
target_language_example: Ella dice que se siente mejor hoy.
native_language_example: She says that she feels better today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or says about a male person. In Spanish, the subject pronoun (él) is often optional, so you’ll also commonly hear "dice que…" (e.g., "Dice que quiere hablar con usted"). Using "él" adds emphasis or clarity about who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Mi hermano dice que él no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: My brother says that he doesn’t have time today.

meaning: “they say that…” / “it’s said that…” (reporting what people say or believe).
additional_notes: Used to introduce hearsay, rumors, or general opinion without saying exactly who said it. It’s the present tense of "decir" (to say) in 3rd person plural: "(ellos) dicen" + "que". Similar meaning to "se dice que…". Often implies the speaker is not fully confirming the information.
target_language_example: Dicen que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "they say that the..." / "people say that the..."
additional_notes: Used to report rumors, common beliefs, or what people say in general. The verb is 3rd person plural (dicen = “they say”) with an unspecified subject (“people”). Often followed by a noun with el (masculine singular): "Dicen que el + noun + ...". For feminine nouns, you’ll hear: "Dicen que la..."; for plural: "Dicen que los/las...".
target_language_example: Dicen que el café ayuda a concentrarse.
native_language_example: They say that coffee helps you concentrate.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people say or what’s commonly believed, without saying who exactly (“they/people”). Very common for rumors, reputation, or general opinions. Usually followed by a description with "ser" (e.g., "Dicen que es honesto").
target_language_example: Dicen que es muy bueno, pero no lo conozco.
native_language_example: They say he’s very good, but I don’t know him.

meaning: “They say that the…” (hearsay/rumor about something feminine).
additional_notes: Used to report what people say in general, without naming who (“they say…”). After this, Spanish often uses the subjunctive if what follows is uncertain or unconfirmed (e.g., “Dicen que la casa esté embrujada”), but the indicative is also common, especially when the speaker treats it like a fact (“Dicen que la casa está embrujada”). “La” is the feminine singular “the,” so it’s followed by a feminine noun (la casa, la Coca-Cola, etc.).
target_language_example: Dicen que la comida de aquí es muy buena.
native_language_example: They say the food here is very good.

additional_notes: Past participle of decir used with haber (e.g., he/has/had) or with modals/conditionals: debiste haber dicho la verdad (you should have told the truth), si me hubieras dicho la verdad (if you had told me the truth). More generally, the base phrase is decir la verdad = “to tell the truth.”
target_language_example: Deberías haber dicho la verdad desde el principio.
native_language_example: You should have told the truth from the beginning.

meaning: 'told/said that' (as part of a past tense with haber).
additional_notes: Used after a form of **haber** to make compound past tenses of **decir**: **he/has/ha/hemos/han dicho que...** (have/has said that) and **había/habías... dicho que...** (had said that). Often implies you communicated information to someone: **Te he dicho que...** = “I told you that...”.
target_language_example: Te había dicho que hoy no podía.
native_language_example: I had told you that I couldn’t today.

additional_notes: Past participle of *decir* used in perfect tenses (*he/has/había dicho...*) to report that someone refused or didn’t allow something. Often appears as *decirle a alguien que no* (to tell someone no): *Te he dicho que no* = “I’ve told you no / I said no.”
target_language_example: Ya le he dicho que no puedo ir.
native_language_example: I’ve already told him/her that I can’t go.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary haber (he/has/ha/hemos, etc.) to form the present perfect: "he dicho" = "I have said/told." You can add more information after it (e.g., "de Alemania" = "about Germany"). Common with "ya" to emphasize that you’ve already shared all you know.
target_language_example: Lo siento, ya te he dicho todo lo que sé sobre el tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’ve already told you everything I know about the topic.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (diciendo) to describe an action in progress, often with estar: está/estaba diciendo la verdad = 'is/was telling the truth.' You can also use it after modal/auxiliary verbs like podría estar: podría estar diciendo la verdad = 'might be telling the truth.'
target_language_example: No te enojes: te lo estoy diciendo la verdad.
native_language_example: Don’t get mad: I’m telling you the truth.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age. With the verb "tener" it means "to be 18": "Tengo dieciocho años" (I’m 18). In comparisons, you’ll often see it with "desde que" (since) or "no… más de" (not more than / no older than).
target_language_example: Cumplo dieciocho años este mes.
native_language_example: I turn eighteen this month.

additional_notes: Used either for age (often with "tener": "Tengo dieciséis años" = "I’m sixteen") or for a period of time ("dieciséis años después" = "sixteen years later"). With ages, it commonly appears as "a los dieciséis años" meaning "at (the age of) sixteen".
target_language_example: A los dieciséis años me mudé a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: At sixteen, I moved to another city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time (duration) or someone’s age. Often appears with time expressions like "hace diez años" (ten years ago), "a los diez años" (at age ten), "tardó diez años en..." (it took [someone] ten years to...), or "pasó diez años..." (spent ten years...).
target_language_example: Viví en México diez años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to state a price, a payment amount, wages, or money owed. With amounts of money, Spanish often uses the verb + amount directly: “cuesta diez dólares” (it costs ten dollars), “me debe diez dólares” (he owes me ten dollars), “son diez dólares” (it’s ten dollars). In many contexts you’ll also hear “por diez dólares” (for ten dollars) and “a diez dólares al día” (at ten dollars a day).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes cambiar un billete de diez dólares?
native_language_example: Can you break a ten-dollar bill for me?

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (e.g., a delay) or frequency (e.g., something happens every ten minutes). You can use it with time expressions like “en diez minutos” (in ten minutes) and “cada diez minutos” (every ten minutes).
target_language_example: Vuelvo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) things and point out how they are not the same. It’s often used with verbs like "hay" (there is/are) and adjectives like "gran" or "clara": "Hay una gran/clara diferencia entre A y B". You can also use it in definitions or explanations: "Es la diferencia entre A y B".
target_language_example: Hay una gran diferencia entre estudiar un poco y estudiar todos los días.
native_language_example: There’s a big difference between studying a little and studying every day.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say an action is hard: "difícil de + infinitive" (difícil de aprender/creer/prever/leer). It agrees in gender and number with what it describes: "difícil" (masc. sing.), "difíciles" (plural), "difícil" (fem. sing. too), e.g., "preguntas difíciles de responder".
target_language_example: Es difícil de entender cuando hablan tan rápido.
native_language_example: It's hard to understand when they speak so fast.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation or decision is hard for a particular person/group. Usually appears with **ser**: *Es/Debe de ser difícil para + pronoun/name* (e.g., *difícil para mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros/ustedes*), or *una decisión difícil para + alguien*.
target_language_example: Sé que es difícil para ti, pero vamos a encontrar una solución.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard for you, but we’re going to find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for you personally. It often follows a form of ser (“es/era/fue”) and can be followed by an infinitive: “Es difícil para mí + infinitive” (e.g., entender, hablar). You can swap “mí” for another person: “difícil para ti/para él/para nosotros.” Note: “mí” (with an accent) is the object pronoun after “para”; “mi” (no accent) means “my.”
target_language_example: Es difícil para mí levantarme temprano los lunes.
native_language_example: It’s difficult for me to get up early on Mondays.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for the person you’re speaking to. Common with verbs like ser/estar: “(Debe) ser difícil para ti” = “(It must) be difficult for you.” You can also add intensity: “demasiado difícil para ti” (too difficult for you).
target_language_example: Entiendo que es difícil para ti hablar de eso.
native_language_example: I understand that it's difficult for you to talk about that.

meaning: "let’s say" / "let’s suppose" (used to introduce an explanation or an approximate/softened statement).
additional_notes: Used to frame what you’re about to say as a way of explaining, giving an example, or speaking approximately rather than 100% precisely. Often softens the statement (like “so to speak” or “kind of”). Common in speech: “Digamos que…” + clause.
target_language_example: Digamos que hoy no tengo muchas ganas de salir.
native_language_example: Let’s say I don’t really feel like going out today.

meaning: "(you) say anything"; usually in "No digas nada" = "Don’t say anything."
additional_notes: Used most often with "no" as a negative command to tell someone to stay quiet or not reveal information: "No digas nada" (Don’t say anything), "No les digas nada" (Don’t tell them anything). "Nada más" means "anything else" in this context: "No digas nada más" (Don’t say anything else).
target_language_example: Por favor, no digas nada hasta que lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Please, don’t say anything until we get home.

meaning: “I’m telling the truth.” / “I tell the truth.”
additional_notes: Often used to insist you’re not lying: “Digo la verdad.” With “si te digo la verdad,” it commonly means “to be honest / truthfully” and introduces a frank opinion or confession.
target_language_example: Te prometo que digo la verdad.
native_language_example: I promise I’m telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you’re stating or expressing an opinion about. It can also be used with an indirect object to mean “I tell (someone) that...”, e.g., "Le digo que..." (I tell him/her that...) or "Me digo que..." (I tell myself that...).
target_language_example: Sólo digo que no es tan fácil.
native_language_example: I’m just saying it’s not that easy.

meaning: "I told" / "I said to" (past tense, used with a person).
additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of decir: dije = “I said/I told.” With people, Spanish often uses the personal a: dije a Tom = “I told Tom.” Very commonly it appears with indirect-object pronouns: le dije a Tom (“I told Tom”), se lo dije a Tom (“I told it to Tom”), se lo dije a ella (“I told it to her”).
target_language_example: Le dije a mi hermana que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: I told my sister that I would arrive late.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of decir (“to say”) + que (“that”), used to introduce reported speech: what you said in the past. What comes after que can vary (e.g., estaba, volvería, fuéramos) depending on the time frame or mood you need.
target_language_example: Dije que no podía ir hoy.
native_language_example: I said that I couldn’t go today.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of decir: dije = “I said/told.” Used to report what you stated earlier. Usually followed by an identity/description (ateo, enfermera, suplente) or an evaluation (posible). Often continues with a verb in the imperfect: “Dije que era…” = “I said that it was/that I was…”.
target_language_example: Dije que era estudiante, pero en realidad ya había terminado la carrera.
native_language_example: I said I was a student, but actually I had already finished my degree.

meaning: 'I said that I would (do) it' / 'I told you that (about) it.'
additional_notes: "Dije" is the simple past of "decir" (to say/tell). "que" introduces what you said (“that…”). "lo" is an object pronoun meaning “it” or “that,” referring to something already known from context (e.g., conseguirlo = get it, pensarlo = think about it, dejarlo = leave/quit it). Often used to remind someone of what you previously said: "Dije que lo haría" = “I said I would do it.”
target_language_example: Dije que lo iba a hacer, pero no tuve tiempo.
native_language_example: I said I was going to do it, but I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Past tense of "decir" (to say/tell) + "que no". Often used to remind someone you already refused or set a boundary. It can stand alone (Dije que no.) or introduce a clause: "Dije que no pagamos nada" = "I said we aren’t paying anything."
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero dije que no voy a ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I said I'm not going to go.

additional_notes: Often used to insist you’ve already shared all the information you have. "Dije" is the past tense of "decir" (I said/told). You’ll frequently add an indirect object pronoun: "Les dije…" (I told them), "Te dije…" (I told you). "Ya" means “already,” emphasizing it’s been said before: "Ya dije todo lo que sé."
target_language_example: Ya te dije todo lo que sé; no tengo más detalles.
native_language_example: I already told you everything I know; I don’t have any more details.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of decir (dijeron) to report what “they” said at a specific moment in the past. It’s often followed by a statement (que + clause) or by “sí/no” as a short answer: “Dijeron que sí/no.”
target_language_example: Dijeron que no tenían tiempo.
native_language_example: They said that they didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (past) of decir: dijiste = "you said" (informal singular tú). "Que" introduces what the person said. Common for reminding someone of their words, asking for clarification, or pointing out a contradiction.
target_language_example: Dijiste que ibas a llamarme hoy.
native_language_example: You said that you were going to call me today.

additional_notes: Used to report or remind someone of what they previously said about something. Common in conversations to correct, confirm, or challenge earlier information. Often appears with an object pronoun too: “me dijiste que era…” = “you told me it was…”.
target_language_example: Pensé que dijiste que era hoy.
native_language_example: I thought you said it was today.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a past statement. "Dijiste" is the simple past of "decir" (you said), and "querías" is the imperfect of "querer" (you wanted/you used to want). Often followed by an infinitive (querías hablar/irte/hacer) or by another clause with "que" (querías que + subjunctive).
target_language_example: Dijiste que querías cambiar de trabajo, ¿todavía lo estás pensando?
native_language_example: You said you wanted to change jobs—are you still thinking about it?

additional_notes: “Dijo” is the preterite (simple past) of **decir** (“to say/tell”). It’s often followed by **a + person** to show *who* was told: **Le dijo a su madre...** = “He/She told his/her mother...”. Very commonly you’ll also see object pronouns with it: **se lo dijo a María** (“he/she told it to María”), where **lo** = “it” and **se** replaces **le** before **lo/la/los/las**.
target_language_example: Se lo dijo a Ana ayer.
native_language_example: He/She told it to Ana yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. It’s the past tense of “decir” (él/ella dijo) + “que” (“that”) to introduce the reported information. You can add an indirect object pronoun when needed: “le dijo que …” = “(he/she) told him/her that …”. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb).
target_language_example: María dijo que llegaría tarde.
native_language_example: María said that she would arrive late.

additional_notes: Past tense of "decir" ("dijo" = "he/she said"). Used to report what someone said: "X dijo que era…". After "que", Spanish typically uses the imperfect "era" to describe what something/someone was (reported speech). The subject of "era" is understood from context (it can refer to he, she, you, or it).
target_language_example: María dijo que era su hermano.
native_language_example: María said it was her brother.

additional_notes: Common narration/reporting phrase: past tense of "decir" (dijo = said) + "que" (that) + "era" (was, imperfect of "ser") + "un" (a/an, masculine). Often followed by a noun (un policía, un asunto, un diamante). For feminine nouns, use "una": "dijo que era una idea".
target_language_example: Ella dijo que era un buen plan.
native_language_example: She said it was a good plan.

meaning: 'he/she said (that) he/she was…' (reported speech in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a past state or condition. You can add a noun/adjective after "estaba" (bien, triste, ocupado, cansada, etc.). The verb form changes with the speaker: "me dijo" (told me), "le dijo" (told him/her), "dijeron" (they said). In English you may or may not include "that."
target_language_example: Mi hermano dijo que estaba enfermo ayer.
native_language_example: My brother said he was sick yesterday.

additional_notes:
Used in reported speech to introduce what someone said about how they were feeling or what condition they were in. 
- dijo = “(he/she) said” (pretérito/past)
- que = “that”
- estaba = “was” (temporary state, from estar)
- muy = “very”
You normally add an adjective after muy (e.g., ocupado/a, aburrido/a, emocionado/a, satisfecho/a). The subject (“he/she”) is often understood from context and not stated.
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que estaba muy cansado.
native_language_example: My boss said that he was very tired.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said ("dijo que" = “said that”) followed by the past perfect ("había" + past participle) to talk about something that happened before another past moment. Subject pronouns (él/ella/usted) are often omitted in Spanish: “Dijo que había…” can mean “He said…” or “She said…”. You can change "dijo" to other people: "dije que había" (I said), "dijeron que había" (they said).
target_language_example: María dijo que había perdido las llaves.
native_language_example: María said that she had lost the keys.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they planned or intended to do in the past. The verb changes with the speaker (dije/dijiste/dijo/dijimos/dijeron) and you can change the subject after “que” (e.g., “dijo que yo iba a…”). In reported speech about the past, “va a” often becomes “iba a”.
target_language_example: Ella dijo que iba a llamarme después.
native_language_example: She said she was going to call me later.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (to him/her)" / "(he/she) said that (it) happened to him/her".
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (indirect speech): "X dijo que..." = "X said that...". The pronoun "le" often refers to the person affected or involved (him/her/you formal), especially with verbs like "robar" (they stole from him/her), "seguir" (they were following him/her), or expressions like "le daba sueño" (he/she felt sleepy). In English you may translate it as "said that he/she..." or "said that to him/her..." depending on context.
target_language_example: El policía dijo que le iban a ayudar.
native_language_example: The police officer said they were going to help him/her.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (he/it/him)…" (reported speech + direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone said in the past: dijo que… = “(he/she) said that…”. The "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it,” referring to something already known from context (e.g., "dijo que lo intentaría" = “said he would try it”; "dijo que lo sentía" = “said he was sorry [about it]”). Often followed by an imperfect or conditional verb to reflect a future-in-the-past idea (intentaría, podría, etc.).
target_language_example: Mi jefe dijo que lo revisaría mañana.
native_language_example: My boss said that he would look it over tomorrow.

meaning: "(He/She) said that I..." / "(He/She) told me that I..."
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, introducing a clause with que (“that”). Often followed by a verb in the imperfect (e.g., me amaba, me extrañaba) for reported feelings, or by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., me lavara) when reporting a command or suggestion. You’ll also see the order flipped as: “Me dijo que…” = “(He/She) told me that…”.
target_language_example: Dijo que me ayudaría mañana.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she would help me tomorrow.

meaning: "(he/she) said no" or "(he/she) said that ... not".
additional_notes: Used with reported speech. It can mean a direct refusal/denial ("He said no"), or it can introduce a negative statement: "dijo que no + verb" ("said that he/she didn’t..."). In commands/advice it often appears as "me dijo que no + imperfect subjunctive": "Me dijo que no condujera..." = "He told me not to drive...".
target_language_example: Le pregunté si venía, pero dijo que no.
native_language_example: I asked if he was coming, but he said no.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., "Él dijo…" / "Ella dijo…"). After "que," Spanish often uses the imperfect: "tenía" = "had" / "didn’t have" at that time. Commonly followed by a noun or by an expression like "dónde + infinitive" ("dónde ir" = "where to go").
target_language_example: Ana dijo que no tenía tiempo para venir.
native_language_example: Ana said that she didn’t have time to come.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said and what they believed at the time. After "dijo" and "pensaba," Spanish often uses "que" (“that”) to introduce the next clause. The subject can change with context: "Tom dijo…" = “Tom said…”, "Ella dijo…" = “She said…”. You’ll also see the present version: "dice que piensa que" (“says he/she thinks that”).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que pensaba que era demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: She said she thought it was too late.

additional_notes: Common reporting structure: **decir (pretérito)** + **que** + verb. Here **podía** is the imperfect of **poder** (“could/was able to”), often used to report what someone said they were able/allowed to do. The subject is often understood from context: **Dijo que podía hacerlo** = “(He/She) said (he/she) could do it.” You can add the subject for clarity: **Él/Ella dijo que podía…**
target_language_example: Ella dijo que podía ayudarme mañana.
native_language_example: She said that she could help me tomorrow.
