Common patterns: el mejor + noun (el mejor plan), el mejor de + plural (el mejor de los cumpleaños = “the best birthday”), el mejor para + noun (“the best for your money”).
target_language_example: Para mí, este es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this is the best restaurant in the city.

el mejor día de mi vida

target_language_multi_word_term: el mejor día de mi vida
additional_notes: A fixed phrase to express that something is/was the happiest or most important day you’ve ever had. Common with different tenses: "Es/Hoy es el mejor día de mi vida" (it is/today is), "Fue/Ese fue" (it was/that was), "Ha sido" (it has been), "Había sido" (it had been). You can swap "mi" for another person: "de tu vida", "de su vida", "de nuestra vida".
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la noticia, pensé: "Este es el mejor día de mi vida".
native_language_example: When they told me the news, I thought: “This is the best day of my life.”

additional_notes: Often refers to (1) a physical place where goods are sold (a market), or (2) the economic “market” for a product (customers and demand), as in “estar en el mercado” (to be on the market/available for sale). It can also be used in a broader, more abstract sense to talk about the market economy.
target_language_example: Este teléfono ya está en el mercado, pero todavía es caro.
native_language_example: This phone is already on the market, but it’s still expensive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific month or about the month as a period of time. Common patterns: "el mes próximo" (next month), "el mes pasado" (last month), "el mes de + [month/event]" (the month of May / the month of lovers). Spanish also often says "en el mes de mayo" where English usually just says "in May."
target_language_example: Tenemos vacaciones el mes que viene.
native_language_example: We have vacation next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the previous month. It’s a time expression; it often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., “El mes pasado fui…” / “Fui… el mes pasado”).
target_language_example: El mes pasado empecé un nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Last month I started a new job.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. It can go at the start or end of the sentence. Also common: "la semana que viene" (next week), "el año que viene" (next year).
target_language_example: Nos vemos el mes que viene para hablar del proyecto.
native_language_example: See you next month to talk about the project.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the city train system that runs underground or on dedicated tracks. Common with verbs like "tomar el metro" (to take the subway) and "ir en metro" (to go by subway). Also used when asking for directions: "¿Dónde está el metro?"
target_language_example: Para llegar al centro, toma el metro en esta estación.
native_language_example: To get downtown, take the subway at this station.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something is identical: el mismo ADN = “the same DNA,” el mismo tipo de auto = “the same type of car.” It agrees with the noun: el mismo (masc. singular), la misma (fem. singular), los mismos / las mismas (plural). Can also emphasize identity (“the very same”).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes el mismo número de teléfono que antes?
native_language_example: Do you have the same phone number as before?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is in an identical location as something else or as before. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: el mismo lugar, la misma casa, los mismos sitios, las mismas cosas. Often appears with que ("the same ... as"): "en el mismo lugar que...".
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el mismo lugar de siempre.
native_language_example: See you at the same place as always.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something is identical: el mismo ADN = “the same DNA,” el mismo tipo de auto = “the same type of car.” It agrees with the noun: el mismo (masc. singular), la misma (fem. singular), los mismos / las mismas (plural). Can also emphasize identity (“the very same”).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes el mismo número de teléfono que antes?
native_language_example: Do you have the same phone number as before?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone repeats an identical mistake (often with verbs like cometer (to make/commit), repetir (to repeat), or seguir (to keep doing)). With a comparison you’ll often see: "el mismo error que..." (“the same mistake as...”).
target_language_example: No quiero cometer el mismo error otra vez.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make the same mistake again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific point in time, or the appropriate time to do something. Common patterns: “Es el momento de + infinitive” (It’s time to…), “el momento perfecto para + noun/infinitive” (the perfect moment/time for…), and “Ya llegará el momento” (The time will come / It’ll happen when the time is right).
target_language_example: No es el momento de discutir ahora.
native_language_example: Now is not the time to argue.

meaning: the right moment; the right time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the best or most appropriate time to do something. Often appears with verbs like ser ("Es el momento adecuado"), esperar ("Hay que esperar el momento adecuado"), or in the phrase "cuando sea el momento adecuado" ("when the time is right"). "Adecuado" agrees with the noun: "el momento adecuado" (masc.), "la hora adecuada" (fem.).
target_language_example: No es el momento adecuado para hablar de eso.
native_language_example: It’s not the right time to talk about that.

additional_notes: Used to say that now is (or isn’t) the appropriate time to do an action. Often appears with verbs like decir, explicar, confiar, tomar. You can change the article or tense depending on context: ahora es el momento de..., no es el momento de..., llegó/era/sería el momento de....
target_language_example: No es el momento de discutir; hablemos mañana.
native_language_example: It’s not the time to argue; let’s talk tomorrow.

meaning: the moment of truth; the decisive moment.
additional_notes: Used when an important test, decision, or outcome is about to happen—when you’ll finally find out what’s really going to happen (e.g., before an exam result, a big presentation, opening an envelope). Often said as a standalone phrase for emphasis: “Bien, el momento de la verdad.”
target_language_example: Respira hondo: ha llegado el momento de la verdad.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath: the moment of truth has arrived.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or cause. It’s often followed by a clause: “El motivo por el que + verb…”. You can also use it with “es”: “El motivo por el que X es que…”. Similar options: “la razón por la que” (same meaning).
target_language_example: El motivo por el que llegué tarde es que perdí el autobús.
native_language_example: The reason why I arrived late is that I missed the bus.

additional_notes: Most often refers to a vehicle’s engine (car, motorcycle, etc.). Common verbs: encender el motor (start/turn on the engine), apagar el motor (turn off the engine), dejar el motor andando/encendido (leave the engine running).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes apagar el motor, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the engine, please?

additional_notes: Refers to a male child or teenager, and sometimes a young man depending on context. In many places it’s a common alternative to “el chico.” Plural: “los muchachos” (the boys / the guys).
target_language_example: El muchacho está esperando afuera.
native_language_example: The boy is waiting outside.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the world” (the planet or the world as a whole): El mundo es muy diferente. It can also mean “everyone / people in general” in some contexts (e.g., Todo el mundo = everybody). Used with verbs like cambiar (change), conocer (know), recorrer (travel).
target_language_example: Todo el mundo quiere vivir en paz.
native_language_example: Everyone wants to live in peace.

additional_notes: Literally “the entire world.” Used for emphasis to mean all people or all places (e.g., “everyone in the world will know”). It’s masculine singular, so you’ll often see it with singular verbs: “El mundo entero está…”.
target_language_example: El mundo entero estaba mirando el partido.
native_language_example: The whole world was watching the game.

additional_notes: Used to describe the world with an adjective or phrase. In Spanish, adjectives agree in gender/number with the noun: mundo is masculine singular, so you typically use masculine singular adjectives (e.g., El mundo es bello/hermoso/pequeño). You can also use it more generally to make statements about life or society.
target_language_example: El mundo es muy grande, pero a veces parece pequeño.
native_language_example: The world is very big, but sometimes it feels small.

meaning: “the world is a place …” (often followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used as a general statement about what the world is like. It’s commonly completed with an adjective (mejor, grande, maravilloso, peligroso, divertido) or a phrase like “para + infinitive.” In sentence 1, it’s part of the fixed idea “el mundo es un lugar mejor” (“the world is a better place”), often used to praise someone’s positive impact.
target_language_example: Con gente amable, el mundo es un lugar más bonito.
native_language_example: With kind people, the world is a nicer place.

meaning: "the world is" / "the world is (in a certain state)".
additional_notes: Uses **estar** (not *ser*) to describe a state or condition of the world that’s seen as temporary, changing, or situational (e.g., *está lleno de..., está de nuestro lado*). You’ll often add an adjective or phrase after it: **el mundo está + adjective/phrase**. In sentences like *Mucha gente en el mundo está...*, it means “many people in the world are...”.
target_language_example: Hoy el mundo está muy dividido.
native_language_example: Today the world is very divided.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement that there are many of something. It’s often followed by a plural noun (e.g., problemas) or an uncountable noun (e.g., ilusiones). You can also change the subject: "La ciudad está llena de turistas" (The city is full of tourists).
target_language_example: El mundo está lleno de oportunidades.
native_language_example: The world is full of opportunities.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression by itself; it’s the start of a sentence where "el mundo" is the subject and "se" introduces a verb that’s reflexive or uses "se" for a passive/impersonal feel. Common patterns you’ll see: "El mundo se está acabando" (the world is coming to an end), "El mundo se queda sin..." (the world runs out of...), "El mundo se detiene" (the world stops). The "se" usually won’t translate as a separate word in English.
target_language_example: El mundo se está calentando rápidamente.
native_language_example: The world is warming up quickly.

additional_notes: Superlative phrase meaning “the most big/great.” Use it to compare within a group: el más grande (masculine singular). It can mean physical size (“the biggest”) or importance/skill (“the greatest”). With nouns it often appears as “el más grande + noun” (e.g., el más grande pintor). Feminine/plural: la más grande, los más grandes, las más grandes.
target_language_example: De todos los edificios, este es el más grande.
native_language_example: Of all the buildings, this is the biggest.

meaning: the doctor (male); also used generically for “the doctor”.
additional_notes: “Médico” means a medical doctor/physician. It’s often used with the definite article (“el médico”) to refer to someone’s doctor or a doctor previously mentioned. Feminine form: “la médica” (also common: “la doctora”). Plural: “los médicos” (male or mixed group), “las médicas” (all female).
target_language_example: Tengo cita con el médico mañana.
native_language_example: I have an appointment with the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often means a business in general (“a company” or “the business side of something”), but in everyday speech it can also mean a small local shop. In the phrase “El negocio es el negocio,” it’s like “business is business,” meaning you make decisions based on business, not feelings. Plural: los negocios.
target_language_example: Tengo que abrir el negocio a las ocho.
native_language_example: I have to open the shop at eight.

additional_notes: “Niño” means “child” or “boy,” depending on context. With “el” it usually refers to a specific boy/child (“the boy/the child”). For a girl, use “la niña.” The plural is “los niños” (can mean “the children” in general, including mixed groups).
target_language_example: El niño no quiere irse a dormir.
native_language_example: The boy doesn’t want to go to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the child’s location (*está allí*), temporary condition/state (*está cansado*), and actions happening right now with the present progressive (*está bebiendo/escuchando*). *El niño* can mean “the boy” or “the child” depending on context.
target_language_example: El niño está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: The boy is at home now.

additional_notes: “Se” is a reflexive pronoun used with many verbs to show the action happens to the subject (the boy): he did something to himself (El niño se ajustó la gorra. = He adjusted his cap) or his state changed (El niño se ensució las manos. = He got his hands dirty). It’s also used in reflexive/progressive forms: El niño se estaba escondiendo… = The boy was hiding…. With body parts you often see: se + verb + la/las + body part(s): se ensució las manos (not *sus manos*).
target_language_example: El niño se lavó la cara antes de salir.
native_language_example: The boy washed his face before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to identify a person, place, or thing ("Ese es el nombre"). Also used in phrases like "llevar el nombre de" (to be named after) and "cambiarse el nombre" (to change your name).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el nombre de esta calle?
native_language_example: What is the name of this street?

additional_notes: Used to identify a person, animal, or thing: El nombre de + noun/pronoun. Very common after verbs like saber (to know), decir (to tell), olvidar (to forget), oír (to hear), querer (to want). With pronouns, you often hear: el nombre de él/ella (his/her name) or the more common possessive: su nombre (his/her name).
target_language_example: No recuerdo el nombre de tu profesor.
native_language_example: I don’t remember your teacher’s name.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s name in relation to something they own or are connected to: “el nombre de su informante” = “the name of his informant.” Note that **su** can mean **his, her, your (formal), or their**—context tells you which. Also appears in the common pattern **llevar el nombre de + person** (“to be named after + person”).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el nombre de su profesor?
native_language_example: What is the name of your professor?

meaning: “the name of the” (masculine singular: of the).
additional_notes: Used to introduce who/what something belongs to or refers to: el nombre del lugar (“the name of the place”), el nombre del caballo (“the horse’s name”). It’s a contraction of de + el → del, so you use it with masculine singular nouns (el lugar, el Señor). With feminine singular you use “de la” (el nombre de la casa), and with plural “de los/de las” (el nombre de los niños). Also appears in set religious phrases like “En el nombre del Padre…” (“In the name of the Father…”).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el nombre del hotel?
native_language_example: What is the name of the hotel?

meaning: the north; northern area (also: direction north).
additional_notes: Used for geography ("el norte de la ciudad/de Suecia" = the northern part) and for the compass direction ("ir hacia el norte" = go north). It can also be figurative in expressions like "perder el norte" (= to lose your sense of direction/purpose).
target_language_example: El hotel está en el norte de la isla, cerca de la playa.
native_language_example: The hotel is in the north of the island, near the beach.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: el nuevo modelo (the new model), el nuevo programa (the new program). It can also be used on its own when the noun is understood from context (e.g., el nuevo = the new one/the new guy). Feminine: la nueva. Plural: los nuevos / las nuevas.
target_language_example: ¿Has visto el nuevo teléfono?
native_language_example: Have you seen the new phone?

meaning: the number (e.g., a phone number or a numerical value).
additional_notes: Commonly used for phone numbers with verbs like decir (Dime el número), marcar (Marque el número / Marcó el número equivocado), and dar (Me dio el número). Also used for choosing a number: elegir un número al azar. In Spanish, phone numbers are often said as “el número de teléfono,” but in context people may just say “el número.”
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar el número de tu teléfono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how many of something there are. Usually followed by a plural noun: el número de abejas/accidentes. With it, Spanish commonly uses a singular verb because the subject is número (singular): El número de abejas está disminuyendo. It can also appear in phrases like “sin importar el número de veces” (“no matter how many times”).
target_language_example: El número de estudiantes en la clase es de veinte.
native_language_example: The number of students in the class is twenty.

additional_notes: Used before a person or place to say who the phone number belongs to: el número de teléfono de ella/él, de mis padres, de su oficina, de casa. In Spanish you usually say “el número de teléfono” (often just “el número”) rather than “número de teléfono” alone.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes el número de teléfono de Marta?
native_language_example: Do you have Marta’s phone number?

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses **el** (singular) and **los** (plural: *los océanos*). Often used when talking about the sea, marine life, pollution, climate change, etc.
target_language_example: Me gusta nadar en el océano cuando hace calor.
native_language_example: I like to swim in the ocean when it’s hot.

additional_notes: Used for the cardinal direction opposite el este (east). Common with prepositions: en el oeste (in/to the west), por el oeste (in/from the west, via the west side), desde el oeste (from the west). Also used to talk about a western region/area (e.g., el oeste del país).
target_language_example: Vivimos en el oeste de la ciudad.
native_language_example: We live in the west of the city.

additional_notes: Refers to the physical eye (vision). Common in phrases like "guiñar el ojo" (to wink) and in metaphorical uses (e.g., "el ojo en el cielo" = an eye in the sky; "el ojo nos lo dirá" personifies the eye/vision as a judge of what’s true). In Spanish, body parts often use the definite article (el/la) where English uses a possessive: "Cúbrete el ojo" = "Cover your eye."
target_language_example: Cierra el ojo y guiña el otro.
native_language_example: Close one eye and wink the other.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the precious metal (“gold”). In sports/competitions, “ganar el oro” means “to win gold” (i.e., the gold medal).
target_language_example: Quiere ganar el oro en la próxima carrera.
native_language_example: He/She wants to win gold in the next race.

additional_notes: Used to point out or contrast a different one from the one you’re talking about. It can refer to another person (el otro tipo), another place (el otro pueblo), another time/day (el otro jueves = the other/next Thursday depending on context), a direction (en el otro sentido), or a body part (el otro brazo). It agrees with the noun: la otra (fem.), los otros/las otras (plural).
target_language_example: No quiero este, quiero el otro.
native_language_example: I don’t want this one; I want the other one.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the opposite side of something (a street, a wall, the Moon) or the opposing side in a conflict (“the other side”). Often appears with de: “el otro lado de la calle / de la Luna”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el otro lado de la calle.
native_language_example: See you on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used to point out or contrast a different one from the one you’re talking about. It can refer to another person (el otro tipo), another place (el otro pueblo), another time/day (el otro jueves = the other/next Thursday depending on context), a direction (en el otro sentido), or a body part (el otro brazo). It agrees with the noun: la otra (fem.), los otros/las otras (plural).
target_language_example: No quiero este, quiero el otro.
native_language_example: I don’t want this one; I want the other one.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses el: el pan. In plural: los panes (“the breads/loaves”). Commonly used with types of bread: pan blanco (white bread), pan integral (whole wheat bread).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes comprar el pan para la cena?
native_language_example: Can you buy the bread for dinner?

additional_notes: Most commonly means the material you write or draw on ("en el papel" = on paper). In acting/theater, "hacer/interpretrar el papel de + character" means to play the role of that character. In some contexts, "el papel" can also mean an official document (like a paper you need to get), depending on what the situation is.
target_language_example: Necesito un papel para escribir tu dirección.
native_language_example: I need a piece of paper to write your address.

meaning: the role/part of (in a play, movie, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like hacer or interpretar to talk about acting a character: hacer el papel de X / interpretar el papel de X. You can also talk about learning the lines: Sé el papel de memoria (“I know the role/part by heart”).
target_language_example: Ella hizo el papel de doctora en la película.
native_language_example: She played the role of a doctor in the movie.

additional_notes: Used when talking about an umbrella that someone left behind on the bus. It often appears with verbs like dejar(se) (“to leave behind”) or olvidar(se) (“to forget”), e.g., “Me he dejado el paraguas en el autobús” = “I left my umbrella on the bus.”
target_language_example: Creo que me he dejado el paraguas en el autobús.
native_language_example: I think I left my umbrella on the bus.

additional_notes: Used literally for a religious/spiritual “heaven” (often after death: “su alma está en el paraíso”) and figuratively for an ideal, wonderful situation (“esto es el paraíso”, “otro día en el paraíso”). You may also hear the set phrase “problemas en el paraíso” meaning that something isn’t as perfect as it seems.
target_language_example: Estar aquí contigo es el paraíso.
native_language_example: Being here with you is paradise.

additional_notes: A common place word. Use **en el parque** for “in/at the park” and **al parque** (a + el) for “to the park.” It’s masculine singular: **el parque / los parques**.
target_language_example: Vamos al parque después de clase.
native_language_example: We’re going to the park after class.

additional_notes: Used for a sports match (e.g., soccer, basketball). Common with verbs like jugar (to play), ganar/perder (to win/lose), and celebrarse (to be held). Also used with tickets: entradas para el partido.
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el partido?
native_language_example: What time does the game start?

additional_notes: "Partido" means a game/match (especially in sports). With "de béisbol," it specifies the sport: a baseball game. You’ll often hear it with verbs like "ver" (to watch), "ir a" (to go to), or in announcements like "fue cancelado" (was canceled) / "será suspendido" (will be suspended), often because of rain.
target_language_example: Vamos al partido de béisbol esta tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to the baseball game this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used for a scheduled soccer match/event. In many Spanish-speaking countries, “fútbol” usually means soccer (not American football). You’ll often hear it with verbs like ver (to watch), jugarse (to be played), and posponerse (to be postponed).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora empieza el partido de fútbol?
native_language_example: What time does the soccer game start?

additional_notes: Used to talk about earlier times or what has already happened. Often appears in contrasts like "el pasado" vs. "el futuro" (the future), and with verbs like "olvidar" (to forget) or "recordar" (to remember).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar del pasado ahora.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about the past right now.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a hallway/corridor inside a building or house, used with directions like “por el pasillo a la derecha/izquierda” (down the hallway to the right/left). It can also mean an aisle in places like a supermarket, plane, or theater (e.g., “el pasillo del avión”).
target_language_example: El baño está al final del pasillo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.

additional_notes: Refers to an outdoor area next to a house or building. In many Spanish-speaking places, "patio" can mean a yard or an inner courtyard (not just a "patio" with paving). You’ll often see it with home activities: "barrer el patio" (sweep the yard) or kids/pets "jugar/correr por el patio" (play/run in the yard). "Patio de recreo" is a playground or schoolyard.
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el patio.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the yard.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a nation/state as a whole (its territory and people). It can also mean “the countryside” in some contexts (like being out of the city), but in these examples it means “country” (e.g., leaving the country; the whole country).
target_language_example: No puedo viajar porque no tengo pasaporte para salir del país.
native_language_example: I can’t travel because I don’t have a passport to leave the country.

meaning: the chest; the breast (front of the torso).
additional_notes: Refers to the front upper part of the body (between neck and stomach). Common in health contexts (dolor en el pecho = chest pain) and to describe body features (pecho peludo = hairy chest). For women, "pecho" can also mean "breast," but "la mama" is more specific/medical.
target_language_example: Me duele el pecho cuando respiro hondo.
native_language_example: My chest hurts when I take a deep breath.

additional_notes: Often used with body-part verbs and reflexive routines: "cepillarse el pelo" (to brush one’s hair), "lavarse el pelo" (to wash one’s hair). In Spanish you typically use the definite article (el/la) with body parts instead of a possessive (mi/tu). In "tener el pelo de punta", it means your hair is standing on end (from fear, surprise, etc.).
target_language_example: Me voy a lavar el pelo esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to wash my hair tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. "Castaño" = brown (for hair); you can add shades like "castaño oscuro" (dark brown). Often used with "tener": "Tengo el pelo castaño" (I have brown hair).
target_language_example: Ella tiene el pelo castaño.
native_language_example: She has brown hair.

additional_notes: Describes hair length. Common with the verb tener (Tiene el pelo corto = He/She has short hair) and with quedar (Te queda bien el pelo corto = Short hair looks good on you).
target_language_example: Ahora tengo el pelo corto.
native_language_example: Now I have short hair.

meaning: '(hair) ... (color)' (used with a hair-color adjective after it).
additional_notes: Used to say what color someone’s hair is dyed (or sometimes naturally is). It often appears with the verb teñirse/teñir (to dye) and an adjective naming a color after de: teñirse el pelo de negro/rojo/rubio. Literally “the hair of…”, but in this pattern it means “hair (in the color) …”.
target_language_example: Me estoy tiñendo el pelo de castaño.
native_language_example: I’m dyeing my hair brown.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair length (often with the verb tener: "tener el pelo largo" = "to have long hair"). You can also use it more generally as a noun phrase: "El pelo largo pasó de moda" ("Long hair went out of style").
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene el pelo largo.
native_language_example: My brother has long hair.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (to have): tener el pelo rubio = to have blond hair. Hair color adjectives agree with pelo (masculine singular): rubio, castaño, negro. You can also say el cabello rubio (more formal/Latin American).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene el pelo rubio y los ojos verdes.
native_language_example: My brother has blond hair and green eyes.

additional_notes: A common way to refer to a (printed or online) newspaper as a source of news or as something you read. Used with verbs like leer (to read): “leer el periódico.” Also used to mean “the paper” in the sense of a news publication that can report or publish something (“una foto para el periódico”).
target_language_example: Cada mañana leo el periódico con un café.
native_language_example: Every morning I read the newspaper with a coffee.

additional_notes: "El" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). "Perro" means “dog.” Used to talk about a specific dog, or dogs in general as a category (e.g., "El perro es un animal fiel").
target_language_example: El perro está en el jardín.
native_language_example: The dog is in the yard.

meaning: “the dog is …” (using estar for location or a temporary/ongoing action).
additional_notes: Use **estar** (not ser) to say where someone/thing is or what they’re doing right now. Very common patterns: **El perro está + en/al lado de…** (location) and **El perro está + gerundio** (present continuous), e.g. **está ladrando/saltando/dando vueltas**.
target_language_example: El perro está durmiendo en el sofá.
native_language_example: The dog is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Usually refers to fish you eat (fish meat), especially in everyday contexts like liking it, buying it, or saying it’s healthy/expensive. It’s masculine singular (el); plural: los pescados. Contrast: el pez = a fish (the animal) when talking about it alive.
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a comer el pescado con arroz.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to eat fish with rice.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses el. With instruments in Spanish, you usually use the definite article: tocar el piano = “to play the piano” (not *tocar piano*). Also used with en to mean “on/at the piano,” especially when accompanying someone: acompañar a alguien en el piano = “to accompany someone on the piano.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes tocar el piano esta noche?
native_language_example: Can you play the piano tonight?

additional_notes: In these examples, "el piso" refers to the surface you walk on indoors. It’s common with cleaning verbs like "barrer" (to sweep): "Barrer el piso" = "to sweep the floor." (In other contexts, "piso" can also mean "apartment" in some countries, but here it clearly means "floor".)
target_language_example: Hay agua en el piso, ten cuidado.
native_language_example: There’s water on the floor—be careful.

meaning: the plan; a plan (idea/strategy for doing something).
additional_notes: Usually refers to an arrangement or strategy that has been decided (or is being discussed): conversar/discutir el plan, mantener el plan en secreto. Common fixed phrase: "Todo va según el plan" = "Everything is going according to plan."
target_language_example: Tenemos un plan para mañana, pero puede cambiar.
native_language_example: We have a plan for tomorrow, but it can change.

meaning: power; the ability/authority to do something.
additional_notes:
Commonly used with:
- "el poder de + infinitive" = the power/ability to do something ("el poder de amar").
- "tener el poder (para) + infinitive" = to have the power/ability ("Tengo el poder para construir...").
- "tomar el poder" = to seize/take power (often political control).
It can mean personal ability/strength, legal authority, or political power depending on context.
target_language_example: No tienes el poder para cambiar el pasado.
native_language_example: You don't have the power to change the past.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an ability or capacity. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (el poder de + verb, e.g., el poder de cambiar “the power to change”) or by a noun (el poder de + noun, e.g., el poder de la mente “the power of the mind”).
target_language_example: Todos tenemos el poder de cambiar nuestras vidas.
native_language_example: We all have the power to change our lives.

meaning: "the power of the" (of a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s or something’s strength, ability, influence, or authority. It’s made of el poder (the power) + del, which is the contraction of de + el (“of the”). Use del before a masculine singular noun: el poder del rey, el poder del fuego. For feminine singular nouns, use de la: el poder de la magia.
target_language_example: Conoces el poder del dinero.
native_language_example: You know the power of money.

additional_notes: In these sentences, the key phrase is usually **de memoria**, meaning you can recite something without looking at the text/notes. Common with verbs like **aprender(se)** or **saber(se)**: *aprender(se) algo de memoria*, *saber(se) algo de memoria*. Often used with poems, speeches, lines, and songs.
target_language_example: Tengo que aprenderme el poema de memoria para mañana.
native_language_example: I have to learn the poem by heart for tomorrow.

meaning: the price; (figuratively) the cost (what you pay for something).
additional_notes: Used for the amount of money something costs: "el precio del auto" (the car’s price). It can also be used figuratively to mean the personal or social “cost” of something: "el precio de la fama" (the price/cost of fame). Common with "de": "el precio de + noun". Often used with verbs like "subir" (to go up), "bajar" (to go down), "aumentar" (to increase), "cambiar" (to change).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el precio de esta camisa?
native_language_example: What’s the price of this shirt?

additional_notes: Used to say how much something costs or to talk about prices in general. Common patterns: “El precio de X es…” (The price of X is…), “El precio de X sube/baja” (goes up/down), and “Dos por el precio de uno” (Two for the price of one).
target_language_example: El precio de este billete incluye una bebida.
native_language_example: The price of this ticket includes a drink.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the cost/value of something. It’s commonly followed by a noun: el precio de la gasolina (gas), el precio de la electricidad (electricity). You’ll also see it in the expression “Es el precio de…” meaning “That’s the price of…” / “That’s the cost of…” (often figurative), e.g., “Es el precio de la fama” (“That’s the price of fame”).
target_language_example: El precio de la comida está subiendo.
native_language_example: The price of food is going up.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to talk about how much something costs or how its price changes (sube, baja, aumenta, cae, varía). For feminine nouns, use “el precio de la” (e.g., el precio de la gasolina). Can also be used figuratively: “el precio del pecado…”.
target_language_example: El precio del billete incluye impuestos.
native_language_example: The price of the ticket includes taxes.

additional_notes: Used for something you win or receive for being the best (a contest, competition, raffle, etc.). Common with verbs like ganar (to win) and recibir (to receive), and in phrases like el premio fue para… (the prize went to…). It can also mean an “award” like at a ceremony.
target_language_example: Si estudias mucho, puedes ganar el premio.
native_language_example: If you study a lot, you can win the prize.

meaning: a feeling/sense that (something is going to happen).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a “hunch” or intuition, often without clear proof. Very common with tener: "Tengo/Tenía/Tuve el presentimiento de que..." followed by a verb (often in imperfect or conditional when talking about what you thought would happen).
target_language_example: Tuve el presentimiento de que hoy iba a llover.
native_language_example: I had a feeling that it was going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used for the head of a country or organization. Often followed by "de" + a place/organization ("el presidente de Francia"). When used in the news or in context, "el presidente" can mean "the current president" without naming them. Feminine form: "la presidenta".
target_language_example: Mañana el presidente dará un discurso en la televisión.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the president will give a speech on TV.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns that come right after it: el primer año, el primer giro. It’s a shortened form of “primero” used before the noun. For feminine nouns, use “la primera …” (la primera vez).
target_language_example: Este es el primer día de clases.
native_language_example: This is the first day of class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the beginning of something (a trip, job, relationship, etc.). In the expression “el primer día del resto de mi/tu vida” it means “the first day of the rest of my/your life,” often said to mark a fresh start. Also common in comparisons like “como el primer día” = “like on the first day,” especially about feelings staying the same over time.
target_language_example: Hoy es el primer día de mi nuevo trabajo.
native_language_example: Today is the first day of my new job.

additional_notes: Used for the top government leader in many countries, usually the head of the executive branch (not necessarily the president). Often appears with political/news verbs like dimitir (to resign), firmar (to sign), and hacer una declaración (to make a statement). Plural: los primeros ministros.
target_language_example: El primer ministro anunció nuevas medidas económicas.
native_language_example: The prime minister announced new economic measures.

meaning: “the first step” (the initial action in a process).
additional_notes: Used to talk about starting a process (solving a problem, learning something, making a change). Often followed by “para + infinitive” (el primer paso para resolver...) or “consiste en + infinitive” (el primer paso consiste en reconocer...).
target_language_example: El primer paso para mejorar es pedir ayuda.
native_language_example: The first step to improving is asking for help.

additional_notes: Used in contests, competitions, raffles, etc. It refers to the highest prize/award. Often used with verbs like ganar (to win) and obtener (to receive).
target_language_example: Si practicas mucho, quizá ganes el primer premio.
native_language_example: If you practice a lot, maybe you’ll win first prize.

meaning: the first train (usually of the day).
additional_notes: Refers to the earliest scheduled train, often in the morning: “tomar/coger el primer tren” = “to take/catch the first train.” It can imply getting up early to leave as soon as possible.
target_language_example: Si queremos llegar a tiempo, tenemos que tomar el primer tren.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we have to take the first train.

meaning: "the first" (1st; the one that comes before the others).
additional_notes: Used for a masculine singular noun or person. Often appears after the verb: "Es el primero" = "He/It is the first." With "que", it can mean "the first (one) who/that...": "El primero que llegue..." = "The first one who arrives...". As an adjective before a masculine singular noun, it shortens to "primer": "el primer día" (not *el primero día*). Feminine: "la primera" / "primer" (before a feminine noun).
target_language_example: Tú fuiste el primero en llegar.
native_language_example: You were the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone is the first person to do an action: "el primero en + infinitive" (e.g., "el primero en llegar"). It can also appear with a noun phrase like "el primero en la lista" = "the first on the list". Changes for gender/number: "la primera en", "los primeros en", "las primeras en".
target_language_example: Ella fue la primera en llegar a la reunión.
native_language_example: She was the first to arrive at the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to identify the first person/thing that does an action, followed by a verb phrase (a relative clause): «El primero que llega…». It agrees with the noun/person: «la primera que…» (feminine), «los primeros que…» (plural), etc. In English it’s often translated as “the first to + verb” (e.g., “the first to arrive”).
target_language_example: El primero que termine el examen puede salir.
native_language_example: The first person to finish the exam can leave.

meaning: the beginning; the start (also: a guiding principle).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “the beginning/start,” often in phrases like “al principio” (at first/in the beginning) or “es/eso es sólo el principio” (it/that’s only the beginning). It can also mean “principle” as in a rule or guiding idea, but in your examples it’s mainly about the start of something (including figuratively).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: esto es sólo el principio.
native_language_example: Relax: this is only the beginning.

additional_notes: Used with the masculine article "el". It can refer to a situation/issue ("Discutimos el problema") or to the person/thing causing trouble ("El problema es ella" / "Tom es el problema"). Common verbs include "discutir el problema" (discuss the problem), "entender el problema" (understand it), "pensar en el problema" (think about it), and "solucionar el problema" (solve it).
target_language_example: No entiendo el problema, ¿me lo explicas?
native_language_example: I don’t understand the problem—can you explain it to me?

additional_notes: Used to point out an obstacle or the reason something can’t happen. It’s often followed by a clause with que + verb: “El problema es que no tengo tiempo.” You can also use it to politely disagree or bring up a concern before giving an explanation.
target_language_example: Quiero ir, pero el problema es que mañana trabajo temprano.
native_language_example: I want to go, but the problem is that I work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main obstacle or difficulty, often as an explanation or excuse. Typically followed by a verb phrase in the present or past (e.g., “no tengo…”, “no hubo…”, “no sabía…”). You can also say “El problema es que…” without “no” when it isn’t negative.
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero el problema es que no tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but the problem is that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used for a male teacher or professor. In everyday Spanish, "profesor" can refer to a school teacher as well as a university professor. The feminine form is "la profesora". Often used with school-related words like "alumnos/estudiantes" (students).
target_language_example: El profesor nos explicó la lección con paciencia.
native_language_example: The teacher explained the lesson to us patiently.

meaning: 'the teacher/professor (to) me' — used before a verb to show the teacher is doing something to/for me.
additional_notes: This is a common sentence pattern: **El profesor me + verb**. The pronoun **me** is an indirect object meaning **“to me / for me”** (e.g., *me advirtió* = “warned me”, *me recomendó* = “recommended to me”, *me echó* = “kicked me out”). Often it translates naturally as “my teacher + verb” or “the teacher + verb + me,” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: El profesor me ayudó con la tarea.
native_language_example: The teacher helped me with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what the weather is expected to be. Common with phrases like “según…” or “de acuerdo con…” (according to), and with future forms like “va a…” (is going to) or “caerá…” (will fall, e.g., snow). Also used with a time reference: “el pronóstico del tiempo de ayer/para mañana”.
target_language_example: ¿Viste el pronóstico del tiempo? Dice que va a hacer frío mañana.
native_language_example: Did you see the weather forecast? It says it’s going to be cold tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for a planned piece of work or an organized effort (at school, at work, or a construction/engineering plan). Common collocations: "el proyecto de construcción" (construction project), "terminar el proyecto" (finish the project), "el proyecto continúa" (the project continues), "estar en marcha" (to be underway).
target_language_example: Tenemos que terminar el proyecto esta semana.
native_language_example: We have to finish the project this week.

additional_notes: Used in politics/government for a proposal that is discussed and voted on in a legislature (e.g., Congreso, Senado). If approved, it can become a law (una ley). Common with verbs like aprobar (pass/approve), retirar (withdraw), and salir adelante (go through/pass).
target_language_example: El proyecto de ley sobre educación no se aprobó.
native_language_example: The education bill was not approved.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to refer to the one that comes immediately after the current one in time or order: el próximo tren, el próximo cruce. With days/dates it means the upcoming one: el próximo jueves, el próximo martes. It can also mean the next person/thing in a sequence or role: el próximo líder. Feminine form: la próxima.
target_language_example: ¿Cuándo llega el próximo autobús?
native_language_example: When does the next bus arrive?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen in the year after the current one. Often paired with the future tense (tendré) or with "ir a" + infinitive (voy a trabajar) to express future plans.
target_language_example: El próximo año vamos a mudarnos a otro país.
native_language_example: Next year we’re going to move to another country.

meaning: next Sunday (the Sunday that is coming).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something scheduled for the Sunday that comes next. Common in plans and appointments (events, meetings, games). You can also say "este domingo" for "this Sunday" (often the soonest Sunday), but "el próximo domingo" emphasizes the upcoming one.
target_language_example: El próximo domingo vamos a visitar a mis abuelos.
native_language_example: Next Sunday we’re going to visit my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately following the current time. Often appears after verbs in the future (va a…, vendrá, espero que…). You can also say “este fin de semana” for “this weekend.”
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer el próximo fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Monday after today. It’s common with future plans and schedules (events starting, meetings, visits). In many contexts it matches English “next Monday.” If you need to be extra clear, you can say “este lunes” for “this Monday” (the coming Monday) vs. “el lunes siguiente” for “the following Monday” (after a specific Monday already mentioned).
target_language_example: Tengo una cita con el médico el próximo lunes.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next Monday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Common with future expressions like "va a" (is going to), the simple future ("saldrá", "terminará"), and scheduled events.
target_language_example: Nos mudamos el próximo mes.
native_language_example: We’re moving next month.

meaning: the town/village; or “the people” (the public/common people).
additional_notes: “Pueblo” has two very common meanings: (1) a small town or village (“Tom dejó el pueblo” = he left town), and (2) the people as a collective group (“No soy el pueblo” = I’m not ‘the people’). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Todo el pueblo vino a la fiesta.
native_language_example: The whole town came to the party.

additional_notes: A common noun for a bridge; it’s masculine, so it uses el/un (el puente, un puente). Often used with en to mean “on/at the bridge” (en el puente) when talking about meeting or where something happened.
target_language_example: Hay un restaurante cerca del puente.
native_language_example: There’s a restaurant near the bridge.

additional_notes: Refers to a group of people as spectators/listeners (at a show, game, speech, etc.) or to people in general (“the public”). Often used with verbs like aplaudir (to applaud), aburrirse (to get bored), ver (to see), and admirar (to admire).
target_language_example: El público guardó silencio durante el discurso.
native_language_example: The audience fell silent during the speech.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for the appliance that keeps food and drinks cold. Commonly used with locations like en el refrigerador (“in the fridge”) and with verbs like abrir (“to open”) or arreglar (“to fix/repair”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner las verduras en el refrigerador?
native_language_example: Can you put the vegetables in the fridge?

additional_notes: "El reloj" can mean either a clock (on a wall/table) or a watch (worn on your wrist). In Spanish, context usually makes it clear: "el reloj de mi padre" is often a watch, while "el reloj" on its own could be either. Common phrases: "¿Qué hora es?" (What time is it?) and "El reloj está haciendo tictac" (The clock/watch is ticking).
target_language_example: Mi reloj está atrasado.
native_language_example: My watch is running slow.

meaning: “the watch that/which …” (a watch with a description after it).
additional_notes: Used when you add a relative clause with **que** to identify or describe **el reloj**: *el reloj que compré* (“the watch that I bought”). **Que** here means “that/which” and is used for people or things. It doesn’t usually translate as a separate word in very natural English, but Spanish needs it to connect the noun to the clause.
target_language_example: No encuentro el reloj que me regalaste.
native_language_example: I can’t find the watch you gave me.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article "el". You’ll often see it with location phrases ("está en...", "estaba lejos de...") and status words like "abierto/cerrado" (open/closed) or "vacío" (empty).
target_language_example: El restaurante está abierto hasta las diez.
native_language_example: The restaurant is open until ten.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the remaining part of something. Very common in the pattern “el resto de + noun” (“the rest of + noun”), e.g., “el resto de la frase” = “the rest of the sentence.” You can also use it on its own when the context is clear: “Ya sabes el resto” (“You know the rest”).
target_language_example: Yo me encargo de la comida y tú del resto.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the food and you take care of the rest.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun to mean what remains: el resto de ustedes (“the rest of you”), el resto de la tarde (“the rest of the afternoon”), el resto de tu vida (“the rest of your life”). It often contrasts with something already mentioned (e.g., one person does X; el resto de… do Y).
target_language_example: Yo me quedo aquí, y el resto de ustedes puede entrar.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here, and the rest of you can go in.

meaning: “the rest of the story” (the remaining part of what happened).
additional_notes: Used when someone has already told (or knows) part of an event and now refers to the remaining details. Common with verbs like contar (to tell), oír (to hear), saber/conocer (to know): «Quiero oír el resto de la historia». It can also imply “you know the rest” when the ending is obvious.
target_language_example: Ya te conté el principio; ahora te cuento el resto de la historia.
native_language_example: I already told you the beginning; now I’ll tell you the rest of the story.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything from now until you die. Often follows verbs like vivir (to live), seguir (to follow), tener (to have time), etc. You can change the possessive to match the person: el resto de tu vida (your), su vida (his/her/their/your formal), nuestra vida (our).
target_language_example: No quiero pasar el resto de mi vida en este trabajo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend the rest of my life in this job.

additional_notes: Used to refer to everyone else in a group that includes the speaker, often in comparisons: "como/el resto de nosotros" (= "like the rest of us"). You can replace "nosotros" with another pronoun (e.g., "el resto de ustedes" = "the rest of you").
target_language_example: No soy diferente; soy como el resto de nosotros.
native_language_example: I'm not different; I'm like the rest of us.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time from now (or from a specific point in the past) until someone dies. The possessive "su" can mean "his," "her," "your (formal)," or "their" depending on context; with "vida" it often means "his/her life." You can also change it to match other people: "el resto de mi vida" (the rest of my life), "el resto de tu vida" (the rest of your life), "el resto de nuestras vidas" (the rest of our lives).
target_language_example: Quiero vivir aquí el resto de mi vida.
native_language_example: I want to live here for the rest of my life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that happens from now on until you die. It often follows a verb phrase: "recordarás el resto de tu vida" (you’ll remember for the rest of your life), "afecta el resto de tu vida" (it affects the rest of your life). You can also change the possessive: "el resto de mi/su/nuestra vida".
target_language_example: Si tomas esa decisión, te afectará el resto de tu vida.
native_language_example: If you make that decision, it will affect you for the rest of your life.

meaning: “the rest of the” (the remaining part of a time period or group).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after del (= de + el): el resto del día/viaje/equipo. For feminine nouns, use: el resto de la semana. You can use it for time (“the rest of the day/trip”) or for people/things (“the rest of the squad/staff”).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en casa el resto del fin de semana.
native_language_example: We stayed home for the rest of the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you get at the end of a test, process, experiment, or investigation. Very common with "de" to say what the result is from: "el resultado del examen" (the exam result).
target_language_example: Todavía no sabemos el resultado del partido.
native_language_example: We still don't know the result of the game.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what something leads to or produces. Often followed by a noun ("el resultado de la guerra") or a longer phrase ("el resultado de todas las decisiones..."). You’ll also see it in cause-and-effect statements: "X es el resultado de Y" ("X is the result of Y").
target_language_example: El cansancio que siento hoy es el resultado de haber dormido poco.
native_language_example: The tiredness I feel today is the result of sleeping little.

additional_notes: Refers to a male monarch or ruler. Use the article: el rey (the king). Plural: los reyes (the kings). Feminine equivalent: la reina (the queen). Can also be used figuratively for “the king of” something (e.g., el rey del pop = the king of pop).
target_language_example: El rey habló con sus consejeros en el palacio.
native_language_example: The king spoke with his advisers in the palace.

meaning: "the king of" (ruler of a place; also "the best/most important of" something).
additional_notes: Used with a place or group: "el rey de Jerusalén" = the king of Jerusalem, "el rey de los animales" = the king of the animals. It can be literal (an actual monarch) or figurative to mean the top/best/most dominant. In card games, "rey" is also the "king" card (e.g., "el rey de picas" = the king of spades).
target_language_example: Mi hermano cree que es el rey de la cocina.
native_language_example: My brother thinks he's the king of the kitchen.

additional_notes: Refers to a king and queen as a pair (often a married royal couple). Use the definite articles (el/la) with titles: el rey, la reina. Common in stories, history, and when talking about a royal family or palace. In Spanish, you can repeat the article before each noun: el rey y la reina.
target_language_example: En el castillo viven el rey y la reina.
native_language_example: The king and the queen live in the castle.

meaning: the risk of; the possibility of (something bad) happening.
additional_notes: Often used in the common expression **correr el riesgo de + infinitive** (“to run the risk of / to risk + -ing”): *Corres el riesgo de perder tu trabajo.* You can also use **hay el riesgo de...** (“there is a risk of...”).
target_language_example: No quiero correr el riesgo de llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I don’t want to risk arriving late.

meaning: “the noise” (a sound, often annoying or loud).
additional_notes: Masculine noun: el ruido. Used for an unwanted/loud sound (e.g., traffic, a bang). Common with verbs like: hacer ruido (to make noise), oír un ruido (to hear a noise), despertar por el ruido (to wake up because of the noise), el ruido me pone nervioso (the noise makes me nervous).
target_language_example: No puedo dormir por el ruido de la calle.
native_language_example: I can’t sleep because of the noise from the street.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el rumor). Used for information people are saying that hasn’t been confirmed. Common with verbs like circular/estar por todas partes (“to be everywhere”), extenderse (“to spread”), and resultar ser + adj. (“to turn out to be…”).
target_language_example: No creas el rumor hasta que haya pruebas.
native_language_example: Don’t believe the rumor until there’s proof.

additional_notes: Used for the best performance ever recorded worldwide in a sport or activity. Common with verbs like tener (to hold) and romper/batir (to break). In Spanish, récord often has an accent: récord.
target_language_example: Ella tiene el récord mundial de salto de altura.
native_language_example: She holds the world record in the high jump.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: el río (the river), los ríos (the rivers). In Spanish you use the article (el) more often than in English when talking about a specific river or the river in your area. With places, you can use prepositions like por (along/by), en (in/at), and cerca de (near).
target_language_example: Vamos a sentarnos cerca del río.
native_language_example: Let's sit near the river.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like cruzar/atravesar (“to cross”) to say you cross a river by swimming: cruzar/atravesar el río a nado. The structure a + noun indicates the method of doing something (e.g., a pie = on foot, a mano = by hand).
target_language_example: Tuvimos que cruzar el río a nado porque no había puente.
native_language_example: We had to cross the river by swimming because there was no bridge.

additional_notes: A simple subject + verb sentence: el río (“the river”) + fluye (he/she/it flows; from fluir). Often followed by phrases like a través de (“through”), hacia (“toward”), or adverbs like lentamente (“slowly”), pacíficamente (“peacefully”), tranquilamente (“calmly”).
target_language_example: El río fluye rápido después de la lluvia.
native_language_example: The river flows fast after the rain.

additional_notes: A noun phrase used for hidden information that someone doesn’t want others to know. Often appears with verbs like saber/conocer (to know), guardar (to keep), revelar (to reveal), and with the expression “salir a la luz” (to come to light).
target_language_example: No le digas a nadie el secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone the secret.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun to talk about something in second place/order: el segundo mes, el segundo premio, el segundo (one). For feminine nouns, use "la segunda": la segunda semana. Can also mean "the second" as a unit of time (segundo), but the examples here are about order/ranking.
target_language_example: Mi casa es la segunda a la derecha.
native_language_example: My house is the second on the right.

meaning: the traffic light on red (red light).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the situation/status of a traffic light showing red, meaning you must stop. Often used with verbs like ver (to see), parar/pararse (to stop), saltarse (to run/ignore), and pasarse (to go through/run).
target_language_example: No cruces; el semáforo en rojo significa que tienes que parar.
native_language_example: Don’t cross; the red light means you have to stop.

additional_notes: A common, slightly philosophical phrase used when talking about what makes life meaningful (love, happiness, etc.). You’ll often see it in statements like “El sentido de la vida es…” (The meaning of life is…).
target_language_example: Para mí, el sentido de la vida es compartir tiempo con mi familia.
native_language_example: For me, the meaning of life is spending time with my family.

meaning: "Mr." / "sir" (polite form of address for a man).
additional_notes: Used before a man’s last name (El señor Smith) or by itself to address him politely (Señor, ¿puede ayudarme?). Often written as “Sr.” in abbreviations. With professions/titles you may also see “el señor” + title, but most commonly it’s “el señor” + surname.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hablar con el señor García, por favor?
native_language_example: May I speak with Mr. García, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what a specific word means, often when looking it up in a dictionary or asking for an explanation. Common pattern: el significado de la palabra + [X] (e.g., “el significado de la palabra ‘sueño’”).
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es el significado de la palabra “amistad”?
native_language_example: What is the meaning of the word “friendship”?

additional_notes: A common philosophical phrase used when talking about life’s purpose or the reason we exist. It’s often used with verbs like saber/entender/buscar (to know/understand/search for).
target_language_example: A veces me pregunto cuál es el significado de la vida.
native_language_example: Sometimes I wonder what the meaning of life is.

meaning: “the system” (an organized set of parts, rules, or processes).
additional_notes: Used for many kinds of systems: a machine/technical system (el sistema de ventilación), a computer/AI system, or an institutional system (e.g., healthcare, education, legal). It’s masculine singular: el sistema; plural: los sistemas.
target_language_example: El sistema no responde, así que voy a reiniciarlo.
native_language_example: The system isn’t responding, so I’m going to restart it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the type or purpose of a system: el sistema de + noun (energía, alerta, ventilación, arranque, túneles). Often followed by a specific thing the system controls, provides, or is related to.
target_language_example: El sistema de calefacción no funciona.
native_language_example: The heating system isn’t working.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for a piece of living-room furniture you sit/lie on. Use it with the masculine article: el sofá (the sofa) / un sofá (a sofa). Plural: los sofás.
target_language_example: Voy a sentarme en el sofá.
native_language_example: I’m going to sit on the sofa.

additional_notes: Refers to the sun (a masculine noun). Common with verbs like salir (to rise/come out) and ponerse (to set). Also used in the expression "tomar el sol" = "to sunbathe" / "to get some sun."
target_language_example: Hoy hace buen tiempo y brilla el sol.
native_language_example: Today the weather is nice and the sun is shining.

additional_notes: Used to describe the sun (el sol) with an adjective or a noun (es = “is”). Very common in simple descriptions: “El sol es + adjective” (El sol es amarillo / grande) or “El sol es + noun” (El sol es rey...).
target_language_example: El sol es brillante hoy.
native_language_example: The sun is bright today.

meaning: “the sun is” (the sun is + a state/location/action).
additional_notes: Used to describe what the sun is doing or what condition it’s in right now. You’ll usually add a gerund (-ando/-iendo) for an action (e.g., está brillando = is shining, está saliendo = is coming up/rising) or an adjective/past participle for a state (e.g., está escondido = is hidden).
target_language_example: El sol está muy alto hoy.
native_language_example: The sun is very high today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about sunset. You’ll often see it in different tenses: «El sol se ha puesto» (the sun has set), «cuando el sol se ponga» (when the sun sets), «antes de que el sol se pusiera» (before the sun set). The verb is «ponerse» in the sense of “to set” (for the sun).
target_language_example: Vamos a salir antes de que el sol se ponga.
native_language_example: We’re going to leave before the sun sets.

additional_notes: Used to talk about sunset. The verb is "ponerse" (to set, for the sun). You can add where it sets: "El sol se pone en el oeste / por el oeste" (in the west / toward the west). You can also say when it sets: "más pronto" = earlier, "más tarde" = later.
target_language_example: En verano, el sol se pone más tarde.
native_language_example: In summer, the sun sets later.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (el). Often used with clothing verbs like ponerse (to put on) and quitarse (to take off): Quítate el sombrero. / Se quitó el sombrero. It can refer to many kinds of hats (not just a cowboy hat).
target_language_example: Me gusta tu sombrero, ¿dónde lo compraste?
native_language_example: I like your hat—where did you buy it?

additional_notes: A common noun used with "de" to say what a sound comes from: "el sonido del trueno" (the sound of thunder), "el sonido de tu risa" (the sound of your laugh). It can refer to pleasant sounds (music, a voice) or general noise. In audio/tech contexts it can also mean "audio" (e.g., "el sonido está muy bajo" = the sound/audio is very low).
target_language_example: No puedo dormir por el sonido de la calle.
native_language_example: I can't sleep because of the noise from the street.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is making the sound (a voice, a bell, a battle, etc.). It often takes a noun after de: el sonido de la campana (the sound of the bell). You can also use it with a clause that identifies the source: Fue el sonido de la campana lo que le despertó (It was the sound of the bell that woke him up).
target_language_example: Me relajó el sonido de la lluvia.
native_language_example: The sound of the rain relaxed me.

additional_notes: A common descriptive phrase using the pattern “el sonido de + [noun]” (“the sound of + [noun]”). It’s often used with verbs like adorar (to love), encontrar (to find), and ser (to be) to talk about how a sound feels or what it’s like.
target_language_example: Por la noche, el sonido de la lluvia me ayuda a dormir.
native_language_example: At night, the sound of the rain helps me sleep.

additional_notes: Often means “the ground” outside (land/earth), and “the floor” inside a building. Common with location phrases like en el suelo (“on the ground/on the floor”) and actions like barrer el suelo (“sweep the floor”).
target_language_example: Se me cayó el teléfono al suelo.
native_language_example: My phone fell on the floor/ground.

additional_notes: A common place to buy food and household items. Uses the masculine article: el supermercado. You often talk about being there with “en el supermercado” (at/in the supermarket) and its opening hours with “está abierto/cerrado” (it’s open/closed).
target_language_example: Voy al supermercado a comprar leche y pan.
native_language_example: I’m going to the supermarket to buy milk and bread.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the southern direction or the southern part of a place (a country, city, region, etc.). Often appears with prepositions like en el sur (in the south), al sur (to the south), desde el sur (from the south), or por el sur (from/via the south).
target_language_example: Vivimos en el sur de la ciudad.
native_language_example: We live in the south of the city.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun and avoid repeating it. It agrees in gender/number with the thing owned, not with the owner: el suyo (masc. singular), la suya, los suyos, las suyas. Often contrasts with another person’s possession: “Este es mi libro, no el suyo.”
target_language_example: Mi teléfono es nuevo, pero el suyo es más viejo.
native_language_example: My phone is new, but theirs is older.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Saturday. With days of the week in Spanish, you often use the article: el sábado = on Saturday / Saturday (this Saturday or Saturdays in general, depending on context). You can add time words like pasado (last) or próximo/que viene (next): el sábado pasado = last Saturday.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes planes el sábado?
native_language_example: Do you have plans on Saturday?

additional_notes: A room or level below the ground floor of a building. Often used with location verbs like estar (“to be”): Está/Están en el sótano (“He/She is / They are in the basement”). It can also refer to a safe place (e.g., during storms) or a dark/dirty storage area, depending on context.
target_language_example: Guardamos las cajas viejas en el sótano.
native_language_example: We keep the old boxes in the basement.

meaning: the theater; theatre (the building or the art form).
additional_notes: Usually refers either to the place where plays/performances happen (a theater) or to theater as an activity/art form. Common with prepositions: en el teatro (at/in the theater).
target_language_example: Vamos al teatro esta noche.
native_language_example: We’re going to the theater tonight.

meaning: “the theater used to open” (it regularly opened in the past).
additional_notes: Uses **soler + infinitive** to talk about a past habit or routine: **solía abrir** = “used to open / would open (usually)”. Often followed by a time expression (**a esta hora**, **al amanecer**) or days (**los domingos**, **solo los lunes**).
target_language_example: Antes, el teatro solía abrir todos los días a las ocho.
native_language_example: Before, the theater used to open every day at eight.

additional_notes: Usually means "the ceiling" when talking about the inside/top of a room (e.g., something is on the ceiling). It can also mean "the roof" when talking about the top of a building, often outdoors (e.g., cats on the roof).
target_language_example: Hay una lámpara en el techo.
native_language_example: There is a lamp on the ceiling.

meaning: the roof (top covering of a building/house).
additional_notes: Refers to the exterior roof structure (often a sloped/tiled roof). Common patterns: "el tejado de + (house/building)" and "estar en el tejado" (to be on the roof). "A dos aguas" describes a gabled roof (two sloping sides).
target_language_example: Hay una gotera en el tejado.
native_language_example: There’s a leak in the roof.

additional_notes: A common noun for a phone (mobile or landline). It’s masculine: el teléfono, los teléfonos. Often used with verbs like sonar (to ring), colgar (to hang up), llevar (to take/bring), and caerse (to fall/drop).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está el teléfono? No lo encuentro.
native_language_example: Where is the phone? I can’t find it.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite of sonar (“to ring/sound”) to describe a completed event: the phone rang (once/at that moment). Often used to set the scene with another action in progress (e.g., estaba/tomaba… cuando el teléfono sonó). For repeated ringing, you’ll often add phrases like varias veces (“several times”) or cada pocos minutos (“every few minutes”).
target_language_example: Estaba cocinando cuando el teléfono sonó.
native_language_example: I was cooking when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to refer to what people are talking about or the subject of a class/text (“el tema de la clase”). It can also mean an issue under discussion or debate (“el tema del aborto”). Common with verbs like cambiar/poner/retirar/dejar el tema and phrases like “sobre el tema” (about the topic) and “no tener voz en el tema” (not having a say in the matter).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de ese tema ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that topic right now.

additional_notes: Very common word with two main meanings. (1) "the weather": often with verbs like estar, hacer, cambiar, mejorar (e.g., "El tiempo estuvo bien", "Parece que el tiempo va a mejorar"). (2) "time": used for how you spend/use time (e.g., "perder el tiempo" = to waste time; "pasar el tiempo" = to spend time). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: No quiero perder el tiempo; el tiempo hoy está perfecto para salir.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time; the weather today is perfect to go out.

additional_notes: Used to define or describe what time is, often in general statements, sayings, or metaphors. It can also introduce common expressions like “El tiempo es dinero” (“Time is money”). Note: “tiempo” can mean “time” or “weather,” but in this phrase it usually means “time.”
target_language_example: Para mí, el tiempo es lo más valioso que tenemos.
native_language_example: For me, time is the most valuable thing we have.

meaning: “the time that…” / “the amount of time that…”
additional_notes: Used before a clause with **que** to talk about a specific period or duration. Common in phrases like **Aprecio el tiempo que…** (“I appreciate the time that…”), **Te sorprendería el tiempo que…** (“You’d be surprised how long…”), and **Tómese el tiempo que necesite** (“Take whatever time you need,” formal; **Tómate** is informal).
target_language_example: No sabía el tiempo que iba a tardar el autobús.
native_language_example: I didn’t know how long the bus was going to take.

meaning: as long as you want; for as much time as you want.
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom about how long they stay or take. Often appears after verbs like quedarse (to stay) or tomarse (to take, as in time). In commands it often becomes: «Tómate el tiempo que quieras» = “Take as much time as you want.”
target_language_example: Quédate el tiempo que quieras; no hay prisa.
native_language_example: Stay as long as you want; there’s no rush.

additional_notes: In home/entrance contexts, "tocar el timbre" or "llamar al timbre" means “to ring the doorbell.” ("Timbre" can also mean other things like a postage stamp in some contexts, but in these examples it’s clearly the doorbell.)
target_language_example: Si nadie abre, toca el timbre otra vez.
native_language_example: If nobody opens, ring the doorbell again.

meaning: the guy; the man; the type/kind.
additional_notes: Most commonly, **el tipo** means “the guy/the man” when talking about a person (often someone unspecified or not named): *El tipo que hizo esto…* It can sound casual and sometimes slightly dismissive depending on tone/context (similar to “that guy”). In other contexts, **tipo** also means “type/kind” (*¿Qué tipo de comida te gusta?*).
target_language_example: ¿Quién es el tipo de la puerta?
native_language_example: Who’s the guy at the door?

meaning: the kind/type of; the sort of.
additional_notes: Used to classify or describe a category: "el tipo de deportes" (the type of sports), "el tipo de verde" (the shade/kind of green), "el tipo de persona" (the kind of person). With people, it can mean "the kind of person who...": "No es el tipo de hombre que...". In some contexts (especially in speech), "el tipo" can also mean "the guy," but that’s slightly different from the phrase "el tipo de".
target_language_example: No es el tipo de comida que me gusta.
native_language_example: It’s not the kind of food I like.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character or typical behavior, followed by a clause with "que" (often with ser: "que es/eres/soy"). Common for making general statements about what someone is like: "No es el tipo de persona que..." = “He/She isn’t the kind of person who...”.
target_language_example: No soy el tipo de persona que se rinde fácilmente.
native_language_example: I’m not the kind of person who gives up easily.

additional_notes: Uses "tipo" (literally "type") in a common, casual way to mean "guy" or "a person". It introduces a relative clause with "que" to describe which person you mean: "el tipo que + verb..." (the person who...). Can sound a bit informal or blunt depending on context; more neutral options include "el hombre que" (the man who) or "la persona que" (the person who).
target_language_example: El tipo que trabaja en recepción siempre nos ayuda.
native_language_example: The guy who works at reception always helps us.

meaning: work; job; task (the work to be done).
additional_notes: Often refers to work in general (El trabajo tuvo éxito = “the work was successful”), a specific task/project (cumplir con el trabajo = “to do/fulfill the work”), or someone’s job/employment (donde está el trabajo = “where the work/jobs are”). Also used for physical work like yard work: el trabajo en el jardín.
target_language_example: Tengo mucho trabajo hoy, pero voy a terminarlo.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work today, but I’m going to finish it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what a person, animal, or thing does (their role or responsibility), or who/what created something: *El trabajo de él es...* (“His job is...”), *el trabajo de un crítico* (“a critic’s job”), *el trabajo de hombres* (“the work of men”). Often followed by a person (*él/ella/Juan*), a group (*los hombres*), or a noun phrase (*un crítico*).
target_language_example: El trabajo de Ana es cuidar a los niños.
native_language_example: Ana’s job is to take care of the children.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning sustained effort. Often used with verbs like hacer (to make/produce), agotar (to exhaust), vencer (to beat/overcome), and ser el motivo de (to be the reason for).
target_language_example: El trabajo duro siempre da resultados.
native_language_example: Hard work always pays off.

additional_notes: A common transport word. Used with verbs like llegar (to arrive), salir (to leave/depart), parar (to stop), irse (to leave), retrasarse (to be delayed), and perder (to miss). You’ll often see it with stations: la estación (the station).
target_language_example: ¿A qué hora sale el tren?
native_language_example: What time does the train leave?

meaning: “the train” + “se” before a verb (it … / the train …).
additional_notes: This isn’t really a fixed expression; it’s just the subject (el tren = the train) followed by **se**, which appears with many verbs.
