In your examples, **se** is used with pronominal/reflexive-style verbs to show what happens to the train (e.g., **se descarriló** = derailed, **se dio la vuelta** = turned around, **se dirigió** = headed, **se haya detenido** = has stopped). In English you often don’t translate **se** directly; you translate the whole verb phrase.
target_language_example: No salgas hasta que el tren se haya ido.
native_language_example: Don’t get off until the train has left.

meaning: the train was delayed / the train ran late.
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "retrasarse" ("to be delayed / to run late"). Often followed by a time amount ("diez minutos", "una hora") or a reason with "por / a causa de / debido a" ("because of / due to").
target_language_example: El tren se retrasó treinta minutos por el mal tiempo.
native_language_example: The train was delayed thirty minutes because of the bad weather.

additional_notes: Usually refers to road traffic and congestion, especially in cities. Common with verbs like estar atrapado en (to be stuck in), evitar (to avoid), cortar (to stop/block), and phrases like la hora punta (rush hour) or tráfico de la hora punta (rush-hour traffic).
target_language_example: Hoy hay mucho tráfico en el centro, así que voy en metro.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of traffic downtown today, so I’m taking the subway.

additional_notes: A possessive pronoun used to replace a noun already understood from context (e.g., *tu libro* → *el tuyo* = “yours/the one that is yours”). It uses the definite article (*el/la/los/las*) and must match the gender and number of the thing owned (not the owner): *el tuyo* (m.sg.), *la tuya* (f.sg.), *los tuyos* (m.pl.), *las tuyas* (f.pl.). Common after verbs like *ver* (to see) or *querer* (to want): *Déjame ver el tuyo*.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo usar el tuyo un momento?
native_language_example: Can I use yours for a moment?

additional_notes: Common masculine noun. Use "el" for tea in general or when referring to a specific tea you’ve mentioned: "Me encanta el té" (I love tea) / "Aquí está el té" (Here is the tea). You can describe how you take it: "con/sin azúcar" (with/without sugar).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres el té con leche o sin leche?
native_language_example: Do you want the tea with milk or without milk?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the whole cosmos (space, stars, galaxies, everything that exists). It can also be used more loosely or humorously to mean “fate/life/the world” (e.g., "El universo me odia" = "The universe hates me"). Masculine noun: el universo.
target_language_example: A veces siento que el universo conspira a mi favor.
native_language_example: Sometimes I feel like the universe is conspiring in my favor.

additional_notes: Used to express that two people do something mutually/reciprocally (talk to each other, be honest with each other, have responsibilities toward each other). Often appears with verbs like hablar, ser, conocer, ayudar, pelear. For more than two people, you’ll also hear: "los unos con los otros".
target_language_example: Tenemos que apoyarnos el uno con el otro en momentos difíciles.
native_language_example: We have to support each other in difficult times.

additional_notes: Used with two people/things to show a mutual relationship (learning from, loving, depending on, keeping secrets from, being independent of). It often pairs with verbs or phrases that take “from/with/of” in English: aprender (mucho) el uno del otro = learn (a lot) from each other; enamorarse el uno del otro = fall in love with each other; depender el uno del otro = depend on each other; ser independiente el uno del otro = be independent of each other; no guardarse secretos el uno del otro = not keep secrets from each other. For mixed-gender pairs you’ll also see: el uno de la otra / la una del otro.
target_language_example: Nos ayudamos el uno al otro cuando tenemos problemas.
native_language_example: We help each other when we have problems.

meaning: (to be) meant for each other; perfect for each other.
additional_notes: Used to say that two people (usually a couple) are a great match. It often appears after verbs like ser/estar: “(No) somos el uno para el otro” (we are/aren’t meant for each other) or in the common expression “estar hechos el uno para el otro” (to be made for each other). You can change gender/number: “el uno para la otra,” “la una para el otro,” “la una para la otra.” For plural groups: “los unos para los otros / las unas para las otras.”
target_language_example: Creo que ustedes son el uno para el otro.
native_language_example: I think you’re meant for each other.

meaning: "the value of"; in "tener el valor de", "the courage to".
additional_notes: Most commonly means the value/importance of something: "el valor de la información" (the value of information). When it appears after forms of "tener" (e.g., "tuvo el valor de"), it means having the courage/bravery to do something and is followed by an infinitive: "tuvo el valor de decir...".
target_language_example: No todos tienen el valor de decir la verdad.
native_language_example: Not everyone has the courage to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article: el verano. Often used with time expressions like todo el verano (all summer), en verano (in summer), and before/after: antes de que empiece el verano (before summer starts), el verano terminó (summer ended).
target_language_example: En verano hace mucho calor aquí.
native_language_example: In summer it’s very hot here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous summer (relative to now). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence as a time expression: “El verano pasado fuimos…” / “Fuimos… el verano pasado.”
target_language_example: El verano pasado hice un viaje con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Last summer I took a trip with my friends.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “dress” (a one-piece garment, typically worn by women). In some contexts, especially with adjectives like "formal" ("vestido formal"), it can mean “attire” or “outfit.” You’ll also see it with a relative clause: "el vestido que..." = “the dress that...”.
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta el vestido que me compré?
native_language_example: Do you like the dress I bought?

meaning: the trip; the journey; travel (as a noun).
additional_notes: A common noun for a trip/journey from one place to another. Often used with prepositions like durante el viaje (“during the trip”) and for parts of a trip: a la ida (“on the way there”) / a la vuelta (“on the way back”).
target_language_example: Durante el viaje, vimos muchos paisajes bonitos.
native_language_example: During the trip, we saw many beautiful landscapes.

additional_notes: A common noun for moving air outdoors. Often used with verbs like soplar (to blow) and ponerse (to start to become): “El viento sopla” (The wind blows), “El viento se puso fuerte” (The wind got strong). You also see it in fixed phrases like “contra el viento” (against the wind).
target_language_example: Hoy hace mucho viento y no puedo abrir el paraguas.
native_language_example: It’s very windy today and I can’t open the umbrella.

additional_notes: A common weather phrase. It’s often followed by direction phrases like: del este (from the east), del mar (from the sea), desde el oeste (from the west), or adverbs describing intensity (fuerte, suavemente). You can also use it more poetically to mean the wind blows wherever it wants.
target_language_example: Hoy el viento sopla muy fuerte.
native_language_example: Today the wind is blowing very strongly.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific Friday or the upcoming/known Friday. In Spanish, days of the week usually take the definite article (el) when you mean “on” that day: el viernes, el jueves. You can add time expressions: el viernes por la mañana = on Friday morning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you on Friday afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific day in the recent past. It’s formed with a day of the week + pasado/a (past), and it usually goes after the verb: "Llegué el viernes pasado." You can also use it after "desde" to mean "since last Friday": "desde el viernes pasado."
target_language_example: No fui a trabajar el viernes pasado.
native_language_example: I didn't go to work last Friday.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens. "El" is the definite article (like “the”), and Spanish often uses it with days of the week when talking about a specific time. "Por la noche" means “at night / in the evening” (typically nighttime).
target_language_example: Nos vemos el viernes por la noche.
native_language_example: See you on Friday night.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning the alcoholic drink made from grapes. Use **el vino** for the general idea or a specific wine in context (e.g., on a menu). In Spanish, the article **el** is often used when talking about something in general: **Me gusta el vino** = “I like wine.”
target_language_example: Me gusta el vino, pero hoy prefiero agua.
native_language_example: I like wine, but today I prefer water.

additional_notes: Used to talk about red wine in general, often contrasted with el vino blanco (white wine). In Spanish you’ll often see the article (el) when speaking about a category or preference: Me gusta el vino tinto (I like red wine).
target_language_example: ¿Tiene el vino tinto por copa?
native_language_example: Do you have red wine by the glass?

additional_notes: A masculine noun for the musical instrument. Often used with the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument): "tocar el violín" = "to play the violin". Plural: "los violines".
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar el violín?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the violin?

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like bajar/el volumen (turn the volume down) and subir el volumen (turn the volume up). You can also say "(Le) subió el volumen al televisor" to mean someone increased the TV’s volume; "le" refers to the person affected (e.g., Tom).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes bajar el volumen, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn the volume down, please?

additional_notes: Use **el** (masculine singular “the”) with **árbol**. In Spanish, you use **el árbol** when talking about a specific tree (“the one we mean”), and **un árbol** for “a tree.” In Christmas contexts, **el árbol** often means **the Christmas tree** (from context). Plural: **los árboles**.
target_language_example: Ese es el árbol que quiero para el jardín.
native_language_example: That’s the tree I want for the garden.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific place/section or region. Common in instructions or warnings: “despejen el área” = “clear the area.” Also used with directions or labels: “el área Este” = “the east area/sector.”
target_language_example: Por favor, manténgase fuera del área restringida.
native_language_example: Please stay out of the restricted area.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun (e.g., el último autobús = “the last bus”). It can also mean “the most recent” when talking about time periods: el último invierno = “last winter.” Feminine: la última (la última vez = “the last time”). Plural: los/las últimos/as.
target_language_example: Lo siento, llegaste tarde: el último tren ya salió.
native_language_example: Sorry, you arrived late: the last train already left.

additional_notes: Used for the final train service of the day on a route. Often appears with travel verbs like perder (to miss/lose) and coger (to catch/take), and in warnings or urgency: Date prisa o perderás el último tren (Hurry up or you’ll miss the last train).
target_language_example: Si no salimos ya, vamos a perder el último tren.
native_language_example: If we don’t leave now, we’re going to miss the last train.

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one person/thing in a group or situation. It usually goes before a noun ("el único asiento" = "the only seat"). It can also stand alone as a noun phrase ("El único.") meaning "The only one." Feminine: "la única".
target_language_example: Eres el único que entiende este problema.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who understands this problem.

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one man in a group or situation. It agrees in gender and number: el único hombre (the only man), la única mujer (the only woman), los únicos hombres (the only men). You can add details after it, like del comité (on the committee) or que conozco (that I know).
target_language_example: Soy el único hombre en la reunión.
native_language_example: I’m the only man in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the only person (or thing) that does something. It’s followed by a verb: “el único que vino” = “the only one who came.” With “ser”: “No soy el único que…” = “I’m not the only one who…”. For feminine, use “la única que”; for plural, “los/las únicos/as que”.
target_language_example: No eres el único que se siente así.
native_language_example: You’re not the only one who feels that way.

meaning: "the one from/of" or "the one that belongs to (someone)".
additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a noun already understood from context. It’s the definite article + de, functioning like a pronoun: el de + place/thing/person = “the one from/of …” (Ese cartel es igual que el de la estación = “the one at the station”). With possession it can mean “the one belonging to …” (no el de usted = “not yours”). It agrees in gender/number with the noun it replaces: el de, la de, los de, las de. It can also describe a role/type: el de un caballero = “that of a gentleman.”
target_language_example: Mi coche es rojo, pero el de mi hermano es azul.
native_language_example: My car is red, but my brother’s is blue.

additional_notes: Used to avoid repeating a masculine noun already understood from context. It means “the one belonging to / associated with / from” a feminine noun introduced with **de la**. Common in comparisons: **más … que el de la India** = “more … than India’s.” The feminine version is **la de la …** and the plural is **los de la … / las de la …**.
target_language_example: Prefiero el de la camisa azul.
native_language_example: I prefer the one with the blue shirt.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman spent her whole life focused on a cause, activity, or field. After "a" you usually use a noun ("la ciencia") or an infinitive verb ("ayudar a los demás"). In other persons: "yo dediqué mi vida a", "él dedicó su vida a", etc.
target_language_example: Ella dedicó su vida a ayudar a los demás.
native_language_example: She dedicated her life to helping others.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl says. It’s followed by a clause introduced by que. In conversation you might also hear Ella dice: … (with a pause) without que. Verb form: dice = “(she) says” (present tense of decir).
target_language_example: Ella dice que no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: She says she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what a woman said). After **dijo que**, you usually follow with a full clause: **Ella dijo que + [sentence]**. In the past, Spanish often uses **imperfect** to report what someone said (e.g., *dijo que no tenía…*).
target_language_example: Ella dijo que llegaba tarde.
native_language_example: She said that she was arriving late / that she would be late.

meaning: “she gave birth to” (she had a baby).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the phrase “dar a luz (a…)” = “to give birth (to…)”. You use it to say a woman had a baby, often followed by who/what was born: “dio a luz a un niño/una niña” or “dio a luz a su hijo/su hija”. In everyday speech you also hear “tuvo un bebé”.
target_language_example: Ella dio a luz a gemelos el mes pasado.
native_language_example: She gave birth to twins last month.

meaning: she started to / she began to.
additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl began doing something. "Empezó" is the past tense (preterite) of "empezar" (to start), and it’s followed by "a" + infinitive: "empezó a bailar" (she started to dance). You can swap the subject: "él empezó a", "yo empecé a", etc.
target_language_example: Ella empezó a estudiar español el año pasado.
native_language_example: She started studying Spanish last year.

meaning: “she was” (past tense of *ser*, describing what someone/something was like or used to be).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past (*era*, from *ser*) to talk about past descriptions, roles/identities, relationships, and ongoing states in the past: *Ella era actriz* (she was an actress), *Cuando ella era pequeña…* (when she was little…). Often sets background or describes what someone was like. Note: *era* can look like the English noun “era,” but here it’s a verb meaning “was.”
target_language_example: Ella era muy amable cuando la conocí.
native_language_example: She was very kind when I met her.

meaning: "she was a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe what a woman/girl was like in the past, usually followed by a feminine noun or a noun phrase (e.g., *una corredora, una joven, una señora, una heroína*). For masculine nouns, you’d say *él era un*.
target_language_example: Ella era una excelente estudiante cuando vivía en Madrid.
native_language_example: She was an excellent student when she lived in Madrid.

meaning: 'she is' (used to describe a woman/girl or say who she is).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives (Ella es muy buena), nouns/roles (Ella es un genio; Ella es una chica educada), or to emphasize that *she* is the one (Ella es la única que lo logró). In some countries, "seca" can mean 'distant/cold' or 'mean' (Ella es seca conmigo).
target_language_example: Ella es mi profesora de español.
native_language_example: She is my Spanish teacher.

meaning: “she is the …” (referring to a woman or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone with a feminine noun/title: ella es la juez / campeona / dueña / jefa. It’s also used before a relative clause with **la que** (“the one who/that”): *Ella es la que alimenta a nuestro perro* (“She’s the one who feeds our dog”), *Ella es la que más me gusta* (“She’s the one I like the most”).
target_language_example: Ella es la doctora que me ayudó.
native_language_example: She is the doctor who helped me.

additional_notes: Used to identify a female person and say her relationship/role: "Ella es mi prima" (She’s my cousin), "Ella es mi esposa" (She’s my wife). "Mi" is the singular possessive "my" and does not change with gender (mi amigo / mi amiga). For plural, use "mis" (Ella es mi amiga / Ellas son mis amigas).
target_language_example: Ella es mi mejor amiga.
native_language_example: She is my best friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person with an adjective or phrase. Structure: "Ella es muy + adjective" (e.g., astuta, atractiva, joven). "Muy" intensifies the description (very/really).
target_language_example: Ella es muy simpática con todos.
native_language_example: She is very nice to everyone.

meaning: “she is a …” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a woman by saying what she is: Ella es una + feminine noun/adjective phrase (e.g., estudiante, cocinera). The article “una” is feminine; for masculine nouns you’d use “él es un …”. Note: the full sentence can be neutral (Ella es una estudiante) but the noun you choose can be offensive (e.g., “puta” is a strong insult).
target_language_example: Ella es una buena amiga.
native_language_example: She is a good friend.

additional_notes: A basic identification sentence using the verb "ser" (to be). Use "Ella es..." to describe who someone is or what they are (often with an adjective: "Ella es una mujer amable."). "Ella" is often optional in Spanish because the verb form "es" already implies "she/he/it"; you can say "Es una mujer" if context is clear. For emphasis or clarity, keep "ella."
target_language_example: Ella es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very intelligent woman.

meaning: “she is a (kind of) person…” (used to describe someone’s character).
additional_notes: Use this pattern to describe what someone is like: "Ella es una persona" + adjective (fiable, seria, difícil, etc.) or + adjective phrase ("difícil de tratar"). It’s a neutral, common way to talk about personality. For other people: "Él es una persona…" (he), "Soy una persona…" (I), "Eres una persona…" (you).
target_language_example: Ella es una persona muy amable.
native_language_example: She is a very kind person.

meaning: 'she was' / 'she used to be' (imperfect past of *estar*).
additional_notes: *Ella* = “she.” *Estaba* is the imperfect of *estar* and is used for ongoing/background situations in the past, temporary states/feelings, and actions in progress (often with a gerund: *estaba durmiendo* = “was sleeping”). It also commonly sets the scene: *Cuando abrí la puerta, ella estaba…* (“When I opened the door, she was…”).
target_language_example: Ayer por la noche, ella estaba muy cansada.
native_language_example: Last night, she was very tired.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past state/condition of a woman or girl. It’s made of: ella (she) + estaba (was, imperfect of estar) + muy (very). You normally follow it with an adjective: aburrida, emocionada, enferma, nerviosa, callada, etc.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ella estaba muy cansada.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was very tired.

additional_notes: Used with *estar* to talk about temporary states, feelings, health, location, or ongoing situations/actions (often with an adjective or a gerund: *ella está preocupada*, *ella está tratando...*). For permanent identity/characteristics, Spanish often uses *ser* instead (*ella es médica*, *ella es inteligente*).
target_language_example: Ella está cansada hoy, pero mañana estará mejor.
native_language_example: She is tired today, but tomorrow she’ll be better.

meaning: “she is buying” / “she is shopping (for something)” (right now).
additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: ella (she) + estar (to be) + comprando (buying). It emphasizes an action happening right now or around this time. Often followed by what she’s buying (e.g., “un ordenador”) or where she’s buying it (“en la panadería”).
target_language_example: Ella está comprando ropa para el viaje.
native_language_example: She is buying clothes for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to express that a woman feels pride about someone or something. Usually followed by a noun (Ella está orgullosa de su hijo.) or by "de que" + a clause (Ella está orgullosa de que...); in that case Spanish often uses the subjunctive after "de que".
target_language_example: Ella está orgullosa de su trabajo.
native_language_example: She is proud of her work.

meaning: she went to / she went (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the preterite (simple past) of **ir**: **ella fue** = “she went.” It’s commonly followed by **a + place** (Ella fue a París.) or **a + infinitive** to say what she went to do (Ella fue a estudiar / a ver a alguien).
target_language_example: Ella fue a la tienda a comprar pan.
native_language_example: She went to the store to buy bread.

additional_notes: “Fue” is the preterite (completed past) form of **ser** (“to be”) and **ir** (“to go”). In these examples it means **“she was”** (often describing who/what she was). It’s also used in the passive voice: **fue + past participle** (e.g., *fue educada* = “was educated”). Context tells you whether it means “was” (ser) or “went” (ir).
target_language_example: Ella fue la mejor estudiante de la clase.
native_language_example: She was the best student in the class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a state or situation that started in the past and continues to now, or has relevance now. Often appears with time expressions like “desde” (since) and “por” (for) and can be followed by a past participle (ha estado ausente/triste/ocupada) or a gerund for an ongoing activity (ha estado estudiando/practicando/viendo).
target_language_example: Ella ha estado trabajando desde temprano.
native_language_example: She has been working since early.

additional_notes: Present tense of hablar with the subject pronoun ella (“she”). Use it to say what languages she can speak (Ella habla inglés.) or that she talks a lot (Ella habla demasiado.). With topics, use hablar de/sobre (“to talk about”): Ella habla sobre/de una red de energía. Often the subject pronoun is optional in Spanish, so Habla inglés can also mean “She speaks English” if the context is clear.
target_language_example: Ella habla español y francés.
native_language_example: She speaks Spanish and French.

additional_notes: Subject pronoun (ella = “she”) + preterite of hacer (hizo). Used for completed actions in the past. Often followed by a direct object: “Ella hizo la tarea” (She did the homework) or “Ella hizo una torta” (She made a cake). In Spanish, the subject pronoun is often omitted if it’s clear: “Hizo la tarea.”
target_language_example: Ella hizo la tarea anoche.
native_language_example: She did the homework last night.

additional_notes: Uses the present tense of jugar (ella juega) to say what she does regularly or as a routine. "Al" is the contraction of "a + el" and is used with some sports/games (jugar al tenis, jugar al fútbol). You can change the subject (él juega…, yo juego…) or the sport (…al baloncesto).
target_language_example: Ella juega al tenis después de la escuela.
native_language_example: She plays tennis after school.

additional_notes: "Ella" is the subject pronoun (“she”). "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him / to her / to you (formal)” depending on context. It’s used with verbs like "dar" (to give) and "aconsejar" (to advise) to show who receives something or who is affected indirectly: "Ella le dio un regalo" = “She gave him/her a gift.” In many parts of Spain, "le" is also sometimes used for a male direct object (leísmo), but for beginners it’s safest to think of "le" as “to him/her/you (formal).”
target_language_example: Ella le explicó la tarea.
native_language_example: She explained the homework to him/her.

additional_notes: Used to report advice someone (ella) gave to another person (le = to him/her/you formal). It’s typically followed by the subjunctive in Spanish: «Ella le aconsejó que se fuera / leyera / viera…». You can swap «ella» for other subjects (Él/Yo/Nosotros) and «le» for «me/te/nos/les» depending on who receives the advice.
target_language_example: Ella le aconsejó que descansara y bebiera agua.
native_language_example: She advised him/her to rest and drink water.

additional_notes: Pattern: "[Someone] le aconsejó que dejara (de + infinitive)". Use "de + infinitive" to mean “to stop doing” (dejar de beber/fumar/trabajar). "Le" can mean “to him” or “to her” depending on context. "Dejara" is the past subjunctive used after "aconsejar que".
target_language_example: Ella le aconsejó que dejara de comer tanta azúcar.
native_language_example: She advised him/her to stop eating so much sugar.

meaning: 'she bought him/her a …' (she bought a … for him/her).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **comprar**. **Le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him / to her / to you (formal).” The thing being bought comes after (**un boleto, un diccionario, un suéter**). You can also add **a + person** for clarity: *Ella le compró un diccionario a su hermana.*
target_language_example: Ella le compró un regalo a su mamá.
native_language_example: She bought her mom a gift.

additional_notes: Used to report that a woman told something to someone. "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (formal), depending on context. "Contó" is the preterite (simple past) of "contar" (to tell). Often followed by "a + person" (e.g., "Ella le contó a Mary...") or by what was told (e.g., "Ella le contó todo...").
target_language_example: Ella le contó a su hermano la verdad.
native_language_example: She told her brother the truth.

meaning: “she told him/her that …” / “she said to him/her that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech. “le” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (you often need context to know which). What comes after “que” can be an order/request (often with the subjunctive: “que parara/parase”, “que siguiera…”) or a statement of information (often with the indicative: “que su padre había muerto”).
target_language_example: Ella le dijo que no viniera mañana.
native_language_example: She told him/her not to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of dar: dio = “gave.” Le is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him” or “to her” (also used for “to you” in formal usted). Often followed by the thing given (direct object): “Ella le dio la llave” = “She gave him/her the key.” You can add who receives it with a clarifier: “Ella le dio leche al gato” (le = to the cat).
target_language_example: Ella le dio un regalo por su cumpleaños.
native_language_example: She gave him/her a gift for his/her birthday.

additional_notes: Used to report a request from a woman (“ella”) to another person (“le” = to him/her/you formal). After “pedir que”, Spanish typically uses the subjunctive (e.g., entrara, no dejase, se casara, se lo leyera) because it’s a request, not a fact.
target_language_example: Ella le pidió que la ayudara con la maleta.
native_language_example: She asked him/her to help her with the suitcase.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite tense (llegó) to talk about a completed past action. The subject pronoun ella (“she”) is often optional in Spanish (Llegó tarde) unless you need emphasis or to clarify who you mean. You can add where/what she was late for with a + place/event: “Llegó tarde a la escuela.”
target_language_example: Ella llegó tarde a la reunión.
native_language_example: She arrived late to the meeting.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of **llevar** to describe what someone had on (clothing/accessories) at a moment in the past: *Ella llevaba un abrigo/sombrero/cinturón…*. Although **llevar** can mean “to carry,” with clothing it commonly means “to wear,” so it’s not usually translated literally as “she carried a.”
target_language_example: Cuando la vi, ella llevaba un vestido rojo.
native_language_example: When I saw her, she was wearing a red dress.

additional_notes: "Ella" is the subject pronoun “she.” "Lo" is an unstressed direct object pronoun meaning “him” (for a male person) or “it” (for a masculine singular thing/idea). With a conjugated verb, "lo" normally goes before the verb: "Ella lo visita" = “She visits him/it.” (With an infinitive or gerund, it can attach: "Ella va a visitarlo" / "Ella está visitándolo").
target_language_example: Ella lo ve todos los días.
native_language_example: She sees him/it every day.

meaning: 'she did it' / 'she made him/it do it'.
additional_notes: Literal pieces: ella = 'she', lo = 'it/him' (direct object pronoun), hizo = 'did/made' (preterite of hacer). Most often it means 'she did it' (e.g., Ella lo hizo a propósito = 'She did it on purpose'). With an infinitive, it can be causative: ella lo hizo + infinitive = 'she made him do (something)' (e.g., Ella lo hizo hacerlo = 'She made him do it').
target_language_example: Ella lo hizo ayer.
native_language_example: She did it yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to show that the subject is "she" (ella) and that "me" is the object affected by the action. "Me" is often an indirect object (to/for me), as in "Ella me sonríe" (she smiles at me) and "Ella me lo contó" (she told it to me). In Spanish, "ella" is often optional because the verb ending already shows the subject; speakers may include it for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Ella me llamó anoche.
native_language_example: She called me last night.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said. After "dijo que", you typically use the past tenses (e.g., "conocía", "iría", "había comprado") or the imperfect subjunctive for requests/commands (e.g., "que la viera" = "that I see/visit her"). Often shortened in speech to "me dijo que..." when it’s clear who "she" is.
target_language_example: Ella me dijo que no podía venir hoy.
native_language_example: She told me that she couldn’t come today.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite (simple past) of **dar**: **dio** = “gave.” **me** is the indirect object pronoun (“to me”). It’s followed by what was given: **Ella me dio un regalo** (“She gave me a gift”). It can also appear in set phrases like **Ella me dio la espalda** (“She turned her back on me / ignored me”).
target_language_example: Ella me dio su número de teléfono.
native_language_example: She gave me her phone number.

additional_notes: "Enseñó" is the simple past (preterite) of "enseñar" (to teach/show). With "me" it means she taught me something (a skill/knowledge): "me enseñó a + infinitive" (she taught me to do...), or she showed me something (a place/thing): "me enseñó" + a noun (she showed me the campus/car/garden).
target_language_example: Ella me enseñó a cocinar paella.
native_language_example: She taught me how to cook paella.

meaning: "she doesn't / she has not" (starts a negative sentence about a woman or girl).
additional_notes: Used to begin a negative statement with the subject "ella" (“she”) followed by "no" (“not”). In Spanish, "no" typically goes directly before the verb: "Ella no habla" = “She doesn’t speak.” You’ll often see it with different tenses: "Ella no ha..." (present perfect) or "Ella no habla..." (present).
target_language_example: Ella no quiere ir hoy.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl does not have a certain quality or identity. Follow it with an adjective (Ella no es joven), a noun (Ella no es mi madre), or part of a longer structure like: "no es solo X sino también Y" (not only X but also Y) and "no es..., sino..." (not ..., but rather ...). For comparisons, you’ll often see: "Ella no es menos + adjective + que..." (She is not less ... than...).
target_language_example: Ella no es de aquí; es de México.
native_language_example: She isn't from here; she's from Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to say a woman/girl is not to the same degree of an adjective as someone/something else. It’s commonly followed by an adjective and then a comparison with "como" (e.g., "Ella no es tan + adjective + como..."). You can swap "ella" for another subject: "yo/tú/él/nosotros... no soy/eres/es/somos tan...".
target_language_example: Ella no es tan alta como su amiga.
native_language_example: She isn’t as tall as her friend.

additional_notes: Used when **ella** (she) is the subject, **no** negates the verb, and **le** is an **indirect object pronoun** meaning “to him,” “to her,” or “to you” (formal). It usually comes right before the conjugated verb: *Ella no le dijo…* / *Ella no le prestó…*. The exact meaning of **le** depends on context (who is receiving the action).
target_language_example: Ella no le contó la verdad a su mamá.
native_language_example: She didn’t tell her mom the truth.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of poder for “she,” used for a specific situation or event where she was unable to do something. Often followed by an infinitive: “Ella no pudo + comprender/entender/venir…”. In “Ella no pudo haber dicho eso,” it can also mean “She couldn’t have said that” (the speaker thinks it’s impossible/unlikely).
target_language_example: Ella no pudo venir a la fiesta porque estaba enferma.
native_language_example: She couldn’t come to the party because she was sick.

additional_notes: From ella (she) + no (not) + tiene (has). Used to negate possession or to say someone lacks something: Ella no tiene dinero/hijos. It’s also used in common expressions like no tener la razón (“to not be right”) and no tener conciencia de… (“to have no awareness of…”). With quantities, no tiene más de… means “she has no more than…”, and no tiene menos de… means “she has no fewer than…”.
target_language_example: Ella no tiene tiempo para salir hoy.
native_language_example: She doesn't have time to go out today.

ella no tiene nada que ver

target_language_multi_word_term: ella no tiene nada que ver
meaning: “She has nothing to do with (it)” / “She isn’t involved.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not connected to, responsible for, or involved in something. Very common with **con**: *no tiene nada que ver con eso/esto/él/ella*. You can also say it without *con* when the context is clear: *Ella no tiene nada que ver.*
target_language_example: Tranquilo: ella no tiene nada que ver con lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Relax: she has nothing to do with what happened.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what a woman/girl wants to do or have. It’s the present tense of querer with the subject pronoun ella (“she”). Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., comprar, jugar, leer, saber, ser, tomar). You can also drop the pronoun in Spanish if it’s clear from context: Quiere leer un libro.
target_language_example: Ella quiere aprender español.
native_language_example: She wants to learn Spanish.

meaning: "she can speak" / "she knows how to speak" (a language).
additional_notes: Uses **saber + infinitive (hablar)** to express ability/skill. It’s commonly followed by the language (e.g., *español, ruso*) and sometimes an adverb like *bien* (“well”). You can add other verbs too: *Ella sabe hablar y escribir en francés* (“She can speak and write in French”).
target_language_example: Ella sabe hablar italiano muy bien.
native_language_example: She can speak Italian very well.

additional_notes: Used before a verb when the subject is "ella" and the verb takes **se**. Often **reflexive** (the action happens to herself): *Ella se bajó del carro* (She got out), *Ella se calentó* (She warmed herself), *Ella se talló los ojos* (She rubbed her eyes). It can also show doing something **for herself**: *Ella se compró un peine* (She bought herself a comb). With forgetting, Spanish commonly uses **se le olvidó**: *Se le olvidó el paraguas* (She forgot the umbrella).
target_language_example: Ella se lavó las manos antes de comer.
native_language_example: She washed her hands before eating.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "casarse con" (to marry / to get married to). Used with "con" before the person someone marries: "Se casó con + [person]". You can swap the subject: "Él se casó con...", "Me casé con...".
target_language_example: Ella se casó con su novia el año pasado.
native_language_example: She married her girlfriend last year.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "casarse con" (to marry / to get married to). "Ella" = she. "Se casó" is the past tense (preterite): “got married / married.” "Con un" introduces a masculine singular noun: un bombero, un músico, un estadounidense. For a woman, use "con una" (e.g., "Ella se casó con una doctora"). For “he married…”, say "Él se casó con…".
target_language_example: Ella se casó con un profesor de historia.
native_language_example: She married a history teacher.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of “casarse con” = “to get married to.” Uses the reflexive pronoun “se” and the preposition “con” before the person: “casarse con alguien.” Often followed by time phrases (el año pasado) or reasons with “por” (por dinero, por su dinero, porque…).
target_language_example: Ella se casó con él cuando tenía veinticinco años.
native_language_example: She married him when she was twenty-five.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "enamorarse de" (to fall in love with). Use "de" before the person/thing: "se enamoró de él/ella", "se enamoró de un artista". The "se" is part of the verb (reflexive) and is required.
target_language_example: Ella se enamoró de él en cuanto lo conoció.
native_language_example: She fell in love with him as soon as she met him.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "irse" (to leave/go away) in the simple past (pretérito): "se fue". It can mean she left (departed) or she went (to another place), and it’s often followed by a destination or direction: "se fue a París" (she went to Paris), "se fue por ese camino" (she went down that way). By itself ("Ella se fue."), it simply means she left.
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, ella se fue sin decir nada.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, she left without saying anything.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **irse** (to leave/go away). **Se fue a + place** means she departed and went to that destination (often implying she’s no longer here). It’s very common with countries/cities: *Ella se fue a México / a Estados Unidos*. You can often translate it as “she went to,” but **se fue** emphasizes leaving.
target_language_example: Ayer ella se fue a Madrid por trabajo.
native_language_example: Yesterday she left for Madrid for work.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect of "irse" (to leave/go away): "se ha ido". It often implies she is no longer here/has departed, and the destination may be added with "a" (a la piscina), "al" (al extranjero), or it can be used alone: "Ella se ha ido." In some contexts it can sound final or emotional (e.g., "Ella se ha ido, pero la vida sigue").
target_language_example: No la busques: ella se ha ido a casa.
native_language_example: Don’t look for her—she has gone home.

additional_notes: From the verb negarse a + infinitive (“to refuse to do something”). This entry is specifically in the past tense (pretérito): se negó = “she refused.” It’s often followed by an infinitive: se negó a admitir / hablar / ir / seguir. You can change the subject and tense: él se negó a… / ella se niega a… / ella se ha negado a….
target_language_example: Ella se negó a ayudarme con la tarea.
native_language_example: She refused to help me with the homework.

meaning: "she put on" (clothing) or "she became/got" (a new state).
additional_notes: From the verb **ponerse** (reflexive). Common uses: **ponerse + clothing** = to put on (Ella se puso su abrigo.); **ponerse + adjective/color** = to become/get (Ella se puso roja.); **ponerse de pie** = to stand up. (In real speech you’ll often change the subject: *me puse, te pusiste, se puso*, etc.)
target_language_example: Ella se puso nerviosa antes del examen.
native_language_example: She got nervous before the exam.

meaning: she started to cry; she burst into tears.
additional_notes: Uses the common pattern "ponerse a" + infinitive to mean "to start doing something" (often suddenly or unexpectedly). In this exact phrase, "se puso" refers to "she" (ella) and "llorar" means "to cry." You can swap the person: "me puse a llorar" (I started to cry), "se pusieron a llorar" (they started to cry).
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó la noticia, ella se puso a llorar.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she started to cry.

additional_notes: From the verb "quedarse" (to stay, remain). It’s commonly used to say someone stayed in a place for a while (por un momento, por varios días) or remained in a situation/position (e.g., "se quedó muy cerca"). Depending on context, "se quedó" can also mean "was left" (e.g., "se quedó sola" = she ended up/was left alone).
target_language_example: Ella se quedó en casa toda la tarde.
native_language_example: She stayed at home all afternoon.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of sentarse (“to sit down”). Uses the reflexive pronoun se, which is required with sentarse. Often followed by en + place (en el piso, en la silla) or paired with another action: “Ella se sentó y…” (“She sat down and…”).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó en la silla y abrió el libro.
native_language_example: She sat down in the chair and opened the book.

additional_notes: Used to describe where a woman sat in relation to someone or something. "Cerca de" means "near/close to" and is followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., cerca de mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros). You can change the subject and tense: "Me senté cerca de…" (I sat near…), "Se sentaron cerca de…" (They sat near…).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó cerca de la ventana para leer.
native_language_example: She sat near the window to read.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe someone’s appearance or impression: "Ella se ve feliz" (She looks happy), "Ella se ve sola" (She looks lonely). It can also be used with "en" to talk about how someone looks in certain clothes: "Ella se ve mejor en..." (She looks better in...). Although it literally uses the verb "ver" (to see), here "verse" works like English "to look/seem," not "to see."
target_language_example: Ella se ve cansada hoy.
native_language_example: She looks tired today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a woman/girl who does something habitually or in every case. It’s the subject pronoun "ella" (she) + the adverb "siempre" (always), usually placed before the verb: "Ella siempre se levanta...". In everyday Spanish, the pronoun is often dropped if it’s clear from context: "Siempre se levanta a las seis."
target_language_example: Ella siempre llega temprano a clase.
native_language_example: She always arrives early to class.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is consistently true about her. Often followed by an adjective (ella siempre está contenta) or by the gerund to talk about a repeated/typical action (ella siempre está fumando = she’s always smoking). Also used with “estar” + adjective to describe a temporary state or condition; with “estar” + gerund it can sound like a habit or something she does all the time (sometimes with a slightly critical tone, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ella siempre está ocupada los lunes.
native_language_example: She’s always busy on Mondays.

additional_notes: “Tenía” is the imperfect past of “tener” (to have). It often describes an ongoing state in the past, a habitual situation, or background information (not a single finished event). Common patterns include: “tenía ganas de + infinitive” (she felt like / wanted to…), “tenía en mente + infinitive” (she had in mind to…), “tenía la opción de + infinitive” (she had the option to…), and “tenía + noun” (she had + a thing/trait, e.g., defects).
target_language_example: Cuando era niña, ella tenía mucho miedo a la oscuridad.
native_language_example: When she was a child, she was very afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman or girl possesses something or has a characteristic. It’s the verb "tener" (to have) conjugated for "ella" (she) in the present tense. Often followed by a noun (ella tiene un perro), an adjective/noun for a trait (ella tiene curiosidad), or other expressions with "tener" (e.g., ella tiene 20 años = she is 20 years old).
target_language_example: Ella tiene un perro y un restaurante.
native_language_example: She has a dog and a restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **tener** to say that a woman has or possesses something, or to describe a characteristic (e.g., *un acento*, *un buen corazón*). **Un** is the masculine singular indefinite article, used before masculine singular nouns (e.g., *un novio*, *un rostro*). For feminine nouns, it changes to **una** (*Ella tiene una hermana*).
target_language_example: Ella tiene un coche nuevo.
native_language_example: She has a new car.

additional_notes: Used to say that a female person possesses or has something. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is used before singular feminine nouns (e.g., "una rosa", "una ventaja"). In Spanish, "tener" can be used for both physical things ("una rosa") and more abstract things ("una manera", "una ventaja").
target_language_example: Ella tiene una idea muy buena.
native_language_example: She has a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (e.g., bajar, convencer, investigar, no llorar) to say that she made an effort to do something. In the past tense (pretérito): trató. You can change the subject: yo traté de (I tried to), él trató de (he tried to), etc.
target_language_example: Ella trató de llegar temprano, pero había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: She tried to arrive early, but there was a lot of traffic.

meaning: "she lives" (she resides; or she is alive).
additional_notes: Most commonly used to talk about where or how a woman/girl lives: location (Ella vive cerca/de aquí/en Madrid), living situation (Ella vive sola/con sus padres), or lifestyle/conditions (Ella vive en la abundancia). It can also literally mean “she is alive,” but that usually needs context (e.g., after an accident).
target_language_example: Ella vive con su hermana en el centro.
native_language_example: She lives with her sister downtown.

meaning: “she lives in” (she resides in; or lives in a certain condition).
additional_notes: Used to say where a woman/girl lives: Ella vive en + place. It can also be figurative: Ella vive en + abstract noun (e.g., en la abundancia = “in abundance”). In Spanish you can’t drop “en” here (not *ella vive Madrid*).
target_language_example: Ella vive en este barrio desde 2020.
native_language_example: She has lived in this neighborhood since 2020.

additional_notes: "Ellos" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Estaban" is the imperfect past of "estar" and is used for states/conditions (cansados, listos, enamorados) or ongoing actions in the past, often with a gerund (estaban discutiendo, estaban jugando). It commonly sets background context: what was happening/what they were like at that time.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ellos estaban esperando afuera.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were waiting outside.

meaning: 'they are' (temporary state/location) or 'they are' + a gerund ('they are ...-ing').
additional_notes: "Ellos" = "they" (often dropped in Spanish unless you need emphasis/contrast). "Están" is the present tense of "estar" (to be) used for temporary states, locations, and many conditions: "Ellos están a favor" (They’re in favor), "Ellos están por empezar" (They’re about to start). With a gerund (-ando/-iendo), it forms the present progressive: "Ellos están leyendo" (They are reading). For marriage, Spanish usually says "Están casados desde hace dos años" (They’ve been married for two years).
target_language_example: Ellos están en casa y están preparando la cena.
native_language_example: They are at home and are preparing dinner.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (ellos quieren más dinero = they want more money) or with an infinitive (ellos quieren estar contigo = they want to be with you). With “que” + verb in the subjunctive, it means “they want (someone) to do something” (ellos quieren que haga… = they want me to do…).
target_language_example: Ellos quieren que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: They want you to come tomorrow.

meaning: "they" + "se" (they themselves / each other), used with reflexive, reciprocal, or pronominal verbs.
additional_notes: "Se" is a pronoun that goes with "ellos" when the subject does the action to itself (reflexive: "Ellos se lavan" = They wash themselves) or to one another (reciprocal: "Ellos se saludaron" = They greeted each other). It also appears in many pronominal verbs where English often just uses a normal verb: "Ellos se escaparon" = They escaped; "Ellos se quedaron" = They stayed/ended up. "Se" usually comes right before the conjugated verb ("Ellos se van") and can attach to an infinitive ("van a encontrarse").
target_language_example: Ellos se ayudan cuando tienen problemas.
native_language_example: They help each other when they have problems.

meaning: "they are" (for a group of men, or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to identify or describe who people are (with nouns, professions, nationality, or adjectives). "Ellos" is the subject pronoun and is often omitted in Spanish when it’s clear from context ("Son jugadores de béisbol"). Use "ellas son" for a group of all women.
target_language_example: Ellos son mis vecinos.
native_language_example: They are my neighbors.

meaning: “they have” / “they’ve got”; also “they have to” (in “tienen que”).
additional_notes: Present tense of "tener" with "ellos" (“they”). Used for possession (Ellos tienen la llave), relationships/attributes (Ellos tienen un lazo sanguíneo), and with "que" to express obligation/necessity: "Ellos tienen que..." = “They have to...”. In everyday speech, Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you may also hear just "tienen" when it’s clear who “they” are.
target_language_example: Ellos tienen que irse ahora, pero tienen el número de teléfono.
native_language_example: They have to leave now, but they have the phone number.

meaning: 'they are going to' (they will / they’re going to do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the near future or an intention/plan. Structure: "ellos" (they) + "van" (they go) + "a" + infinitive: "van a hacer" = they’re going to do. In some contexts it can also mean "they go to" as movement (e.g., "Ellos van a la escuela" = They go to school), but in your examples it’s followed by a verb, so it’s the future/intention meaning.
target_language_example: Ellos van a salir temprano mañana.
native_language_example: They’re going to leave early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of empezar: it describes the moment you began doing an action. It’s followed by an infinitive: empecé a + verb (empecé a estudiar, empecé a trabajar). For other subjects: empezó a (he/she started to), empezamos a (we started to).
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español el mes pasado.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish last month.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haber** (e.g., **he/has/ha/había empezado a**) + an infinitive to say someone has begun doing something: **He empezado a estudiar** (“I’ve started to study”). It’s common in the present perfect (**he/has/ha empezado a**) and past perfect (**había empezado a**).
target_language_example: He empezado a trabajar aquí esta semana.
native_language_example: I’ve started working here this week.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the “to ___” form): empezando a + infinitive. Often appears in the progressive with estar (estoy/está/están empezando a…) or with se for things that are starting to happen on their own (se está empezando a acabar = “it’s starting to run out”).
target_language_example: Estoy empezando a sentirme mejor.
native_language_example: I'm starting to feel better.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: "empezar a + infinitive" (empezar a comer, empezar a hablar). Common in many tenses (empecé a…, voy a empezar a…, acaba de empezar a…). It’s often interchangeable with "comenzar a".
target_language_example: Voy a empezar a estudiar ahora.
native_language_example: I’m going to start studying now.

meaning: to start over; to start again.
additional_notes: Used when you restart something from the beginning, often after a mistake, failure, or a big change in life. It can be literal (redo a task) or more personal (restart your life/routine). Also commonly said as "volver a empezar".
target_language_example: Me equivoqué con el formulario, así que tengo que empezar de nuevo.
native_language_example: I made a mistake on the form, so I have to start over.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "empezar" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes": "empezaron". It’s used to say that a group started doing something at a specific moment in the past, and it’s typically followed by "a" + infinitive (e.g., "empezaron a hablar"). In the present tense you’ll often see "empiezan a" (stem change e→ie).
target_language_example: Después de la música, todos empezaron a cantar.
native_language_example: After the music started, everyone began to sing.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "empezar a" + infinitive. Used to say that someone/something began an action at a specific moment in the past (often translated as “started to” or “began to”). The verb that follows stays in the infinitive: empezó a ladrar / trabajar / tocar.
target_language_example: Cuando llegó la lluvia, empezó a correr hacia casa.
native_language_example: When the rain arrived, he/she started running toward home.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of empezar a + infinitive to talk about starting an action at a specific moment in the past. It agrees with the subject (e.g., empecé a estudiar = I started studying; empezamos a estudiar = we started studying). Often followed by details like when, why, or what you studied.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, empezó a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she started studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito): empezó = "started" (from empezar), a + infinitive is used to say you start doing something. Llorar = "to cry." Use it with a subject if needed: "Mi hermana empezó a llorar" = "My sister started to cry."
target_language_example: Cuando vio el perro perdido, empezó a llorar.
native_language_example: When she saw the lost dog, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of empezar (empezó = “(it) began/started”) + a + infinitive (llover = “to rain”). Common for describing a change in weather at a specific moment; often with time phrases like de repente (“suddenly”) or tan pronto como… (“as soon as…”).
target_language_example: Íbamos a caminar, pero empezó a llover otra vez.
native_language_example: We were going to go for a walk, but it started to rain again.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say that someone or something begins an action: "Empieza a hablar" (He/She starts to talk). Often follows commands or suggestions: "Empieza a practicar" (Start practicing). Note: "empieza a" can also mean "starts at" when followed by a time (not an infinitive): "La escuela empieza a las ocho y media" (School starts at 8:30).
target_language_example: Empieza a llover, mejor nos vamos.
native_language_example: It’s starting to rain; we’d better go.

additional_notes: Used to give a schedule: "empieza a las [time] y…" is usually followed by another verb like "acaba"/"termina" (ends/finishes) or another time. With times in Spanish, you normally use "a las" (at + the) plus the hour: "a las nueve" = at nine o’clock.
target_language_example: La tienda empieza a las nueve y cierra a las cinco.
native_language_example: The store starts at nine and closes at five.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) the exact location. Common with verbs like estar (to be), haber (there is/are), esconder (to hide), dejar (to leave/forget), and with clues/evidence: “Debe estar en alguna parte” = “It must be somewhere.” You can also use it more abstractly: “en alguna parte de…” = “somewhere in…”.
target_language_example: Mis llaves tienen que estar en alguna parte.
native_language_example: My keys have to be somewhere.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to mean an unspecified location or moment (often when you don’t know or don’t want to say exactly where/when). Common patterns: "en algún lugar" (somewhere), "en algún lago" (in some lake), "en algún punto" (at some point). Feminine singular is "en alguna" (e.g., "en alguna parte").
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves en algún lugar de la casa.
native_language_example: I left the keys somewhere in the house.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t say) the exact place. Very common in conversation. Often appears with verbs like estar/haber (to be/there is) and with “por aquí” to mean “around here somewhere”: “Tiene que estar por aquí en algún lado.”
target_language_example: Dejé mis llaves en algún lado y no las encuentro.
native_language_example: I left my keys somewhere and I can’t find them.

additional_notes: Used when the exact place is unknown, not specified, or not important. It can be used alone as a short answer (e.g., “En algún lugar.” = “Somewhere.”). Also common with extra details: “en algún lugar del oeste” = “somewhere in the west.”
target_language_example: Déjame las llaves en algún lugar seguro.
native_language_example: Leave the keys somewhere safe.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified time in the past or future. It can mean “eventually” when you expect something to happen sooner or later (Tenía que pasar en algún momento). It can also sound vague/noncommittal in plans (Podemos quedar… en algún momento).
target_language_example: En algún momento te llamaré para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you at some point to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know (or don’t want to say) the exact place. With verbs like estar/haber it means a location (“There’s a hotel somewhere around here”). With actions like cenar it can mean you need to choose a place (“You’ll have to have dinner somewhere”). It’s also common with leer/ver/oír: “I read/saw/heard it somewhere” (the source isn’t specific).
target_language_example: Creo que dejé mis llaves en algún sitio de la casa.
native_language_example: I think I left my keys somewhere in the house.

meaning: in/at that (over there); at that time.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to refer to something farther away (in space, time, or in the story) than "este/ese". Common with time expressions: "en aquel tiempo" = "at that time (back then)". It’s often followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., "en aquel banco", "en aquel juicio").
target_language_example: En aquel momento no entendí lo que estaba pasando.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t understand what was happening.

meaning: at that moment; back then (at that time).
additional_notes: Points to a specific time in the past that’s distant from “now” (often like “at that point” or “back then”). It can appear at the start of a sentence as a time marker: “En aquel momento, …”.
target_language_example: En aquel momento, no entendí lo que estaba pasando.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t understand what was happening.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (the means of transport). It often contrasts with other options: en tren (by train), en barco (by boat). You can use it alone as a short answer (e.g., to “How will you go?”).
target_language_example: Vamos en avión porque es más rápido.
native_language_example: We’re going by plane because it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, venir, llegar) to say how someone travels. You can also say "ir en bici" (more casual) as a shorter version.
target_language_example: Hoy voy al parque en bicicleta.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the park by bike.

additional_notes: Used mainly for images, photos, films, or TV that have no color. Often follows the noun (e.g., “televisión en blanco y negro”) or is used after verbs like dejar/poner (“dejar las fotos en blanco y negro”).
target_language_example: Prefiero imprimir esta foto en blanco y negro.
native_language_example: I prefer to print this photo in black and white.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is working well or hasn’t been damaged or worn out. It can also be used with health: “en buen estado de salud” = “in good health.” Often used with the verb “estar” (to be): “está/están en buen estado.”
target_language_example: El teléfono está viejo, pero todavía está en buen estado.
native_language_example: The phone is old, but it’s still in good condition.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes somewhere or does something with the purpose of finding or achieving something. Common with verbs like ir, salir, viajar, andarse/ir de viaje. Usually followed by a noun (en busca de aventuras, en busca de trabajo).
target_language_example: Salimos temprano en busca de un buen restaurante.
native_language_example: We left early in search of a good restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at your home together with your family. Often appears with common routines (cenar, comer) and with estar/quedarse (to be/stay) plus en casa.
target_language_example: Hoy prefiero quedarme en casa con mi familia.
native_language_example: Today I’d rather stay at home with my family.

additional_notes: Used to say someone spends the entire day at home. Often appears with verbs like “quedarse” (to stay) or “estar” (to be): “Me quedé en casa todo el día” = “I stayed at home all day.”
target_language_example: Hoy estoy en casa todo el día porque no trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m at home all day because I’m not working.

additional_notes: Used to explain what you should do if an emergency happens. Often appears in instructions, signs, and safety rules. You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence, and it’s commonly followed by a command (imperative), like "llama" (call) or "presione" (press).
target_language_example: En caso de emergencia, salga por esta puerta.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, exit through this door.

additional_notes: Used in emergency instructions and signs. It introduces what you should do if a fire happens; commonly followed by the subjunctive/imperative (e.g., use, don’t use, break, press).
target_language_example: En caso de incendio, salga del edificio y llame al 112.
native_language_example: In case of fire, leave the building and call 112.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after five minutes have passed from now, or as a deadline: En cinco minutos quiero verte... It can also be a short standalone answer to mean “in five minutes.” Similar pattern: en + number + minutos/horas/días.
target_language_example: Llego en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/poner/mantenerse/ponerse: estar en contacto = to be in touch; poner a alguien en contacto con alguien = to put someone in touch with someone; mantenerse en contacto = to stay in touch; ponerse en contacto con alguien = to get in touch with someone (often by phone/email). Often followed by "con" + person/group.
target_language_example: ¿Te puedo poner en contacto con mi compañero?
native_language_example: Can I put you in touch with my coworker?

additional_notes: Used with estar/seguir/mantenerse/ponerse to talk about staying or getting in touch with someone or something: Estoy en contacto con…, Me mantengo en contacto con…, Ponte/Póngase en contacto con…. Often implies ongoing communication (by email, phone, etc.).
target_language_example: Me mantengo en contacto con mis amigos por WhatsApp.
native_language_example: I stay in touch with my friends on WhatsApp.

meaning: 'in touch with him' / 'in contact with him'.
additional_notes: Used with estar or mantenerse to say you are (or stay) in communication with him (by phone, email, messages, etc.). Very common with the verb phrase ponerse en contacto con + persona = 'to get in touch/contact someone' (me pondré en contacto con él = I'll contact him). The pronoun él means 'him' (with accent to distinguish it from el = 'the').
target_language_example: No estoy en contacto con él desde hace meses.
native_language_example: I haven’t been in touch with him for months.

meaning: against the war; opposed to the war.
additional_notes: Used with estar (or sometimes ser) to express opposition to something: estar en contra de + noun/infinitive. Here, de la guerra means “of the war,” so the whole phrase expresses being opposed to war (or to a specific war, depending on context). You can swap in other nouns: en contra del plan, en contra de la decisión.
target_language_example: Mucha gente está en contra de la guerra.
native_language_example: Many people are against the war.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something you didn’t want to do, often because someone pressured you or forced you. You can also change the possessive pronoun: en contra de tu/su/nuestra voluntad (against your/his/her/our will). Common with verbs like hacer, tomar, casarse, obligar.
target_language_example: Firmé el contrato en contra de mi voluntad.
native_language_example: I signed the contract against my will.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something because they were forced or pressured, not because they wanted to. It often appears with verbs like "hacer" (to do), "casarse" (to get married), or expressions like "verse obligado/a" (to be forced). You can change the possessive: "en contra de mi/tu/su/nuestra/su voluntad".
target_language_example: Aceptó el trato en contra de su voluntad.
native_language_example: He accepted the deal against his will.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean it doesn’t matter which one: en cualquier sitio (any place), en cualquier lugar (anywhere), en cualquier sociedad (any society). Typically you’ll see it as “en cualquier + [noun]”.
target_language_example: Puedes sentarte en cualquier mesa.
native_language_example: You can sit at any table.

additional_notes: Used to say that location doesn’t matter or is unknown/uncertain. Often follows verbs like estar (to be), dormir (to sleep), encontrar(se) (to find / be found): “puede estar en cualquier parte” = “it could be anywhere.”
target_language_example: Mis llaves pueden estar en cualquier parte.
native_language_example: My keys could be anywhere.

meaning: as for me; as far as I’m concerned.
additional_notes: Used to shift the topic to your own situation/opinion. Often followed by a comma: “En cuanto a mí, …”. You can change the pronoun: “en cuanto a ti/él/ella/nosotros…”. Similar to “por mi parte”.
target_language_example: En cuanto a mí, prefiero quedarme en casa esta noche.
native_language_example: As for me, I’d rather stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to show that one action happens immediately after another: en cuanto + present subjunctive for future situations (En cuanto vuelva, te llamo.). With past events, it often uses the indicative (Vine en cuanto pude.). It can also mean “as for/regarding” in other contexts, but in these examples it’s about time.
target_language_example: En cuanto llegues a casa, mándame un mensaje.
native_language_example: As soon as you get home, send me a message.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future action that will happen immediately after an arrival. After **en cuanto**, Spanish typically uses the **present subjunctive** (here, **llegue**) when the arrival is in the future or not yet certain. The subject is understood from context (e.g., “as soon as you arrive,” “as soon as I arrive,” etc.).
target_language_example: En cuanto llegue al hotel, te mando un mensaje.
native_language_example: As soon as I arrive at the hotel, I’ll send you a message.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern **en cuanto + [verb]** to mean “as soon as…”. **Me vio** is the preterite of **ver** (“to see”) and means “(he/she) saw me.” Often used to show that one action happened immediately after seeing someone: *En cuanto me vio, + [reaction/action].*
target_language_example: En cuanto me vio, me saludó con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: As soon as he/she saw me, he/she greeted me with a smile.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something at the earliest possible moment. It commonly follows a future idea (volveré, lo haré, te lo devolveré) and uses the subjunctive after en cuanto: en cuanto pueda (not *en cuanto puedo* in this meaning).
target_language_example: Te llamaré en cuanto pueda.
native_language_example: I’ll call you as soon as I can.

additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like **tener en cuenta** (to keep in mind / take into account), **tomar en cuenta** (to take into account / consider), and **tener a alguien en cuenta** (to consider someone). Also appears in **tomando en cuenta...** meaning “considering...” or “given...”.
target_language_example: Toma en cuenta el clima antes de salir.
native_language_example: Take the weather into account before you go out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acted to protect themselves (often in legal or police contexts). It can appear alone as a short explanation ("En defensa propia.") or inside a sentence ("Actuó en defensa propia").
target_language_example: Solo lo empujé en defensa propia.
native_language_example: I only pushed him in self-defense.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a 10-minute wait from the current moment (future time). It answers “When?” and is common with future tense or “ir a” (e.g., va a...). You can swap the number: en cinco minutos, en dos horas, etc. Not the same as “during ten minutes” (that would be “durante diez minutos”).
target_language_example: Te llamo en diez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in ten minutes.

meaning: in two days; within two days (two days from now).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a time frame or deadline. With future events (llegará, será, llámame) it often means “two days from now.” With completed actions (hizo el trabajo) it means “in two days” as the duration it took to finish.
target_language_example: Te mando los documentos en dos días.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the documents in two days.

meaning: in two hours (from now); within two hours.
additional_notes: Used to say how long until something happens (a point in the future) or how long it will take to finish something. With other numbers: en una hora, en tres horas, en cinco minutos, en dos días, etc.
target_language_example: Termino el informe en dos horas.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the report in two hours.

meaning: "in two weeks" (from now; within a two-week period).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after two weeks have passed from a reference point (often now): "Vuelvo en dos semanas". It can also describe what happened over a two-week span: "Subí tres libras en dos semanas". Similar idea to "dentro de dos semanas" when talking about a future deadline.
target_language_example: Te llamaré en dos semanas para confirmar la cita.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in two weeks to confirm the appointment.

meaning: "in the / on the / at the" (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to locate something in a place, time, or event: en el Ártico (in the Arctic), en el campeonato (in the championship). It’s simply en + el. Don’t confuse it with “en él” (with an accent), which means “in him / in it.” For feminine nouns, use “en la.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el parque a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you in the park at five.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened during a specific accident (often a car crash). It commonly follows a verb to explain how/when someone got hurt or something was damaged: “Me lesioné… en el accidente.” You can also hear “en un accidente” (in an accident) when the accident isn’t specific.
target_language_example: Perdió un diente en el accidente.
native_language_example: He lost a tooth in the accident.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. Common with verbs like estar (to be), despedirse (to say goodbye), dejar (to drop off), recoger (to pick up), and with travel phrases like tengo una conexión (I have a connection/layover).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el aeropuerto a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the airport at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is inside the water or happening there. Common with verbs like meter (to put in), tener (to have), explotar (to explode), estar (to be), and navegar (to sail).
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el agua.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the water.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens: inside the elevator. "Ascensor" = elevator; "en el" = in the. Common with verbs like subir/bajar (go up/down), ir (go), and rules like "No se puede..." (You can’t...).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el ascensor a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you in the elevator at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside a car. With verbs of movement you may also hear "meterse/subirse al auto" (“get into the car”) vs. "estar/esperar en el auto" (“be/wait in the car”). "Auto" is common in many Latin American countries; in Spain, "coche" is more common.
target_language_example: Los niños están esperando en el auto.
native_language_example: The kids are waiting in the car.

meaning: on the bus; in the bus.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens while you are riding a bus. With vehicles in Spanish, both “en” (in/on) and “a” (by) can be used depending on the verb, but with actions like sitting, sleeping, talking, etc., “en el autobús” is very common. You can change the article for gender/number: “en la guagua” (bus in some countries), “en los autobuses” (on buses).
target_language_example: Hablamos en el autobús camino al trabajo.
native_language_example: We talked on the bus on the way to work.

meaning: on the plane; in the airplane.
additional_notes: Common way to say someone/something is physically inside a plane during a flight. With verbs like "ir" (to go), it can mean traveling by plane: "Voy en avión" is more common than "voy en el avión" unless you mean a specific plane/flight.
target_language_example: Nos vimos en el avión y hablamos un rato.
native_language_example: We saw each other on the plane and talked for a while.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located on a specific balcony. "En" + "el" (masculine singular) becomes "en el". With places, Spanish often uses "en" where English uses "on" (e.g., sitting/smoking/standing there).
target_language_example: Hace frío, pero quiero tomar un café en el balcón.
native_language_example: It’s cold, but I want to have a coffee on the balcony.

meaning: in/on the bench; at/in the bank.
additional_notes: "Banco" has two very common meanings: (1) "bench" (a seat, often in a park) and (2) "bank" (the place for money). Context usually makes it clear: "sentarse" or "del parque" → bench; "ahorros" (savings), "trabaja" (works), or people inside → bank. With places like a bank, "en" often means "at" in English ("Estoy en el banco" = "I’m at the bank").
target_language_example: Tengo que ir en el banco a sacar dinero.
native_language_example: I have to go to the bank to withdraw money.

meaning: in the bar; at the bar.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside a bar (a place to drink), or present there. It’s a common location phrase: en + el ("in" + "the") + bar.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en el bar a las ocho.
native_language_example: See you at the bar at eight.

meaning: on the boat; in the ship.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located aboard a boat/ship. With transport, Spanish often uses “en” (not “sobre/on”) to mean “on/in” a vehicle: en el barco, en el tren, en el avión.
target_language_example: ¿Quién está en el barco?
native_language_example: Who is on the boat?

meaning: in the bathroom; in the restroom.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside the bathroom/restroom. Often answers “¿Dónde está…?” (Where is…?). With verbs like “estar” it means someone is in there (possibly using it).
target_language_example: Perdón, estoy en el baño ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in the bathroom right now.

meaning: in (your/his/her) pocket; also figuratively, “in your control” / “in your back pocket.”
additional_notes: Literal use: describes something physically inside a pocket (often with verbs like tener, llevar, meter, ponerse).
