additional_notes: Used to say someone is holding something. Very common with verbs like tener (to have), llevar (to carry), venir/ir (to come/go), andar/pasear (to walk), estar/quedarse (to be/stay): "con X en la mano" = "with X in (their) hand." Also appears in instructions: "Ponlo en la mano" (Put it in your hand).
target_language_example: Entró en la sala con el teléfono en la mano.
native_language_example: He walked into the room with his phone in his hand.

additional_notes: Common in Latin American Spanish to mean a morning time period, especially with a day reference (e.g., ayer/en la mañana = yesterday morning). In Spain you’ll often hear “por la mañana” for the same idea. Use it to say when something happened during the morning.
target_language_example: Mañana en la mañana tengo una reunión.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning I have a meeting.

additional_notes: Used with actions that happen on a specific body part (often with a kiss): *besar a alguien en la mejilla* = “to kiss someone on the cheek.” *Mejilla* is feminine, so it takes *la* (the).
target_language_example: Me dio un beso en la mejilla.
native_language_example: He/She gave me a kiss on the cheek.

meaning: on the table; at the table.
additional_notes: Literally means “on the table.” With verbs like ver/poner/dejar, it usually means something is physically on the surface (Veo un libro en la mesa). With manners or behavior (modales, comportamiento), it often means “at the table” while eating (malos modales en la mesa).
target_language_example: Deja las llaves en la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: "in the same" (feminine form), used before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used to say two things happen in the same place/thing. It must agree with the noun: en el mismo (masculine), en la misma (feminine), en los mismos / en las mismas (plural). Often followed by a noun: en la misma fábrica/cama/habitación.
target_language_example: Vivimos en la misma calle.
native_language_example: We live on the same street.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people study together in the same group/course. Often follows estar (to be): "Estamos en la misma clase." You can also add a time phrase like "el año pasado" (last year) or "por entonces" (back then).
target_language_example: ¿Estamos en la misma clase de matemáticas?
native_language_example: Are we in the same math class?

meaning: in the mountains; on the mountain.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in a mountainous area or on a particular mountain. Often translates as “in the mountains” when talking generally about the mountain region, and “on the mountain” when referring to a specific mountain (context usually makes it clear).
target_language_example: Hay un refugio en la montaña donde podemos dormir.
native_language_example: There’s a shelter in the mountains where we can sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens on the nose (the body part). With contact/placement it often translates as “on the nose” (e.g., put/hold something on your nose). With sensations or injury it can be “in the nose” or “on the nose,” depending on context (itching in the nose, a hit on the nose).
target_language_example: Me duele en la nariz.
native_language_example: It hurts on my nose.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or happens within snowy conditions. Common with verbs like perderse (to get lost), congelarse (to freeze), encontrar (to find), and abandonar (to abandon/leave behind).
target_language_example: Dejé mi mochila en la nieve.
native_language_example: I left my backpack in the snow.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the night/evening period. In many places you’ll also hear "por la noche" with the same meaning; "en la noche" can sound a bit more specific (during the night) or more common in some regions. You can add a day: "el lunes en la noche" = "Monday night".
target_language_example: Trabajo en la noche y descanso en la mañana.
native_language_example: I work at night and rest in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens as part of a stage play (at school, daycare, etc.). Common with verbs like hacer de / interpretar (to play a role) and with roles like el papel de... (“the role of...”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano hizo de príncipe en la obra de teatro del colegio.
native_language_example: My brother played a prince in the school play.

meaning: in the office; at the office.
additional_notes: Used to say where something is happening or where someone/something is located. With "en" + a place, it can mean either physical location ("It’s in the office") or being there as an activity ("I’m at the office/working at the office"), depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Nos vemos en la oficina mañana por la mañana?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at the office tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used literally for situations with little or no light: "buscar algo en la oscuridad" (to look for something in the dark). It also appears in the fixed expression "un tiro en la oscuridad", meaning "a shot in the dark" (a random guess). Similar: "a oscuras" = in the dark.
target_language_example: No puedo leer en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: I can't read in the dark.

additional_notes: Used to say that something appears or is shown on a screen (phone, computer, TV, etc.). In contexts like "debut en la pantalla," it can mean debut on screen/in film or television.
target_language_example: No puedo leer el texto en la pantalla porque es muy pequeño.
native_language_example: I can’t read the text on the screen because it’s very small.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located/placed on (or attached to) a wall. Common with verbs like "colgar" (to hang) and "poner" (to put/place): "Está colgado en la pared" / "Ponlo en la pared". You can specify which wall with "la pared de..." (the wall of...): "en la pared de su oficina".
target_language_example: Quiero colgar este cuadro en la pared.
native_language_example: I want to hang this painting on the wall.

meaning: in the part (of); in the (upper/lower/right/left) part.
additional_notes: Used to locate something within an object, image, screen, page, house, etc. It’s usually followed by a location phrase like "superior" (upper), "inferior" (lower), "de arriba" (upstairs/upper part), "de abajo" (downstairs/lower part), "derecha" (right), or "izquierda" (left): e.g., "en la parte superior" = "at the top"; "en la parte inferior derecha" = "in the lower-right part". Often translates naturally as "at the top/bottom" rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: El botón está en la parte superior izquierda de la pantalla.
native_language_example: The button is in the upper-left part of the screen.

meaning: in the back (in the rear part).
additional_notes: Used to point out a location behind something or in the rear area of a place/object (a room, a chair, a book, a building, etc.). Often answers “Where?” and can stand alone as a short reply: “En la parte de atrás.”
target_language_example: Los baños están en la parte de atrás del restaurante.
native_language_example: The bathrooms are in the back of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens on the body (pain, an injury, a cut, a burn, etc.). With accidents you’ll often see it after a verb like: cortarse (to cut oneself), quemarse (to burn oneself), hacerse un corte (to get a cut), tener/dar un calambre (to get a cramp).
target_language_example: Me duele en la pierna derecha.
native_language_example: It hurts in my right leg.

meaning: in the pool; at the swimming pool.
additional_notes: Used with "estar", "nadar", "haber", etc. to say someone/something is inside the pool (in the water) or at the pool facility, depending on context. "Piscina" is a swimming pool; in sports contexts, "una calle" means a lane (e.g., "Tuve una calle para mí solo" = "I had a lane to myself").
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la piscina a las cinco.
native_language_example: See you at the pool at five.

additional_notes: Used to say something is written or shown on a classroom board. Often appears with verbs like "escribir" (to write), "poner" (to put), or "estar escrito" (to be written). "Pizarra" can mean a blackboard or a whiteboard depending on the context.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes escribir la fecha en la pizarra?
native_language_example: Can you write the date on the board?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of location or activities to say something happens at the beach. With a specific beach you can also say “en Playa X” (e.g., “en Playa del Carmen”), but “en la playa” is the general idea of being at the beach.
target_language_example: Vamos a comer en la playa.
native_language_example: We’re going to eat at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in the main open public area of a town or neighborhood (la plaza). Often refers to a central square where people gather, walk, and where you might see pigeons, children, markets, etc. You can also specify which one: en la plaza central / en la plaza de la ciudad.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la plaza a las seis.
native_language_example: See you in the square at six.

meaning: in the first (one); in the front row.
additional_notes: Uses the feminine article because it refers to an implied feminine noun like curva (curve), vuelta (lap), or fila (row): en la primera curva/vuelta/fila. In contexts like seating, it often means “in the front row” (en la primera fila).
target_language_example: ¿Hay asientos en la primera fila?
native_language_example: Are there seats in the front row?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next place/stop/turn/event in a sequence: en la próxima calle (on the next street), en la próxima parada (at the next stop), en la próxima esquina (at the next corner), en la próxima lección (in the next lesson). In casual conversation, "en la próxima" can be a shortened way to mean "next time" (i.e., next occasion).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la próxima reunión.
native_language_example: See you at the next meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located right by the door or at the entrance. Often followed by "de" + a place to specify which door ("en la puerta de al lado" = "at the next door / next door").
target_language_example: Hay alguien en la puerta; voy a abrir.
native_language_example: There's someone at the door; I'm going to open it.

meaning: "in which" / "where" (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses after a feminine singular noun (e.g., habitación, época, situación) to mean “in which/where.” It’s the combination of the preposition en + la (feminine singular “the”) + que (relative pronoun). For masculine you often see “en el que,” and for plural “en los/las que.”
target_language_example: Esa es la casa en la que crecí.
native_language_example: That’s the house where I grew up.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like escuchar/oir/sonar/estar to say something was heard or was being broadcast on the radio. It can refer to a specific radio station/program, or to the radio as a device. Contrast: “en la tele” = on TV; “por la radio” can also mean “on/over the radio,” focusing on the medium.
target_language_example: Dicen en la radio que va a llover mañana.
native_language_example: They say on the radio that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: in the meeting; at the meeting.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened or someone was present during a specific meeting (reunión = meeting). Often used with verbs like estar/ser/decir/hablar/presentarse: “Estuve en la reunión” (I was at the meeting), “Lo dije en la reunión” (I said it in the meeting).
target_language_example: No pude hablar en la reunión porque no levanté la mano.
native_language_example: I couldn’t speak in the meeting because I didn’t raise my hand.

meaning: in the room; in the hall (meeting room).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside a particular room or hall. "Sala" often means a larger room such as a meeting room, classroom, courtroom, or hall (not necessarily a living room). You’ll also hear "¡Orden en la sala!" as “Order in the court/room!” (a fixed phrase).
target_language_example: Hay mucha gente en la sala, así que hablemos en voz baja.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the room, so let’s speak quietly.

meaning: in the … room (e.g., in the conference room / classroom).
additional_notes: Used with a following noun to specify what kind of room someone/something is in: en la sala de conferencias (conference room), en la sala de clases (classroom), en la sala de interrogación (interrogation room). In Spanish you often say “sala de + [noun]” where English uses “[noun] room.”
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la sala de reuniones a las tres.
native_language_example: See you in the meeting room at three.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone should wait or where people are waiting (commonly at a doctor’s office, hospital, or office). Often used with verbs like esperar (to wait) and hay (there is/are): “Espere en la sala de espera” / “Hay mucha gente en la sala de espera.”
target_language_example: El médico está listo; por favor, espere en la sala de espera.
native_language_example: The doctor is ready; please wait in the waiting room.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone or something is located. "Sala de estar" is the common term for "living room" (also "sala" in some countries). It usually takes "en" for location: "Estoy en la sala de estar."
target_language_example: Deja el bolso en la sala de estar, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the bag in the living room, please.

meaning: 'in the meeting room' / 'in the conference room'.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "Sala de reuniones" is a room for meetings at an office, school, etc. Often follows verbs like "estar", "ver", "tener" (una entrevista/reunión), "encontrarse".
target_language_example: La presentación es en la sala de reuniones.
native_language_example: The presentation is in the meeting room.

meaning: in high school; during high school.
additional_notes: Refers to the period when someone attended secondary school (high school). Use it to say when something happened ("they met in high school") or where someone currently is ("he’s still in high school"). In many Spanish-speaking countries, "secundaria" is roughly ages 12–18, but exact school levels can vary by country.
target_language_example: Nos hicimos amigos en la secundaria.
native_language_example: We became friends in high school.

additional_notes: Used when talking about public transport (especially trains/subways) to say where you will get off. Common with verbs like “bajar” (to get off) or “bajarse” (to get off oneself): “bajar/bajarse en la siguiente estación.”
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿me puede avisar cuando lleguemos en la siguiente estación?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you let me know when we arrive at the next station?

additional_notes: Common in transit contexts (bus/metro/train) with verbs like "bajarse" (to get off) or "parar" (to stop). "Siguiente" agrees with the noun: "la siguiente parada" (feminine), but you may also hear "en el siguiente (alto/paradero)" depending on the word used for "stop".
target_language_example: Por favor, avísame cuando estemos en la siguiente parada.
native_language_example: Please let me know when we’re at the next stop.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is seated on a chair or something is located on a chair. With verbs like sentarse (to sit down) and estar sentado/a (to be seated). In Spanish you typically say "sentarse en la silla" (literally “sit in the chair”) where English often prefers “sit on the chair.”
target_language_example: El gato está en la silla.
native_language_example: The cat is on the chair.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is located or happening on the outer/top layer of something (water, film, a material, etc.). It can describe a physical surface; in other contexts it can also mean "superficially" (not deeply), but the examples here are physical.
target_language_example: Hay manchas en la superficie de la mesa.
native_language_example: There are stains on the surface of the table.

meaning: in the afternoon; later today (in the afternoon).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during the afternoon period. With "hoy" it often means "this afternoon" (e.g., "hoy en la tarde"). You may also hear "por la tarde" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la tarde para tomar un café.
native_language_example: See you this afternoon to have a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you watch something on television, or that someone/something appeared on television (e.g., “salió/apareció en la tele”). Very common in everyday speech; more formal: “en la televisión”.
target_language_example: ¿Lo viste en la tele anoche?
native_language_example: Did you see it on TV last night?

additional_notes: Used to say something is shown, heard, or happens via television (a TV broadcast). Very common with verbs like ver (to see/watch), escuchar (to hear), aparecer (to appear), and poner (to put on). Also used with specific programs: en la televisión / en la tele (more informal).
target_language_example: No lo dieron en la televisión, pero lo vi en internet.
native_language_example: They didn’t show it on TV, but I saw it on the internet.

meaning: in the store; at the shop.
additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is located or where something happens. Often followed by a type of store: "en la tienda de mascotas" (at the pet store). You can also answer a question about location with just "En la tienda."
target_language_example: Nos vemos en la tienda después de clase.
native_language_example: See you at the store after class.

meaning: on earth; in the ground; on land.
additional_notes: Often refers to (1) being on Earth/in the world (“here on earth”), (2) being in/under the soil (“in the ground”), or (3) being on land (not in the air/sea). In phrases like “un infierno en la tierra,” it means “a hell on earth” (something terrible in real life).
target_language_example: Encontraron agua en la tierra después de cavar un poco.
native_language_example: They found water in the ground after digging a little.

meaning: at the university; in college (as a student).
additional_notes: Used to talk about studying/being a student at a university. Often follows verbs like estudiar (to study), conocer (to meet), and estar + gerund (to be studying). You can add the university name after de: en la universidad de Boston.
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en la universidad y todavía somos amigos.
native_language_example: We met in college and we're still friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about life in general (your life, people’s lives, or life as a whole). Very common in phrases like "en la vida" (in life), "en la vida futura" (in future life), and "único/a en la vida" (once in a lifetime).
target_language_example: En la vida, lo más importante es aprender de los errores.
native_language_example: In life, the most important thing is to learn from mistakes.

additional_notes: Used before feminine plural nouns: en las sombras (in the shadows), en las peores circunstancias (in the worst circumstances), en las mentes (in the minds). It’s the plural feminine form of “en el” (in the, masculine singular). Often followed by a specific place, time, or situation.
target_language_example: Nos vemos en las oficinas a las nueve.
native_language_example: See you at the offices at nine.

meaning: on the outskirts; in the suburbs (outside the city center).
additional_notes: Used to say someone lives or something is located outside the main part of a city/town. Often appears as “en las afueras de + place” (e.g., en las afueras de Boston). Typically refers to the outer areas rather than the downtown/center.
target_language_example: El hotel está en las afueras de la ciudad, cerca del aeropuerto.
native_language_example: The hotel is on the outskirts of the city, near the airport.

meaning: in the streets; out on the streets.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in public street areas (everyday life, conditions, crime, protests, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean learning from real life rather than in school ("street education"). Often appears with extra details: "en las calles de [place]" or "en las calles cubiertas de hielo".
target_language_example: De noche, es mejor no andar solo en las calles.
native_language_example: At night, it’s better not to walk alone in the streets.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically on your hands (blood, cracks, calluses), or that someone is holding something (e.g., un arma en las manos = a weapon in their hands). Spanish often uses "en" where English uses "on" (en las manos, en la cara, etc.).
target_language_example: No quiero nada en las manos cuando entremos al museo.
native_language_example: I don’t want anything in my hands when we go into the museum.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the mountain area, or that an action happens there. Often answers “where?” (¿Dónde?) and can be used with verbs like estar (to be), vivir (to live), esconderse (to hide), buscar (to look for), pasar (to spend time).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos en las montañas todo el fin de semana.
native_language_example: We stayed in the mountains all weekend.

meaning: 'in the news' (on TV, radio, newspapers, or online news).
additional_notes: Used to say something was reported or mentioned by the news media. Often follows verbs like decir (to say), ver (to see), escuchar (to hear), and salir (to appear).
target_language_example: Lo vi en las noticias esta mañana.
native_language_example: I saw it in the news this morning.

meaning: 'in what' / 'in the thing that' (refers to an action/thing).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to refer back to a specific thing, activity, or situation: "en lo que creo" (in what I believe), "en lo que haces" (in what you do), "en lo que estoy trabajando" (in what I'm working on). Often follows a noun like "algo" or "todo" and can be close to "about what" or "on what" depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Estoy concentrado en lo que tengo que hacer.
native_language_example: I'm focused on what I have to do.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say someone is right about something: estar en lo cierto. Common in questions (¿Estoy en lo cierto?) and for emphasis (Estás absolutamente en lo cierto). Also: Creo que estoy en lo cierto (“I think I’m right”).
target_language_example: Creo que estás en lo cierto: el museo cierra a las seis.
native_language_example: I think you’re right: the museum closes at six.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to say someone is right about something: "estar en lo correcto". You can add emphasis with words like "completamente" (completely) or specify the topic with "en" (about): "Estabas en lo correcto en todo" / "en esto".
target_language_example: Creo que estás en lo correcto sobre el precio.
native_language_example: I think you're right about the price.

additional_notes: Used almost always with negation (no, nada, nunca) to emphasize that something is zero/none. It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “Not at all.”
target_language_example: No me molesta en lo más mínimo.
native_language_example: It doesn’t bother me at all.

meaning: 'in what' / 'in the thing that' (refers to an action/thing).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to refer back to a specific thing, activity, or situation: "en lo que creo" (in what I believe), "en lo que haces" (in what you do), "en lo que estoy trabajando" (in what I'm working on). Often follows a noun like "algo" or "todo" and can be close to "about what" or "on what" depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Estoy concentrado en lo que tengo que hacer.
native_language_example: I'm focused on what I have to do.

additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns to express location, setting, membership, or time frames: en los asuntos (in the affairs), en los Dodgers (on/in the Dodgers), en los colegios (in the schools), en los próximos diez segundos (in the next ten seconds). It’s the preposition "en" + the plural masculine article "los" (no contraction, unlike "a + el" → "al" and "de + el" → "del").
target_language_example: Nos vemos en los próximos días.
native_language_example: See you in the next few days.

meaning: in the eyes; in someone’s eyes (in their opinion).
additional_notes: Literal location: something is physically in/into the eyes (often with verbs like meterse, hacer daño, tener). Figurative: "en los ojos de + person" means "in that person’s eyes" = how they see/judge something (their viewpoint). Also used to talk about what can be seen in someone’s eyes (e.g., emotions, honesty).
target_language_example: No había miedo en sus ojos.
native_language_example: There was no fear in his eyes.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears/was reported in printed or online newspapers. Often with verbs like ver (to see), leer (to read), salir/estar (to appear/be) + en los periódicos.
target_language_example: Salió en los periódicos esta mañana.
native_language_example: It was in the newspapers this morning.

meaning: 'in the old days' / 'back in the day'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the present to the past, often with a nostalgic feeling. Common in phrases like "como/igual que en los viejos tiempos" (just like in the old days). It refers to a past period in general, not a specific date.
target_language_example: Volvimos a reunirnos y fue como en los viejos tiempos.
native_language_example: We got together again and it was like in the old days.

meaning: in the last (…); over the past (…).
additional_notes: Used with a time period to talk about something that happened within the most recent period up to now: en los últimos dos años (in the last two years). It can also be used with moments/instants: en los últimos momentos (in the final moments).
target_language_example: En los últimos días he estado muy ocupado.
native_language_example: In the last few days, I've been very busy.

meaning: in half an hour; in 30 minutes.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after 30 minutes from now (a time from the present). Very common for plans and future actions: “Nos vemos en media hora.” You can also say “en una media hora” (in about half an hour). Don’t confuse with “durante media hora” (= for half an hour, duration).
target_language_example: Te llamo en media hora.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in half an hour.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens inside a place/group (a crowd, the street) or during an event/situation (a storm, a class). Often followed by a noun: en medio de la multitud / en medio de una tormenta. Similar to "entre" in some contexts, but focuses on being in the center or surrounded by something.
target_language_example: Nos llamaste en medio de la cena.
native_language_example: You called us in the middle of dinner.

meaning: in the middle of; in the midst of (something).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is located within an event/situation or physical place. It’s usually followed by a feminine singular noun (la discusión, la avenida). With masculine nouns, use “en medio del”. You can also use “en medio de” before plural nouns (en medio de las/los).
target_language_example: Me llamaron en medio de la reunión.
native_language_example: They called me in the middle of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re in a very remote place with nothing around (often implying it’s hard to find, isolated, or you’re lost). You can use it after a verb of being/ending up ("estoy", "estamos", "me desperté") or as a standalone phrase for emphasis.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio de la nada.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of nowhere.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at a very late hour while it’s still nighttime (often unexpectedly). It’s a time expression: en medio de + [time period] = “in the middle of + [time period].”
target_language_example: Nos llamaron en medio de la noche por una emergencia.
native_language_example: They called us in the middle of the night because of an emergency.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/exists within a larger place, time period, or situation. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: en medio del invierno / del campo / del desierto. With feminine singular, use en medio de la (en medio de la noche). Often implies being surrounded by something.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin gasolina en medio del camino.
native_language_example: We ran out of gas in the middle of the road.

additional_notes: Used with a time period, quantity, or number to say something happens/exists before that limit is reached: en menos de + number + unit (minutos, horas, días, meses, etc.). Often answers “How long?” or “How much?”
target_language_example: Terminé la tarea en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: I finished the homework in less than an hour.

meaning: in less than an hour; within an hour.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen before one hour passes, or that something took under an hour to do. It often follows verbs like llegar (to arrive), estar aquí (to be here), or terminar (to finish). You can swap the time unit: en menos de cinco minutos, en menos de dos días.
target_language_example: Podemos hacerlo en menos de una hora.
native_language_example: We can do it in less than an hour.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something is located in/on you or belongs to you (my…). Which English preposition fits (“in” vs “on”) depends on the noun: en mi calendario = “in my calendar,” en mi mesa = “on my table,” en mi ojo = “in my eye.” Often appears in set phrases like “en mi caso” (“in my case”) and “Póngase en mi lugar” (“put yourself in my shoes” / “put yourself in my place”).
target_language_example: Guárdalo en mi mochila, por favor.
native_language_example: Put it in my backpack, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located inside your pocket. With verbs like estar/poner/guardar (to be/put/keep), it describes where an item is: «Está en mi bolsillo» (It’s in my pocket), «Lo puso en mi bolsillo» (He/She put it in my pocket). You can swap «mi» for another possessive: «en tu bolsillo», «en su bolsillo», etc.
target_language_example: Tengo las llaves en mi bolsillo.
native_language_example: I have the keys in my pocket.

meaning: “in my head” (literally: “in my head/skull” or “in my mind”).
additional_notes: Often used literally for something physically in/on your head (hair, a sound ringing in your head), and also figuratively for thoughts, imagination, or inner voices (“it’s only in my head”). You can change the possessive: en tu cabeza (in your head), en su cabeza (in his/her head), etc.
target_language_example: No sé si es real o si solo está en mi cabeza.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it’s real or if it’s just in my head.

meaning: in my house; at my place (my home).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside your home, or that an activity happened at your home. Often translates as “at my place” in English even though it literally means “in my house.”
target_language_example: Vamos a cenar en mi casa esta noche.
native_language_example: Let’s have dinner at my place tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unfavorable to you or that someone is working/opposing you. Common with verbs like estar (La evidencia está en mi contra), ir (Todo va en mi contra), or poner a alguien en contra de alguien (He’s trying to turn her against me).
target_language_example: Parece que todo el mundo está en mi contra hoy.
native_language_example: It seems like everyone is against me today.

additional_notes: Used to express deep feelings like love, affection, gratitude, or emotional certainty. Common in romantic or emotional contexts (“forever in my heart”), and also with verbs like llevar (“to carry”) or sentir (“to feel”) to show something is emotionally important.
target_language_example: Aunque estés lejos, siempre estás en mi corazón.
native_language_example: Even if you’re far away, you’re always in my heart.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is inside your room. In many contexts, "cuarto" means "bedroom" (especially at home or in a hotel). In hotels, you may also hear "en mi habitación" for the same idea.
target_language_example: Deja la maleta en mi cuarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the suitcase in my room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your family as a group (the people you’re related to). It often introduces a general statement, habit, or fact about your relatives (e.g., “In my family, we say…”, “There are three boys in my family”). You can swap the possessive: en tu familia (in your family), en su familia (in his/her/their family), en nuestra familia (in our family).
target_language_example: En mi familia celebramos los cumpleaños juntos.
native_language_example: In my family, we celebrate birthdays together.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "En" means "in/on/at" depending on context; here it’s typically "in." "Habitación" usually means a bedroom or a room in a home (can also mean a hotel room).
target_language_example: Voy a estar en mi habitación un rato.
native_language_example: I’m going to be in my room for a while.

meaning: in my place; instead of me.
additional_notes: Used when someone does something instead of you (replacement): "Mi hermano hizo eso en mi lugar." It’s also used to ask someone to imagine being you (empathy), often with "ponerse": "Ponte/Póngase en mi lugar" = "Put yourself in my shoes."
target_language_example: ¿Podrías venir en mi lugar mañana?
native_language_example: Could you come instead of me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside your office, or to tell someone to come to your office for a meeting or conversation. Often appears with verbs like estar (to be), entrar (to enter), volver/regresar (to return), and querer/ver (to want to see).
target_language_example: Nos vemos en mi oficina después de la reunión.
native_language_example: See you in my office after the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal viewpoint. Often comes at the beginning of the sentence (sometimes followed by a comma), but it can also appear later: "Y en mi opinión..." You can change the possessive: "en tu opinión" (in your opinion), "en su opinión" (in his/her/their opinion), "en nuestra opinión" (in our opinion).
target_language_example: En mi opinión, este restaurante es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is too expensive.

meaning: 'in my opinion,' (followed by a masculine noun: 'the…').
additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal view. In these examples it’s followed by a masculine noun introduced by "el" (e.g., el alcohol, el alemán). You can also say "En mi opinión," without adding "el", or use "la" for feminine nouns ("En mi opinión, la música…").
target_language_example: En mi opinión, el café sabe mejor sin azúcar.
native_language_example: In my opinion, coffee tastes better without sugar.

additional_notes: Used to say what you do outside of work/school or other obligations. Often followed by a verb (e.g., "En mi tiempo libre leo...") or placed at the end of the sentence for emphasis ("Leo en mi tiempo libre"). You can change the possessive to match the person: en tu/su/nuestro tiempo libre.
target_language_example: En mi tiempo libre voy al gimnasio y veo series.
native_language_example: In my free time I go to the gym and watch TV shows.

additional_notes: Literally means “in my life.” Very common with negation words like "nunca" to emphasize that something has never happened: "Nunca en mi vida" / "No… en mi vida." It can also mean having someone as part of your life (relationships): "Te quiero en mi vida" = “I want you in my life.”
target_language_example: Nunca en mi vida había probado algo tan rico.
native_language_example: Never in my life had I tried something so delicious.

additional_notes: Used for holding someone (a baby, partner, injured person) or when someone is physically lying against you. Common with verbs like coger/tomar (to pick up/hold), dormir (to sleep), and morir (to die), e.g., “murió en mis brazos” = “he died in my arms.” Often matches the literal idea of being inside/within your embrace.
target_language_example: El gato se quedó dormido en mis brazos.
native_language_example: The cat fell asleep in my arms.

meaning: “in my dreams.” (sometimes: “yeah right,” to show something won’t happen)
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something happens only in your dreams/imagination. Often used sarcastically to reject an idea or express disbelief (like “As if!” / “Yeah right!”). You can also change the possessive: en tus sueños (in your dreams), en sus sueños (in his/her/their dreams).
target_language_example: ¿Que me van a subir el sueldo este mes? En mis sueños.
native_language_example: They’re going to raise my salary this month? Yeah right.

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened for a long period up to now, or that this is the best/most/first time within a long period. Often appears in expressions like "no ... en mucho tiempo" (not in a long time), "la primera vez ... en mucho tiempo" (the first time in a long time), and with superlatives like "mejor ... en mucho tiempo" (the best in a long time).
target_language_example: No me reía así en mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: I hadn’t laughed like that in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true in a large number of countries. Common in general statements: "se habla/se usa/se enseña en muchos países" (“it’s spoken/used/taught in many countries”).
target_language_example: Este producto se vende en muchos países.
native_language_example: This product is sold in many countries.

meaning: in/on me; in me (with certain verbs).
additional_notes: Used after prepositions like "en" to mean "in/on me" (the stressed form of "mí" is used after prepositions). Very common with verbs that take "en" such as: "confiar en mí" (to trust me), "creer en mí" (to believe in me), "fijarse en mí" (to notice/look at me), and "dejar una impresión en mí" (to leave an impression on me).
target_language_example: Puedes confiar en mí.
native_language_example: You can trust me.

meaning: "in our" / "on our" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: en nuestra casa, en nuestra mesa, en nuestra área. Spanish uses en for several English prepositions (in/on/at), depending on context. It can also be used in expressions like pensar en nuestra situación (“to think about our situation”) or jugar en nuestra contra (“to play against us”).
target_language_example: Hoy comemos en nuestra cocina.
native_language_example: Today we’re eating in our kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is located at your place (you and your group/family). In Spanish, "casa" often means "home" as well as "house."
target_language_example: ¿Quieres cenar en nuestra casa el sábado?
native_language_example: Do you want to have dinner at our place on Saturday?

additional_notes: Used with "en" to talk about things that happen during the autumn season (general facts, habits, or plans). You can place it at the start of the sentence (often with a comma) or later: "En otoño..." / "... en otoño."
target_language_example: En otoño hace más fresco por las tardes.
native_language_example: In the fall it’s cooler in the afternoons.

meaning: on something else; about something else.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like pensar (to think), estar pensando (to be thinking), or tener la mente (to have your mind) to say someone’s attention is elsewhere or they’re distracted. Often implies you’re not focused on what’s happening now: "Tienes la mente en otra cosa" = "Your mind is elsewhere."
target_language_example: Perdón, estaba pensando en otra cosa y no escuché la pregunta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was thinking about something else and didn’t hear the question.

additional_notes: Used to postpone something to a different time in the future. Common in polite refusals or to suggest continuing the conversation later (often like “maybe another time”).
target_language_example: Hoy no puedo; mejor en otra ocasión.
native_language_example: I can’t today; better another time.

meaning: at another time; some other time (later).
additional_notes: Used to postpone something or say you’ll do it later, often politely. You can use it alone as a short response (“En otro momento.”) or inside a sentence (“Lo haremos en otro momento.”). Often implies “not now.”
target_language_example: Ahora estoy ocupado; mejor lo vemos en otro momento.
native_language_example: I’m busy right now; we’d better look at it another time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening quickly or within a relatively brief period. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence: “En poco tiempo, …” or “… en poco tiempo.”
target_language_example: Aprenderás a pedir comida en español en poco tiempo.
native_language_example: You’ll learn to order food in Spanish in a short time.

additional_notes: Used with estar/seguir (temporary state) or with verbs like morir to say someone is/was imprisoned. In many contexts “prisión” and “cárcel” both translate as “prison/jail,” but “prisión” can sound a bit more formal. The literal idea is “in (a) prison.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano estuvo en prisión dos años, pero ahora está libre.
native_language_example: My brother was in prison for two years, but now he’s free.

additional_notes: Used with estar ("estar en problemas") to say you’re in trouble or in a difficult situation. You can also describe someone/something "en problemas" ("un amigo en problemas" = a friend in trouble). Common warning: "No te metas en problemas" = Don’t get yourself into trouble.
target_language_example: Si llego tarde otra vez, voy a estar en problemas.
native_language_example: If I’m late again, I’m going to be in trouble.

additional_notes: Used to correct or contradict what someone thinks or expects, or to clarify the truth. It can be a full reply (“En realidad no.”) or appear inside a longer sentence. Often softens a disagreement compared to a blunt “No.”
target_language_example: ¿Vas a venir mañana? En realidad no, tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? Actually no, I have to work.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives/phrases like "rico/a", "abundante" or verbs like "abundar" to say a place has a lot of natural resources (e.g., "rica en recursos naturales" = “rich in natural resources”).
target_language_example: Chile es rico en recursos naturales.
native_language_example: Chile is rich in natural resources.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say you’ll do something very soon or without delay. Often appears with near-future plans (e.g., "Voy a... en seguida") and with commands ("Hazlo en seguida"). In many contexts it overlaps with "enseguida" (one word), which is very common in writing.
target_language_example: Te llamo en seguida.
native_language_example: I’ll call you right away.

additional_notes: Used to say something is serious/true (not a joke), or to talk about doing something with seriousness. Very common with verbs like “tomarse (algo) en serio” (to take something seriously) and “hablar en serio” (to mean it/seriously). Can also be used alone for emphasis: “¿En serio?” = “Seriously?/Really?”
target_language_example: ¿En serio vas a renunciar?
native_language_example: Are you seriously going to quit?

additional_notes: It’s the preposition **en** (“in/on/into”) + the possessive **su** (“his/her/your [formal]/their”). **Su** is ambiguous, so you usually figure out whose it is from context or from a clarifying phrase like **su misión de usted** (your mission), **su misión de él** (his), **su misión de ella** (her).
target_language_example: Puso toda su energía en su trabajo.
native_language_example: He/She put all his/her energy into his/her work.

additional_notes: Means something is inside someone’s pocket. "Su" can mean "his," "her," or formal "your" (usted) depending on context. Often used with verbs like meter/poner (to put in) and sacar (to take out).
target_language_example: No tengo efectivo; lo dejé en su bolsillo sin querer.
native_language_example: I don’t have cash; I left it in his/her pocket by accident.

meaning: in his/her/their home; at his/her/their place.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is at home or something is located in their home. "Su" can mean his, her, their, or formal "your" (usted), so the meaning depends on context. Often followed by "de + place" to specify the location (e.g., "en su casa de Kitakamakura").
target_language_example: Te espero en su casa a las seis.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you at his/her place at six.

additional_notes: Used after verbs or nouns to show that something is unfavorable to a person/group (a ruling, evidence, public opinion). Often with verbs like estar/ir/ser “en su contra” (to be/go against them) or usar algo “en su contra” (to use something against them). The possessive changes: en mi contra, en tu contra, en su contra, en nuestra contra, etc.
target_language_example: La evidencia está en su contra.
native_language_example: The evidence is against him/her.

additional_notes: Uses "en" (= in) + "su" (= his/her/your/their) + "cuarto" (= room/bedroom). "Su" is ambiguous, so context tells you whose room it is. Common with activities done privately: studying, sleeping, listening to music, etc. You can swap the possessive: "en mi cuarto" (in my room), "en tu cuarto" (in your room), "en nuestro cuarto" (in our room).
target_language_example: Los niños están en su cuarto jugando.
native_language_example: The kids are in their room playing.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located inside their bedroom. "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context; often you clarify with "de él/de ella/de ellos" if needed.
target_language_example: El gato está en su dormitorio.
native_language_example: The cat is in his/her bedroom.

meaning: in his/her/your (formal) room; in their room.
additional_notes: A location phrase: en (“in”) + su (“his/her/your formal/their”) + habitación (“room/bedroom”). In context, su usually refers to someone already mentioned, and it can be ambiguous in English without extra context (his vs. her vs. their). Often used with activities done privately, like sleeping, studying, or listening to music.
target_language_example: Está en su habitación, estudiando para el examen.
native_language_example: He/She is in his/her room, studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is located or happens in someone’s garden/yard. "Su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their"—the meaning depends on context. If you want to be extra clear, you can replace "su" with "mi" (my), "tu" (your, informal), "nuestro" (our), etc.: "en mi jardín," "en tu jardín."
target_language_example: Hay un perro en su jardín.
native_language_example: There is a dog in his/her garden.

meaning: in his/her youth; when he/she was young.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a period in someone’s life in the past (their younger years). The possessive changes with the person: en mi juventud (in my youth), en tu juventud (in your youth), en nuestra juventud (in our youth), etc. It can go at the start of the sentence for emphasis or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: En su juventud, él viajaba mucho.
native_language_example: In his youth, he traveled a lot.

additional_notes: Common uses: (1) With ponerse: "ponte en su lugar" = imagine being that person / try to understand their perspective. (2) As a connector meaning "instead": "en su lugar, + verb" or "haz X; en su lugar, haz Y".
target_language_example: No voy a salir; en su lugar, voy a quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: I’m not going out; instead, I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside or at someone’s office. The possessive adjective (su) can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so the meaning depends on context. For clarity, Spanish can specify: en la oficina de él (his), en la oficina de ella (her), en la oficina de usted (your formal), en la oficina de ellos/ellas (their).
target_language_example: Te espero en su oficina a las tres.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you in his/her office at three.

meaning: “in his/her/its own” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs to or happens within that person/thing itself: en su propia voluntad (in his/her own will), en su propia manera (in his/her own way), en su propia lengua (in his/her own language). Because propia is feminine, it must match a feminine noun (manera, lengua, mente, trampa). For masculine nouns, use en su propio (e.g., en su propio país).
target_language_example: Cada quien lo hace en su propia manera.
native_language_example: Everyone does it in their own way.

additional_notes: "Sus" is a possessive meaning "his/her/their" (it doesn’t show gender). It’s used with plural nouns (e.g., *sus hombros*, *sus espaldas*). With certain expressions involving body parts, *en* is often best translated as "on" in English: *cargar a alguien en sus hombros* = "carry someone on his/her shoulders."
target_language_example: El niño se quedó dormido en sus brazos.
native_language_example: The child fell asleep in her arms.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is holding another person (often a baby/child) or embracing them. It agrees with the possessor: en mis brazos (in my arms), en tus brazos (in your arms), en sus brazos (in his/her/their arms), en nuestros brazos (in our arms). You’ll also see it with verbs like tener, tomar, coger, llevar, and estar.
target_language_example: Cuando entré, el bebé estaba en sus brazos.
native_language_example: When I came in, the baby was in her arms.

meaning: in their hands; in their care/control.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: something is physically being held in someone’s hands (e.g., “Tiene una muñeca en sus manos”). Very commonly used figuratively to mean you leave something up to someone or it’s under their responsibility/control: “Lo dejo en sus manos” = “I’ll leave it to you / it’s in your hands.” With “caer en sus manos,” it often means to fall into someone’s power (sometimes an enemy), implying danger or capture.
target_language_example: La decisión final está en sus manos.
native_language_example: The final decision is in their hands.

meaning: in his/her/their eyes; in their gaze; in their view.
additional_notes: Used both literally (something visible in someone’s eyes, like tears or an emotion) and figuratively (someone’s perspective/opinion: “in their eyes”). Often appears with verbs like ver (“to see”) or with nouns like lágrimas (“tears”).
target_language_example: Puedo ver la tristeza en sus ojos.
native_language_example: I can see the sadness in their eyes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something considered alone, separate from its effects, context, or consequences. Often appears after a noun: “la idea en sí misma” = “the idea itself.” It agrees with the noun: en sí mismo (masc.), en sí misma (fem.), en sí mismos / en sí mismas (plural).
target_language_example: La tecnología en sí misma no es buena ni mala; depende de cómo se use.
native_language_example: Technology in itself isn’t good or bad; it depends on how it’s used.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is considered alone (its own nature), separate from context or effects: "X en sí mismo" = "X in itself." With people it becomes reflexive and agrees in gender/number: en sí mismo (he/himself), en sí misma (she/herself), en sí mismos/as (they/themselves). Often appears after a noun: "El diseño en sí mismo..."
target_language_example: La idea en sí misma es buena, pero el plan no funciona.
native_language_example: The idea in itself is good, but the plan doesn’t work.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "en" + the prepositional pronoun "ti" (used after many prepositions like en/para/por/sin). Common in phrases like "creer en ti" = "to believe in you". For plural, use "en ustedes" (formal) or "en vosotros" (Spain).
target_language_example: Siempre he creído en ti.
native_language_example: I’ve always believed in you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like creer (to believe) or pensar (to think) to refer back to “you” (reflexive emphasis). It agrees with the person and gender: en ti misma (to a woman), en ti mismos/mismas (to more than one person). Common in phrases like creer en ti mismo (“believe in yourself”) and pensar en ti mismo (“think about yourself”).
target_language_example: Tienes que confiar en ti mismo.
native_language_example: You have to trust in yourself.

meaning: in my whole life; ever in my life.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has (or hasn’t) happened at any time up to now in your entire life. Common in comparisons and superlatives ("la mejor... en toda mi vida" = "the best ... in my life") and with negatives ("no... en toda mi vida" = "never in my life").
target_language_example: Nunca había probado algo tan rico en toda mi vida.
native_language_example: I had never tasted anything so delicious in my whole life.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/exists in every one of a set of places/things (feminine plural noun): en todas las ciudades, en todas las fiestas. With directions it often means “in every direction”: en todas las direcciones. For masculine plural, use “en todos los”.
target_language_example: Hay baños en todas las plantas del edificio.
native_language_example: There are bathrooms on every floor of the building.

additional_notes: Used to say something is present in many places or in all places. It often answers “Where?” (¿Dónde?) and can be used literally (physical locations) or more generally (e.g., “injustice everywhere”). Common with verbs like estar/haber/ser: “Está en todas partes” (It’s everywhere), “Hay … en todas partes” (There is/are … everywhere).
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves y estaban en todas partes.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys and they were everywhere.

meaning: "in the whole" / "all over the" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens throughout an entire place or period of time: en todo el mundo (all over the world / in the whole world), en todo el viaje (throughout the whole trip), en todo el piso / rancho / brazo (all over the floor / ranch / arm). With feminine nouns, it becomes en toda la (en toda la casa = all over the house). With plural nouns: en todos los / en todas las.
target_language_example: Había gente en todo el estadio.
native_language_example: There were people all over the stadium.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true everywhere on Earth. Common after nouns or at the end of a sentence: "es famoso en todo el mundo". It can also be used more personally to mean “in the whole world” (= more than anywhere else): "mi persona favorita en todo el mundo".
target_language_example: Esta canción es famosa en todo el mundo.
native_language_example: This song is famous all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places, or that someone searches/looks in many places. Often interchangeable with "por todas partes". The verb usually gives the context: "ver" (see), "buscar" (search), "estar" (be).
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves en todos lados, pero no las encontré.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys everywhere, but I didn’t find them.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “in every” or “in all the.” It often introduces a broad/general statement: En todos los aspectos/sentidos (“in every respect/way”), en todos los pueblos (“in every town”). For feminine plural use en todas las; for singular use en todo el / en toda la.
target_language_example: Lo revisaron en todos los detalles antes de firmar.
native_language_example: They reviewed it in every detail before signing.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something being inside your body/object/place or within your personal “space” (like your life, world, dream). It’s formed by en (in/on/at) + tu (your, singular informal). Use it before a singular noun: en tu bolsillo (in your pocket), en tu mundo (in your world). For plural nouns, use en tus: en tus sueños (in your dreams).
target_language_example: En tu casa siempre hay café.
native_language_example: In your house there is always coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located inside the listener’s pocket (often with verbs like llevar/poner/guardar). With body-related nouns you may hear bolsillo interno (“inside pocket”). You can change tu to another possessive: en mi bolsillo (in my pocket), en su bolsillo (in his/her/their pocket).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes las llaves en tu bolsillo?
native_language_example: Do you have the keys in your pocket?

meaning: in your house/home; at your place.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside or staying at the other person’s home (“en tu casa”). With verbs like quedarse/estar/hacer it often means “at your place.” In the set phrase “Siéntete como en tu casa,” it means “Make yourself at home.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedo dejar mi mochila en tu casa?
native_language_example: Can I leave my backpack at your place?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in someone else’s situation or to give advice from their perspective. Common patterns: “Yo, en tu lugar, …” (If I were you, I’d …). Can also appear as “estar en tu lugar” = “to be in your place/situation.”
target_language_example: Yo, en tu lugar, hablaría con el jefe primero.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d talk to the boss first.

meaning: “in your hands” (literally), or “up to you / your responsibility” (figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (you are holding something: “con un libro en tus manos”) and figuratively to mean that a decision or outcome depends on you (“Dejo en tus manos qué hacer”). It also appears in set phrases like “tener sangre en tus manos” (“to have blood on your hands,” meaning responsibility/guilt). You can change the possessive: en mis manos, en sus manos, en nuestras manos, etc.
target_language_example: Ahora está en tus manos decidir si aceptas el trabajo.
native_language_example: Now it’s in your hands to decide whether you accept the job.

additional_notes: "En" is usually "in" or "on" depending on context, and "un" means "a/an" for a singular masculine noun. Used to say where something is or happens: en un póster (on a poster), en un circuito (in a circuit), en un circo (in a circus). Before a feminine noun, use "en una".
target_language_example: Hay una foto de mi familia en un marco.
native_language_example: There’s a photo of my family in a frame.

additional_notes: Used to say that an injury, death, or other bad event happened as the result of an accident. Often follows verbs like herirse (to get hurt), quedarse (to end up/become), morir (to die), perder la vida (to lose one’s life), romperse (to break a bone), etc.
target_language_example: Se lastimó el brazo en un accidente de coche.
native_language_example: He injured his arm in a car accident.

meaning: in a (type of) accident; in an accident involving…
additional_notes: Used to say that an injury or death happened as a result of a particular kind of accident. It’s typically followed by the activity or vehicle (e.g., esquí, tráfico/circulación, coche/auto, automóvil). You can also say "en un accidente" without "de" if you don’t specify the type.
target_language_example: Se lastimó la pierna en un accidente de bicicleta.
native_language_example: He injured his leg in a bicycle accident.

meaning: in a plane crash (in an airplane accident).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "morir" (to die) to say someone died as a result of a plane crash. "En" here means "in" (the circumstance/event). You may also hear "en un accidente aéreo" (more formal) or "en un accidente de avión" (more common/clear).
target_language_example: El piloto resultó herido en un accidente de avión.
native_language_example: The pilot was injured in a plane crash.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during/because of a car crash. Often used with verbs like resultar herido/a (to be injured), morir (to die), and quemarse (to be burned). You can also hear en un accidente de auto (Latin America) or en un accidente de tráfico (traffic accident).
target_language_example: Ella se lastimó en un accidente de coche.
native_language_example: She got hurt in a car accident.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened as a result of a road/vehicle accident. Very common with verbs like perder (to lose), morir (to die), resultar herido (to be injured), and perder la vida (to lose one’s life). Also written as accidente de tránsito in some countries.
target_language_example: Se rompió la pierna en un accidente de tráfico.
native_language_example: He broke his leg in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during a car/road accident. Very common with verbs like perder (to lose someone), lastimarse (to get hurt), and perder la memoria (to lose one’s memory). In many places you may also hear: en un accidente de tráfico.
target_language_example: Se rompió la pierna en un accidente de tránsito.
native_language_example: He broke his leg in a traffic accident.

meaning: in one year; in a year (within a year from now).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens within a one-year period. It can mean (1) during the course of one year ("in a year" as a time span: en un año gano X) or (2) one year from now ("a year from now": en un año lo repetimos).
target_language_example: Terminaré el curso en un año.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the course in a year.

meaning: in/at a bank; on a bench (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Banco" has two very common meanings: (1) a financial bank (el banco) and (2) a bench/seat (un banco), especially in a park. With places like "trabajar en un banco" it means a bank (financial). With locations like "en el parque" or actions like "sentarse", it usually means a bench (in English you often say "on a bench").
target_language_example: Nos sentamos en un banco en el parque.
native_language_example: We sat on a bench in the park.

meaning: in one day; within a day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the time it takes to complete something (duration), often emphasizing speed or that it can be done in a single day. It can also mean "within a day" (before a day passes), depending on context.
target_language_example: Terminamos el proyecto en un día.
native_language_example: We finished the project in one day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is located in a hospital or that an event (like being born) happened there, or that someone works there. Also used after verbs like trabajar (to work), estar (to be), nacer (to be born), and morir (to die).
target_language_example: Mi hermano está en un hospital desde ayer.
native_language_example: My brother has been in a hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone is staying or located. Often used with estar (Estoy en un hotel.) or quedarse/alojarse (Nos quedamos en un hotel...).
target_language_example: Voy a estar en un hotel cerca del aeropuerto.
native_language_example: I’m going to be in a hotel near the airport.

meaning: in a place; in one spot/location.
additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or is located. Often followed by an adjective or description: en un lugar remoto (in a remote place), en un lugar fresco y seco (in a cool, dry place), en un lugar como éste/ése (in a place like this/that).
target_language_example: Deja las llaves en un lugar seguro.
native_language_example: Leave the keys in a safe place.

meaning: in a minute; in a moment (soon).
additional_notes: Often used to mean “very soon,” not necessarily exactly 60 seconds. You can use it by itself as a short reply: “En un minuto.” It can also be literal when talking about time/seconds, but in everyday conversation it usually just means “in a little bit.”
target_language_example: En un minuto termino y salimos.
native_language_example: I’ll finish in a minute and we’ll go out.

meaning: in a moment; at a particular time.
additional_notes: Used either (1) to mean "in a moment" / "just a second" when said on its own as a short reply, or (2) to refer to a specific period or point in time, often modified with adjectives: "en un momento peligroso / extraño de mi vida" ("at a dangerous/strange time in my life").
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo hablar; en un momento te llamo.
native_language_example: I can't talk right now; I'll call you in a moment.

meaning: in a fantasy world; in an unrealistic dream world.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not being realistic or is disconnected from real life. Often used with "vivir" (e.g., "Vive en un mundo de fantasía") to criticize or tease someone for having unrealistic expectations. Can also be more neutral when talking about children using their imagination.
target_language_example: Si crees que todo será perfecto sin esfuerzo, vives en un mundo de fantasía.
native_language_example: If you think everything will be perfect without effort, you’re living in a fantasy world.

meaning: in a couple of days; in a few days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening soon, typically about two days from now (sometimes loosely meaning “in a few days”). Common with the future tense or near-future expressions like “te llamaré…” / “nos vemos…”.
target_language_example: Te mando el documento en un par de días.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the document in a couple of days.

meaning: in a couple of hours; in a few hours.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after a short amount of time (roughly around two hours, often not exact). Common with future or implied future: Estaré/volveré/lo tendremos... en un par de horas.
target_language_example: Te llamo en un par de horas.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in a couple of hours.

meaning: in a couple of weeks; in about two weeks.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a time in the (near) future when something will happen or when you’ll see someone again. "Un par de" often means "a couple of" (roughly two, sometimes just “a few”).
target_language_example: Terminaré el proyecto en un par de semanas.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the project in a couple of weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives/lived or grew up. With place names, Spanish often uses "en" (en Madrid, en México), and also with general places like "en un pueblo". "Pueblo" can mean either "town" or "village" depending on context; "pequeño" agrees with the masculine noun (pueblo).
target_language_example: Mis abuelos viven en un pequeño pueblo cerca de la costa.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in a small town near the coast.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens (eating, having dinner, working). Often follows verbs like comer, cenar, trabajar, conseguir trabajo. You can swap in another place: en un café, en un bar. Plural: en restaurantes (in restaurants).
target_language_example: Hoy vamos a comer en un restaurante cerca de casa.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to eat in a restaurant near home.

meaning: in a second; in just a moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen very soon. It can be literal (in one second) but is very often an exaggeration meaning “right away / in a moment.” Common with the future (Estaré…) or near-future expressions.
target_language_example: Vuelvo en un segundo.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a second.

meaning: in a dream; (figuratively) like in a dream.
additional_notes: Used literally to talk about something you experienced while dreaming: “en un sueño”. It’s also used figuratively with “como” or “como si” to describe something that feels unreal, dreamy, or surreal: “Me sentía como en un sueño” / “como si estuviese en un sueño.”
target_language_example: Todo se veía tan perfecto que pensé que estaba en un sueño.
native_language_example: Everything looked so perfect that I thought I was in a dream.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after "en" to indicate location, situation, or medium (e.g., "en una habitación" = in a room, "en una camilla" = on a stretcher, "en una encuesta en línea" = in an online survey). It’s simply "en" + "una" (no contraction). For masculine singular, use "en un".
target_language_example: Nos vemos en una cafetería cerca de tu casa.
native_language_example: See you in a café near your house.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or placed inside a box/container. Often followed by more detail like the type of box (en una caja de cartón) or where it is (en una caja, en la oficina).
target_language_example: Guardé los documentos en una caja para que no se mojaran.
native_language_example: I stored the documents in a box so they wouldn’t get wet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located inside a house or lives in a house. "En" can mean both "in" and "at" depending on context, but with buildings it often means "in/inside." You’ll often see it with verbs like vivir (to live) or estar (to be/located): "Vive en una casa" / "Está en una casa."
target_language_example: Ahora vivimos en una casa cerca del parque.
native_language_example: Now we live in a house near the park.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens or where someone is/grew up. The article changes depending on the city: en una ciudad (a city), en la ciudad (the city), en esa/esta ciudad (that/this city). You can add adjectives like nueva, grande, etc.: en una ciudad nueva.
target_language_example: Encontré trabajo en una ciudad grande.
native_language_example: I found a job in a big city.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" or other verbs to say the location/event where something happens. "En" = in/at, and "una fiesta" = a party. You can change it to "en la fiesta" when referring to a specific party ("at the party").
target_language_example: Nos vimos en una fiesta el sábado.
native_language_example: We saw each other at a party on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone works, is located, or is hiding. Often followed by “de + product” to specify what the factory makes: “una fábrica de herramientas” (a tool factory).
target_language_example: Ella trabaja en una fábrica de automóviles.
native_language_example: She works in a car factory.

meaning: on a farm; at a farm.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is located or works/lives in a farm setting. With verbs like trabajar (to work), vivir (to live), or crecer/criarse (to grow up/be raised), it describes where the action happens. Literally “in a farm,” but in English it’s often “on a farm.”
target_language_example: Vivo en una granja desde niño.
native_language_example: I’ve lived on a farm since I was a kid.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after one hour has passed from the present moment. Common with the future tense or near future (ir a + infinitive): "Te llamo en una hora" / "Te voy a llamar en una hora".
target_language_example: Estoy ocupado ahora, pero puedo ayudarte en una hora.
native_language_example: I’m busy now, but I can help you in an hour.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to say something happens/exists/grew up "in a small ..." (place or thing). "En" = in/on/at, "una" = a, and "pequeña" agrees with a feminine noun (cafetería, granja, ciudad, maleta, aldea). With a masculine noun, you use "en un pequeño" (e.g., "en un pequeño pueblo").
target_language_example: Vivimos en una pequeña casa cerca del parque.
native_language_example: We live in a small house near the park.

meaning: in a week; within one week.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening during the span of one week ("Dos veces en una semana" = two times in one week) or by the time one week has passed ("Lo haré en una semana" = I’ll do it within a week).
target_language_example: Terminaré el informe en una semana.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the report in a week.

meaning: in a situation (in a particular set of circumstances).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives or a descriptor to say what circumstances someone/something is in: en una situación difícil/delicada/de emergencia. Very common with verbs like estar (to be) and encontrarse (to find oneself).
target_language_example: Estamos en una situación complicada, pero vamos a resolverlo.
native_language_example: We’re in a complicated situation, but we’re going to solve it.

meaning: in a store; at a shop.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens inside a store or in the context of a store (shopping, working, finding/buying something). Often followed by a type of store: “en una tienda de antigüedades” (in an antique shop).
target_language_example: Compré este regalo en una tienda cerca de mi casa.
native_language_example: I bought this gift in a store near my house.

additional_notes: Used to say where something was bought/found or where someone works, followed by the kind of store: "en una tienda de ropa" (in a clothing store), "en una tienda de antigüedades" (in an antiques shop). Often you can also use "en una tienda" without "de" if you don’t specify the type.
target_language_example: Encontré este libro en una tienda de segunda mano.
native_language_example: I found this book in a second-hand store.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen a short time from now, but without saying the exact number of days. Literally "in some days" ("unos" = "some/a few"), but the natural English translation is usually "in a few days."
target_language_example: Te llamo en unos días para confirmarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in a few days to confirm it.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly (after a short wait). It can refer to the near future ("I’ll be there in a few minutes") or a countdown until an action starts ("We’ll begin in a few minutes"). You can also say it by itself as a short answer: "En unos minutos."
target_language_example: Te llamo en unos minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happen in the summer season in general (habits, weather, typical situations). It often answers “when?” and can go at the start of the sentence for emphasis: “En verano, …”.
target_language_example: En verano, vamos a la playa casi todos los fines de semana.
native_language_example: In the summer, we go to the beach almost every weekend.

additional_notes: Used with estar (or sometimes quedarse) to describe being in love with someone: estar enamorado/a de + person. Match gender/number: enamorado (male), enamorada (female), enamorados/enamoradas (plural). Intensifiers like totalmente/locamente make it stronger. For a lighter “I like you,” Spanish often uses me gustas rather than estoy enamorado/a de.
target_language_example: Estoy enamorada de mi novio desde hace dos años.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with my boyfriend for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say a man/boy is romantically in love with a specific woman/girl. It agrees with the speaker: a woman would say “enamorada de ella.” You can also change the person: “enamorado/a de él” (in love with him), “enamorado/a de ti” (in love with you).
target_language_example: Creo que está enamorado de ella desde hace meses.
native_language_example: I think he’s been in love with her for months.

additional_notes: Used to say you have romantic love for the person you’re talking to. It agrees with the speaker’s gender: a man says “estoy enamorado de ti” and a woman says “estoy enamorada de ti.” You can also say “enamorado/a de + [person]” (e.g., “enamorado de ella”).
target_language_example: Creo que estoy enamorado de ti.
native_language_example: I think I’m in love with you.

additional_notes: Almost always used with the reflexive pronoun: **se enamoró de** (he/she/it fell in love with). It can be romantic (a person) or non-romantic (a hobby, music, a place): **se enamoró de la música**. For other subjects/tenses you change the verb: **me enamoré de** (I fell in love with), **se enamoran de** (they fall in love with).
target_language_example: Me enamoré de esta ciudad en cuanto llegué.
native_language_example: I fell in love with this city as soon as I arrived.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. Structure: (A + person) + pronoun + encanta el + noun. The thing liked is grammatically the subject: “A él le encanta el béisbol” = “Baseball is delightful to him” → “He loves baseball.” With plural nouns, use encantar in plural: “Me encantan los tacos.”
target_language_example: A mí me encanta el café.
native_language_example: I love coffee.

additional_notes: Used in polite conversation to express that you’re happy about an action or situation, very commonly with greetings: “Encantado/a de conocerle/conocerte” (“Nice to meet you”). It agrees with the speaker: encantado (male speaker) / encantada (female speaker). Often followed by an infinitive (encantado de verle = pleased to see you) or by a noun phrase (encantado de la visita = delighted about the visit).
target_language_example: Encantada de ayudarte hoy.
native_language_example: Pleased to help you today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "encantar" to say someone really likes/loves something. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you often see it with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les encantan los…". Use "encanta" (singular) with a singular thing ("Me encanta el café") and "encantan" (plural) with plural things ("Me encantan los perros"). Often appears with "A + person": "A ella le encantan los animales".
target_language_example: A mí me encantan los libros de misterio.
native_language_example: I love mystery books.

additional_notes: Used to say something is resting/placed on the surface of a table. Common with verbs like dejar (to leave), poner (to put), estar/haber (to be/there is). In Spanish you often say encima de + [place] (“on top of”).
target_language_example: Pon el vaso encima de la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the glass on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on the upper surface of something else (on top of it) or higher than it. It’s often followed by a noun with the definite article: encima del escritorio (on top of the desk), encima del armario (on top of the wardrobe). Feminine form: encima de la mesa.
target_language_example: Dejé las llaves encima del sofá.
native_language_example: I left the keys on top of the couch.

additional_notes: Used with the personal “a” before a specific person (or a pet) who is the direct object: “encontrar a Tom”, “encontrar a tu padre”.
