Without “a”, “encontrar” often refers to finding things: “encontrar las llaves”. It can also mean “to run into/meet (by chance)” in contexts like “Me acabo de encontrar a tu padre.”
target_language_example: No puedo encontrar a mi hermano por ningún lado.
native_language_example: I can’t find my brother anywhere.

meaning: “to find a …” (to locate or to discover a …).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (un + noun): encontrar un lugar/un refugio/un amigo/un departamento. Conjugate encontrar to match the subject and tense (encuentro, encuentras, encuentra, encontré, etc.). For feminine nouns, use “encontrar una”.
target_language_example: No puedo encontrar un lugar tranquilo para estudiar.
native_language_example: I can’t find a quiet place to study.

additional_notes: Use this when you mean getting a job (finding a position and being hired). Common patterns: "encontrar un trabajo" (find a job), "encontrar trabajo" (find work), and in the past: "encontré un trabajo" (I found a job).
target_language_example: Me mudé a Madrid para encontrar un trabajo.
native_language_example: I moved to Madrid to find a job.

additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem or difficult situation. Very common with a problem mentioned explicitly ("para el problema") or implied by context. You can also say "buscar una solución" (to look for a solution) when you haven’t found it yet.
target_language_example: Tenemos que encontrar una solución antes de mañana.
native_language_example: We have to find a solution before tomorrow.

meaning: "I ran into (someone) by chance" / "I found (something) by chance."
additional_notes: Used with the verb *encontrarse* (often with an indirect object pronoun like *me/te/se*): *me encontré por casualidad con él* = “I ran into him by chance.” With people you usually add *con* (especially for “run into”): *me encontré por casualidad con una amiga*. With things, *encontrar por casualidad* can mean “find by chance”: *encontré por casualidad una foto vieja*. In your examples, *me lo/le encontré* uses pronouns (*lo* = him/it, *le* = him/her in some dialects; *me le* is common in parts of Spain).
target_language_example: Ayer me encontré por casualidad con mi profesor en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher by chance at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone found/discovered something in the past. *Encontró* is the completed past (“found”), and *un* is “a/an” for a masculine singular noun (e.g., *un restaurante, un sobre*). With an indirect object, it can mean “found (someone) a …” = arranged/located something for them: *Tom le encontró un departamento a Mary* (“Tom found Mary an apartment”).
target_language_example: Ayer encontré un libro interesante en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: Yesterday I found an interesting book at the library.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or a school) teaches the English language. "Enseña" is the present tense of "enseñar" (to teach) for él/ella/usted. You can add who is being taught with an indirect object: "nos enseña inglés" = "teaches us English," and you can add the group with "a": "enseña inglés a los estudiantes" = "teaches English to the students."
target_language_example: Mi profesora enseña inglés en la universidad.
native_language_example: My teacher teaches English at the university.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of enseñar: “he/she taught/showed.” It’s commonly followed by an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) for “to someone.” Use “enseñó a + infinitive” for teaching how to do something (Él me enseñó a pronunciar…), and “enseñó + noun” for showing/teaching something (Me enseñó su colección).
target_language_example: Mi papá me enseñó a conducir.
native_language_example: My dad taught me to drive.

additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by “lo que” (“what/that which”) to refer to the content of what someone said or what occurred. Often followed by verbs like dice/decía/digo/pasó/estaba diciendo: “No puedo entender lo que pasó.” You can add an object pronoun to show who is speaking to you: “entender lo que me decía” = “understand what he/she was telling me.”
target_language_example: No entiendo lo que quieres decir.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used when you want to know the reason/cause for something. Often followed by a full clause: “entender por qué + [subject] + [verb]”. Very common with “no puedo/no podía” (I can’t/I couldn’t understand why).
target_language_example: No logro entender por qué están tan enojados.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to understand why they’re so angry.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand the content of what someone says, means, thinks, or feels. It’s typically followed by a verb clause (e.g., lo que dices/quieres decir/sientes). You may also see other tenses or subjects: entiendo/entendí/entiendo; entiendo/entiende/entendemos lo que…
target_language_example: Entiendo lo que dices, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I understand what you’re saying, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the key point or specific information after some discussion or as a transition (entonces = “so/then”). Often followed by a noun: “Entonces, ¿cuál es el problema/el plan/la conclusión…?” It can also stand alone (“Entonces, ¿cuál es?”) when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿cuál es la respuesta correcta?
native_language_example: So, what’s the correct answer?

meaning: "So, how…?" (asking how something happened/works, or how someone is doing).
additional_notes: Used to follow up on what was just said: entonces = “so/then,” and ¿cómo…? = “how…?” You’ll often hear it when asking for an explanation (Entonces, ¿cómo ocurrió esto? = “So, how did this happen?”) or when checking in with someone (Entonces, ¿cómo va todo…? = “So, how’s everything going…?”). You can also use it alone (Entonces, ¿cómo?) to mean “So, how (are we going to do it)?” or “So, what now?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿cómo vamos a resolver esto?
native_language_example: So, how are we going to solve this?

additional_notes: Used to question someone’s reasons after what was just said or shown. It often expresses skepticism or a follow-up: “If that’s true, then why…?” You can use it as a full question (“Entonces, ¿por qué?”) or before a verb (“Entonces, ¿por qué lo hiciste?”).
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿por qué no me lo dijiste antes?
native_language_example: So why didn’t you tell me earlier?

additional_notes: Used to follow up on what was just said and ask for clarification or the next logical detail. Often starts a question and can sound like you’re saying “OK, in that case…” or “So…” before asking who did something or who will do something.
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿quién viene conmigo?
native_language_example: So, who’s coming with me?

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation forward and ask what happens next, what someone is doing, or what the next step is. Often introduces a direct question and can sound a bit impatient or pressing depending on tone: “So, what are we going to do?”
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿qué quieres que haga ahora?
native_language_example: So, what do you want me to do now?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question as a follow-up or conclusion (often after hearing an explanation or when moving the conversation forward). It’s very commonly followed by a noun or pronoun ("Entonces, ¿qué es esto?") or by "lo que" for emphasis/clarification ("Entonces, ¿qué es lo que…?").
target_language_example: Entonces, ¿qué es lo que necesitas para empezar?
native_language_example: So, what do you need to get started?

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **darse cuenta** (“to realize”). It’s commonly followed by **de + noun/infinitive** (*me di cuenta de la verdad*, *me di cuenta de lo que pasó*) or **de que + clause** (*me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado*). You can also hear **sólo entonces me di cuenta** = “only then did I realize.”
target_language_example: Entonces me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: Then I realized that I had forgotten the keys.

meaning: to enter / to go into (a specific feminine place).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: entrar a la habitación, entrar a la casa, entrar a la cueva. Often interchangeable with “entrar en la” in many regions; “entrar a la” emphasizes movement into a place.
target_language_example: No puedes entrar a la oficina sin identificación.
native_language_example: You can’t enter the office without ID.

additional_notes: "Entrar" means "to enter." "Al" is a contraction of "a + el" and is used with masculine singular nouns (el cuarto, el aula, el país, el auto). Often used with movement into a place (entrar al cuarto / al país) or letting someone/something in (dejar entrar al perro/gato). For feminine nouns, use "entrar a la" (entrar a la casa).
target_language_example: No puedes entrar al edificio sin identificación.
native_language_example: You can’t enter the building without ID.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular places/rooms/things: entrar en el almacén, entrar en el quirófano, entrar en el local. With feminine nouns use entrar en la (entrar en la casa). Often implies being allowed/forbidden to go in: Sólo la familia puede entrar en el quirófano.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo entrar en el museo?
native_language_example: Can I go into the museum?

meaning: to enter the (feminine noun); to go into the.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to say someone/something goes into a place/area or enters a situation: entrar en la cabina, entrar en la atmósfera, entrar en la Zona. Often it’s simply “enter the” in English. You can also see “entrar en” (without la) before other nouns, and in some regions people say “entrar a” instead of “entrar en”.
target_language_example: No puedes entrar en la sala sin permiso.
native_language_example: You can’t enter the room without permission.

entre el bien y el mal

target_language_multi_word_term: entre el bien y el mal
meaning: between good and evil (right and wrong).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like distinguir (to tell apart) or ver (to see) to talk about a moral contrast or conflict. Often appears in phrases like distinguir entre el bien y el mal (“to distinguish right from wrong”) or una pelea/lucha entre el bien y el mal (“a fight between good and evil”).
target_language_example: A veces cuesta distinguir entre el bien y el mal.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to tell right from wrong.

additional_notes: Used to talk about interactions within a group (they do something with each other: "Hablan/pelean entre ellos" = they talk/fight among themselves). It can also be used when choosing from a set: "elegir entre ellos" = to choose between them. Changes with gender/number: "entre ellas" (all female), "entre ellos" (mixed or all male), "entre nosotros/nosotras", "entre vosotros/vosotras", "entre ustedes".
target_language_example: No discutas con ellos; déjalos que lo resuelvan entre ellos.
native_language_example: Don’t argue with them; let them sort it out among themselves.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like mezclarse (to blend in), encontrar (to find), or abrirse paso (to make your way) to say someone is within a group of many people. Often implies being hard to see or identify because there are so many people.
target_language_example: Lo vi entre la multitud, pero lo perdí de vista.
native_language_example: I saw him in the crowd, but I lost sight of him.

additional_notes: Used to place something in the middle of or within a group of feminine plural nouns: entre las ramas (among the branches), entre las personas (among the people). It’s the preposition entre + the feminine plural article las.
target_language_example: El gato duerme entre las mantas.
native_language_example: The cat sleeps among the blankets.

meaning: "among the" / "between the" (before a masculine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns (los) to locate something within a group ("among") or between two items/people ("between"). Very common pattern: "entre los dos" = "between the two of them / the two of them together"; also "entre los + plural noun" = "among the + plural noun".
target_language_example: Entre los estudiantes, ella habla más español.
native_language_example: Among the students, she speaks the most Spanish.

meaning: "between you and me" (often: just between us / confidential).
additional_notes: Literally means the space/relationship "between you and me" (El gato está entre tú y yo; La relación entre tú y yo...). Very commonly used to mean something is private or a secret: Esto es sólo/queda entre tú y yo = "Let’s keep this between us." You can also add it as an aside to share a candid opinion: Y entre tú y yo, ... = "Between you and me, ..."
target_language_example: Entre tú y yo, no creo que él diga la verdad.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I don’t think he’s telling the truth.

additional_notes: This is the past tense (pretérito) of **entrar**: **entró** = “he/she entered.” **a la** is “to the” (feminine singular), used before places like **la casa, la tienda, la sala**. In many regions you’ll hear **entrar a + place**; in others, **entrar en + place** is also common. For masculine singular, it becomes **entró al** (a + el).
target_language_example: Ella entró a la tienda y compró pan.
native_language_example: She entered the store and bought bread.

additional_notes: "Entró" is the preterite (completed past) of "entrar" (to enter). It usually takes "en" (entró en la habitación) or, in many places, "a" (entró a la habitación) with the same meaning. Used to describe someone going into a room at a specific moment.
target_language_example: En cuanto entró a la habitación, todos se callaron.
native_language_example: As soon as he entered the room, everyone went quiet.

meaning: “entered (into/in)” or “went into” (past tense of entrar en).
additional_notes: Used for someone physically going into a place: Entró en mi casa / en su habitación / en un restaurante. It can also be used with certain nouns for “to go into a state,” especially common in Entró en pánico (“He panicked”).
target_language_example: Cuando oyó el ruido, entró en la cocina.
native_language_example: When he heard the noise, he went into the kitchen.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of entrar: entró = “entered” (a completed action). Often used in stories to describe what happened next. You can replace habitación with another place: entró en la casa / entró en el baño. If you want to specify who entered, add a subject: Él/Ella/Un hombre entró en la habitación.
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó el ruido, entró en la habitación.
native_language_example: When he/she heard the noise, he/she entered the room.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of entrar: entró = “entered/came in.” Used to describe someone entering a place via a specific door; you can add details like por la puerta trasera/delantera (“through the back/front door”). Often used with justo cuando (“just when”) or justo a tiempo (“just in time”).
target_language_example: Cuando entró por la puerta, todos se quedaron en silencio.
native_language_example: When he/she came in through the door, everyone went silent.

meaning: 'team of' / 'crew of' / 'unit of' (a group for a specific activity).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say what kind of team/group it is: equipo de rescate (rescue team), equipo de investigación (research team), equipo de esgrima (fencing team). It can also mean a set of items used for something: equipo de primeros auxilios (first-aid kit).
target_language_example: Llamaron a un equipo de rescate para ayudar en la montaña.
native_language_example: They called a rescue team to help in the mountains.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of players who play baseball. Very common with verbs like estar en / pertenecer a (to be on / belong to) and roles like capitán (captain). You may also see it without “de” as “equipo béisbol” in some contexts, but “equipo de béisbol” is the standard form.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está en el equipo de béisbol de la escuela.
native_language_example: My brother is on the school's baseball team.

additional_notes: Refers to a team that plays fútbol (soccer). In many Spanish-speaking countries, fútbol usually means soccer (not American football). Often used with estar en (to be on a team) and with school teams: el equipo de fútbol de la escuela.
target_language_example: Mi hermano está en el equipo de fútbol de su escuela.
native_language_example: My brother is on his school's soccer team.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was (or wasn’t) aware of a fact, mistake, presence, or situation. It’s the imperfect past (era) of ser + consciente (aware) + de (of). Commonly negated: "no era consciente de..." = "wasn’t aware of...". You can also use it with an infinitive to express awareness of an action: "era consciente de estar...".
target_language_example: No era consciente de que ya era tarde.
native_language_example: I wasn’t aware that it was already late.

additional_notes: Used to say something was excessive in the past. Common pattern: "Era demasiado + adjective" (Era demasiado honesto = He was too honest). With an infinitive: "Era demasiado + adjective + para + infinitive" (Era demasiado tímido para hacer eso = He was too shy to do that). You can also use it impersonally: "Era demasiado + adjective + infinitive" (Era demasiado peligroso contactar contigo = It was too dangerous to contact you).
target_language_example: Era demasiado tarde para llamar.
native_language_example: It was too late to call.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ser (era) to describe a past situation: by that point, it was already too late. Often followed by "para" + infinitive: "Era demasiado tarde para + verbo" (It was too late to + verb). You’ll also commonly see it with "ya": "Ya era demasiado tarde" (It was already too late).
target_language_example: Lo intenté llamar, pero era demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: I tried to call him, but it was too late.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe what something/someone was in the past (background or ongoing past situation). Often followed by a noun or a noun phrase: *Mi carta era el tres de espadas.* Note: Spanish **era** is a verb form meaning “was,” and can be confused with English *era* (a time period).
target_language_example: Ese ruido era el viento.
native_language_example: That noise was the wind.

meaning: 'he/she/it was the only one' / 'was the only (person/thing)'.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of "ser" (era = was) to describe a past situation/background. "Único" agrees with the noun it refers to: "era el único" (masc.), "era la única" (fem.), "eran los únicos/las únicas" (plural). Often followed by "en" + place (era el único en la habitación) or "que" + verb (era el único que tenía).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, era el único en la oficina.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I was the only one in the office.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of ser (era) to describe a past state/background situation: "He/She/I was innocent." You can also say "era inocente de + [something]" to mean "was innocent of" a crime/accusation (e.g., "era inocente del crimen").
target_language_example: Cuando lo arrestaron, yo sabía que era inocente.
native_language_example: When they arrested him, I knew he was innocent.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of **ser** (**era**) to describe an ongoing past state/background information (age, description, situation). Often contrasted with the preterite (**fue joven**) which is much less common and would focus on the fact of being young as a completed stage.
target_language_example: Cuando mi abuelo era joven, vivía cerca del mar.
native_language_example: When my grandfather was young, he lived near the sea.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of ser (era) to describe a past situation: something/someone was the only option/solution/opportunity/person, etc. "Única" agrees with a feminine noun (la forma, la oportunidad, la solución, la profesora, la chica, la persona). For a masculine noun, use "era el único".
target_language_example: Era la única manera de hacerlo a tiempo.
native_language_example: It was the only way to do it on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something in the past was the thing someone wanted/meant/needed, etc. It uses the imperfect tense of ser (era = “was”), often in phrases like: “No era lo que quería” (It wasn’t what I wanted) or “Era lo que faltaba” (It was what was missing / just what we needed).
target_language_example: No era lo que esperaba, pero estuvo bien.
native_language_example: It wasn’t what I expected, but it was fine.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to say something met the needed degree or level. Very common pattern: "era lo suficientemente + adj. + para + infinitive" ("was + adj. + enough to + verb"). The adjective usually agrees in gender/number with the subject: "lo suficientemente insensato" (masc.), "lo suficientemente insensata" (fem.).
target_language_example: La habitación era lo suficientemente grande para todos.
native_language_example: The room was big enough for everyone.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there was just one possible/necessary option. Commonly followed by a verb phrase: “Era lo único que podía/quería/tenía que (hacer) …”. You can add “eso” at the start (“Eso era lo único que…”) to refer back to something already mentioned. Note: “era” is imperfect past (background/description), while “fue” would sound more like a specific completed event (“it was the only thing that happened/that I did”).
target_language_example: Era lo único que podía decir en ese momento.
native_language_example: It was the only thing I could say at that moment.

additional_notes: Used to say that something in the past was the thing someone wanted/meant/needed, etc. It uses the imperfect tense of ser (era = “was”), often in phrases like: “No era lo que quería” (It wasn’t what I wanted) or “Era lo que faltaba” (It was what was missing / just what we needed).
target_language_example: No era lo que esperaba, pero estuvo bien.
native_language_example: It wasn’t what I expected, but it was fine.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect form of **ser** (**era**) + a possessive (**mi**) to describe what something/someone used to be or was considered in the past (background/description). Often followed by a noun: **era mi casa** (it was my house), **era mi mejor amiga** (she was my best friend).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, esa casa era mi hogar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, that house was my home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (era) to describe a past situation/relationship that lasted for a period of time (e.g., when you were a kid, in high school). You can change the person/gender: "era mi mejor amiga" (she was my best friend). If you mean a completed past fact at a specific moment, Spanish often uses "fue" instead of "era" depending on context.
target_language_example: Antes, era mi mejor amigo, pero ya no hablamos.
native_language_example: Before, he was my best friend, but we don’t talk anymore.

meaning: "was very" (used to describe how something/someone was).
additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past tense of "ser" (to be), used for descriptions, background information, and ongoing states in the past. "Muy" intensifies an adjective or adverb: era muy aburrido/anormal/rico = was very boring/abnormal/rich. For a past event/change (not a description), Spanish often uses "fue" instead.
target_language_example: La película era muy larga, pero me gustó.
native_language_example: The movie was very long, but I liked it.

meaning: “(he/I) was a child” / “when (he/I) was a child.”
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of ser (era) to talk about an ongoing past state/background, often in phrases like “cuando era niño” (when I/he was a child) or “desde que era niño” (since I/he was a child). Add an article for gender/number: “era un niño / era una niña” (I/he was a boy/girl).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, me gustaba jugar en el parque.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I liked to play in the park.

meaning: “(he/she/I) was little / was a child” (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of **ser** (**era**) to describe someone’s age/state during childhood. Very common in time clauses with **cuando**: **Cuando yo era pequeño...** = “When I was a kid...”. You can change for gender/number: **era pequeña**, **éramos pequeños/as**.
target_language_example: Cuando era pequeño, me gustaban mucho los dinosaurios.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I really liked dinosaurs.

meaning: 'was so' / 'was such (a)…' (introduces a result or comparison).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of **ser** (**era**) + **tan** to intensify an adjective or adverb: **era tan + adj./adv. + que...** = “it was so … that …”. Often followed by **que** to give the consequence/result. In questions like **¿Qué era tan…?**, it means “What was so…?”.
target_language_example: La comida era tan buena que pedimos otra porción.
native_language_example: The food was so good that we ordered another portion.

meaning: “it was all that / it was everything that …”
additional_notes: Used to say that something was the only thing needed/possible/known/had, followed by a clause with a verb (often in the imperfect: necesitaba, podía, conocía). Also common in the fixed phrase “Eso era todo lo que quería decir” (“That was all I wanted to say”).
target_language_example: Era todo lo que necesitábamos para empezar.
native_language_example: It was all we needed to get started.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ser (era) + the masculine singular indefinite article (un) before a masculine noun: "Era un médico" = "He was a doctor." The imperfect often describes background information, identity, or a general/ongoing state in the past (not a single completed event). For a woman, use "era una".
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, mi padre era un maestro.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, my dad was a teacher.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of ser: "era" is used for descriptions/background in the past (who someone was, what something was like). "buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" used before a masculine singular noun (buen + noun). For feminine nouns, use "era una buena …".
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, mi abuelo era un buen maestro.
native_language_example: When he was a child, my grandfather was a good teacher.

meaning: “was a great / an excellent …” (describing someone or something in the past).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to praise someone/something, often about a person’s qualities or role: "era un gran periodista" (he/she was a great journalist). "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" that goes before a singular noun (gran + noun).
target_language_example: Cuando era joven, mi abuelo era un gran músico.
native_language_example: When he was young, my grandfather was a great musician.

meaning: “he was a man” / “(it) was a man.”
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect form of "ser" (era) to describe someone in the past or give background information. Often followed by an adjective or a relative clause: "Era un hombre valiente" (He was a brave man), "Era un hombre que…" (He was a man who…). If you want to specify "he," you can say "Él era un hombre…" (note the accent on "Él").
target_language_example: Cuando lo conocí, era un hombre muy amable.
native_language_example: When I met him, he was a very kind man.

meaning: "he was a very ..." (describing a man with an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man in the past with an adjective: "Era un hombre muy + adjective" (e.g., honesto, decente, pequeño, gracioso, sabio). "Era" is the imperfect of "ser" (was), commonly used for descriptions/background information.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo era un hombre muy trabajador.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a very hard-working man.

meaning: "I/he was a child" / "I/he was a boy. "
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of ser (era) to describe someone in the past (age, background description, or an ongoing state). It can refer to the speaker or another person depending on context: Yo era un niño = “I was a child,” Él era un niño = “He was a child.” Also common with todavía (“still”): todavía era un niño = “I/he was still a child.”
target_language_example: Cuando era un niño, me gustaban mucho los dinosaurios.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I liked dinosaurs a lot.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** in the **imperfect past** to describe what something/someone *was like* or *was* over a period of time (background description). **Una** is the feminine form of “a/an”; with masculine nouns you use **era un**. Note: **era** can look like the English noun “era,” but here it’s a verb form meaning “was.”
target_language_example: Cuando yo era niño, era una persona muy tímida.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I was a very shy person.

additional_notes: Used to clarify that something you said/did wasn’t serious (often after someone reacts or misunderstands). Also appears with emphasis words like “sólo/solo” (just) or “sí” (yes): “Sólo era una broma.”
target_language_example: Lo dije en serio… bueno, no: era una broma.
native_language_example: I said it seriously… well, no: it was a joke.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often something someone did or planned to do) was not a good decision. It uses the imperfect tense (era), common for descriptions and background information in the past. You can also use it after verbs like pensar/saber: "Pensó/Sabía que era una mala idea". You can add an action with an infinitive: "Era una mala idea hacer eso" (It was a bad idea to do that).
target_language_example: Salir sin abrigo era una mala idea.
native_language_example: Going out without a coat was a bad idea.

meaning: 'she was a woman' / 'it was a woman' (describing someone in the past).
additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past tense of "ser" (to be), used for descriptions in the past (age, personality, appearance, background). "Era una mujer + adjective" means "She was a + adjective + woman" (e.g., "Era una mujer sabia" = "She was a wise woman"). It can also refer to an unidentified person in a story: "Era una mujer embarazada" = "It was a pregnant woman."
target_language_example: Cuando la conocí, era una mujer muy amable.
native_language_example: When I met her, she was a very kind woman.

meaning: "she was a girl" / "I was a girl" ("used to be a little girl").
additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" and is used for descriptions and ongoing past situations (age, personality, background). "Una niña" means "a girl" or "a (little) girl." The subject (yo/ella/etc.) is often omitted and understood from context.
target_language_example: Cuando era una niña, me gustaban mucho los animales.
native_language_example: When I was a little girl, I really liked animals.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of **ser** (**eran**) to describe a past situation/state (e.g., who someone used to be to you). The subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes) is often omitted because **eran** already implies “they/you (plural) were.”
target_language_example: Cuando vivía en Madrid, ellos eran mis amigos.
native_language_example: When I lived in Madrid, they were my friends.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t have enough age or maturity to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., entender, viajar) or sometimes by a noun phrase (e.g., tener novio). You can change the subject: «soy demasiado joven para…», «es demasiado joven para…», «eres demasiado mayor para…».
target_language_example: Eres demasiado joven para conducir sin un adulto.
native_language_example: You are too young to drive without an adult.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** (to be) to identify someone or say they belong to a category. **El** is masculine singular; for a female, use **eres la**. Very common with superlatives: **eres el más + adjective** (“you are the most …”).
target_language_example: Eres el mejor amigo que tengo.
native_language_example: You are the best friend I have.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone directly. It agrees with the person you’re talking to: to a female, say "eres la mejor". You can add a noun after it (as in the examples): "Eres el mejor piloto" = "You’re the best pilot."
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme; eres el mejor.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me; you’re the best.

meaning: “you are the only one” (the only person).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are the only person who can do something or the only one in a group (often with que / con el que / en el que / en quien + verb). For a woman, say: “eres la única”. Spanish also distinguishes between “en el que” and “en quien” (“in whom”), but both are common in speech.
target_language_example: Eres el único en quien confío.
native_language_example: You’re the only one I trust.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** + **el/la único/a(s)** + **que** to say someone is the only person who does something. **Único** agrees with the person: *eres el único que...* (male), *eres la única que...* (female). For plural: *sois los únicos que... / son las únicas que...*. After **que**, you typically add a verb phrase: *eres el único que puede/queda/sabe...*.
target_language_example: Eres la única que entiende mi situación.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who understands my situation.

additional_notes: Used to say that only “you” (and nobody else) is able to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive to name the action: “Eres el único que puede + ayudar / hacerlo / protegerlos…”. You can change gender/number: “eres la única…” (female), “sois los únicos…” (you all), “es el único…” (he/it), “son los únicos…” (they).
target_language_example: Eres el único que puede solucionar este problema.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who can solve this problem.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone by saying they are the most + adjective (más fuerte, más importante, más maravillosa, etc.). It’s often followed by extra information, like: que conozco/que he conocido (“that I know / that I’ve ever known”) or en mi vida (“in my life”). Word-by-word it’s: eres (you are) + la persona (the person) + más (most).
target_language_example: Eres la persona más amable que conozco.
native_language_example: You’re the kindest person I know.

meaning: "you’re the only one" (speaking to a woman).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the person you’re speaking to is the only one who fits a description (the only one I trust / miss / have). It agrees with the person’s gender: eres el único (to a man). It often continues with a clause like “en quien/en la que puedo confiar” (that I can trust) or “que yo extraño” (that I miss).
target_language_example: Eres la única en quien confío.
native_language_example: You’re the only one I trust.

meaning: "you’re the only one who can" (addressing a woman).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one specific person is the only person capable of doing something. It’s directed at a female (única). For a male, say: "eres el único que puede". You normally add an infinitive or verb phrase after "puede" (e.g., ayudarme, hacerlo, protegerlos).
target_language_example: Eres la única que puede decirle la verdad.
native_language_example: You’re the only one who can tell him the truth.

meaning: “you are my …” (talking to one person, informally).
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular verb form (tú): eres. Follow it with a noun or noun phrase to say what someone means to you (e.g., amigo, felicidad, esperanza). For a formal or plural ‘you are’, use: usted es mi… / ustedes son mi….
target_language_example: Eres mi familia.
native_language_example: You are my family.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe someone directly in the tú form: eres = “you are” (informal singular), muy = “very.” It’s a compliment or description depending on the adjective (bella/hermosa = beautiful, generoso = generous, diferente = different). For formal “you,” use: usted es muy …
target_language_example: Eres muy amable conmigo.
native_language_example: You are very kind to me.

additional_notes: A common compliment using **ser** (“to be”) in the **tú** form: *eres* = “you are.” **Bueno** agrees with the person: **bueno** (male), **buena** (female). Often followed by what someone is good at: **eres muy bueno cosiendo** (“you’re very good at sewing”) or **eres muy bueno en + noun/thing** (“you’re very good at what you do”). Can also be said alone (*Eres muy bueno.*) to praise someone; tone can make it sound sarcastic in some contexts.
target_language_example: Eres muy bueno con los niños.
native_language_example: You’re very good with kids.

additional_notes: "Eres" = "you are" (for a permanent or general trait) and "tan" = "so/as". Use it to intensify an adjective: "Eres tan amable" (You’re so kind). It’s also used in comparisons with "como": "Eres tan alto como yo" (You’re as tall as me). You can repeat "tan" for emphasis: "tan, tan".
target_language_example: Eres tan amable conmigo.
native_language_example: You are so kind to me.

additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize the person being talked about (often like “it’s YOU”). It can appear after a noun or clause for emphasis: “X eres tú” = “You are X” / “X is you.” Often used in dramatic, emotional, or accusatory statements.
target_language_example: La persona que busco eres tú.
native_language_example: The person I’m looking for is you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that *you* (and not someone else) are the person doing something. It’s a cleft sentence with **quien** (“who”). Can be negated: **No eres tú quien…** (“You’re not the one who…”). Often followed by a verb in the present or past: **Eres tú quien quería…**.
target_language_example: Eres tú quien siempre llega tarde.
native_language_example: You’re the one who always arrives late.

meaning: “you are a …” (speaking to one person, informal tú).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to identify or describe someone: eres un + masculine singular noun (or a noun phrase). For feminine nouns, use “eres una …” (Eres una doctora.). For plural (talking to more than one person, vosotros/ustedes), it changes (Sois/Son …). Often used for labels, insults, or compliments: “Eres un genio”, “Eres un idiota”.
target_language_example: Eres un buen amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: "you are a good" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone: "Eres" = "you are" and "un buen" is the shortened form of "un bueno" placed before a masculine singular noun (e.g., buen amigo, buen padre, buen cocinero). For feminine nouns, use "Eres una buena..." (e.g., una buena hermana). For plural, use "Eres un buen + plural noun" only if the noun stays singular in meaning; otherwise typically use "Eres un buen + singular role" or "Eres muy buen/ buena...".
target_language_example: Eres un buen amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone (often a male child/teen) with an adjective: “Eres un chico bueno/inteligente.” In many contexts, chico can also mean “guy” (a young man) in a friendly, informal way. For an adult man, you’ll often hear “Eres un hombre…”.
target_language_example: Eres un chico muy amable.
native_language_example: You’re a very kind guy.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a man, often followed by an adjective or phrase: “Eres un hombre adulto/con suerte/de palabra/libre.” It can also be used as a challenge to “be a man” (“Si eres un hombre…”), which can sound confrontational or stereotyped depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Eres un hombre bueno y honesto.
native_language_example: You are a good, honest man.

meaning: "you are a" (addressing someone with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (tú) + feminine singular noun: eres una + [noun]. It can introduce a description, a compliment, an insult, or a profession/role: “Eres una profesora” (You’re a teacher), “Eres una monada” (You’re adorable). Use “eres un” before a masculine singular noun (e.g., “Eres un amigo”).
target_language_example: Eres una buena amiga.
native_language_example: You’re a good friend.

meaning: “you are a good …” (to a female), used before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used to compliment or describe someone/something with a feminine noun after it: *Eres una buena amiga/chica/cocinera.* The adjective must match gender/number: **un buen** (masculine), **una buena** (feminine), **unos buenos/unas buenas** (plural). By itself, *Eres una buena…* sounds incomplete—you normally add the noun.
target_language_example: Eres una buena estudiante.
native_language_example: You’re a good student.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ser (eres = “you are”) to describe someone (a girl). Commonly followed by an adjective or description: “Eres una chica inteligente.” In real life, Spanish often drops the subject pronoun (tú), so you’ll usually hear “Eres…” rather than “Tú eres…”.
target_language_example: Eres una chica muy valiente.
native_language_example: You are a very brave girl.

meaning: "you are a woman" (said to one person).
additional_notes: "Eres" is the informal singular form of "to be" (ser), used when addressing someone as "tú." It can be neutral for stating someone’s gender/identity ("Eres una mujer"), but in contexts like "Eres una mujer hermosa/atractiva" it can sound like a compliment and may feel too direct depending on the relationship and situation. For formal "you" (usted), use "Usted es una mujer."
target_language_example: Eres una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: You are a very intelligent woman.

meaning: "that’s what I…" / "that’s what I’m referring to…" (introduces what you mean, do, dedicate yourself to, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as the start of a longer sentence: **Es/Eso/Esto + a lo que me + verb**. The part **a lo que** means “to what/what … to,” and it links back to something already mentioned (eso/esto) or understood from context. Common verbs after it include **dedico** (I dedicate myself to / I do for work) and **refería** (I was referring to).
target_language_example: Eso es a lo que me refería.
native_language_example: That’s what I was referring to.

additional_notes: Used to say something (a thing, situation, or person) fits a purpose, task, or group. You can also negate it: "no es adecuado para" = "is not suitable for". For people, it often means "is a good fit/qualified for" a job or role.
target_language_example: Este curso es adecuado para estudiantes con poco tiempo.
native_language_example: This course is suitable for students with little time.

additional_notes: Use **es algo** to say something is *at least a little positive or helpful*: **Al menos es algo** (“At least it’s something”). It’s also used to soften an adjective: **es algo difícil** = “it’s somewhat / kind of difficult.” Often followed by an adjective (**es algo bueno, es algo raro**) or used alone to mean “that already counts for something.”
target_language_example: No es perfecto, pero al menos es algo.
native_language_example: It’s not perfect, but at least it’s something.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific thing/idea, usually followed by more information (often a relative clause with verbs like conviene, debemos, tiene que ver, etc.). Very common for giving explanations or emphasizing that a topic matters: Es algo que + (verb/description).
target_language_example: Es algo que no puedo explicar ahora.
native_language_example: It’s something that I can’t explain right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is your responsibility or something you have the right to know about. Often said as “(Eso) es asunto mío” (“That’s my business”) or in the negative to set boundaries: “No es asunto tuyo” (“It’s none of your business”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es asunto mío.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s my business.

additional_notes: Used to say something is someone’s responsibility or concern. Often appears in the negative to mean “it’s none of your business”: “No es asunto suyo” / “Esto no es asunto suyo.” You can also change the person: “es asunto mío/tu/su/nuestro.”
target_language_example: Si quieres ir o no, es asunto tuyo.
native_language_example: Whether you want to go or not is up to you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is someone else’s responsibility or concern. Often sounds firm or dismissive; in the negative ("No es asunto tuyo" / "Esto no es asunto tuyo") it means “It’s none of your business.” You can swap the subject: "Eso/Esto/Ese" + "es asunto tuyo".
target_language_example: Si quieres decírselo o no, es asunto tuyo.
native_language_example: Whether you want to tell them or not, that’s your business.

meaning: “it’s like that / that’s how it is.”
additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true or to state that a situation is simply that way. Common in phrases like “Es así de sencillo” (“It’s that simple”) and in conditional sentences: “Si es así…” (“If that’s the case…”). It can also mean “it’s done that way” depending on context.
target_language_example: No me gusta, pero es así.
native_language_example: I don’t like it, but that’s how it is.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to soften or moderate a description (similar to "quite" or "pretty" in English): Es bastante + adjective. It can sound less absolute than “es muy…”. Also common with other subjects: “Es/está/son/están bastante…”.
target_language_example: El examen es bastante difícil, pero se puede aprobar.
native_language_example: The exam is quite difficult, but you can pass it.

meaning: “is good” (talking about something feminine or using a feminine adjective).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (agua, economía, fruta, etc.): *El agua es buena.* Literally “is good.” In conversation, *Esa sí que es buena* can mean “That’s a good one!”—often reacting to a surprising statement or a joke (sometimes ironic, depending on tone). You can also add *para + someone* to mean “is good for (someone)”: *La fruta fresca es buena para ti.*
target_language_example: La idea es buena, pero necesitamos más tiempo.
native_language_example: The idea is good, but we need more time.

meaning: “is good for” / “is good at” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular subjects (la zanahoria, ella, la guerra, cualquier excusa). With an activity/verb in the infinitive, it often means “good for (doing something)” or “a good excuse/opportunity to do something” (Es buena para sacar...). With a skill or task, it means “good at” (Es buena para hablar/jugar; No es buena para las tareas domésticas). With a thing/purpose, it means “good for” (La zanahoria es buena para la sopa; La guerra es buena para los negocios). Variants: es bueno para (masc.), son buenos/as para (plural).
target_language_example: Este cuchillo es bueno para cortar pan, pero no es bueno para carne.
native_language_example: This knife is good for cutting bread, but it’s not good for meat.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to say something is good in general: *Comer es bueno.* It’s also common with an infinitive: *Es bueno leer...* You can add **que + subjunctive** to express that it’s good that something happens/doesn’t happen: *Es bueno que no seas...* With people, **ser bueno** can mean “to be a good person” (*Él es bueno.*). To say someone is good at something, Spanish often uses **ser bueno + gerund** (*Él es bueno conduciendo* = he’s good at driving) or **ser bueno en + subject** (*Él es bueno en matemáticas*).
target_language_example: Es bueno descansar un poco antes del examen.
native_language_example: It’s good to rest a little before the exam.

meaning: is good for; is good at (doing something).
additional_notes: Use **ser bueno/a para + noun** to say something is beneficial or suitable: *Es bueno para el estómago* (good for the stomach), *Es bueno para ese trabajo* (good for that job). Use **ser bueno/a para + infinitive** to say someone is good at doing an activity: *Es bueno para conducir* (good at driving). Match **bueno/a** to the subject (bueno = masculine, buena = feminine).
target_language_example: Este té es bueno para dormir.
native_language_example: This tea is good for sleeping.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity or habit has a positive effect on health. It often follows an infinitive or noun: "Correr es bueno para la salud" (Running is good for your health) / "El deporte es bueno para la salud" (Sports/exercise is good for your health). You can also say "Esto es bueno para la salud" (This is good for your health).
target_language_example: Beber suficiente agua es bueno para la salud.
native_language_example: Drinking enough water is good for your health.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability or capacity to do something, usually followed by an infinitive: es capaz de + infinitive (e.g., es capaz de nadar). In the negative (no es capaz de), it means “is not able to / can’t bring themselves to,” especially for emotional or difficult actions.
target_language_example: ¿Crees que él es capaz de decir la verdad?
native_language_example: Do you think he’s capable of telling the truth?

additional_notes: Used to confirm that a statement is true. Often followed by "que" + a clause ("Es cierto que..." = "It’s true that..."). You can also use it to agree with someone’s point: "Sí, es cierto."
target_language_example: Sí, es cierto que mañana no trabajamos.
native_language_example: Yes, it’s true that we’re not working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to state or confirm that a fact is true. Often introduces a clause with a contrast, like: "Es cierto que…, pero…" (“It’s true that…, but…”). In questions/conditions it can express doubt or a premise: "¿Es cierto que…?" (“Is it true that…?”), "Si es cierto que…" (“If it’s true that…”). Also common: "Es cierto." (“That’s true.”).
target_language_example: Es cierto que no tengo tiempo, pero quiero ayudarte.
native_language_example: It’s true that I don’t have time, but I want to help you.

meaning: “is like” (used to compare or give an analogy).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) + como (“like/as”) to compare one thing to another: “X es como Y.” It’s also common for explaining a concept by analogy (often like “it’s like…” in English). For other subjects, ser changes: “soy como…”, “eres como…”, “somos como…”.
target_language_example: Aprender un idioma es como entrenar: necesitas práctica todos los días.
native_language_example: Learning a language is like training: you need practice every day.

meaning: “is like a…” (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare one thing/person to another in a figurative or literal way. It’s often followed by a noun with an article (un/una), and it can also appear in other forms like “es como una…”, “son como…”, or “es como…” (without un/una).
target_language_example: Para mí, esta ciudad es como un laberinto.
native_language_example: To me, this city is like a maze.

meaning: 'it’s like a…' (comparison with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to something else. The noun after "una" is feminine (e.g., una computadora, una ola). For a masculine noun, you say "es como un" (e.g., es como un coche).
target_language_example: Este programa es como una guía paso a paso.
native_language_example: This program is like a step-by-step guide.

meaning: “is like” (used to compare or give an analogy).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) + como (“like/as”) to compare one thing to another: “X es como Y.” It’s also common for explaining a concept by analogy (often like “it’s like…” in English). For other subjects, ser changes: “soy como…”, “eres como…”, “somos como…”.
target_language_example: Aprender un idioma es como entrenar: necesitas práctica todos los días.
native_language_example: Learning a language is like training: you need practice every day.

meaning: "it’s as if" / "it’s like" (introducing an unreal or hypothetical situation).
additional_notes: Used to compare a real situation to an imagined one: “It’s as if…”. It’s commonly followed by the imperfect subjunctive (as in the examples: estuviera, fuera, viniera, se diera). You can also see it without the “es” in other tenses: “Era/Fue como si…”.
target_language_example: Es como si no me escuchara nadie.
native_language_example: It’s as if nobody were listening to me.

additional_notes: Used to say a person (or their name) is familiar to everyone in a place or group. Structure: ser + conocido/a + por todos (gender/number changes: es conocida…, son conocidos…, son conocidas…). Often followed by a location: en el pueblo, en la ciudad, etc.
target_language_example: La historia del castillo es conocida por todos en el pueblo.
native_language_example: The story of the castle is known by everyone in the town.

additional_notes: Used to take responsibility or blame. Often appears in questions/defensive statements like “¿Acaso es culpa mía?” (“Is it my fault?”). You can swap the pronoun: “es culpa tuya” (it’s your fault), “es culpa suya” (it’s his/her/their/your fault—formal).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es culpa mía.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it’s my fault.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is impolite or socially unacceptable. Often followed by an infinitive to name the action: "Es de mala educación + infinitive" (e.g., "Es de mala educación interrumpir"). You can also say "Eso es de mala educación" = "That’s rude."
target_language_example: Es de mala educación interrumpir cuando alguien está hablando.
native_language_example: It’s rude to interrupt when someone is talking.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives or adverbs to say something is excessive. Common pattern: “es demasiado + adjective + para + infinitive” (e.g., “es demasiado peligroso para…” = “it’s too dangerous to…”). You can also use it alone to mean “that’s too much.”
target_language_example: Esto es demasiado caro para mí.
native_language_example: This is too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs more than is acceptable or affordable. Often followed by “para mí” (“for me”) to make it personal: “Es demasiado caro para mí.” You can replace the subject: “El alquiler es demasiado caro.” / “Este anillo es demasiado caro.”
target_language_example: No lo voy a comprar; es demasiado caro para mí.
native_language_example: I’m not going to buy it; it’s too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is beyond someone’s ability or understanding. Common patterns: (1) "Es demasiado difícil para + noun/pronoun" + optional noun (e.g., "para mí", "para mi comprensión"). (2) "Es demasiado difícil para que + subjunctive" to express “too difficult for (someone) to + verb”: "Es demasiado difícil para que yo lo entienda". After "para que", use the subjunctive (entienda, lea, resuelva).
target_language_example: Este ejercicio es demasiado difícil para que lo haga hoy.
native_language_example: This exercise is too difficult for me to do today.

meaning: “is too big for (someone/something)” or “is too big to (do something)”
additional_notes: Used to say something is bigger than what a person needs or can use, or bigger than what will fit/allow an action. Structure: (subject) + es + demasiado grande + para + [person/thing] (e.g., para ti) or para + [infinitive] (e.g., para entrar). You can change "es" to match the subject (son, era, etc.).
target_language_example: El coche es demasiado grande para este garaje.
native_language_example: The car is too big for this garage.

additional_notes: Use it to say someone doesn’t have the age (or maturity/permission) to do something. Structure: [ser] + demasiado joven + para + infinitive. You can change the verb to match the subject: soy/eres/es/somos/son demasiado joven(es) para… In plural, use jóvenes: Son demasiado jóvenes para conducir.
target_language_example: Es demasiado joven para salir solo por la noche.
native_language_example: He/She is too young to go out alone at night.

additional_notes: Used to say something (often a thing, room, house, or a person) is not big enough for someone or for doing an activity. Structure: **[subject] + es + demasiado + pequeña/o/a/os/as + para + [person/thing]** or **para + infinitive**. Agreement: use **pequeño/pequeña** to match the subject (e.g., *El cuarto es demasiado pequeño...*, *Las sillas son demasiado pequeñas...*).
target_language_example: El coche es demasiado pequeño para cinco personas.
native_language_example: The car is too small for five people.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t fit or isn’t suitable because it’s not big enough. It can be followed by a person (para mí, para nosotros) or by an action with an infinitive (para nadar). You can change the adjective for gender/number: es demasiado pequeña / son demasiado pequeños.
target_language_example: Este abrigo es demasiado pequeño para mí.
native_language_example: This coat is too small for me.

additional_notes: Used to say an action can no longer be done in time ("too late to" + infinitive: Es demasiado tarde para llamar) or that it’s too late for someone/something ("too late for" + person/thing: Es demasiado tarde para mí). Often appears with "Nunca" to express that it’s not too late: "Nunca es demasiado tarde para aprender" (“It’s never too late to learn”).
target_language_example: Es demasiado tarde para cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: It’s too late to change your mind.

additional_notes: Used to compare things or situations. Often followed by "de" to say what something differs from: "es diferente de..." (different from...). Can also react to new information: "Bueno, eso es diferente."
target_language_example: Para mí, esta situación es diferente.
native_language_example: For me, this situation is different.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is hard to do: Es difícil convencer..., Es difícil decir.... You can also use it with a noun/verb phrase as the subject: Dominar el inglés es difícil. Often implies a general statement (not tied to a specific person).
target_language_example: Es difícil aprender un idioma sin practicar.
native_language_example: It’s hard to learn a language without practicing.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is not easy to do/understand: Es difícil de + infinitive (describir, entender, explicar, creer, etc.). In everyday Spanish you’ll also hear "Es difícil" without "de" (Es difícil entenderlo), but both are common.
target_language_example: Es difícil de creer, pero es verdad.
native_language_example: It’s hard to believe, but it’s true.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is not easily satisfied and has high expectations. Often said about a boss, customer, or anyone who complains easily. You can change the subject: "Soy difícil de complacer" (I’m hard to please), "Mi jefe es difícil de complacer" (My boss is hard to please).
target_language_example: A mi profesora le cuesta quedar satisfecha; es difícil de complacer.
native_language_example: My teacher has a hard time being satisfied; she’s hard to please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not easy to understand (because it’s complex, confusing, or unclear). You can use it by itself (Es difícil de entender.) or specify the subject: X es difícil de entender. Also common: Es difícil de entender, pero… (“It’s hard to understand, but…”).
target_language_example: Lo que dijo el profesor es difícil de entender.
native_language_example: What the teacher said is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult for a particular person or group. Pattern: "Es difícil para + [person/group] + [infinitive/thing]". With pronouns: "para mí, para ti, para él/ella, para nosotros/as". Note the accent: "mí" (me) vs "mi" (my).
target_language_example: Es difícil para mí levantarme temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to get up early every day.

additional_notes: Used with ser (es) + adjective (divertido) to describe something as fun or entertaining: Es divertido bailar. It can describe an activity/thing (Esto es divertido) or a person (Tom es divertido = Tom is fun/funny). In the negative, ya no es divertido means 'it’s not fun anymore.' You may also see a similar structure with an indirect object: Me es divertido (less common than Es divertido para mí or Me resulta divertido) = 'It’s fun for me / I find it fun.'
target_language_example: Ya no es divertido jugar así.
native_language_example: It’s not fun to play like that anymore.

meaning: "is where" (used to say/define the place where something happens or exists).
additional_notes: Used to identify or emphasize a location. Often follows a place phrase for emphasis (e.g., "En mi casa es donde...") or starts a sentence to define a place ("Es donde vivo"). It can also be used in general definitions: "Una mina es donde...".
target_language_example: Aquí es donde nos conocimos.
native_language_example: This is where we met.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: **ser + number of years + mayor que + person**. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., *soy / eres / es / somos / son*). You can replace *dos* with any number: *es tres años mayor que…*. For “younger,” use *menor que*: *es dos años menor que…*.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es dos años mayor que yo, pero parece más joven.
native_language_example: My sister is two years older than me, but she looks younger.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** (to be): **es** = “is” and **el** = “the” (masculine singular noun). Common in definitions and statements of identity: *X es el Y* (“X is the Y”). Use **es la** for feminine singular (*la casa*), and **son los/son las** for plural.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es el médico de la familia.
native_language_example: My brother is the family doctor.

meaning: 'it is love' / 'love is' (used when defining or identifying love).
additional_notes: Literally "is the love," but in Spanish the article (el) is often used in definitions or general statements: "X es el amor" = "X is love" / "That’s what love is." Very common inside the question "¿Qué es el amor?" ("What is love?") or in phrases like "Sé lo que es el amor" ("I know what love is").
target_language_example: Para mí, ayudar a los demás es el amor.
native_language_example: For me, helping others is love.

additional_notes: Use this pattern to say it’s a family member’s (or someone’s) birthday: **Es el cumpleaños de mi + [person]**. **cumpleaños** = “birthday” (always masculine: **el cumpleaños**). **de** means “of,” and **mi** means “my.” In English you usually switch to **’s**: “my mom’s birthday.”
target_language_example: Es el cumpleaños de mi hermana.
native_language_example: It’s my sister’s birthday.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, prices, or sizes. Often followed by a number (Ocho es el doble de cuatro) or by a clause/noun phrase (Es el doble de lo que pagamos ahora). With adjectives like grande, you commonly add “que” to compare: “es el doble de grande que …” = “is twice as big as …”.
target_language_example: Este apartamento es el doble de caro que el otro.
native_language_example: This apartment is twice as expensive as the other one.

meaning: "it’s the day" (used to say what day it is, or that a particular day is for something).
additional_notes: Used with a specific day ("Mañana es el día…" = "Tomorrow is the day…") or with "de" to name an occasion ("es el día de mi boda" = "it’s my wedding day"). It can also introduce a relative clause: "es el día en el que…" ("it’s the day when/on which…").
target_language_example: Hoy es el día para descansar.
native_language_example: Today is the day to rest.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has finished or is over. Often followed by a noun phrase: es el fin de la historia (the story is over), es el fin de la diversión y los juegos (the fun and games are over). You can also use it in a bigger sentence (e.g., La muerte es el fin de...).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: no es el fin del mundo.
native_language_example: Relax: it’s not the end of the world.

meaning: 'he is the man' / 'you’re the man' (the right person).
additional_notes: Used to identify someone as the person you mean (e.g., “He’s the man in the photo”) or to say someone is the right person for a job/role (“He’s the man for the job,” “the man of the house,” “the man of my dreams”). It can also be used as praise, especially in direct address: “Usted eres el hombre” ≈ “You’re the man.”
target_language_example: Si alguien puede arreglarlo, él es el hombre.
native_language_example: If anyone can fix it, he’s the man.

additional_notes: Used to say that a particular place is the safest option. The structure is: es = “it is”, el lugar = “the place”, más seguro = “safest/more safe” (masculine singular). You can add details with para… (“for…”) or specify the place: “El sótano es el lugar más seguro.”
target_language_example: En una tormenta, es el lugar más seguro.
native_language_example: In a storm, it’s the safest place.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is the best (the top choice) in a group or category. It agrees with the subject: for a woman you usually say “es la mejor”; for more than one, “son los/las mejores.” You can add “en + [activity/field]” (e.g., “es el mejor en lo que hace”) or use it with other superlatives like “el más barato es el mejor” (“the cheapest is the best”).
target_language_example: Para mí, este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right time has arrived to do something, often followed by **de + infinitive**: *Es el momento de + verbo* ("It’s time to + verb"). You can add words like *ahora* (now), *perfecto* (perfect), or *apropiado* (appropriate) to emphasize timing.
target_language_example: Es el momento de irnos.
native_language_example: It’s time for us to go.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something has the highest degree of a quality in a group. Pattern: "[Subject] es el más + adjective" (masculine singular). Change it to match what you’re talking about: "es la más" (feminine), "son los más / son las más" (plural). You can add "de..." to specify the group: "es el más alto de la clase".
target_language_example: Este restaurante es el más barato del barrio.
native_language_example: This restaurant is the cheapest in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person (or thing) with a group. Structure: [person/thing] + es + el/la más + adjective + de + [group]. With "alto" it usually refers to height (tall). You can change the adjective: "es el más rápido de…" (the fastest of…), "es la más alta de…" for a female subject.
target_language_example: Lucía es la más alta de mis hermanas.
native_language_example: Lucía is the tallest of my sisters.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is the biggest in size or the greatest in importance/ability. Often followed by “de…” (of…) to compare within a group: “Es el más grande de los dos” (the bigger of the two), “Es el más grande de los artistas vivos” (the greatest of the living artists). “Grande” can mean physical size (big) or figurative greatness (great).
target_language_example: Para mí, este edificio es el más grande de la ciudad.
native_language_example: For me, this building is the biggest in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say a country has the highest degree of an adjective within a group. Structure: [Country] + es el país más + adjective (+ de/del + group). The adjective usually agrees with “país” (masculine): más pequeño/chico, más grande, más occidental, etc.
target_language_example: Canadá es el país más grande de América del Norte.
native_language_example: Canada is the largest country in North America.

additional_notes: Used to compare countries by size. It’s a full statement: **es** (“is”) + **el país** (“the country”) + **más grande** (“biggest/largest”). Often followed by **de** or **del** (“of the”) + a region/group (**de Escandinavia**) or **del mundo** (“in the world”). You can swap the subject before it: *Rusia es el país más grande…*
target_language_example: Canadá es el país más grande de América del Norte.
native_language_example: Canada is the largest country in North America.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person/thing is number one in order or rank. It comes before a masculine singular noun: "es el primer día / es el primer presidente / es el primer lugar". Before a masculine singular noun, "primero" shortens to "primer".
target_language_example: Este es el primer día de clases.
native_language_example: This is the first day of classes.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is starting now (the first day of school, a new job, a new period of life, etc.). Often followed by “de…” (of) to say what it’s the first day of: “Es el primer día de clases.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es el primer día y todo es nuevo.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s the first day and everything is new.

meaning: "is the one who/that" (used to identify the person/thing that does something).
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize who/what fits a description or performed an action. Often followed by a verb in the past or present: "Es el que pagó..." / "Es el que vive...". In comparisons/superlatives you may see it with "más/menos": "es el que más...". It changes for gender/number: "es la que", "son los que", "son las que".
target_language_example: Ella es la que organiza las reuniones.
native_language_example: She’s the one who organizes the meetings.

meaning: "he's the one who told me" / "he's the one who said (to me)".
additional_notes: Used to identify who gave you the information or instruction. Often followed by a clause explaining what the person told you (e.g., qué hacer, cómo hacerlo, cuándo sería la reunión, a quién dárselo). You can change the subject for gender/number: Ella es la que me dijo… / Son los que me dijeron…
target_language_example: Ana es la que me dijo qué hacer en la reunión.
native_language_example: Ana is the one who told me what to do in the meeting.

es el que más me gusta

target_language_multi_word_term: es el que más me gusta
meaning: “It’s the one I like the most.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is your favorite among several options. Literally: “it is the one that I like the most.” You can change it to match gender/number: **es la que más me gusta** (feminine), **son los que más me gustan** (plural), etc. Often used after mentioning a group: **De todos…, es el que más me gusta.**
target_language_example: De todas las pizzas, la de pepperoni es la que más me gusta.
native_language_example: Of all the pizzas, pepperoni is the one I like the most.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is the longest river in a place. Structure: **[X] es el río más largo de/en [place]**. Use **de** with continents/countries/regions (de África, de Europa) and **en** to mean “in” a place (en Japón). **más largo** is the superlative “longest” (literally “more long”).
target_language_example: El Amazonas es el río más largo de Sudamérica.
native_language_example: The Amazon is the longest river in South America.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the final one in an order or sequence (time, list, warnings, etc.). It can also mean “the latest/newest model” in product contexts ("el último modelo"). Changes with gender/number: "es la última" (fem.), "son los últimos/las últimas" (plural).
target_language_example: Este es el último tren a Madrid.
native_language_example: This is the last train to Madrid.

meaning: “is the last refuge” (the final excuse or fallback).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern “X es el último refugio de Y” to criticize something as a desperate last resort (often a moral judgment). It’s a set, quote-like expression; you can also say “el último refugio” on its own.
target_language_example: Decir que no te importa es el último refugio de quien no quiere admitir que está herido.
native_language_example: Saying you don’t care is the last refuge of someone who doesn’t want to admit they’re hurt.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is the only one in a group. It agrees with gender/number: es el único (masc.), es la única (fem.), son los únicos / son las únicas (plural). Often followed by a noun (modo, testigo) or by “de + place/group” (de aquí).
target_language_example: Ella es la única persona que conoce la verdad.
native_language_example: She is the only person who knows the truth.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize that something matches perfectly or is precisely correct. Often followed by a noun phrase ("Es exactamente la misma idea") or by "lo que…" ("Es exactamente lo que quiero"). For plural subjects you use "son exactamente" ("Son exactamente iguales").
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesitamos.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what we need.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm that something matches your meaning, plan, or expectation. It’s followed by a verb phrase: “Es exactamente lo que quiero decir” (what I mean), “Eso es exactamente lo que voy a hacer” (what I’m going to do). Often appears after “eso” (“that”): “Eso es exactamente lo que…”.
target_language_example: Eso es exactamente lo que necesito ahora.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective: "Es extremadamente + adjetivo". It’s a formal/neutral way to say something is very intense (peligroso, aburrido, despistado, etc.). Often followed by an adjective, not a noun.
target_language_example: Este examen es extremadamente difícil.
native_language_example: This exam is extremely difficult.

meaning: "is famous for its/her" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to say a place or person is well-known because of something. The adjective changes for gender/number: es famoso por su (masc. singular), es famosa por su (fem. singular), son famosos/as por su. Use "por" + "su" + noun; "su" agrees with what is owned, and the owned thing is often singular here (e.g., su vino, su arquitectura).
target_language_example: La región es famosa por su queso.
native_language_example: The region is famous for its cheese.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe something as easy: **[subject] + es fácil** (El examen es fácil). You can also use it impersonally with an infinitive to mean “it’s easy to…”: **Es fácil + infinitive** (Es fácil viajar).
target_language_example: Es fácil aprender español con práctica.
native_language_example: It’s easy to learn Spanish with practice.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb after de: Es fácil de + usar/aprender/decir/hacer. You can change the subject (e.g., Esta cámara es fácil de usar) and gender/number to match it: es fácil (singular), son fáciles (plural).
target_language_example: Este programa es fácil de entender.
native_language_example: This program is easy to understand.

additional_notes: Used to react positively to something (an idea, news, a plan, a situation). Often appears as “Esto es genial” (“This is great”) or “Eso es genial” (“That’s great”). “Genial” in Spanish usually means “great/awesome/brilliant,” not “genius.”
target_language_example: ¡Tu idea es genial!
native_language_example: Your idea is great!

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe size (a general characteristic). **Es** is for singular subjects (El lago/La habitación). For plural: **son grandes**. **Grande** stays the same for masculine/feminine singular (el coche es grande / la casa es grande), and becomes **grandes** in plural. Watch out: **grande** can look like English **grand**, but it usually just means **big/large**.
target_language_example: Tu casa es grande, pero muy acogedora.
native_language_example: Your house is big, but very cozy.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment has come to do an action: Es hora de + infinitive (Es hora de cerrar). With a noun, it can mean “it’s time for…” (Es hora de mi inyección). You’ll also see Es hora de que + subjunctive (Es hora de que nos vayamos). Ya es hora de… adds emphasis: “it’s (about) time to…”.
target_language_example: Es hora de irnos a casa.
native_language_example: It’s time to go home.

meaning: “it’s time for us to go / leave.”
additional_notes: Used to say it’s time to leave. Often appears with a lead-in like “Bueno/Bien,” and can be softened with “Creo que…” (“I think…”). Literally “it’s the hour of leaving (ourselves),” where “irnos” = “to go/leave” + “nos” (“us”), meaning “for us to leave.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de irnos.
native_language_example: It’s already late; it’s time for us to go.

meaning: "it’s time to leave" / "it’s time to go."
additional_notes: Used to say that the moment to leave has arrived. Often followed by a place or destination: "irse a casa" (to go home) or "irse de aquí" (to get out of here). "Irse" is the reflexive form of "ir" and emphasizes leaving/going away from the current place.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de irse.
native_language_example: It’s already late; it’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say the moment has come for someone to do something, often as a suggestion, insistence, or a sense of urgency. After "es hora de que," Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: "Es hora de que vayas," "…salgamos," "…sepas." You can also use "ya" for emphasis: "Ya es hora de que…".
target_language_example: Ya es hora de que empecemos a trabajar.
native_language_example: It’s (really) time for us to start working.

meaning: “it’s time for you to…” (often with the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone (you) should do something now, or that the moment has come. It’s typically followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: “Es hora de que te marches / te perdones / te decidas.” Can be firm or urging depending on tone (e.g., “Vamos, es hora de que te…”).
target_language_example: Es hora de que te vayas a casa.
native_language_example: It’s time for you to go home.

es hora de que te vayas

target_language_multi_word_term: es hora de que te vayas
meaning: “it’s time for you to leave / go.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (often firmly) that the right time has come for them to go. After “es hora de que…”, Spanish typically uses the present subjunctive: “te vayas” (from “irse,” to leave/go away). You can add a destination: “Es hora de que te vayas a casa / al colegio.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; es hora de que te vayas.
native_language_example: It’s late; it’s time for you to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t change or is identical/similar. Very common in comparisons: **es igual que** (same as), **es igual al/a la** (same as + noun). It can also imply “it’s always the same” when talking about repeated situations (e.g., *Siempre es igual*).
