Change **alta** to match the person being described: **alto** (masc.), **alta** (fem.), **altos/altas** (plural). For other adjectives, swap in the adjective you need (e.g., *tan rápido como* = as fast as).
target_language_example: Mi hermana es tan alta como yo.
native_language_example: My sister is as tall as me.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things have the same height: **ser + tan + adjective + como**. You can change the adjective: *Es tan grande como…*, *Es tan rápido como…*. Often used with **de** for measurement: *Es tan alto como su hermano, pero mide 1,90 m.*
target_language_example: Mi hermana es tan alta como yo.
native_language_example: My sister is as tall as me.

meaning: it’s so good; it’s that good.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize how good something is. Often followed by an infinitive to say it’s good to do something (Es tan bueno verte = “It’s so good to see you”), or used with comparisons: tan + adjective + como (“as … as”): Es tan bueno como… (“It’s as good as…”). You can also use it alone as a strong opinion: Es tan bueno. (“It’s so good.”).
target_language_example: Es tan bueno tener amigos como tú.
native_language_example: It’s so good to have friends like you.

meaning: “is as good as” (as good as something/someone else).
additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say they’re equally good. Pattern: **[X] es tan bueno(a) como [Y]**. Agree **bueno** with what you’re describing: *es tan buena como…* (feminine), *son tan buenos(as) como…* (plural). With **cualquiera / cualquier otro**, it means “as good as any/anyone else.”
target_language_example: Mi español es tan bueno como el tuyo.
native_language_example: My Spanish is as good as yours.

additional_notes: Used to compare or emphasize difficulty. Common patterns: **es tan difícil como + noun** (“as difficult as…”): *El latín no es tan difícil como el griego.*; and **es tan difícil que + clause** (“so difficult that…”): *La tarea es tan difícil que no puedo hacerla.* You can change **es** for other forms (e.g., *era tan difícil*, *será tan difícil*) and replace **difícil** with other adjectives (e.g., *es tan caro*).
target_language_example: Aprender a conducir es tan difícil al principio que me estreso.
native_language_example: Learning to drive is so difficult at first that I get stressed.

additional_notes: Used with **tan + adjective** to mean **“so + adjective”**: *Es tan fácil (hacerlo / entenderlo).* You can also negate it: **No es tan fácil** (“It’s not so easy / It’s not that easy”). Often followed by an infinitive: *Es tan fácil comprenderlo.*
target_language_example: Aprender estas palabras es tan fácil.
native_language_example: Learning these words is so easy.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things that are equal in size (or amount). Pattern: [Subject] + ser (es/son) + tan + adjective + como + [comparison]. You can swap in other adjectives: es tan alto como (as tall as), es tan caro como (as expensive as). In negative comparisons you often use: No es tan grande como… (not as big as…).
target_language_example: Mi casa no es tan grande como la tuya.
native_language_example: My house isn't as big as yours.

additional_notes: Comparison pattern: ser + tan + adjective + como + (noun/pronoun/clause). Use it to say someone/something has the same level of a quality as someone/something else. For 'not as ... as', add no: "no es tan inteligente como...". You can swap the adjective: "es tan alto como", "es tan amable como", etc.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es tan inteligente como mi hermano.
native_language_example: My sister is as smart as my brother.

meaning: “it’s all / it’s the only thing” (often in “es todo lo que…”); also “a real/quite a …” (in “es todo un/una …”).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- **Es todo lo que + verb** = “It’s all that…” / “It’s the only thing that…”: *Es todo lo que tengo* (“It’s all I have”).
- **Es todo lo mismo** = “It’s all the same” / “It’s all the same to me.”
- **Es todo un/una + noun** emphasizes the noun: “a real/quite a …”: *Es todo un caballero* (“He’s a real gentleman”), *Es todo un logro* (“Quite an achievement”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es todo lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: Relax, that’s all I wanted to say.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing, the complete extent of something, or the only requirement. Often followed by a verb clause: es todo lo que + verb (e.g., es todo lo que se me ocurre = “that’s all I can think of”; es todo lo que tiene que hacer = “that’s all you have to do”).
target_language_example: Es todo lo que necesito por ahora.
native_language_example: That’s all I need for now.

additional_notes: Used to say you can’t do more than this (because of limits, rules, ability, or circumstances). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive or verb phrase like "darte" (give you), "decirte" (tell you), "hacer" (do), "pedir" (ask for). You can change the verb to fit the context: "Es todo lo que puedo hacer" = "It’s all I can do."
target_language_example: Lo siento, es todo lo que puedo hacer por ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s all I can do for now.

es todo lo que puedo hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: es todo lo que puedo hacer
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve done as much as you’re able to do, often implying there’s nothing more you can do. It can be followed by phrases like "para ayudarte" (to help you), "por ahora" (for now), or "por ti" (for you).
target_language_example: Lo siento, es todo lo que puedo hacer.
native_language_example: Sorry, that’s all I can do.

meaning: “That’s all I have.” / “That’s all I’ve got.”
additional_notes: Used to say you have nothing more to give, show, or say. You can add what it refers to: “Es todo lo que tengo para decir” (that’s all I have to say) or time expressions like “por ahora / hasta ahora” (for now / so far). Often appears with “Lo siento” (I’m sorry) or “Por favor” (please) to sound more apologetic or pleading.
target_language_example: Aquí está el dinero; lo siento, es todo lo que tengo.
native_language_example: Here’s the money; sorry, that’s all I have.

meaning: “it’s all / it’s the only thing” (often in “es todo lo que…”); also “a real/quite a …” (in “es todo un/una …”).
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- **Es todo lo que + verb** = “It’s all that…” / “It’s the only thing that…”: *Es todo lo que tengo* (“It’s all I have”).
- **Es todo lo mismo** = “It’s all the same” / “It’s all the same to me.”
- **Es todo un/una + noun** emphasizes the noun: “a real/quite a …”: *Es todo un caballero* (“He’s a real gentleman”), *Es todo un logro* (“Quite an achievement”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, es todo lo que quería decir.
native_language_example: Relax, that’s all I wanted to say.

meaning: "means everything to me" / "is everything to me."
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is the most important thing in your life. You can change the subject: "Él/ella es todo para mí" (He/She means everything to me), "Mi familia es todo para mí" (My family means everything to me). Often said with strong emotion.
target_language_example: Eres todo para mí.
native_language_example: You mean everything to me.

additional_notes: Used to wrap up a talk, class, meeting, broadcast, or conversation. Often preceded by filler like “Bueno,” or “Pues,” and sometimes said as “Eso/Esto es todo por hoy” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Bueno, es todo por hoy. Nos vemos mañana.
native_language_example: Well, that’s all for today. See you tomorrow.

es tres años mayor que yo

target_language_multi_word_term: es tres años mayor que yo
additional_notes: Use **ser + number of years + mayor/menor que + person** to compare ages. **Mayor** = older; **menor** = younger. You can change the number and the person: *Ella es dos años mayor que tú.* (She’s two years older than you.)
target_language_example: Mi hermana es cinco años mayor que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is five years older than me.

meaning: “it’s your …” (referring to something that belongs to you).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something is someone’s: Es tu auto. It uses the verb ser (es = “is”) + the possessive adjective tu (“your,” informal singular). For plural “your,” use su: Es su turno. If the noun is plural: Son tus amigos (“They’re your friends”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es tu responsabilidad.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s your responsibility.

additional_notes: Used to blame someone for a problem or bad situation. Common variations: “No es tu culpa” (It’s not your fault), “Es mi culpa” (It’s my fault), “Fue tu culpa” (It was your fault). You can also say “La culpa es tuya” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es tu culpa que llegáramos tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s your fault we arrived late.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to say something belongs to the person you’re speaking to. It agrees with the thing owned: es tuyo (masc. singular), es tuya (fem. singular), son tuyos (masc. plural), son tuyas (fem. plural). You can also use it in offers/permission: "Es tuyo si lo quieres" = "You can have it if you want."
target_language_example: Si nadie lo reclama, es tuyo.
native_language_example: If no one claims it, it’s yours.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to identify or describe what someone/something is: **Es un + noun** (e.g., *Es un arquitecto*). Before a **feminine** singular noun, use **es una** (*Es una doctora*). For plurals, use **son** (*Son unos estudiantes / Son unas estudiantes*).
target_language_example: Mi padre es un médico.
native_language_example: My father is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a friend. Often said about a man or male friend; for a female friend, say “es una amiga.” You can also use it to reassure someone (e.g., “Es un amigo, no?” = “He’s a friend, right?”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es un amigo del trabajo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a friend from work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify someone as your friend. You can add adjectives after "amigo" (e.g., "un amigo mío muy cercano"). For a female friend, use "es una amiga mía". In Spanish it’s common to say both "un amigo" + "mío" for emphasis/clarity; you can also say "es mi amigo" (or "es amigo mío").
target_language_example: Ella es una amiga mía del trabajo.
native_language_example: She’s a friend of mine from work.

meaning: "is an animal" (literally); also "is a beast" (very intense/strong or very good at something).
additional_notes: Literally it identifies something as an animal: “El delfín es un animal…”. When said about a person, it’s usually informal and figurative: it can be a compliment (someone is incredibly good/strong) or a criticism (someone is brutal/rude). Context and tone make the difference.
target_language_example: En el gimnasio, Juan es un animal: levanta muchísimo peso.
native_language_example: At the gym, Juan is a beast: he lifts a lot of weight.

meaning: “it’s an art” (a skill that takes creativity, practice, or subtlety).
additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t just a simple task—it requires talent, technique, or good judgment. Often said about activities like cooking, love, or living, and can be complimentary (admiring how hard or refined something is). You can also use it with an adjective: “Es un arte muy sutil.”
target_language_example: Negociar es un arte: tienes que escuchar y ser paciente.
native_language_example: Negotiating is an art: you have to listen and be patient.

additional_notes: Used with ser to describe someone’s profession or identity: "X es un artista." You can add adjectives after artista (e.g., famoso, visual) or use "artista nato" to mean someone is a natural/born artist. "Artista" can refer to a painter, visual artist, performer, etc., depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es una artista muy creativa.
native_language_example: My sister is a very creative artist.

meaning: “it’s a matter/issue (of…)” or “it’s a private affair.”
additional_notes: Used to identify what something is about, often followed by an adjective (serio, trivial, familiar, privado) or by “de” + noun (e.g., es un asunto de dinero). “Asunto” can mean “matter,” “issue,” or “affair,” depending on context.
target_language_example: No te metas: es un asunto privado.
native_language_example: Don’t get involved: it’s a private matter.

additional_notes: Used to classify something as a bird: **X es un ave** (“X is a bird”). You’ll often see it with extra information, like **un ave de presa** (“a bird of prey”) or **un ave de agua** (“a water bird”). Note: **ave** is feminine, so you also say **es un ave** (and in plural **son aves**).
target_language_example: El colibrí es un ave muy pequeña.
native_language_example: The hummingbird is a very small bird.

meaning: “it’s a good …” / “he’s a good …” (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (“to be”) + un + buen (short form of bueno) before a masculine singular noun: es un buen lugar, es un buen nombre, es un buen momento. With people/animals it means “he/she/it is a good …” depending on context (Spanish can drop the subject). For feminine nouns, use es una buena…. For plural, use son buenos / son buenas.
target_language_example: Tu idea es un buen plan.
native_language_example: Your idea is a good plan.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male (often a child or young person) as good, nice, well-behaved, or kind. For an adult, it often sounds like “good guy” or “nice guy.” You can change the subject: “Él es un buen chico.” / “Mi hijo es un buen chico.” Feminine: “Es una buena chica.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: él es un buen chico.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a good guy.

meaning: “he is a good man” / “(you) are a good man.”
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character positively. It commonly appears after a name or family word (Mi esposo/mi marido/papá/tu padre + es un buen hombre). With no subject, “es” usually refers to “he” (él), but it can also refer to “you” in formal address (Usted es un buen hombre). In Spanish you can drop the subject pronoun because the verb form gives the meaning.
target_language_example: Creo que tu hermano es un buen hombre.
native_language_example: I think your brother is a good man.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place is suitable for doing an activity (verb in the infinitive) or for a purpose. You can change the subject and tense: “Boston es un buen lugar para visitar”, “Aquí no es un buen lugar para estudiar”.
target_language_example: Esta cafetería es un buen lugar para estudiar.
native_language_example: This café is a good place to study.

meaning: “it’s a good time” / “it’s a good moment.”
additional_notes: Used to say that the timing is good (often with “para + infinitive”): “Es un buen momento para hablar.” In the negative (“no es un buen momento”), it means it’s not a good time right now and can sound like a gentle refusal.
target_language_example: Es un buen momento para hacer una pregunta.
native_language_example: It’s a good time to ask a question.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male person (often a child/teen, but also a young man) with **ser** for more lasting traits (age, personality, identity). For a girl you’d say **es una chica**. In Latin America, **chico** can also mean “kid” or “young person” depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es un chico muy simpático.
native_language_example: My brother is a very nice guy.

additional_notes: Used with professions or roles (artista, escritor, músico, ingeniero, etc.) to emphasize that someone is very experienced and skilled. Agree in gender and number: es un consumado artista / es una consumada artista; son consumados músicos / son consumadas escritoras. It’s fairly formal and common in writing.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es una consumada pianista.
native_language_example: My sister is an accomplished pianist.

additional_notes: Used to say something is illegal or morally very wrong. Often appears in statements like “X no es un crimen” (“X isn’t a crime”) to defend or justify something, or “X es un crimen” to strongly condemn it. Common pattern: “Es un crimen + adjective” (e.g., “Es un crimen horrible”).
target_language_example: Robar es un crimen.
native_language_example: Stealing is a crime.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe an activity as a sport. Often followed by an adjective or a phrase with de: Es un deporte interesante (an interesting sport), Es un deporte de equipo (a team sport), Es un deporte de contacto (a contact sport).
target_language_example: El tenis es un deporte muy popular.
native_language_example: Tennis is a very popular sport.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in very bad condition, messy, chaotic, or went very badly. You can use it for places (Esta casa es un desastre), things (La alfombra es un desastre), or situations/results (El vídeo… es un desastre). Often said with emphasis: “Esto sí que es un desastre” = “Now THIS is a disaster.”
target_language_example: Tu cuarto es un desastre; por favor, límpialo hoy.
native_language_example: Your room is a mess; please clean it today.

additional_notes: Used to define or describe something/someone as a dictionary. In a figurative expression like "un diccionario ambulante" (literally “a walking dictionary”), it means someone who knows a lot of words/facts and corrects others.
target_language_example: Este libro es un diccionario de español-inglés.
native_language_example: This book is a Spanish-English dictionary.

meaning: “it’s a day” / “it is a (kind of) day”.
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe what the day is like or what kind of day it is: **Es un día hermoso / importante / pésimo.** Often followed by an adjective, **de + noun** (**Es un día de viaje** = “It’s a travel day”), or **como...** (**Es un día como cualquier otro** = “It’s a day like any other”). For a specific day (today/that day), Spanish often uses **Hoy es un día...** or **Ese es un día...**
target_language_example: Hoy es un día muy especial para mi familia.
native_language_example: Today is a very special day for my family.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a student. It’s the verb ser (es = “is”) + indefinite article un (“a”) + estudiante (“student”). Commonly followed by de + place/type of school (e.g., "es un estudiante de instituto"). Use "es estudiante" (without "un") when speaking more generally about someone’s status/profession.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es un estudiante de la universidad.
native_language_example: My brother is a university student.

meaning: “(he/she) is a genius” (also: “(he/she) is awesome / really smart”).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s intelligence or talent. In context it often means “so smart” or “amazing,” not necessarily a literal IQ/genius claim. You can change the subject: “Soy un genio” (I’m a genius), “Eres un genio” (you’re a genius), “Son unos genios” (they’re geniuses).
target_language_example: ¡Gracias por ayudarme con la tarea! Eres un genio.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the homework! You’re a genius.

meaning: “it is a great / big …” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to say something is great/important or big: Es un gran + noun (desafío, momento, país). The full base form is “grande,” but it shortens to “gran” before a singular noun. For feminine nouns, use “Es una gran …” (una gran idea).
target_language_example: Aprender español es un gran paso para mí.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish is a big step for me.

meaning: “it’s a great day” (a special or very good day).
additional_notes: Use it to say that today (or another day mentioned in context, like mañana) is important, exciting, or very positive. You can add para + someone to say who it’s great for: “Es un gran día para nosotros / para ti”. Often used for events like celebrations, big news, or something you’ve been waiting for.
target_language_example: ¡Hoy es un gran día para celebrar!
native_language_example: Today is a great day to celebrate!

meaning: “it’s a great pleasure to be…” (here/with you).
additional_notes: A polite, formal-sounding phrase used to express pleasure at being somewhere or being with someone. You normally complete it with a place (aquí, en Madrid) or with someone (con usted = formal singular; contigo = informal singular; con vosotros/con vosotras = informal plural in Spain). Often used in greetings, speeches, or when meeting someone.
target_language_example: Es un gran placer estar en su casa esta noche.
native_language_example: It’s a great pleasure to be in your home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true and not up for debate. Very common in the pattern “Es un hecho que + [statement]” (“It’s a fact that…”). You can also say “Y eso es un hecho” to strongly underline what you just said.
target_language_example: Es un hecho que necesitamos descansar para estar bien.
native_language_example: It’s a fact that we need to rest to be well.

meaning: “he is a man” / “it’s a man” (saying someone is a man, often followed by a description).
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to identify someone as a man and commonly to describe him with an adjective or phrase: **Es un hombre casado / con suerte / ocupado / divertido / capaz**. You can also add **de + noun/infinitive** to describe a quality: **un hombre de fiar** (“a trustworthy/reliable man”), or a relative clause: **un hombre en quien se puede confiar** (“a man you can trust”).
target_language_example: Es un hombre muy amable, siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: He’s a very kind man; he always helps others.

meaning: 'he is a man of…' (used to describe a man’s qualities, appearance, age, etc.).
additional_notes: Common pattern: **Es un hombre de + noun phrase**. It can describe a trait (**un hombre de palabra** = a man who keeps his word), a quality (**de una fe tremenda**), a physical description (**de aspecto agradable**), or age (**de treinta años**). In English you often translate more naturally as “He’s a … man” or “He’s a …-year-old man,” depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Es un hombre de gran paciencia.
native_language_example: He’s a very patient man.

meaning: "he is a very ... man" / "he's a very ... guy".
additional_notes: Used to describe a man with an adjective (or adjective phrase) after "muy". Common in descriptions: "Es un hombre muy capaz/discreto/paciente/peligroso". "Hombre" is more formal than "tipo" (guy), and you can swap the subject: "Es una mujer muy...", "Es un chico muy...".
target_language_example: Mi jefe es un hombre muy amable.
native_language_example: My boss is a very kind man.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser ("to be") to say that something is a language, either literally (Greek is a language) or metaphorically (math/music is a language). Often followed by an adjective or description: "es un idioma encantador" (it's a charming language).
target_language_example: El español es un idioma muy hablado en muchos países.
native_language_example: Spanish is a widely spoken language in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is hard to learn. You can swap in the language name before it: “El japonés es un idioma difícil.” You can also compare difficulty with “pero no tanto como…” (but not as much as…).
target_language_example: Para mí, el alemán es un idioma difícil.
native_language_example: For me, German is a difficult language.

additional_notes: Used to describe something literally as a game (a sport, chess, etc.) or figuratively as a “game” in the sense of a strategy, trick, or mind game (juego mental). Often followed by details: “Es un juego + adjective” (Es un juego aburrido) or “Es un juego que…” (Es un juego que se juega con tus reglas).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, es un juego; solo estamos practicando.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s a game; we’re just practicing.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something as a book. Often appears with adjectives (e.g., “Es un libro genial/muy útil”). With a longer noun phrase, you may also see “Es un libro de…” (“It’s a book about/on…”). The subject is usually understood from context, so Spanish often just says “Es…” without “It.”
target_language_example: ¿Qué es eso? Es un libro de cocina.
native_language_example: What is that? It’s a cookbook.

meaning: "it’s a place" (used to describe a location).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe a place: “Es un lugar + adjective” (Es un lugar bonito/lindo/agradable). You can add “para + infinitive” to say it’s a good place to do something: “Es un lugar interesante para descubrir” = “It’s an interesting place to discover.”
target_language_example: Es un lugar tranquilo para descansar.
native_language_example: It’s a quiet place to rest.

additional_notes: Used to label a man as someone who lies. Often appears after a name ("Tom es un mentiroso") or after a conditional like "si..." ("Es un mentiroso si dice..."). For a woman: "es una mentirosa." You can also use it with other subjects: "soy un mentiroso" (I’m a liar), "eres un mentiroso" (you’re a liar), "son unos mentirosos" (they’re liars). Strong/accusatory in tone.
target_language_example: No le creas: es un mentiroso.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: he’s a liar.

additional_notes: Used to identify or classify a material as a metal. It’s the verb "ser" (permanent characteristic) in 3rd person singular: "X es un metal" = “X is a metal.” You can add adjectives after "metal" (e.g., "metal blando" = soft metal, "metal tóxico" = toxic metal).
target_language_example: El hierro es un metal muy resistente.
native_language_example: Iron is a very strong metal.

meaning: “is a very good …” (describing someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone/something is very good at something or of high quality: “Es un muy buen amigo/tenista/intérprete.” Note that Spanish often uses “muy buen” (not *“muy bueno”*) before a masculine singular noun: “un muy buen amigo.” For feminine nouns: “una muy buena amiga.”
target_language_example: Ella es una muy buena profesora.
native_language_example: She is a very good teacher.

meaning: "(he/she) is a child" or "(he) is a boy."
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (to be) to state someone’s identity/description: X es un niño. Often you’ll add an adjective after niño: es un niño listo/sensible. For a girl, use es una niña. To specify age, Spanish usually says Tiene X años rather than *Es X años*.
target_language_example: Es un niño muy curioso y siempre hace preguntas.
native_language_example: He’s a very curious kid and he always asks questions.

meaning: "it’s a name" (used to say what type of name something is).
additional_notes: Used to identify something as a name and often to add a description: *Es un nombre + adjective* (Es un nombre bonito.) or *Es un nombre + nationality/language adjective* (Es un nombre español / francés / alemán). For feminine nouns you change it to *es un nombre* anyway, because *nombre* is masculine: *Carmen es un nombre español.*
target_language_example: ¿Sofía? Sí, es un nombre muy común.
native_language_example: "Sofía"? Yes, it’s a very common name.

es un número de la suerte

target_language_multi_word_term: es un número de la suerte
additional_notes: Used to say that a number is considered to bring good luck. Often appears with verbs like creer (“to believe”) or decir (“to say”): Se cree/Se dice que X es un número de la suerte (“It’s believed/said that X is a lucky number”). You can change the number: El siete/trece es un número de la suerte.
target_language_example: Para mí, el ocho es un número de la suerte.
native_language_example: For me, eight is a lucky number.

additional_notes: Used with a place name + “es un país” + adjective or descriptor to say what kind of country it is (e.g., europeo, democrático, rico, hermoso). It can also be followed by a noun phrase: “Es un país de…” (e.g., Es un país de montañas.).
target_language_example: Canadá es un país grande.
native_language_example: Canada is a big country.

additional_notes: Used to describe a country with an adjective after "muy" (very): "Es un país muy seguro/hermoso/bello/poderoso". It commonly comes after a country name: "Colombia es un país muy…".
target_language_example: España es un país muy diverso.
native_language_example: Spain is a very diverse country.

meaning: “it’s a small/a little …” (introducing a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to downplay size/importance: “Es un pequeño favor / un pequeño avance / un pequeño resfriado.” For feminine nouns, use “es una pequeña …” (e.g., “una pequeña pausa”). Adjective agreement matters: pequeño/pequeña, pequeños/pequeñas. Often “pequeño” comes before the noun (“un pequeño favor”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: es un pequeño problema.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s a small problem.

additional_notes: A polite, formal phrase used when meeting someone, welcoming them, or expressing that you’re happy to do something. Often followed by an infinitive ("Es un placer estar aquí") or a verb like conocer/ver/tener + object pronoun ("Es un placer conocerlo/la/los/las"). You can also say "Un placer" as a shorter version.
target_language_example: Es un placer ayudarle.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to help you.

meaning: “It’s a pleasure to meet you.” (formal, to a man).
additional_notes: Polite, formal greeting when meeting someone for the first time. Uses the formal object pronoun “lo” (you, masculine or mixed group) with “conocer” (to meet). You can also hear “es un placer conocerla” (formal, to a woman) or “es un placer conocerle” (more common in some regions). Often used with titles like “señor/señora” and can be answered with “Para mí también” (“For me too”).
target_language_example: Es un placer conocerlo, señor Martínez.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to meet you, Mr. Martínez.

additional_notes: A polite, friendly phrase used when meeting someone (often for the first time). You can add words like “al fin / por fin / finalmente” to mean “at last / finally.” Also common: “Es un placer conocerlo/la” (more formal, for “you” = usted) and “Es un placer conocerles” (to meet you all).
target_language_example: Hola, soy Ana. Es un placer conocerte.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Ana. It’s a pleasure to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to state what something is (classification/definition). It’s the verb ser in the present tense (es = “is”) + un planeta (“a planet”). For negation, use “no es un planeta” (“is not a planet”).
target_language_example: Marte es un planeta muy frío.
native_language_example: Mars is a very cold planet.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives or phrases to soften what you say or indicate a small degree: “Es un poco + adjective” (e.g., tarde, idiota, duro de oído). You can also say “Es un poco + noun” in informal speech to mean “kind of a …”.
target_language_example: Es un poco caro para mí.
native_language_example: It’s a bit expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that the time is late, or that it’s too late to do something (often with para: Es un poco tarde para eso = “It’s a bit late for that.”). Adding ya (“already”) makes it stronger: Ya es un poco tarde = “It’s already a bit late.”
target_language_example: Es un poco tarde para llamar; mejor mañana.
native_language_example: It’s a bit late to call; better tomorrow.

meaning: "it’s a privilege" (an honor or special advantage).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is an honor (e.g., meeting someone, being part of something) or that something is a special advantage not everyone has. Often followed by an infinitive: "Es un privilegio conocerte". You can also negate it: "No es un privilegio".
target_language_example: Es un privilegio trabajar contigo.
native_language_example: It’s a privilege to work with you.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is an issue, difficulty, or concern. Often followed by details like: “es un problema grave” (it’s a serious problem), “es un problema común” (it’s a common problem), or “es un problema que hay que resolver” (it’s a problem that needs to be solved). You can replace “un problema” with “un problema de…” to specify the type (e.g., “de vida o muerte” = life-or-death).
target_language_example: Llegar tarde siempre es un problema en este trabajo.
native_language_example: Being late is always a problem at this job.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a gift/present, or more figuratively that something is a gift in life (a blessing). You’ll often see it with adjectives ("Es un regalo maravilloso") or with "para" (a gift for someone) and "de" to say who it’s from ("Es un regalo de mi tía").
target_language_example: Para mí, tu ayuda es un regalo.
native_language_example: For me, your help is a gift.

additional_notes: Used to say what occasion the gift is for (es un regalo de boda / de graduación). With “de + source” it can also mean “a gift from” (e.g., un regalo de los dioses = a gift from the gods). Often you’ll also hear “Es un regalo para...” to emphasize who it’s for.
target_language_example: Es un regalo de cumpleaños para mi hermana.
native_language_example: It’s a birthday gift for my sister.

additional_notes: Use it to say who the present is intended for. Follow with a person or pronoun: para mi mamá, para él/ella/usted, para un amigo. You can change the verb/person as needed: Es/era/será un regalo para…
target_language_example: No lo abras: es un regalo para mi hermana.
native_language_example: Don’t open it: it’s a gift for my sister.

additional_notes: Used to say that something indicates or suggests a quality or situation. It’s often followed by a noun (e.g., confianza, fuerza, debilidad) and can be used in general statements or explanations.
target_language_example: Su sonrisa es un signo de alegría.
native_language_example: Her smile is a sign of happiness.

additional_notes: Used literally to say something is happening in a dream (e.g., “Sólo es un sueño”). It can also be used figuratively to mean something feels unreal or like a fantasy (“Es un sueño, tiene que serlo”), or to say something used to be only a dream/hope but is becoming real (“ya no es un sueño”).
target_language_example: Ganar este premio es un sueño para mí.
native_language_example: Winning this prize is a dream for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man or person, often followed by an adjective: Es un tipo simpático (a nice guy), un tipo rudo (a tough guy). In many contexts, tipo is like "guy" in English: informal and conversational, but not necessarily rude. It can also mean "a kind/type" of something, but with people it usually means "guy/person."
target_language_example: Tu hermano es un tipo muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: Your brother is a very calm guy.

additional_notes: Used to classify or define something by putting it into a category. You can also change it for gender/number: es un tipo de (masc. singular), es una clase de / es una especie de (common alternatives), son un tipo de (plural subject; often also son tipos de).
target_language_example: Un SUV es un tipo de coche.
native_language_example: An SUV is a type of car.

meaning: “is a real / a true …” (used to emphasize a noun).
additional_notes: Used to strongly describe what someone/something is: **Es un verdadero + noun**. Change for gender/number: **un verdadero** (masc. sing.), **una verdadera** (fem. sing.), **unos verdaderos / unas verdaderas** (plural). Common with nouns like *caballero*, *señor*, *psicópata*, etc., to mean “a true/real …”.
target_language_example: Ella es una verdadera amiga.
native_language_example: She’s a true friend.

meaning: “he/she is an old friend of mine.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce someone by saying you have known them for a long time ("viejo" here means long-time, not necessarily elderly). "Es" can refer to a person of any gender; you can replace the name or pronoun before it (e.g., "Tom es…"). You can also shorten it to "Es un amigo mío" (a friend of mine).
target_language_example: Ella es una vieja amiga mía; fuimos a la escuela juntos.
native_language_example: She’s an old friend of mine; we went to school together.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to identify or describe what someone/something is, followed by a **feminine singular** noun: *Es una serpiente.* If the noun is masculine, use **es un** (*Es un médico*). Depending on context, it can mean **he/she/it is a**.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es una doctora.
native_language_example: My sister is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t serious, or to check if someone is joking (often with a surprised/annoyed tone: “Are you kidding?”). You’ll also hear “solo es una broma” (“it’s just a joke”). In questions: “¿Es una broma?” or “¿Es una broma, verdad?”
target_language_example: ¿Es una broma o hablas en serio?
native_language_example: Is it a joke, or are you serious?

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good option/choice/thing, and it normally continues with a feminine noun: Es una buena idea/decisión/elección/apuesta/lección. Because "buena" is feminine, it agrees with feminine nouns; with masculine nouns you’d say: Es un buen plan / Es un buen chico.
target_language_example: Es una buena idea esperar hasta mañana.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to wait until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or suggestion is smart/recommendable. You can follow it with an infinitive to say what is a good idea: "Es una buena idea + verbo" (e.g., "Es una buena idea leer..."). Often used alone to agree with someone, and it can be turned into a question with intonation: "Es una buena idea, ¿verdad?"
target_language_example: Es una buena idea llamar antes de ir.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to call before going.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to describe someone’s character/morals (a general quality). Change the subject as needed: Él/ella es una buena persona; Usted es una buena persona. For the negative, add no: No es una buena persona. You can also swap in names (Tom/Alí es una buena persona) or add details after it.
target_language_example: Mi profesor es una buena persona y siempre ayuda a los estudiantes.
native_language_example: My teacher is a good person and always helps the students.

meaning: “she is a girl” / “she’s a young woman.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) to describe someone (often followed by an adjective): Es una chica simpática. Chica usually means “girl,” but it can also mean “young woman,” depending on age and context.
target_language_example: Laura es una chica muy inteligente.
native_language_example: Laura is a very smart girl/young woman.

additional_notes: Used to identify/classify a place as a city. It’s a basic structure: **[place] + es + una ciudad (+ adjective)** (e.g., *una ciudad grande* = “a big city”). For plural: *son ciudades*.
target_language_example: Madrid es una ciudad muy bonita.
native_language_example: Madrid is a very beautiful city.

meaning: “is a very … city” (used to describe a city with an adjective).
additional_notes: Use this pattern to describe a city: [Place] es una ciudad muy + adjective. The adjective agrees with “ciudad” (feminine singular), so many adjectives end in -a (segura, cara, bonita). With adjectives that don’t change for gender (e.g., moderna, interesante), the form stays the same. You can also drop “una” in some contexts, but “es una ciudad muy…” is very common and natural.
target_language_example: Barcelona es una ciudad muy bonita.
native_language_example: Barcelona is a very beautiful city.

meaning: “is one thing” (used to contrast with something else).
additional_notes: Most commonly used in the pattern “X es una cosa, Y es otra” to highlight a contrast: one action/idea is different from another (often implying “they’re not the same” or “one doesn’t automatically lead to the other”). In English it’s usually “X is one thing; Y is another.”
target_language_example: Decirlo es una cosa; hacerlo es otra.
native_language_example: Saying it is one thing; doing it is another.

meaning: 'it's kind of / sort of' (a type of).
additional_notes: Used to compare or classify something by saying it is similar to, or a type of, something else. Common in definitions and explanations. You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: "son una especie de..." (they are), "era una especie de..." (it was).
target_language_example: Este aparato es una especie de cámara, pero también graba audio.
native_language_example: This device is kind of a camera, but it also records audio.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to identify someone or something as a star. Literally it means an astronomical star (El Sol es una estrella). Figuratively, it can mean someone famous or outstanding, often with an extra description like “una estrella del rock” (a rock star). You can also say “Es una estrella” by itself when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Para mí, ella es una estrella.
native_language_example: To me, she’s a star.

meaning: "it’s a way of" (doing something); "it’s a form/type of" (something).
additional_notes: Used to define or describe something by comparing it to a broader category ("X es una forma de Y") or to explain a purpose/approach ("es una forma de + infinitive"). Very common for giving explanations: "Es una forma de decir(lo)" = "It’s a way of saying it" (not meant literally).
target_language_example: Para mí, viajar es una forma de aprender.
native_language_example: For me, traveling is a way to learn.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as a phrase (often in grammar, writing, or when quoting someone). You can add a description or source: “Es una frase de Sonny” (It’s a phrase/quote from Sonny), “Es una frase obvia” (It’s an obvious phrase). For negation: “Eso no es una frase” (That’s not a phrase).
target_language_example: Es una frase muy común en español.
native_language_example: It’s a very common phrase in Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to classify something: **X es una fruta** = “X is a fruit.” It’s the verb **ser** (to be) + **una** (a) + **fruta** (fruit). Note: In some contexts, calling a person **una fruta** can be slang/objectifying and may sound rude or inappropriate; for literal descriptions of food, it’s neutral.
target_language_example: La piña es una fruta.
native_language_example: Pineapple is a fruit.

meaning: “it’s a great…” / “he’s a great…” / “she’s a great…”
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something positively. In Spanish, the adjective "grande" shortens to "gran" before a singular noun (gran chica, gran película, gran manera). You can change "es" to match the subject: "soy" (I’m), "eres" (you are), "es" (he/she/it is), "somos" (we are), "son" (they are).
target_language_example: Es una gran idea.
native_language_example: It’s a great idea.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something is: a story, tale, or narrative. Very often followed by “de …” (es una historia de amor = it’s a love story) or by a relative clause (es una historia que… = it’s a story that…). In more formal/academic contexts, “una historia de…” can mean “a history of…” (e.g., human history is a history of ideas).
target_language_example: Es una historia de amor muy bonita.
native_language_example: It’s a very beautiful love story.

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe what something is (often a language): “X es una lengua + adjective” (difficult, beautiful), or “X es una lengua + type” (bereber, construida). You can also use it figuratively, as in “La música es una lengua común…”. Note: “lengua” can mean both “language” and the physical “tongue”; in these examples it means “language”.
target_language_example: El español es una lengua muy hablada en muchos países.
native_language_example: Spanish is a language that is widely spoken in many countries.

additional_notes: Used to classify a language: "[Language] es una lengua eslava". You can add a subgroup after it, e.g. "es una lengua eslava occidental/oriental" (“a West/East Slavic language”). "Lengua" and "idioma" are often interchangeable here.
target_language_example: El polaco es una lengua eslava occidental.
native_language_example: Polish is a West Slavic language.

additional_notes: Used to say something is wild, unbelievable, chaotic, or unreasonable. Can describe a situation (¡Adentro es una locura! = It’s crazy in there!) or an activity (Es una locura leer esa revista = It’s crazy to read that magazine). Often said with emphasis; can be negative (too much, dangerous) or playful/exaggerated.
target_language_example: Ir sin dormir al trabajo es una locura.
native_language_example: Going to work without sleeping is crazy.

additional_notes: Used to express regret or disappointment about a situation. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive because it comments on a fact rather than stating it neutrally (e.g., “Es una lástima que no puedas venir”). You can also say “Qué lástima que…”.
target_language_example: Es una lástima que no puedas quedarte más tiempo.
native_language_example: It’s a shame you can’t stay longer.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to say something is bad: es una mala broma (a bad joke), es una mala costumbre (a bad habit), es una mala traducción (a bad translation), es una mala influencia (a bad influence). For masculine nouns, use: es un mal + noun (e.g., es un mal ejemplo).
target_language_example: Mentir es una mala idea.
native_language_example: Lying is a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used to explain how something is done or understood, or to soften/rephrase what you’re saying (like “it’s a way of saying it/looking at it”). Common patterns: “Es una manera de decirlo” (a way to put it), “Es una manera de verlo” (a way to see it). Often followed by an infinitive (decir, hacerlo, verlo, etc.).
target_language_example: Es una manera de explicarlo sin entrar en detalles.
native_language_example: It’s a way to explain it without going into details.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is false. You can add an adjective for nuance: “una mentira blanca” = “a white lie” (a small lie meant to avoid hurting someone). Word order is flexible in speech: “Es una mentira” / “Eso es una mentira” / “¡Es mentira!”
target_language_example: No le creas: es una mentira.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: it’s a lie.

meaning: "is a mixture of" / "is a mix of".
additional_notes: Used to describe what something is made up of or composed of. It’s often followed by a plural noun (es una mezcla de gases) or by two things joined with y (es una mezcla de verdad y error). You can add qualifiers like varios/muchos/diferentes: es una mezcla de varios gases.
target_language_example: Este té es una mezcla de hierbas y especias.
native_language_example: This tea is a mix of herbs and spices.

additional_notes: Strong, vulgar way to say something is very bad, disappointing, or terrible. Often used with a specific subject: “X es una mierda” (“X sucks”). You can intensify it: “es una mierda enorme” (“it’s huge crap / it really sucks”). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Este trabajo es una mierda, pero tengo que terminarlo.
native_language_example: This job sucks, but I have to finish it.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es = “is”) to identify someone’s gender/identity. Often followed by an adjective: “Es una mujer guapa” (“She’s a pretty woman”). You can add “Sí, por supuesto” to strongly confirm something: “Sí, por supuesto que es una mujer.”
target_language_example: Es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart woman.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to describe a woman’s general/lasting qualities. You normally add an adjective after muy (e.g., rica, atractiva, elegante, obstinada, ocupada, talentosa). For temporary states, Spanish often uses estar instead (e.g., Está muy ocupada = She is very busy).
target_language_example: Ana es una mujer muy inteligente.
native_language_example: Ana is a very intelligent woman.

additional_notes: Used to praise or evaluate something/someone with a feminine noun: Es una muy buena idea/elección/persona/pregunta. For masculine nouns, use: Es un muy buen … (Es un muy buen libro). With professions/nationalities you usually drop “una”: Es muy buena tenista.
target_language_example: Es una muy buena idea.
native_language_example: It’s a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (es) to identify someone as a girl/young female (niña). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., es una niña encantadora). Negative form: no es una niña. Can also be used as an announcement like “¡Es una niña!” (It’s a girl!).
target_language_example: Es una niña muy inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart girl.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as artistically impressive or beautifully made. It can be literal (a real artwork) or figurative for things like a garden, a conversation, a performance, etc. You can change the subject (e.g., “Tu pastel es una obra de arte”).
target_language_example: Tu dibujo es una obra de arte.
native_language_example: Your drawing is a work of art.

meaning: “It’s an order.” (a command that must be obeyed).
additional_notes: Used to give a firm command, often from someone with authority (a boss, officer, etc.). You can say it strongly as “¡Es una orden!” In legal contexts, “una orden” can also mean an official order/warrant (e.g., “una orden de la corte” = “a court order”).
target_language_example: Cierra la puerta ahora mismo: es una orden.
native_language_example: Close the door right now: it’s an order.

meaning: “is a person” (used to describe what someone is like).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description to talk about someone’s character or qualities: “X es una persona + adjective” (agradable, complicada, decente, honesta, inteligente). In polite/formal contexts, you may see “usted es una persona…”. Often interchangeable with “X es + adjective” (e.g., “Tom es honesto”), but “es una persona…” can feel a bit more descriptive/reflective about the person overall.
target_language_example: Mi jefe es una persona muy justa.
native_language_example: My boss is a very fair person.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality or qualities. It’s followed by an adjective (independiente, gentil, ocupada, sabia, sensible, trabajadora, simpática). The adjective agrees in gender and number with persona (feminine singular), so you typically use the feminine form: persona muy ocupada / simpática, even if the person is male. For a group: son personas muy amables.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es una persona muy amable.
native_language_example: My brother is a very kind person.

meaning: “it’s a pigsty” (a very dirty, filthy place).
additional_notes: Used to criticize a place as extremely dirty or messy (a room, a house, a neighborhood, etc.). It’s insulting/derogatory in tone. You can also hear: “Esto parece una pocilga” (“This looks like a pigsty”).
target_language_example: No puedo invitar a nadie: mi departamento es una pocilga.
native_language_example: I can’t invite anyone over: my apartment is a pigsty.

additional_notes: Used to point out that something is a question (often to clarify tone or intent). You can add an adjective after “pregunta” (e.g., “Es una pregunta interesante.”). With “sólo/solo” it can mean “It’s just a question,” to downplay it or say you’re not accusing or insisting.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, sólo es una pregunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, plan, or place isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring results or value. Common pattern: "[Something] es una pérdida de tiempo" (e.g., Estudiar eso es una pérdida de tiempo). You can also hear the plural: "son una pérdida de tiempo" for plural subjects.
target_language_example: Discutir otra vez es una pérdida de tiempo.
native_language_example: Arguing again is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a good moral quality or admirable trait. Often follows an abstract noun (La honestidad es una virtud.) or an infinitive phrase acting as a noun (Aprender de tus errores es una virtud.). You can add emphasis with adjectives: es una gran virtud / es una virtud muy valiosa.
target_language_example: La paciencia es una virtud, especialmente con niños.
native_language_example: Patience is a virtue, especially with kids.

meaning: "is one of" (refers to a female noun; for a male noun: "es uno de").
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to a group: "Es una de mis amigas" = she is one of my friends. Very common before plural nouns with an article/possessive: "una de las...", "una de mis...". Often used with superlatives: "una de las más..." (one of the most...).
target_language_example: Sofía es una de mis profesoras favoritas.
native_language_example: Sofía is one of my favorite teachers.

meaning: “it is one of the” (feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group: “It’s one of the + [plural noun].” Use **es uno de los** with a masculine plural noun, and **son uno/una de los/las** for plural subjects. Often followed by a superlative or description: **una de las + más + adjective + noun** (e.g., “one of the most beautiful capitals”).
target_language_example: Es una de las mejores razones para aprender español.
native_language_example: It’s one of the best reasons to learn Spanish.

es una de las ciudades más grandes

target_language_multi_word_term: es una de las ciudades más grandes
additional_notes: Used to describe something as belonging to a group of the largest cities. Often followed by a place: del mundo (in the world), de Japón (in Japan). You can swap the noun and adjective to fit other things: es uno de los países más grandes (one of the biggest countries).
target_language_example: Madrid es una de las ciudades más grandes de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the biggest cities in Spain.

es una de las cosas que

target_language_multi_word_term: es una de las cosas que
additional_notes: Used to introduce one item from a list of reasons, characteristics, habits, etc. After "que" you usually add a verb clause describing the thing: "Es una de las cosas que me gustan" (one of the things I like). Often followed by emphasis like "más" (most): "una de las cosas que más me gusta".
target_language_example: Es una de las cosas que más me gustan de este lugar.
native_language_example: It’s one of the things I like most about this place.

meaning: “it’s one of my …” (used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Use this to say something belongs to a group of your favorites/best/etc. The noun after it is typically plural: "Es una de mis canciones favoritas" = one of my favorite songs. Use "Es uno de mis" with masculine nouns ("Es uno de mis amigos"). With plural subjects, use "Son una(s) de mis…" ("Son unas de mis películas favoritas").
target_language_example: Es una de mis comidas favoritas.
native_language_example: It’s one of my favorite foods.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to a larger group: Es uno de + noun (often plural). With superlatives it’s very common: es uno de los más + adjective ("one of the most..."). It agrees in gender/number: es uno de (masc. singular), es una de (fem. singular), son uno(s) de / son una(s) de (plural).
target_language_example: Madrid es una de las ciudades más grandes de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the biggest cities in Spain.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone/something as belonging to a group. For people, Spanish often uses the masculine plural pronoun “ellos” for mixed-gender groups; for an all-female group you’d say “es una de ellas.” You can also change the verb: “soy uno de ellos” (I’m one of them), “eres uno de ellos” (you’re one of them), “somos uno de ellos” (we’re one of them).
target_language_example: Se nota que él es uno de ellos.
native_language_example: You can tell that he’s one of them.

meaning: “is one of the” (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a group: “X is one of the + plural noun.” Often followed by a superlative like “más…” (most/more) or “peores/mejores” (worst/best): “es uno de los más hermosos,” “es uno de los peores.” For feminine singular subjects, use “es una de las” before a plural feminine noun.
target_language_example: Madrid es uno de los destinos más visitados de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is one of the most visited destinations in Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to the top group. It often continues with a plural noun: “Es uno de los mejores países/lugares/restaurantes…”. You can make it feminine/plural depending on what you’re describing: “Es una de las mejores (ciudades/opciones)”, “Son unos de los mejores (equipos)”, “Son unas de las mejores (películas)”.
target_language_example: Este restaurante es uno de los mejores de la ciudad.
native_language_example: This restaurant is one of the best in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to your personal group of favorites or choices. It’s followed by a plural noun phrase: es uno de mis lugares/autores/platos favoritos. For feminine groups, use: es una de mis … (e.g., es una de mis películas favoritas).
target_language_example: Este café es uno de mis sitios favoritos para estudiar.
native_language_example: This café is one of my favorite places to study.

additional_notes: Use this to say someone belongs to your group of friends. You can add details after “amigos,” like “más cercanos” (closest) or “más íntimos” (closest/intimate). You can also add “también” (also) for emphasis: “También es uno de mis amigos.”
target_language_example: María es una de mis amigas.
native_language_example: María is one of my friends.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true, agree with someone, or insist on a fact (often like “that’s true”). You can also use it to politely correct or emphasize: “No quiero…, pero es verdad” (“I don’t want to…, but it’s true”). Related: “¿Es verdad?” = “Is it true?” and “Es verdad que…” = “It’s true that…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero es verdad: no hay más entradas.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s true: there are no more tickets.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific shirt that’s not right next to the speaker (often “that one” rather than “this one”). "Esa" agrees with the noun: camisa is feminine singular, so you say "esa camisa" (not *ese camisa*). Often used when choosing between items: "Esa camisa no, la otra."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde compraste esa camisa?
native_language_example: Where did you buy that shirt?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "esa" to point to a particular song that’s known from context (for example, one you just mentioned, heard, or are referring to). "Esa" often implies the song is not right here with the speaker (e.g., over there, or already known), but in many conversations it simply means “that” vs. “this.”
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta esa canción que está sonando?
native_language_example: Do you like that song that's playing?

meaning: that house (over there / not this one).
additional_notes: "Esa" points to something not close to the speaker (often near the listener, or at some distance). It’s used with feminine singular nouns like "casa" (house). Contrast: "esta casa" = this house; "aquella casa" = that house over there (far away).
target_language_example: ¿Quién vive en esa casa?
native_language_example: Who lives in that house?

meaning: “that girl” (a specific girl, not near the speaker).
additional_notes: “Esa” is the feminine singular demonstrative meaning “that” (often something/someone not close to you). It agrees with the noun: esa + chica (girl). Common in identification and description: “Esa chica es… / se parece a…”.
target_language_example: No conozco a esa chica, pero parece simpática.
native_language_example: I don’t know that girl, but she seems nice.

meaning: “that girl” (a specific girl, not near the speaker).
additional_notes: “Esa” is the feminine singular demonstrative meaning “that” (often something/someone not close to you). It agrees with the noun: esa + chica (girl). Common in identification and description: “Esa chica es… / se parece a…”.
target_language_example: No conozco a esa chica, pero parece simpática.
native_language_example: I don’t know that girl, but she seems nice.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific kind of person/thing/comment/etc., often with an implied opinion (“that kind of people/comments”). It agrees in gender/number with *clase*: *esa clase de* (feminine singular) is very common as a fixed phrase; also possible: *ese tipo de* (“that type of”).
target_language_example: No me gusta esa clase de películas.
native_language_example: I don’t like that kind of movies.

meaning: “that thing” (used when you don’t know or don’t want to name it).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative “esa” (“that”, feminine) + “cosa” (“thing”). Common for pointing something out or asking what it is: “¿Qué es esa cosa?” You can use it when the object/person isn’t identified yet, or when you’re being vague. For masculine nouns you’d usually say “ese (algo/objeto)” or name the noun (e.g., “ese perro”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes quitar esa cosa de la mesa?
native_language_example: Can you remove that thing from the table?

meaning: "that story" (referring to a specific story/claim already mentioned or understood).
additional_notes: "Esa" is the feminine singular form of "that" (for something not right here, often already mentioned). "Historia" can mean "story" (an anecdote, explanation, or even a made-up excuse) and can also mean "history" depending on context; in these examples it means "story."
target_language_example: No me creo esa historia.
native_language_example: I don’t believe that story.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific way of doing or thinking, usually already mentioned or clear from context. Very common in the pattern "de esa manera" = "in that way". Also used as "esa manera de + infinitive" (e.g., "esa manera de hablar" = "that way of speaking").
target_language_example: No me gusta esa manera de hablar.
native_language_example: I don't like that way of speaking.

meaning: “that shit” (a very vulgar, dismissive way to refer to something).
additional_notes: Used to express anger, contempt, or frustration about a thing, situation, or what someone is talking about. It can refer to a specific object (“Turn that shit off”) or a whole series of events (“All that crazy shit happened…”). Strong profanity—avoid in polite/formal contexts; with friends it can be common but still harsh.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de esa mierda ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that shit right now.

meaning: “that woman” (a specific woman, not here or not the closest one).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “esa” + “mujer” to point out a particular woman. Often refers to someone previously mentioned or identified in context. Contrast: “esta mujer” = this woman (near/just mentioned), “aquella mujer” = that woman over there / more distant (in space or time).
target_language_example: No conozco a esa mujer, pero parece amable.
native_language_example: I don’t know that woman, but she seems kind.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular night that both people know about or that was mentioned before. It can point to the recent past (“that night I didn’t sleep”) or to a memorable event (“that night when…”). Often appears at the start of a sentence for emphasis: “Esa noche, …”.
target_language_example: Esa noche no pudimos dormir por el ruido.
native_language_example: That night we couldn’t sleep because of the noise.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific word that has been mentioned, is understood from context, or is being singled out (sometimes because it’s important, offensive, or very precise). It agrees with the feminine noun palabra: esa (that) + palabra (word).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se escribe esa palabra?
native_language_example: How do you spell that word?

additional_notes: "Esa" is a demonstrative meaning "that" (usually something not right here, or something you and the other person can identify). It agrees with the feminine noun "película". You can also hear "ese" (masculine) and "eso" (neuter for "that" idea/thing).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto esa película?
native_language_example: Have you seen that movie?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative adjective “esa” (feminine singular) to refer to a specific question that’s already known from context or was mentioned before. Often used with verbs like contestar/responder (“to answer”) and can sound a bit pointed depending on tone (e.g., refusing to answer).
target_language_example: No entiendo esa pregunta; ¿puedes repetirla?
native_language_example: I don’t understand that question; can you repeat it?

meaning: 'that door' (a specific door over there/previously mentioned).
additional_notes: "Esa" is a demonstrative meaning "that" (near the listener or not right next to the speaker). Use it to point out or refer back to a particular door: "Cierra/abre esa puerta". "Puerta" is feminine, so it’s "esa" (not "ese").
target_language_example: ¿Puedes cerrar esa puerta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you close that door, please?

additional_notes: "Esa" is the feminine singular demonstrative meaning "that" (not "this"), used for something not right next to you—often near the listener or a bit farther away. "Tienda" means "store/shop" and is feminine, so it takes "esa" (not "ese"). Used to point out or refer back to a specific store: "Esa tienda está cerrada" = "That store is closed."
target_language_example: No me gusta esa tienda porque es muy cara.
native_language_example: I don’t like that store because it’s very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something feminine (esa = 'that' feminine; es = 'is'). Often followed by a noun: "Esa es la verdad". For masculine, use "ese es"; for plural, "esas son" / "esos son".
target_language_example: Esa es mi mochila.
native_language_example: That is my backpack.

meaning: “that is the” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to point out, identify, or emphasize something: “That is the + [feminine noun].” It agrees with a feminine singular noun (la noticia, la excepción, la belleza). For a masculine noun you’d use “ese es el.”
target_language_example: Esa es la razón por la que no fui.
native_language_example: That is the reason why I didn’t go.

additional_notes: Used to highlight the key issue or the main thing everyone wants to know. It can be said on its own (“Esa es la pregunta.”) or followed by more detail (e.g., “Esa es la pregunta correcta / del millón / que hacemos todos”). Often implies uncertainty or that the answer isn’t clear yet.
target_language_example: ¿Va a funcionar el plan? Esa es la pregunta.
native_language_example: Is the plan going to work? That’s the question.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify something that belongs to you. "Esa" = "that" (feminine, singular) and "mi" = "my"; the noun that follows is feminine (e.g., cama, chica, especialidad, oferta, teoría). For a masculine noun, use "ese es mi" (e.g., Ese es mi coche).
target_language_example: Esa es mi mochila.
native_language_example: That is my backpack.

additional_notes: Used to point something out (“esa” = “that” for feminine nouns) and identify who it belongs to or relates to (“su”). “Su” can mean his, her, your (formal), or their, so context matters; you can clarify with “de él / de ella / de usted / de ellos(as)”. Often followed by a noun: “Esa es su firma” (That’s his/her signature).
target_language_example: Esa es su casa, no la nuestra.
native_language_example: That is their house, not ours.

additional_notes: Used to point out, identify, or comment on something: “Esa es una teoría / una idea / una pregunta.” It agrees with gender and number: esa (feminine singular) + es (is) + una (a/an, feminine). For masculine nouns, use “ese es un …” (e.g., “Ese es un macho”).
target_language_example: Esa es una buena opción para mañana.
native_language_example: That is a good option for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used as an incomplete sentence where the noun is implied: *Esa es una buena (idea/pregunta/broma)*. With a noun, you’ll usually see: *Esa es una buena noticia/pregunta/señal.* In speech it can sound like you’re praising what someone just said, or reacting as if something is clever or funny.
target_language_example: —¿Y si vamos mañana temprano? —Esa es una buena.
native_language_example: —What if we go early tomorrow? —That’s a good one.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the final time (often followed by “que” + a verb: “Esa fue la última vez que la vi” = “That was the last time I saw her”). You can change “esa” to “esta” (this) or “aquella” (that over there/that one long ago), and “fue” to “era” depending on context.
target_language_example: Esa fue la última vez que hablamos.
native_language_example: That was the last time we talked.

esa fue la última vez que

target_language_multi_word_term: esa fue la última vez que
additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the final time in the past. It’s often followed by a verb in the past (e.g., vi, estuve, habló) describing what happened that last time. You can also hear it as "esa fue la última vez que + [verb]" in storytelling or explanations.
target_language_example: Esa fue la última vez que fuimos al cine juntos.
native_language_example: That was the last time we went to the movies together.

additional_notes: Refers to things not near the speaker (physical or abstract). Common when you don’t want to name something directly or when it’s understood from context (habits, actions, events): No hago esas cosas. Can be negative or dismissive (“that stuff”), but can also be neutral (“those things did happen”).
target_language_example: No me gusta hablar de esas cosas.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about that kind of thing.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify multiple feminine things at some distance (or already known in context). "Esas" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., noticias, cosas, órdenes, opciones) or can stand alone as a pronoun. Contrast: "estos son" (masculine), "esas son" (feminine), "esos son" (masculine).
target_language_example: Esas son mis llaves.
native_language_example: Those are my keys.

additional_notes: Used to point out or identify specific things that are farther away, previously mentioned, or understood from context. It agrees with a feminine plural noun: esas son las gafas / esas son las órdenes. The noun can also be implied: Y esas son las buenas noticias. (Compare: estas son las = these are the; aquellas son las = those over there are the.)
target_language_example: Esas son las llaves que estaba buscando.
native_language_example: Those are the keys I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used in instructions on forms, documents, sign-in books, etc. “Escriba” is the formal usted command of “escribir,” and “su” refers to the person being addressed (your, formal). Often followed by where/how: “en esta hoja” (on this sheet), “con lápiz” (in pencil).
target_language_example: Por favor, escriba su nombre aquí.
native_language_example: Please write your name here.

additional_notes: An affirmative tú command (informal singular) using "escribir". Common in instructions on forms, exams, or notes. You can add where/how: "al final" (at the end), "con lápiz" (in pencil), "junto al mío" (next to mine). For a formal command to one person, use "Escriba su nombre".
target_language_example: Por favor, escribe tu nombre aquí.
native_language_example: Please, write your name here.

additional_notes: "Escribiendo" is the gerund (-ing form) of "escribir" (to write). This phrase is commonly used with "estar" to talk about something in progress right now or at a specific time in the past: "está/estaba escribiendo una carta". You may also see it after "estar ocupado/a" to mean "to be busy writing a letter."
target_language_example: No puedo hablar ahora; estoy escribiendo una carta.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m writing a letter.

additional_notes: Literally “to write his/her own name.” Used to talk about a basic skill (often emphasizing that someone can’t do something simple: “ni siquiera puede escribir su propio nombre”). Change the possessive to match the person: escribir mi propio nombre (my), escribir tu propio nombre (your), escribir su propio nombre (his/her/your formal/their).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes escribir tu propio nombre aquí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you write your own name here, please?

additional_notes: A common phrase meaning to create a book (fiction or non-fiction). It’s often used with verbs like querer (to want), comenzar (to start), poder (can/could), or deber (should) + infinitive: “Quiero/comencé/podríamos escribir un libro.” In “Deberías escribir un libro,” it can also be a suggestion or compliment meaning “You have so much to say/so many stories that it could be a book.”
target_language_example: Algún día voy a escribir un libro sobre mis viajes.
native_language_example: Someday I’m going to write a book about my travels.

additional_notes: Used for writing a (usually formal or traditional) letter, typically on paper. You can add who it’s for with "a": "Escribirle una carta a María" = “to write Mary a letter.” In everyday speech, people may also say "mandar/enviar una carta" (to send a letter) once it’s written.
target_language_example: Voy a escribir una carta a mi abuela esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to write a letter to my grandmother tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say what the subject of a book is. The verb is in the simple past (pretérito): escribió = “wrote.” Change the subject as needed: Yo escribí…, Tú escribiste…, Él/Ella escribió…, Nosotros escribimos…, Ellos escribieron…. After sobre you can use a noun (sobre animales), a topic (sobre el tema), or a clause with cómo (“about how…”).
target_language_example: Mi abuelo escribió un libro sobre su infancia.
native_language_example: My grandfather wrote a book about his childhood.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "escribir": "escribió" means "wrote" (completed action). Often used with an indirect object for the recipient: "Le escribió una carta a su amiga" = "She wrote a letter to her friend" (literally, "She wrote her a letter"). You can also use "a + [person]" to make the recipient clear.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo me escribió una carta cuando yo era niño.
native_language_example: My grandpa wrote me a letter when I was a kid.

additional_notes: "Escribí" is the simple past (preterite) of "escribir" for "yo" (I). Use it for a completed action in the past. With an indirect object, you often say "le escribí una carta" = "I wrote him/her a letter" (literally, "to him/her I wrote a letter").
target_language_example: Le escribí una carta para agradecerle su ayuda.
native_language_example: I wrote him/her a letter to thank them for their help.

additional_notes: This is a past participle phrase and is normally used with the auxiliary verb **haber** to form perfect tenses: **he escrito una carta** (I have written a letter), **habrá escrito una carta** (will have / probably has written a letter), **habría escrito una carta** (would have written a letter). You’ll often see an indirect object pronoun before the auxiliary to show who you wrote to: **le he escrito una carta** (I wrote him/her a letter), **te he escrito una carta** (I wrote you a letter).
target_language_example: Ya le he escrito una carta a mi abuela.
native_language_example: I’ve already written my grandmother a letter.

meaning: “listen to what …” (pay attention to what someone is saying).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to listen carefully to the words that follow. "Escucha" is the informal command (tú) form of "escuchar"; it can also appear as "escuche" (formal usted) or "escuchas" (you listen). "Lo que" means “what/that which” and introduces the thing being said: "Escucha lo que te digo" = “Listen to what I’m telling you.”
target_language_example: Escucha lo que te estoy diciendo: no vayas solo.
native_language_example: Listen to what I’m telling you: don’t go alone.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (escuchando) to describe an action in progress or happening at the same time as another action. Often appears with estar (están/estaban escuchando la radio) or after another verb to show simultaneous action (Me dormí escuchando la radio = I fell asleep while listening to the radio).
target_language_example: Estoy escuchando la radio mientras cocino.
native_language_example: I'm listening to the radio while I cook.

additional_notes: "Escuchando" is the gerund of "escuchar" (to listen). It’s used to describe an action in progress, often with "estar" ("está/estamos escuchando música" = "is/are listening to music"). It can also be used after another verb to say how/when something happens: "Me levanté el ánimo escuchando música" ("I cheered myself up by listening to music").
target_language_example: Estoy en casa escuchando música.
native_language_example: I'm at home listening to music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "escuchar" (to listen) + "la radio" (the radio). Common with verbs like "gustar" (Me gusta escuchar la radio), "preferir" (Prefiero escuchar la radio a...), and in the past/habitual (Solía escuchar la radio...).
target_language_example: Cuando cocino, me gusta escuchar la radio.
native_language_example: When I cook, I like to listen to the radio.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the content of what someone says or what happened: escuchar lo que + verb (dice, pasó, etc.). Often followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., “escuchar lo que dijo”).
target_language_example: Escucha lo que te estoy diciendo, por favor.
native_language_example: Listen to what I’m telling you, please.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase: escuchar = “to listen (to)” and música = “music.” Use it after verbs like gustar (Me gusta escuchar música), ser (Mi hobby es escuchar música), and disfrutar (Disfruto escuchar música). You may also hear the variant “escuchar la música,” meaning “to listen to the music” (a specific music).
target_language_example: Me gusta escuchar música cuando estudio.
native_language_example: I like to listen to music when I study.

additional_notes: Used to express that you want (or are happy) to hear someone speaking—often on the phone, in a voice message, or in person. You can change the possessive: escuchar mi/su/nuestra voz (“to hear my/his/her/your(pl)/our voice”).
target_language_example: Me alegra escuchar tu voz después de tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to hear your voice after so long.

meaning: “I listen to this song” / “I’m listening to this song.”
additional_notes: “Escucho” is the 1st-person singular present tense of “escuchar” (to listen/to hear). It’s often used with a direct object: “escucho + [thing]”.
