additional_notes: A common direction/instruction (often in the tú command form). Used when giving driving or walking directions: “Gira a la derecha en el cruce / al llegar al semáforo.” You may also hear the more formal/plural command: “Gire a la derecha” (usted) or “Giren a la derecha” (you all).
target_language_example: Sigue todo recto y luego gira a la derecha en la esquina.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and then turn right at the corner.

additional_notes: Common in directions and navigation. Often used as an informal command (tú): “Gira a la izquierda (en la esquina / en el semáforo / después de dos cuadras)”. You may also hear the formal/usted command: “Gire a la izquierda”.
target_language_example: En el próximo cruce, gira a la izquierda.
native_language_example: At the next intersection, turn left.

additional_notes: Used for giving directions. It’s the formal command form (usted) of "girar" (to turn). In casual speech you may also hear "gira a la derecha" (tú) or "giren a la derecha" (plural). Often followed by a place or landmark: "en el banco" (at/by the bank) or "en el tercer semáforo" (at the third traffic light).
target_language_example: En la próxima esquina, gire a la derecha.
native_language_example: At the next corner, turn right.

meaning: 'thanks to you' (because of you; due to you).
additional_notes: Used to give credit to someone for a positive result (“Thanks to you, I can…”). Depending on context and tone, it can also be sarcastic/blaming (“…and it’s all thanks to you” meaning “because of you” in a negative way). Similar to “por tu culpa” when clearly blaming, but “gracias a ti” can be either sincere or sarcastic.
target_language_example: Lo logré, gracias a ti.
native_language_example: I did it, thanks to you.

additional_notes: Used to thank a group of people for a specific action. Put an infinitive after por (por venir, por participar) or a noun/thing (por esto). Common in speeches, meetings, and events.
target_language_example: Gracias a todos por ayudarme con el proyecto.
native_language_example: Thanks to everyone for helping me with the project.

additional_notes: Use it to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s typically followed by a noun (Gracias por el espectáculo; Gracias por vuestra atención) or by an infinitive verb (Gracias por estar aquí; Gracias por llamarme de vuelta; Gracias por explicarme...). You can also use it in set phrases like Gracias por todo (“thanks for everything”).
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme hoy.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me today.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for helping you. You can add details after it (e.g., ayer “yesterday”, siempre “always”) or continue with pero… (“but…”) to add a contrast.
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudarme con la tarea.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing introduced by the masculine singular definite article el (e.g., el apoyo, el consejo). If the noun is feminine, use “gracias por la …”; if it’s plural, “gracias por los/las …”. You can also say “gracias por + [noun]” without an article in some cases.
target_language_example: Gracias por el regalo.
native_language_example: Thanks for the gift.

additional_notes: Use this to thank someone for a specific thing or action, followed by a feminine noun: Gracias por la información / ayuda / explicación. For masculine nouns, use “gracias por el …” (Gracias por el café). You can also use it to thank someone for an abstract thing like a conversation or correction.
target_language_example: Gracias por la ayuda, de verdad.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help, really.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely in formal situations. "Su" is the formal singular "your" (usted). It’s typically followed by a noun: gracias por su tiempo (your time), su atención (your attention), su confianza (your trust). For informal "your," use "gracias por tu …".
target_language_example: Gracias por su ayuda, doctora.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, doctor.

meaning: “Thanks for your …” (to thank someone for something they did/are doing).
additional_notes: Use it before a masculine singular noun to say what you’re thankful for: Gracias por tu + [noun] (e.g., tu ayuda, tu tiempo). If the noun is feminine, use “Gracias por tu” + noun too (tu works for both genders), but the noun changes (e.g., gracias por tu ayuda). In very formal situations, you may see “Gracias por su …” (your = su).
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for showing up or attending. You can add details with "a + place/event" (Gracias por venir a nuestro cine) or "hasta aquí" to emphasize they came a long way (Gracias por venir hasta aquí). Often said when greeting someone or at the end of a meeting.
target_language_example: Gracias por venir a mi fiesta.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to my party.

additional_notes: Used when talking about temperature that is below zero, especially with Celsius in Spanish-speaking contexts. Common patterns: “hace X grados bajo cero” (it’s X degrees below zero), “está/estuvo a X grados bajo cero” (it is/was at X below zero), “bajar/descender a X grados bajo cero” (to drop to X below zero). You can also say “menos de X grados bajo cero” (less than X below zero).
target_language_example: Mañana por la noche vamos a estar a cuatro grados bajo cero.
native_language_example: Tomorrow night it will be four degrees below zero.

meaning: a great day; the big day (an important, awaited day).
additional_notes: Gran is the shortened form of grande used before a singular noun (gran día, gran momento). In context, el gran día often means “the big day” for a special event (wedding, exam, trip).
target_language_example: ¡Mucha suerte en tu entrevista mañana: es tu gran día!
native_language_example: Good luck on your interview tomorrow: it’s your big day!

additional_notes: Gran is a shortened form of grande used before a singular noun (gran error, gran idea). It emphasizes importance or severity. Common patterns: Fue un gran error. / Ese fue mi gran error. / Cometer un gran error (“to make a big mistake”).
target_language_example: Decir eso en la reunión fue un gran error.
native_language_example: Saying that in the meeting was a big mistake.

meaning: “(as) big/large as” in comparisons like “X times bigger than …”.
additional_notes: Used in size comparisons, especially with quantities: **el doble de grande que** (twice as big as), **el triple de grande que** (three times as big as), **la mitad de grande que** (half as big as). It normally appears as **de grande que + [noun/pronoun]** after a number/amount, not by itself. In everyday Spanish you’ll also hear **más grande que** (“bigger than”).
target_language_example: Este apartamento es el doble de grande que el mío.
native_language_example: This apartment is twice as big as mine.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons, usually with **más/menos/tan**: **más grande que la mía** (“bigger than mine”), **tan grande como la mía** (“as big as mine”). **La mía** means “mine” and agrees with the noun you’re comparing (feminine singular here, e.g., **mi ciudad / mi habitación**). You can also change it: **el mío** (masc. sing.), **los míos / las mías** (plural).
target_language_example: Tu casa es más grande que la mía.
native_language_example: Your house is bigger than mine.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say what the group is made up of or what kind of group it is: grupo de gente (a group of people), grupo de rescate (rescue team), grupo de apoyo (support group), grupo de amigos (group of friends). Often followed by a plural noun, but can also be followed by a singular noun that names a category or type (e.g., grupo de rescate).
target_language_example: Somos un grupo de estudiantes de intercambio.
native_language_example: We are a group of exchange students.

meaning: to keep quiet; to remain silent.
additional_notes: Used to talk about deliberately not speaking, often as a rule, order, or personal decision (e.g., in class, during an operation, or as a vow). Also common as an instruction: «¡Guarden silencio!» = “Be quiet!”
target_language_example: Por favor, guarden silencio mientras empieza la película.
native_language_example: Please be quiet while the movie starts.

additional_notes: Used to say you will not tell other people private information. It often appears with verbs like poder (can) and saber (know how to): «No puedo guardar un secreto» / «Sé guardar un secreto». Also common with «Debo guardar un secreto» (I must keep a secret).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: sé guardar un secreto.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can keep a secret.

meaning: '(he/she/you) likes the' (used with gustar + a singular masculine noun).
additional_notes: With **gustar**, the thing you like is the grammatical subject, so Spanish literally works like “**the X is pleasing to (someone)**.” In real Spanish you’ll almost always see this with an indirect object pronoun: **me/te/le/nos/os/les gusta el + singular masculine noun**. To say who likes it, you can add **a mí, a ti, a Tom, a ella**, etc. For plural nouns use **gustan**: *Me gustan los tacos.*
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta el chocolate.
native_language_example: My sister likes chocolate.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "gustar," which works like "to be pleasing" in English: the thing liked ("el helado") is the grammatical subject, and the person is an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les." Often you add "A + person" for clarity or emphasis: "A Tomás le gusta el helado." Use "gusta" (singular) with a singular noun like "el helado," and "gustan" with plural nouns ("Me gustan los helados"). To say you don’t like it: "No me gusta el helado."
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta el helado de fresa.
native_language_example: My sister likes strawberry ice cream.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar + infinitive: (A mí) me gusta estar…, (A él/ella) le gusta estar…, (A nosotros) nos gusta estar… to say someone likes being in a certain state or situation (alone, wet, surrounded by people, etc.). The person is often introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Tom le gusta…").
target_language_example: A mí me gusta estar en casa los domingos.
native_language_example: I like being at home on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gustar**, which works differently from English: the thing liked is the grammatical subject. So **A María le gusta la música** literally means “Music pleases María,” but in natural English it’s “María likes music.” You’ll almost always see it with an indirect object pronoun (**me/te/le/nos/os/les**) and sometimes **a + person** for clarity or emphasis. **La** is the feminine singular article; for masculine you’d use **gusta el**; for plural things: **gustan los/las**.
target_language_example: A mi hermana le gusta la pizza.
native_language_example: My sister likes pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to express strong liking. The thing/person liked is the grammatical subject: “Me gusta mucho esta sopa” = “I like this soup a lot” (literally: “This soup pleases me a lot”). You’ll often see it with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les) and sometimes an explicit person: “A María no le gusta mucho el fútbol.” Note: “Ella me gusta mucho” means “I like her a lot” (often with a romantic sense).
target_language_example: Me gusta mucho esta canción.
native_language_example: I like this song a lot.

meaning: “(they) like the …” (used with plural feminine nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to talk about things people like. The person is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/os/les" (e.g., "A ella le gustan las fresas" = she likes strawberries). Because "las" is feminine plural, it’s followed by a feminine plural noun (las verduras, las fresas, las minifaldas). For masculine plural, use "gustan los"; for singular, use "gusta el/la".
target_language_example: A mí me gustan las películas de comedia.
native_language_example: I like comedy movies.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar. What is liked (“las chicas”) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les. Often appears as: “Me/Te/Le/Nos/Les gustan las chicas.” Use “gusta” (singular) if what you like is one thing (e.g., “Me gusta la chica”).
target_language_example: A mí me gustan las chicas inteligentes.
native_language_example: I like smart girls.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **gustar**. In Spanish, the thing you like (**las manzanas**) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is **plural**: *gustan*. The person who likes them is shown with an **indirect object pronoun**: *me/te/le/nos/les* (often with emphasis: *a mí, a ti, a él/ella, a nosotros, a ellos*). Example: *Me gustan las manzanas* = “I like apples” (literally, “Apples are pleasing to me”).
target_language_example: A ella le gustan las manzanas, pero a mí no.
native_language_example: She likes apples, but I don't.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gustar to say someone likes things. In Spanish the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/os/les): “Me gustan los pasteles” = “I like cakes.” Use “gustan” with plural nouns; with a singular noun you use “gusta” (e.g., “Me gusta el café”). “Los” is the masculine plural “the”; for feminine plural use “las” (“Me gustan las flores”).
target_language_example: ¿Te gustan los videojuegos?
native_language_example: Do you like video games?

additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar to say that beans are pleasing to someone. The thing liked (los frijoles) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is plural: gustan. Add an indirect object pronoun for who likes them: me (I), te (you), le (he/she/you formal), nos (we), les (they/you all). Often you can add “a + name/pronoun” for clarity: A Mary le gustan los frijoles. (Note: a literal translation like “Beans please me” matches the grammar, but in English you usually say “I like beans.”)
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los frijoles, pero a mi hermano no le gustan.
native_language_example: I like beans, but my brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar" to say someone likes cats. The person who likes them is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. "Los gatos" is the thing liked, so the verb is plural: "gustan". You can add "a + person" for clarity/emphasis: "A ella le gustan los gatos."
target_language_example: ¿Te gustan los gatos?
native_language_example: Do you like cats?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gustar". In Spanish, the thing being liked ("los mariscos") is the grammatical subject, so the verb is usually plural here: "gustan". Add an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: me (I), te (you), le (he/she/you formal), nos (we), les (they/you all). You can also add "a + person" for clarity: "A Mary le gustan los mariscos."
target_language_example: A mí me gustan los mariscos, pero a mi hermano no le gustan.
native_language_example: I like seafood, but my brother doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used when meeting someone (or after meeting them) to express pleasure at knowing them. Very common variants: «(Mucho) gusto conocerte» and «Qué gusto conocerte». You’ll also hear it in longer phrases like «Es un gusto conocerte», «Fue un gusto conocerte» (nice meeting you / it was a pleasure meeting you), and «Me dio gusto conocerte» (it made me happy to meet you). In many places it’s also common to say «Encantado/a» as a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Mucho gusto conocerte, soy Laura.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, I’m Laura.

meaning: Nice to see you. / Glad to see you.
additional_notes: Common greeting (and sometimes a friendly closing) when you see someone. Often used as: «(Fue) un gusto verte» (It was nice to see you), «Qué gusto verte» (So nice to see you), or «Me dio gusto verte» / «Le dio mucho gusto verte» (I’m/He’s/She’s happy to see you; literally “It gave me/him/her pleasure to see you”). You can add a name or «amigo/a».
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte otra vez, Ana!
native_language_example: So nice to see you again, Ana!

additional_notes: Written to show laughing in text or in dialogue. It can be genuine laughter or used sarcastically to mock or tease. Often repeated (“ha ha ha”) and usually separated by commas or exclamation marks depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ha ha, qué gracioso eres.
native_language_example: Haha, you’re so funny.

additional_notes: Used to say something is over or finished. It’s the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (acabado), often translated as “has ended/has finished.” Common with events, periods of time, games, wars, negotiations, etc. Word order can vary: “El juego ha acabado” / “Ha acabado el juego.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, la reunión ya ha acabado.
native_language_example: Sorry, the meeting has already ended.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle (**cambiado**) to talk about a change that has happened already, often with a result that matters now. Used with a subject (*El mundo ha cambiado*) or with a direct object using **a** for people/countries (*La guerra ha cambiado a Japón* = “The war has changed Japan”).
target_language_example: Desde que te fuiste, todo ha cambiado.
native_language_example: Since you left, everything has changed.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haber + participle) to talk about a change that has happened up to now: someone/something is different now compared to before. Often followed by "desde..." (since...) or "ya no..." (no longer...). You can change the subject/pronoun: "he/has/hemos/han cambiado mucho".
target_language_example: Mi ciudad ha cambiado mucho en los últimos diez años.
native_language_example: My city has changed a lot in the last ten years.

additional_notes: Present perfect of caer (“to fall”). Used for physical falling (often with se: Se te ha caído algo = “You dropped something / Something fell from you”), for decreases (La temperatura ha caído = “The temperature has dropped”), and for institutions/regimes collapsing (El régimen ha caído = “The regime has fallen”). Also in the expression caer en desgracia = “to fall from favor.”
target_language_example: Se me ha caído el vaso al suelo.
native_language_example: I dropped the glass on the floor.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "ha" (from haber) + "comprado" (past participle). It’s followed by "un" because the noun is masculine singular (e.g., un abrigo, un ordenador). With "se ha comprado un…", it often means "has bought (himself/herself) a…" (for their own use).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha comprado un coche usado.
native_language_example: My brother has bought a used car.

meaning: "has/have given" (present perfect of "dar"); often used in set phrases like "has begun" or "had/got" (an attack, etc.).
additional_notes: "Ha" is from "haber" and "dado" is the past participle of "dar". It forms the present perfect: "él/ella/usted ha dado" = "he/she/you (formal) has given". In idioms, "ha dado comienzo" means "has begun/has started", and "le ha dado un ataque" means "he/she had/got an attack" (something happened to them).
target_language_example: El profesor ha dado la respuesta.
native_language_example: The teacher has given the answer.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle (**decidido**). Used with a third-person singular subject (él/ella/usted) or a singular noun/name (e.g., *Tom*). Often implies the decision is relevant now or has just been made.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha decidido cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister has decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **dejar** (él/ella/usted): **ha dejado**. Common patterns: **ha dejado + objeto** = “has left (something/someone)”, **ha dejado de + infinitive** = “has stopped (doing something)”, and **se ha dejado + objeto** = “has forgotten/left behind (something)” (often unintentionally), e.g., *Se ha dejado el cambio*. With body/hair: **se ha dejado la barba** = “has grown/let his beard grow.”
target_language_example: Tom ha dejado de hablarme.
native_language_example: Tom has stopped talking to me.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (dejar de + infinitive) to say an action has stopped. “Ha” is the present perfect (he/she/it has), so it often implies it stopped recently or by now: ha dejado de llover (it has stopped raining). Change the person as needed: he dejado de, has dejado de, hemos dejado de, etc.
target_language_example: Mi móvil ha dejado de cargar.
native_language_example: My phone has stopped charging.

additional_notes: Present perfect of desaparecer (“to disappear”): ha (has) + desaparecido (disappeared). Used for something that is no longer there or has gone away, often with a result that matters now. The subject can come after the verb: Ha desaparecido el dolor (“The pain has disappeared”).
target_language_example: Mi cartera ha desaparecido.
native_language_example: My wallet has disappeared.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + **dicho** (past participle of *decir*). Used for what **he/she/it has said** (often recently or with relevance now). It can also mean **has told** when there’s a person receiving the message: *Me ha dicho...* = “He/She has told me...”.
target_language_example: Mi jefe ha dicho que mañana no hay clase.
native_language_example: My boss has said that there’s no class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "[someone] ha dicho que + clause". It's the present perfect of "decir" (he/she/it has said). Often corresponds to English "said (that)" or "has said (that)" depending on context. You can change the subject and tense: "He dicho que..." (I said...), "dijo que..." (he/she said...).
target_language_example: El guía ha dicho que el museo abre a las diez.
native_language_example: The guide said that the museum opens at ten.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "empezar" + "a" + infinitive. Used to say someone/something has recently begun doing an action: "ha empezado a + infinitive" (ha empezado a nevar, a cantar, a buscar...). Often implies a new change or recent development. Other persons: he empezado a (I’ve started to), has empezado a (you’ve started to), hemos/han empezado a (we/they’ve started to).
target_language_example: Últimamente, mi hermano ha empezado a levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Lately, my brother has started getting up early.

additional_notes: Formed with **haber (ha)** + past participle **encontrado**. Used to talk about something someone **has found** or that **has happened already** (often with a result now). With people, **encontrar a + person** = “to find/meet (someone).” Reflexive **se ha encontrado** can mean “has been found” (passive/impersonal: “a dagger has been found”).
target_language_example: La policía ha encontrado al sospechoso.
native_language_example: The police have found the suspect.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" (ha) + past participle (escrito) to talk about something someone has done, often with a result or relevance now. It can also be used to talk about life experience (e.g., how many books someone has written). Common with quantities like "tres", "muchos", "cientos de".
target_language_example: María ha escrito un artículo para el periódico.
native_language_example: María has written an article for the newspaper.

meaning: "has been" (often used as part of "ha estado" + gerund = "has been doing").
additional_notes: "Ha estado" is the present perfect form of **estar** (3rd person singular: "he/she/it has been"). Very commonly it’s followed by a **gerund** (verb ending in -ando/-iendo) to form **ha estado + gerund**, meaning an action has been happening recently or up to now: *ha estado mirando* = "has been looking/staring." With indirect object pronouns it becomes *me/te/le/nos/os/les ha estado...* (e.g., *te ha estado mirando* = "has been looking at you").
target_language_example: Mi jefe ha estado hablando de ese proyecto toda la semana.
native_language_example: My boss has been talking about that project all week.

meaning: "has been in / has been to" (has spent time in a place or situation).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **ha** (has) + **estado** (been) + **en** (in/on). It often talks about life experience or repeated visits (**Ha estado en Australia dos veces** = he’s been to Australia twice). It can also mean being in a situation/activity for some time: **ha estado en el teléfono por horas** = he’s been on the phone for hours. With media/activities, it can mean participation: **ha estado en películas** = he has been in movies.
target_language_example: Ella ha estado en España varias veces.
native_language_example: She has been to Spain several times.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (haber + estado) to talk about a period up to now or a recently relevant situation: Ha estado enfermo durante mucho tiempo (“He has been sick for a long time”). Often followed by time expressions like durante…, por…, desde…. You can add en cama (“in bed”) to say someone has been sick in bed. Note: with a finished past time like la semana pasada, Spanish more naturally uses the simple past (Estuvo enfermo la semana pasada).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha estado enfermo desde el viernes.
native_language_example: My brother has been sick since Friday.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect of gustar: ha gustado = “has been pleasing.” In Spanish, the thing you like is the grammatical subject, and the person is shown with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/os/les. Examples: Me ha gustado el libro. (I liked the book.) / Le ha gustado el concierto. (He/She liked the concert.) Often used with a + person for emphasis: A mí también me ha gustado.
target_language_example: ¿Te ha gustado la película?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie?

meaning: “there has been / there have been” (it has existed/occurred).
additional_notes: Impersonal form of haber used to say something has happened or existed. It’s the present perfect: ha (has) + habido (past participle). It’s always singular (ha), even with plural nouns: “Ha habido muchas quejas” = “There have been many complaints.” Common with events/changes: “Ha habido un accidente/un cambio/dificultades.”
target_language_example: Ha habido varios retrasos esta semana.
native_language_example: There have been several delays this week.

meaning: "there has been a" / "there has been one".
additional_notes: Impersonal use of the verb "haber" to say that something has occurred or existed. It’s used for news, events, changes, incidents, etc. Even if the noun is plural, "haber" often stays singular: "Ha habido problemas" = "There have been problems." (Also: "ha habido una" for feminine nouns, e.g., "ha habido una reunión").
target_language_example: Ha habido un problema con la reserva.
native_language_example: There has been a problem with the reservation.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **ha** (from *haber*) + past participle **hecho** (from *hacer*). Used for actions completed in the past with a connection to the present (often similar to English “has done/has made”). Refers to **él/ella/usted** or a thing/idea (3rd person singular). In some set phrases it can mean “has caused” (e.g., *no le ha hecho mal* = “hasn’t harmed him/her”).
target_language_example: ¿Quién ha hecho esto?
native_language_example: Who has done this?

meaning: "has gone" / "has gone (to...)"; also "has gone (for you)" (has turned out).
additional_notes: Present perfect of ir (él/ella/usted ha ido). Often used with destinations: "ha ido a + place" = "has been/has gone to...". With "te/le ha ido" it means how things have gone for someone: "te ha ido bien/mal" = "things have gone well/badly for you" (how you’ve been doing).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo te ha ido en el trabajo?
native_language_example: How have things gone at work?

meaning: "has gone to" / "has been to" (he/she/it has gone to…).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect of "ir": "haber" (ha) + past participle (ido). Use it to talk about someone going somewhere at an unspecified time, or about life experience ("ha ido a Francia tres veces" = has been to France three times). With "a" + infinitive, it often means "has gone to (do something)": "ha ido a montar" (has gone to ride), "ha ido a buscar" (has gone to get/pick up). With "se ha ido a", it often means "has left/gone away to" a place.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha ido al supermercado a comprar pan.
native_language_example: My sister has gone to the supermarket to buy bread.

additional_notes: Used with a singular subject to say something/someone has arrived or has come (often just now or by now): El juez ha llegado. With things like trains, messages, or mail, it means they have arrived/been received: El tren no ha llegado; Me ha llegado una oferta. With abstract nouns it can mean “has come” or “has reached”: La época… ha llegado a su fin (“has come to an end”). Negative: no ha llegado (“hasn't arrived/hasn't come”).
target_language_example: Todavía no ha llegado el correo.
native_language_example: The mail still hasn’t arrived.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "llegar" (to arrive/reach) + "a". Used for arriving at a place ("ha llegado a Kioto"), reaching a stage/age ("ha llegado a una edad..."), or arriving at an abstract result like a decision or conclusion ("ha llegado a una decisión").
target_language_example: Después de horas de hablar, por fin ha llegado a un acuerdo.
native_language_example: After hours of talking, he/she has finally reached an agreement.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (llevado), used for actions in the past connected to the present. With a person/place as the object, it often means “has taken (someone) (to somewhere)” (e.g., No me ha llevado a Shanghai). With things, it can mean “has carried” or “has taken away.” In the reflexive form (se ha llevado), it often means “has been taken away” or “has carried off” (e.g., by a wave). With “una vida,” it means “has led a life” (Ha llevado una vida emocionante).
target_language_example: Mi hermana me ha llevado al aeropuerto dos veces esta semana.
native_language_example: My sister has taken me to the airport twice this week.

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (mejorado). Used to talk about improvement that happened in the past and is true/relevant now. Often followed by something like “mucho” (a lot) or “desde…” (since…).
target_language_example: Mi situación ha mejorado desde el año pasado.
native_language_example: My situation has improved since last year.

additional_notes: Past tense form of *morir* used to report a death: **haber (ha) + muerto**. It’s common in news or announcements (e.g., *Ha muerto Stephen*). You can add details with **en**: *Ha muerto en un accidente* (“He/She died in an accident”). It can also be used figuratively: *La justicia ha muerto* (“Justice is dead,” meaning it no longer exists/works).
target_language_example: Ha muerto mi abuelo esta mañana.
native_language_example: My grandfather died this morning.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "ocurrir" (to happen). Used to talk about something that happened in the past but is still relevant now, often with words like "jamás", "antes", "hoy", or "desde entonces". In questions: "¿Qué ha ocurrido?" = "What happened?/What has happened?"
target_language_example: No sé qué ha ocurrido, pero todos están preocupados.
native_language_example: I don't know what happened, but everyone is worried.

additional_notes: It’s the present perfect of pasar (él/ella/usted ha pasado). Meaning depends on context: (1) time passing: Ha pasado tanto tiempo. = So much time has passed. (2) something happening: Eso es lo que ha pasado. = That’s what happened. (3) spending time somewhere/doing something: Ella ha pasado horas en el gimnasio. = She’s spent hours at the gym. It can also refer to serving time in prison: Ha pasado diez años entre rejas. = He spent ten years behind bars.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero ya ha pasado; no podemos cambiarlo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it already happened; we can’t change it.

meaning: "a long time has passed" / "it’s been a long time."
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ha pasado) to say that a lot of time has gone by up to now. Very common with "desde" (since) or "desde que" + a verb: "Ha pasado mucho tiempo desde que lo vi" (It’s been a long time since I saw him). It can also stand alone as a full sentence to comment that it’s been a while.
target_language_example: Ha pasado mucho tiempo desde que hablamos por última vez.
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since we last talked.

meaning: “a year has passed” / “it’s been a year.”
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ha pasado) to say that one year has elapsed up to now. Very often followed by desde (“since”) or desde que (“since [something happened]”): Ha pasado un año desde entonces (since then); Ha pasado un año desde que ella vino (since she came). You can also use it alone to emphasize the amount of time: Ha pasado un año.
target_language_example: Ha pasado un año desde la última vez que nos vimos.
native_language_example: It’s been a year since the last time we saw each other.

additional_notes: Used with many kinds of “loss”: objects (ha perdido su tarjeta), abilities/health (ha perdido el oído, ha perdido mucha sangre), abstract things (ha perdido la esperanza), and also opportunities/time in set phrases like "no ha perdido el tiempo" (= he/she hasn’t wasted time). It’s formed with "haber" (ha) + past participle (perdido).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ha perdido las llaves.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she has lost the keys.

additional_notes: "Ha puesto" = haber (ha) + past participle (puesto). It describes something completed in the recent past or with relevance to the present. "Poner" is very common and can mean "to put/place," "to set" (e.g., rules/a date), "to lay" (eggs), or "to make/cause" a feeling (e.g., "me ha puesto nervioso"). "Puesto" is the irregular past participle of "poner."
target_language_example: Él ha puesto las llaves en la mesa.
native_language_example: He has put the keys on the table.

meaning: “has ended up / has been left” (shows the result after something happens).
additional_notes: It’s the present perfect of **quedar** (“to remain / to end up / to be left”). Very common in the pattern **ha quedado + adjective/past participle** to describe the final state: *ha quedado cancelado* (“has ended up canceled”), *ha quedado corto* (“has fallen short / been too short”). Don’t confuse with **se ha quedado**, which often means “has stayed” somewhere or with someone (*Tom se ha quedado conmigo*).
target_language_example: La puerta ha quedado abierta.
native_language_example: The door has been left open.

additional_notes: Used with **haber** to form the present perfect: **(él/ella/usted) ha roto** = “he/she/you (formal) has broken.” With **se** it often means something broke on its own: **Se ha roto** = “It broke / It’s broken.” With people, **ha roto conmigo** means “has broken up with me.”
target_language_example: Mi móvil se ha roto otra vez.
native_language_example: My phone broke again / My phone is broken again.

meaning: "has gone out" / "has come out" / "has left" (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect: haber (ha) + past participle (salido). With things like the moon/sun, it means “has come out/appeared” (Ha salido la luna). With transportation or people, it often means “has left/departed” (El avión ya ha salido).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el tren ya ha salido.
native_language_example: Sorry, the train has already left.

additional_notes: Formed with the auxiliary verb "haber" (ha) + the past participle of "ser" (sido). It’s used in the present perfect, often in passive constructions with a past participle: "ha sido + participio" = "has been + past participle" (e.g., "ha sido enviado" = "has been sent").
target_language_example: El paquete ha sido entregado.
native_language_example: The package has been delivered.

additional_notes: Formed with the auxiliary verb "haber" (ha) + the past participle of "ser" (sido). It’s used in the present perfect, often in passive constructions with a past participle: "ha sido + participio" = "has been + past participle" (e.g., "ha sido enviado" = "has been sent").
target_language_example: El paquete ha sido entregado.
native_language_example: The package has been delivered.

meaning: it was (someone’s) fault / it was to blame.
additional_notes: Used with "de" to say who is responsible: "Ha sido culpa de Ah Hoi" (It was Ah Hoi’s fault). Often appears in negatives to reassure someone: "No ha sido culpa tuya" (It wasn’t your fault). You can also add a noun after it to say what caused the problem: "Ha sido culpa del ciervo" (It was the deer’s fault).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ha sido culpa mía.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, it was my fault.

meaning: “it was the…” / “it has been the…” (used to identify or blame something/someone).
additional_notes: “Ha sido” is the present perfect of *ser* (it has been/it was). It’s commonly used to point out who did something or what caused something: *Esto ha sido el X* (“This was X / This was caused by X”). With a masculine noun you’ll often see *el*; with a feminine noun it would be *ha sido la*.
target_language_example: Esto ha sido el jefe; yo no he hecho nada.
native_language_example: This was the boss; I didn’t do anything.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "ser" (él/ella/usted): "ha sido" = "has been". It’s commonly used to describe how someone/something has been up to now (often connected to "hasta ahora", "últimamente", etc.). Put an adjective after "muy" and make it agree in gender/number: "ha sido muy exitoso/existosa", "ha sido muy paciente".
target_language_example: El viaje ha sido muy largo.
native_language_example: The trip has been very long.

meaning: "has been a" (talking about a past situation or experience).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns (un encanto, un éxito, un privilegio) to describe how something turned out or what the experience was like. For feminine nouns, use "ha sido una" (e.g., Ha sido una sorpresa). Common in polite endings: "Ha sido un placer."
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; ha sido un placer conocerte.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; it’s been a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: 'it has been a day' / 'it’s been a day' (used to describe how the day was).
additional_notes: Very common with an adjective or description after it: “Ha sido un día duro/perfecto/agotador.” Uses the present perfect (haber + sido), often to talk about how today has gone so far or how a recent day felt. You can also add “Hoy”: “Hoy ha sido un día…”
target_language_example: Ha sido un día largo, pero ya terminó.
native_language_example: It’s been a long day, but it’s over now.

additional_notes: A polite way to end a conversation or meeting, or to thank someone after an interaction. Often followed by an infinitive: “Ha sido un placer + conocerle/conocerla” (to meet you), “hablar con usted” (to speak with you). Uses the present perfect (“has been”), common in Spain; in many Latin American contexts you may also hear “Fue un placer.”
target_language_example: Ha sido un placer hablar con usted. Que tenga un buen día.
native_language_example: It’s been a pleasure speaking with you. Have a good day.

meaning: "has been a" (used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Present perfect of ser (ha + sido) used to describe what something/someone has been (an experience, an afternoon, a burden, etc.), often up to now or with relevance to the present. It must agree with the noun: ha sido una experiencia/tarde/carga (feminine), but ha sido un día/un problema (masculine). You can add an adjective after the noun: ha sido una experiencia maravillosa.
target_language_example: Ha sido una semana muy intensa.
native_language_example: It has been a very intense week.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **haber (ha)** + past participle (**sucedido**). Used to talk about something that has happened in the past and is relevant now (often with words like **ya** "already" or **antes** "before"). Also appears in phrases like **lo que ha sucedido** ("what has happened"). Note: **suceder** means "to happen," not "to succeed" (so it can be confused with English "succeeded").
target_language_example: ¿Qué ha sucedido aquí?
native_language_example: What has happened here?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about past experiences or results that matter now. It’s the third-person singular form (él/ella/usted): "ha tenido". Often followed by a noun: "ha tenido suerte" (has had luck), "ha tenido tiempo" (has had time).
target_language_example: Ella ha tenido un día muy largo.
native_language_example: She has had a very long day.

additional_notes: Present perfect of tener: “ha tenido” = “has had” (also used for “has been in”). Commonly used to report that someone was involved in an accident (car accident, workplace accident, etc.). You can add details with de/en/con: “un accidente de coche” (a car accident), “un accidente en la carretera” (on the road), “un accidente con…” (involving/with…).
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha tenido un accidente de coche, pero está bien.
native_language_example: My brother has had a car accident, but he’s okay.

additional_notes: Used to say something is over or completed. It’s the formal written/spoken way to express “it’s finished” in the recent past or with present relevance. Often used with events/processes: La clase/la reunión/la conversación ha terminado. In Spain you may also hear pretérito perfecto (ha terminado) more than in much of Latin America, where terminó is often preferred in everyday speech.
target_language_example: El partido ha terminado, vámonos a casa.
native_language_example: The game is over; let’s go home.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary haber + past participle (tomar → tomado) to talk about something that has happened (often recently or with a present connection). Depending on context, tomar can mean “take,” “have (food/drink/medicine),” or “make” (e.g., tomar una decisión = to make a decision). With a reflexive pronoun (se ha tomado), it can appear in set phrases like tomarse molestias (“to go to a lot of trouble”) or tomarse libertades (“to take liberties”).
target_language_example: Él ha tomado una decisión hoy.
native_language_example: He has made a decision today.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb haber + past participle to talk about something that has happened up to now. "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular form (he/she/it/you-formal: "has"). It often appears with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le ha traído" = "has brought me/you/him-her (something)".
target_language_example: El trabajo me ha traído mucha experiencia.
native_language_example: The job has brought me a lot of experience.

meaning: “has come / has arrived” (present perfect, he/she/it has come).
additional_notes: Formed with **haber** (ha) + past participle (**venido**) to talk about something that has happened already. The subject is usually **él/ella/usted** (he/she/you formal) and can be omitted: **Ha venido** = “(He/She) has come.” Negative: **No ha venido** = “hasn’t come.”
target_language_example: ¿Ya ha venido tu hermana?
native_language_example: Has your sister arrived yet?

additional_notes: Present perfect of venir + a. Use it for someone who has arrived at a place (ha venido a nuestro país / a Río) or who has come in order to do something (ha venido a ayudarnos). With places, English often uses "has come to" or simply "has been to" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha venido a casa para cenar con nosotros.
native_language_example: My sister has come to our house to have dinner with us.

additional_notes: "Ha visto" is the 3rd-person singular present perfect: "él/ella/usted ha visto" = "he/she/you (formal) has seen". It can refer to something seen at an unspecified time in the past, or to an experience up to now. With a direct object pronoun, it often appears as "le/la/lo ha visto" ("has seen him/her/it").
target_language_example: ¿Usted ha visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: Have you (formal) seen my keys?

additional_notes: Present perfect of vivir: haber (ha) + past participle (vivido) + en + place. Used to talk about life experience or a period of time up to now; often followed by “durante + time period” (e.g., durante diez años).
target_language_example: Ella ha vivido en Madrid desde 2019.
native_language_example: She has lived in Madrid since 2019.

meaning: 'has returned / has come back'; also used to mean 'again' (ha vuelto a + infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect of volver (to return). It can mean something/someone has come back: Ha vuelto la paz. With "ha vuelto a + infinitive," it means the action is happening again: Ha vuelto a salir el sol (= The sun has come out again). Note: with reflexive "se ha vuelto + adjective/noun," it means "has become": Él se ha vuelto importante.
target_language_example: Mi hermana ha vuelto a casa.
native_language_example: My sister has come back home.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has done an action again: **ha vuelto a + infinitive** (e.g., *ha vuelto a ocurrir* = “it happened again,” *ha vuelto a meterlo* = “he/she put it back in”). It can also introduce a return to a place with **ha vuelto a + place** (e.g., *ha vuelto a la ciudad* = “he/she has returned to the city”). It’s the present perfect: **ha** (has) + **vuelto** (returned) + **a** (to), often implying repetition or “back to” a previous state.
target_language_example: Mi hermano ha vuelto a llamar esta mañana.
native_language_example: My brother called again this morning.

meaning: "to have said" (to have said something before another action/feeling).
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: haber + past participle (dicho). It’s used after other verbs to talk about something that happened earlier, often with feelings (Lamento haber dicho eso. = I’m sorry I said that) or possibility/impossibility (No pudo haber dicho eso. = He couldn’t have said that). Common patterns: poder + haber dicho (could/couldn’t have said), lamentar + haber dicho (regret/sorry to have said), arrepentirse de + haber dicho (to regret having said).
target_language_example: No creo que él pueda haber dicho eso.
native_language_example: I don’t think he could have said that.

additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: haber + past participle (dicho). It’s used after modal/auxiliary verbs (deber, debería, podría, etc.) to talk about a past action that was possible, likely, or would have been better to do (often expressing speculation, regret, or criticism).
target_language_example: Podrías haber dicho algo antes de irte.
native_language_example: You could have said something before leaving.

additional_notes: Uses the perfect infinitive (haber + past participle) to talk about something someone said in the past, often with verbs/modals showing regret, doubt, or possibility (e.g., no debí/puede/no pudo/no creo). It refers back to a specific thing already mentioned: “that.”
target_language_example: Perdón por haber dicho eso; no lo pensaba en serio.
native_language_example: Sorry for having said that; I didn’t mean it seriously.

meaning: "to have done that" (to have already done it).
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive: **haber + past participle** (here, *hecho*). It’s commonly used after modal/auxiliary verbs like **deber**, **poder**, **querer**, **no poder**, etc., to talk about a past action in relation to obligation, possibility, regret, or conclusions. *Eso* means “that.”
target_language_example: Lamento haber hecho eso.
native_language_example: I regret having done that.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "nacer" (to be born). It’s used after another verb to talk about being born at an earlier time, often in phrases like "estar + adjective + de haber nacido..." (to be [adjective] about having been born...) or "alegrarse de no haber nacido..." (to be glad not to have been born...).
target_language_example: Está orgullosa de haber nacido en México.
native_language_example: She’s proud to have been born in Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past state/identity from the point of view of another time (often with verbs like lamentar, desear, parecer, or in phrases like sin haber sido...). Common patterns: (1) lamentar/dese(ar)/parecer + haber sido + adjective/noun: "Lamento haber sido grosero" = "I regret having been rude." (2) sin haber sido + past participle: "Se fue sin haber sido visto" = "He left without having been seen." It agrees with "ser" uses (adjective/noun), not "estar".
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber sido parte del equipo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have been part of the team.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past state/identity from the point of view of another time (often with verbs like lamentar, desear, parecer, or in phrases like sin haber sido...). Common patterns: (1) lamentar/dese(ar)/parecer + haber sido + adjective/noun: "Lamento haber sido grosero" = "I regret having been rude." (2) sin haber sido + past participle: "Se fue sin haber sido visto" = "He left without having been seen." It agrees with "ser" uses (adjective/noun), not "estar".
target_language_example: Me alegro de haber sido parte del equipo.
native_language_example: I'm glad to have been part of the team.

meaning: "to have had" (past action/state, often with regret or a past expectation).
additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive of *tener* (formed with *haber* + past participle *tenido*). It’s used after another verb (often a modal like *deber*, *poder*, *querer*) to talk about something that was supposed to happen, could have happened, or is assumed to have happened in the past: *Deberíamos haber tenido más cuidado* = “We should have been/had more careful”; *Debe haber tenido sus razones* = “He/She must have had their reasons”; *Quisiera haber tenido…* = “I wish I had had…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento; deberíamos haber tenido más paciencia.
native_language_example: I’m sorry; we should have had more patience.

additional_notes: Used after another verb to talk about having already come before that moment (often in regrets, thanks, or wishes): Debería/Deberías/Ojalá pudiera + haber venido. It’s the past infinitive: haber + past participle (venido).
target_language_example: Gracias por haber venido tan temprano.
native_language_example: Thanks for having come so early.

additional_notes: Used with impersonal **haber** to say that something exists or is present: **hay algo** (there is something), **debe de haber algo** (there must be something), **ha de haber algo** (there has to be something). **Haber** here does *not* mean “to have,” so don’t translate it as “to have something.”
target_language_example: Tiene que haber algo que podamos hacer para ayudar.
native_language_example: There has to be something we can do to help.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal verb **haber** to say that something exists or happens, without naming who does it. Common forms: **hay un...** (there is/are a...), **había/solía haber un...** (there used to be a...), **va a haber un...** (there is going to be a...). Note: the noun can be singular or plural (e.g., *hay un libro* / *hay unos libros*).
target_language_example: En la reunión va a haber un anuncio importante.
native_language_example: At the meeting, there’s going to be an important announcement.

meaning: 'there is/there was a' (used to say something exists).
additional_notes: Impersonal use of **haber** + a feminine singular noun (**una**). It means “there is/was a …” (not “to have”). Tense changes with context: **hay una** (there is a), **había una** (there was a/used to be a), **hubo una** (there was a—one-time event), **debería haber una** (there should be a).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad debería haber una estación de tren.
native_language_example: In this city, there should be a train station.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "hacer" (haber + lo + hecho). It talks about an action completed before another time or action. Common after phrases like "deber" (should have) and "arrepentirse de" (regret having done).
target_language_example: Lamento haberlo hecho tan tarde.
native_language_example: I’m sorry I did it so late.

additional_notes: From the verb hablar (to talk) + con (with). "Habla con…" is the tú imperative, used to tell one person you address as tú to talk to someone. For formal you, use "Hable con…"; for plural (Spain), "Hablad con…"; for you all (Latin America), "Hablen con…".
target_language_example: Habla con tu profesora después de clase.
native_language_example: Talk to your teacher after class.

additional_notes: From the verb hablar (to speak) + español (Spanish). It’s often used to say what language someone speaks. Change it depending on the subject: yo hablo español (I speak Spanish), tú hablas español (you speak Spanish), él/ella/usted habla español (he/she/you formal speak Spanish), nosotros hablamos español (we speak Spanish), ellos/ellas/ustedes hablan español (they/you all speak Spanish).
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla español y también inglés.
native_language_example: My brother speaks Spanish and also English.

additional_notes: Used to say someone speaks the French language. Often appears with an explicit subject (Ella habla francés) or implied by context. You can change the subject by changing the verb: yo hablo francés (I speak French), tú hablas francés (you speak French), él/ella habla francés (he/she speaks French), nosotros hablamos francés (we speak French).
target_language_example: Mi hermano habla francés y alemán.
native_language_example: My brother speaks French and German.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s language ability or how well they express themselves. Conjugated form of hablar for él/ella/usted (habla). You can add the language after it (habla muy bien inglés/francés) or use it alone when the context is clear.
target_language_example: ¡Hablas muy bien español!
native_language_example: You speak Spanish very well!

meaning: 'was speaking on the radio' / 'used to speak on the radio'.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (hablaba) to describe an ongoing or habitual past action. Often appears in sentences identifying someone (e.g., “Era usted/tú quien…” = “It was you who…”). “En la radio” means “on the radio” (i.e., heard via radio).
target_language_example: Pensé que tú eras quien hablaba en la radio.
native_language_example: I thought it was you who was speaking on the radio.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb (he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han) to form the present perfect: "he hablado con..." = "I have spoken with...". "Con" introduces the person you spoke to (often interchangeable with "hablar con" = "to talk to/with").
target_language_example: Ya he hablado con el doctor.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with the doctor.

additional_notes: "Hablando" is the gerund (-ing form) of "hablar" (to talk/speak). Use it often with "estar" to talk about something happening right now or in progress: "Estoy hablando con…" = "I’m talking with…". It can also describe someone/something: "La chica hablando con Jim…" = "The girl talking with Jim…". In some contexts, "hablar con + [noun]" can describe the way someone speaks: "hablando con acertijos" = "speaking in riddles."
target_language_example: Estoy hablando con mi mamá ahora.
native_language_example: I’m talking with my mom right now.

additional_notes: Used with estar to say what the conversation/topic is about: “Estamos hablando de una máquina” = “We’re talking about a machine.” It’s also common at the start of a phrase to introduce a topic or make a quick connection/segue: “Hablando de donaciones…” = “Speaking of donations…”. You can also say “Hablando de eso” = “Speaking of that.”
target_language_example: Hablando de eso, ¿ya pagaste la cuenta?
native_language_example: Speaking of that, did you already pay the bill?

additional_notes: Used with forms of estar (e.g., están/estuvo/ha estado) to say that someone is/was/has been discussing you. It can be neutral or imply gossip depending on context. The preposition de is required: hablar de alguien = to talk about someone.
target_language_example: Creo que están hablando de ti otra vez.
native_language_example: I think they’re talking about you again.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (hablando) to describe an action in progress. Often used with estar (está/estoy hablando por teléfono) or to describe someone you saw/heard doing something (lo vi/lo escuché hablando por teléfono).
target_language_example: Ahora no puedo; estoy hablando por teléfono.
native_language_example: I can't right now; I'm talking on the phone.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a conversation. Often interchangeable with "hablar de" (more common) and "hablar sobre". After "acerca de" you can use a noun ("acerca de Tom"), a pronoun ("acerca de él"), or a clause with "cómo/lo que" ("acerca de cómo ganaba dinero").
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar acerca de tu plan para mañana?
native_language_example: Can we talk about your plan for tomorrow?

meaning: to talk to him / to speak with the (male).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun or title that starts with el (e.g., el capitán, el Papa, el gobernador). Note the two common uses: (1) hablar con él (with accent) = “talk to him”; (2) hablar con el (no accent) + noun/title = “talk to the …”. Often used when asking or trying to get access to an important person.
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hablar con el doctor un momento?
native_language_example: Can I speak with the doctor for a moment?

meaning: to talk to her; to speak with her.
additional_notes: "Hablar con" means "to talk to/with." "Ella" = "she/her" (used for a female person). You can change the pronoun: hablar con él (him), hablar con usted (you, formal), hablar con ellos/ellas (them). In "voy a ir a hablar con ella," the "a" marks an action you’re going to do ("I’m going to go talk to her").
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con ella hoy.
native_language_example: I need to talk to her today.

meaning: to talk to them; to speak with them.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "hablar" (to talk/speak) + "con" (with) + "ellos" (them, masculine or mixed-gender group). Common for saying you need/want/are going to talk to a group of people: "Tengo que hablar con ellos" (I have to talk to them), "Voy a hablar con ellos" (I’m going to talk to them).
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, necesito hablar con ellos.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I need to talk to them.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person politely (e.g., a stranger, an older person, a customer, a boss). It uses the formal "usted" form; with friends or family you’d usually say "hablar contigo" or "hablar con ti" (less common). Often appears in polite phrases like "Quisiera hablar con usted" (I’d like to speak with you).
target_language_example: ¿Podría hablar con usted un momento?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you for a moment?

additional_notes: Used in voseo regions (especially Argentina, Uruguay, and parts of Central America) where “vos” replaces “tú” for informal “you.” It’s the same idea as “hablar contigo,” but with “vos” instead of “ti”/“tú.” Often appears when someone wants a conversation, sometimes a serious one: “Necesito/Tengo que hablar con vos.”
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, quiero hablar con vos un momento.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I want to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: to talk to him; to speak with him.
additional_notes: "Hablar" means "to talk/to speak" and "con" means "with." "Él" (with an accent) means "he/him". Use it when you want to talk directly to a male person. In real conversation, Spanish often uses the indirect object pronoun instead: "hablarle" or "hablarle a él" (to talk to him), especially when "a" + person is used: "Voy a hablarle" / "Voy a hablar con él."
target_language_example: Tengo que hablar con él mañana.
native_language_example: I have to talk to him tomorrow.

meaning: to talk to me; to speak with me.
additional_notes: Uses the verb hablar (to talk/speak) + conmigo (with me). Often used for requests or invitations to talk: ¿Puedes hablar conmigo? / Tengo que hablar contigo. If you’re addressing someone informally (tú), you’ll also hear hablar contigo (“talk to you”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar conmigo un momento?
native_language_example: Can you talk to me for a moment?

additional_notes: Uses the informal “you” (tú): hablar + contigo (“with you”). Common for requesting a conversation or saying it was nice talking to someone. For formal “you” (usted), use “hablar con usted”.
target_language_example: ¿Podemos hablar contigo después de clase?
native_language_example: Can we talk to you after class?

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re talking about is already known from context. It’s often used with verbs like preferir (to prefer) or with phrases like no hay necesidad de… (there’s no need to…). You’ll also see the related fixed expression "he oído hablar de ello" = "I’ve heard about it" (literally, "I’ve heard to talk about it").
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de ello ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it right now.

meaning: to talk about that; to discuss that.
additional_notes: Used when referring back to a topic already mentioned or understood from context (eso = “that”). Often appears with “no quiero / no puedo” to refuse or postpone the conversation, or with time phrases like “ahora”, “en otra ocasión”. You can also say “hablar de ello” (more formal) or replace “eso” with a specific topic: “hablar de política”.
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de eso todavía; hablemos mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about that yet; let’s talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or insist on discussing a specific topic or situation (“esto” = “this”). Common in serious or urgent conversations: “Tenemos que hablar de esto” = “We need to talk about this.” You can also soften it with “quizás” (maybe) or make it firm with “por última vez” (for the last time).
target_language_example: No quiero hablar de esto ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about this right now.

additional_notes: Used to say which language someone speaks (or is speaking) in. You can swap in another language: hablar en español / hablar en francés. After verbs like poder, saber, or querer, Spanish often uses the infinitive: Puedo hablar en inglés. Also common with adverbs like bien (well) and con fluidez (fluently): Habla bien en inglés; Habla en inglés con fluidez.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar en inglés, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak in English, please?

meaning: to speak in public; public speaking.
additional_notes: Used for giving a talk or addressing an audience (a class, a meeting, etc.). Often appears with verbs like gustar (no le gusta hablar en público), ser difícil (es difícil hablar en público), and estar acostumbrado/a a (be used to public speaking).
target_language_example: Me da miedo hablar en público, pero necesito hacerlo para la presentación.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public, but I need to do it for the presentation.

additional_notes: Use it to say you can/can’t speak French (or how well you speak it). With a language, Spanish often uses no article: "hablo francés" (not *"hablo el francés"*). "Apenas" means "hardly/barely," so "Apenas puedo hablar francés" = "I can barely speak French."
target_language_example: ¿Hablas francés?
native_language_example: Do you speak French?

additional_notes: Future tense of "hablar" (yo hablaré) + "con". Used to say you will speak with someone later, often to promise or plan to discuss something: "Lo hablaré con…" = "I’ll talk it over with…". You can also use the present for near future in Spanish: "Hablo con ella mañana."
target_language_example: Mañana hablaré con el profesor sobre la tarea.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll talk to the teacher about the homework.

meaning: “I’ll talk to him.” / “I will speak with him.”
additional_notes: Future tense of hablar (hablaré = “I will talk/speak”). Used to promise or plan to talk to a male person (él). Often implies you’ll handle something by discussing it with him; you can add details like a solas (“in private”) or luego (“later”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: hablaré con él mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll talk to him tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you are not joking and you want to be taken seriously. You can say it alone (Hablo en serio.) or add more information (Hablo en serio cuando te digo que…). With te, it means “I’m speaking to you seriously” / “I’m telling you seriously” (Te hablo en serio).
target_language_example: No estoy bromeando; hablo en serio.
native_language_example: I’m not joking; I’m serious.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *hablar* in the first-person singular present (*hablo* = “I speak/I talk”). Add details with *con* (“with”), *en* (“in/at”), frequency words like *casi todos los días* (“almost every day”), or combine languages with *e* (used instead of *y* before an *i-* sound: *francés e inglés*). *Ya hablo francés* often means “I already speak French.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hablo alemán; hablo francés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak German; I speak French.

additional_notes: Used to say you have basic ability in a language. It’s often followed by a language name: “Hablo un poco de español.” You can swap the verb form for other people: “Hablas un poco de…”, “Habla un poco de…”, “Hablamos un poco de…”.
target_language_example: Hablo un poco de italiano, pero entiendo más de lo que hablo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Italian, but I understand more than I speak.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "hablar": it means you talked to/with someone at a specific time. Use it with a person or group: "Hablé con Ana", "Hablé con ellos". For "I spoke to him/her", use the pronoun after "con": "Hablé con él/ella" (note: "él" has an accent).
target_language_example: Ayer hablé con mi jefe por teléfono.
native_language_example: Yesterday I spoke with my boss on the phone.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of hablar: hablé = “I spoke/I talked” (a completed action). con él means “with him” (él = “him/he,” with an accent to distinguish it from el = “the”). Often used with time references like la última vez (“the last time”) or cuando (“when”).
target_language_example: Ayer hablé con él por teléfono.
native_language_example: Yesterday I talked to him on the phone.

additional_notes: "Habló" is the simple past (pretérito) of "hablar" for él/ella/usted. Use "habló con + person" to say someone talked to/with someone. It can also be followed by something like "una sonrisa" to describe the manner (e.g., "spoke with a smile").
target_language_example: Ayer habló con su jefe sobre el problema.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she spoke with his/her boss about the problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone would have said in a hypothetical past situation (often with a “si…” clause). It can also express a guess about what someone probably said (“I/He would have said…”). The person is shown by the ending: yo habría dicho, tú habrías dicho, él/ella habría dicho, nosotros habríamos dicho, etc.
target_language_example: Si lo hubiera sabido, te habría dicho la verdad.
native_language_example: If I had known, I would have told you the truth.

meaning: “would have done” (conditional perfect: hypothetical past action).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone would have done in a past situation that didn’t happen or is imagined. Often appears with a condition: **Si + imperfect subjunctive** → **habría hecho** (“If…, I would have done…”). Frequently used with object pronouns: **lo/la habría hecho** = “I would have done it.”
target_language_example: Si lo hubiera sabido, lo habría hecho antes.
native_language_example: If I had known, I would have done it earlier.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of ser (haber in conditional + sido). Used for hypothetical past situations (“It would have been…”), and also for making guesses/speculation about the past (“Yesterday would have been his birthday” = presumably/it would have been).
target_language_example: Sin tu ayuda, habría sido imposible.
native_language_example: Without your help, it would have been impossible.

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive of "decir" (haber + participle: dicho) with attached pronouns: me (to me) + lo (it). Common after verbs like deber/poder in sentences such as "Deberías/Podrías habérmelo dicho" = "You should/could have told me (it)." The accent in "habérmelo" marks the stress when pronouns are attached.
target_language_example: ¡Podrías habérmelo dicho antes!
native_language_example: You could have told me earlier!

additional_notes: This is the perfect infinitive of "decir" with pronouns attached: haber + te (to you) + lo (it/that) + dicho (told). It’s commonly used after expressions like "debería", "debí", "tendría que", "podría", etc. to talk about something you should/could have told someone in the past (often implying regret).
target_language_example: Lo siento, debería habértelo dicho ayer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I should have told you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was bought before another past moment/event. Often appears with time expressions like "la semana anterior", "el día antes", or in patterns like "Para cuando llegué, ya había comprado...". You’ll also see it with object pronouns ("lo había comprado" = "I/he/she had bought it") and in relative clauses ("el reloj que había comprado" = "the watch that (I/he/she) had bought").
target_language_example: Cuando empezó la reunión, ya había comprado los boletos.
native_language_example: When the meeting started, I had already bought the tickets.

additional_notes: Formed with the imperfect of haber (había) + past participle (dado) to talk about something that happened before another past event. Often followed by an object: me/te/le había dado (I/you/he had given). Also appears inside common expressions like “me había dado cuenta” (I had realized) and “había dado a luz” (had given birth).
target_language_example: No me había dado cuenta de que ya te lo había dado.
native_language_example: I hadn’t realized that I had already given it to you.

additional_notes: This is part of the verb phrase **darse cuenta (de)** = “to realize / to notice.” **Había dado cuenta** is the **past perfect** ("had realized") and usually appears with a reflexive pronoun: **me/te/se/nos/os había dado cuenta**. It often takes **de** + noun or **de que** + clause: *No me había dado cuenta de eso* / *No me había dado cuenta de que era tarde*. You may also hear it alone: *No me había dado cuenta.*
target_language_example: Lo siento, no me había dado cuenta de que estabas esperando.
native_language_example: Sorry, I hadn’t realized you were waiting.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (había + past participle) to talk about something that happened before another past moment. With objects/places it usually means “had left (something somewhere)” or “had left (a person).” With “de” it often means “had stopped/quit” (e.g., había dejado de fumar = had quit smoking). With the reflexive form “se había dejado,” it commonly means “had forgotten/left behind” something (especially at home, on the train, etc.).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, me di cuenta de que había dejado las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I realized I had left the keys at home.

meaning: “had said / had told” (past perfect of decir).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something someone said earlier than another past moment (e.g., “I thought you had told me…”). It’s built with imperfect haber (había) + past participle (dicho). Often followed by que + clause (había dicho que…), and it frequently includes an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les había dicho (“had told me/you/him-her…”).
target_language_example: Ya te había dicho que no podía ir.
native_language_example: I had already told you that I couldn’t go.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (*haber* in imperfect + past participle) to talk about an expectation that happened before another past moment. Very common in comparisons with **más/menos... de lo que había esperado** (“more/less... than I had expected”). Subject comes from context: **yo había esperado** = “I had expected”; **no había esperado mucho** = “I hadn’t waited long / I didn’t expect much” depending on context (because *esperar* can mean “to expect” or “to wait for”).
target_language_example: La reunión fue más larga de lo que había esperado.
native_language_example: The meeting was longer than I had expected.

meaning: 'had been' (past perfect of estar), often used for earlier states or ongoing actions before another past moment.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive auxiliary "había" + past participle "estado". It forms the past perfect with estar: "había estado" = "had been". Use it to talk about something that started before and was already true/going on prior to another event in the past (often with "cuando..."). With a gerund it forms the past perfect continuous: "había estado leyendo/trabajando" = "had been reading/working". Also common with adjectives: "había estado enferma" (had been sick), "había estado asustado" (had been scared).
target_language_example: Yo ya había estado aquí antes de mudarme.
native_language_example: I had already been here before I moved.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of *hacer*: **había** (imperfect of *haber*) + **hecho** (past participle). Used to talk about something completed **before** another moment in the past (often when telling a story or explaining a past feeling/reaction). *Hecho* doesn’t change for gender/number here.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya había hecho la cena.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I had already made dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened before another past moment. Often appears in reported speech (e.g., "me dijo que...") or when explaining earlier past events. With "se" ("se había ido"), it commonly means "had left" / "was gone."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ella ya había ido al supermercado.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she had already gone to the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone died before another past moment or action. It’s common in reported speech (Ella dijo que…) and with time markers like “cuando” (Ya había muerto cuando llegué = he/she was already dead when I arrived). Agree for gender/number: había muerto (he/it), había muerta (she, less common but possible as an adjective), habían muerto (they).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos al hospital, el abuelo ya había muerto.
native_language_example: When we got to the hospital, Grandpa had already died.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of olvidar: it talks about something that was already forgotten before another moment in the past. Often used with "(me/te/se/nos) había olvidado" and "de" (to forget about something/someone): "Me había olvidado de él." You may also hear "se me había olvidado" (literally “it had slipped my mind”), which is very common in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué al aeropuerto, me di cuenta de que había olvidado mi pasaporte.
native_language_example: When I got to the airport, I realized I had forgotten my passport.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (haber + past participle) to talk about something that was heard before another past moment or event. Often appears with "ya" (already) or "hasta que" (until) to show sequence in the past. The participle is "oído" (from "oír"), and the person changes: yo había oído, tú habías oído, él/ella había oído, nosotros habíamos oído, etc.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya había oído la noticia.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I had already heard the news.

additional_notes: Past perfect: había + pasado, used to talk about something that happened before another past moment (e.g., “I wondered what had happened”). Depending on context, pasar can mean “to happen” (¿Qué te había pasado?), “to go by/stop by” (había pasado por la oficina), “to go through/spend time” (dónde había pasado el fin de semana), or “to slip one’s mind” in se me había pasado (“I completely forgot”).
target_language_example: No sabía qué había pasado cuando llegué.
native_language_example: I didn’t know what had happened when I arrived.

additional_notes: Past perfect of pensar (to think): haber (había) + past participle (pensado). Used to talk about a thought that happened before another past moment. Very common with "nunca" + "en" to mean "I had never thought about (it/that)": "Nunca había pensado en eso."
target_language_example: No había pensado en llamarte ayer, pero se me hizo tarde.
native_language_example: I hadn’t thought about calling you yesterday, but it got late.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluperfect) of perder (“to lose”): había (imperfect of haber) + perdido (past participle). Used to talk about something that happened before another past event, often in relative clauses like “que había perdido” (“that [someone] had lost”). Person/number can change: yo había perdido, ella había perdido, nosotros habíamos perdido, etc.
target_language_example: Por fin encontré el documento que había perdido ayer.
native_language_example: I finally found the document I had lost yesterday.

meaning: 'had left / had gone out'; also 'had turned out' (with bien/mal).
additional_notes: This is the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): haber (imperfect) + past participle. It describes something that happened before another past action (often with cuando/apenas: "as soon as..."). With results, you’ll often see it with an adverb like bien/mal: "La obra había salido muy bien" = "The play/performance had turned out very well."
target_language_example: Cuando llegaste, yo ya había salido.
native_language_example: When you arrived, I had already left.

meaning: “had been” (past perfect of ser); often used to form the passive: “had been + past participle.”
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (escrito, destruida, robado, abolido, arrestada) to say something was already done before another past moment: había sido + participle = “had been (done).” It agrees in gender/number when used in the passive (había sido destruida / habían sido destruidas).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, el puente ya había sido cerrado.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the bridge had already been closed.
