meaning: “had been” (past perfect of ser); often used to form the passive: “had been + past participle.”
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (escrito, destruida, robado, abolido, arrestada) to say something was already done before another past moment: había sido + participle = “had been (done).” It agrees in gender/number when used in the passive (había sido destruida / habían sido destruidas).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, el puente ya había sido cerrado.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the bridge had already been closed.

additional_notes: Past perfect: haber (imperfect) + past participle. "Había terminado" says something was already finished before another past event (often with "cuando"). Used for events ending: a battle, class, meeting, show, etc. You can replace "terminado" with other participles (había llegado, había comido).
target_language_example: Cuando llamaste, la película ya había terminado.
native_language_example: When you called, the movie had already ended.

additional_notes: Past perfect of ver: haber (había) + past participle (visto). Used to talk about something you saw before another moment in the past (often implied or mentioned). Example: Cuando llegué, ya lo había visto = "When I arrived, I had already seen it." You can use object pronouns before the verb: lo/la había visto (I had seen him/it/her), te había visto (I had seen you). In some regions you may hear le había visto for a male person (leísmo).
target_language_example: Ya había visto esa película antes de conocer a mi pareja.
native_language_example: I had already seen that movie before I met my partner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about seeing a person earlier than another past moment (“already had seen”). Often appears in reported speech (e.g., “dijo que…”). The “a” is the personal a: it goes before a direct object that is a person or pet (había visto a María / la había visto a ella).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya había visto a Carlos esa mañana.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I had already seen Carlos that morning.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (haber in imperfect: había + past participle: visto) to say you had seen someone/something earlier than another past moment. Often appears with negatives like nunca/jamás: “Nunca/Jamás lo/la/los/las había visto antes” = “I had never seen him/her/them before.” The pronoun (lo/la/los/las) can change depending on what you saw.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a la ciudad, ya había visto ese edificio antes.
native_language_example: When I arrived in the city, I had already seen that building before.

meaning: 'had ever seen in my life' (usually: 'I had never seen ... in my life').
additional_notes: Commonly used with a negative (No/Nunca) to emphasize that something has never happened before: “No/Nunca lo/la/le había visto en mi vida.” Uses the past perfect (había visto) to mean “had seen” relative to another past moment, often translated naturally as “I had never seen … before” or “I’d never seen … in my life.” The pronoun changes with what you’re talking about: lo (him/it, masculine), la (her/it, feminine), le (him/her as an indirect object, used in some regions).
target_language_example: Nunca había visto tanta gente en mi vida.
native_language_example: I had never seen so many people in my life.

additional_notes: This is the pluperfect tense (había visto = “had seen”) used with nunca (“never”). In real usage it’s almost always with negation: no había visto nunca… = “I/He/She had never seen…”. Word order can vary: no había visto nunca / nunca había visto. The ending changes with the subject: había (I/he/she) vs. habías (you) vs. habían (they).
target_language_example: No había visto nunca una casa tan grande.
native_language_example: I had never seen a house that big.

additional_notes: Used to describe a crowded situation in the past. "Había" is the imperfect of "haber" used to mean "there was/there were" (it doesn’t agree with plural), and "mucha gente" is singular in Spanish even though it refers to many people. Common with places or events: "Había mucha gente en..."
target_language_example: Ayer en el centro había mucha gente.
native_language_example: Yesterday downtown there were a lot of people.

additional_notes: Used to say that something existed or was present in the past. It’s the imperfect past of "hay" (there is/are): "había" + a masculine singular noun ("un"). For feminine nouns, use "había una"; for plural, "había" + "unos/unas" or just the plural noun (e.g., "había dos cines").
target_language_example: En la mesa había un libro abierto.
native_language_example: There was an open book on the table.

meaning: "there was a" (referring to a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb haber (imperfect: había) to say something existed or was present in the past. Common for setting the scene/background or describing what was there. Because it uses "una," it must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., una lluvia, una mezquita, una niebla). For masculine nouns, use "había un"; for plural, "había" + "unos/unas".
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, había una tienda abierta cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was an open shop near the station.

meaning: "Once upon a time, there was a…"
additional_notes: A classic opening for fairy tales and stories. It uses the impersonal form "había" (there was/there were) + "una vez" (once) + a noun with an article (often "un"/"una"). You can change the last word for gender/number: "había una vez una princesa…", "había una vez unos niños…".
target_language_example: Había una vez un gato que quería volar.
native_language_example: Once upon a time, there was a cat who wanted to fly.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluperfect) of decir: habías dicho = “you had said” (informal singular tú). Used to refer back to something someone said earlier, often to remind them or point out a contradiction: “Creía que habías dicho que…”, “No me habías dicho que…”. You can swap the subject pronoun depending on context (e.g., Tú habías dicho que…).
target_language_example: Pensé que habías dicho que no podías venir hoy.
native_language_example: I thought you had said you couldn’t come today.

meaning: “you had gone” / “you had been” (past perfect, tú form).
additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): **haber (imperfect)** + **past participle**. Here it’s **tú habías** + **ido** (from *ir*). Used to talk about something that happened **before** another past moment/event. Often with **ya** (“already”): *ya te habías ido* = “you had already left.” With places, it can mean either “had gone” or “had been,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando llamé, ya habías ido al banco.
native_language_example: When I called, you had already gone to the bank.

meaning: The weather is nice / it’s good weather.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "hacer" to talk about weather in general (not that someone ‘does’ something). It’s often said on its own ("Hace buen tiempo.") or in conditions: "Si mañana hace buen tiempo..." = "If the weather is nice tomorrow..." Similar to "hace mal tiempo" (bad weather).
target_language_example: Vamos a caminar; hace buen tiempo.
native_language_example: Let’s go for a walk; the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the temperature, especially the weather or how a place feels. Spanish often uses “hacer” (“to make/do”) in weather expressions: hace calor (it’s hot), hace frío (it’s cold). You can add time phrases: Hoy hace calor (It’s hot today), En verano hace calor (It’s hot in summer).
target_language_example: Hoy hace mucho calor, mejor nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: It’s very hot today; it’s better we stay home.

meaning: five years ago; five years ago (for)
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say how long ago something happened: "Me gradué hace cinco años" = "I graduated five years ago." It can also start a sentence: "Hace cinco años, ...". You can swap the number: "hace dos años" (two years ago), "hace diez años" (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace cinco años.
native_language_example: I started this job five years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how much time has passed since an event or since a situation started. Structure: Hace + time period + que + present tense (if the situation continues) or past tense (if it ended). Example: Hace cinco años que no tengo noticias de él = “I haven’t heard from him in five years.” You can also use it with “Hoy” to mark an anniversary: Hoy hace cinco años que… = “Today marks five years since…”.
target_language_example: Hace cinco años que vivo en esta ciudad.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in this city for five years.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Pattern: "hace + time period" (hace un día, hace dos semanas, hace muchos años). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence, and it can also be used alone as a short answer to "¿Cuándo...?"
target_language_example: Terminé la universidad hace cuatro años.
native_language_example: I finished university four years ago.

meaning: ten years ago (ten years ago from now / from the time being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how long ago something happened. It’s built from "hace" (it has been/makes) + a time period. Very common pattern: "hace + [time]" (hace dos días, hace un mes, hace mucho tiempo). In some regions people also say "hace diez años atrás"—it means the same, but "hace diez años" is enough.
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace diez años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Pattern: "hace + time period" (hace un minuto / hace dos horas / hace tres días). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Hace diez minutos salió" / "Salió hace diez minutos". You can also say it alone as a short answer to "¿Cuándo?".
target_language_example: Llegué hace diez minutos.
native_language_example: I arrived ten minutes ago.

additional_notes: Used in time expressions with a period of time after it: "hace dos días" (two days ago), "hace dos semanas" (two weeks ago), "hace dos años" (two years ago). It often appears with "hace" + number (+ optional "o tres", etc.) + time unit. Sometimes you may also hear "hace dos años atrás"; "hace dos años" already means "two years ago," so "atrás" is redundant.
target_language_example: Llegué hace dos horas.
native_language_example: I arrived two hours ago.

meaning: two years ago; two years ago/from now (when talking about how long ago something happened).
additional_notes: Used to talk about time elapsed since a past event: "hace + time period" = "... ago" (e.g., hace una semana, hace tres meses). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence. With duration, Spanish typically says "Hace dos años que..." or "Desde hace dos años..." (e.g., "Hace dos años que están casados" = "They’ve been married for two years").
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace dos años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish two years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past action to say how long ago it happened: Hace + time period (hace dos días, hace una semana, hace un año). You can also see the pattern “Hace dos días que + present tense” to mean “It’s been two days since…” (duration up to now): Hace dos días que está ahí. In some regions people add “atrás” (hace dos días atrás), but “hace dos días” is enough and more standard.
target_language_example: Lo vi hace dos días.
native_language_example: I saw him two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. In Spanish you often use **hace + time period** to mean “... ago”: *hace cinco minutos* (five minutes ago), *hace un año* (a year ago). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Llegué hace dos horas, pero todavía estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I arrived two hours ago, but I’m still tired.

meaning: two weeks ago; two weeks ago (it has been two weeks).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a point in the past: "hace + time period" = "... ago" (e.g., hace dos semanas = two weeks ago). You can also use it with "que" to mean "it’s been ... since" something happened: "Hace dos semanas que llegué" = "I arrived two weeks ago / It’s been two weeks since I arrived."
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace dos semanas.
native_language_example: I started this job two weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used with the verb hacer to describe the weather: hace frío = it’s cold. You can add time/place: Aquí hace frío. / Hoy hace frío. Negation: No hace frío. Emphasis: Sí que hace frío = It really is cold.
target_language_example: En la montaña hace frío por la noche.
native_language_example: In the mountains it’s cold at night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acts however they like, without following rules or other people’s advice. You can change the subject and the verb: yo hago lo que quiero (I do whatever I want), tú haces lo que quieres, ellos hacen lo que quieren. Often implies criticism or annoyance, especially with "siempre" (always).
target_language_example: Mi hermano siempre hace lo que quiere y nunca escucha a nadie.
native_language_example: My brother always does whatever he wants and never listens to anyone.

additional_notes: Used with "hace + time" to say how long ago something happened. It refers to a point in the past (not a duration), and often goes at the end of the sentence: "Llegó hace media hora." It can also be used alone as a short answer to "¿Cuándo?".
target_language_example: Llegaron hace media hora, pero todavía no han llamado.
native_language_example: They arrived half an hour ago, but they still haven’t called.

meaning: "It’s been a long time since (I/we/etc.)…" / "Not in a long time."
additional_notes: Used to say you haven’t done something for a long time. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the present tense (e.g., "Hace mucho que no como…" = "I haven’t eaten… in a long time"). It can also be used alone: "Hace mucho que no." = "Not in a long time."
target_language_example: Hace mucho que no hablo con mis abuelos.
native_language_example: I haven’t talked to my grandparents in a long time.

meaning: “a lot” (often after hacer: “does a lot / is very…”).
additional_notes: Common with **hacer** to mean a large amount or high intensity: **hacer mucho + noun** (“to do a lot of [something]”), **hacer mucho + noun (weather)** (“it’s very windy/hot/cold”), and **hacer mucho + noun** in general (“to cause a lot of damage”). Often used with **más**: **no hace mucho más** = “doesn’t do much else.” (Not the same as **hace mucho** meaning “a long time ago,” which uses a time expression: *Hace mucho que…* / *Hace mucho tiempo*.)
target_language_example: Aquí hace mucho calor en verano.
native_language_example: It’s very hot here in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather. Spanish often uses **hacer** (“to make/do”) to describe weather conditions: **hace calor** = “it’s hot,” **hace frío** = “it’s cold.” **mucho** intensifies it (“very/a lot”). You can add time or place: **hace mucho calor hoy** (today), **en verano** (in summer), **en Japón** (in Japan).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad hace mucho calor en agosto.
native_language_example: In this city it’s very hot in August.

meaning: a long time ago; (it’s been) a long time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past, or to emphasize that a lot of time has passed. Often appears at the start of a sentence (Hace mucho tiempo visité París) or after a time reference (Hace mucho tiempo de eso). By itself (¡Hace mucho tiempo!) it means “It’s been a long time!”
target_language_example: No nos vemos hace mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

meaning: "It’s been a long time since (I/we) last…"
additional_notes: Used to say that something hasn’t happened for a long time. It’s usually followed by a verb (often in the present or imperfect, depending on context): Hace mucho tiempo que no lo veo. / Hace mucho tiempo que no estábamos tan cerca. Similar idea to "Hace mucho que no…"; adding "tiempo" just makes it more explicit.
target_language_example: Hace mucho tiempo que no vamos al cine.
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since we last went to the movies.

meaning: many years ago; for many years (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long ago something happened or how long something has been true. Common patterns: (1) "[Verb] hace muchos años" = "[verb] many years ago" (e.g., Desapareció hace muchos años). (2) "Hace muchos años que + [present]" = "I have been + -ing for many years / It’s been many years since..." (e.g., Hace muchos años que quiero ir...).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos hace muchos años.
native_language_example: We met many years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Pattern: "hace + time period" (e.g., hace un día, hace dos meses, hace seis años). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence: "Hace seis años tomaste..." / "...hace seis años."
target_language_example: Me mudé aquí hace seis años.
native_language_example: I moved here six years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built with hace + a time period (hace dos días, hace un año). You can use it on its own as a short answer (—¿Cuándo? —Hace seis meses.)
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace seis meses.
native_language_example: I started this job six months ago.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "hacer" + "sentir". It’s used to say that something causes an emotion or feeling in someone: "X me/te/le hace sentir + adjective" (makes me/you/him/her feel + adjective) or "hace sentir + noun" (makes someone feel something). Often followed by an adjective like "poderoso", "mal", "inseguro".
target_language_example: Ese comentario me hace sentir nervioso.
native_language_example: That comment makes me feel nervous.

additional_notes: From "hacer" (to make) + "sentir" (to feel) + "mejor" (better). Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les hace sentir mejor" = "it makes me/you/him-her/ us/them feel better." Very common in the phrase "Si te hace sentir mejor..." meaning "If it makes you feel better..." (sometimes said with a slightly dismissive or reassuring tone, depending on context).
target_language_example: Si te hace sentir mejor, puedo llamarte cuando llegue a casa.
native_language_example: If it makes you feel better, I can call you when I get home.

meaning: “It’s been a long time since…” (I haven’t … for a long time).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened for a long time. It’s often followed by a verb (usually in the present: “hace tiempo que no + [present]”, or in the past: “hace tiempo que no + [imperfect/pluperfect]” depending on context). It can also stand alone as a short reply: “Hace tiempo que no.” = “Not in a long time.”
target_language_example: Hace tiempo que no veo a mis amigos.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen my friends in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It uses "hace + time period" (literally "it makes/does + time"), often placed at the end of the sentence: "Llegué hace tres años." You can change the number/time unit: "hace dos días" (two days ago), "hace un mes" (a month ago), "hace mucho tiempo" (a long time ago).
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace tres años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish three years ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. Spanish uses “hace + time period” for “ago”: hace tres días, hace una semana, hace dos años. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (Hace tres días ocurrió eso / Eso ocurrió hace tres días). You may also see “Hace tres días que + present tense” to mean “It’s been three days since…”
target_language_example: Llegué a Madrid hace tres días.
native_language_example: I arrived in Madrid three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often comes at the end of the sentence (Lo vi hace tres horas.) but can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis (Hace tres horas, cayó un asteroide...). You can swap in other time amounts: hace dos días (two days ago), hace un minuto (a minute ago).
target_language_example: Salí de casa hace tres horas.
native_language_example: I left home three hours ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often goes with the past tense: "Se casaron hace tres meses". You may also hear "hace tres meses atrás" (redundant but common in some regions); "hace tres meses" is enough. Pattern: "hace + time period" (e.g., hace dos días, hace un año).
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace tres meses.
native_language_example: I started this job three months ago.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say how long ago something happened: "hace un rato" (a little while ago), "hace un mes" (a month ago). In some varieties of Spanish (especially in Latin America), "hace un + noun" can describe the weather: "Hace un clima pésimo" = "The weather is awful."
target_language_example: Hace un minuto te llamé, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: I called you a minute ago, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It often appears with the imperfect or preterite (e.g., fue, sucedió, murió). You can swap in other time amounts: hace dos años (two years ago), hace un mes (a month ago), hace una semana (a week ago).
target_language_example: Me mudé aquí hace un año.
native_language_example: I moved here a year ago.

meaning: a month ago; for a month (up to now).
additional_notes: With a completed past action, it means “a month ago”: “Eso fue hace un mes.” With an action/state that continues to the present, Spanish often uses “desde hace un mes” to mean “for a month (now)”: “Está en el hospital desde hace un mes.” (In casual speech you may still hear “Está … hace un mes,” but “desde hace” is the standard form.)
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace un mes.
native_language_example: I started this job a month ago.

meaning: a moment ago; just a moment ago.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a very short time before now. It commonly appears with the pattern "hace + time period" (e.g., hace dos días = two days ago). You can place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Te llamé hace un momento.
native_language_example: I called you a moment ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened some time in the past (roughly two years, often meaning “a few years” loosely). Commonly goes at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Hace un par de años, …” / “…, hace un par de años.”
target_language_example: Nos mudamos aquí hace un par de años.
native_language_example: We moved here a couple of years ago.

meaning: a little while ago; not long ago.
additional_notes: Used with expressions of time to say something happened recently in the past. Often used with the simple past (pretérito): "Se fue hace un rato" = "He/She left a little while ago." By itself ("Hace un rato."), it’s a short answer meaning “A little while ago.”
target_language_example: Llegué hace un rato, pero todavía no he comido.
native_language_example: I arrived a little while ago, but I still haven’t eaten.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It goes after the verb or at the end of the sentence: "Llamó hace una hora" (He called an hour ago). With other time amounts, you can swap the unit: "hace dos horas" (two hours ago), "hace un minuto" (a minute ago).
target_language_example: Salí de casa hace una hora.
native_language_example: I left home an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used with "hace + time period" to say how long ago something happened: "hace una semana" = "one week ago." It can also appear in "hace una semana que..." meaning "it’s been a week since..." (e.g., "Hoy hace una semana que la vi" = "Today it’s been a week since I saw her").
target_language_example: Empecé este trabajo hace una semana.
native_language_example: I started this job a week ago.

meaning: "about ... ago" (for an approximate amount of time in the past).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say roughly how long ago something happened: "hace unos + número + (días/meses/años...)". It commonly corresponds to English "about" or "around". Often appears as "hace unos años" (a few years ago) or "hace unos tres días" (about three days ago). Sometimes you may hear it with "atrás" ("hace unos años atrás"), but "hace unos años" already means "years ago".
target_language_example: La conocí hace unos seis meses.
native_language_example: I met her about six months ago.

additional_notes: Used with past events to say how long ago something happened. "Hace" + time period works like "ago" in English (e.g., hace dos años = two years ago). Often placed at the end of the sentence: "Lo compramos hace unos años."
target_language_example: Empecé a estudiar español hace unos años.
native_language_example: I started studying Spanish a few years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened (counting back from now). It often goes at the end of the sentence: “Lo vi hace unos días.” You can also put it at the beginning for emphasis: “Hace unos días, lo vi.”
target_language_example: Hablé con ella hace unos días.
native_language_example: I talked to her a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used with past actions to say how long ago something happened: "hace" + time period. "Unos" here means “about/around” (an approximate amount), so it’s not an exact number of minutes. Often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can appear earlier too.
target_language_example: Llegamos hace unos minutos.
native_language_example: We arrived a few minutes ago.

meaning: twenty years ago; for twenty years (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Hace + time" expresses time relative to now. With a completed past event, it means "... ago" (El Muro cayó hace veinte años = The Wall fell twenty years ago). With an action/state that started in the past and continues to the present (often with present tense), it means "for ..." (Lo conozco hace veinte años = I’ve known him for twenty years).
target_language_example: Vivo aquí hace veinte años.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for twenty years.

meaning: to do about it (to deal with the situation).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like saber/no saber, poder, or pensar to talk about what action someone can take regarding a problem or situation. Very common in the pattern “(no) hay nada que puedas hacer al respecto” = “there’s (nothing) you can do about it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no hay nada que pueda hacer al respecto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but there’s nothing I can do about it.

meaning: to do something; to make/do an action.
additional_notes: A very common, general phrase used when the specific action isn’t stated (or isn’t important). It can be followed by more details: hacer algo por alguien (do something for someone), hacer algo más (do something more).
target_language_example: Si tienes tiempo, ¿puedes hacer algo para ayudarme?
native_language_example: If you have time, can you do something to help me?

additional_notes: Used to say you will take action to fix or deal with a problem or situation. Very common with obligation or future forms like “tener que” (have to), “deber” (must), “ir a” (going to), or “pensar” (plan to). “Al respecto” refers back to what was just mentioned (about that matter).
target_language_example: Hay muchas quejas, y la empresa tiene que hacer algo al respecto.
native_language_example: There are many complaints, and the company has to do something about it.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (is needed/wanted).
additional_notes: Means there’s no limit on what someone can do. Often followed by “por + alguien” to mean “do anything for someone” (Estoy preparado para hacer cualquier cosa por ti). You can also add a clause with “que” to mean “whatever you want”: “hacer cualquier cosa que quieras”. In negative sentences it can mean “do anything at all” (no puedes hacer cualquier cosa).
target_language_example: Si quieres, puedo hacer cualquier cosa para ayudarte.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do anything to help you.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase for doing physical activity for fitness/health. You can use it generally (Hago ejercicio) or with frequency words like regularmente/a diario (regularly/daily). Often appears with advice or obligation: Deberías / Debo / Tienes que hacer ejercicio. You can add a place or manner: hacer ejercicio afuera (outside), hacer ejercicio en el gimnasio (at the gym).
target_language_example: Intento hacer ejercicio tres veces por semana.
native_language_example: I try to work out three times a week.

meaning: to do good (to do what is right/helpful).
additional_notes: Means acting in a morally good way or helping others. It’s often used in general statements about values or ethics (e.g., “We should do good”). Don’t confuse with “hacerlo bien” = “to do it well” (do something correctly).
target_language_example: Ella siempre intenta hacer el bien, incluso cuando nadie la ve.
native_language_example: She always tries to do good, even when no one is watching her.

meaning: to do the job/work (complete the task).
additional_notes: Used for carrying out or completing a specific task or piece of work. Often appears with "me fue/resultó imposible" + infinitive ("it was impossible for me to...") or with someone "dispuesto a" + infinitive ("willing/ready to...").
target_language_example: Si quieres, yo puedo hacer el trabajo esta tarde.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do the work this afternoon.

meaning: all you/we can do is wait.
additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like: “Lo único que podemos hacer es esperar” (The only thing we can do is wait) or “Todo lo que tenemos que hacer es esperar” (All we have to do is wait). It’s used when there’s nothing else to do right now except be patient and wait for something to happen.
target_language_example: Lo único que podemos hacer ahora es esperar.
native_language_example: The only thing we can do now is wait.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific action already mentioned or understood from context. It often appears after verbs like poder (can), saber (know how), and deber (should): puedo hacer eso = I can do that; no sé cómo hacer eso = I don’t know how to do that. In questions, add cómo: ¿Cómo hago eso? = How do I do that?
target_language_example: No puedo hacer eso ahora; estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: I can't do that now; I'm busy.

additional_notes: Uses hacer + esto to refer to performing a specific action mentioned or implied in context. Often used with modal verbs or expressions like poder (can), deber (must), tener que (have to), or gracias por (thanks for): No puedes hacer esto; Todo el mundo debe hacer esto; Gracias por hacer esto. In many cases English uses “do,” while Spanish uses hacer.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hacer esto por mí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you do this for me, please?

additional_notes: Used with a person (often with an indirect object pronoun like me/te/le/nos/les): “hacer feliz a alguien.” For emphasis you can add “a + name/person”: “hacer feliz a Mary.” In past/future you conjugate hacer: “hizo feliz a…”, “va a hacer feliz a…”, “hará feliz a…”.
target_language_example: Quiero hacer feliz a mi familia.
native_language_example: I want to make my family happy.

additional_notes: A general way to talk about actions or tasks without naming them specifically. Often used with adverbs like mejor (better), bien (well), or rápido (quickly).
target_language_example: Tenemos que hacer las cosas con calma.
native_language_example: We have to do things calmly.

additional_notes: Used to say someone should repeat an action or behave in the same way as another person or situation. Often followed by "que" + a person/pronoun: "hacer lo mismo que yo" (do the same as me). Very common with advice or recommendations: "deberías hacer lo mismo" (you should do the same).
target_language_example: Si yo llevo paraguas, tú deberías hacer lo mismo.
native_language_example: If I bring an umbrella, you should do the same.

meaning: to do what (…); to do whatever (…).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to say what action someone does. With the subjunctive (e.g., "haga", "quiera"), it often means "whatever" (freedom/permission or no matter what). It can also appear with an implied verb: "hacer lo que tenía que hacerse" = "do what had to be done."
target_language_example: Haz lo que te dije, por favor.
native_language_example: Do what I told you, please.

meaning: to do what (…); to do whatever (…).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to say what action someone does. With the subjunctive (e.g., "haga", "quiera"), it often means "whatever" (freedom/permission or no matter what). It can also appear with an implied verb: "hacer lo que tenía que hacerse" = "do what had to be done."
target_language_example: Haz lo que te dije, por favor.
native_language_example: Do what I told you, please.

meaning: to do my job / to do my work.
additional_notes: Used when you mean doing your responsibilities or tasks (at a job or in a role). Often said to ask someone not to interfere: “Déjame hacer mi trabajo” (Let me do my job). You can swap the possessive to match the person: hacer tu trabajo (your), hacer su trabajo (his/her/their/your formal), hacer nuestro trabajo (our).
target_language_example: Por favor, déjame hacer mi trabajo en paz.
native_language_example: Please, let me do my job in peace.

meaning: to do anything / to do nothing (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with negatives (no, nunca) it means “to do anything” in English: “No puedo hacer nada” = “I can’t do anything.” Without a negative, it usually means “to do nothing”: “No quiero hacer nada” = “I don’t want to do anything / I want to do nothing” (often interchangeable in English). Common in the phrase “No se puede hacer nada” = “There’s nothing you can do (about it).” You can add “por” or “para” to show who you’re helping: “No puedo hacer nada por ti” = “I can’t do anything for you.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora mismo no puedo hacer nada.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do anything right now.

meaning: to do anything about it; to do something about it (usually in the negative: “can’t do anything about it”).
additional_notes: Very often used with a negative (no, no se puede, no podía, etc.): “No puedo hacer nada al respecto” = “I can’t do anything about it.” "Al respecto" means “about it / regarding that.” You can also say “hacer algo al respecto” for “do something about it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no puedo hacer nada al respecto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I can’t do anything about it.

meaning: to make a deal; to reach an agreement.
additional_notes: Used when two people/groups agree on terms, often involving an exchange (money, services, promises). Very common in everyday situations and business. Also used in offers: "¿Hacemos un trato?" = "Deal? / Do we have a deal?"
target_language_example: Si me ayudas hoy, mañana te ayudo yo: hacemos un trato.
native_language_example: If you help me today, I’ll help you tomorrow: we have a deal.

meaning: to do/make a (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to talk about doing an action or making/creating something: hacer una pregunta (ask a question), hacer una declaración (make a statement), hacer una traducción (do a translation), hacer una torta (make a cake). If the noun is masculine, use "hacer un" instead.
target_language_example: Tengo que hacer una reserva para mañana.
native_language_example: I have to make a reservation for tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common everyday way to talk about placing a phone call. It often appears with phrases like "Necesito..." (I need to...), "Déjame..." (Let me...), and can be modified: "hacer una llamada urgente" (make an urgent call).
target_language_example: Voy a salir un momento para hacer una llamada.
native_language_example: I’m going to step out for a moment to make a call.

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to introduce a question. Conjugate "hacer" to match the subject (quiero hacer, quisiera hacer, me gustaría hacer). You can also add an indirect object: "Te/le/les quiero hacer una pregunta" = "I want to ask you (informal/formal/them) a question."
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿puedo hacer una pregunta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a question?

additional_notes: "Hacerle" = "hacer" (to do/make) + "le" (to you/him/her, formal/indirect object), but in this fixed expression it’s commonly used to mean "to ask" questions. Very common in polite situations (interviews, customer service, talking to a stranger). You can swap "le" for another pronoun: "hacerte" (ask you, informal), "hacerles" (ask you all/them), or replace "algunas" with "unas" (some) or "varias" (several).
target_language_example: Antes de ayudarle, necesito hacerle algunas preguntas.
native_language_example: Before helping you, I need to ask you some questions.

additional_notes: "Hacer" (to do/make) is commonly used with "una pregunta" to mean "ask a question." The "-le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him/her/you (formal)," so the full idea is "to ask a question to someone." You can change it: "hacerme una pregunta" (ask me), "hacerte" (ask you), "hacerles" (ask them/you all). Often used in polite requests like "¿Puedo/Quisiera hacerle una pregunta?"
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿puedo hacerle una pregunta?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I ask you a question?

meaning: to ask you/him/her a few questions.
additional_notes: "Hacerle" includes the indirect object pronoun "le" (= to you / to him / to her, formal or third person). It’s a polite, common way to introduce questions, often with phrases like "Me gustaría / Necesito / Quiero / Quisiera hacerle unas preguntas". Add the person with "a + name": "hacerle unas preguntas a Tom". You can change "le" to fit: "hacerte" (to ask you, informal), "hacerles" (to ask you all / them).
target_language_example: Perdón, ¿puedo hacerle unas preguntas?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask you a few questions?

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Used when you need to question someone briefly. It’s built from hacer (to do/make) + te (to you) + algunas (some/a few) + preguntas (questions), but the natural translation is “to ask you a few questions.” You’ll often see it with necesitar/tener que/querer (need/have to/want) + hacerte algunas preguntas.
target_language_example: El doctor va a hacerte algunas preguntas antes del examen.
native_language_example: The doctor is going to ask you a few questions before the exam.

meaning: to ask you the same question.
additional_notes: Used when someone was about to ask (or could ask) exactly what the other person just asked or said. "Hacer" (to do/make) is often used with "pregunta" to mean "to ask a question." "Hacerte" = "ask you" (literally "do/make to you"), and "la misma" = "the same." Common with tenses like "iba a..." (was going to), "estaba a punto de..." (was about to), or "podría..." (could).
target_language_example: ¡Qué coincidencia! Iba a hacerte la misma pregunta.
native_language_example: What a coincidence! I was going to ask you the same question.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase hacer una pregunta (“to ask a question”) plus the indirect object pronoun te (“to you”). Commonly used to politely introduce a question: Quería/Quiero hacerte una pregunta (“I wanted/I want to ask you a question”). You can swap te for other pronouns: hacerle una pregunta (to ask him/her/you [formal] a question), hacerles una pregunta (to ask you all/them a question).
target_language_example: Perdona, ¿puedo hacerte una pregunta?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I ask you a question?

meaning: to ask you a few questions.
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you want to ask someone some questions. Literally it’s “to make you some questions,” but English uses “ask,” not “make.” Structure: hacer + indirect object pronoun (te = to you) + unas preguntas (“some/a few questions”). You can change the pronoun: hacerle unas preguntas (to ask him/her/you-formal), hacerles unas preguntas (to ask them/you all). Often used with acerca de / sobre / con respecto a (about/regarding).
target_language_example: ¿Puedo hacerte unas preguntas sobre el trabajo?
native_language_example: Can I ask you a few questions about the job?

additional_notes: Used to show direction or movement toward a specific masculine noun: hacia el buzón, hacia el arroyo. It’s a combination of hacia (“toward”) + el (“the” for masculine singular). For feminine nouns, use hacia la (e.g., hacia la puerta).
target_language_example: Camina hacia el parque, por favor.
native_language_example: Walk toward the park, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction (movement or orientation) toward the north. Often follows verbs of movement like ir, seguir, caminar, conducir: "Vamos/Sigan hacia el norte". Can also be used alone as a short direction: "Hacia el norte."
target_language_example: Camina hacia el norte hasta la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Walk north (toward the north) until the next street.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or direction in the sense of “heading toward” a place or point on the compass. Often follows verbs like ir, dirigirse, moverse, navegar, poner rumbo, etc. (Note: “al oeste” usually means “to the west (of something),” while “hacia el oeste” emphasizes the direction of travel.)
target_language_example: Conduce hacia el oeste por la autopista.
native_language_example: Drive west on the highway.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement to the opposite side (of a street, room, door, etc.). With verbs like “mirar” (mirar hacia el otro lado), it can also mean “to look the other way,” i.e., to ignore something on purpose.
target_language_example: Cruza la calle hacia el otro lado.
native_language_example: Cross the street to the other side.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to show direction (Ir/Volar/Caminar hacia el sur = “go/fly/walk south”). With places/things like windows or a house, it often means the direction they face (Mirar hacia el sur = “to face south”). Often answers “¿Hacia dónde?” (“Which direction?”).
target_language_example: Conduce hacia el sur y verás el mar.
native_language_example: Drive south and you’ll see the sea.

meaning: "toward the" / "in the direction of" (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to show movement or orientation in the direction of something feminine: *hacia la casa* (toward the house), *hacia la estación* (toward the station). It can also be figurative: *hacia la salvación* (toward salvation). For masculine nouns, use **hacia el**.
target_language_example: Vamos hacia la playa.
native_language_example: We’re going toward the beach.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward the right side. Common in giving directions (often after verbs like girar/voltear “to turn”) and with mirar “to look.” In politics, it can mean leaning toward the right (conservative ideas).
target_language_example: Sigue todo recto y luego gira hacia la derecha.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and then turn to the right.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement/orientation (where to look, turn, or head). Often follows verbs like mirar (to look) or girar (to turn). You can also hear it alone as an instruction: “Hacia la izquierda.”
target_language_example: Gira hacia la izquierda en la próxima calle.
native_language_example: Turn left at the next street.

additional_notes: Used to describe past weather. "Hacía" is the imperfect of "hacer" used for general conditions (especially weather): "hace frío" (it’s cold), "hacía frío" (it was cold). "Mucho" intensifies it: very/really cold. Often followed by a time expression: "ayer", "por la noche", "durante...".
target_language_example: En la montaña hacía mucho frío, así que nos quedamos en casa.
native_language_example: In the mountains it was very cold, so we stayed home.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "hacer" to describe past weather/background conditions. Often followed by "que" + a result: "Hacía tanto calor que..." (It was so hot that...). You’ll also see it without "que" when giving the reason for an action: "Como hacía tanto calor, ..." (Since it was so hot, ...).
target_language_example: Ayer hacía tanto calor que nos quedamos en casa con el aire acondicionado.
native_language_example: Yesterday it was so hot that we stayed home with the air conditioning.

additional_notes: Used to describe the weather in the past (imperfect: hacía) and introduce a consequence with que. Common pattern: “Hacía tanto + noun + que …” (e.g., hacía tanto calor que…). Often followed by a verb in the past describing what happened as a result.
target_language_example: Hacía tanto frío que se me quedaron las manos heladas.
native_language_example: It was so cold that my hands got freezing cold.

additional_notes: Very polite/formal way to ask someone to do something; it uses the usted command form (haga). Often followed by an infinitive (haga el favor de + verb). Common in service situations or when you want to sound extra courteous; with the wrong tone it can also sound a bit stern.
target_language_example: Haga el favor de cerrar la puerta, por favor.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

additional_notes: Uses the usted command form of **hacer** (*haga*). Common patterns: **Haga lo que + verb (subjunctive)** = “Whatever you do…” (*Haga lo que haga…*), **Haga lo que pueda** = “Do what you can,” **Haga lo que tenga que hacer** = “Do what you have to do,” and **Haga lo que + clause** = “Do what…” (*Haga lo que le han dicho*).
target_language_example: Haga lo que haga, no se rinda.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, don’t give up.

meaning: “do whatever you want / let him (or her) do whatever (he or she) wants.”
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive (haga, quiera). Often said as a permissive/indifferent response meaning “Fine—let him/her do whatever he/she wants.” Common with dejar/deja/deja que (“let”) or alone: “Que haga lo que quiera.” You can change the person: haga (usted/él/ella), hagas (tú), hagan (ustedes/ellos/ellas); quiera/quieras/quieran.
target_language_example: Si no quiere escuchar, que haga lo que quiera.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t want to listen, let him do whatever he wants.

additional_notes: Used with the ustedes command hagan (“do”) followed by lo que (“what/whatever”). It often introduces something like “hagan lo que les digo” = “do what I tell you.” The verb after lo que can change (digo/diga) depending on meaning and grammar, but the overall idea is giving instructions to a group (or to one person in some regions where ustedes is used).
target_language_example: Por favor, hagan lo que les pido.
native_language_example: Please do what I’m asking you.

meaning: “Do whatever you want.” (to more than one person)
additional_notes: Uses the ustedes command form of hacer: hagan. lo que quieran means “whatever you want,” referring to an unspecified action. Often said to give permission or show indifference (“Fine, do what you want”). You may also see it after que: Que hagan lo que quieran (“Let them do whatever they want”).
target_language_example: Si no les gusta el plan, hagan lo que quieran.
native_language_example: If you don’t like the plan, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: Formal plural command (ustedes) of hacer: “make/do.” Used by an announcer or dealer to tell a group to bet (e.g., in a casino, game, or competition). Can also be used humorously before revealing an outcome: “Place your bets (and let’s see what happens).”
target_language_example: ¡Hagan sus apuestas, que el juego va a empezar!
native_language_example: Place your bets—the game is about to start!

meaning: “no matter what you do” / “whatever you do”.
additional_notes: Used to introduce advice, instructions, or a warning that applies in every case. It uses the present subjunctive of hacer (hagas) in a fixed pattern: “Hagas lo que hagas, …”. You can also say it alone for emphasis, like “Whatever you do.”
target_language_example: Hagas lo que hagas, no abras esa puerta.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, don’t open that door.

meaning: "I do things" (how I do tasks / handle things).
additional_notes: "Hago" is the "I" form of "hacer" (to do/make). "Hago las cosas" is often followed by an adverb or phrase that explains *how* you do things: "bien" (well), "a mi manera" (my way), "de la misma manera" (the same way). It can refer to tasks, habits, or your way of doing things in general.
target_language_example: Perdón, hago las cosas despacio, pero las hago bien.
native_language_example: Sorry, I do things slowly, but I do them well.

meaning: “I do what …” (followed by a verb or phrase).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you do, often with a following expression like quiero (I want), debo hacer (I must do), es mejor (is best), etc. It’s the first-person singular present of hacer (to do/make) + lo que (“what/that which”).
target_language_example: Hago lo que puedo para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I do what I can to help you.

additional_notes: From the verb cambiar (“to change”) in the present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (cambiado). Used to say that something has changed up to now, often with time expressions like “en los últimos…”, “desde entonces”, or “nunca”. The subject is plural: ellos/ellas/ustedes, or a plural thing (las reglas, las circunstancias).
target_language_example: Desde el año pasado, las cosas han cambiado mucho.
native_language_example: Since last year, things have changed a lot.

meaning: “they have given” / “they gave” (present perfect of dar).
additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Common with object pronouns: me/te/le/nos/les han dado… (“they’ve given me/you/him/us/them…”). With "dar a" it can mean “to hit / to shoot (and hit)”: ¿Le han dado a X? = “Did they hit X?”
target_language_example: Me han dado la llave del cuarto.
native_language_example: They gave me the room key.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decidir (to decide): ellos/ellas/ustedes han decidido + infinitive (han decidido no comprar…) or + que + clause (han decidido que…). In many contexts it can be translated as either “have decided” or simple past “decided,” depending on how recent/relevant the decision is.
target_language_example: Mis padres han decidido mudarse a otra ciudad.
native_language_example: My parents have decided to move to another city.

additional_notes: Present perfect (ellos/ellas/ustedes) of decir + que. Often used in an impersonal way to report information from others (like “they say…” or “I’ve heard…”), without saying exactly who said it. You can also use it literally when the subject is clear: "Mis padres han dicho que..."
target_language_example: Han dicho que la tienda cierra a las seis.
native_language_example: They said the store closes at six. / I’ve been told the store closes at six.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to describe an activity that has been happening recently or up to now: "Han estado rastreando..." = "They've been tracking...". It can also mean "have been" in a state/situation: "Han estado juntos" (have been together), "han estado casados" (have been married), "nunca han estado con una mujer" (have never been with a woman). Sometimes it's used in set phrases like "ha(n) estado a la venta" = "has/have been on sale".
target_language_example: Últimamente han estado trabajando hasta tarde.
native_language_example: Lately, they've been working late.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haber** (**han**) + past participle **hecho** to talk about something **they** did at an unspecified time in the past that matters now (often used like English “have done”). The subject can be explicit (**ellos/ellas/ustedes**) or implied by context.
target_language_example: No sé qué han hecho, pero están muy felices.
native_language_example: I don’t know what they’ve done, but they’re very happy.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ir** for **ellos/ellas/ustedes**: **han ido** = “they/you (plural) have gone.” With **las cosas han ido bien/mal/a peor**, it often means “things have gone/been going well/badly/gotten worse” (more about how something turned out than physical movement). With **se** (**se han ido**), it means “they have left / everyone has gone.”
target_language_example: Últimamente, las clases han ido mejor.
native_language_example: Lately, the classes have been going better.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "llegar" (to arrive): haber (han) + past participle (llegado). Used with a plural subject (they/you all). Often followed by "a" + place: "Han llegado a Madrid." You can negate it: "No han llegado todavía" = "They haven't arrived yet."
target_language_example: Ya han llegado los invitados.
native_language_example: The guests have already arrived.

additional_notes: Present perfect of pasar (to pass) with an implied subject like el tiempo / los años / los meses (“time/years/months have passed”). Often used with a time expression (Han pasado cinco años) or with desde que / desde (“since”) to say how much time has passed since something happened. It can also be used more generally with cosas (“things/events have happened”).
target_language_example: Han pasado dos semanas desde que empezé el trabajo.
native_language_example: Two weeks have passed since I started the job.

meaning: “It’s been ten years since…” / “Ten years have passed since…”
additional_notes: Used to say how much time has elapsed since an event. Very common pattern: **Han pasado + [amount of time] + desde + ...**. Use **desde que + verb clause** (Desde que la vi / Desde que murió) or **desde + noun** (Desde su muerte). You can change the time: *Han pasado dos meses desde…*, *Han pasado muchos años desde…*.
target_language_example: Han pasado diez años desde que nos mudamos aquí.
native_language_example: It’s been ten years since we moved here.

meaning: two years have passed / it’s been two years.
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (han pasado) to say that two years have elapsed up to now. Very common with "desde que" (since) to mark the starting point: "Han pasado dos años desde que…" You can swap the number: "Han pasado tres meses", "Han pasado cinco días". Also used alone as a full sentence: "Han pasado dos años."
target_language_example: Han pasado dos años desde que me mudé a esta ciudad.
native_language_example: It’s been two years since I moved to this city.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ser**: **han** (they/you all have) + **sido** (been). Used to talk about something true up to now or recently. Very common in the **passive voice**: *han sido vistos/leídos* = “have been seen/read.”
target_language_example: Las entradas han sido vendidas.
native_language_example: The tickets have been sold.

additional_notes: Present perfect of **ser**: **han** (they/you all have) + **sido** (been). Used to talk about something true up to now or recently. Very common in the **passive voice**: *han sido vistos/leídos* = “have been seen/read.”
target_language_example: Las entradas han sido vendidas.
native_language_example: The tickets have been sold.

additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (han) + past participle (visto). Used for experiences or things seen up to now. Often means “they have seen” (ellos/ellas/ustedes), with the subject understood from context.
target_language_example: ¿Ya han visto la película?
native_language_example: Have you all seen the movie yet?

additional_notes: Used with **estar**: **estar harto/a/os/as de + noun** or **de + infinitive**. It agrees with the subject (**harto, harta, hartos, hartas**) and expresses strong annoyance or having had too much of something/someone.
target_language_example: Estoy harto de esperar; vámonos ya.
native_language_example: I’m sick of waiting; let’s go now.

additional_notes: Future tense of hacer (“to do/make”): haré = “I will do.” Used to promise or emphasize willingness to do whatever is necessary, often with por (“for”) or para (“in order to”), or followed by que + subjunctive: “haré cualquier cosa que me digas (que haga)” = “I’ll do anything you tell me (to do).”
target_language_example: Haré cualquier cosa para ayudarte a salir de aquí.
native_language_example: I’ll do anything to help you get out of here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with what you will do, often followed by subjunctive (e.g., "haré lo que me pidas"). Common extensions: "haré lo que sea necesario" (I’ll do whatever is necessary), "haré lo que tenga que hacer" (I’ll do what I have to do), "haré lo que usted quiera" (I’ll do what you want).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: haré lo que haga falta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll do whatever is needed.

meaning: "I’ll do what …" / "I’ll do whatever …" (with me = “to/for me”).
additional_notes: Used as a set-up before another verb: "Haré lo que me + (subjunctive)". Commonly: "haré lo que me pidas/pida" = “I’ll do what you/he/she asks me (to do).” You change the verb ending to match who is doing the asking (pidas = you, pida = he/she/you-formal, pides = you in statements like “you ask,” though after "lo que" Spanish often uses the subjunctive). "Haré lo que me plazca" means “I’ll do whatever I want/please.”
target_language_example: Haré lo que me digas.
native_language_example: I’ll do what you tell me.

meaning: I’ll do whatever it takes / I’ll do anything.
additional_notes: Expresses strong determination or willingness to do anything to achieve a goal or help someone. Often followed by para + infinitive (purpose): “Haré lo que sea para salir…”. Also common with por + someone (for someone’s sake): “Haré lo que sea por ti.” The verb is future tense (haré = “I will do”) and lo que sea means “whatever (it may be)”.
target_language_example: Haré lo que sea para recuperar mi trabajo.
native_language_example: I’ll do whatever it takes to get my job back.

meaning: “I’ll do everything I can…” / “I’ll do all that’s (within my power)…”.
additional_notes: Used to promise you’ll make your best effort. It’s typically followed by phrases like “a mi alcance” (within my reach), “en mi mano” (in my hands), or “en mi poder” (within my power) to emphasize you’ll do whatever is possible.
target_language_example: Haré todo lo que esté en mi poder para resolverlo hoy.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to solve it today.

meaning: I’ll do everything I can / I’ll do my best.
additional_notes: A promise to make a strong effort. Uses the future tense (haré = “I will do”) plus the subjunctive (pueda = “I can / may be able to”) after lo que (“what/whatever”). Often followed by para + infinitive (“in order to…”) or por + someone (“for you”).
target_language_example: No puedo garantizarlo, pero haré todo lo que pueda para ayudarte.
native_language_example: I can’t guarantee it, but I’ll do everything I can to help you.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense (haría = “would do”) to express willingness/hypothetical devotion. Follow it with an object pronoun or person: por ti (for you, informal), por usted (for you, formal), por ustedes (for you all), por vosotros (for you all, Spain), por él/ella (for him/her).
target_language_example: Haría cualquier cosa por mi familia.
native_language_example: I would do anything for my family.

meaning: “I’d do anything for …” / “I’d do whatever it takes for …”
additional_notes: Uses the conditional haría (“I would do”) plus lo que fuera (“whatever it might be”) to express willingness to do anything to help someone or to achieve a goal. Often followed by a person (por ti, por ella) or an objective/idea (por amor, por ganar dinero). You can change the subject: Yo haría…, Él/Ella haría…, Haríamos…
target_language_example: Haría lo que fuera por ayudarte.
native_language_example: I’d do anything to help you.

additional_notes: Present perfect of cambiar, used to say someone has changed from before to now. Often appears with adverbs like mucho (“a lot”) or nada (“at all”): No has cambiado nada = “You haven’t changed at all.” You can add the subject for emphasis: Tú has cambiado.
target_language_example: Has cambiado mucho desde el año pasado.
native_language_example: You’ve changed a lot since last year.

meaning: 'you have said' / 'you said' (present perfect of *decir*, informal singular).
additional_notes: Used with **tú** to talk about what someone has said, often with **que**: *Has dicho que...* (“You said that…”). In many contexts it translates as simple past in English (“you said”), especially when referring to something just said or relevant now. Negative: *No has dicho...*; also common in questions/complaints: *Aún no me has dicho...* (“You still haven’t told me…”).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has dicho eso?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

additional_notes: Used with tú to say someone has been in a place or state up to now (or at some time before now that matters in the present). Often followed by an adjective (ausente, enfermo), a place (ahí, en casa), or a gerund to show an ongoing/repeated action (has estado dando vueltas = “you’ve been hanging around/going around”).
target_language_example: ¿Has estado en México alguna vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Mexico?

meaning: “you have been in/to …” (you’ve visited or spent time somewhere).
additional_notes: Present perfect (tú): haber (has) + estado (past participle of estar) + en. Used to talk about life experience or something that happened at an unspecified time in the past, often with “alguna vez” (ever) or “ya” (already). With places it usually means “have been to,” but it can also mean “have been in” (present in) a situation or group for a period of time (e.g., “has estado en mi familia…”).
target_language_example: ¿Has estado en Madrid alguna vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Madrid?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to talk about actions that are completed but connected to the present (results, experience, or recent past). It agrees with “tú” (informal singular “you”): has = you have; hecho = done/made. Common patterns: “¿Qué has hecho?” (What have you done?), “Has hecho una promesa” (You’ve made a promise).
target_language_example: ¿Qué has hecho con las llaves?
native_language_example: What have you done with the keys?

meaning: you did the right thing; you did well.
additional_notes: Used to approve or reassure someone about something they already did. Often followed by an action with "al + infinitive": "Has hecho bien al llamar..." (You did well to call...). Can also be said on its own: "Has hecho bien."
target_language_example: Has hecho bien al decir la verdad.
native_language_example: You did the right thing by telling the truth.

additional_notes: Present perfect of oír (“to hear”), used to ask if someone heard something or to say they have. Often appears with a direct object: ¿Lo has oído? (“Did you hear it?”) / Has oído lo que he dicho (“You heard what I said”). Can also be followed by de to mean “have you heard from/about”: ¿Has oído de él? / No has oído nada de ella (“You haven’t heard anything from/about her”).
target_language_example: ¿Has oído la noticia?
native_language_example: Have you heard the news?

additional_notes: Second-person singular present perfect of perder (haber + perdido). Used to say someone has lost a game/competition (“Has perdido”), or that they’ve lost/missed something or a step in a process (“has perdido un paso”). It can also be followed by what was lost: “has perdido la cabeza” = “you’ve lost your mind/head.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, has perdido la llave otra vez.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’ve lost the key again.

meaning: “you have put/placed” (also, with a reflexive pronoun: “you’ve gotten / you’ve put on”).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect: haber (has) + past participle (puesto). It’s used for things you’ve done recently or that matter now. Common patterns: **has puesto + object** (“you’ve put X”): *Has puesto a mamá muy enferma* (“You’ve made Mom very sick”); **te has puesto + adjective** (from *ponerse* = “to become/get”): *Te has puesto celosa* (“You’ve gotten jealous”); **te has puesto + clothing** (“to put on”): *Ya te has puesto el uniforme* (“You’ve already put on your uniform”).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde has puesto las llaves?
native_language_example: Where have you put the keys?

meaning: "you have been" (present perfect of ser, tú).
additional_notes: Used to describe what someone has been like up to now (often with adjectives or nouns): Has sido muy amable / Has sido una buena amiga. It uses the tú form: has + sido. For usted, use ha sido; for vosotros, habéis sido.
target_language_example: Has sido muy paciente hoy.
native_language_example: You’ve been very patient today.

additional_notes: Present perfect (tú) of tener: haber (has) + past participle (tenido). Used to talk about something you’ve had/experienced up to now, often with words like alguna vez (ever), ya (already), nunca (never). Depending on context, it can mean having an illness/fever, having time/work, having enough of something, or having had an experience before.
target_language_example: ¿Has tenido tiempo para comer hoy?
native_language_example: Have you had time to eat today?

additional_notes: Present perfect of "venir" (venir → venido) with "tú": "haber" (has) + past participle (venido). It’s used to say that someone has arrived or came (often with a sense of a recent or relevant past), and it can be followed by extra details: "has venido aquí", "has venido en coche", "has venido a + infinitive" (you came to do something), "has venido al lugar adecuado" (you came to the right place).
target_language_example: ¿Por qué has venido tan temprano?
native_language_example: Why did you come so early?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb haber (has) + past participle (visto) to talk about something you’ve seen at an unspecified time up to now. Common in questions like "¿Has visto...?" and in statements like "Has visto miles de ellos" (You’ve seen thousands of them).
target_language_example: ¿Has visto mis llaves?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

meaning: "you’ve come back / you’ve returned"; also "you’ve done (something) again" (with a + infinitive).
additional_notes: Present perfect: haber (has) + past participle (vuelto). It can mean you have returned (often implied: to a place or situation): "¡Qué bien que has vuelto!". Very commonly it’s followed by "a" + infinitive to mean “you’ve ___ again” (repetition): "Has vuelto a cometer el mismo error" = “You made the same mistake again.”
target_language_example: Has vuelto a llegar tarde otra vez.
native_language_example: You’ve arrived late again.

additional_notes: Used to limit what you’re saying to your current knowledge or information (often implying it could be wrong or incomplete). Common at the start of a sentence: “Hasta donde sé, …”.
target_language_example: Hasta donde sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement as being based on your current knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). It often comes at the beginning of a sentence and is followed by a comma. You can change the person: “hasta donde yo sé” (I know), “hasta donde él/ella sabe” (he/she knows), “hasta donde sabemos” (we know).
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, la reunión es mañana a las diez.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting is tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to give information with some uncertainty, meaning “based on what I know.” Often followed by a statement about someone/something. You can swap the subject: “Hasta donde yo sé, ella… / ellos… / usted…” or omit it: “Hasta donde yo sé, es honesto.”
target_language_example: Hasta donde yo sé, él trabaja aquí desde 2020.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he has worked here since 2020.

meaning: 'until the' or 'to the' (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with destinations or limits (physical or figurative): *hasta el asiento trasero* = 'as far as the back seat', *hasta el fin del mundo* = 'to/until the end of the world'. It also appears in farewells and scheduling: *Hasta el jueves* = 'See you on Thursday' / 'Until Thursday'. Use **hasta la** before feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Camina hasta el parque y luego vuelve a casa.
native_language_example: Walk to the park and then come back home.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the last moment or the last part of something (a game, meeting, movie, etc.), or up to the end point of a route. Often answers “How long?” (stay until the end) or “How far?” (go all the way to the end of the street). Can also imply persistence: insistir hasta el final (“keep insisting to the very end”).
target_language_example: Me quedé hasta el final de la película.
native_language_example: I stayed until the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize going all the way to the end, without leaving anything out: time (hasta el último segundo), effort/life (hasta el último aliento), completeness (hasta el último detalle), or money (hasta el último dólar). It agrees with what follows: hasta el último segundo/detalle/dólar; hasta la última vez; hasta los últimos minutos; hasta las últimas consecuencias.
target_language_example: Lo revisaré hasta el último detalle antes de enviarlo.
native_language_example: I’ll check it down to the very last detail before sending it.

additional_notes: Used to mark an end point in time, distance, or limit: hasta la una (until 1 o’clock), hasta la mitad (up to halfway). Also common in set phrases like Hasta la próxima (until next time). It’s the same as hasta el, but with feminine nouns (la).
target_language_example: El restaurante está abierto hasta la medianoche.
native_language_example: The restaurant is open until midnight.

meaning: to the last drop; completely (leaving nothing).
additional_notes: Used literally with drinks/liquids (drinking/using every last bit), and figuratively to mean taking or squeezing every last bit of something (time, money, effort, etc.). Often follows verbs like "beber" (to drink), "exprimir" (to squeeze), or "aprovechar" (to make the most of).
target_language_example: Aproveché mis vacaciones hasta la última gota.
native_language_example: I enjoyed my vacation to the fullest.

meaning: 'until further notice' (until you hear a new update/instruction).
additional_notes: Used in announcements to say something will continue indefinitely, and will only change when someone informs you. Common with closures, freezes/suspensions, policies, or temporary arrangements.
target_language_example: La reunión queda pospuesta hasta nuevo aviso.
native_language_example: The meeting is postponed until further notice.

additional_notes: Used to mark an endpoint in time: an action continues up to the moment when something happens. The "se" is often part of a reflexive verb (e.g., acostarse = to go to bed) or a change-of-state verb (e.g., oscurecerse/oscurecer = to get dark), and it can also appear with passive/impersonal ideas (e.g., hasta que se demuestre = until it is proven). After "hasta que", Spanish often uses the subjunctive when the event is not yet known/hasn’t happened, and the indicative when it’s a completed/past fact.
target_language_example: Esperamos aquí hasta que se abra la tienda.
native_language_example: We’ll wait here until the store opens.

additional_notes: Used to set a condition that lasts up to the moment you do something. It’s often followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (vuelva, llegue, diga, baje) because it refers to a future/unknown moment. In commands, it can sound firm or authoritative: "Nadie sale… hasta que yo lo diga."
target_language_example: Quédate aquí hasta que yo vuelva.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays awake or something lasts until a late time. Often with verbs like "quedarse" (to stay) and "estar" (to be): "quedarse despierto/a hasta tarde" = "to stay up late."
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; me quedé despierto hasta tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I stayed up late.

additional_notes: Used to say an action continues late into the night. Common with ongoing activities (trabajar, estudiar, escuchar música) and often implies “later than usual.” You can also hear the shorter version “hasta tarde” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos despiertos hasta tarde por la noche hablando.
native_language_example: We stayed up until late at night talking.

additional_notes: Uses "hay" (from haber) to say something exists or is present. Often followed by a place: "Hay algo aquí" (There’s something here), or by a relative clause with "que": "Hay algo que necesito decirte" (There’s something I need to tell you). In questions, intonation (or "¿") makes it mean "Is there something…?": "¿Hay algo que pueda hacer?"
target_language_example: ¿Hay algo que te preocupe?
native_language_example: Is there something that’s worrying you?

meaning: 'there's something that' (I/we need/want to talk about).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic you want or need to discuss. Structure: "hay algo" (there is something) + "de lo que" (about which/that) + a verb like "hablar" (to talk). Often followed by "debemos/tenemos que/quiero" + "hablar" + "contigo/te".
target_language_example: Hay algo de lo que quiero hablar contigo cuando tengas un momento.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to talk to you about when you have a moment.

meaning: "is there anything else that" / "there is something else that".
additional_notes: Used to introduce an additional thing (a question, fact, or task) beyond what was already mentioned. It often comes before a verb in the subjunctive after a question (e.g., "¿Hay algo más que quieras?") and before an infinitive or obligation phrase (e.g., "hay algo más que debo hacer").
target_language_example: ¿Hay algo más que necesites hoy?
native_language_example: Is there anything else that you need today?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unspecified thing you want to say/do/show/mention. Often followed by a verb phrase: "Hay algo que quiero decirte" (something I want to tell you) or "Hay algo que debes ver" (something you should see). "Hay" is the common way to say "there is/there are" in Spanish.
target_language_example: Hay algo que necesito preguntarte.
native_language_example: There’s something I need to ask you.

meaning: “There’s something I need to / I must …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce something important you feel obligated to say, do, show, or know. It’s followed by an infinitive: hay algo que debo + decirte (tell you), decirle (tell you—formal/you/he/she), mostrarte (show you), saber (know). Common for serious or sensitive topics.
target_language_example: Hay algo que debo preguntarte antes de irme.
native_language_example: There’s something I need to ask you before I leave.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you want to say/show/teach/protect, etc. It’s often followed by an infinitive: "Hay algo que quiero decirte/mostrarte/enseñarte". You can also add an indirect object: "Hay algo que quiero decirle" (to you/formal you).
target_language_example: Hay algo que quiero preguntarte.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to ask you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone exists or is present in a place/situation. "Hay" is the impersonal form of "haber" meaning "there is/there are" (it doesn’t change for singular/plural), and it’s often followed by a location: "Hay alguien aquí / ahí / en casa". You can also add "más" for “someone else”: "Hay alguien más".
target_language_example: ¿Hay alguien en casa?
native_language_example: Is there anyone at home?

additional_notes: Used to put something in perspective and say you shouldn’t focus too much on one issue because other things matter more. Often followed by “que + noun/infinitive”: “Hay cosas más importantes que el dinero” (…than money), “Hay cosas más importantes de las que preocuparse” (…to worry about).
target_language_example: No te enojes por eso; hay cosas más importantes.
native_language_example: Don’t get mad about that; there are more important things.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about certain tasks, facts, or situations. Often followed by a verb clause: "Hay cosas que necesito hacer" (There are things I need to do). In negative statements it’s common with "no se pueden" / "no se pueden dejar": "Hay cosas que no se pueden dejar al azar" (There are things you can’t leave to chance).
target_language_example: Hay cosas que no puedo explicar ahora.
native_language_example: There are things I can’t explain right now.

additional_notes: Uses **hay** (from *haber*) to say that something exists/there is/there are. **Estaciones** here means the seasons of the year (primavera, verano, otoño, invierno). Often used with a place or time: *En Japón hay cuatro estaciones* / *Hay cuatro estaciones al año*.
target_language_example: En mi país hay cuatro estaciones, pero el invierno es muy corto.
native_language_example: In my country there are four seasons, but winter is very short.

additional_notes: Used to say that two of something exist or are present. “Hay” is used for existence/presence (not *estar*). Often followed by a noun or by “que + verb” to describe which two: “Hay dos que…”.
target_language_example: En mi clase hay dos estudiantes nuevos.
native_language_example: In my class there are two new students.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about some people (not everyone). It’s common for talking about habits, opinions, or beliefs. Verb agreement: "hay" is always singular, but the following verb changes depending on the people mentioned (e.g., "hay gente que cree" / "hay gente que creen").
target_language_example: Hay gente que prefiere caminar en vez de tomar el autobús.
native_language_example: There are people who prefer to walk instead of taking the bus.

meaning: "there are thousands of" / "there are lots of".
additional_notes: Used to say that a very large number of something exists. It’s built with: hay (there is/are) + miles de (thousands of) + a plural noun. For emphasis you may also see bigger numbers, e.g., "hay miles de millones de" = "there are billions of".
target_language_example: En esta playa hay miles de conchas.
native_language_example: There are thousands of shells on this beach.

meaning: "there is/are a lot of" (with a feminine singular noun).
