additional_notes: Comparative form of cuidadoso (“careful”). Often used with ser (Sé más cuidadoso…), or with subjunctive after advice/wishes (que sea/fuera/fuese más cuidadoso). You’ll commonly see it followed by: con (“with/about”), en (“in/with what you do”), or cuando + verb (“when you…”).
target_language_example: Por favor, sé más cuidadoso con el vaso; es de vidrio.
native_language_example: Please be more careful with the glass; it’s made of glass.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or amounts, usually with numbers: "más de + número + sustantivo" (más de dos horas). It can also appear in phrases like "poco más de" = "a little more than". Sometimes it’s used in instructions/texts to mean "more about this" ("Ve más de esto más adelante"), similar to "see more on this later."
target_language_example: Hay más de cincuenta personas en la sala.
native_language_example: There are more than fifty people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to say a quantity is above 100. Often followed by a noun (más de cien kilómetros / personas / naciones). With numbers, Spanish commonly uses “más de” (more than) and “menos de” (less than).
target_language_example: Hay más de cien estudiantes en esta clase.
native_language_example: There are more than a hundred students in this class.

additional_notes: Used to compare an amount/degree to what is possible, expected, seen, or believed. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb: más de lo que puedo…, más de lo que creía, más de lo que se ve. Similar to “más … que”, but “más de lo que” is used when the comparison is to an entire idea/action (“than what/how much…”), not just a single noun/adjective.
target_language_example: Gasté más de lo que quería en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I spent more than I wanted to at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to compare an amount/degree to what is possible, expected, seen, or believed. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb: más de lo que puedo…, más de lo que creía, más de lo que se ve. Similar to “más … que”, but “más de lo que” is used when the comparison is to an entire idea/action (“than what/how much…”), not just a single noun/adjective.
target_language_example: Gasté más de lo que quería en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I spent more than I wanted to at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the reality is greater/stronger/more frequent than the listener expects. Often follows a verb (pasa, esconde, sé, conozco) and can be said alone as a dramatic response meaning “More than you think.”
target_language_example: Esto ocurre más de lo que crees.
native_language_example: This happens more than you think.

additional_notes: Used to compare an amount/degree to what is possible, expected, seen, or believed. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb: más de lo que puedo…, más de lo que creía, más de lo que se ve. Similar to “más … que”, but “más de lo que” is used when the comparison is to an entire idea/action (“than what/how much…”), not just a single noun/adjective.
target_language_example: Gasté más de lo que quería en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I spent more than I wanted to at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration that is longer than 30 years. Very common with time expressions like "desde hace" (since … ago/for), "hace" (for), and "por" (for). You can replace "treinta" with other numbers: "más de diez años", "más de dos años".
target_language_example: Vivo aquí desde hace más de treinta años.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for more than thirty years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or amount of time that exceeds three hours. It can modify verbs like durar (to last), esperar (to wait), perder (to waste/lose time), or arrive late (llegar tarde). You can replace tres with any number: más de dos horas, más de cinco minutos, etc.
target_language_example: El vuelo se retrasó y estuvimos en el aeropuerto más de tres horas.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed and we were at the airport for more than three hours.

meaning: more than one; more than a/an.
additional_notes: Used to say a number or amount is greater than 1 (or greater than a specific unit), often followed by a singular noun: más de un siglo (more than a century), más de un tres por ciento (more than three percent). Even though the noun is singular, it can refer to multiple items: Hay más de un cofre valioso (There’s more than one valuable chest).
target_language_example: He estado aquí por más de un año.
native_language_example: I’ve been here for more than a year.

meaning: more than a year; over a year.
additional_notes: Used to say a time period is longer than one year. Often appears with time expressions like "hace" ("Hace más de un año" = "more than a year ago") or with "durante" ("durante más de un año" = "for more than a year"). You can also soften/approximate it with "poco más de un año" or "un poco más de un año" ("a little over a year").
target_language_example: Hace más de un año que no lo veo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him for more than a year.

additional_notes: Used to say a period of time is longer than 60 minutes. Often appears after time-related verbs like esperar (to wait) and pasar (to pass): “Esperé más de una hora” = “I waited more than an hour.” You can swap in other amounts: “más de dos horas”, “más de un día”.
target_language_example: Esperamos más de una hora para entrar.
native_language_example: We waited more than an hour to get in.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to slow down, especially when speaking (e.g., "Hable/Hablen más despacio"), but also for walking or driving. Often used alone as a short request: "Más despacio." You can soften it with "por favor" or "un poco" (a bit).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak more slowly, please?

meaning: 'more difficult' / 'harder' (also: 'the most difficult' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used for comparisons: "más difícil" = harder than something else (often with "que": "más difícil que..."). With "el/la/lo" it becomes a superlative: "el/la/lo más difícil" = the hardest / most difficult part/thing. Agree "difícil" with gender/number only when it becomes plural: "más difíciles".
target_language_example: Para mí, lo más difícil es levantarme temprano.
native_language_example: For me, the hardest thing is getting up early.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to say someone should put in more effort or intensity, especially with work or studying: “estudiar/trabajar más duro.” You can also hear “más fuerte” or “con más empeño” with a similar idea.
target_language_example: Tengo que entrenar más duro si quiero ganar.
native_language_example: I have to train harder if I want to win.

additional_notes: Comparative form of feliz (“happy”). Use it to compare how happy someone is (often with que: más feliz que… = “happier than…”). Common with verbs like sentirse (“to feel”): sentir(se) más feliz = “to feel happier,” and with verse (“to look/seem”): verse más feliz = “to look happier.”
target_language_example: Desde que cambió de trabajo, está más feliz.
native_language_example: Since he changed jobs, he’s happier.

additional_notes: Used with a noun like "momento" or "época" to say it was the happiest time in your whole life. "Más feliz" is the superlative idea (“happiest”) and "de mi vida" means “of my life.” You can also change the person: "de tu vida" (of your life), "de su vida" (of his/her life).
target_language_example: Mi graduación fue el día más feliz de mi vida.
native_language_example: My graduation was the happiest day of my life.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength or intensity: más + adjective (fuerte). With el/la/lo + más fuerte it means “the strongest” or “the most intense” (e.g., lo más fuerte del mundo = the strongest thing in the world). It can describe physical strength (más fuerte que tú), but also sounds/nature (el trueno se hizo más fuerte = the thunder got louder) or anything becoming more intense.
target_language_example: Habla más fuerte, por favor; no te oigo.
native_language_example: Speak louder, please; I can’t hear you.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, usually with a verb like parecer (“to seem”) or creer (“to think/believe”): más + adjective/adverb + de lo que + verb/clause. Often implies “than you thought/seemed.” You can swap in other adjectives: más alto de lo que…, más rápido de lo que….
target_language_example: Eres más fuerte de lo que pensabas.
native_language_example: You’re stronger than you thought.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with "que" after the adjective: "más + adjective + que + [person/thing]". "Fuerte" can mean physically strong, intense, or loud depending on context. You can add emphasis with "mucho": "mucho más fuerte que".
target_language_example: Habla más fuerte que yo; no te oigo bien.
native_language_example: Speak louder than me; I can’t hear you well.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "fácil" (easy): "más + adjective" = "more + adjective." Often used with "ser" or "estar" ("Esto es/está más fácil") and with "hacer" to mean "to make (something) easier" ("hacer más fácil la vida"). Common pattern: "más fácil de lo que + verb" = "easier than (what) I thought/it seemed."
target_language_example: Si lo hacemos juntos, será más fácil.
native_language_example: If we do it together, it will be easier.

additional_notes: Used to compare size: **más grande (que...)** = “bigger (than...)”. With **el/la/los/las + más grande** it becomes the superlative: “the biggest/largest.” It can also mean “older/more grown-up” in some contexts (e.g., *Quiero ser más grande* = “I want to be older / grown up”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más grande que yo, pero yo soy el más grande en mi clase.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me, but I’m the oldest in my class.

additional_notes: Used in superlatives to compare size: **el/la más grande de + place/group** (“the largest in/of …”). It agrees with the noun: **el más grande** (masc.), **la más grande** (fem.). Often followed by **de +** a group (“de todos”) or a place (“de Japón”, “de esta ciudad”).
target_language_example: Madrid es la ciudad más grande de España.
native_language_example: Madrid is the largest city in Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the largest worldwide. Structure: "el/la/los/las + [noun] + más grande del mundo" (superlative). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: el coche…, la ciudad…, los bancos…, las ciudades…
target_language_example: Barcelona no es la ciudad más grande del mundo, pero es muy bonita.
native_language_example: Barcelona isn’t the biggest city in the world, but it’s very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to compare size or importance between two things. It’s the comparative form of grande (“big/large”), followed by que (“than”). Often paired with a second item after que: más grande que + noun/pronoun/time expression (e.g., más grande que ahora).
target_language_example: Este cuarto es más grande que el otro.
native_language_example: This room is bigger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone or something to you with más + adjective + que + pronoun. With people, grande often means “older” (especially in Latin America), and the contrast with más bajo (“shorter”) shows it can also refer to physical size/height depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi prima es más grande que yo, pero yo soy más alta.
native_language_example: My cousin is older than me, but I’m taller.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "grande" (big/large). Used with "que" to compare two things: "más grandes que..." = "bigger/larger than...". It agrees in gender and number with the noun: "más grande" (sing.), "más grandes" (plural).
target_language_example: Necesitamos zapatos más grandes.
native_language_example: We need bigger shoes.

additional_notes: Used to compare size (or more generally magnitude) between two things. Structure: **[noun] + ser + más grande(s) + que + [comparison]**. Make **grande** agree in number: **más grande que** (singular) / **más grandes que** (plural). Often used with articles/pronouns: **más grandes que los de...**, **más grandes que las de...**.
target_language_example: Mis zapatos son más grandes que los tuyos.
native_language_example: My shoes are bigger than yours.

additional_notes: Used to compare importance ("X es más importante que Y" = "X is more important than Y"). With "el/la/lo + más importante" it means "the most important" (superlative), often followed by "de" (e.g., "la más importante del día" = "the most important of the day").
target_language_example: Para mí, la salud es más importante que el dinero.
native_language_example: For me, health is more important than money.

additional_notes: Used to compare importance between two things. It follows the comparative pattern “más + adjective + que” (more + adjective + than). You can intensify it with “mucho” (“mucho más importante que” = “much more important than”). It’s often followed by a noun, pronoun, or an idea/phrase.
target_language_example: Tu salud es más importante que el trabajo.
native_language_example: Your health is more important than work.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: **más + adjective + que + person/thing**. You can intensify with words like **mucho**: *mucho más inteligente que...* The opposite comparison is **menos inteligente que** (“less intelligent than”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana es más inteligente que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is smarter than me.

additional_notes:
Used to compare interest level. 
- With a comparison: "más interesante que..." = "more interesting than..." 
- With "de lo que": "más interesante de lo que esperaba" = "more interesting than I expected." 
- With "el/la/lo" it becomes a superlative: "el libro más interesante" = "the most interesting book." 
- Often appears with "cada vez más" to show a change over time: "cada vez más interesante" = "more and more interesting."
target_language_example: La conversación se está volviendo cada vez más interesante.
native_language_example: The conversation is becoming more and more interesting.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: "más + adjective + que + noun/pronoun". Often intensified with words like "mucho" (much more) or "de lejos" (by far). The adjective agrees with the noun being described (e.g., "más interesante" with masculine/feminine singular nouns; plural would be "más interesantes").
target_language_example: Este museo es más interesante que el otro.
native_language_example: This museum is more interesting than the other one.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "joven" (young): "más joven (que...)" = "younger (than...)". It can describe age or how someone looks: "parece más joven" = "looks younger". Often used with "de lo que" to compare with an expectation: "más joven de lo que piensas" = "younger than you think."
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más joven que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons: **más + adjective + de lo que + verb** (“more [adjective] than [someone/something] is/was”). Here it’s often followed by **es/era**: *más joven de lo que es/era*. Common with verbs like **parecer**, **verse**, **aparentar** (“to seem/look”).
target_language_example: Te ves más joven de lo que eres.
native_language_example: You look younger than you are.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages or how old someone looks. Structure: [person/thing] + (ser / parecer / verse) + más joven que + [other person/thing]. You can add "algo" to soften it: "algo más joven que" = "a bit younger than."
target_language_example: Mi hermano es más joven que yo.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: **más + adjective + que + pronoun** (“more + adjective + than + me/you/him…”). With ages, **joven** = “young,” so **más joven que yo** = “younger than me.” In everyday Spanish you’ll also hear **más joven que mí** after **que**, though **que yo** is very common.
target_language_example: Creo que mi primo es más joven que yo.
native_language_example: I think my cousin is younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare distance or how far something goes (physical or sometimes figurative). Often appears with comparisons like “más lejos que…” (farther than…) and with the superlative: “lo más lejos (posible/que puedas)” = “as far as possible / as far as you can.”
target_language_example: Camina más lejos y luego me llamas.
native_language_example: Walk farther and then call me.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things: **más + listo/a/os/as + que + ...**. *Listo* often means “smart/clever” (sometimes “quick-witted”). It agrees with the subject: *más listo que*, *más lista que*, *más listos que*, *más listas que*.
target_language_example: Mi hermana es más lista que yo.
native_language_example: My sister is smarter than me.

meaning: 'I like it more' / 'I like it the most.'
additional_notes:
Uses the verb gustar (literally 'to be pleasing'), so Spanish says 'it pleases me' = 'I like it.' The pronoun me means 'to me.' With más, it becomes a comparison or a superlative depending on context:
- Cuanto más..., más me gusta... = 'The more..., the more I like...'
- lo que más me gusta (de...) = 'what I like most (about...)'.
Often followed by a noun/pronoun as the thing liked: 'más me gusta el lugar' (I like the place more).
target_language_example: De todos los postres, el helado es el que más me gusta.
native_language_example: Of all desserts, ice cream is the one I like the most.

additional_notes: Used in emphatic phrases like “al más mínimo + noun” (at the slightest + noun), “no tener el más mínimo + noun” (to not have the slightest + noun), and “ni en lo más mínimo” (not even in the slightest). Often appears with “el/lo” before it: “el más mínimo error”, “en lo más mínimo”.
target_language_example: No me molestes por el más mínimo detalle.
native_language_example: Don’t bother me about the slightest detail.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "profundo" (deep). Used to compare depth (literal or figurative): "más profundo que..." = "deeper than...". Often follows a verb like "ir", "llegar" or "cavar": "ir más profundo" (go deeper), "cavar más profundo" (dig deeper). "Profundo" can look like English "profound"; in Spanish it commonly means "deep".
target_language_example: Tenemos que cavar más profundo para encontrar agua.
native_language_example: We have to dig deeper to find water.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not enough or that there’s something additional/bigger beyond what was mentioned. Often appears after a statement (Pero es más que eso.) or as a warning (Vas a necesitar más que eso.)
target_language_example: No basta con pedir perdón: es más que eso.
native_language_example: It’s not enough to apologize: it’s more than that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the amount/quality is not just enough, but plenty (sometimes implying “so stop/that’s all we need”). It can stand alone as a short answer (Más que suficiente.) or modify a noun: más que suficiente comida/evidencia/dinero. With people (Eres más que suficiente), it often means “you are enough / you’re more than enough” in an emotional/relationship sense.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: con tres botellas de agua es más que suficiente.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: three bottles of water is more than enough.

additional_notes: Used to compare how much/many or how often someone does/has something, with tú as the comparison point. Common patterns: (verb) + más que tú (Trabajo más que tú = I work more than you); (noun) + más que tú (Tengo diez bolígrafos más que tú = I have ten more pens than you); (me importa/te quiero) + más que tú (+ a mí) for comparisons in feelings (Nadie me importa más que tú = No one matters to me more than you).
target_language_example: Yo estudio más que tú, pero tú duermes más que yo.
native_language_example: I study more than you, but you sleep more than me.

meaning: "more than a"; in negatives, "nothing more than a".
additional_notes: Used to compare or to emphasize what something/someone really is. In positive statements, it often means something exceeds a basic category: "Es más que un amigo" = "He’s more than a friend." In negative statements with "no" ("no... más que un/una"), it usually downplays: "No es más que un niño" = "He’s nothing more than a kid" / "He’s just a kid."
target_language_example: Para mí, este trabajo es más que un empleo.
native_language_example: For me, this job is more than a job.

additional_notes: Often used to compare or emphasize that something is beyond a simple category: “Es más que una X” (“It’s more than a X”). With “no” it often flips meaning to “nothing but”: “No es más que una ilusión” / “No es nada más que una ilusión” = “It’s nothing but an illusion.” You may also see “más que un/una + noun” depending on the noun’s gender.
target_language_example: Para mí, esto es más que una amistad.
native_language_example: For me, this is more than a friendship.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone has/does something to a greater degree than you. Common with verbs like necesitar (to need) or saber (to know): "Tú lo necesitas más que yo" = "You need it more than I do." In casual speech, "más que yo" is often used instead of the more formal "más que yo lo hago" (more than I do).
target_language_example: Creo que te gusta el café más que yo.
native_language_example: I think you like coffee more than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed or how long something takes. With "ser" it describes something/someone as faster ("Es más rápido", "El ciervo es más rápido que..."). With an infinitive, it often means a faster option: "Será más rápido + infinitive" (e.g., "Será más rápido ir/atravesar por aquí"). Can also be used adverbially to talk about doing an action more quickly ("Hazlo más rápido").
target_language_example: Si vamos en metro, será más rápido.
native_language_example: If we go by subway, it will be faster.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed or how long something takes. With "ser" it describes something/someone as faster ("Es más rápido", "El ciervo es más rápido que..."). With an infinitive, it often means a faster option: "Será más rápido + infinitive" (e.g., "Será más rápido ir/atravesar por aquí"). Can also be used adverbially to talk about doing an action more quickly ("Hazlo más rápido").
target_language_example: Si vamos en metro, será más rápido.
native_language_example: If we go by subway, it will be faster.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed between two people/things/actions: X va/hace (algo) más rápido que Y. You can swap in other adjectives/adverbs in the same pattern (más + adverb/adjective + que). Often used with verbs like ir, correr, hacer.
target_language_example: Tengo que caminar más rápido que tú para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I have to walk faster than you to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Comparative structure: **más + adjective/adverb + que + person**. Here **rápido** means "fast/quick" and **que yo** is "than me/I." Often used with actions (walk, do something, run). You can swap **yo** for another pronoun/name: *más rápido que ella*, *más rápido que Tom*.
target_language_example: No puedo escribir más rápido que yo cuando estoy cansado.
native_language_example: I can’t write faster than I do when I’m tired.

additional_notes: Comparative form of "seguro" (safe/secure). Often used with "ser" or "estar": "Es/Está más seguro" = "It’s safer." With "el/la/los/las" it means "the safest" (e.g., "el camino más seguro"). With "lo", it can mean "the safest thing" or, in predictions, "the most likely" ("Lo más seguro es que…" = "Most likely…").
target_language_example: Lo más seguro es que lleguemos tarde si salimos ahora.
native_language_example: Most likely we’ll arrive late if we leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after now. Common in plans and conversations: Hablamos más tarde. / Nos vemos más tarde. It can refer to later today or generally later, depending on context. In longer timeframes, it can mean “later” in the sense of “months/years later.”
target_language_example: Estoy ocupado ahora, pero te llamo más tarde.
native_language_example: I’m busy now, but I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used to compare times or to say something happens earlier than usual (often with "que": "más temprano que nosotros/de costumbre"). Also common in requests like "Ven más temprano" (Come earlier).
target_language_example: Si salimos más temprano, llegaremos a tiempo.
native_language_example: If we leave earlier, we’ll arrive on time.

meaning: "You'd better..." / "It’d be best if..." (a warning or strong advice).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or strongly recommend an action, often implying consequences if they don’t do it. It commonly introduces a verb in the present subjunctive: "Más vale que te vayas". You can also hear "más vale" + infinitive: "Más vale irse" (It’s better to leave).
target_language_example: Más vale que me llames cuando llegues.
native_language_example: You’d better call me when you get there.

additional_notes: Usually used in the pattern **(no) tener más alternativa que + infinitive** to express that someone is forced to do something because there are no other options. Very common with **no**: *No tuve más alternativa que…*
target_language_example: No tenemos más alternativa que cancelar el viaje.
native_language_example: We have no choice but to cancel the trip.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like "tener" (to have) to mean "to be more careful": "tener más cuidado". Common with advice/criticism, especially with "deber" (should/must) and in conditional sentences ("Si yo fuera tú...": If I were you...). Also used with "al" + infinitive to say when to be careful: "tener más cuidado al manejar" (be more careful when driving).
target_language_example: Tienes que tener más cuidado al cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: You have to be more careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an additional amount of money (often meaning “extra” or “a larger amount than before”). Typically follows verbs like conseguir (to get), ganar (to earn), necesitar (to need), or haber (there is/are): “conseguir más dinero”, “tiene que haber más dinero”.
target_language_example: Necesito más dinero para pagar el alquiler.
native_language_example: I need more money to pay the rent.

meaning: "more money than" (used to compare with someone/something).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: **más dinero que + noun/person**. Often appears in fixed, insulting/humorous expressions like **más dinero que cerebro/sesos** (“more money than brains”) or **más dinero que gusto** (“more money than taste/class”). You’ll frequently see a full comparison with **que**: *gana más dinero que su marido*.
target_language_example: Tiene más dinero que paciencia.
native_language_example: He/She has more money than patience.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an increase in the number of people in general (not a specific group). Very common in patterns like: “cada vez más gente...” (more and more people...), “ojalá hubiera más gente como tú” (I wish there were more people like you), and “donde haya más gente” (where there are more people). Note: “gente” is singular in Spanish, so you say “más gente es...” / “más gente tiene...”, not *“más gente son...”*.
target_language_example: En verano hay más gente en la playa.
native_language_example: In the summer there are more people at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or point someone to additional details (common in signs, emails, websites: “Para más información…” / “Haga clic aquí para más información”). Often used without an article: “más información” (not usually “la más información”).
target_language_example: Si necesitas más información, envíame un correo.
native_language_example: If you need more information, send me an email.

additional_notes: Used in the fixed pattern "(no) tener más opción que + infinitive" to say someone is forced to do something. It’s usually preceded by "no" ("no tengo más opción que...") and followed by an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: No tenemos más opción que esperar.
native_language_example: We have no choice but to wait.

meaning: "no choice but to" / "have no option but to".
additional_notes: Used with (no) tener/quedar + más remedio que + infinitive to say you are forced to do something because there’s no alternative. Very common in the negative: “no tengo más remedio que…” (I have no choice but to…).
target_language_example: No me queda más remedio que llamar a la policía.
native_language_example: I have no choice but to call the police.

additional_notes: Used when you need additional time or when something takes longer. Common with verbs like necesitar/pedir (to need/ask for) and tomar/llevar (to take): “Necesito más tiempo.” / “Esto va a tomar más tiempo.”
target_language_example: Necesito más tiempo para terminar.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say you need or want additional time in order to do an action. It’s often followed by an infinitive (para hablar, para completar, para estudiar). You can use it with tener/necesitar/no tener: "Necesito más tiempo para…" / "No tengo más tiempo para…".
target_language_example: Necesito más tiempo para terminar el informe.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish the report.

meaning: 'me, please' (with mí used after a preposition).
additional_notes: Mí is the stressed form of 'me' used after prepositions (e.g., detrás de mí = 'behind me', por mí = 'for me', después de mí = 'after me'). 'Por favor' adds politeness and can go at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Ven después de mí, por favor.
native_language_example: Come after me, please.

meaning: myself (often for emphasis, after a preposition).
additional_notes: Used with prepositions like de/a/para/por/en: de mí (mismo) = “of me (myself)”, a mí (mismo) = “to me (myself)”. The word mismo adds emphasis (“myself” vs just “me”). Note the accent: mí (pronoun “me”) vs mi (possessive “my”).
target_language_example: Tengo que cuidar de mí mismo.
native_language_example: I have to take care of myself.

additional_notes: Imperative command (tú) meaning “look at me in the eyes,” often used to ask for attention, honesty, or seriousness. It’s a direct request and can sound intense depending on tone. Variants: "Mira" (informal tú), "Mírame" (look at me), "Mírame a la cara" (look me in the face), "Míreme a los ojos" (formal usted).
target_language_example: Mírame a los ojos y dime la verdad.
native_language_example: Look me in the eyes and tell me the truth.

additional_notes: A common genre label for music (often Western art music) and composers like Beethoven or Bach. Usually used with verbs like escuchar/oir (to listen to) and gustar (to like): “Me gusta la música clásica.”
target_language_example: Cuando estudio, pongo música clásica para concentrarme.
native_language_example: When I study, I put on classical music to concentrate.

meaning: “music to my ears” (something very pleasing to hear).
additional_notes: Used as an idiomatic reaction when someone says good news or something you really want to hear. Often said on its own ("Música para mis oídos") or with "Eso es..."/"Es...". It can be used literally about music too, but it’s most common as a figurative expression.
target_language_example: Si de verdad vas a ayudarme, eso es música para mis oídos.
native_language_example: If you’re really going to help me, that’s music to my ears.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone was born. It’s the 3rd-person singular, past tense of "nacer" (to be born): "él/ella/usted nació". Follow it with a place (city, country, etc.). For "I was born in...": "nací en..."
target_language_example: Mi abuela nació en México.
native_language_example: My grandmother was born in Mexico.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was born in a place and spent their childhood there. It’s the past tense (3rd person singular) of the verbs nacer (to be born) and crecer (to grow up). You can change the subject: nací y crecí (I), naciste y creciste (you), nacieron y crecieron (they). Often followed by en + place.
target_language_example: Mi abuela nació y creció en un pueblo pequeño.
native_language_example: My grandmother was born and grew up in a small town.

additional_notes: "Nací" is the preterite (simple past) of "nacer" (to be born) for "yo". Use "nací en" before a location: a country, city, or even an unusual place ("en un taxi").
target_language_example: Nací en Nueva York, pero vivo en Miami.
native_language_example: I was born in New York, but I live in Miami.

additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay something: “that’s his opinion, that’s all” (…nada más). It can also mean “just like that / simply” (así nada más). With an action in time, it can mean “as soon as”: “Nada más + infinitive” = “as soon as (someone) does something” (Nada más conocerse = as soon as they met).
target_language_example: Dame agua nada más, por favor.
native_language_example: Just give me water, please.

additional_notes: Used with a negative verb (e.g., no saber / no recordar / no decir) to emphasize that there is zero information or mention about something. Often appears as “no… nada acerca de…”. Similar to “nada sobre…”.
target_language_example: No sé nada acerca de ese problema.
native_language_example: I don't know anything about that problem.

meaning: “nothing about it/that” (no information or comment regarding something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like saber, decir, comentar, or negar to mean you know/say/comment “nothing about” a topic. Often appears with another negative word (no, nadie) in Spanish: “no… nada al respecto”, “nadie… nada al respecto”.
target_language_example: No sé nada al respecto, lo siento.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about it, sorry.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or clause to mean “none of it/any of it.” Often used as a firm command: “¡Nada de + noun!” = “No + noun!” (e.g., “Nada de excusas” = “No excuses.”). Also appears in “nada de lo que…” (“none of what…”) and “nada de + possessive + noun” (“none of my/your…”).
target_language_example: ¡Nada de quejas, por favor!
native_language_example: No complaining, please!

additional_notes: Used to say that no part of the current situation/thing(s) is included or matters. Often appears in negative or emotional statements (e.g., nada de esto importa; nada de esto hubiera pasado). You can also say it alone (“Nada de esto.”) to reject or dismiss what’s being discussed.
target_language_example: No entiendo nada de esto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand any of this.

meaning: “nothing about the galaxy of …” (you don’t know anything about …).
additional_notes: Used with a specific galaxy name: “la galaxia de Andrómeda”, “la galaxia de la Vía Láctea”, etc. The core pattern is “no saber nada de + [noun/topic]” = “to not know anything about + [topic]”. “de la galaxia de” is just the “about the galaxy of …” part.
target_language_example: No sé nada de la galaxia de Andrómeda.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about the Andromeda galaxy.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero things from a group (usually things said, heard, done, or understood) apply. It’s followed by a verb clause: “nada de lo que + verb” (often with past: había dicho, escuché, decía). Common in negative statements and emphasizes “not any of it.”
target_language_example: No entendí nada de lo que explicó el profesor.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand any of what the teacher explained.

meaning: "nothing in the world" (used for strong emphasis: "nothing at all").
additional_notes: Often used in comparisons to express that something is loved/liked more than anything else: "más que (a) nada en el mundo" / "más que nada en el mundo". With verbs like "gustar" or "querer/amar," you may see the personal "a" before "nada" ("más que a nada en el mundo"), especially when it's treated like the object of affection.
target_language_example: No hay nada en el mundo que me haga más feliz que estar contigo.
native_language_example: There’s nothing in the world that makes me happier than being with you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize priorities or values. It’s followed by a noun (“…que la salud”) or a verb in the infinitive (“…que dormir bien”). You can add context first (e.g., “En la vida, …”).
target_language_example: Para mí, nada es más importante que pasar tiempo con mi familia.
native_language_example: For me, nothing is more important than spending time with my family.

additional_notes: Common after a negative: "no hizo nada malo" = "he/she didn’t do anything wrong." It can also be used in predictions: "nada malo pasaría" = "nothing bad would happen."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no has hecho nada malo.
native_language_example: Relax, you haven’t done anything wrong.

additional_notes: Used to limit something to just one thing. Common patterns: **no... nada más que + infinitive** ("do nothing but...") and **no... nada más que + noun** ("have nothing but..."). **Nada más que** can also mean "nothing more than" to downplay something ("he was nothing more than a liar").
target_language_example: Hoy no hice nada más que trabajar.
native_language_example: Today I did nothing but work.

additional_notes: Used to end a discussion or indicate you have finished speaking. Often appears as "No tengo nada más que decir" (I have nothing more to say) or "No hay nada más que decir" (There’s nothing more to say). Can also be said alone: "Nada más que decir."
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada más que decir.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I have nothing more to say.

meaning: "nothing that…" (introduces a clause describing what doesn’t exist / doesn’t happen).
additional_notes: Used before a relative clause with **que** to mean “nothing that…/nothing which…”. It often appears in negative or limiting contexts: **No hay nada que…** (“There’s nothing that…”), **No dijo nada que…** (“She didn’t say anything that…”). After **nada que**, Spanish frequently uses the **subjunctive** because it refers to something non-existent or unspecified: **No hay nada que pueda hacer** (“There’s nothing I can do”). Common fixed expression: **no dejar nada que desear** = “to leave nothing to be desired” (to be excellent).
target_language_example: No hay nada que pueda hacer ahora.
native_language_example: There’s nothing I can do now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no comment, no response, or nothing relevant to add. Often appears with verbs like tener (“to have”) or haber (“there is/are”): “No tengo nada que decir” (I have nothing to say), “No hay nada que decir” (There’s nothing to say).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada que decir sobre ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to say about that topic.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no tasks, plans, or obligations at the moment. Often appears after verbs like tener (“to have”) or haber (“there is/was”): “No tengo nada que hacer” (I have nothing to do), “No había nada que hacer” (There was nothing to do / Nothing could be done). In “No había nada que hacer salvo…” it means “there was nothing to do except…”.
target_language_example: Hoy no tengo nada que hacer, así que voy a descansar en casa.
native_language_example: Today I have nothing to do, so I’m going to rest at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no secrets or wrongdoing. Often appears with tener (to have): “No tengo nada que ocultar” = “I have nothing to hide.” You may also see it with queda/quedar (“nothing left to hide”).
target_language_example: Puedes revisar mi bolso; no tengo nada que ocultar.
native_language_example: You can check my bag; I have nothing to hide.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no risk or that the situation can’t really get worse, so it’s worth trying. Often appears after a form of "tener" (tengo/tienes/tenemos…): "No tenemos nada que perder." Also common in sayings like "Quien no tiene nada, no tiene nada que perder."
target_language_example: Inténtalo: no tienes nada que perder.
native_language_example: Try it—you have nothing to lose.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no possible action or solution. Often appears in the common structure “No hay nada que puedas hacer …” and is followed by phrases like “al respecto” (about it) or “por él/ella” (for him/her). Uses the subjunctive “puedas” after “nada que…”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que puedas hacer para cambiar la decisión.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, there’s nothing you can do to change the decision.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that there is no danger or reason to be afraid. Very common after "no hay" or "no tienes" (e.g., "No hay nada que temer" / "No tienes nada que temer").
target_language_example: Tranquilo: aquí no hay nada que temer.
native_language_example: Relax: there’s nothing to fear here.

meaning: “nothing to do with it / nothing to see / not related at all.”
additional_notes: Commonly used to say something is unrelated or that you had no involvement: “No tengo nada que ver en ese asunto” = “I have nothing to do with that matter.” Also used as a short reaction meaning “That has nothing to do with it” / “Not at all.” In “No hay nada que ver,” it literally means there’s nothing to look at (nothing to see). Often intensified with “absolutamente”: “no tuvo absolutamente nada que ver.”
target_language_example: Lo que dices no tiene nada que ver con el problema.
native_language_example: What you’re saying has nothing to do with the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say there is zero knowledge, information, or mention about something/someone. Very often appears with another negative word: **no ... nada sobre ...** (Spanish uses double negatives). For people, it commonly follows **nada sobre + mí/ti/él/ella/nosotros**.
target_language_example: No encontré nada sobre el restaurante en internet.
native_language_example: I didn’t find anything about the restaurant online.

additional_notes: Used to say that no information was told/mentioned/heard regarding the accident. Often appears with verbs like contar (to tell), decir (to say/tell), escuchar (to hear), saber (to know), and with negatives like nunca/no: Spanish commonly uses double negatives (e.g., “Nunca me dijo nada…” = “He/She never told me anything…”).
target_language_example: No sé nada sobre el accidente.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about the accident.

additional_notes: "Nadando" is the gerund of "nadar" (to swim) and is used to describe an action in progress (often with "estar": "está nadando") or an activity someone did/enjoyed (e.g., "disfruté nadando..."). "En el río" means the location: in the river.
target_language_example: Estamos nadando en el río ahora mismo.
native_language_example: We’re swimming in the river right now.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action happening now (often with estar: "está/están nadando en la piscina") or an activity someone was doing in the past (with estar in the imperfect: "estuvo/estaba nadando..."). "Nadando" is the gerund (-ing form) of "nadar" (to swim), and "la piscina" means "the pool."
target_language_example: Mis amigos están nadando en la piscina ahora.
native_language_example: My friends are swimming in the pool right now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about swimming in a river (not a pool or the sea). You can change the person/tense of the verb (nado, nadas, nada, nadamos, nadan; nadé, nadaba; etc.). With permission or possibility, it often appears with phrases like “Me dejan…” (They let me…) or “Podría…” (I could…).
target_language_example: En verano, a veces vamos a nadar en el río.
native_language_example: In summer, sometimes we go to swim in the river.

additional_notes: A literal phrase: the verb "nadar" (to swim) + "en" (in) + "este río" (this river). It’s often used with safety or rules, e.g. "Es (muy) peligroso..." (It’s (very) dangerous...) or "No está permitido..." (It’s not allowed...). You can also talk about habits in the past with "solía" (used to): "Yo solía nadar..."
target_language_example: No deberías nadar en este río; hay mucha corriente.
native_language_example: You shouldn't swim in this river; there's a strong current.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have a person you can go to when you need help, advice, or support. It’s built with a relative clause: “nadie” + “a quien” (to whom) + “acudir” (to turn/go for help). Often followed by something like “que me ayude / que me aconseje”.
target_language_example: En esta ciudad no tengo a nadie a quien acudir si tengo un problema.
native_language_example: In this city, I don’t have anyone to turn to if I have a problem.

additional_notes: Used when **nadie** (“nobody”) is followed by the indirect object pronoun **le** (“to him/her/you [formal]”). It often appears in negative contexts and **le** comes before the verb: *nadie le escucha* = “nobody listens to him/her.” Depending on the verb, English may translate it as “nobody **helps him/her**,” “nobody **listens to him/her**,” “nobody **bothers him/her**,” etc.
target_language_example: A nadie le importa lo que digo.
native_language_example: Nobody cares about what I say.

additional_notes: From "creer" (to believe). "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/her/you (usted)”; you can add the person with "a": "Nadie le creyó a Kevin". Often used when someone says something but others think it’s not true.
target_language_example: Le conté la verdad, pero nadie le creyó.
native_language_example: I told him the truth, but nobody believed him.

additional_notes: Used when you are the person affected and “no one” does something to you. It’s typically followed by a verb: “nadie me contestó” (no one answered me), “nadie me reconocía” (no one recognized me), “nadie me creyó” (no one believed me), “nadie me escuchó” (no one listened to me).
target_language_example: Llamé varias veces, pero nadie me respondió.
native_language_example: I called several times, but no one answered me.

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s impossible for any person to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie puede + verb": Nadie puede oír/enseñar/negar/usar). In conversation it can also be left unfinished for emphasis ("Nadie puede, después de lo que hice"), implying "...do that / accept that / forgive me," etc. For plural or formal contexts you may also hear "nadie puede" with "nadie" meaning "nobody" in general (always singular in Spanish).
target_language_example: Nadie puede ayudarte si no dices la verdad.
native_language_example: No one can help you if you don’t tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person wants something. Often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie quiere morir"), a noun ("Nadie quiere una guerra"), or "que" + subjunctive to express what nobody wants to happen ("Nadie quiere que pase eso").
target_language_example: Nadie quiere esperar tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to wait that long.

additional_notes: Common in news or after accidents to say there were no injuries. "Resultar herido" means "to end up injured"; you can add details like "de gravedad" (seriously) or "por..." (by/from...). In other tenses: "nadie ha resultado herido" (no one has been injured).
target_language_example: Hubo un accidente, pero nadie resultó herido.
native_language_example: There was an accident, but no one was injured.

additional_notes: Commonly followed by a question word or clause describing what is unknown: nadie sabe + dónde/qué/cuánto/si... You can also use it with a noun: Nadie sabe su nombre. It’s a straightforward statement (not a question) and is often used to emphasize that information is unknown or secret.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe cuándo va a llegar el tren.
native_language_example: Nobody knows when the train will arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say that a fact is unknown to everyone (often implying it’s secret or not widely known). It’s followed by a clause introduced by que + a verb (usually in the indicative): Nadie sabe que vivo aquí.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe que estoy estudiando español.
native_language_example: No one knows that I’m studying Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to express that nobody knows what to say/what happened/what became of someone. It’s often followed by an infinitive ("Nadie sabe qué decir") or by a verb clause ("Nadie sabe qué le pasó"). Note the accent in “qué” when it means “what” in an indirect question.
target_language_example: Nadie sabe qué hacer ahora.
native_language_example: No one knows what to do now.

additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence/clause meaning “nobody/no one …” when the verb uses **se**. The **se** can be reflexive or part of a pronominal verb (a verb that commonly goes with se), and it comes before the conjugated verb: *Nadie se rió* (Nobody laughed), *Nadie se dio cuenta* (Nobody realized). If there are extra pronouns like **lo/la/los/las**, they also go before the verb: *Nadie se lo cree* (Nobody believes it).
target_language_example: Nadie se acordó de llamarme.
native_language_example: Nobody remembered to call me.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of "darse cuenta (de)" = "to notice/realize". Often followed by "de" + noun/phrase: "Nadie se dio cuenta de mi nuevo corte de pelo" (Nobody noticed my new haircut). You can also leave it implied: "Nadie se dio cuenta" (Nobody noticed).
target_language_example: Nadie se dio cuenta de que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Nobody realized that we arrived late.

additional_notes: "Nadie" is a negative pronoun meaning "no one." "Te" is the object pronoun for "you" (tú), meaning "you" as the person receiving the action ("you," "to you"). It’s commonly followed by another object pronoun: e.g., "Nadie te lo ha dicho" = "No one has told you (it)." With "nadie" before the verb, you normally don’t add "no" ("Nadie te obliga," not *"No nadie te obliga").
target_language_example: Nadie te entiende cuando hablas tan rápido.
native_language_example: No one understands you when you talk so fast.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody will do a future action. It’s formed with nadie (“no one”) + ir a + infinitive (a very common way to talk about the near future). Often used to reassure someone (Nadie va a buscarte) or to emphasize that something won’t happen.
target_language_example: Nadie va a ayudarte si no lo pides.
native_language_example: No one is going to help you if you don’t ask for it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a vehicle that travels in space. Most common with the article (la/una) and with verbs like aparecer (to appear) or estar a bordo de (to be on board). You may also see the more technical synonym “nave espacial” = “spacecraft” in news/science contexts.
target_language_example: Vimos una nave espacial en el museo.
native_language_example: We saw a spacecraft in the museum.

additional_notes: Used to express a necessity or strong requirement. "Necesidad de + infinitive" = need to do something (La necesidad de aprender). "Necesidad de + noun" = need for something (necesidad de amor). "Verse en la necesidad de + infinitive" means "to find yourself having to" (often because of circumstances).
target_language_example: Tengo necesidad de descansar un poco.
native_language_example: I need to rest a bit.

additional_notes: "Necesita" is the usted (formal you) form and also the he/she form of "necesitar" (to need). Used to say someone needs help or to politely offer help: "Si necesita ayuda, dígame" = "If you need help, tell me." For "I need help": "Necesito ayuda." For "Do you (informal) need help?": "¿Necesitas ayuda?"
target_language_example: Si necesita ayuda, puedo explicárselo otra vez.
native_language_example: If you need help, I can explain it to you again.

additional_notes: Used with the verb necesitar in the third-person singular (necesita) to say that someone or something needs one of something. Usually followed by a masculine singular noun (un trabajo) or by a noun phrase like "un poco de" (un poco de aire). For feminine nouns, use "necesita una" (e.g., "necesita una pausa").
target_language_example: Mi coche necesita un lavado.
native_language_example: My car needs a wash.

meaning: "I need to talk to / speak with" (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you must speak with a specific person or group. Follow it with a person, pronoun (él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted/ustedes), or an institution (la policía, mi abogado). You can add time/urgency words like "primero" (first) or "ahora mismo" (right now).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con usted un momento.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say you want a conversation with someone. It can sound serious depending on tone and context. You can add details: de algo (about something), en privado (in private), un minuto (for a minute), or a place (en mi oficina). Also common with a name: "Tom, necesito hablar contigo".
target_language_example: Necesito hablar contigo en privado, por favor.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you in private, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater amount of something. Typically followed by a noun (necesito más práctica) or a quantity/measure (necesito más tiempo). You can also add "de" before an uncountable noun: "necesito más de agua" (though "necesito más agua" is more common).
target_language_example: Necesito más tiempo para terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: I need more time to finish the work.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone else to do something. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: "Necesito que firmes", "Necesito que veas", "Necesito que te quedes". With "yo" (I), the subjunctive form often looks different from the normal present (e.g., "hagas" not "haces").
target_language_example: Necesito que me llames mañana.
native_language_example: I need you to call me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you. It uses the present subjunctive after “necesito que” because it expresses a need/wish about another person’s action. “Hagas” is the tú form of “hacer” (to do/make). You can add details like “por mí” (for me) or “primero” (first).
target_language_example: Necesito que hagas algo hoy, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to do something today, please.

meaning: "I need you to" (do something to/for me).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you need, followed by a verb in the present subjunctive because it comes after "necesitar que". The "me" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to/for me" (or sometimes the person affected). Common patterns: "Necesito que me + verb" (Necesito que me ayudes / llamen / dejen / lleven). You can often drop "me" if the action isn’t directed at you: "Necesito que respondas" vs. "Necesito que me respondas" (answer me).
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esto, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this, please.

meaning: I need you to help me.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for help. After “necesito que…”, Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive: “ayudes” (from “ayudar”). You can add what you need help with using “a + infinitive” (e.g., “a encontrarlo/a hacerlo”).
target_language_example: Necesito que me ayudes con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this homework assignment.

additional_notes: Used to express that you require some information. Often followed by a question word like dónde (where), por qué (why), qué (what), quién (who), or a noun phrase: Necesito saber su nombre (I need to know his/her name).
target_language_example: Necesito saber a qué hora empieza la reunión.
native_language_example: I need to know what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes: Used when you’re asking for an explanation of what happened or what something is. It’s typically followed by a verb or clause: qué pasó/ocurrió/sucedió (what happened), qué significa (what it means), qué quieres (what you want). Note that the accent matters: qué = "what" (question/indirect question).
target_language_example: Necesito saber qué estás haciendo aquí.
native_language_example: I need to know what you’re doing here.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: "Necesito un + noun". Use "un" with masculine singular nouns (un cable, un bolígrafo, un visado). For feminine nouns, use "necesito una" (e.g., "Necesito una silla"). You can also add adjectives after the noun: "Necesito un cable nuevo".
target_language_example: Necesito un taxi, por favor.
native_language_example: I need a taxi, please.

additional_notes: Use it to ask for or state you need a small amount of something. It’s followed by a noun (usually uncountable: jabón, papel, información; but it can also be abstract like tiempo). You can make it more polite by adding “por favor”: “Necesito un poco de agua, por favor.”
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de ayuda con esta tarea.
native_language_example: I need a little help with this homework.

additional_notes: Used to ask for assistance politely. You can add location or detail: “Necesito un poco de ayuda aquí” (here). You can also say who you need help from: “Necesito un poco de ayuda tuya” (I need a little help from you). In more urgent situations you might say “Necesito ayuda” without “un poco de.”
target_language_example: Perdón, necesito un poco de ayuda con esta puerta.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need a little help with this door.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: necesito (I need) + una (a/an). Use it before feminine singular nouns: una ambulancia, una bicicleta, una habitación. For masculine nouns, use "necesito un" (e.g., necesito un médico). You can drop "yo" because the verb form already shows who needs it.
target_language_example: Necesito una mesa para la cocina.
native_language_example: I need a table for the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to deny a past action or experience: **negar + haber + past participle**. The verb **negar** is conjugated (here, **negó** = 'he/she denied'), and **haber** introduces a completed past action (like English 'having done'). Common after this: *negó haber dicho* (denied having said), *negó haber sabido* (denied having known).
target_language_example: Ella negó haber tomado el dinero.
native_language_example: She denied having taken the money.

additional_notes: Used with **negar** (to deny) + **haber** + past participle to deny a past action: *negó haber robado…* = “denied having stolen…”. The noun that was allegedly stolen comes after **el** (or **la/los/las**): *negó haber robado el dinero / la cartera*.
target_language_example: El hombre negó haber robado el reloj.
native_language_example: The man denied having stolen the watch.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is surprising or below the minimum expected. Often appears before the verb ("ni siquiera se dio cuenta") or before what’s being emphasized ("ni siquiera me acuerdo", "ni siquiera debería tocarlo"). It can be followed by "si" for hypothetical emphasis: "ni siquiera si..." (“not even if...”).
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; ni siquiera he comido hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; I haven’t even eaten today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is far from being true/achieved. Very common in comparisons like “no estar ni cerca de + noun/infinitive” (to be nowhere near + noun/doing something). It can also appear in contrasts like “ni cerca ni lejos” (neither close nor far).
target_language_example: Todavía no está ni cerca de terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: He’s still not even close to finishing the project.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (often "no") to emphasize that someone doesn’t know or understand something at all: "no tengo ni idea de..." / "no tienes ni idea de...". It’s commonly followed by a noun ("ni idea de la hora") or by "lo que / quién / qué / cuál(es)" + a clause ("ni idea de quién fue").
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de dónde está mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my phone is.

meaning: "Don’t you dare" / "Don’t even think about it."
additional_notes: A strong warning or command telling someone not to do something. Often followed by an infinitive: "Ni se te ocurra decirlo" (Don’t you dare say it). You may also hear "Que ni se te ocurra" for extra emphasis. Uses the verb "ocurrirse" (for an idea to occur to someone) with an indirect object pronoun: "se te" = "to you."
target_language_example: Ni se te ocurra tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t you dare touch that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen at all: not even trying/thinking/reading it. "Ni siquiera" = "not even"; "lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him/that"). Often followed by a verb: "Ni siquiera lo + verb".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I don’t even understand it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen at all, not even in the most basic or expected way. It’s often followed by a verb: “ni siquiera me conoces” (you don’t even know me), “ni siquiera me miras” (you don’t even look at me), “ni siquiera me estás escuchando” (you’re not even listening to me). You can move it for emphasis: “Tú ni siquiera me conoces.”
target_language_example: Ni siquiera me llamaste para avisar.
native_language_example: You didn’t even call me to let me know.

meaning: "I don't even know" / "I don't even know (that...)"
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you don’t know something at all, often showing surprise, frustration, or that you lack basic information. It’s commonly followed by a question word or clause: "ni siquiera sé qué...", "ni siquiera sé lo que...", "ni siquiera sé cómo...", "ni siquiera sé a qué...".
target_language_example: Ni siquiera sé dónde dejé las llaves.
native_language_example: I don't even know where I left the keys.

meaning: “not a cent; not even one cent” (nothing at all).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero amount of money. Common in phrases like “ni un centavo más” (“not a cent more”) or “no tener ni un centavo” (“to not have a cent / to be broke”). “Centavo” is the smallest coin unit in many Spanish-speaking countries.
target_language_example: No pienso pagarte ni un centavo más.
native_language_example: I’m not going to pay you one cent more.

meaning: not even a single; not a single (one).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero quantity, often with a negative idea (no, nunca, nadie, etc.) or in negative contexts. It’s a strong way to say “not one” of something: “No vi ni un solo… / Nunca… ni un solo…”. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: ni un solo día (masc.), ni una sola vez (fem.).
target_language_example: No tengo ni un solo minuto libre hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have a single free minute today.

meaning: not even one; not a single (feminine).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize zero amount of something, often after a negative word like "no" (e.g., "No queda ni una..."). It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: "ni una gota" (fem.), "ni un minuto" (masc.). It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “not one.”
target_language_example: No tengo ni una idea de cómo hacerlo.
native_language_example: I don’t have even one idea of how to do it.

meaning: not a word; not a single word.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize total silence or that someone said nothing at all, often with negatives like "no" ("No dijo ni una palabra"). It can also be used as a command: "Ni una palabra más" = "Not another word."
target_language_example: No digas ni una palabra hasta que lleguemos a casa.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word until we get home.

additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis to mean “not even one.” It agrees in gender/number with the noun: ni un solo día (not a single day), ni una sola persona (not a single person). Often appears with other negatives like no/nunca, and can also be used with time expressions: ni una sola vez (not once).
target_language_example: No vi ni una sola señal de vida.
native_language_example: I didn’t see a single sign of life.

meaning: not a single word (none at all).
additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis with negatives like no, jamás, sin, or questions/short answers. Can refer to understanding (“I didn’t understand a thing”), speaking (“without saying a word”), believing (“I didn’t believe a word he said”), or the absence of something said (“not a single word of thanks”). Often works as a standalone comment: “Ni una sola palabra.”
target_language_example: No entendí ni una sola palabra de la película.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a single word of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is surprising or below the minimum expected. Often appears before the verb ("ni siquiera se dio cuenta") or before what’s being emphasized ("ni siquiera me acuerdo", "ni siquiera debería tocarlo"). It can be followed by "si" for hypothetical emphasis: "ni siquiera si..." (“not even if...”).
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; ni siquiera he comido hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; I haven’t even eaten today.

additional_notes: Used with negatives (no, nadie, nunca, etc.) to mean “nowhere / not anywhere.” Common patterns: **a ninguna parte** with movement verbs (ir, salir, llevar) = “(to) nowhere / not anywhere,” and **en ninguna parte** for location = “nowhere.” Also appears in the set phrase **en medio de ninguna parte** = “in the middle of nowhere.”
target_language_example: No encuentro mis llaves en ninguna parte.
native_language_example: I can’t find my keys anywhere.

additional_notes: Used when talking about two feminine things (e.g., dos cartas, dos opciones) to say that not one of them applies/was done. It can also be used alone as a short answer: “¿Cuál prefieres?” — “Ninguna de las dos.” For masculine nouns, use “ninguno de los dos”.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres té o café? — Ninguna de las dos; prefiero agua.
native_language_example: Do you want tea or coffee? — Neither; I prefer water.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people/things in a group apply. It’s followed by a noun phrase (often with a definite/possessive: "ninguno de los...", "ninguno de mis...") or by a pronoun: "ninguno de ellos". Often appears with "no" when it comes before a verb: "No conozco a ninguno de..." (double negation is normal in Spanish). "Ninguno" can change to feminine "ninguna" if the noun is feminine: "ninguna de las...".
target_language_example: No he visto a ninguno de mis vecinos hoy.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen any of my neighbors today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a group of people/things and say that zero of them do something or apply. Often appears with “no” in the sentence (double negative in Spanish): “No conozco a ninguno de ellos.” You can also use it as a subject: “Ninguno de ellos sabe…”. For feminine groups, use “ninguna de ellas” (none of them, women/things).
target_language_example: Ninguno de ellos quiere ir hoy.
native_language_example: None of them want to go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people/things in a specific group meet a condition. It’s normally followed by a plural noun: "ninguno de los candidatos". You can also use it with pronouns like "ninguno de los presentes" (“none of the people present”). With feminine plural nouns, it changes to "ninguna de las" (e.g., "ninguna de las opciones").
target_language_example: Ninguno de los estudiantes llegó a tiempo.
native_language_example: None of the students arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero out of two people/things apply. It agrees in gender/number with what it refers to: masculine singular is most common (ninguno), but with feminine nouns you often use “ninguna de las dos” (e.g., Ninguna de las dos opciones es buena). Often answers a choice between two: “¿Té o café?” — “Ninguno de los dos.”
target_language_example: ¿Quieres pollo o pescado? — Ninguno de los dos; soy vegetariano.
native_language_example: Do you want chicken or fish? — Neither; I’m vegetarian.

meaning: none of us; not one of us.
additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group “we/us” did something or are something. It’s normally followed by a singular verb (Ninguno de nosotros es / puede / tiene), although plural agreement can appear in some contexts. For mixed genders, Spanish typically uses the masculine form ninguno; for an all-female group you may hear ninguna de nosotras (“none of us [women]”).
target_language_example: Ninguno de nosotros entiende la pregunta.
native_language_example: None of us understand the question.

additional_notes: Means “no place.” It’s commonly used with negation words like no, nadie, nunca (e.g., “No voy a ningún lado” = “I’m not going anywhere”). You’ll also hear it after “ni” in the pattern “Ni aquí ni en ningún lado” (“Neither here nor anywhere”).
target_language_example: Hoy no salgo a ningún lado porque tengo mucho trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going anywhere because I have a lot of work.

meaning: a little girl; a young girl.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a female child. "Niña" means "girl" and "pequeña" means "small/little"; together it’s a common way to emphasize that the girl is young. You can also say "una niña" or "una niña chica" in some regions.
target_language_example: Esa niña pequeña está jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: That little girl is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say what children are doing or what state they’re in right now. "Están" is the present tense, ellos/ellas/ustedes form of "estar" (to be). It’s often followed by a gerund (-ando/-iendo) for actions in progress: "Los niños están nadando" = "The children are swimming."
target_language_example: Los niños están jugando en el parque.
native_language_example: The children are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Refers to children who are very young (often toddlers or early elementary age). Used as a noun phrase ("the little/young kids"). You can also say "los niños pequeños" = "the young children."
target_language_example: En este parque hay muchos niños pequeños.
native_language_example: In this park there are lots of young children.

additional_notes: Repeating **no** is a common way to add emphasis or sound more firm/polite when disagreeing or refusing. It often comes at the start of a sentence, followed by the verb: **No, no + verb** (e.g., *No, no necesito…*).
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today.

meaning: "No, I don’t / it isn’t (it hasn’t been / I’m not)."
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or correct something, often before a verb that takes the object pronoun “lo” (“it/that”). The second “no” adds emphasis or can sound like a quick self-correction: “No—no, I don’t.” Common with verbs like comprender (understand), ser/estar (to be), and haber sido (have been).
target_language_example: No, no lo sé.
native_language_example: No, I don’t know it.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., No creo que sea…, No creo que haga…). Often you can drop “que” in English: “I don’t think it’s necessary.”
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to politely express doubt or disagreement about an action. After "creo que" (I think that), Spanish often uses the present subjunctive in the next verb when it’s negated: "debamos" is the subjunctive of "deber" (to have to / should). Typically followed by an infinitive or clause: "No creo que debamos + infinitive" (e.g., hacerlo, ir, entrar).
target_language_example: No creo que debamos hablar de eso ahora.
native_language_example: I don’t think we should talk about that now.

meaning: "I don’t think that" / "I don’t believe that."
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement about what was just mentioned. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (e.g., pase, sea, suceda, vaya a pasar) because you’re talking about something uncertain or not confirmed.
target_language_example: No creo que eso funcione.
native_language_example: I don’t think that will work.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt/uncertainty. After a negative opinion like “no creo que…”, Spanish normally uses the subjunctive. Here, “haya + participle” is the present perfect subjunctive (haya dicho/hecho/entendido/salido, etc.). Often translates naturally as “I don’t think (he/she/they) has…” or “I don’t think there has been…”.
target_language_example: No creo que haya terminado el trabajo todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t think (he/she/they) has finished the work yet.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt/uncertainty. After a negative opinion like “no creo que…”, Spanish normally uses the subjunctive. Here, “haya + participle” is the present perfect subjunctive (haya dicho/hecho/entendido/salido, etc.). Often translates naturally as “I don’t think (he/she/they) has…” or “I don’t think there has been…”.
target_language_example: No creo que haya terminado el trabajo todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t think (he/she/they) has finished the work yet.

meaning: "I don’t think (that) … it" / "I don’t believe (that) … it."
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., entienda, hagan, haya hecho, supiera) because the speaker is not stating it as a fact. "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" or "him" (sometimes "her"), referring to something already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: No creo que lo sepan todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t think they know it yet.

additional_notes: Used to say you doubt you’re able to do something. After expressions like “creo que / no creo que”, Spanish uses the subjunctive (here, “pueda” from “poder”). Often followed by an infinitive: “No creo que pueda hacerlo/ir/volver.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no creo que pueda ir mañana.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t think I can go tomorrow.

meaning: "I don’t think it is" / "I don’t believe it is" (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief about something. Because "creer" is negated ("no creo"), Spanish normally uses the present subjunctive after "que" (here: "sea" from "ser"). Often followed by an adjective or a noun clause: "No creo que sea correcto" / "No creo que sea eso."
target_language_example: No creo que sea una buena idea.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, a recommendation, or a mild warning/reproach. It uses the conditional of deber (deberías), which often sounds like a suggestion rather than a strict order. Followed by an infinitive: “No deberías + infinitive” (e.g., no deberías decir, venir, hacer).
target_language_example: No deberías conducir tan rápido.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t drive so fast.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not supposed to be in a place (because it’s not allowed, it’s unsafe, or it’s not the right time). Commonly followed by a time clause like “cuando…” (when…) or “durante…” (during…). Uses the conditional of deber (deberías) to give advice/soft obligation; stronger alternatives include “no puedes estar aquí” (you can’t be here).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no deberías estar aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, you shouldn’t be here right now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something is not allowed or not advisable. It’s the negative of “debes” (from deber), and it’s often followed by an infinitive: “No debes fumar.” It can sound like a rule/obligation (“must not”) or advice (“shouldn’t”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No debes hablar durante la prueba.
native_language_example: You mustn’t/shouldn’t talk during the test.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to prevent something from happening. It’s the negative command (tú) of **dejar** (“to let/allow”) + **que** + a verb in the **subjunctive**: *No dejes que entre.* (“Don’t let him/her come in.”).
target_language_example: No dejes que te hablen así.
native_language_example: Don’t let them talk to you like that.

additional_notes: Negative tú command of decir (“to say/tell”), used to tell one person not to say something: No digas eso (“Don’t say that”). It can also be an exclamation meaning “No way!” or “You don’t say!” (showing surprise), often said as ¡No digas! or ¡No me digas! (“You’re kidding!”).
target_language_example: No digas eso, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t say that, please.

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) used to tell one person to stay quiet or keep a secret. Often used with names or “por favor”: “No digas nada, por favor.”
target_language_example: No digas nada cuando llegue mi mamá.
native_language_example: Don’t say anything when my mom arrives.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of decir: no + dijo + nada. Often used to describe someone staying silent or not commenting in a specific moment. You can add context with phrases like “en absoluto” (at all) or “con respecto a…” (regarding…).
target_language_example: Le pregunté qué pasó, pero no dijo nada.
native_language_example: I asked him/her what happened, but he/she didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Used to express confusion or disagreement about the reason for something. Often followed by a clause (por qué + subject + verb): “No entiendo por qué lo hiciste.” It can also be used before a noun phrase to mean “why so much/so many”: “No entiendo por qué tanto alboroto.” (Note: “por qué” = “why” in questions/indirect questions; “porque” = “because”.)
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué no me lo dijiste antes.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you didn’t tell me earlier.

additional_notes: *No era* is the negative of **era** (imperfect past of **ser**, “to be”). Use it to say someone/something **was not** a certain identity, description, or characteristic in the past (often background info or a continuing past situation): *Tom no era bueno* (“Tom wasn’t good”). For plural, use **no eran** (“they weren’t”).
target_language_example: De niño, no era muy alto.
native_language_example: As a kid, I wasn’t very tall.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb **ser** in the **tú** form (**eres**). It’s commonly followed by a noun or adjective: **No eres estudiante** (“You’re not a student”), **No eres creativo/a** (“You’re not creative”). For emphasis you may see **no eres más que...** (“you’re nothing more than...”).
target_language_example: No eres mi jefe.
native_language_example: You're not my boss.

meaning: "you are not a" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *ser* to say someone is not a certain type of person/thing (identity or description): *No eres un Nazi / un asesino / un sucesor adecuado.* For a feminine noun, use *no eres una* (e.g., *No eres una doctora*).
