With plural, use *no eres* + plural noun/adjective (e.g., *No eres mi amigo* / *No eres mi amigo* vs. *No eres mi amiga*).
target_language_example: No eres un problema; eres parte de la solución.
native_language_example: You’re not a problem; you’re part of the solution.

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb **ser** (to be) in the **he/she/it/you (formal)** present tense: **no + es**. Used to say something isn’t true about someone/something (e.g., identity, description, origin): *No es cierto*, *No es médico*, *No es de aquí*.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero eso no es verdad.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t happen often, isn’t normal/acceptable, or isn’t possible. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "No es algo que se haga" (It’s not something people do), "No es algo que se pueda enseñar" (It’s not something that can be taught).
target_language_example: No es algo que puedas resolver en un día.
native_language_example: It’s not something you can solve in a day.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone something doesn’t concern them. Often sounds firm or rude, especially said alone (“No es asunto tuyo.”). You can also use it with a clause: “No es asunto tuyo dónde estoy” = “Where I am is none of your business.” Variations: “no es asunto mío” (none of my business), “no es asunto nuestro” (none of our business).
target_language_example: No es asunto tuyo con quién salgo.
native_language_example: It’s none of your business who I’m dating.

meaning: “it’s not like that / that’s not true.”
additional_notes: Used to disagree or correct someone (“No, that’s not how it is”). It can also be used as a tag question (often with ¿…?) to ask for confirmation: “..., isn’t that right?” In questions it’s common to add the person’s name: “no es así, Damien?”
target_language_example: No, no es así; lo entendiste mal.
native_language_example: No, that’s not true; you misunderstood it.

meaning: “it’s not good” / “it’s not a good idea.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is bad quality (a road, a referee, a product) or to warn that an action is unhealthy, unsafe, or inappropriate. Often followed by an infinitive: “No es bueno + verb” (No es bueno fumar). You can add “para” to specify for whom: “No es bueno para ti.”
target_language_example: No es bueno conducir cuando estás cansado.
native_language_example: It’s not good to drive when you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a negative effect on a person, thing, or situation. Follow it with a noun or pronoun (para el bebé, para mí, para los negocios). You can also use it with an infinitive as the subject: "Fumar no es bueno para la salud."
target_language_example: Comer demasiada azúcar no es bueno para los dientes.
native_language_example: Eating too much sugar isn’t good for your teeth.

no es bueno para la salud

target_language_multi_word_term: no es bueno para la salud
additional_notes: Used to warn or advise that an action or habit is unhealthy. Often follows an activity: “Fumar no es bueno para la salud.” You can also add “tu/su” for “your/his/her/their”: “No es bueno para tu salud.”
target_language_example: Comer tanta azúcar no es bueno para la salud.
native_language_example: Eating that much sugar isn’t good for your health.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct something that was said or implied. Often appears with a tag question like “¿verdad?” or “¿no es cierto?” (similar to “right?” / “isn’t that so?”). You can also say “Eso no es cierto” = “That isn’t true.”
target_language_example: No es cierto; yo nunca dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I never said that.

meaning: “is not the …” / “it’s not the one who …”.
additional_notes: Used to negate an identity with the verb *ser*: *no es el/la/los/las + noun* (“is not the …”). It’s also common in contrast/emphasis structures: *No es el/la + noun/pronoun + quien/que + verb* (“It’s not the … who …”), often followed by *sino* (“but rather”). Gender/number changes: *no es el* (masc. singular), *no es la* (fem. singular), etc.
target_language_example: No es el profesor quien decide eso, sino el director.
native_language_example: It’s not the teacher who decides that, but the principal.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is difficult. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., “No es fácil estudiar”) or a clause about an activity (“No es fácil hablar una lengua extranjera”). You can also use it to comment on a person or situation: “No es fácil lidiar contigo.”
target_language_example: No es fácil levantarse temprano todos los días.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to get up early every day.

meaning: “it’s not what…” / “it’s not the same as…” (often: “it’s not what it used to be”).
additional_notes: Used to say something has changed or isn’t as good as before: “No es lo que era” = “It’s not what it used to be.” Also used to correct someone or clarify a misunderstanding: “No es lo que pregunté/oí” = “That’s not what I asked/heard.” It’s typically followed by a clause (e.g., “no es lo que pensé”) or by “era / solía ser.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante ya no es lo que era.
native_language_example: This restaurant isn’t what it used to be anymore.

meaning: “it’s not my …” (to say something doesn’t belong to you or isn’t your responsibility).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after it: “No es mi culpa” (It’s not my fault), “No es mi día” (It’s not my day), “No es mi especialidad” (It’s not my specialty). Often the full phrase is “Eso/Esa/Este/Esta no es mi …” = “That/This isn’t my …”.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es mi problema.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it’s not my problem.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes an adverb) to soften a negative evaluation: *no es muy + adj.* It can mean “not very” or, depending on tone, “not particularly.” You can change **es** to match the subject: *no soy muy*, *no eres muy*, *no somos muy*, etc.
target_language_example: La película no es muy buena, pero vale la pena verla.
native_language_example: The movie isn’t very good, but it’s worth watching.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something, often followed by a noun: No es más que + un/una + noun. Can sound dismissive depending on context (e.g., “No es más que una niña” = “She’s just a girl”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un rumor.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a rumor.

meaning: “it’s nothing more than a” / “it’s just a”.
additional_notes: Used to downplay or reduce something/someone to what the speaker considers its true or lesser nature. Often has a dismissive tone. It agrees with gender/number: no es más que un (masc. sing.), no es más que una (fem. sing.), no es más que unos/unas (plural).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: no es más que un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’s just a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t required. Often followed by a noun (No es necesario el algodón.) or by “que” + subjunctive to talk about an action (No es necesario que estés sola.). You can change the verb for other subjects/tense: No era necesario…, No será necesario….
target_language_example: No es necesario que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something cannot happen or cannot be done. Often followed by an infinitive (No es posible + verbo: “No es posible concebir…”) or by “que” + clause (No es posible que…: “It’s not possible that…” / “You can’t possibly…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no es posible terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s not possible to finish the project today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t meet a need, requirement, or expectation. Often followed by “para” + someone/something: “No es suficiente para mí” (It’s not enough for me). Can also be used alone as a complete sentence: “No es suficiente.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero eso no es suficiente para aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that’s not enough to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons or soften a statement. Often followed by an adjective/adverb and sometimes by "como" to compare: "no es tan + adjective + como…" ("not as… as…"). It can refer to something (no es) or a person (él/ella no es), depending on context.
target_language_example: No es tan difícil como parece.
native_language_example: It isn’t as difficult as it seems.

meaning: “isn’t as tall as” (not as tall as).
additional_notes: Used to compare height and say someone/something is less tall than another. Pattern: [subject] + no es tan + adjective + como + [comparison]. You can swap in other adjectives: no es tan grande como (not as big as), no es tan caro como (not as expensive as). In past comparisons you may see: no es tan alto como lo era/como era (not as tall as he/she/I used to be).
target_language_example: Esta silla no es tan alta como esa.
native_language_example: This chair isn’t as tall as that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty and say something is harder than it seems/than something else. Often followed by "parece" (it seems) or by another thing to compare with (e.g., "ese", "pensé").
target_language_example: Aprender español no es tan fácil como creía.
native_language_example: Learning Spanish isn’t as easy as I thought.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say the first one is less big than the second. Structure: [thing 1] + no es tan + adjective + como + [thing 2]. You can swap in other adjectives: no es tan caro como (isn’t as expensive as), no es tan rápido como (isn’t as fast as).
target_language_example: Este apartamento no es tan grande como el otro.
native_language_example: This apartment isn’t as big as the other one.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to say something does not belong to the person you’re talking to (possession/ownership) or that something is not their role/strength. It’s followed by a **singular noun**: *No es tu taza / No es tu fuerte.* For plural nouns, use **no son tus**: *No son tus llaves.* Note agreement with **es** (singular) vs **son** (plural), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no es tu asiento.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it isn't your seat.

additional_notes: Used to negate an identification or classification: “X no es un Y.” Use **no es una** for feminine nouns (e.g., *una idea*), and **no son** for plural (e.g., *no son unos/unas*). Often appears in contrasts with **sino** (“but rather”): *No es un lujo, sino una necesidad.*
target_language_example: Esto no es un juego.
native_language_example: This is not a game.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone does not belong to a category or is not described by a certain label: “No es una opción / excepción / vergüenza…”. It’s the negative form of “es una …”. For masculine nouns, you say “no es un …” (e.g., “No es un problema”).
target_language_example: Eso no es una buena idea.
native_language_example: That isn’t a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something is false or to contradict what someone said. Often followed by what isn’t true: “Lo que dijiste no es verdad” (“What you said isn’t true”). You can also use it on its own as a direct denial: “No es verdad, señor.”
target_language_example: No es verdad; yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: That’s not true; I didn’t say that.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar in the first person singular (yo) to say you are not in a certain state/condition (busy, interested, working, etc.), often temporary. Common patterns: no estoy + adjective (No estoy ocupado.) or no estoy + gerund (-ando/-iendo) for an action in progress (No estoy trabajando.). For more permanent identity/traits, Spanish often uses no soy (ser) instead.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no estoy disponible ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not available right now.

additional_notes: Used to express disagreement. Often followed by **con** + a person/idea: *No estoy de acuerdo con eso / con lo que dices.* You can soften it with phrases like *Con todo respeto,* before it.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no estoy de acuerdo contigo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I don’t agree with you.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty. It often appears by itself (“No estoy segura.”), with a time word like “todavía” (not yet), or followed by “de + infinitive” to mean you’re not sure about doing something: “No estoy segura de querer…” (I’m not sure I want to…). For a man: “No estoy seguro.”
target_language_example: No estoy segura de poder ir mañana.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I can go tomorrow.

meaning: "I’m not sure that..." (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express doubt/uncertainty about what follows. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "sea", "pueda", "tenga"). You can also say "No estoy seguro de que" if the speaker is a man. Often interchangeable with "No sé si..." in everyday speech.
target_language_example: No estoy segura de que podamos ir mañana.
native_language_example: I’m not sure we can go tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty. You can leave it alone (“No estoy seguro.” / “No estoy segura.”) or follow it with information like “pero…” (but…), “todavía” (yet), or an embedded question (“No estoy seguro qué…” / also common: “No estoy seguro de qué…”). “Seguro/segura” agrees with the speaker’s gender.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de la hora, pero puedo preguntar.
native_language_example: I’m not sure about the time, but I can ask.

additional_notes:
Used to express uncertainty. It’s followed by:
- a noun/idea: No estoy seguro de la hora.
- an indirect question: No estoy seguro de cuándo / qué / cómo…
- an infinitive: No estoy seguro de poder / ir / ganar…
- “que” + verb (often subjunctive): No estoy seguro de que me guste… (very common in speech). You can change the subject/person: No estamos seguros de…, ¿Estás seguro de…?
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de si mañana tenemos clase.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if we have class tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to negate *estar*: for temporary states/conditions (no está contenta), location/presence (no está aquí / no está cerca), availability (no está disponible), or ongoing actions with the gerund (no está usando…, no está siendo…). Often corresponds to “isn’t” or “is not” in English, but specifically with *estar* (not *ser*).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono no está cargado.
native_language_example: My phone isn’t charged.

meaning: "It’s not OK / it’s not right" or "it’s not well (in good condition)."
additional_notes: Used for (1) things that aren’t working or aren’t in good condition: "La mira no está bien" (the sight/scope isn’t working right), "La carretera no está bien" (the road isn’t in good condition); (2) people who don’t feel well: "No está bien, no quiere comer" (he/she isn’t well; he/she doesn’t want to eat); and (3) to say something is wrong or unacceptable: "No está bien mentir" (it’s not right to lie).
target_language_example: Lo que hiciste no está bien.
native_language_example: What you did isn’t OK.

additional_notes: Used to give mild praise or to say something is okay/acceptable, often with an understated tone. Common with comparisons like “para ser…” (“for being…”): “No está mal para ser la primera vez.” It can also react to news or results: “No está mal, ¿eh?/¿verdad?” = “Not bad, huh?/right?”
target_language_example: Tu español no está mal; te entiendo bien.
native_language_example: Your Spanish isn’t bad; I understand you well.

additional_notes: Used to state that something is prohibited by a rule, law, or policy. Often followed by an infinitive (No está permitido fumar / aparcar / nadar) or by a clause with que + subjunctive (No está permitido que nadie vaya allá). Also common as a short standalone answer: No está permitido.
target_language_example: No está permitido entrar sin identificación.
native_language_example: It’s not allowed to enter without ID.

additional_notes: Used to negate *estar*: for temporary states/conditions (no está contenta), location/presence (no está aquí / no está cerca), availability (no está disponible), or ongoing actions with the gerund (no está usando…, no está siendo…). Often corresponds to “isn’t” or “is not” in English, but specifically with *estar* (not *ser*).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono no está cargado.
native_language_example: My phone isn’t charged.

additional_notes: Uses **estar** (not *ser*) to talk about someone’s location. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., *El gerente no está aquí* or just *No está aquí*). **Aquí** means “here” (near the speaker); compare **allí/ahí** for “there.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor no está aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor isn’t here right now.

meaning: “is not in” / “is not on” (it isn’t located there; it isn’t included).
additional_notes: Used with location words (en la habitación, en casa, en Madrid) to say someone/something isn’t there. Also used with lists/documents to mean “not included/on” (no está en la lista, no está en el documento). The verb changes with the subject: no estoy en…, no estás en…, no están en….
target_language_example: Mi pasaporte no está en mi bolso.
native_language_example: My passport isn’t in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t at home right now (present tense of estar). You can add a subject for clarity: “Mi mamá no está en casa.” Often paired with time phrases like “en este momento” (at the moment). In questions, “¿verdad?” works like “right?” to confirm.
target_language_example: Lo siento, el señor no está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the man isn’t at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "estar" for "tú" (you). Common with adjectives or states/conditions: "No estás listo" (You’re not ready), "No estás seguro" (You’re not sure). You can also use it to negate an ongoing action with the gerund: "No estás comiendo" (You’re not eating). Often appears without the subject "tú" because it’s understood.
target_language_example: Ahora no estás en casa.
native_language_example: You’re not at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not real, not present, or not available. Often followed by a noun: “No existe la persona perfecta” (“The perfect person doesn’t exist”). Also used with ideas/concepts (“Dios no existe”) or things that used to exist (“ya no existe” = “no longer exists”).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad no existe el metro.
native_language_example: In this city, there is no subway.

additional_notes: “No fue” is the negative preterite (simple past) of **ser** (“to be”) and **ir** (“to go”), so meaning depends on context. Commonly it means **“it/he/she wasn’t…”** with adjectives or nouns: *No fue agradable* (“It wasn’t pleasant”). It’s also used in set time expressions like **“No fue hasta que…”** = “It wasn’t until…” and **“No fue mucho antes de que…”** = “It wasn’t long before…”.
target_language_example: No fue mi culpa.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my fault.

additional_notes: Used with devices, machines, services, or systems to say they aren’t operating properly (e.g., elevator, phone, printer, TV). Also used more generally to mean “it doesn’t work” in the sense of “it won’t work / it doesn’t work out” (an idea, method, relationship, plan). Present tense of funcionar; for a temporary situation you can also hear “no está funcionando.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, mi tarjeta no funciona aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, my card doesn’t work here.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "haber" ("ha") to form the present perfect in the negative: "no ha" + past participle (e.g., "no ha resuelto", "no ha faltado", "no ha funcionado"). Refers to something that has not happened up to now (or up to a point in time).
target_language_example: Ella no ha terminado el trabajo todavía.
native_language_example: She hasn't finished the work yet.

additional_notes: Negative present perfect of **ser** for **él/ella/usted** (and also used with things: **esto/eso**). Common in polite set phrases like **No ha sido molestia** = “It wasn’t any trouble.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no ha sido mi intención.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, it hasn't been my intention.

additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (él/ella/usted) or with a named subject: “Mi madre no habla inglés.” For “I don’t speak English,” say “No hablo inglés.” For “we/they don’t,” use “no hablamos / no hablan.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no habla inglés.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she/you (formal) doesn’t speak English.

meaning: “there won’t be / there will not be” (future of “there is/are”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something will not exist or be present in the future. It’s the negative form of “habrá” (from haber). Common with nouns: “no habrá clase” (there won’t be class), “no habrá nadie” (there won’t be anyone), “no habrá más…” (there won’t be any more…).
target_language_example: Si llueve, no habrá partido.
native_language_example: If it rains, there won’t be a game.

meaning: "there wasn’t / there weren’t" (imperfect past of "there is/are").
additional_notes: Used to say something did not exist or was not available in the past. "Había" is the past (imperfect) of "hay" (there is/are). Common patterns: "No había + noun" (No había ningún problema = There was no problem), and "No había + dónde/cuándo + infinitive" (No había dónde esconderse = There was nowhere to hide).
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, no había nadie en casa.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was nobody at home.

meaning: "there was nothing that…" / "there was nothing (someone) could do…"
additional_notes: Used to say there was no possible action or solution. It’s commonly followed by a verb describing what someone could do, often in the imperfect subjunctive in careful Spanish: «No había nada que pudiera hacer». In everyday speech you may also hear «podía/pudo haber hecho», as in the examples.
target_language_example: No había nada que pudiéramos hacer para ayudar.
native_language_example: There was nothing we could do to help.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of haber (había) to say that at a certain time, nobody was present somewhere. Often followed by a place: “No había nadie en casa/en el parque.” “Nadie” is negative here, so it goes with “no” (double negative is normal in Spanish).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, no había nadie en la oficina.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was nobody in the office.

meaning: “there was nobody/no one in …” (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say a place was empty at a past moment. The verb is imperfect: “había” = “there was/there were” (background description). Common pattern: “No había nadie en + place” (No había nadie en la casa / en el auto). You can also add details: “No había nadie en la habitación además de…” = “There was no one in the room besides…”.
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, no había nadie en el restaurante.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there was nobody in the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (ningún + noun) to say that none existed/was present in the past. It’s the imperfect of haber in an impersonal expression: no había ningún asiento = there weren’t any seats / there was no seat. For feminine nouns use: no había ninguna + noun (e.g., no había ninguna mesa).
target_language_example: No había ningún restaurante abierto a esa hora.
native_language_example: There weren’t any restaurants open at that time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is unnecessary. Common patterns: **No hace falta + infinitive** (No hace falta decirlo.) and **No hace falta que + subjunctive** (No hace falta que te quedes.). Often implies “it’s obvious” with **(ni) decirlo**: *No hace falta (ni) decirlo* = “it goes without saying.”
target_language_example: No hace falta que vengas mañana.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something considered obvious or already understood. Often followed by a full clause: “No hace falta decir que + [statement]”. You can also hear “No hace falta decirlo” (“Needless to say”).
target_language_example: No hace falta decir que tienes que traer tu pasaporte.
native_language_example: Needless to say, you have to bring your passport.

meaning: "you don't need to..." / "it's not necessary to..."
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary. It’s commonly followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive): No hace falta que + (yo/tú/él...) + verb. Also very common without “que”: No hace falta + infinitive (e.g., No hace falta decirlo = “No need to say it”).
target_language_example: No hace falta que vengas mañana; puedo hacerlo yo.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow; I can do it myself.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something only does one action repeatedly or continuously. It’s followed by an infinitive: no hace más que + verb (e.g., llorar, empeorar, crecer). Common with verbs like llorar (cry), quejarse (complain), empeorar (get worse), crecer (grow).
target_language_example: Últimamente no hace más que quejarse del trabajo.
native_language_example: Lately he does nothing but complain about work.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone only does one activity (often repeatedly or for a long time). It’s followed by an infinitive: no hace nada más que + ver/leer/estudiar. You can also use it with other persons/tenses: no hago nada más que…, no hacía nada más que….
target_language_example: Hoy no hago nada más que trabajar.
native_language_example: Today I do nothing but work.

additional_notes: Present perfect: **no + has (haber) + cambiado (past participle of cambiar)**. Often said about a person’s personality/appearance/behavior (**No has cambiado en nada.** = “You haven’t changed at all.”). It can also be used when **cambiar** takes an object: **No has cambiado mucho el cuarto.** = “You haven’t changed the room much.”
target_language_example: Te veo igual: no has cambiado nada.
native_language_example: You look the same: you haven’t changed at all.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t exist or isn’t available. It’s the negative of "hay" (there is/there are). Followed by a noun: "No hay reglas" = "There are no rules."
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay agua caliente.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no hot water.

meaning: “there’s no way to…” / “it’s impossible to…”; also “no way that…”
additional_notes:
Used to say something can’t be done or can’t be true.

Common patterns:
- **No hay forma de + infinitive**: *No hay forma de deshacer esto.* (“There’s no way to undo this.”)
- **No hay forma de que + subjunctive** (often shortened to **no hay forma que** in casual speech): *No hay forma de que esto sea real.* (“There’s no way this is real.”)

Meaning is similar to **“no way”**, but the expression itself is neutral (not slang).
target_language_example: No hay forma de llegar a tiempo sin un taxi.
native_language_example: There’s no way to arrive on time without a taxi.

additional_notes: Used to say something can’t be done or can’t happen (because it’s impossible, not allowed, or there’s no solution). Often followed by an infinitive (no hay manera de abrirlo) or by “que” + subjunctive (no hay manera de que yo pueda…).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay manera de llegar a tiempo con este tráfico.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no way to get there on time with this traffic.

additional_notes: Used to say that nothing exists or is available. Very common with a following clause: “No hay nada que + verb (subjunctive)” = “There’s nothing that (someone) can / could …” (e.g., No hay nada que pueda hacer).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que podamos hacer.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s nothing we can do.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best, most comforting, or most enjoyable option. It’s often followed by a noun (No hay nada como el hogar.) or by an infinitive/reflexive verb to talk about an action (No hay nada como descansar / darse un baño.).
target_language_example: Después de un día largo, no hay nada como dormir bien.
native_language_example: After a long day, there’s nothing like sleeping well.

meaning: "there's no" / "there isn't any" (often: "there's nothing [wrong/to worry about/etc.]").
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say there isn’t any of something: «No hay nada de viento» (“There’s no wind at all”). Very commonly appears in the pattern «No hay nada de malo + con/en + [infinitive]» (“There’s nothing wrong with/in …”). With «de qué + infinitive» it means “nothing to …”: «No hay nada de qué preocuparse» (“There’s nothing to worry about”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no hay nada de qué preocuparse.
native_language_example: Relax, there's nothing to worry about.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the best or most enjoyable option, often as a general statement or after an experience (e.g., after work). It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase or an infinitive (e.g., “no hay nada mejor que descansar”).
target_language_example: Después de correr, no hay nada mejor que una ducha caliente.
native_language_example: After running, there’s nothing better than a hot shower.

additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t anything additional or beyond what’s being talked about. Very common pattern: "No hay nada más que + infinitive" (There’s nothing else to + verb), e.g., "No hay nada más que decir" = there’s nothing else to say. Also used for comparisons with adjectives: "No hay nada más + adjective + que..." (There’s nothing more ... than ...), meaning something is the most extreme/best/worst, e.g., "No hay nada más hermoso que el amor" = nothing is more beautiful than love. Note spelling: "que" (not "qué") in "no hay nada más que decir".
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada más que pueda hacer.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s nothing else I can do.

additional_notes: Used to say that no thing/action exists that can (or should) be done. Very often followed by a verb in the subjunctive: “No hay nada que pueda hacer” = “There’s nothing I can do.” It can also introduce a strong statement with a double negative: “No hay nada que no pueda pasar” = “There’s nothing that can’t happen.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que pueda hacer para cambiar la decisión.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, there's nothing I can do to change the decision.

meaning: "There’s nothing to do" / "There’s nothing we can do."
additional_notes: Used to say there are no activities available (bored) or that a situation can’t be changed (resigned/helpless tone). Often followed by details: "No hay nada que hacer al respecto" = "There’s nothing we can do about it."
target_language_example: Lo intentamos todo, pero no hay nada que hacer.
native_language_example: We tried everything, but there’s nothing we can do.

no hay nada que pueda hacer

target_language_multi_word_term: no hay nada que pueda hacer
additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to help or change the situation. Very often followed by phrases like al respecto (“about it”), para + infinitive (“to…”), or por + someone (“for someone”). Uses the subjunctive pueda after que because it refers to something that does not exist (nothing that I can do).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nada que pueda hacer para arreglarlo hoy.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, there’s nothing I can do to fix it today.

additional_notes: Used to say nobody is present or nobody exists in a place/situation. Often followed by a location (no hay nadie aquí/en casa). It can also be used in comparisons to mean “there’s nobody (better/smarter) than…” (no hay nadie mejor que tú), or with a clause: no hay nadie que + verb (“there’s no one who…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no hay nadie en casa ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no one at home right now.

meaning: "there’s no need to" / "you don’t have to".
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., no hay necesidad de + esperar/explicarlo). You can also use it with a noun: No hay necesidad de eso. Common in polite reassurance or to calm someone down.
target_language_example: No hay necesidad de preocuparte; todo está bajo control.
native_language_example: There’s no need to worry; everything is under control.

meaning: “There isn’t any / there are no (female noun).”
additional_notes: Used to say that something does not exist or is not present. It’s the negative form of “hay” (there is/are) + “ninguna” (not any, none) and it agrees with a feminine singular noun: “No hay ninguna duda” (duda is feminine). With masculine nouns you use “no hay ningún …” and with plural nouns: “no hay ningunas / ningunos …” (less common) or more naturally “no hay …” + plural noun: “No hay reglas.”
target_language_example: No hay ninguna solución fácil.
native_language_example: There isn’t any easy solution.

meaning: “there isn’t any” / “there are no” (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something does not exist or is not present. It’s the negative form of “hay” (there is/are) + “ningún” (any/no) before a masculine singular noun: “No hay ningún error.” For feminine nouns use “no hay ninguna …” (e.g., “No hay ninguna razón.”). For plural, use “no hay …” + plural noun, often with “ningunos/ningunas” depending on the context (e.g., “No hay ningunos planes” or more commonly “No hay planes”).
target_language_example: No hay ningún café en la cocina.
native_language_example: There isn’t any coffee in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary or isn’t justified. It can be followed by an infinitive ("No hay razón para temer" = no reason to be afraid) or by "que" + subjunctive when a clause follows ("No hay razón para que nos quedemos" = no reason for us to stay).
target_language_example: No hay razón para discutir; podemos hablar tranquilos.
native_language_example: There’s no reason to argue; we can talk calmly.

meaning: "I haven't" / "I have not" (used with a past participle).
additional_notes: Used to make the negative **present perfect** in the **yo** form: **no he + participle** (e.g., *no he comido* = “I haven’t eaten”). Here **he** is from the verb **haber** (auxiliary “to have”), not **tener**. Often used with time expressions like **desde** (since), **durante** (for), and **nunca** (never).
target_language_example: No he terminado mi tarea todavía.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished my homework yet.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **no + he hablado** (I have not spoken). It’s followed by **con** + a person/group (con él, con ella, con mis vecinos). Often used with time expressions like **desde** (since), **hace** (for/ago), or **durante** (for/during): *No he hablado con ella desde ayer / hace semanas / durante mucho tiempo.*
target_language_example: No he hablado con mi jefe desde la reunión.
native_language_example: I haven’t spoken to my boss since the meeting.

meaning: "I haven't been able to" (up to now).
additional_notes: Present perfect of poder (yo): no + he podido + infinitive. It means you were unable to do something during a period that includes the present (e.g., today/this week/up to now). Often followed by an infinitive: no he podido dormir/encontrar/hacer/ver.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no he podido llamarte hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I haven't been able to call you today.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (he sabido) to say you haven’t received any news, message, or update about someone (or from them) up to now. Very common with time words like "últimamente" (lately), "todavía" (still), or "desde entonces" (since then). You can also change the person: "no has sabido nada de..." (you haven’t), "no hemos sabido..." (we haven’t).
target_language_example: Todavía no he sabido nada de mi hermano desde ayer.
native_language_example: I still haven’t heard anything from my brother since yesterday.

additional_notes: Present perfect: "no" + "he" (I have) + "terminado" (finished). Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you haven’t finished doing: "No he terminado de hablar" (I haven’t finished talking). With "contigo," it means "I’m not done with you" (the situation with you isn’t over).
target_language_example: No he terminado de escribir el informe.
native_language_example: I haven’t finished writing the report.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "no hacer nada". Common for saying you did nothing (e.g., during a trip) or for defending yourself/insisting you’re not guilty: "¡No hice nada!" Also used with qualifiers like "fuera de lo ordinario" (nothing out of the ordinary).
target_language_example: No hice nada ayer; me quedé en casa todo el día.
native_language_example: I didn’t do anything yesterday; I stayed home all day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone only did one thing (often in a complaining or critical tone). Follow it with an infinitive: “no hizo nada más que + verb” (e.g., bromear, llorar, quejarse). You can change the tense/person: “no hice…”, “no hicieron…”, “no hacía…”, etc.
target_language_example: Durante la reunión, no hizo nada más que interrumpir.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he did nothing but interrupt.

meaning: “wasn’t going to” (not going to do something; not going to happen).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of **ir** + **a** to talk about a future action from a past point of view (“was going to…”). With **no**, it means someone didn’t intend to do it, or it wasn’t going to happen (often suggesting it was impossible or inevitable). Common before an infinitive: **no iba a volver / no iba a luchar / no iba a dejarte / no iba a ir / no iba a parar**.
target_language_example: Pensé que no iba a llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: I thought I wasn’t going to arrive on time.

meaning: "it doesn’t matter" / "never mind"; also "no matter (when/what/how much)".
additional_notes: Used to say something is unimportant or to dismiss an issue: "No importa" = “It doesn’t matter / Never mind.” It can also introduce an idea meaning “no matter…”, often followed by a question word: no importa qué (no matter what), no importa cuándo (no matter when), no importa cuánto (no matter how much), no importa cómo (no matter how).
target_language_example: No importa lo que digas, yo te creo.
native_language_example: No matter what you say, I believe you.

additional_notes: Used to say that something does not change the result or does not matter, regardless of the thing that follows. It’s often followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (e.g., pase, digas, hagas): No importa lo que + (subjunctive).
target_language_example: No importa lo que elijas, yo te apoyaré.
native_language_example: No matter what you choose, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to negate an action involving a feminine direct object (“her” or “it”). The pronoun “la” goes before a conjugated verb: “No la traerán” = “They won’t bring her/it.” With an infinitive, it can go before the first verb or be attached to the infinitive: “No la quiero ver” / “No quiero verla” = “I don’t want to see her.”
target_language_example: No la conozco, pero me parece simpática.
native_language_example: I don’t know her, but she seems nice.

meaning: "I haven’t seen her" / "I haven’t seen it".
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "he visto" = "I have seen." "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" (a female person) or "it" (a feminine noun). It’s often followed by a time expression with "desde" (since): "No la he visto desde ayer" (since yesterday), "desde hace mucho tiempo" (for a long time).
target_language_example: No la he visto desde la semana pasada.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen her since last week.

meaning: "I don’t see her" / "I don’t see it."
additional_notes: "La" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (for a feminine noun). "Veo" is "I see" (from *ver*). Often used literally for not seeing a person (e.g., you don’t meet/see her often), but it can also mean "I don’t see it" in the sense of "I don’t understand/agree" when the context is an idea.
target_language_example: No la veo los fines de semana porque trabajo.
native_language_example: I don’t see her on weekends because I work.

additional_notes: "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (usted). It usually goes before a conjugated verb: "No le he oído" (I haven’t heard him/her/you). With affirmative commands it attaches to the verb (e.g., "Dígale"), but with negative commands it stays before the verb: "No le mires" (Don’t look at him/her). It’s also used with verbs like "gustar": "A María no le gusta..." (María doesn’t like...).
target_language_example: No le digas la verdad.
native_language_example: Don’t tell him/her the truth.

additional_notes: Negative command with tú: no + (indirect object pronoun) + verb. Here le means “to him,” “to her,” or “to you” (usted). Often followed by que + clause: No le digas que te lo dije (“Don’t tell him I told you”). You can clarify who le is by adding a + person: No le digas a Marta.
target_language_example: No le digas a tu mamá que llegué tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t tell your mom that I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to share information with a specific person. Structure: No + indirect object pronoun (le = to him/her/you-formal) + digas (tú command of decir) + a + person. With a name/role after a (mamá, papá, mi padre, Leila). You can change le to les for plural: No les digas a ellos.
target_language_example: No le digas a tu mamá que llegué tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t tell your mom that I arrived late.

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) of decir: no digas. Le = “to him/to her” (indirect object). Nada = “anything.” Often used to tell someone to keep something secret; you can change le to me/te/nos/les (No me digas nada = Don’t tell me anything) and add who: No le digas nada a mamá/a nadie.
target_language_example: Por favor, no le digas nada a tu hermano todavía.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell your brother anything yet.

meaning: "he/she doesn’t like it" (it doesn’t please him/her).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gustar. The person who dislikes something is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: me/te/le/nos/les. The thing disliked is the grammatical subject: No le gusta hablar… = “Speaking… doesn’t please him/her.” Common pattern: A + person + no + (me/te/le/nos/les) + gusta + infinitive / noun; or No le gusta que + subjunctive for actions by others (e.g., “he doesn’t like that they tell him what to do”).
target_language_example: A Marta no le gusta levantarse temprano.
native_language_example: Marta doesn’t like getting up early.

meaning: "he/she doesn’t care" / "it doesn’t matter to him/her".
additional_notes: Used with the verb "importar" (to matter). Spanish commonly phrases this as: "(A alguien) le importa (algo)" = "(To someone) something matters." So "no le importa" means the person referred to by "le" (to him/her/you-formal) doesn’t care. You can add the person with "a + person": "A Juan no le importa" (Juan doesn’t care).
target_language_example: A Marta no le importa llegar tarde.
native_language_example: Marta doesn’t care about arriving late.

meaning: "not to them" / "not to you (plural)" (with an indirect object).
additional_notes: "No" negates the verb, and "les" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to them" or "to you (plural, Spain: ustedes)." It’s very common with verbs like "decir" (to tell/say to) and "importar" (to matter to): e.g., "No les dije nada" = "I didn’t tell them anything," and "No les importa" = "It doesn’t matter to them."
target_language_example: No les voy a contar el secreto.
native_language_example: I’m not going to tell them the secret.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t do/need/know something, where “lo” means “it/that” (often an idea, fact, or masculine noun). “Lo” goes before the verb: “No lo necesito” = “I don’t need it.” With commands: “No lo tomes…” = “Don’t take it…”.
target_language_example: No lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I don't understand it.

meaning: “I don’t think so” / “I don’t believe it.”
additional_notes: Used to disagree or to say something is unlikely. “Lo” refers to the idea or situation being discussed (“it/that”). You can use it alone as a short reply (“—¿Vienes? —No lo creo.”).
target_language_example: —¿Crees que va a llover? —No lo creo.
native_language_example: —Do you think it’s going to rain? —I don’t think so.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t understand a situation or idea (often with emphasis or frustration). "Lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it/that” (the thing being discussed). Also common: "No entiendes" (“You don’t understand”), "No lo entiendo" (“I don’t understand it”).
target_language_example: No lo entiendes: no se trata de dinero, se trata de confianza.
native_language_example: You don’t understand it: it’s not about money, it’s about trust.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (an idea, explanation, word, situation). "Lo" means "it" (referring to what was just mentioned). You can add emphasis with "para nada" (“not at all”): "No lo entiendo para nada."
target_language_example: Perdón, no lo entiendo. ¿Puedes repetirlo?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand it. Can you repeat it?

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) of hacer (“to do/make”): no + lo (“it”) + hagas (subjunctive form used for negative tú commands). Used to tell someone not to do a specific thing; you can add emphasis or politeness: Por favor, no lo hagas. / Mejor que no lo hagas (“You’d better not do it”).
target_language_example: Si es peligroso, por favor no lo hagas.
native_language_example: If it’s dangerous, please don’t do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t do a particular action that’s already known from context. "lo" = “it” (a thing/idea/action previously mentioned), and "hago" is the present tense of "hacer" (to do/make). Often appears with emphasis or frequency words: "nunca" (never), "tampoco" (either/neither), "yo" (to stress “I” in contrast to someone else).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no lo hago.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t do it.

additional_notes: Future tense of hacer (haré = “I will do/make”). lo is a pronoun meaning “it/that,” referring to an action already mentioned or understood. Used to refuse or promise not to do something; can be strengthened with words like definitivamente (“definitely”) or nunca más (“never again”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no lo haré.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I won't do it.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **he decidido** = “I have decided.” **No** negates it. **Lo** means “it/that” and refers to the thing you’re deciding (plans, choice, etc.). Often used with **todavía** or **aún** (“yet/still”): *Todavía/Aún no lo he decidido* = “I haven’t decided yet.”
target_language_example: ¿Vienes mañana? No lo he decidido todavía.
native_language_example: Are you coming tomorrow? I haven’t decided yet.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: **he visto** = “I have seen.” **Lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it” or “him” (for a woman you’d say **no la he visto**). Often used with time expressions like **nunca** (never), **desde entonces** (since then), and **últimamente** (lately).
target_language_example: No lo he visto hoy.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him/it today.

additional_notes: Used to deny having done something. "Lo" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "it/that" (something understood from context), and "hice" is the preterite (completed past) of "hacer" for "I". You can add emphasis with words like "yo" (I) or "yo mismo" (myself): "No lo hice yo" / "No lo hice yo mismo."
target_language_example: Te lo juro: no lo hice.
native_language_example: I swear: I didn’t do it.

additional_notes: Uses the negative "no" + the direct object pronoun "lo" (“it/that”) + "hiciste" (preterite of "hacer" for "tú"). Often used to deny, accuse, or confirm something: "No lo hiciste." / "¿Por qué no lo hiciste?" / "No lo hiciste, ¿verdad?" The "lo" refers to an action or thing already known from context.
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no lo hiciste a propósito.
native_language_example: Relax, you didn't do it on purpose.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of hacer (“hizo” = “did”) with “lo” meaning “it/that” (a thing or action already mentioned). Often answers a question like “¿Lo hizo?” or emphasizes denial: “Por supuesto que no lo hizo.” You can replace the subject with a name: “Tom no lo hizo.”
target_language_example: Te dije que lo haría, pero al final no lo hizo.
native_language_example: I told you he would do it, but in the end he didn’t.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: "No lo puedo + infinitive" (e.g., ayudar, comprender). "Lo" is an object pronoun meaning "it" (sometimes "him" in context). You can swap in other object pronouns: "no la puedo" (it/her, feminine), "no los puedo" (them, masculine), "no las puedo" (them, feminine). Often interchangeable with "no puedo + infinitive" when "it" is understood, but "no lo puedo" makes the object explicit.
target_language_example: No lo puedo hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I can't do it today.

additional_notes: Used to say you lacked that information. "Lo" means "it/that" and refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), often used for background knowledge in the past. It can change with the subject: "No lo sabía nadie" = "Nobody knew."
target_language_example: Perdón, no lo sabía; nadie me lo dijo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn't know; nobody told me.

additional_notes: Used to admit you don’t know something (No lo sé) and then add a guess, opinion, or contrast (pero = “but”). Often followed by creo que… (“I think…”) or a statement you do know.
target_language_example: No lo sé, pero creo que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I don’t know, but I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: "don’t/doesn’t" + "them" (masculine plural direct object), before a verb.
additional_notes: "No" negates the verb, and "los" is a direct object pronoun meaning "them" (or sometimes "you" plural, formal, in some regions). It goes before a conjugated verb: "No los tengo" (I don’t have them). With infinitives/gerunds, it can go before the first verb or attached to the end: "No los puedo dejar" / "No puedo dejarlos" (I can’t leave them).
target_language_example: No los encuentro por ninguna parte.
native_language_example: I can’t find them anywhere.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to mean that something does NOT happen to you or is NOT done to you. It combines the negation "no" with the object/reflexive pronoun "me" (me/to me/myself). Common patterns: "No me dice..." = "He/She doesn’t tell me..."; "No me mires" = "Don’t look at me"; "No me lastima" = "It doesn’t hurt me."
target_language_example: No me llames tan tarde.
native_language_example: Don’t call me so late.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase acordarse de (to remember). You must use de before the thing/person you don’t remember: No me acuerdo de él/eso/tu nombre. Often strengthened with para nada, en absoluto, or nada (“not at all” / “nothing”). You can change the indirect object pronoun: no te acuerdas de… (you don’t remember), no se acuerda de… (he/she/you formal doesn’t remember), no nos acordamos de… (we don’t remember).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no me acuerdo de tu dirección.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember your address.

additional_notes: Used to react to what you’ve just heard or to push back on an idea. Often implies “I can’t believe it” or “surely not,” and it can also be used to emphasize a complaint (e.g., “don’t tell me you didn’t hear it”). Common in exclamations; can be followed by indicative: "No me digas que perdiste..."
target_language_example: ¡No me digas que ya se fueron sin mí!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me they already left without me!

additional_notes: Used to express dislike. "Me" means “to me” and "gusta" comes from "gustar" (literally “to be pleasing”), so the thing you don’t like is the subject: "No me gusta la lluvia" = “The rain isn’t pleasing to me.” Use "no me gustan" with plural nouns: "No me gustan los gatos." You can also use it alone to react to a situation: "Nos siguen de cerca y no me gusta."
target_language_example: No me gusta este plan.
native_language_example: I don’t like this plan.

meaning: "I don’t like it when/that..." (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to express that something bothers you or you disapprove of an action. After "no me gusta que", Spanish normally uses the subjunctive (e.g., "No me gusta que hables así"). You can change the person: "no te/le/nos/les gusta que..."
target_language_example: No me gusta que fumes en mi casa.
native_language_example: I don’t like it when you smoke in my house.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to express dislike: **No me gustan + plural noun** (e.g., *No me gustan las patatas*). Literally means “they don’t please me.” For singular nouns, use **no me gusta** (e.g., *No me gusta el café*). You can add emphasis with **nada** (“at all”): *No me gustan nada…*.
target_language_example: No me gustan los perros.
native_language_example: I don’t like dogs.

additional_notes: Uses the verb gustar, which works like “to be pleasing (to someone).” The thing you don’t like is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: gustan for plural (los cabos sueltos), gusta for singular (no me gusta el café). Use los for masculine plural nouns and las for feminine plural nouns (no me gustan las mentiras).
target_language_example: No me gustan los deportes de contacto.
native_language_example: I don’t like contact sports.

meaning: “don’t make me…” / “don’t do that to me…”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to force you to do something or not to put you in a difficult situation. Often followed by an infinitive (no me hagas + verb: “No me hagas esperar”) or by “esto/eso” (“No me hagas esto”). It uses the tú command form of hacer (hagas) with an indirect object pronoun (me).
target_language_example: No me hagas esperarte otra vez.
native_language_example: Don’t make me wait for you again.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t interest you or doesn’t matter to you. Often followed by a noun: “No me interesa la política.” You can also use it alone as a complete sentence: “No me interesa.” (tone can sound dismissive depending on context).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no me interesa ese trabajo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m not interested in that job.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to refer to you with a certain name/label ("Don’t call me that") or not to call you on the phone ("Don’t call me at work," "Don’t call me until next month"). "Llámame" = call me; "no me llames" is the negative command (tú form).
target_language_example: Por favor, no me llames durante la reunión.
native_language_example: Please don’t call me during the meeting.

meaning: "don’t … it to/for me" / "I didn’t … it" (with object pronouns "me" + "lo").
additional_notes: This is a very common pronoun cluster used before a verb: **no** (not) + **me** (to/for me) + **lo** (it). The exact translation depends on the verb: *No me lo agradezcas* = “Don’t thank me for it”; *No me lo esperaba* = “I didn’t expect it”; *No me lo perdería* = “I wouldn’t miss it.” **Lo** refers to an idea/thing already known from context.
target_language_example: No me lo digas todavía.
native_language_example: Don’t tell me yet.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop giving you a certain look (often judging, accusing, intense, or teasing). Common in tense or awkward moments, and can be softened with “por favor.” You’ll also hear it with a reason: “...que me pones nerviosa” (“...you’re making me nervous”).
target_language_example: No me mires así; no he hecho nada malo.
native_language_example: Don’t look at me like that; I haven’t done anything wrong.

meaning: "I don’t have any ... left" / "I have no ... left."
additional_notes: From the verb "quedar" (to remain/be left). It’s used to say you have nothing left of something: "No me queda dinero" (I don’t have any money left), "No me queda nada" (I have nothing left). It can also be used with "otra opción" to mean "I have no other choice": "No me queda otra opción".
target_language_example: Lo siento, ya no me queda tiempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any time left.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone something isn’t necessary. It’s the negative of “necesitas” (you need) and is often followed by an infinitive (no necesitas hacerlo) or a noun (no necesitas eso). You can add “ya” or “ya no” to mean “(not) anymore” (ya no necesitas hacerlo).
target_language_example: No necesitas venir mañana; podemos hablar por teléfono.
native_language_example: You don’t need to come tomorrow; we can talk on the phone.

additional_notes: "No" goes before the verb to make it negative. "Nos" is an object/reflexive pronoun meaning "us" (or "each other" in reflexive use). Common patterns: "No nos + verb" = "(Someone) doesn’t/didn’t + verb + us" (e.g., No nos avisaron = They didn’t tell us). With reflexive verbs it can mean "we don’t/didn’t (do something)" or "we haven’t (done something)"; for example, "No nos hemos visto" often means "We haven’t seen each other."
target_language_example: No nos entienden.
native_language_example: They don’t understand us.

meaning: "we have no ... left" / "we have no choice but ..."
additional_notes: From the verb "quedar" (to be left, to remain). Use it to say something is no longer available or remaining: "No nos queda más comida" = "We don’t have any more food left." With "más remedio que + infinitive", it means there’s no alternative: "No nos queda más remedio que esperar" = "We have no choice but to wait."
target_language_example: No nos queda dinero, así que no podemos salir a cenar.
native_language_example: We don’t have any money left, so we can’t go out to dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues nonstop or repeatedly. It’s the negative of "parar de" (to stop doing something). Common patterns: "No para de + infinitive" (No para de llover = It keeps raining) and with reflexive verbs: "No para de quejarse" (He/She keeps complaining).
target_language_example: Desde esta mañana no para de sonar el teléfono.
native_language_example: Since this morning, the phone hasn’t stopped ringing.

additional_notes: Very common reassuring phrase. Literally “nothing happens,” and it’s used to calm someone down, forgive a small mistake, or say something is not an issue (similar to “no worries” or “it’s fine”). Often said on its own or after “pero”/“tranquilo/a”: “No pasa nada.”
target_language_example: Perdón por llegar tarde—no pasa nada.
native_language_example: Sorry for being late—no problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t expect something or you were wrong about what would happen. It’s the preterite (past) of pensar: pensé = “I thought.” After que, Spanish commonly uses the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estuvieras, fuera, fueras) for something you didn’t believe/expect, and sometimes the conditional (e.g., vendrías) or imperfect (e.g., volvería) depending on meaning and context.
target_language_example: No pensé que fuera tan tarde.
native_language_example: I didn’t think it was so late.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” are not able to do something or that something is not allowed/possible. Often followed by an infinitive: no podemos hacer/aceptar/obtener... You can add emphasis with words like “realmente” (really) or “bajo ninguna circunstancia” (under no circumstances).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no podemos ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that you and others should not trust a person or rely on something. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: confiar en ellos/ella/él, confiar en alguien, confiar en su + noun (e.g., su amabilidad). In Spanish, confiar takes the preposition en.
target_language_example: No podemos confiar en lo que nos dijo.
native_language_example: We can’t trust what he/she told us.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s nothing you (we) can do in a situation (helplessness or lack of options). Very common with additions like “al respecto” (“about it”) and “más que + infinitive” (“nothing to do but…”): “No podemos hacer nada al respecto” = “We can’t do anything about it”; “No podemos hacer nada más que continuar” = “We can’t do anything but continue.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no podemos hacer nada al respecto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, we can’t do anything about it.

additional_notes: Used to express that you are extremely happy/satisfied—basically as happy as possible. You can swap the adjective: “no podría estar más contento/a” (I couldn’t be more pleased), “no podría estar más emocionado/a” (I couldn’t be more excited).
target_language_example: Con este trabajo nuevo, no podría estar más feliz.
native_language_example: With this new job, I couldn’t be happier.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of poder (“to be able to”) in the negative: yo no podía = “I couldn’t / I wasn’t able to.” Used for ongoing inability in the past, repeated situations, or background context (not a one-time action). Often followed by an infinitive (no podía ir, no podía confiar) or used with another verb for inability to achieve something (no podía encontrarlo).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, no podía nadar.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I couldn’t swim.

additional_notes: From the verb poder (“to be able to”). "No pude" is the simple past (preterite) for “I couldn’t,” often used for a specific situation that happened and finished in the past. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "no pude dormir" (I couldn’t sleep), "no pude resistir" (I couldn’t resist), "no pude contener" (I couldn’t hold back).
target_language_example: Lo intenté, pero no pude abrir la puerta.
native_language_example: I tried, but I couldn’t open the door.

meaning: "I couldn't help (doing something)" / "I couldn't stop myself."
additional_notes: Used to say you couldn’t control a reaction or feeling. Very common with an infinitive (e.g., no pude evitar llorar / reírme / sentir). In the present tense you’ll often hear "no puedo evitar" (I can’t help).
target_language_example: No pude evitar mirarla cuando entró.
native_language_example: I couldn't help looking at her when she came in.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of *no poder* for a completed situation in the past: *no pudo + infinitive* (no pudo llegar, no pudo abrir). Often implies a specific failure at that moment, rather than a general inability. Used for he/she/it/you (formal) and also *él/ella/usted no pudo*.
target_language_example: Lo intenté, pero ella no pudo venir.
native_language_example: I tried, but she couldn’t come.

additional_notes: "No puede" is the negative of the verb poder (to be able to) in the él/ella/usted form. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "No puede escribir" (She can’t write). The subject can be stated ("Ella no puede") or implied. With "haber" + past participle ("No puede haber ido"), it often means "can’t have" as a logical conclusion (it’s not possible that he went).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no puede venir.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is impossible or very unlikely: No puede ser él. You can also use it as an exclamation of surprise/disbelief (like “No way!”), often with an implied “it”: ¡No puede ser! Grammar: no (not) + puede (can) + ser (be).
target_language_example: ¡No puede ser! Se me olvidaron las llaves.
native_language_example: No way! I forgot my keys.

additional_notes: Formed by **no** + **pueden** (present tense of *poder*, “to be able to”). Used to say someone lacks the ability, permission, or possibility to do something. **Pueden** is for **ellos/ellas/ustedes**; for “I can’t” use **no puedo**, and for “he/she can’t” **no puede**.
target_language_example: Ellos no pueden venir hoy.
native_language_example: They can’t come today.

meaning: "you can’t" / "you are not able to" (informal singular "you").
additional_notes: Used to tell one person that they are not able to do something or that they are not allowed to do it. It’s the negative of "puedes" (tú) from "poder" (to be able to / can). For "you can’t" to more than one person or formally, use "no pueden" (ustedes/ellos) or "no puede" (usted).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedes entrar aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t go in here.

meaning: “you can’t do” / “you’re not allowed to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is unable to do something (lack of ability) or is not permitted to do it (rules, restrictions). Often followed by an infinitive or a noun: “No puedes hacer magia” (do magic), “No puedes hacer eso” (do that).
target_language_example: No puedes hacer ruido aquí.
native_language_example: You can’t make noise here.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something (because you lack ability, time, permission, or it’s not possible). It’s the negative of "puedo" (I can). Often followed by an infinitive: "No puedo + verb" (No puedo ir, No puedo decirlo).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say something is unacceptable. Often followed by a noun (un regalo, estas condiciones, una excusa), or said alone as a complete statement: “No puedo aceptar.” It can express a polite refusal (e.g., of a gift) or a firm rejection (e.g., of terms or an excuse).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo aceptar tu oferta.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I can't accept your offer.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, shock, or disbelief. Often followed by **que + verb** (“I can’t believe that…”) or **lo que + clause** (“I can’t believe what…”). You can also say it alone: **No puedo creer.**
target_language_example: No puedo creer que ya sea viernes.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it’s already Friday.

additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise, shock, disbelief, or indignation. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “no puedo creer que estés…”), though you may also hear the indicative in casual speech.
target_language_example: No puedo creer que hayas hecho eso.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you did that.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable or not allowed to say something, or that you don’t know for sure. Often followed by: "nada" (anything), "nada más" (anything else), "que sí/que no" (yes/no), "si..." (whether/if), or a noun like "una mentira" (a lie). In conversation you can add "lo": "No lo puedo decir" = "I can't say it."
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo decirte más por ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't tell you more for now.

meaning: "I can’t leave" / "I can’t stop" / "I can’t let."
additional_notes:
Used with different structures:
- **no puedo dejar + (a) alguien/algo** = “I can’t leave (someone/something)” (often meaning you can’t abandon them or leave them alone): *No puedo dejar a la chica sola.*
- **no puedo dejar de + infinitive** = “I can’t stop + -ing”: *No puedo dejar de comer.*
- **no puedo dejar que + subjunctive** = “I can’t let (someone)…”: *No puedo dejar que hagas eso.*
target_language_example: No puedo dejar de pensar en eso.
native_language_example: I can’t stop thinking about that.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (de + infinitive) to say you can’t stop doing something, often because it’s hard to control (thinking, crying, laughing, etc.). You can change the subject/tense: "no puedo" (I can’t), "no puede" (he/she can’t), "no podemos" (we can’t), "no podía" (I couldn’t).
target_language_example: No puedo dejar de reír cuando escucho esa historia.
native_language_example: I can’t stop laughing when I hear that story.

meaning: "I can't be" / "I can't stay" (in a place, state, or situation).
additional_notes: Used with **estar** to talk about a temporary state, location, or situation you can’t be in. Common patterns: **no puedo estar + en** (place) = “I can’t be in…”, **no puedo estar + con/sin** (person) = “I can’t be with/without…”, **no puedo estar + adjective** = “I can’t be (nervous/sure/etc.).” Often implies inability or impossibility in that moment.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo estar aquí ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't be here right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is involuntary or hard to control. Common patterns: (1) no puedo evitar + infinitive: "No puedo evitar pensar..." / "No puedo evitar reírme..."; (2) no puedo evitar + noun/pronoun: "No puedo evitar eso." Often implies "even if I want to".
target_language_example: No puedo evitar preocuparme cuando no me respondes.
native_language_example: I can't help worrying when you don't reply to me.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to talk (right now or in general), or that you can’t speak a certain way or language. It can also extend to what you can’t talk about (e.g., “sobre eso” = “about that”). For “I can’t speak for him,” Spanish uses “No puedo hablar por él.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, ahora mismo no puedo hablar; te llamo luego.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now; I’ll call you later.

meaning: “I can’t do” / “I’m not able to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something. It’s followed by a noun (no puedo hacer el trabajo) or by “más” (no puedo hacer más = I can’t do any more). You can also add “nada” for emphasis (no puedo hacer nada sobre eso = there’s nothing I can do about that). Often you’ll add “solo/sola” (alone) or another detail at the end.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo hacer eso hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do that today.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable or not allowed to do something. In conversation it can also sound like a refusal depending on tone. You’ll often hear it with verbs like saber/decir: “Sabes que no puedo hacer eso” (“You know I can’t do that”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo hacer eso ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do that right now.

meaning: “I can’t do anything” / “There’s nothing I can do.”
additional_notes:
Used to say you’re unable to take action or help. It can be followed by details: 
- "no puedo hacer nada por ti" = I can’t do anything for you (can’t help you)
- "no puedo hacer nada sobre eso" = there’s nothing I can do about that
- "no puedo hacer nada con mi tiempo" = I can’t do anything with my time (don’t know what to do).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo hacer nada al respecto.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s nothing I can do about it.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to do something. You can add details after it, like how/why: “no puedo hacerlo solo” (I can’t do it alone), “no puedo hacerlo yo” (I can’t do it myself), “no puedo hacerlo de ninguna manera” (I can’t do it any way / at all).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't do it today.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to go somewhere or leave. Often followed by a place with "a" (e.g., "no puedo ir a la fiesta") or by a time word like "ahora". The verb "poder" changes with the subject: "no puedo" (I can’t), "no puedes" (you can’t), "no puede" (he/she/you-formal can’t), etc.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go today.

meaning: "I can't think about" / "I can't think of".
additional_notes: Used when you’re unable (or don’t want) to focus your mind on something, or when you can’t come up with an idea/person/thing. It’s often followed by: eso/esto (“that/this”), nada (“anything/nothing”), nadie (“anyone/no one”), or a person (él/ella). You can change the subject and tense: no puedes pensar en… (“you can’t…”), no podía pensar en… (“I couldn’t…”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo pensar en otra cosa ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t think about anything else right now.

meaning: "I can't continue" / "I can't go on"; also "I can't follow."
additional_notes: With "seguir con + noun/verb" it means to continue doing something: "No puedo seguir con esto" (I can’t continue with this). With a direct object, "seguir" often means to follow (track/understand): "No puedo seguir la bola" (I can’t follow the ball) or "No puedo seguir su lógica" (I can’t follow his/her logic). By itself, "No puedo seguir" can mean "I can’t go on" (continue).
target_language_example: Lo siento, estoy muy cansado; no puedo seguir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m very tired; I can’t go on.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intolerable, either because you strongly dislike it (people, music, noise) or because you can’t endure it (pain, suffering). Often appears with “más” to mean “I can’t take it anymore” (No puedo soportar más...). With “a” before a person: “No puedo soportar a…” = “I can’t stand…”. Note: “pedazo de mierda” is very vulgar/insulting.
target_language_example: No puedo soportar más este ruido.
native_language_example: I can’t take this noise anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to see something (because of darkness, distance, poor eyesight, an obstacle, etc.). Often followed by what you can’t see: "No puedo ver la torre" (I can’t see the tower), "No puedo ver nada" (I can’t see anything). With people, Spanish commonly uses "ver a" + person: "No puedo ver a nadie" (I can’t see anyone). It can be intensified with informal/vulgar expressions like "No puedo ver un carajo" (I can’t see a damn thing).
target_language_example: Perdón, no puedo ver el menú sin mis gafas.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t see the menu without my glasses.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something (because you lack ability, time, permission, or it’s not possible). It’s the negative of "puedo" (I can). Often followed by an infinitive: "No puedo + verb" (No puedo ir, No puedo decirlo).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (quería) to talk about not wanting to do something in the past, often as background, a repeated feeling, or a polite/softened way to introduce what you’re about to say ("I didn’t mean to..."). Common pattern: "No quería + infinitive" (no quería interrumpir / mentirte / decir nada). Subject depends on context: yo no quería, él/ella no quería.
target_language_example: Perdón, no quería molestarte.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t want to bother you.

additional_notes: Used to refuse something or say you don’t want to do something. Often followed by an infinitive: no quiero + verb (No quiero vivir). It can also be followed by a noun/pronoun: no quiero nada (I don’t want anything). You can use it alone as a short refusal: No quiero. In radio/phone talk, “cambio” means “over.”
target_language_example: No quiero salir hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t want a specific action to happen. It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., No quiero que entres / lleguen / sigas). You can add a subject for clarity: “No quiero que tú…” / “No quiero que ellos…”.
target_language_example: No quiero que me hables así.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to talk to me like that.

meaning: "I don’t want you to…" (said to someone informally).
additional_notes: Used to express what you don’t want the other person (tú) to do or to have happen to them. It’s followed by a verb in the present subjunctive: no quiero que te vayas, no quiero que te preocupes. The "te" is an object/reflexive pronoun that depends on the next verb (te vayas, te pase, te escapes, te muestres).
target_language_example: No quiero que te vayas todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to leave yet.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to repeat an action. It’s followed by an infinitive (volver a + infinitive = “to do again”): No quiero volver a caerme (I don’t want to fall again). You can also use it for “not want to go back” with a place: No quiero volver a España (I don’t want to go back to Spain) — here it’s volver a + noun/place, not a verb.
target_language_example: Lo intenté una vez y no quiero volver a hacerlo.
native_language_example: I tried it once and I don’t want to do it again.

additional_notes: Used to say you have no memory of what happened (often after an event, shock, alcohol, sleep, an accident, etc.). In the present tense: "(yo) no recuerdo nada". You can add a time reference: "de ayer", "de anoche", "después de eso".
target_language_example: Me golpeé la cabeza y no recuerdo nada.
native_language_example: I hit my head and I don’t remember anything.

additional_notes: “No sabe” is the negation of “sabe” (3rd-person singular, present tense of *saber*). It’s used for not knowing information (No sabe con qué está jugando.) and also for not knowing how to do something / not being able to do it (No sabe nadar.). The subject can be a name (Cleo no sabe…) or implied (No sabe…).
target_language_example: Mi hermano no sabe cocinar.
native_language_example: My brother can’t cook. / My brother doesn’t know how to cook.

additional_notes: Used with the verb saber to say someone has no knowledge about something. Often followed by sobre (about) or de (about/in the area of): No sabe nada sobre el asunto; No sabe nada de política. In everyday speech you may also hear the more emphatic double negative: No sabe nada de nada (“doesn’t know anything at all”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero ella no sabe nada sobre la reunión.
native_language_example: Sorry, but she doesn’t know anything about the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has zero knowledge about a topic. It’s often followed by a noun (no sabe nada sobre radiación) or a situation/issue (no sabe nada sobre el asunto). The verb changes with the subject: no sé nada sobre… (I), no sabes nada sobre… (you), no saben nada sobre… (they/you all). In everyday Spanish you can also hear “de” instead of “sobre” (no sabe nada de…).
target_language_example: Mi hermano no sabe nada sobre coches, pero quiere comprar uno.
native_language_example: My brother doesn’t know anything about cars, but he wants to buy one.

meaning: "they don't know what…" / "you (all) don't know what…"
additional_notes: Used with ustedes/ellos/ellas to say someone doesn’t know what something is, what is happening, what they’re doing, or what is coming next.
