Often followed by: + es ("no saben lo que es…" = they don’t know what it’s like to…), + les espera ("no saben lo que les espera" = they don’t know what awaits them), or another verb phrase ("no saben lo que están haciendo" = they don’t know what they’re doing).
target_language_example: No saben lo que significa esta palabra.
native_language_example: They don’t know what this word means.

meaning: “they don’t know anything about …” / “they know nothing about …”.
additional_notes: Used to say a group of people (they = “saben”) has no knowledge or information about a topic or person. You can change the verb to match the subject (no sé nada de, no sabes nada de, no sabe nada de, no sabemos nada de, etc.). Often followed by a noun/person: “No saben nada de Sara” = they don’t know anything about Sara.
target_language_example: No saben nada de este tema.
native_language_example: They don’t know anything about this topic.

additional_notes: Uses tú (sabes) and is addressed to one person. Common before question words: “no sabes quién…” (you don’t know who…), “no sabes lo que…” (you don’t know what…), “no sabes qué…” (you don’t know what/which…). Often used to say someone lacks information or doesn’t know what to do; by itself (“No sabes.”) it can sound blunt/critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: No sabes lo mucho que te agradezco tu ayuda.
native_language_example: You don’t know how much I appreciate your help.

additional_notes: Uses the negative (no) + verb (sabes) + nada (“anything”) for emphasis. It can be a neutral statement about lack of knowledge (No sabes nada sobre eso.) or a sharp/critical comment meaning “You have no idea” (No sabes nada, mamá.). Often followed by de or sobre to say what someone doesn’t know: no sabes nada de mí / sobre mí.
target_language_example: Perdón, pero no sabes nada de lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you don’t know anything about what happened.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no knowledge/understanding of a person, topic, or situation. Often sounds critical or accusatory. Usually followed by a noun, pronoun (mí, ella, nosotros), or an infinitive: "No sabes nada de ser...". Note: you normally say either "no sabes nada de mí" or "no sabes nada acerca de mí" (not *"de acerca de").
target_language_example: No sabes nada de mi trabajo, así que no opines.
native_language_example: You don’t know anything about my job, so don’t give your opinion.

additional_notes: Used to say someone lacked knowledge/awareness in the past, often as background info or describing an ongoing situation (“I didn’t know what to do”). Commonly followed by a clause: no sabía que… (I didn’t know that…), no sabía qué… (I didn’t know what…), or no sabía nada (I didn’t know anything).
target_language_example: No sabía que hoy era feriado.
native_language_example: I didn’t know today was a holiday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you didn’t know in the past. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), often implying you lacked the information at that time. It’s commonly followed by a clause with "que"; after "no sabía que", Spanish often uses the subjunctive (e.g., "fuera") when the information is new/unknown to the speaker.
target_language_example: No sabía que vivías tan lejos.
native_language_example: I didn’t know you lived so far away.

additional_notes: Used when someone is speechless, unsure how to respond, or can’t find the right words. It’s the imperfect past of saber (sabía), often describing a situation in progress or a repeated state in the past. You can change the subject: no sabía / no sabías / no sabíamos / no sabían qué decir.
target_language_example: Cuando me dieron la noticia, no sabía qué decir.
native_language_example: When they gave me the news, I didn’t know what to say.

additional_notes: Used to express being unsure how to respond or what action to take. "Sabía" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), suggesting an ongoing state in the past. Often appears with context showing confusion, worry, or desperation.
target_language_example: Cuando empezó a llover tan fuerte, no sabía qué hacer.
native_language_example: When it started raining so hard, I didn’t know what to do.

meaning: "it is not" / "one does not" (impersonal/passive with *se*), often meaning "you can’t" or "isn’t allowed."
additional_notes: Used with *se* to talk about rules, general truths, or things people in general do/don’t do—without saying who the subject is. Common in signs and regulations: *No se permite…* (“…is not allowed”), *No se pueden…* (“…can’t be done”), *No se + verb* (“People don’t / You don’t (in general)”).
target_language_example: Aquí no se puede fumar.
native_language_example: You can’t smoke here / Smoking is not allowed here.

meaning: Don’t come closer; don’t approach. (formal command)
additional_notes: Negative command in the usted form of acercarse (to come closer/approach). Often used with “a” + person/place: “No se acerque a la puerta.” You can add distance words like “mucho/demasiado”: “No se acerque demasiado.”
target_language_example: Por favor, no se acerque a la ventana.
native_language_example: Please, don’t go near the window.

meaning: "has/have not" (with impersonal/passive se: "it hasn't been…", "no one has…").
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the negative present perfect: no se ha + participle. The "se" often makes the sentence impersonal or passive-like, so English usually uses "it hasn't been…" or "no one has…" (e.g., No se ha sabido… = "Nothing has been known / We haven't heard…").
target_language_example: Todavía no se ha decidido nada.
native_language_example: Nothing has been decided yet.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to show a negative action with two object pronouns: **se** + **lo**. Here **se** usually stands for **le/les** (to him/her/you formal/them) because **le/les** changes to **se** when it comes before **lo/la/los/las** (e.g., *No se lo pedí* = *No le lo pedí* ❌). The exact meaning depends on the verb: *no se lo comió* (he didn’t eat it), *no se lo pedí* (I didn’t ask him/her for it), *no se lo pregunté* (I didn’t ask him/her), *no se lo tome* (don’t take it), *no se lo mostrará* (he won’t show it).
target_language_example: No se lo dije a mi jefe.
native_language_example: I didn’t tell it to my boss (I didn’t tell my boss).

meaning: “Don’t tell it to him/her/them.” / “Don’t tell them.”
additional_notes: Negative command (tú) of "decir". It uses two pronouns: "se" (indirect object = to him/her/them; it replaces "le/les" before "lo") + "lo" (direct object = it/that). You can add who not to tell: "No se lo digas a nadie" (Don’t tell anyone), "No se lo digas al elfo" (Don’t tell the elf).
target_language_example: Por favor, no se lo digas a tu mamá todavía.
native_language_example: Please, don’t tell your mom yet.

additional_notes: A negative command (tú) meaning “don’t tell it to [someone].” It uses object pronouns: **se** = “to him/her/them” (replaces *le/les* before **lo**), **lo** = “it/that.” Common with people: *No se lo digas a mamá / a nadie.*
target_language_example: Es un secreto: no se lo digas a nadie.
native_language_example: It’s a secret: don’t tell anyone.

meaning: “I can’t think of (anything/any reason/what to say).”
additional_notes: Literally “it doesn’t occur to me.” Uses the verb **ocurrirse** with an indirect object pronoun: **no se me ocurre** (to me), **no se te ocurre** (to you), **no se le ocurre** (to him/her/you formal). Often followed by **nada** (“anything”), **ninguna + noun** (“any + noun”), or a question word: **qué decir**, **por qué**, **cómo**.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no se me ocurre qué responder.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t think of what to say.

additional_notes: A common sign/notice. Literally "it is not permitted to smoke" (impersonal/passive "se"), so it doesn’t say who forbids it. Often used with a place or time: "No se permite fumar en..." / "durante...".
target_language_example: En este restaurante no se permite fumar.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed in this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used for rules and signs to say something is prohibited. It’s an impersonal passive construction: literally “(they) are not permitted,” often followed by a noun (e.g., perros, mascotas) or an activity (e.g., peleas). Common in formal contexts like hotels, clubs, and public notices.
target_language_example: En la piscina no se permiten bebidas de vidrio.
native_language_example: Glass drinks/containers aren’t allowed in the pool.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to be concerned. It uses the formal usted form (preocupe), so it’s appropriate with strangers, customers, older people, or in polite situations. Informal version: “no te preocupes.” You can also add “por eso/por ello” = “about that.”
target_language_example: No se preocupe, yo me encargo de todo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of everything.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with "se" used to talk about a general rule or impossibility (not about a specific person). It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "No se puede + infinitive" (e.g., no se puede entrar, no se puede saber).
target_language_example: Aquí no se puede fumar.
native_language_example: You can’t smoke here.

additional_notes: Impersonal phrase with **se** + **poder**: it means “it’s not possible to trust…” / “you can’t trust…”. It’s often used as a general statement rather than blaming a specific person. Use **confiar en + person/thing**: *No se puede confiar en ella / en los políticos.*
target_language_example: No se puede confiar en esa persona.
native_language_example: You can’t trust that person.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with **se** (no specific person is doing the knowing). It’s used when the information is unknown or uncertain, often followed by a question word or clause: **no se sabe qué/cuál/lo que…**.
target_language_example: No se sabe a qué hora llegará el autobús.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what time the bus will arrive.

additional_notes: Used to clarify the real point of a situation and correct a misunderstanding. Often followed by a noun ("No se trata de mí") or an infinitive verb ("No se trata de ganar dinero"). You can also use it to reject an interpretation: "No se trata de un chiste" (It’s not a joke).
target_language_example: No se trata de quién tiene la culpa; se trata de cómo lo vamos a arreglar.
native_language_example: It’s not about who’s to blame; it’s about how we’re going to fix it.

additional_notes: Used to say something is more important or broader than one thing. The pattern is: No se trata sólo de + noun/infinitive. You can also hear: No se trata solo de (same meaning).
target_language_example: No se trata sólo de ganar; se trata de aprender.
native_language_example: It’s not just about winning; it’s about learning.

meaning: "You can't see it" / "it isn't visible"; also "it doesn't look (like)".
additional_notes:
Used with an implicit subject (it/that/he/she): 
- Visibility: "El avión no se ve" = the plane can’t be seen.
- Appearance/impression: "No se ve feliz" = he/she doesn’t look happy; "No se ve nada bien" = it doesn’t look good at all.
Often expanded as "no se ve + adjective" (doesn’t look + adjective) or "no se ve nada" (you can’t see anything).
target_language_example: Con esta niebla, la montaña no se ve.
native_language_example: With this fog, you can’t see the mountain.

meaning: "may not be" / "isn't" (subjunctive form of "ser", to be).
additional_notes: “Sea” is the present subjunctive of “ser” (to be). You often see “no sea” after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (uncertainty, doubt, wishes), like “ojalá que…”, “puede que…”, “quizás/tal vez…”. It also appears in phrases like “no tenemos otra opción que no sea…” meaning “we have no other option but to… / other than…”.
target_language_example: Espero que no sea demasiado tarde.
native_language_example: I hope it isn’t too late.

meaning: “don’t be …” (telling someone not to act a certain way).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) not to be something or not to behave in a certain way. It’s the negative tú command of ser: no seas + adjective/noun (No seas ridículo / No seas un bebé). In other contexts it can also be part of a subjunctive clause meaning “that you are not …” (Es bueno que no seas parte…).
target_language_example: No seas tan impaciente; ya casi llegamos.
native_language_example: Don’t be so impatient; we’re almost there.

meaning: “don’t be so…” (telling someone to stop being so ___).
additional_notes: Used as an informal/neutral way to criticize or scold someone. Grammatically it’s the negative tú command of **ser** (“no seas”) + **tan** (“so/as”), followed by an adjective: **No seas tan + adj.** The adjective agrees with the person you’re talking to (e.g., *tan malo/tan mala*).
target_language_example: No seas tan impaciente; ya voy.
native_language_example: Don’t be so impatient; I’m coming.

meaning: “it means nothing to me” / “it doesn’t matter to me.”
additional_notes: Used to say something has no importance, value, or emotional significance for you. With people ("Él/Ella no significa nada para mí"), it can sound cold and implies you don’t care about them or don’t have feelings for them. Pattern: [subject] + no significa nada para mí.
target_language_example: Ese comentario no significa nada para mí.
native_language_example: That comment means nothing to me.

meaning: “It’s no use / it doesn’t help / it’s pointless.”
additional_notes: Used to say something has no benefit or effect. Often followed by an infinitive: “No sirve de nada + infinitive” (No sirve de nada quejarse = Complaining is no use). You can also use it alone as a full sentence: “Pero no sirve de nada.”
target_language_example: No sirve de nada preocuparse por eso ahora.
native_language_example: There’s no point in worrying about that now.

additional_notes: Used to say your group/person isn’t alone in doing, thinking, or experiencing something. Often followed by: **en + infinitive** ("no somos los únicos en pensar...") or **que + verb** ("no somos los únicos que creemos..."). You can change the subject: *no soy el único / no eres el único / no son los únicos*, etc. (Agree **único** with gender/number: *la única, los únicos, las únicas*.)
target_language_example: No somos los únicos que estamos preocupados por el examen.
native_language_example: We’re not the only ones who are worried about the exam.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "ser" in the present tense, 3rd person plural: "ellos/ellas no son" = "they are not". In Spain it also matches "vosotros/vosotras no son" (less common than "no sois"). Common for stating what something is not, classifying/identifying, or saying something isn’t true/real.
target_language_example: Esos zapatos no son míos.
native_language_example: Those shoes are not mine.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** (soy) to deny identity, description, or a characteristic: **No soy + noun/adjective** (No soy el único / No soy rica / No soy sorda). Often paired with **tan ... como** for comparisons: **No soy tan X como para...** (“I’m not so X as to…”).
target_language_example: No soy estudiante; soy profesor.
native_language_example: I’m not a student; I’m a teacher.

meaning: "I’m not a" (said by a male speaker).
additional_notes: Used to deny being a specific kind of person/thing before a masculine singular noun: No soy un + noun/adjective phrase. For a female speaker, use “no soy una”. If the noun is feminine but the speaker is male, you still use the noun’s gender: “No soy una persona…”
target_language_example: No soy un experto, pero puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: I’m not an expert, but I can help you.

additional_notes: Used as a conversational filler to show uncertainty or soften what you’re about to say, then add a guess, opinion, contrast, or warning. Often implies “I’m not sure, but…” or “I don’t know (the full story), but…”.
target_language_example: No sé, pero creo que deberíamos irnos ya.
native_language_example: I don’t know, but I think we should leave now.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you have zero knowledge about something. Often followed by a topic with: acerca de / sobre (“about”) or al respecto (“about it/that”). You can also say it alone as a complete answer.
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé absolutamente nada de ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything at all about that topic.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the way/method to do something, or you can’t explain how something happened. It’s often followed by an infinitive (No sé cómo usarla) or by a clause (No sé cómo lo hace / No sé cómo encontró la casa). In conversation it can also express worry or uncertainty about what you’ll do next (No sé cómo voy a...).
target_language_example: No sé cómo decirle la verdad.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to tell him/her the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something surprising or hard to explain: the speaker doesn’t know the method or reason, but states that the result is true. Often followed by a statement like "happened," "works," or "it is."
target_language_example: No sé cómo, pero llegamos a tiempo.
native_language_example: I don’t know how, but we got there on time.

meaning: “I don’t know what…” / “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you don’t know or don’t understand. Most often followed by a verb like hablar (hablas/estás hablando/hablan): “No sé de qué hablas” = “I don’t know what you’re talking about.” In questions, it becomes “¿De qué hablas?” (“What are you talking about?”).
target_language_example: No sé de qué me acusas.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you’re accusing me of.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the location of something (or someone). Often appears with a noun after it: “No sé dónde está el baño/el oro/mi teléfono.” You can add emphasis with “de verdad” (really) or “para ser sincero” (to be honest).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé dónde está mi llave.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where my key is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unknown thing or situation, followed by a clause: “No sé lo que + verb …”. Often uses “lo que” (what/that which) rather than “qué” because it refers to “the thing that…”. You can use it with different tenses: “No sé lo que fue” (what it was), “No sé lo que había hecho” (what I had done), “No sé lo que traerá el mañana” (what tomorrow will bring).
target_language_example: No sé lo que pasó anoche.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Often used with de/acerca de/sobre to say you don’t know anything about a topic: No sé nada de eso / sobre esto. You can intensify it with repetition: No sé nada de nada (“I don’t know anything at all”). In Spanish, double negatives are normal (no + nada).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé nada de ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about that topic.

meaning: "I don’t know anything about" / "I know nothing about".
additional_notes: Used to say you have no knowledge or information about a topic, situation, or person. The part after de can be a subject (de ciencia), a person (de él/ella), or an event (de ningún secuestro). Often implies ignorance or denial of involvement: No sé nada de eso = “I know nothing about that.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé nada de este tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about this topic.

additional_notes: Used to say you have zero knowledge/information about a topic. Follow it with a noun (no sé nada sobre arte), a pronoun (no sé nada sobre eso/ello), or a person (no sé nada sobre él). In speech you can also hear the same idea as “No sé nada de …” (e.g., No sé nada de Linux).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no sé nada sobre ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about that topic.

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t know the reason for something. Often followed by a full clause ("No sé por qué dijo eso"), but it can also be said alone as a complete answer ("No sé por qué."). You’ll also hear the variant "No sé por qué + infinitive" (e.g., "No sé por qué ir"), meaning “I don’t know why (to) …”.
target_language_example: No sé por qué no me contestas.
native_language_example: I don’t know why you’re not answering me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something surprising or hard to explain, followed by a statement or feeling. Often expresses uncertainty about the reason: “No sé por qué, pero me encanta…” / “No sé por qué, pero pensé…” You can drop the comma in casual writing, but the pause is natural in speech.
target_language_example: No sé por qué, pero hoy me siento nervioso.
native_language_example: I don’t know why, but today I feel nervous.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person’s identity. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., "no sé quién fue/era/es") or a clause ("no sé quién lo tomó"). You may also hear the subjunctive in some contexts ("no sé quién sea ese tipo"), especially when the identity is unknown or uncertain. It can also be used alone as a short answer: "Sí, pero no sé quién."
target_language_example: No sé quién me llamó anoche.
native_language_example: I don't know who called me last night.

meaning: I don’t know what to do.
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or being stuck about what action to take. You can add extra details with "con + [person/thing]" (e.g., "no sé qué hacer con ella" = "I don’t know what to do with her"). Often said on its own as a complete sentence, and you may hear it with fillers like "es que" to sound more natural in conversation.
target_language_example: Estoy muy nervioso y no sé qué hacer.
native_language_example: I’m very nervous and I don’t know what to do.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about whether something is true or will happen. It’s often followed by a verb in the indicative (No sé si llueve / lloverá) and can also be used to soften an opinion or question (No sé si es buena idea…).
target_language_example: No sé si tengo tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: I don't know if I have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun te (“you” informal singular) to make a negative statement or command. Common patterns: No te + verb (command: “Don’t ...”: No te acerques = Don’t come closer) and no + verb + te (statement: No te he visto = I haven’t seen you).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is going to be fine.

meaning: “Don’t come closer / Don’t get close (to me/it).”
additional_notes: Negative informal command (tú) of the verb *acercarse* (“to come closer”). It’s used as a warning or instruction, often with **a / al** (“to the”): *No te acerques a la ventana* (“Don’t go near the window”). You can also say *No te acerques más* (“Don’t come any closer”).
target_language_example: No te acerques al perro; puede morder.
native_language_example: Don’t get close to the dog; it might bite.

additional_notes: A strong warning/command telling someone not to do something. Uses the verb "atreverse" (to dare) in the present subjunctive: "te atrevas". It’s followed by an infinitive: "no te atrevas a decir / hablar / ponerte...". Common in arguments and can sound threatening or very firm.
target_language_example: No te atrevas a tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t you dare touch that.

additional_notes: Used to point out that someone isn’t noticing or understanding something obvious. Often followed by **de + noun** (No te das cuenta de la verdad) or by a **que** clause (No te das cuenta que es tarde). In more formal Spanish, **No te das cuenta de que...** is common.
target_language_example: ¿No te das cuenta de que ya es muy tarde?
native_language_example: Don’t you realize it’s already very late?

additional_notes: Commonly used to call someone out for pretending or acting innocent: “No te hagas (el/la) + noun/adjective” (e.g., “No te hagas el listo” = don’t act smart). It also appears with reflexive idioms like “no te hagas ilusiones” (don’t get your hopes up) and other “hacerse + …” expressions (e.g., “no te hagas explotar” = don’t blow yourself up / don’t get yourself blown up). Often sounds colloquial in the standalone form “No te hagas.”
target_language_example: No te hagas; sé que tú también quieres ir.
native_language_example: Don’t pretend; I know you also want to go.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative present perfect: **no** + **te** (object pronoun “you”) + **he** (from *haber*, “I have”) + a past participle (e.g., *entendido, preguntado, enseñado*). It often means “I haven’t [done something] to/with you” or “I haven’t [verb]-ed you,” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: No te he visto hoy.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you today.

additional_notes: Present perfect of ver: he visto = “I have seen.” Used to say you haven’t seen someone (often “lately/recently”: últimamente), or “never” (nunca). It can also be a lead-in to a comment after running into someone unexpectedly: “I haven’t seen you—You look great.”
target_language_example: ¡Hola! No te he visto desde la fiesta.
native_language_example: Hi! I haven’t seen you since the party.

additional_notes: With "si" + verb, it’s a common way to ask permission or check if something is okay: "¿No te importa si…?" = "Do you mind if…?" (often polite). Said on its own, it can mean "You don’t care" or, in a sharper tone, "It’s none of your business." Uses "te" (tú), so it’s informal in the sense of being the tú form (vs. "no le importa").
target_language_example: ¿No te importa si abro la ventana?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: “don’t … it / you can’t … it” (no + te + lo before a verb).
additional_notes: This is a common pronoun cluster used before a verb: **no** (not/don’t) + **te** (“to you” or “for yourself”) + **lo** (“it”). It depends on the verb that follows: **No te lo pienses** = “Don’t think about it,” **No te lo pierdas** = “Don’t miss it,” **No te lo puedes imaginar** = “You can’t imagine it,” **No te lo tomes a pecho** = “Don’t take it so personally.”
target_language_example: No te lo digas a nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t tell it to anyone.

meaning: Don’t get involved; don’t meddle / don’t mess with it.
additional_notes: Negative command (tú) from "meterse". Common patterns: "No te metas con + alguien/algo" = don’t mess with / don’t pick on; "No te metas en + problema/lío" = don’t get into trouble/a mess; used alone ("No te metas") to tell someone to stay out of it.
target_language_example: No te metas en esto; no es asunto tuyo.
native_language_example: Don’t get involved in this; it’s none of your business.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (informally) not to interfere, not to get involved, or not to poke their nose into a situation or someone else’s business. It’s the negative tú command of meterse en (“to get into / get involved in”). Often followed by esto/eso (“this/that”), mis asuntos (“my business”), la vida de los demás (“other people’s lives”), lo que no te importa (“what doesn’t concern you”).
target_language_example: No te metas en mis asuntos; yo lo arreglo.
native_language_example: Don’t meddle in my business; I’ll handle it.

additional_notes: An informal command using the negative tú imperative of "moverse" (to move). Common in urgent situations (e.g., during a photo, when someone might be in danger). You can add location: "No te muevas de ahí" = "Don’t move from there / Stay right there."
target_language_example: No te muevas, ya vuelvo.
native_language_example: Don’t move; I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone (one person you address as tú) to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (no te olvides de + infinitive): No te olvides de llamar / traer / sacar…. For formal you: No se olvide de….
target_language_example: No te olvides de cerrar la puerta cuando salgas.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to close the door when you leave.

meaning: "Don’t get" / "don’t become" (in a certain mood or state).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to start feeling or acting a certain way, especially with emotions or reactions: no te pongas celoso/a (don’t get jealous), no te pongas histérico/a (don’t get hysterical), no te pongas así (don’t get like that). It comes from the verb ponerse (“to get/become” in a temporary state). Often followed by an adjective or “así.”
target_language_example: No te pongas nervioso, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t get nervous; everything is going to be fine.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone and tell them not to worry about a person/thing/situation. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (por él, por eso, por el problema). You can also hear: “No te preocupes” = “Don’t worry.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes por mí; estoy bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me; I’m fine.

additional_notes:
Negative tú command of **quedarse** (“to stay/remain/end up”). It’s often followed by:
- **a place/position**: *No te quedes ahí sentado* (“Don’t stay sitting there.”)
- **an adjective/state**: *No te quedes dormido / hambriento* (“Don’t fall asleep / don’t end up hungry.”)
- **a gerund (-ando/-iendo)**: *No te quedes mirando* (“Don’t keep staring/watching.”)
- **an adverb**: *No te quedes atrás* (“Don’t fall behind.”)
target_language_example: No te quedes callado; dime qué pasó.
native_language_example: Don’t stay quiet; tell me what happened.

meaning: Don’t just stand (sit) there; don’t stay there.
additional_notes: An informal-sounding imperative using quedar(se) (“to stay/remain”) + ahí (“there”). It’s used to urge someone to move or take action instead of remaining where they are. Often expanded with an adjective/participle that agrees with the person: no te quedes ahí parado/parada (standing), sentado/sentada (sitting).
target_language_example: ¡No te quedes ahí, ven a ayudarme!
native_language_example: Don’t just stand there—come help me!

meaning: “you’re not going to …” / “it’s not going to … (to you)”.
additional_notes: Used to make a negative near-future statement with the structure: no + te + va a + infinitive. It often means “you won’t (do something)” (No te va a gustar = You’re not going to like it) or “it won’t happen to you” with certain verbs (No te va a pasar/ocurrir nada = Nothing is going to happen to you).
target_language_example: No te va a servir esa explicación.
native_language_example: That explanation isn’t going to help you.

additional_notes: Negative command (tú) of the verb irse (“to leave/go away”). Often used to ask someone to stay, sometimes with extra details: no te vayas sin mí (“don’t go without me”), no te vayas a ninguna parte / a ningún lado (“don’t go anywhere”).
target_language_example: No te vayas todavía, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t leave yet, please.

meaning: "I'm not going to (do something to/for you)".
additional_notes: Used to start a negative "near future" with **ir a + infinitive**: **(yo) voy a + verb** = "I’m going to + verb". **No** makes it negative. **Te** is the indirect/direct object pronoun meaning "to you" or "you" (depending on the verb): *No te voy a ayudar* = "I’m not going to help you"; *No te voy a perdonar* = "I’m not going to forgive you." Often followed by an infinitive (ayudar, traer, hacer, perdonar, etc.).
target_language_example: No te voy a mentir.
native_language_example: I'm not going to lie to you.

meaning: "we don't have" / "we don't have any" (present tense).
additional_notes: Used with "tener" (to have) in the present tense for "we" (nosotros). Often followed by a noun (no tenemos clase/comida/acceso) or an expression like "no tenemos nada" (we have nothing). Common set phrases: "No tenemos más remedio" = "We have no choice"; "No tenemos nada en común" = "We have nothing in common"; "No tenemos adónde volver" = "We have nowhere to return".
target_language_example: Hoy no tenemos tiempo para hacerlo.
native_language_example: Today we don't have time to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say “we” don’t possess something, don’t share anything, or don’t have anything to do/continue (“no tenemos nada más de que hablar” = “we have nothing else to talk about”). Often appears with add-ons like: “en común” (in common), “más” (anything else), “más que + infinitive” (nothing more than / nothing else to + verb), or “en absoluto” (at all).
target_language_example: Si no tenemos nada en común, es difícil ser amigos.
native_language_example: If we have nothing in common, it’s hard to be friends.

additional_notes: Negative tú command of tener (“tengas” is the present subjunctive): literally “don’t have fear.” Used to reassure someone. Often followed by a reason with porque (e.g., “No tengas miedo, porque…”). Common with affectionate words like bebé or cariño.
target_language_example: No tengas miedo, estoy aquí contigo.
native_language_example: Don’t be afraid, I’m here with you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (to have) in the 1st person singular present (tengo). Put no directly before the verb to make it negative. It’s used for possession (No tengo gato.), lack of something (No tengo tiempo.), and not having an option/place (No tengo otro sitio adonde ir.).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo efectivo ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have cash right now.

meaning: "I don't have anyone" (to talk to / help me / trust / etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say you have nobody available for something. With people as a direct object, Spanish often uses "a" (personal a): "No tengo a nadie". It’s commonly followed by a relative clause that explains what you need: "a quien contarle..." (to tell), "con quien jugar" (to play with), "en quien confiar" (to trust), "que me ayude" (who helps me).
target_language_example: No tengo a nadie que me acompañe al médico.
native_language_example: I don't have anyone to go with me to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have money right now. Often said as a simple reason/explanation (e.g., why you can’t buy something). You can add time words like hoy (today) or ahora (now): “Hoy no tengo dinero.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo dinero para pagar ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have money to pay right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have the desire or motivation to do an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: no tengo ganas de + cantar/ir/hablar. You can change the person: no tienes ganas de… (you don’t feel like…), no tenemos ganas de… (we don’t feel like…). Often implies “not in the mood” rather than a permanent refusal.
target_language_example: Hoy no tengo ganas de salir; prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel like going out; I’d rather stay home.

meaning: "I have no idea (about)…" / "I don’t know… (at all)."
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something (often strongly). It’s followed by a question word like cómo (how), dónde (where), por qué (why), quién (who), or qué (what/which/what it means). You can also say: "No tengo idea" by itself.
target_language_example: No tengo idea de a qué hora empieza la reunión.
native_language_example: I have no idea what time the meeting starts.

additional_notes:
Used to say you don’t possess or have something available. It’s often followed by a clarification: 
- no tengo nada para ti = I don’t have anything for you
- no tengo nada en contra de... = I have nothing against... (no objection or bad feelings).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no tengo nada que decir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have anything to say today.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say you don’t have anything to do/say/eat/add/offer. Often appears as: “No tengo nada que + infinitive” (e.g., no tengo nada que decir). You can add emphasis with “ya”: “Ya no tengo nada que decir.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo nada que añadir.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to add.

meaning: "I have nothing to say" / "I have nothing to add" (no comment).
additional_notes: Used to state that you don’t want to comment, or that you don’t have any opinion or extra information. Often appears with phrases like "por el momento" (for now) or "al respecto" (about it). You can change the person: "no tenemos nada que decir" (we have nothing to say), "no tiene nada que decir" (he/she/you formal has nothing to say).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no tengo nada que decir sobre ese tema.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I have nothing to say about that topic.

meaning: 'I have nothing to do' / 'I’ve got nothing to do.' (Sometimes: 'It’s none of my business / I’m not involved.')
additional_notes: Literally “I don’t have anything to do.” Used to say you’re free/not busy: “No tengo nada que hacer esta tarde.” With topics like “en este asunto” (in this matter), it can mean you have no role or responsibility in it: “No tengo nada que hacer en este asunto” = “This doesn’t concern me / I have nothing to do with this.” You can add time phrases like “por el momento” (for now) or “en particular” (in particular).
target_language_example: Hoy no tengo nada que hacer, así que puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: Today I have nothing to do, so I can help you.

no tengo nada que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: no tengo nada que ver con
meaning: "I have nothing to do with" / "I have nothing to do with it/them."
additional_notes: Used to deny involvement or connection with a person, situation, or problem. It’s a fixed expression: tener que ver con = “to have to do with / to be related to,” and adding no...nada makes it “nothing to do with.” You can change the subject/person: no tienes nada que ver con..., no tiene nada que ver con..., no tenemos nada que ver con....
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero no tengo nada que ver con eso.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I have nothing to do with that.

meaning: "I have no idea" / "I don’t know at all."
additional_notes:
A very common way to say you have zero information or you’re completely unsure. Often followed by:
- "de" + noun/pronoun: "No tengo ni idea de eso." (I have no idea about that.)
- "de" + question word: "No tengo ni idea del por qué." (I have no idea why.)
- a question word clause: "No tengo ni idea cómo llegué aquí." (I have no idea how I got here.)
You can also say it alone: "No tengo ni idea."
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea dónde están mis llaves.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my keys are.

meaning: “I have no idea (about)…” / “I don’t know at all…”
additional_notes: Used to strongly say you don’t know something. Often followed by a question word (adónde, cuáles, cuántos, dónde, qué) or by “lo que…”. You can also hear it without “de” when the next word is a question word: “No tengo ni idea qué es esto.”
target_language_example: No tengo ni idea de dónde está mi móvil.
native_language_example: I have no idea where my phone is.

additional_notes: Used to say you have none of something. "Ninguna" agrees with a feminine noun that usually follows (e.g., ninguna duda/queja/razón/prueba). It commonly appears with a double negative in Spanish: "no" + "ninguna" = "any" in English (not "no any"). With masculine nouns, use "no tengo ningún" (e.g., no tengo ningún problema).
target_language_example: No tengo ninguna idea de dónde está.
native_language_example: I have no idea where it is.

additional_notes: Used to say you have zero of something. It must match a masculine singular noun: no tengo ningún plan/interés/lugar/tiempo. With feminine singular, use "no tengo ninguna" (ninguna idea). With plural nouns, use "no tengo ningunos/ningunas" (less common) or more naturally "no tengo ningún + noun" when you mean "any kind of" (no tengo ningún tipo de planes).
target_language_example: Lo siento, hoy no tengo ningún tiempo libre.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any free time today.

meaning: "I have no problem" / "I don't have any problem."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re fine with something or you don’t mind (often followed by "con eso/esto" = "with that/this" or by an action: "No tengo ningún problema (en) dejando..." = "I have no problem letting..."). In conversation it can also mean "No worries" or "That's fine."
target_language_example: No tengo ningún problema con esperar cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I have no problem waiting five minutes.

meaning: “I don’t have to” / “I have no reason to.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t feel obligated or you don’t see any justification for doing something. Often followed by an infinitive: “No tengo por qué + infinitive” (e.g., disculparme, hacerlo). It can also be used alone to mean “I don’t have to (do that).”
target_language_example: No tengo por qué explicarte nada.
native_language_example: I don’t have to explain anything to you.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy or unavailable. Often followed by "para" + infinitive or noun to specify what you don’t have time for: "No tengo tiempo para estudiar" / "...para ti". You can add time words for clarity: "ahora" (right now), "hoy" (today).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo tiempo para hablar ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have time to talk right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy to do something. Follow it with a noun (para eso/esto), an infinitive (para ayudarte), or a person/pronoun (para ti/para mí). You can change the verb to match the subject: no tengo (I), no tienes (you), no tiene (he/she/you formal), no tenemos (we).
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tengo tiempo para hablar ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time to talk right now.

additional_notes: Negative form of "tener" in the imperfect tense (yo tenía = I had / I used to have). Use it to say someone lacked something in the past, often describing an ongoing situation, background detail, or repeated past circumstance: "No tenía agua" (He didn't have water). It’s also common with expressions like "no tenía dónde + infinitive" (didn’t have anywhere to...) and "no tenía otro remedio" (had no other choice).
target_language_example: Cuando era estudiante, no tenía tiempo para salir.
native_language_example: When I was a student, I didn't have time to go out.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (tenía) to describe a past situation/background state. The subject is often understood from context (yo/él/ella), but you can add it for clarity: “Yo no tenía dinero.” Often followed by a result with “así que / por eso” (so/that’s why).
target_language_example: Yo no tenía dinero, así que no pude comprar el boleto.
native_language_example: I didn’t have any money, so I couldn’t buy the ticket.

meaning: "I/He/She didn’t have any idea (about...)"; "had no idea (that/what/why...)."
additional_notes: Used to say someone didn’t know or didn’t understand something at all. Commonly followed by a question word clause: de lo que (what), de qué (what), de por qué (why), de a qué hora (what time), etc. Tense can change with the subject/time: no tengo idea de (I have no idea), no tenía idea de (I had no idea), no tendrás idea de (you won’t have any idea).
target_language_example: Yo no tenía idea de que la reunión era hoy.
native_language_example: I had no idea the meeting was today.

meaning: "I had no idea that..." / "I didn't know that..."
additional_notes: Used to say you were unaware or surprised about a fact. It’s in the imperfect past (tenía), common when talking about what you didn’t know at that time. Often followed by a clause with que + verb: No tenía idea de que vinieras. In conversation you’ll also hear: No tenía ni idea de que... (a bit stronger).
target_language_example: No tenía idea de que ya habías llegado.
native_language_example: I had no idea that you had already arrived.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did not plan or mean to do something. It’s in the imperfect past (tenía), often used for ongoing intentions in the past. Follow it with an infinitive: no tenía intención de + infinitivo (e.g., ir, dar, rendirse). You can change the subject/person: no tenías intención de…, no tenía intención de…, no teníamos intención de….
target_language_example: No tenía intención de molestarte, lo siento.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to bother you; I’m sorry.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of tener (tenía) with negation (no) and nada. Used to describe a past situation or ongoing lack in the past: no tenía nada para comer (nothing to eat), no tenía nada en común (nothing in common), no tenía nada mejor que hacer (nothing better to do). Change the subject by changing the verb: yo no tenía nada, tú no tenías nada, él/ella no tenía nada, nosotros no teníamos nada.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué al hotel, no tenía nada de dinero.
native_language_example: When I arrived at the hotel, I didn’t have any money.

meaning: "(he/she) didn’t have anything to…" / "there was nothing (for him/her) to…"
additional_notes: Used to say someone had nothing to do/say/add/hide, followed by an infinitive: no tenía nada que + infinitive (decir, ocultar, agregar/añadir, esconder, etc.). You can change the subject and tense: no tengo nada que…, no teníamos nada que…, no tendrá nada que….
target_language_example: No tenía nada que perder, así que aceptó el trabajo.
native_language_example: He didn’t have anything to lose, so he accepted the job.

meaning: “I/He/She didn’t have anything to do” (had nothing to do).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (tenía) to describe a past state/background situation. Often followed by a result with “así que” (“so”), e.g., because there was nothing to do, someone did something else. You can change the subject: “yo no tenía…”, “ella no tenía…”, “Tom no tenía…”.
target_language_example: No tenía nada que hacer, así que me fui a caminar.
native_language_example: I didn’t have anything to do, so I went for a walk.

meaning: “I/He/She had no idea (about)…” / “I/He/She didn’t know at all…”.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of tener (“tenía”), so it commonly refers to not knowing something at that time in the past (“had no idea”). It’s often followed by an indirect question word like qué (what), dónde/adónde (where/to where), quién (who), cómo (how). You can change the person: no tenía (I/he/she), no tenías (you), no teníamos (we), etc. “Ni idea” adds emphasis: “no idea at all.”
target_language_example: No tenía ni idea de que la tienda cerraba tan temprano.
native_language_example: I had no idea the store closed so early.

no tenía ni idea de que

target_language_multi_word_term: no tenía ni idea de que
additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t know something before (past). Often followed by a clause with que + verb. Very common for expressing surprise or new information. You can change the subject/person: no tenías ni idea de que… (you had no idea), no teníamos ni idea de que… (we had no idea).
target_language_example: No tenía ni idea de que ya habías estado en España.
native_language_example: I had no idea that you had already been to Spain.

additional_notes: Form of the verb tener (“to have”): él/ella/usted no tiene (“he/she/you (formal) don’t have”). Used to say someone/something lacks or does not possess something: no tiene objetivos (has no goals), no tiene deudas (has no debts), no tiene valor (has no value), no tiene dominio aquí (has no control/authority here).
target_language_example: Ella no tiene tiempo hoy.
native_language_example: She doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have any person available (often family/friends) to help, care for, or accompany them. It can be followed by a clause with que + verb: “No tiene a nadie que le ayude” = “She has no one to help her.” The “a” is used because “nadie” refers to people (personal a).
target_language_example: Desde que se mudó, no tiene a nadie con quien hablar.
native_language_example: Since he moved, he has no one to talk to.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has no friends (often in a specific place or situation). It’s built from: no (not) + tiene (has, he/she/you-formal) + amigos (friends). You can add details like aquí (here) or con quienes + infinitive: “no tiene amigos con quienes jugar” (he doesn’t have friends to play with).
target_language_example: En esta ciudad no tiene amigos.
native_language_example: In this city, he/she doesn’t have any friends.

meaning: (he/she) has no idea about; doesn’t know.
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t know something at all, often followed by an indirect question word: cuánto (how much), cuánto tiempo (how long), dónde (where), por qué (why), quién (who), qué (what). You can change the person/tense: no tengo idea de (I have no idea), no tenemos idea de (we have no idea), no tenía idea de (I had no idea).
target_language_example: No tengo idea de cuánto cuesta.
native_language_example: I have no idea how much it costs.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has nothing (no objects, no money, no plans, etc.). It’s often followed by an infinitive to mean “has nothing to + verb”: “no tiene nada que perder” = “has nothing to lose.” You can also add “mejor” to mean “has nothing better to do.”
target_language_example: Ahora mismo, ella no tiene nada que decir.
native_language_example: Right now, she has nothing to say.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things share zero similarities. Usually followed by "con" + a person/thing: "No tiene nada en común conmigo/contigo/con él/con ella". You can add "con respecto a" (or "en cuanto a") to specify the area: "…con respecto a sus gustos" (regarding their tastes).
target_language_example: No tenemos nada en común, pero podemos llevarnos bien.
native_language_example: We have nothing in common, but we can get along well.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone has no reason or opportunity to do something: "No tiene nada que + infinitive" (e.g., reclamar, esconder, decir, perder). The verb changes with the subject: "no tengo nada que…", "no tienes nada que…", "no tenemos nada que…".
target_language_example: No tengo nada que decir.
native_language_example: I have nothing to say.

meaning: “It has nothing to do with…” / “It’s not related.”
additional_notes: Used to say there is no connection, relationship, or relevance between two things. Very common with **con**: *No tiene nada que ver con X* (“It has nothing to do with X”). You can also say it about people: *Él no tiene nada que ver con eso* (“He has nothing to do with that” / “He wasn’t involved”).
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con lo que estamos hablando.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what we’re talking about.

no tiene nada que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: no tiene nada que ver con
meaning: “has nothing to do with” / “is not related to”.
additional_notes: Used to say there is no connection or relevance between two things. The basic structure is: (subject) + no tiene nada que ver con + noun / person / situation. It can change for tense and person: no tengo nada que ver con… (I have nothing to do with…), no tiene nada que ver con… (it has nothing to do with…).
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con mi decisión.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with my decision.

no tiene nada que ver con esto

target_language_multi_word_term: no tiene nada que ver con esto
meaning: “it has nothing to do with this” / “it has nothing to do with it.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not related to the situation, or not involved/responsible. Often appears as: «(Él/Ella) no tiene nada que ver con esto/eso» or «no tiene nada que ver con + [noun]» (e.g., «no tiene nada que ver con el problema»). You can change «tiene» to match the subject: «no tengo…», «no tienes…», «no tienen…».
target_language_example: Yo no tengo nada que ver con esto; pregúntale a él.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with this; ask him.

no tiene nada que ver contigo

target_language_multi_word_term: no tiene nada que ver contigo
meaning: “It has nothing to do with you.” / “It doesn’t concern you.”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not involved in a situation and shouldn’t interfere. You can also use it with other pronouns: “no tiene nada que ver conmigo” (with me), “con él/ella” (with him/her), “con ustedes” (with you all).
target_language_example: Esto no tiene nada que ver contigo, así que por favor no te metas.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with you, so please don’t get involved.

meaning: “doesn’t have any” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has none of something: no tiene ningún + noun (atractivo, orden, valor, derecho, mensaje). “Ningún” is the shortened form of “ninguno” before a masculine singular noun; for feminine singular use “ninguna” (no tiene ninguna razón). For plural nouns, use “ningunos/ningunas” or more commonly “no tiene” + plural noun + “ningún/ninguna” is not used (e.g., no tiene excusas).
target_language_example: Este plan no tiene ningún sentido.
native_language_example: This plan doesn’t make any sense.

additional_notes: Used to say something is illogical, confusing, or has no meaning. You can use it with different subjects: “Eso/Esto no tiene ningún sentido” (That/This doesn’t make any sense), “Lo que dice no tiene ningún sentido” (What he/she says doesn’t make any sense). You can add “para mí” to mean “to me / for me.”
target_language_example: Tu explicación no tiene ningún sentido para mí.
native_language_example: Your explanation doesn’t make any sense to me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not necessary or not required. Often followed by an infinitive ("No tiene por qué ir") or by "ser" + adjective ("No tiene por qué ser así"). It can also suggest “there’s no reason why it should be that way.”
target_language_example: No tiene por qué preocuparte ahora.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry right now.

meaning: “It doesn’t make sense.” / “It has no meaning.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is illogical, unclear, or pointless. It can refer to an idea/explanation/story (“Esto no tiene sentido.”) or to life having (or lacking) meaning (“Mi vida no tiene sentido sin ti.”). Also appears as “no tiene sentido de…” meaning someone lacks a certain quality or attitude (e.g., “no tiene sentido de la aventura” = “has no sense of adventure”).
target_language_example: Lo que dices no tiene sentido.
native_language_example: What you’re saying doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb **tener** in the **ellos/ellas/ustedes** form (**tienen**). It can mean lacking something (“Las plantas no tienen cerebro”) or not possessing/holding something (“No tienen el expediente”). In questions, **no** stays before the verb: “¿No tienen…?”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no tienen esa información aquí.
native_language_example: Sorry, they don't have that information here.

additional_notes: Used with the plural subject (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Often followed by more information: + para + infinitive (no tienen nada para comer = they have nothing to eat), or with common phrases like en común (in common) and en contra (against).
target_language_example: No tienen nada de dinero.
native_language_example: They don’t have any money.

meaning: 'you don't have' / 'you don't have to' (with que).
additional_notes: From tener (to have), 2nd person singular (tú). Common patterns: **no tienes que + infinitive** = 'you don’t have to ...' (no obligation): *No tienes que ser mi amiga.* Also **no tienes nada que + infinitive** = 'you have nothing to ...': *No tienes nada que temer.* And **no tienes más que + infinitive** = 'you only have to / all you have to do is ...': *No tienes más que pulsar el botón.*
target_language_example: No tienes que venir hoy si estás cansado.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come today if you’re tired.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they’re not allowed to do something, or that it’s not fair/acceptable for them to do it. Typically followed by an infinitive (e.g., decir, hacer, preguntar). Can change for other people/tense: no tienes/ no tiene/ no tienen derecho a…
target_language_example: No tienes derecho a hablarme así.
native_language_example: You have no right to talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t know or understand something, or to emphasize how surprising/important something is. Often followed by a noun or an indirect question: "no tienes ni idea de cavar" (about digging), "no tienes ni idea de lo que..." (what...), "no tienes ni idea de lo importante que..." (how important...), "no tienes ni idea de qué..." (what...). Can sound critical depending on tone.
target_language_example: No tienes ni idea de lo difícil que fue para mí.
native_language_example: You have no idea how hard it was for me.

meaning: "you don’t have to" / "there’s no need for you to".
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not obliged to do something, or that there’s no reason/need to do it. It’s often followed by an infinitive (no tienes por qué + decir/hacer/quejarte) and can sound reassuring or slightly firm depending on tone. You can change the person: no tengo por qué, no tienes por qué, no tiene por qué, etc.
target_language_example: No tienes por qué preocuparte; yo me encargo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to worry; I’ll take care of it.

meaning: you don’t have to (you’re not required to).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person informally (tú) that something is not necessary or not required. It’s the negative of "tienes que" (“you have to”). Commonly followed by an infinitive: "no tienes que + infinitive" (e.g., hacer, decir, escuchar, faltar, preocuparte). For a formal "you": "no tiene que"; for "you all": "no tienen que".
target_language_example: No tienes que venir si no quieres.
native_language_example: You don’t have to come if you don’t want to.

meaning: "you don't have to do it" / "you don't need to do it."
additional_notes: Used to say something is not necessary (it removes an obligation). It’s the negative of "tener que" (to have to). You can add timing or conditions: "No tienes que hacerlo ahora" (not now), "No tienes que hacerlo si no quieres" (if you don’t want to).
target_language_example: No tienes que hacerlo hoy; puedo encargarme yo.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do it today; I can take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to say a statement isn’t true for all people. Often followed by a verb: “No todo el mundo puede…” = “Not everyone can…”. Uses singular verb (“es”, “puede”, “quiere”) because “todo el mundo” is treated as singular.
target_language_example: No todo el mundo entiende esta broma.
native_language_example: Not everyone understands this joke.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement doesn’t apply to every member of a group. It’s typically followed by a plural noun ("no todos los errores") or by "que" + verb ("No todos los que vienen..."), and often contrasts with a generalization.
target_language_example: No todos los estudiantes tienen tiempo para estudiar hoy.
native_language_example: Not all (the) students have time to study today.

no tuvo nada que ver con

target_language_multi_word_term: no tuvo nada que ver con
meaning: “had nothing to do with”; “had no involvement in.”
additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility, involvement, or connection to an event or situation. Often used when someone is accused or suspected: “X no tuvo nada que ver con Y.” You can change the tense/person: “no tengo nada que ver con…”, “no tenía nada que ver con…”, “no tendrás nada que ver con…”.
target_language_example: Yo no tuve nada que ver con ese accidente.
native_language_example: I had nothing to do with that accident.

meaning: “is not going to” (negative of *ir a* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about a future plan or something expected to happen (often in the near future). Conjugate **ir** for the subject: *no voy a*, *no vas a*, *no va a*, *no vamos a*, *no van a* + infinitive. Example: *No va a llegar* = “He/She isn’t going to arrive / won’t make it.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, no va a poder venir hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she isn’t going to be able to come today.

meaning: “it’s not going to work” / “it won’t work.”
additional_notes: Used to say something won’t succeed or won’t have the desired result (a plan, an idea, a relationship, a device, etc.). Very common in conversation. Often said emphatically on its own: “No va a funcionar.”
target_language_example: Si seguimos así, no va a funcionar.
native_language_example: If we keep going like this, it’s not going to work.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(no) va a pasar** = “(it’s not) going to happen.” Often said to predict or insist that something won’t occur. With **de + time** it can mean “won’t last past…”: **No va a pasar de esta noche** = “It won’t last past tonight.”
target_language_example: Tranquilo, eso no va a pasar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, that’s not going to happen.

meaning: “it’s not worth it / it’s not worth the trouble.”
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing (because it’s too much effort, risk, time, money, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: “No vale la pena + infinitive” (No vale la pena discutir / hablar). You can also use it alone as a reaction: “¡No vale la pena!”
target_language_example: No vale la pena preocuparse por eso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth worrying about that.

meaning: “we’re not going to …” / “we’re not going to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about a future plan/intention that won’t happen, or to refuse/deny doing something: no vamos a + infinitive (ir, trabajar, volver, etc.). In speech it can sound like a firm decision (“we won’t…”).
target_language_example: No vamos a hablar de eso hoy.
native_language_example: We’re not going to talk about that today.

meaning: "you’re not going to..." (near future; tú form).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something will not happen (or someone won’t be able to do it): no vas a + infinitive. It’s the negative of the common future structure ir a + infinitive (“to be going to”). This is for tú; other forms include: no voy a (I’m not going to), no va a (he/she isn’t going to), no vamos a (we aren’t going to), no van a (they aren’t going to).
target_language_example: No vas a entender si no escuchas.
native_language_example: You’re not going to understand if you don’t listen.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to promise or assure that something won’t be repeated. Common verbs here are ocurrir/pasar/suceder (“to happen”). Formal with “Le prometo…”, informal with “Te prometo…”.
target_language_example: No volverá a ocurrir, se lo aseguro.
native_language_example: It won’t happen again, I assure you.

additional_notes: Used to say you do not intend to do something (near-future plan) or to refuse/decide not to do something. It’s the negative of "voy a" + infinitive. For other subjects: "no vas a" (you), "no va a" (he/she/you formal), "no vamos a" (we), "no van a" (they/you all).
target_language_example: No voy a hablar de eso ahora.
native_language_example: I’m not going to talk about that now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to repeat an action. It’s a negative command with "volver a" (to do something again). After "a" you use an infinitive: "No vuelvas a decir...", "No vuelvas a hacer...". It can sound strict or threatening depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: No vuelvas a hablarme así.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that again.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to contradict what was just said or assumed, then give the correct information. Often followed by a noun/adjective clause: “No, es de…”, “No, es en serio”, “No, es que…”. In speech it’s a common correction/clarification marker.
target_language_example: No, es que no tengo tiempo ahora.
native_language_example: No, it’s just that I don’t have time right now.

meaning: "No, I am…" (used to correct or contradict).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is NOT the case and then state your situation with the verb estar (yo estoy). Common patterns: (1) + adjective: "No, estoy cansado" (I’m tired). (2) + en + place/location: "No, estoy en…" (I’m in/at…). (3) + gerund to describe what you’re doing right now: "No, estoy hablando…" (I’m speaking…).
target_language_example: No, estoy ocupado ahora.
native_language_example: No, I’m busy right now.

additional_notes: "No," is often used to answer or correct someone, followed by a sentence. "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "him"), referring to something already known from context. It usually goes right before a conjugated verb: "No, lo hice" = "No, I did it." (In "No, lo que...", "lo que" means "what/that which"—a different use of "lo".)
target_language_example: No, lo compré ayer.
native_language_example: No, I bought it yesterday.

meaning: “No, …” followed by “me” (“me / myself”) starting the next clause.
additional_notes: This isn’t a set phrase; it’s just a very common pattern in conversation: you say “No,” and then your next sentence begins with the object/reflexive pronoun **me**. You’ll see it with verbs like **gustar** (**No, me gusta…** = “No, I like…”), with accidents/things happening to you (**No, me lo perdí** = “No, I missed it”), or with reflexive verbs (**No, me voy** = “No, I’m leaving”). The comma is a pause in speech; in writing it may or may not appear.
target_language_example: No, me siento bien hoy.
native_language_example: No, I don’t feel well today.

additional_notes: Repeating **no** is a common way to add emphasis or sound more firm/polite when disagreeing or refusing. It often comes at the start of a sentence, followed by the verb: **No, no + verb** (e.g., *No, no necesito…*).
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to correct or deny a statement about what something is. Often followed by a noun (No, no es gato.), an article + noun (No, no es la verdad.), or a negative word like nada/ninguno for emphasis (No, no es nada. / No, no es ninguna prueba.). In Spanish, double negatives are normal and correct.
target_language_example: —¿Es tuyo este libro? —No, no es mío.
native_language_example: —Is this book yours? —No, it isn't mine.

meaning: "No, I don’t / it isn’t (it hasn’t been / I’m not)."
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or correct something, often before a verb that takes the object pronoun “lo” (“it/that”). The second “no” adds emphasis or can sound like a quick self-correction: “No—no, I don’t.” Common with verbs like comprender (understand), ser/estar (to be), and haber sido (have been).
target_language_example: No, no lo sé.
native_language_example: No, I don’t know it.

additional_notes: Repeating **no** is a common way to add emphasis or sound more firm/polite when disagreeing or refusing. It often comes at the start of a sentence, followed by the verb: **No, no + verb** (e.g., *No, no necesito…*).
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” is a common way to make a refusal stronger, show disagreement, or stop/correct someone (similar to “No, no, no!” in English). The number of “no”s varies with emotion/urgency. Often followed by a term of address like “cariño” (honey) or “hombre” (man/dude) to soften it or make it more conversational.
target_language_example: No, no, no, gracias; hoy no puedo.
native_language_example: No, no, no, thanks; I can’t today.

additional_notes: Repeating “no” shows strong refusal, disagreement, or alarm (like “No, no, no!” in English). Tone matters: it can mean “Don’t do that,” “That’s not true,” or “This is going badly.” Often used in speech; in writing it can be followed by a reason (e.g., “...nos hemos quedado sin opciones”).
target_language_example: No, no, no, no—eso no es lo que dije.
native_language_example: No, no, no, no—that’s not what I said.

meaning: “No, but …” (a refusal/disagreement followed by a contrast, correction, or extra point).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to reject or disagree with what was said or implied, then add a contrasting idea or important detail. Often sets up a correction (“No, pero…”), an exception (“No, pero…”), or a request after saying no (“No, pero dame detalles.”). In speech it’s usually said with a brief pause after “no”.
target_language_example: No, pero mañana sí puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: No, but tomorrow I can help you.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to correct what someone assumed or to downplay something. It’s often followed by an explanation: “No, sólo quería charlar” (“No, I just wanted to chat”). Note: Spanish “sólo/solo” usually means “only/just” in this use, not English “solo” (alone), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: No, sólo estaba preguntando.
native_language_example: No, I was just asking.

meaning: "No, YOU..." (used to correct or emphasize that the other person is the one who did/is something).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to contradict someone or shift the focus to the other person. It often comes before a statement about the listener: "No, tú eres..." (No, you are...), "No, tú lo hiciste..." (No, you did it...). It can also be used before giving a direct instruction to the listener for emphasis: "No, tú sé realista" (No, you be realistic).
target_language_example: No, tú tienes la razón.
native_language_example: No, YOU are right.

additional_notes: Used to start an answer that corrects or reassures someone by saying something has already happened or is already true (often with the sense of “don’t worry/it’s taken care of”). Common with verbs like: “No, ya he comido” (I’ve already eaten), “No, ya lo sé” (I already know), “No, ya los tengo” (I already have them). It can also introduce something expected soon: “No, ya vendrá …” (She’ll come later / She’ll show up). The comma reflects a pause; in speech it’s the intonation that matters.
target_language_example: —¿Te llamo un taxi? —No, ya viene mi hermano.
native_language_example: “Should I call you a taxi?” “No, my brother is already coming.”

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct someone and emphasize that *you* (not someone else) will/won’t do something. In Spanish you can omit the subject pronoun, so adding "yo" here is for emphasis or contrast: "No, (yo) no..." = "No, *I* don't..."
target_language_example: No, yo no dije eso.
native_language_example: No, I didn't say that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly contradict or refuse, often to emphasize that *you* specifically do not do something ("Not me"). It’s commonly followed by a verb ("No, yo no voy") or can stand alone when the verb is understood from context ("—¿Vienes? —No, yo no."). Word order adds emphasis: "yo" highlights the subject.
target_language_example: —¿Quieres café? —No, yo no tomo café.
native_language_example: —Do you want coffee? —No, I don’t drink coffee.

additional_notes: Repeating **no** is a common way to add emphasis or sound more firm/polite when disagreeing or refusing. It often comes at the start of a sentence, followed by the verb: **No, no + verb** (e.g., *No, no necesito…*).
target_language_example: No, no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: No, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something does not change the result or does not matter, regardless of the thing that follows. It’s often followed by a verb in the present subjunctive (e.g., pase, digas, hagas): No importa lo que + (subjunctive).
target_language_example: No importa lo que elijas, yo te apoyaré.
native_language_example: No matter what you choose, I’ll support you.

additional_notes: Negative tú command (informal singular) from the verb "llorar" (to cry). Used to tell one person not to cry, often to comfort them. You may also see it in the proverb "No llores sobre la leche derramada" (“Don’t cry over spilled milk”). For a formal or plural command: "no llore" (usted) / "no lloren" (ustedes).
target_language_example: No llores; todo va a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t cry; everything is going to be okay.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the night of a wedding (often the first night the couple spends together as married partners). It’s usually said with a possessive: "mi/tu/nuestra noche de bodas". "Bodas" is plural in Spanish here.
target_language_example: Reservaron una suite para su noche de bodas.
native_language_example: They booked a suite for their wedding night.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to tell you their name, often in formal/service situations (reception, forms, phone calls). It can be a full question (“¿Su nombre, por favor?”) or just said on its own as a prompt. You can also hear “Nombre y apellido, por favor” (“First and last name, please”).
target_language_example: Perdón, su nombre, por favor.
native_language_example: Excuse me, your name, please.

meaning: "name of"; used to identify what someone/something is called.
additional_notes:
Common in fixed expressions like:
- "el nombre de X" = "X’s name / the name of X"
- "bajo el nombre de X" = "under the name of X" (i.e., known as X)
- "responder al nombre de X" = "to go by the name of X" (to respond when called X)
Note: "nombre" looks like English "number" but means "name" (false friend).
target_language_example: Lo conocí bajo el nombre de Miguel.
native_language_example: I knew him under the name Miguel.

additional_notes: Used on forms, registrations, deliveries, and official requests when someone needs your identifying info. Often appears as a prompt by itself (e.g., “Nombre y dirección, por favor.”).
target_language_example: Para enviar el paquete, necesito tu nombre y dirección.
native_language_example: To send the package, I need your name and address.

additional_notes: From the verb casarse (to get married). Nos is the “we/us” reflexive pronoun here (“we marry ourselves” → “we get married”). Often used with time phrases like hace siete años (seven years ago) or with places like en Las Vegas. Without context, it can mean either past (“we got married”) or present/future for a planned event (“we’re getting married”).
target_language_example: Nos casamos el próximo sábado.
native_language_example: We’re getting married next Saturday.

additional_notes: Used when two people are familiar with each other (not “I know you” in the sense of knowing information). It’s the reciprocal form of conocer: conocer = to meet/know (a person), conocerse = to know each other. Often used with time/degree words: Hace mucho que nos conocemos (We’ve known each other for a long time), Apenas nos conocemos (We barely know each other).
target_language_example: ¿De verdad? Pensé que nos conocemos desde la escuela.
native_language_example: Really? I thought we’ve known each other since school.

meaning: "we've known each other for" (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say how long two people have known each other. It’s typically followed by a duration (e.g., "cinco años", "mucho tiempo"). "Desde hace" combines: "desde" (since) + "hace" (ago) to express “for (how long)”. You can change "nos" to other pronouns: "se conocen desde hace..." (they’ve known each other for...), "os conocéis desde hace..." (you all have known each other for...).
target_language_example: Mi mejor amiga y yo nos conocemos desde hace tres años.
native_language_example: My best friend and I have known each other for three years.

meaning: “we met” (we got to know each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "conocerse" for "we" (nosotros). Use it to talk about the moment two people first met: "Nos conocimos ayer/en la universidad". Often used with time expressions like "desde el día en que nos conocimos" (“since the day we met”) or "aquí es donde nos conocimos" (“this is where we met”).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en una fiesta hace dos años.
native_language_example: We met at a party two years ago.

meaning: "we met in/at/on" (a place, event, or platform).
additional_notes: Used with the verb conocerse in the simple past (pretérito) to say where two people first met. Use en for countries/cities (en Australia, en Boston), venues or groups (en un grupo de teatro), and also platforms/apps (en Facebook).
target_language_example: Nos conocimos en una fiesta de un amigo.
native_language_example: We met at a friend's party.

additional_notes: "Nos" is the indirect object pronoun meaning "to us." It’s used with the verb "dar" (to give): "(alguien/ algo) nos da + noun". In Spanish the subject can be omitted, so "Nos da..." often means "It gives us..." or "He/She gives us..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Nos da las llaves mañana.
native_language_example: He/She will give us the keys tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to the speaker and other people (nos = “to us”). The verb is usually in past tense (dijo = “said/told”), and que introduces the message/clause. You’ll often need to infer who the subject is from context (e.g., Ella/Tom).
target_language_example: El profesor nos dijo que no había clase hoy.
native_language_example: The teacher told us that there was no class today.

meaning: “we had a lot of fun” / “we really enjoyed ourselves.”
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "divertirse" = "to have fun". "Nos" shows it’s "we" (reflexive: "we enjoyed ourselves"). "Mucho" intensifies it: "a lot"/"really". Often used to talk about a completed event (last night, on vacation, at a party).
target_language_example: En el concierto nos divertimos mucho.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the concert.

additional_notes: Used with **de** to say your group will be responsible for something or someone: *Nos encargaremos de X.* It often appears with object pronouns like **ello/eso/esto** (“it/that/this”) or **él** (“him”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: nos encargaremos de todo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’ll take care of everything.

additional_notes: From the verb "encontrarse" (to meet). It often implies meeting in a place or bumping into each other unexpectedly. You’ll commonly add a location with "en" (Nos encontramos en...).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos en la estación a las seis.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the station at six.

additional_notes: From enseñar (to teach, to show) + nos (us). Used when someone or something teaches a group that includes the speaker. Often followed by: a + infinitive (nos enseña a ver...), a subject clause with que (nos enseña que...), or a direct object (nos enseña francés / historia). The subject can be a person (Ella nos enseña...) or a thing/field (La gramática nos enseña...).
target_language_example: El profesor nos enseña a usar estas palabras.
native_language_example: The teacher teaches us how to use these words.

additional_notes: "Nos" is an object pronoun meaning "us" (the people receiving the action). "Ha" is the present perfect helper verb (haber) for él/ella/usted: "has".
