additional_notes: Used to reassure someone after mentioning a problem or something negative. It’s addressing one person informally (tú). You can also say “pero no se preocupe” (formal, usted) or “pero no se preocupen” (to multiple people).
target_language_example: Llegaré un poco tarde, pero no te preocupes: te aviso cuando esté cerca.
native_language_example: I’ll be a little late, but don’t worry: I’ll let you know when I’m close.

additional_notes: Used to contrast an expectation or statement with something that has *never* happened. Common before a verb phrase ("pero nunca + verb"), often emphasizing refusal, denial, or impossibility: "...pero nunca me rindo" (but I never give up).
target_language_example: Quise llamarte, pero nunca encontré el momento.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you, but I never found the right moment.

meaning: "but if" / "but (it) is/was...!" (often to contradict or insist).
additional_notes: Often used in two ways: (1) Literal conditional: "pero si + clause" = "but if..." ("But if there’s no ticket, you have to pay a fine."). (2) Very common conversational/emphatic use to correct someone, show surprise, or insist on a fact: "¡Pero si...!" ≈ "But it is...! / But I did...!" ("But we’ve looked a hundred times!"). The "si" here doesn’t really mean "if" in English; it’s more like emphasis.
target_language_example: ¡Pero si ya te lo dije!
native_language_example: But I already told you!

meaning: “but yes” / “but actually (yes/it does)” (a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to contradict or qualify what was just said or implied (similar to “but yes,” “but actually,” “but I do,” “but it is/they are”). Often followed by a verb or pronoun for emphasis: “pero sí lo tienen” = “but they do have it.” It can also stand alone as a brief reluctant agreement: “..., pero sí.” As a stronger emphatic form you may hear “pero sí que …” (e.g., “Pero sí que está enfermo” = “He really is sick”).
target_language_example: No es barato, pero sí vale la pena.
native_language_example: It’s not cheap, but it is worth it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce doubt, an alternative possibility, or a softer correction after what was just said. Very common when you want to reconsider or qualify a statement. Often followed by the imperfect/subjunctive in more speculative sentences (e.g., "pero tal vez sería/mejor...", "pero tal vez sea...").
target_language_example: Quiero ir contigo, pero tal vez no pueda mañana.
native_language_example: I want to go with you, but maybe I can’t tomorrow.

meaning: “but I have to…” (I need to / must…).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or a polite excuse before saying an obligation or necessity. Commonly followed by an infinitive: “pero tengo que + preguntar/salir/recoger/decir/hacer…”. You can change the subject: “pero tienes que…”, “pero tenemos que…”.
target_language_example: Quiero quedarme más, pero tengo que irme.
native_language_example: I want to stay longer, but I have to go.

meaning: “but you have to / but you need to.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast (“pero” = “but”) and then state an obligation or necessity with “tienes que” + infinitive: “pero tienes que + hacer/decir/ir…”. The subject is “tú” (you, informal singular).
target_language_example: Entiendo que estás cansado, pero tienes que terminar la tarea.
native_language_example: I understand you’re tired, but you have to finish the homework.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what was just said with what *you* did/are/need, often with strong emphasis on “tú” (you). It commonly appears at the start of a sentence to object, correct, or point out an exception: “Pero tú no estabas…” = “But you weren’t there…”. In speech, it can also be left hanging to show surprise or protest: “Pero tú…” = “But you…!”.
target_language_example: Quería irme, pero tú me convenciste de quedarme.
native_language_example: I wanted to leave, but you convinced me to stay.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection, often correcting someone or pointing out a fact about them. It’s usually followed by a noun or adjective: "Pero tú eres mi amigo" (noun phrase) / "Pero tú eres soltero" (adjective). The stress on "tú" emphasizes that *you* (not someone else) are.
target_language_example: Pero tú eres el que lo dijo primero.
native_language_example: But you’re the one who said it first.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what you just said with the fact that something has already happened or is true now. Often introduces a correction or an objection: "Pero ya me asignaron..." (but they already assigned me...), "Pero ya es tarde" (but it’s already late). In some contexts it means "but now" or "but by now" (things have changed since before).
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, pero ya lo resolviste.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but you already solved it.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with something that used to be true but isn’t now. Often refers back to a previously mentioned action or situation: "Lo era, pero ya no" = "I/he/she used to be (that), but not anymore." You’ll also see it before a verb: "pero ya no lo hace" = "but he/she doesn’t do it anymore."
target_language_example: Antes vivía aquí, pero ya no.
native_language_example: I used to live here, but not anymore.

meaning: 'but I…' (contrasts what you say about yourself with someone/something else).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or exception focused on the speaker (yo). Often appears in comparisons like “Ellos no, pero yo sí” (“They don’t, but I do”), or to push back/clarify your own point: “No sé tú, pero yo…” (“I don’t know about you, but I…”). Spanish often includes “yo” here for emphasis, even though the verb ending already shows who the subject is.
target_language_example: No sé ustedes, pero yo prefiero quedarme en casa.
native_language_example: I don’t know about you all, but I’d rather stay home.

meaning: "but I don't" / "but I didn't" (in contrast to someone else).
additional_notes: Used to disagree or contrast your situation/actions with what was just said. The verb is often understood from context and left out: *Yo sí, pero yo no* (“I did, but I didn’t”). It can sound emphatic, especially when said alone: *Pero yo no.*
target_language_example: Ellos quieren ir, pero yo no.
native_language_example: They want to go, but I don’t.

meaning: "But why?" (asking for a reason, often with surprise or protest).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question something someone just said/did. "Pero" adds contrast or objection (“but...”), so it often sounds like “Wait, why?” or “But why would you...?” You can follow it with a noun/phrase ("pero ¿por qué en mi auto?") or with "no" + verb ("pero ¿por qué no paras ya?").
target_language_example: Pero ¿por qué te vas ahora?
native_language_example: But why are you leaving now?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to react to something unexpected or confusing. It often expresses surprise, disbelief, impatience, or concern, and is usually followed by a verb: “pero ¿qué pasa?” (what’s going on?), “pero ¿qué pasó?” (what happened?), “pero ¿qué harás?” (what will you do?).
target_language_example: Pero ¿qué estás diciendo?
native_language_example: But what are you saying?

additional_notes: This is the noun perro (“dog”) + the verb está (3rd person singular of estar, “is”). Use estar for temporary states and locations: está sediento (is thirsty), está aquí/allí (is here/there). In real Spanish you usually include an article or possessive: el perro está…, mi/tu/su perro está… (just “perro está” by itself is uncommon). Note the accent: está (he/she/it is) vs esta (this).
target_language_example: Mi perro está en casa ahora.
native_language_example: My dog is at home now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a person. It usually follows an article or determiner (la/una/cualquier persona que…) and then a verb: "la persona que ayudó…". "Que" doesn’t change for gender or number (la persona que…, las personas que…).
target_language_example: Busco a una persona que hable inglés.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a person who speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes which people you mean. It’s often followed by a verb: “personas que trabajan” (people who work). You’ll also see singular “persona que” (a person who/that).
target_language_example: Busco personas que hablen inglés.
native_language_example: I’m looking for people who speak English.

additional_notes: Used to show ownership (who something belongs to) or membership/classification (what group, category, or place someone/something is part of). It’s the verb "pertenecer" + "a". With people/pronouns: "pertenece a Tom", "pertenece a ella".
target_language_example: ¿Este paraguas pertenece a alguien?
native_language_example: Does this umbrella belong to anyone?

meaning: to go fishing at the river.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **ir a pescar al río** (“to go fishing at the river”). Here **al** = **a + el** (“to the”), emphasizing going to that place to fish. You may also hear **pescar en el río** (“to fish in the river”), which focuses more on the location where you fish rather than the trip there.
target_language_example: Los fines de semana vamos a pescar al río.
native_language_example: On weekends we go fishing at the river.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("pidiendo" = "asking/requesting") to describe an action happening at the same time as another action, often after verbs like gritar (to shout), llorar (to cry), or llamar (to call). Common in emergencies: "gritó pidiendo ayuda" = "he shouted for help."
target_language_example: Corrí hacia ellos cuando los oí pidiendo ayuda.
native_language_example: I ran toward them when I heard them asking for help.

additional_notes: “Pidió” is the past tense (preterite) of “pedir” = “to ask for / to request.” It often uses “a” before a person: “pidió a sus amigos ayuda” = “he asked his friends for help.” Very common pattern: “pidió a [person] que + verb (subjunctive)” to say someone asked another person to do something: “pidió a la niñera que cuidara…”. Pronouns can be added: “le pidió a ella…” or “les pidió a todos…”.
target_language_example: El jefe me pidió a mí que llegara temprano.
native_language_example: The boss asked me to arrive early.

additional_notes: Common pattern: "pedir consejo a + person" = to ask someone for advice. "Pidió" is the simple past (preterite) of "pedir" (to ask for/request). "Su" means "his/her/your(formal)/their"—the owner is understood from context. You’ll usually continue with a noun like "amigo/a", "profesor/a", etc.: "le pidió consejo a su amigo".
target_language_example: Le pidió consejo a su hermana antes de aceptar el trabajo.
native_language_example: She asked her sister for advice before accepting the job.

additional_notes: Used to report a request in the past (preterite of pedir). After “pidió que”, Spanish typically uses the imperfect subjunctive: pidieron que fuéramos / hiciéramos / ayudáramos. Often followed by an object pronoun: “Nos pidió que…”, “Me pidió que…”.
target_language_example: El jefe pidió que llegáramos temprano.
native_language_example: The boss asked that we arrive early.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "pedir" to make a request: "pidió que" + verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "pidió que le llamara"). "Le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to him," "to her," or "to you" (formal), depending on context. Often the full pattern is "[Someone] le pidió a [someone] que le + [subjunctive verb]".
target_language_example: El jefe le pidió que le enviara el informe hoy.
native_language_example: The boss asked him/her to send him/her the report today.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to apologize. Literally “I ask (for) apologies,” often used in customer service, speeches, or when speaking respectfully. Common patterns: “(Le/Les/Te) pido disculpas” (I apologize to you), and “Pido disculpas por…” (I apologize for…).
target_language_example: Le pido disculpas por la demora.
native_language_example: I apologize for the delay.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to apologize for something you did (or didn’t do). Use it before a noun or a clause introduced by what/that (e.g., “por lo que dije” = “for what I said”). You can also say “te pido disculpas por …” to address the person directly (“I apologize to you for …”).
target_language_example: Te pido disculpas por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I apologize for being late.

additional_notes: "Piensa" is the tú (informal singular) command form of pensar. Use "piensa en + noun/pronoun/thing" to tell someone to think about something or someone (e.g., "Piensa en mí", "Piensa en esto"). It can also imply "consider" or "keep in mind," especially in advice or reminders.
target_language_example: Piensa en lo que vas a decir antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Think about what you're going to say before you speak.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person informally (tú) to consider or reflect on something, usually followed by a clause: piensa en lo que dije/haces/vas a hacer (“think about what I said/you’re doing/you’re going to do”). You can change the verb form for other people: piense en lo que… (usted), piensen en lo que… (ustedes).
target_language_example: Piensa en lo que vas a decir antes de hablar.
native_language_example: Think about what you’re going to say before you speak.

additional_notes: Used to introduce someone’s opinion or belief. "Piensa" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "pensar" (he/she/it thinks). Often followed by a full clause: "piensa que + [sentence]". You can change the subject: "Yo pienso que..." (I think that...), "¿Piensas que...?" (Do you think that...?).
target_language_example: Mi hermano piensa que vamos a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother thinks that we’re going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what a group of people believes or assumes. "Piensan" is the present tense of "pensar" (to think) for "ellos/ellas/ustedes"; the subject is often implied, and "que" introduces the clause that follows.
target_language_example: Piensan que no entiendo, pero sí entiendo.
native_language_example: They think I don't understand, but I do.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **pensar en** (“to think about”). **Piense en** is the **usted** imperative (formal), used to tell someone to think about or consider something. You’ll often see it followed by a noun (**Piense en su familia**) or by **lo que…** (**Piense en lo que gana** = “Think about what you gain”).
target_language_example: Piense en las consecuencias antes de decidir.
native_language_example: Think about the consequences before deciding.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pensar + en + noun/pronoun to say what someone has in mind (a person, thing, memory, idea). It can be general/habitual ("I think about...") or right now ("I’m thinking of..."). With an infinitive, it often means "to plan/intend to": No pienso en ir = "I’m not planning to go."
target_language_example: Pienso en mi familia cuando estoy lejos.
native_language_example: I think about my family when I’m far away.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is on your mind. The verb is pensar + en + person/thing: “pienso en ti” (I think about you), “pienso en eso” (I think about that). Often implies remembering, missing, or having someone in your thoughts. Negative form: “No pienso en ti (de ese modo)” = “I don’t think of you (like that).”
target_language_example: Pienso en ti cuando te extraño.
native_language_example: I think about you when I miss you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about a statement. Often followed by a verb in the indicative (e.g., "deberíamos", "había estado", "va a ser"). You can also say "Creo que…" with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Pienso que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion. Often followed by an adjective or noun: “Pienso que es lo mejor” (I think it’s the best). You may also see the pattern “Pienso que es + adjective + que + subjunctive” when what follows is a reaction or judgment: “Pienso que es extraño que no haya…” (I think it’s strange that there isn’t…).
target_language_example: Pienso que es importante hablar con el profesor hoy.
native_language_example: I think it’s important to talk to the teacher today.

additional_notes: Used to describe a picture/painting that is hanging or placed on a wall. Very often you’ll see it with verbs like colgar (to hang): "Colgué una pintura en la pared" / "Está colgando una pintura en la pared."
target_language_example: Esa pintura en la pared es nueva.
native_language_example: That painting on the wall is new.

meaning: “nice to meet you” / “it was a pleasure to meet you.”
additional_notes: Most commonly said as **(Fue) un placer conocerte** (“It was a pleasure to meet you”), especially when saying goodbye after meeting someone. You can also say **Es un placer conocerte** when meeting someone (more formal). Add emphasis with **un gran placer** (“a great pleasure”) or **un verdadero placer** (“a real pleasure”). Uses **conocerte** = “to meet you” (informal ‘you’, *tú*). For formal ‘you’ (*usted*), say **(Fue) un placer conocerlo/la**.
target_language_example: Fue un placer conocerte; que te vaya bien.
native_language_example: It was nice to meet you; take care.

meaning: "plans for" (intentions/arrangements for something in the future).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone intends to do or has arranged, often followed by a time period (mañana, este fin de semana) or a noun (vacaciones, su vida). Very common with tener: "No tengo planes para mañana" / "Ya tengo planes para el fin de semana". Also appears in broader contexts like "planes para la humanidad" (big goals/intentions).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes planes para el verano?
native_language_example: Do you have plans for the summer?

meaning: the main course; the main event (highlight).
additional_notes: Most commonly used on menus and in meals to mean the main dish served after an appetizer (la entrada) and before dessert (el postre). It’s also used figuratively to introduce the most important or anticipated part of something (a show, presentation, announcement): “And now, the main event.”
target_language_example: De plato fuerte pedí pollo con arroz.
native_language_example: For the main course I ordered chicken with rice.

additional_notes: Used to say a small number of people do something or are in a place. Often followed by a verb: “Poca gente sabe…” (“Few people know…”). You can intensify it with “muy”: “muy poca gente” (“very few people”).
target_language_example: Poca gente entiende este acento.
native_language_example: Few people understand this accent.

additional_notes: Used to say that only a small number of people do something or have something. Often appears as (muy) pocas personas + verb. Because it's an adjective + noun, it changes for gender/number (e.g., pocas cosas, pocos hombres).
target_language_example: Pocas personas entienden este tema.
native_language_example: Few people understand this topic.

additional_notes: Used literally in fantasy stories (a drink that causes a special effect). It can also be used figuratively to mean a “miracle cure” or “quick fix” that doesn’t really exist. Often appears with an article: "la/una poción mágica".
target_language_example: Se terminó el efecto de la poción mágica.
native_language_example: The effect of the magic potion wore off.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a small amount of money (often implying it’s not enough). You can strengthen it with "muy" ("muy poco dinero" = very little money). Often contrasted with "mucho" ("mucho trabajo, poco dinero").
target_language_example: Ahora tengo poco dinero, así que no voy a comprar nada.
native_language_example: I have little money right now, so I’m not going to buy anything.

meaning: little time; not much time (a short amount of time).
additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t enough time or that the available time is short. Common patterns: “me queda poco tiempo” = “I have little time left”; “poco tiempo para + infinitive” = “little time to do something”; “por poco tiempo” = “for a short time.”
target_language_example: Nos queda poco tiempo para llegar al aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We have little time left to get to the airport.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about a small quantity: un poco de + noun (un poco de frío, un poco de champaña). With some expressions, it refers to a small degree/amount of something abstract (un poco de mal gusto).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little bit of water, please?

additional_notes: Means a small amount of water. Very common with requests (Dame un poco de agua.) or to describe what’s in something (Hay un poco de agua en la botella.). Often used with un: un poco de agua. With only/just: sólo/solamente un poco de agua.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

meaning: a little air; a bit of fresh air.
additional_notes: Used literally for air in something that can be filled (like a tire: “needs a little air”), and figuratively/idiomatically to mean needing to breathe or step outside to get some fresh air (often after stress or feeling overwhelmed). You’ll often hear it as “Necesito un poco de aire” or “Tomar un poco de aire” (to get some air).
target_language_example: Después de la reunión, salí a tomar un poco de aire.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I went out to get a bit of fresh air.

meaning: a little (bit) of money; some money.
additional_notes: "Un poco de" means “a little (bit) of” and is used with uncountable nouns like dinero (money). In requests, "Dame un poco de dinero" is common but can sound direct; "¿Me das un poco de dinero, por favor?" is more polite.
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de dinero para el autobús.
native_language_example: I need a little money for the bus.

meaning: a slight fever; a little fever.
additional_notes: Almost always used as "un poco de fiebre" with the verb "tener" (to have): "Tengo un poco de fiebre". It means you have a mild temperature—not a high fever. You can also use it with "llevar" to say how long you’ve had it: "Llevo desde esta mañana con un poco de fiebre".
target_language_example: Creo que tengo un poco de fiebre, así que voy a descansar.
native_language_example: I think I have a slight fever, so I'm going to rest.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount of milk. Very common with drinks ("con un poco de leche" = "with a little milk"). For quantities with an uncountable noun like leche, Spanish uses "un poco de" (or just "poco de").
target_language_example: ¿Me pones un poco de leche en el café?
native_language_example: Can you put a little milk in the coffee for me?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a small amount of time. Very common with verbs like necesitar (Necesito un poco de tiempo), dar (Dame un poco de tiempo), or tener (No tengo mucho tiempo). You can add more detail with phrases like a solas (“alone”) or para + infinitive (un poco de tiempo para pensar).
target_language_example: Dame un poco de tiempo para pensarlo.
native_language_example: Give me a little time to think about it.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate a small additional amount (more time, money, food, etc.). It can also mean a small additional distance (“un poco más lejos”). Often appears with “solo/sólo” to mean “just a little more.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes esperar un poco más, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer, please?

meaning: “a little more (of)”; “just over / a little more than”.
additional_notes: Used before a noun or quantity. With nouns it means “a little more of” (Necesito un poco más de espacio). With numbers, time, age, etc., it often means “a little more than / just over” (un poco más de cuarenta años; un poco más de una hora).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes darme un poco más de agua?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more water?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a small extra amount of time to finish something or make a decision. Common with verbs like "dame" (give me) and "necesito" (I need): "Dame/Necesito un poco más de tiempo." You can also say it by itself as a brief request: "Solo/Sólo un poco más de tiempo."
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco más de tiempo para terminar?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time to finish?

additional_notes:
Used to say that only a small number of students understood something. 
- **pocos** = few (emphasizes that the number is small).
- Often you’ll also hear **(solo) unos pocos estudiantes entendieron…** (“only a few students understood…”), which sounds a bit more neutral.
- **entendieron** is the **preterite** (simple past) of *entender* (“to understand”), used for a completed action in the past.
target_language_example: Pocos estudiantes entendieron la explicación.
native_language_example: Few students understood the explanation.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” (nosotros) can trust or rely on someone/something. It’s the present tense of the verb phrase “confiar en” (to trust in/rely on). Often followed by a person: “confiar en él/ella/ellos/ella” or “en alguien/en nadie”.
target_language_example: Podemos confiar en ellos para terminar el trabajo a tiempo.
native_language_example: We can rely on them to finish the work on time.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or offer discussing a topic. Common with a pronoun or noun after de: de eso/esto (about that/this), de lo que quieras (about whatever you want). It can be polite and practical (“We can talk about it later”) or, depending on tone, a challenge (“We can talk about this, man.”).
target_language_example: Si quieres, podemos hablar de tus planes mañana.
native_language_example: If you want, we can talk about your plans tomorrow.

additional_notes: From poder (to be able to) + hacer (to do/make). Use it to talk about what “we” are able to do, offer help, or propose solutions: ¿Qué podemos hacer? (“What can we do?”). With que + verb, it often means “we can make/ensure that…”: Podemos hacer que el mundo se detenga (“We can make the world stop”).
target_language_example: No se preocupe: podemos hacer algo para ayudar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we can do something to help.

additional_notes: Uses the verb poder (“to be able to/can”) in the present tense for nosotros (“we”): podemos + infinitive (hacer). The pronoun lo (“it”) is attached to the infinitive: hacer + lo → hacerlo. You can add emphasis or details after it, e.g., “podemos hacerlo solos” (“we can do it alone/by ourselves”).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: podemos hacerlo juntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we can do it together.

meaning: "we can go to" / "can we go to?"
additional_notes: Used to talk about the possibility/permission of going somewhere. In questions (¿Podemos ir a...?) it often means asking for permission: “Can we go to…?” After "a" you can use a place (a casa, al parque) or an infinitive to say an activity (a nadar, a cenar).
target_language_example: ¿Podemos ir a la playa mañana?
native_language_example: Can we go to the beach tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + estar to express a possibility about someone’s location, state, or condition: "Podría estar en casa" (He/She could be at home), "podría estar cansado" (might be tired). In the negative, "no podría estar" often means "couldn’t be" (it’s not possible) or "wouldn’t be able to be," depending on context.
target_language_example: Ahora no contesta; podría estar conduciendo.
native_language_example: He’s not answering right now; he might be driving.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something may be in a place, but you’re not sure. It’s the conditional of poder (podría = might/could) + infinitive estar (to be) + en (in/at). Often used with uncertainty phrases like “por lo que sé/sabemos” (as far as I know/we know).
target_language_example: Mi teléfono podría estar en la cocina.
native_language_example: My phone might be in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past possibility or missed opportunity, often in conditional sentences (Si..., podría haber...). It’s the conditional of poder (podría) + haber + past participle (ganado, decidido, conseguido) to form the conditional perfect: “could have + done.”
target_language_example: Lo siento: podría haber llegado antes, pero había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: I could have arrived earlier, but there was a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + haber + past participle (sido) to talk about something that was possible, but did not happen or is uncertain in hindsight. Often followed by a noun or pronoun: “podría haber sido cualquiera/cualquier cosa” = “it could have been anyone/anything.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: podría haber sido un malentendido.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it could have been a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Conditional perfect of poder: podría (would/could) + haber + past participle (hecho). It talks about a past possibility/ability, often implying it was possible in theory (or under certain conditions). “lo” means “it” and attaches to haber (haberlo). Often used with negatives or conditions: “No podría haberlo hecho sin…” = “I couldn’t have done it without…”.
target_language_example: Yo podría haberlo hecho, pero no tenía tiempo.
native_language_example: I could have done it, but I didn’t have time.

additional_notes: From poder (can/be able to) in the conditional tense + ser (to be). Used to express possibility or a polite/soft suggestion: "Podría ser útil" = "It might/could be useful." Often followed by an adjective or noun.
target_language_example: Podría ser una buena idea.
native_language_example: It could be a good idea.

meaning: "could be a" / "might be a" (expressing a possibility).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + ser to say something is possible or uncertain. It’s commonly followed by a masculine singular noun with un; for feminine use "podría ser una" (e.g., "podría ser una mentira"). With plural: "podrían ser" (e.g., "podrían ser unos errores").
target_language_example: Con ese acento, podría ser un turista.
native_language_example: With that accent, he could be a tourist.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of poder (podría) + ser to suggest something is possible rather than certain. The article changes with the noun: podría ser un / podría ser una. Common for guesses, hypotheses, or polite/soft statements: "Podría ser una buena idea".
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero podría ser una buena idea.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but it could be a good idea.

additional_notes: From poder (can/be able to) in the conditional tense + ser (to be). Used to express possibility or a polite/soft suggestion: "Podría ser útil" = "It might/could be useful." Often followed by an adjective or noun.
target_language_example: Podría ser una buena idea.
native_language_example: It could be a good idea.

meaning: 'you could have' (had the possibility to do something in the past).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the conditional perfect: podrías haber + participle (e.g., podrías haber venido = you could have come). It often talks about a missed possibility, an alternative past, or a mild criticism/suggestion about what someone should have done.
target_language_example: Podrías haberme llamado ayer, pero no lo hiciste.
native_language_example: You could have called me yesterday, but you didn’t.

additional_notes: Uses the Spain-only plural “you” form (vosotros/vosotras): podéis = “you all can/are able to.” It often appears with a direct-object pronoun before the verb (la = “it” feminine, lo = “it” masculine/neuter): “La/lo podéis poner ahí” = “You can put it there.” “Ahí” means “there” (near the listener).
target_language_example: ¿Lo podéis poner ahí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you (all) put it there, please?

additional_notes: Uses the vosotros form (common in Spain) to talk to a group informally: podéis = “you all can/are able to.” Often you’ll see a direct object pronoun placed before the verb: la podéis poner allí (“you can put it there” referring to a feminine noun), lo podéis poner allí (masculine/neuter). Allí means “there” (over there, not here).
target_language_example: ¿Podéis ponerlo allí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you all put it there, please?

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect (podía) to talk about a past belief/assumption or an ongoing ability to trust someone. Often appears after verbs like dije/pensé/sabía (“I said/thought/knew”) in sentences like “Pensé que podía confiar en ti.” Note: “confiar en” usually means “to trust,” not “to confide” (though in some contexts it can mean “to confide in”).
target_language_example: Creí que podía confiar en ti, pero me mentiste.
native_language_example: I thought I could trust you, but you lied to me.

meaning: "could do" / "was able to do" (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of poder (podía) + infinitive (hacer) to talk about past ability, what was possible, or what someone was allowed to do. Often implies an ongoing situation in the past (not a single completed attempt). For a specific one-time successful action, Spanish often uses "pude hacer".
target_language_example: No podía hacer nada sin ayuda.
native_language_example: I couldn't do anything without help.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase ponerse + adjective (“to become” a certain state). Most often used reflexively: se pone nervioso/a = “gets nervous.” If talking about something that causes the feeling, use poner + adjective with a direct object: Eso me pone nervioso/a = “That makes me nervous.” Adjective agrees: nervioso (masc.), nerviosa (fem.).
target_language_example: Antes del examen, me pongo nervioso.
native_language_example: Before the exam, I get nervous.

additional_notes: Used to talk about animals that reproduce by laying eggs (birds, insects, reptiles, etc.). It’s the present tense, third-person plural of "poner" (to lay/put): *ponen* = “they lay.” With a singular animal, use *pone huevos* (“lays eggs”).
target_language_example: Las tortugas ponen huevos en la playa.
native_language_example: Turtles lay eggs on the beach.

additional_notes: Used when telling someone where to place something. Often appears with an object pronoun before the verb (lo/la/los/las): “Lo/La puede(s) poner ahí” = “You can put it there.” You can also say “ponerlo/ponerla ahí.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ponerlo ahí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put it there, please?

additional_notes: Used to say where to place something. Often appears with object pronouns: lo/la = “it” (masc./fem.), and puede/pueden = “you can” (formal singular) / “you all/they can.” “Allí” means “there” (a bit more specific than “ahí,” which is “there” near you).
target_language_example: ¿Puede poner la bolsa allí, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put the bag there, please?

meaning: to get in touch with; to contact.
additional_notes: Used when you want to communicate with someone (by phone, email, etc.). It’s the reflexive form of “poner en contacto con” (to put someone in contact with). You can change “me” to match the person: “ponerte / ponerse / ponernos / ponerse en contacto con”.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ponerme en contacto con tu jefe, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you get me in touch with your boss, please?

meaning: to contact him; to get in touch with him.
additional_notes: Literally “to put myself in contact with him.” Used for making communication (call, message, email, etc.). You can change the pronoun and person: ponerme/ponerte/ponerse/ponernos/ponerse en contacto con + persona (con ella, con ellos, con usted). Often used with intentar, poder, querer, or in the past: Me fue imposible ponerme en contacto con él.
target_language_example: No puedo ponerme en contacto con él hoy, pero le escribiré mañana.
native_language_example: I can’t get in touch with him today, but I’ll write to him tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative of poner + direct object pronoun lo (“it”) + en (“on/in”). Used to tell someone where to place an object: en un sobre (in an envelope), en la mesa (on the table), en la pared (on the wall), en la mano (in your hand). With “tú” commands: Ponlo en…, and in negative: No lo pongas en….
target_language_example: Ponlo en la mochila, por favor.
native_language_example: Put it in the backpack, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the expected time. Common with thanks and apologies: “Gracias por adelantado” = “Thanks in advance,” and “disculparse por adelantado” = “to apologize in advance.” Also used with payments: “pagar por adelantado” = “to pay in advance/upfront.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes enviarme la información por adelantado?
native_language_example: Can you send me the information in advance?

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact reason, or when you suggest there may be a (possibly meaningful) reason. It can go at the beginning of the sentence ("Por alguna razón, ...") or after the verb ("... por alguna razón"). In expressions like "Todo pasa por alguna razón," it can imply "everything happens for a reason."
target_language_example: Por alguna razón, hoy estoy de buen humor.
native_language_example: For some reason, I’m in a good mood today.

additional_notes: Used to politely direct someone to come or go through a specific place, often while guiding them (e.g., in an office, store, or waiting room). Common with verbs like pase/pasen (“come in/go ahead”), venga (“come”), or just said alone as an instruction.
target_language_example: Por aquí, por favor. La doctora lo atenderá enseguida.
native_language_example: This way, please. The doctor will see you right away.

additional_notes: Use this to casually introduce new information (often a small topic change). "Por cierto" = "by the way". "Tengo algo" usually needs a follow-up like "para ti" (for you) or "que + infinitive" (something to give/tell/show you): "tengo algo que decirte".
target_language_example: Por cierto, tengo algo que preguntarte.
native_language_example: By the way, I have something to ask you.

meaning: by mail; through the postal service.
additional_notes: Used to say something is sent or communicated using postal mail (letters/packages). With "correo" it often implies regular mail (snail mail), not email (which is usually "por correo electrónico" or "por e-mail"). Common with verbs like "enviar", "mandar", and "comunicarse".
target_language_example: Te lo envío por correo mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll send it to you by mail tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is being sent through the postal service by air (faster than regular surface mail). Often used with verbs like "enviar" or "mandar" (to send): "enviar/mandar algo por correo aéreo".
target_language_example: ¿Puedes mandarme los documentos por correo aéreo?
native_language_example: Can you send me the documents by airmail?

additional_notes: Used to say how something is sent/communicated (the method). Often goes with verbs like enviar (to send), mandar (to send), or comunicar (to inform). You can use it in both informal and formal contexts: Envíame… (informal) vs. Envíeme… (formal).
target_language_example: Te lo mando por correo electrónico ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I’ll send it to you by email right now.

additional_notes: Used to assign blame or responsibility for a negative outcome. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (del = de + el): por culpa del accidente, por culpa del atasco. For feminine singular use por culpa de la; for plural use por culpa de los/las.
target_language_example: No pude dormir por culpa del ruido.
native_language_example: I couldn’t sleep because of the noise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce bad news or an undesirable situation. Commonly placed at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma), but it can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Por desgracia, no puedo ir a la fiesta.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can’t go to the party.

additional_notes: Used to express duration (how long something lasts). Common with actions like esperar (to wait), estudiar (to study), trabajar (to work), caminar (to walk). Often interchangeable with “durante dos horas.”
target_language_example: Estuve esperando por dos horas.
native_language_example: I was waiting for two hours.

meaning: “for the,” “because of the,” or “through the” (por + el).
additional_notes: “Por el” is the contraction of “por” + “el” (never *por el* when it’s “por + él” = “for him”). It’s used for several common ideas: cause/reason (“por el mal tiempo” = “because of the bad weather”), movement through/along a place (“por el campus” = “through the campus”), and “for” in the sense of competition/aim (“por el puesto” = “for the position”).
target_language_example: No salimos por el frío.
native_language_example: We didn’t go out because of the cold.

meaning: for the good of; for the sake of.
additional_notes: Used to say you do something to benefit someone/something (a person, a group, your health, etc.). It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: por el bien de todos / por el bien de mi salud / por el bien de los dos. Similar to “por el beneficio de,” but much more common.
target_language_example: Lo hice por el bien de mi familia.
native_language_example: I did it for the good of my family.

meaning: through the forest; in/around the forest.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or activity (caminar, pasar, pasear, dar vueltas) to say someone goes or does something in/through a forest. "Por" often means "through" or "along" when talking about movement through a place.
target_language_example: Fuimos por el bosque para llegar al lago.
native_language_example: We went through the forest to get to the lake.

meaning: along the way; via/on the path/road.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, venir, pasar, perderse, irse) to say someone goes/comes/travels via a path/road, or that something happens or is lost “along the way.” Often followed by a more specific path: "por el camino del oeste" (along the western road).
target_language_example: Nos detuvimos por el camino para comprar agua.
native_language_example: We stopped along the way to buy water.

meaning: for the money; because of money (as the motive).
additional_notes: Used to say that money is the reason someone does something (often implying a selfish or purely financial motive). Common with phrases like "solo/sólo por el dinero" (only for the money) or in negatives like "No lo hago por el dinero" (I’m not doing it for the money).
target_language_example: No acepté el trabajo por el dinero, sino por la experiencia.
native_language_example: I didn’t take the job for the money, but for the experience.

meaning: through/around the park; in the park (moving around).
additional_notes: Uses por to express movement through a place or along an area (not a fixed location). Common with verbs like caminar, pasear, correr, and guiar. Contrast: en el parque = located in the park (no focus on movement).
target_language_example: Fuimos por el parque para llegar más rápido.
native_language_example: We went through the park to get there faster.

additional_notes: Uses "por" + "ello" (“that/it”) to refer back to something already mentioned. Common with feelings or thanks ("gracias por ello", "mi gratitud por ello" = “thanks for that/it”), and with causes/consequences ("y por ello..." = “and because of that...”).
target_language_example: No estudié y, por ello, no aprobé el examen.
native_language_example: I didn’t study and, because of that, I didn’t pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement at a higher level than something else. Often used with verbs of movement (volar, pasar, trepar, saltar). Similar to "sobre" in many cases, but "por encima de" often emphasizes going across/over something (like an obstacle).
target_language_example: El gato saltó por encima de la mesa.
native_language_example: The cat jumped over the table.

additional_notes: Used to express that someone or something is above a surface, obstacle, or level. With movement verbs like "saltar" it means going over something (por encima de la valla). With measurements or comparisons, it means above a level/average (por encima de la altura media). Often appears as "por encima de" + noun; here it’s specifically with feminine singular nouns that take "la".
target_language_example: El avión pasó por encima de la ciudad.
native_language_example: The plane flew over the city.

additional_notes: Used literally to describe being higher than cloud level (e.g., a plane flying over the clouds or a mountain peak rising above them). Built from por encima de (“above/over”) + las nubes (“the clouds”).
target_language_example: Desde la ventanilla, vimos el sol por encima de las nubes.
native_language_example: From the window, we saw the sun above the clouds.

meaning: above all; more than anything else.
additional_notes: Used to say something is the top priority or most important thing. Often set off with commas as a comment (“..., por encima de todo, ...”). You can also use it after a noun/idea to emphasize priority (“X por encima de todo”).
target_language_example: Tu seguridad está por encima de todo.
native_language_example: Your safety is above all else.

additional_notes: Used for physical position or movement higher than something else. Often follows a verb of movement (e.g., saltar por encima de...) or describes location (estar/colgar por encima de...). The full phrase is "por encima de" + noun; it becomes "por encima del" before a masculine singular noun starting with "el" (por encima de + el = del).
target_language_example: El avión voló por encima del mar.
native_language_example: The plane flew over the sea.

meaning: for speeding; for driving over the speed limit.
additional_notes: Used with "por" to give the reason for a ticket, stop, or arrest. Often follows verbs like "detener" (to stop/detain), "arrestar" (to arrest), or nouns like "multa" (ticket/fine): "una multa por exceso de velocidad".
target_language_example: Me pusieron una multa por exceso de velocidad.
native_language_example: They gave me a speeding ticket.

meaning: because of a lack of; due to not having enough (of something).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason something happened: there wasn’t enough of a necessary thing (money, water, oxygen, time, etc.). It’s typically followed by a noun: por falta de dinero/agua/fondos. Often implies a negative outcome (couldn’t continue, failed, died).
target_language_example: Llegamos tarde por falta de tiempo.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of lack of time.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form of abrir (“to open”): abra (usted). Common in polite requests from strangers, staff, police, etc. Often followed by what to open: la puerta (the door), el maletero (the trunk), su bolsa (your bag). By itself (“Por favor, abra.”) it means “Please open (it/the door).”
target_language_example: Por favor, abra la ventana.
native_language_example: Please open the window.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to help you. "Ayúdame" is the informal (tú) command of "ayudar" + "me" (me). Often followed by "a + infinitive" to say what you need help doing: "Ayúdame a bajar esto" (help me carry/lower this), "Ayúdame a preparar esta clase" (help me prepare this class). For the formal version, use "Por favor, ayúdeme" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, ayúdame a estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: Please, help me study for the exam.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or to give you something (an object, a photo, a drink, etc.). Use it before a noun: "Por favor, dame + [thing]". "Dame" is the informal (tú) command form of "dar"; with someone you address as "usted," say "Por favor, deme ...".
target_language_example: Por favor, dame un vaso de agua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **dejar** (“to leave/let”). Common patterns: **deja de + infinitive** = “stop doing something” (Deja de fumar = Stop smoking). **deja + noun/pronoun** = “leave it/leave it alone” or “leave something (as it is / somewhere)” (Deja eso = Leave that; Deja la puerta abierta = Leave the door open). **deja un mensaje** = “leave a message.”
target_language_example: Por favor, deja de gritar.
native_language_example: Please stop shouting.

additional_notes: Used to politely (and sometimes impatiently) tell someone to stop doing something. Structure: "Por favor, deja de" + infinitive (e.g., gritar, mentir, silbar). You can also drop "por favor" to sound more direct: "Deja de gritar."
target_language_example: Por favor, deja de hacer eso; me está distrayendo.
native_language_example: Please stop doing that; it's distracting me.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request. “Deme” is the formal command (usted) of “dar” (to give). Common in customer-service situations (restaurants, shops) and when speaking formally to someone you don’t know well. With “tú” you’d usually say: “Por favor, dame …”.
target_language_example: Por favor, deme la cuenta.
native_language_example: Please, give me the bill/check.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (tú) to pass a message to another person. "Dile" is the tú command form of "decir" (to tell), and "a" introduces the person who will receive the message (e.g., "dile a Tom..."). If you’re speaking formally (usted), you’d say "por favor, dígale a...".
target_language_example: Por favor, dile a Juan que llegue temprano.
native_language_example: Please tell Juan to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to say something. Often followed by a noun or a clause: “por favor, dime la verdad” (tell me the truth) / “por favor, dime que…” (tell me that…). In speech you may also hear “Por favor, dime…” or “Dime, por favor…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, dime dónde estás.
native_language_example: Please, tell me where you are.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for instructions or an explanation. Often followed by an infinitive (cómo + arreglar/hacer/llegar) or by a full clause (cómo puedo… / cómo se…). You can also change the person: “dime” (tell me, informal tú); formal: “dígame” (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, dime cómo usar esta aplicación.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to use this app.

meaning: “please, let me…” (asking someone to allow you to do something / stop bothering you).
additional_notes: Used to politely (sometimes firmly) ask for permission or space. "Déjame" is the informal (tú) command of "dejar" + "me" (“let me / leave me”). Common patterns: "Por favor, déjame + infinitive" (déjame ir/entrar/comer) and "Por favor, déjame en paz" (“please leave me alone”). For a more formal version, use "Por favor, déjeme" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, déjame terminar de hablar.
native_language_example: Please, let me finish speaking.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request to someone you address as usted. Déjeme is the usted command form of dejar + the object pronoun me (“me”), and it’s followed by an infinitive (déjeme salir = “let me leave”) or a phrase (déjeme en paz = “leave me alone”). For tú, use: por favor, déjame.
target_language_example: Por favor, déjeme pasar.
native_language_example: Please, let me through.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form dígame (“tell me”), used with usted (not tú). Often followed by a question word (cómo, dónde, adónde) or by si (“if/whether”): Por favor, dígame si… You can also say it alone (“Por favor, dígame.”) to invite someone to speak or explain.
target_language_example: Por favor, dígame cómo llegar a la estación.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to get to the station.

additional_notes: Polite request used with strangers/customer service. "Espere" is the formal (usted) command form of "esperar". Often followed by a time/amount ("cinco minutos", "un poco") or "hasta" + time ("hasta las cinco").
target_language_example: Por favor, espere aquí un momento.
native_language_example: Please wait here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to talk or to speak in a certain way (e.g., with me, slowly, louder, seriously). “Habla” is the informal (tú) command form of “hablar.” With a name it can sound like a gentle but firm request: “Tom, por favor, habla…”
target_language_example: Por favor, habla más despacio; no te entiendo.
native_language_example: Please, speak more slowly; I don’t understand you.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to speak (a language) or to change their speaking speed. "Hable" is the formal command form (usted) of "hablar"; use it with strangers, service staff, or in formal situations. With someone you address as "tú," you’d usually say: "Por favor, habla..."
target_language_example: Por favor, hable más despacio; no entiendo.
native_language_example: Please speak more slowly; I don’t understand.

additional_notes: "Haz" is the tú (informal singular) command form of "hacer" (to do/make). It’s used to give an instruction or request to one person you address as "tú"; for a formal request to one person, use "Por favor, haga..." and for more than one person, "Por favor, hagan...".
target_language_example: Por favor, haz la tarea antes de cenar.
native_language_example: Please, do your homework before dinner.

meaning: "Please, talk to me" / "Please, speak to me."
additional_notes: Used to politely ask one person (tú) to talk or to speak. "Háblame" is the tú command (imperative) of "hablar" + "me" (to/with me). You can add what you want them to talk about with "de" or "acerca de" (both mean "about"), or specify the language with "en" (e.g., "Háblame en inglés").
target_language_example: Por favor, háblame de tu día.
native_language_example: Please, talk to me about your day.

additional_notes: A polite request using the informal command (tú) form: “llámame” = “call me.” You can add details like when/why: “antes de venir” (before coming), “de vuelta” (back), “en cuanto…” (as soon as…), “mañana por la mañana” (tomorrow morning), “siempre que…” (whenever…). It can also mean “please call me [name]” when followed by a name (e.g., “Llámame Ángela”).
target_language_example: Por favor, llámame cuando tengas un momento.
native_language_example: Please call me when you have a moment.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone not to do something. "No" goes right before the verb: "Por favor, no entren" (Please don’t come in). It can also be used by itself to express a polite objection or refusal: "Por favor, no" (Please, no). "Por favor" may sometimes be used as a general plea (like “please”) even when the next words aren’t a command.
target_language_example: Por favor, no hagas ruido en la biblioteca.
native_language_example: Please, don’t make noise in the library.

additional_notes: "Por favor" means “please.” "No" makes a negative command. "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “that” (referring to something already known). It’s commonly followed by a verb: negative commands use the present subjunctive form (e.g., "no lo hagas", "no lo olvides").
target_language_example: Por favor, no lo digas.
native_language_example: Please, don’t say it.

additional_notes: A common pattern: **Por favor, no me + verb**. **No** comes before **me**, and **me** goes right before the verb (e.g., *no me preguntes*, *no me golpee*). The verb form changes depending on who you’re talking to: **tú** often uses *no me + verb* (negative command, e.g., *no me preguntes*), and **usted** uses *no me + verb* with the formal command (e.g., *no me golpee*).
target_language_example: Por favor, no me llames tan tarde.
native_language_example: Please don’t call me so late.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite negative request/command, often with usted/ustedes forms (e.g., No se levante / No se levanten; No se mueva). The “se” may be part of a reflexive verb (levantarse = to get up) or it can replace le/les before lo/la/los/las (e.g., No se lo diga = Don’t tell it to him/her/them).
target_language_example: Por favor, no se preocupe.
native_language_example: Please don’t worry.

additional_notes: Use it to apologize and ask for forgiveness before explaining what you did (or didn’t do). Follow with an infinitive (decir, no contestar) or with “lo que + verb” (“lo que he dicho” = “what I said”). More formal options: “Por favor, perdón por …” or “Perdóname por …” (without “por favor”).
target_language_example: Por favor, perdóname por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: Please forgive me for arriving late.

additional_notes: Repeating por favor adds emphasis. It’s used when begging, pleading, or asking someone to take you seriously. The tone depends on context: it can sound desperate, impatient, or even sarcastic (like “Oh, please”).
target_language_example: Por favor, por favor, no te vayas todavía.
native_language_example: Please, please, don’t leave yet.

additional_notes: Polite request using the tú command form of sentarse (siéntate = “sit down”). Often followed by a place word like aquí (“here”) or ahí (“there”). Use “por favor, siéntese” for a more formal/polite you (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, siéntate un momento.
native_language_example: Please, sit down for a moment.

meaning: “Please, have/keep …” (telling someone to do or maintain something).
additional_notes: Used to politely give an instruction with the tú command (imperative) of tener: ten. Common patterns: ten cuidado (be careful), ten paciencia (be patient), ten las ventanas abiertas (keep the windows open), ten un poco de… (have/take some…). With a noun it often means “have” (possess/consume); with something like “abiertas/cerradas/listas” it often means “keep” (maintain a state).
target_language_example: Por favor, ten la puerta cerrada.
native_language_example: Please, keep the door closed.

additional_notes: "Tome" is the formal command (usted) form of "tomar". It’s used in polite instructions or offers: take a seat (tome asiento), take the next exit/turn (tome el próximo acceso), take this (tome esto). In casual speech with friends you’d usually use "por favor, toma" (tú).
target_language_example: Por favor, tome su recibo y espere aquí.
native_language_example: Please, take your receipt and wait here.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come (often to a place like your home, or to come see you). "Ven" is the informal (tú) command form of "venir"; for a more formal request to one person, use "por favor, venga" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, ven conmigo un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come with me for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses the usted command form "venga" (from "venir"), so it’s a polite or formal way to ask someone to come. Often followed by "con nosotros" (with us), "por aquí" (this way), or "cuando lo crea conveniente" (when you find it convenient).
target_language_example: Por favor, venga a la recepción.
native_language_example: Please, come to the front desk.

additional_notes: Uses the tú command form of irse (vete), so it’s addressed to one person informally (someone you’d call tú). It often sounds firm because it tells someone to leave; you can add a place: vete a casa (go home), vete de aquí (get out of here), or vete a por… (go get…).
target_language_example: Por favor, vete de aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Please, get out of here right now.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to return. "Vuelve" is the tú (informal singular) command form of "volver" (to come back/return). It can also be used with other phrases like "vuelve a casa" (come back home) or "vuelve a intentarlo" (try again). For a more formal/polite command to one person, you can say "por favor, vuelva" (usted).
target_language_example: Por favor, vuelve mañana.
native_language_example: Please, come back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Use it to ask someone to do something politely. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "Por favor, ¿puedes + infinitivo…?" (e.g., "ayudar", "venir", "salir"). You can add a name before it for emphasis: "Griff, por favor, ¿puedes…?"
target_language_example: Por favor, ¿puedes hablar más despacio?
native_language_example: Please, can you speak more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to give you information or say something. Often followed by a question word (cuándo, qué, dónde) or by "que" + a full sentence: "Por favor dime que estás bien." You can also add what you want them to tell you: "Por favor dime tu versión."
target_language_example: Por favor dime dónde está el baño.
native_language_example: Please tell me where the bathroom is.

additional_notes: Used when something happens after a long wait, effort, or delay. It can go at the beginning of the sentence (Por fin terminé...) or before the verb (Él por fin aprobó...).
target_language_example: Por fin llegamos a casa.
native_language_example: We finally got home.

meaning: for the; because of the; by/through the (feminine singular).
additional_notes: “Por la” = “por” + “la” (no contraction). Common uses: (1) reason or motivation: “por la seguridad” = “for the sake of security”; (2) thanking/cause: “gracias por la tarjeta” = “thanks for the card”; (3) movement/location ‘through/past’: “pasamos por la oficina” = “we go by/through the office”; (4) ‘by’ meaning ‘by way of/holding onto’: “lo agarró por la manga” = “he grabbed him by the sleeve.” It’s used before feminine singular nouns (la seguridad, la manga, la amistad).
target_language_example: Gracias por la ayuda.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help.

meaning: in the street; along/down the street.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (caminar, correr, marchar) to show that something happens out on the street or along it. It can also mean “out and about/on the street” when you run into someone by chance (Me lo encontré por la calle). In Spain you’ll also hear it used to mean “in public” (e.g., No lo digas por la calle = don’t say it publicly).
target_language_example: Me encontré a Ana por la calle y hablamos un rato.
native_language_example: I ran into Ana on the street and we talked for a while.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “by/through the back,” often used with violence (e.g., apuñalar/disparar por la espalda = stab/shoot from behind). Figuratively, it can mean doing something without the person knowing, often in a negative way: criticar a alguien por la espalda = criticize someone behind their back.
target_language_example: No hables de mí por la espalda.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about me behind my back.

meaning: for freedom; in the cause of freedom.
additional_notes: Uses por to express purpose or cause (“for”). Often appears in contexts like fighting, protesting, or sacrificing something to achieve or defend freedom.
target_language_example: Lucharon por la libertad de su país.
native_language_example: They fought for their country’s freedom.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the morning. It often answers “When?” and can be repeated in schedules: por la mañana (in the morning) vs. por la tarde (in the afternoon) vs. por la noche (at night). You can also specify a day: los lunes por la mañana = on Monday mornings.
target_language_example: Suelo estudiar por la mañana.
native_language_example: I usually study in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say when something usually happens during the nighttime hours. It often describes a routine or habit (similar to "at night" / "in the evenings"). You can contrast it with other times of day: por la mañana (in the morning), por la tarde (in the afternoon/evening).
target_language_example: Por la noche hace más frío aquí.
native_language_example: At night it’s colder here.

meaning: through the door; out/in by the door.
additional_notes: Uses por to indicate the route/way someone goes (entering or leaving). Often with verbs like entrar (to enter) and salir (to leave). You can specify which door: por la puerta principal (through the main door), por la puerta oeste (through the west door).
target_language_example: No entres por la ventana; entra por la puerta.
native_language_example: Don’t come in through the window; come in through the door.

meaning: through the back door; via a hidden/less noticeable way.
additional_notes: Often used literally (entering/exiting through a building’s back door). It can also suggest doing something quietly or secretly to avoid being seen, or taking an indirect/less official route (context decides). Used with verbs like entrar, salir, pasar, sacar.
target_language_example: Salimos por la puerta trasera para no hacer ruido.
native_language_example: We left through the back door so we wouldn’t make noise.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses with a feminine singular noun (la mujer, la persona, la razón, la parte) to mean “the one/thing that… for which/for whom…”. It’s por + la que, where que refers back to the noun. Variations: por el que (masc. sing.), por los que / por las que (plural). Often used with reasons, motives, and people you do something for (e.g., “la razón por la que…” = “the reason why…”).
target_language_example: Esta es la razón por la que no fui ayer.
native_language_example: This is the reason why I didn’t go yesterday.

meaning: in the afternoon; in the evening (before night).
additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the later part of the day, after the morning (por la mañana). In many contexts it covers both “afternoon” and the earlier “evening,” depending on local usage and the time of year. You can use it with routines or schedules: Trabajo/Estudio por la tarde.
target_language_example: Nos vemos por la tarde.
native_language_example: See you in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (especially "saltar" = to jump) to say movement goes through and out of a window. "Por" here indicates the route/way something happens (passing through the window opening).
target_language_example: El gato salió por la ventana cuando abrí las cortinas.
native_language_example: The cat went out the window when I opened the curtains.

additional_notes: “Por” + “las” (the feminine plural form of “the”) introduces a feminine plural noun. Depending on context, it can mark a route or movement (“through the”), a means/way (“by the”), or a cause (“because of the”). Examples: “pasar por las calles” = go through the streets; “resolverlo por las vías normales” = solve it by the normal channels; “ocupado por las Olimpiadas” = busy because of the Olympics.
target_language_example: Caminamos por las calles del centro.
native_language_example: We walked through the streets downtown.

meaning: through/along the streets; around the streets.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or activity (e.g., caminar, correr, pasear, dar vueltas) to say someone is moving or spending time in the streets in a general, non-specific way (not on one particular street). Often implies going around different streets.
target_language_example: Estuvimos caminando por las calles toda la tarde.
native_language_example: We were walking around the streets all afternoon.

meaning: up/down the stairs; via the stairs.
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs to show the path taken (not using the elevator). Often appears with verbs like subir (to go up), bajar (to go down), caer(se) (to fall), and llevar/subir/bajar something (to carry something up/down).
target_language_example: Subimos por las escaleras porque el ascensor no funcionaba.
native_language_example: We went up the stairs because the elevator wasn’t working.

meaning: at night; in the evenings (as a usual time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone typically does at night/in the evenings. It often implies a routine or repeated habit ("I usually… at night"), not just one specific night. You’ll also hear the singular "por la noche" for a particular night or a more general “at night.”
target_language_example: Por las noches, me gusta leer antes de dormir.
native_language_example: At night, I like to read before going to sleep.

meaning: for being late; for arriving late.
additional_notes: Uses por + infinitive (por llegar) to give the reason for an apology, scolding, etc. Often follows verbs like disculparse, ofrecer una disculpa, perdonar/perdona, regañar, echar una bronca. You can add where/when: por llegar tarde a la escuela / a la cena.
target_language_example: Lo siento por llegar tarde; había mucho tráfico.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for being late; there was a lot of traffic.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **por lo que + clause**. It introduces the *reason/cause* or the thing you’re referring to: **por lo que dijiste** (“because of what you said”), **por lo que estás pasando** (“because of what you’re going through”). In **por lo que sea**, it means “for whatever reason.”
target_language_example: Te agradezco por lo que hiciste por mí.
native_language_example: I thank you for what you did for me.

meaning: at least (minimum); or at least (in any case).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum number/amount (Por lo menos sesenta personas = at least sixty people). It can also soften or qualify what you just said, meaning “or at least / at any rate” (O por lo menos, así lo cuenta él = Or at least, that’s how he tells it). Often used with negation: Por lo menos no durante el primer año = At least not during the first year.
target_language_example: Podemos vernos el viernes, o por lo menos llamarnos por teléfono.
native_language_example: We can meet on Friday, or at least call each other on the phone.

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to the best of my knowledge."
additional_notes: Used to qualify a statement with your limited knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). It often goes at the beginning of the sentence: “Por lo que yo sé, …”. Similar to “que yo sepa” or “hasta donde yo sé”.
target_language_example: Por lo que yo sé, la reunión empieza a las tres.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the meeting starts at three.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or result based on what was just said. It’s common in formal writing and speech, but also appears in everyday explanations. Often set off with commas: "..., por lo tanto, ...". Similar to "por eso" and "así que" (usually more conversational).
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo; por lo tanto, no voy a ir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time; therefore, I’m not going to go.

meaning: at least (minimum); or at least (in any case).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a minimum number/amount (Por lo menos sesenta personas = at least sixty people). It can also soften or qualify what you just said, meaning “or at least / at any rate” (O por lo menos, así lo cuenta él = Or at least, that’s how he tells it). Often used with negation: Por lo menos no durante el primer año = At least not during the first year.
target_language_example: Podemos vernos el viernes, o por lo menos llamarnos por teléfono.
native_language_example: We can meet on Friday, or at least call each other on the phone.

meaning: “for what / for which”; often “because of what” or “as (someone) said”.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something previously mentioned (a thing, event, or reason). With responsibility/blame it commonly means “for what” someone did (e.g., responsable por lo que has hecho = responsible for what you’ve done). It can also mean “as/according to what” someone said (por lo que decían = as they were saying / according to what they said).
target_language_example: Me disculpé por lo que dije ayer.
native_language_example: I apologized for what I said yesterday.

meaning: “for what / for which”; often “because of what” or “as (someone) said”.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something previously mentioned (a thing, event, or reason). With responsibility/blame it commonly means “for what” someone did (e.g., responsable por lo que has hecho = responsible for what you’ve done). It can also mean “as/according to what” someone said (por lo que decían = as they were saying / according to what they said).
target_language_example: Me disculpé por lo que dije ayer.
native_language_example: I apologized for what I said yesterday.

meaning: on my own; on my tab (I’ll pay).
additional_notes: Often means doing something independently (“by myself/without help”): Lo hice por mi cuenta. With verbs like ir/venir/estar + por mi cuenta, it commonly means you will cover the cost (“it’s on me/my treat”): Las bebidas van por mi cuenta / Va por mi cuenta. Changes with the person: por tu cuenta (on your own), por su cuenta (on his/her/their own).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, la cena va por mi cuenta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, dinner is on me.

meaning: for a long time; for long.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration of time (how long something lasts or has been happening). Often goes with the present perfect to mean “for a long time” up to now (e.g., "He estado... por mucho tiempo"), and with "no" it can mean “not for a long time” / “in a long time” (e.g., "No nos hemos visto por mucho tiempo").
target_language_example: No puedo quedarme por mucho tiempo porque tengo que trabajar.
native_language_example: I can't stay for long because I have to work.

meaning: by myself; on my own (for myself).
additional_notes: Used to say you will do something alone or without help, or that you want to see/check something personally. It changes with the person and gender: por ti mismo/a, por sí mismo/a, por nosotros/as mismos/as, etc. You can also say "yo mismo/a" for emphasis ("I myself").
target_language_example: Prefiero hacerlo por mí mismo.
native_language_example: I prefer to do it by myself.

meaning: "for not having written to you" / "for not writing to you."
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for an apology or request for forgiveness: "(I’m sorry) for…". Structure: "por" + infinitive. "no haberte escrito" is a perfect infinitive (haber + past participle) meaning the not-writing happened earlier. "haberte" = "haber" + "te" (to you). Often followed by time expressions like "antes" (before) or "en tanto tiempo" (in so long).
target_language_example: Perdón por no haberte escrito antes; he estado muy ocupado.
native_language_example: Sorry for not writing to you before; I’ve been really busy.

meaning: “for the first time to/at …” (or “for the first time, …” before a person).
additional_notes: Use **por primera vez** to say something happens for the first time. It’s often followed by **a** when you’re going **to a place** (e.g., *por primera vez a Japón*) or when the next word is a **person** because Spanish uses the **personal a** (e.g., *vi por primera vez a Tom* = “I saw Tom for the first time”). Word order can vary: *Vino por primera vez a Boston* / *Por primera vez vino a Boston*.
target_language_example: Viajé por primera vez a México en 2023.
native_language_example: I traveled to Mexico for the first time in 2023.

meaning: for the first time in (a period/place).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens for the first time within a time span (en cinco años, en meses, en su vida) or in a location/context (en Australia). Often followed by a time expression or place, and it can start a sentence for emphasis: «Por primera vez en su vida, ...».
target_language_example: Por primera vez en mucho tiempo, me sentí tranquilo.
native_language_example: For the first time in a long time, I felt calm.

meaning: "why did you do that?" / "why you did that."
additional_notes: Uses **por qué** (two words) meaning “why” to ask for a reason or to introduce the reason in an indirect statement. **Hiciste** is the tú preterite of *hacer* (“you did/made”), and **eso** means “that.” In a question: **¿Por qué hiciste eso?** In a statement: **(Yo) sé por qué hiciste eso** (“I know why you did that”).
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué hiciste eso.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you did that.

additional_notes: Used with **por qué** (with accent) to ask or explain the reason for something, followed by the direct object pronoun **lo** (“it” or sometimes “him” in some regions) before a verb: **por qué lo + verb** (e.g., *por qué lo hiciste* = “why did you do it”). It also appears in indirect questions after verbs like *saber/decir* (e.g., *No sé por qué lo hice* = “I don’t know why I did it”).
target_language_example: No entiendo por qué lo hiciste así.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you did it like that.

meaning: "why I" / "why (something happens to) me" (introduces an indirect question).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like preguntar, saber, entender, explicar to introduce an indirect question: por qué + subject pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) + verb. It often appears in reported speech ("He asked why I..."). Written with an accent: qué.
target_language_example: No sé por qué me miras así.
native_language_example: I don’t know why you’re looking at me like that.

meaning: "why not?" / "how come (we/you) don't...?" (a suggestion or question).
additional_notes: Used to propose an idea politely or challenge a situation: ¿Por qué no + verb (present)? = “Why don’t we/you...?” It can also be a standalone response meaning “Why not?” Note: with accent (por qué) it’s a question; without accent (porque) it means “because.”
target_language_example: ¿Por qué no vamos al cine después de cenar?
native_language_example: Why don’t we go to the movies after dinner?

meaning: "why" + "you" (used to ask why something is happening to you / why you did something).
additional_notes: Used in questions before a verb that goes with te (object/reflexive pronoun), e.g. ¿Por qué te llamaron? (Why did they call you?), ¿Por qué te ríes? (Why are you laughing?), ¿Por qué te molestas? (Why are you getting upset?). Remember: por qué (two words, with accent) is used in questions and means “why”.
target_language_example: ¿Por qué te vas tan temprano?
native_language_example: Why are you leaving so early?

meaning: "to take it for granted that" / "to assume that".
additional_notes: Used with verbs like dar/tomar (present/past/imperfect): doy por sentado que…, damos por sentado que…, dieron por sentado que…, daba por sentado que…. It means you treat something as true or certain without checking, or you assume it as the default.
target_language_example: No des por sentado que voy a decir que sí.
native_language_example: Don’t take it for granted that I’m going to say yes.

additional_notes: Used with **por** + a possessive adjective (**su** = his/her/your(formal)/their) to give a reason/cause (*por su acento* = because of his accent), express what something is for (*por su seguridad* = for her safety), or show what someone is being thanked/criticized for (*gracias por su cooperación* = thanks for your cooperation). **Su** can be ambiguous; context tells whose it is (often formal 'your' when addressing someone with usted/ustedes).
