additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of saludar: saludó = “he/she greeted.” Use it to describe how someone said hello in a friendly way. Often followed by an indirect object pronoun: me/te/nos/lo/la (e.g., Me saludó con una sonrisa = “She greeted me with a smile”).
target_language_example: El recepcionista nos saludó con una sonrisa.
native_language_example: The receptionist greeted us with a smile.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "salvar la vida". Usually used with an indirect object pronoun to show who was saved: "me/te/le/nos/les salvó la vida" = "saved my/your/his-her/our/their life." It can be literal (preventing death) or figurative (helping in a very serious situation).
target_language_example: Gracias por llamar a la ambulancia; me salvaste la vida.
native_language_example: Thanks for calling the ambulance; you saved my life.

meaning: (Someone’s) nose is bleeding / to have a nosebleed.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sangrar" (to bleed). In these examples, the person is shown with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les" + "sangra" + "la nariz" (literally, “the nose bleeds to me/you/him…”). In everyday English you usually say “My/your/his nose is bleeding” or “I have a nosebleed.”
target_language_example: Si te sangra la nariz, inclina la cabeza hacia adelante.
native_language_example: If your nose is bleeding, tilt your head forward.

additional_notes: A respectful Catholic title for the Pope. It’s most often used with the article and capitalized: "el Santo Padre". In everyday conversation you can also say "el Papa" (the Pope).
target_language_example: Mañana el Santo Padre dará una misa en Roma.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the Holy Father will celebrate a Mass in Rome.

additional_notes: Use this to say someone feels happy with how something turned out. "Satisfecho" agrees with the person: "satisfecho" (male), "satisfecha" (female), "satisfechos/satisfechas" (plural). Common with "estar" or "quedarse": "Estoy satisfecho..." (I’m satisfied), "Se quedó satisfecho..." (He ended up satisfied / was left satisfied).
target_language_example: No estoy del todo satisfecho con el resultado, pero está bien.
native_language_example: I’m not completely satisfied with the result, but it’s okay.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened **a moment ago**. With **irse** (to leave/go away), it becomes **se acaba de ir** (“just left”). You can add who left (e.g., *Tom se acaba de ir*) or where to (e.g., *se acaba de ir de compras* = “just went shopping”).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el doctor se acaba de ir.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor just left.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has ended (a game, a show, a period of life, a situation). Often appears as a complete sentence for emphasis (“Se acabó.” = “That’s it / It’s over.”). You can also put the subject after it: “Se acabó el espectáculo.”
target_language_example: Ya discutimos suficiente; se acabó.
native_language_example: We’ve argued enough; that’s it.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, phase, or privilege has ended, often with a firm or final tone. It’s usually followed by a noun phrase: "Se acabó el recreo" (recess is over), "Se acabó el cuento de hadas" (the fairy tale is over). You can also hear it with feminine nouns: "Se acabó la fiesta".
target_language_example: Se acabó el descanso; volvamos al trabajo.
native_language_example: Break is over; let’s get back to work.

meaning: 'the ... is over' / 'the ... ran out' (for a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something has ended or there is none left. Common with feminine nouns like la batería (battery), la visita (visit), la discusión (discussion). In many contexts it’s an emphatic “That’s it—no more.” In full form you’ll often see: “Se acabó la + noun.”
target_language_example: Se acabó la paciencia.
native_language_example: We've run out of patience. / That's it—no more patience.

additional_notes: From the verb acercarse (“to approach / come closer”). Used for things, times, events, or weather that are coming soon: Se acerca el examen / el invierno / la hora. Often followed by a noun (Se acerca un tifón) or by "a" to show what something is getting close to (El día se acerca a su fin).
target_language_example: Se acerca el fin de semana.
native_language_example: The weekend is approaching.

additional_notes: Present tense, 3rd person plural of **acercarse** (to come closer/to approach). **Se** is reflexive here (the subject is moving closer by itself). Often used to warn that people/animals/enemies are getting nearer, and it can translate as “they’re approaching” or “they’re coming up.”
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Se acercan demasiado rápido.
native_language_example: Careful! They’re coming closer too fast.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "acercarse a" = to move closer to or go up to a person/thing. It often implies physically coming near, and it’s commonly followed by a person/object: "se acercó a ella" (he came up to her), "se acercó a mí" (she came up to me). You can add an infinitive to show purpose: "se acercó a consolarla" (she approached to comfort her).
target_language_example: Me asusté cuando un perro se acercó a mí.
native_language_example: I got scared when a dog came up to me.

meaning: he lay down; he went to bed.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "acostarse" (a reflexive verb). Often used for going to bed to sleep: "Se acostó temprano". With context it can also mean lying down (e.g., on a bed or couch). For other subjects: "me acosté" (I went to bed), "te acostaste" (you went to bed), "se acostaron" (they went to bed).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, se acostó temprano.
native_language_example: After dinner, he went to bed early.

meaning: 'they feed on' / 'they eat' (as a regular diet).
additional_notes: Used to describe what an animal or creature eats as its main food source. It’s the verb "alimentarse de" in the third-person plural (they). You can change it to match the subject: "me alimento de" (I feed on), "se alimenta de" (he/she/it feeds on), "nos alimentamos de" (we feed on).
target_language_example: Los murciélagos vampiro se alimentan de sangre.
native_language_example: Vampire bats feed on blood.

additional_notes: From the verb **arrepentirse de** (“to regret/to be sorry about”). It’s reflexive, so you change **se** depending on the subject: **me arrepiento de** (I regret), **te arrepientes de** (you regret), **se arrepiente de** (he/she/you formal regrets), **nos arrepentimos de**, **se arrepienten de**. It’s commonly followed by **de + infinitive** (e.g., *de haber ido*, *de no estudiar*) or **de + noun/phrase** (e.g., *de la decisión*), or **de lo que + verb** (“what [someone] did”).
target_language_example: Él se arrepiente de no haber dicho la verdad.
native_language_example: He regrets not telling the truth.

meaning: looks like; resembles; is similar to.
additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things. The verb is pronominal: asemejarse a + noun/pronoun ("Ella se asemeja a su madre"). Often followed by “en…” to specify what is similar ("en muchos aspectos", "en todos los sentidos"). In the negative: “no se asemeja a…” (doesn’t resemble / isn’t like).
target_language_example: Esta ciudad se asemeja a la mía, pero es más grande.
native_language_example: This city looks like mine, but it’s bigger.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "bajarse de" + "el" = "del". It means to get off a vehicle (bus, taxi) or get out of a vehicle (car), and also to climb down from something (a tree). Use it with a reflexive pronoun: me/te/se/nos/se + bajé/bajaste/bajó..., e.g., "me bajé del bus" = "I got off the bus."
target_language_example: Me bajé del metro en la próxima estación.
native_language_example: I got off the subway at the next station.

additional_notes: Used to say what something depends on or has as its foundation. It’s the reflexive verb basarse: (algo) se basa en (algo). You can change it for tense/person: se basan en (they are based on), se basaba en (was based on), se basará en (will be based on).
target_language_example: Esta decisión se basa en la información que tenemos ahora.
native_language_example: This decision is based on the information we have now.

additional_notes: From the verb "burlarse de" (to make fun of). Use it with a person/thing after "de": "Se burla de mí" (He/She makes fun of me). The subject is the person doing the mocking, and it can be followed by a reason with "por": "Se burla de John por su dialecto" (…because of his dialect).
target_language_example: No te burles de mí, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t make fun of me, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb phrase “burlarse de” + a person/thing: “to make fun of / to mock.” Often implies being unkind or humiliating. Other forms: “se burla de” (he/she makes fun of), “me burlé de” (I made fun of).
target_language_example: Se burló de mi acento, pero no me importó.
native_language_example: He/She made fun of my accent, but I didn’t care.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of asking, requesting, convincing, or refusing (e.g., pedir, convencer, negar) to talk about marrying someone. It’s the imperfect subjunctive of "casarse con" (to marry). The full pattern is "que + (él/ella/yo) se casara con + persona". Often appears in proposals: "Le pidió que se casara con él/ella" (= He/She asked them to marry him/her).
target_language_example: Mis padres querían que me casara con alguien de mi ciudad.
native_language_example: My parents wanted me to marry someone from my town.

meaning: they got married; they married (each other).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of casarse, used for a completed event: they got married. It’s often used with time expressions like hace tres meses (three months ago) or el mes pasado (last month). The "se" is part of the reflexive verb casarse (to get married).
target_language_example: Mis abuelos se casaron en 1975.
native_language_example: My grandparents got married in 1975.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: casarse = “to get married.” "Se casó" is the preterite (completed past action). Often used with "con" to say who someone married: "Se casó con él/ella." You can add time expressions like "ayer" or "cuando tenía...".
target_language_example: Mi hermana se casó en junio.
native_language_example: My sister got married in June.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb casarse (to get married). In the preterite, se casó is used for a completed past event: se casó con + person. It changes with the subject: me casé (I got married), te casaste, se casó, nos casamos, se casaron.
target_language_example: Mi primo se casó con su mejor amiga el año pasado.
native_language_example: My cousin got married to his best friend last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "casarse con" = “to marry / to get married to.” It’s used with "se" because it’s reflexive in Spanish: "casarse". You typically add a noun after "con un/una" (a person): "Se casó con un músico" / "Se casó con una doctora". For other subjects: "Me casé con…" (I married…), "Nos casamos con…" (we married…).
target_language_example: Se casó con una ingeniera el año pasado.
native_language_example: He/She married an engineer last year.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb **caerse** (“to fall down”). **Se** shows it happened to the subject (often accidentally). Commonly used for people/objects physically falling (*Se cayó en el tren*), and also for services or systems being down (*El servidor se cayó*).
target_language_example: Me asusté porque mi teléfono se cayó al suelo.
native_language_example: I got scared because my phone fell on the floor.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb "caerse" (to fall). "Se" changes with the subject (me/te/se/nos/os/se): "Me caí al suelo" = I fell to the ground. Used for people or objects accidentally falling.
target_language_example: Me resbalé y me caí al suelo.
native_language_example: I slipped and fell to the ground.

additional_notes: Used with the verb caerse (to fall, accidentally) in the past: se cayó = “(he/she) fell.” Add de + place to say where someone fell from (bed, stairs, roof, etc.). Often implies an accidental fall.
target_language_example: Se cayó de la bicicleta y se lastimó la rodilla.
native_language_example: He/She fell off the bike and hurt his/her knee.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the verb phrase “caerse (de)” = “to fall (from/off)”. “Del” is the contraction of “de + el” (“from/off the”). Used for falling from a place or vehicle: “del puente” (from the bridge), “del techo” (off the roof), “del camión” (off the truck). In some contexts “caerse del caballo” can also be figurative (suddenly realizing the truth), but it’s often literal too.
target_language_example: Mi hermano se cayó del árbol, pero está bien.
native_language_example: My brother fell from the tree, but he’s okay.

additional_notes: "Se cayó" is the past tense (preterite) of "caerse" = "to fall" (often accidental). "Del" = "de + el" ("from/out of the"). The subject changes with context: "El mono se cayó..." (the monkey fell), "Mi hermano se cayó..." (my brother fell). Often followed by what happened as a result: "pero no se rompió nada" (but nothing got broken) or "y se rompió una pierna" (and he broke a leg).
target_language_example: Ayer mi primo se cayó del árbol y se lastimó el brazo.
native_language_example: Yesterday my cousin fell out of the tree and hurt his arm.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **comerse**. The **se** often adds emphasis that someone ate the whole thing or finished it (similar to “ate it all up”). Often used with a direct object: *Se comió mi almuerzo* = “He ate my lunch.”
target_language_example: Me distraje y mi hermano se comió toda la pizza.
native_language_example: I got distracted and my brother ate up all the pizza.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (completed past) of **comerse**: **se comió** = “he/she ate (it),” often implying eating it up/entirely. **una** is an indefinite article (“a”) when followed by a feminine noun (**una naranja**), or a pronoun meaning “one” when the noun is understood from context (**nadie se comió una** = “nobody ate one [of them]”).
target_language_example: Había muchas galletas, pero Ana se comió una.
native_language_example: There were many cookies, but Ana ate one.

additional_notes: Used to describe what something is made of or what parts/members it has. Structure: [thing] + se compone de + [components]. Often in the present tense, but can change for tense: “se componía de” (used to consist of), “se compondrá de” (will consist of).
target_language_example: El equipo se compone de jugadores de diferentes países.
native_language_example: The team is made up of players from different countries.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (se) to show the subject bought something for themselves. It’s the preterite (past) of comprarse. You can change it to match the person: me compré (I bought myself), te compraste (you bought yourself), nos compramos (we bought ourselves). Often followed by an item with un/una (or plural: se compró unos/unas).
target_language_example: Me compré una chaqueta nueva.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new jacket.

additional_notes: Future tense of “convertirse en” (to become/turn into). Used to say that someone or something will become a person/role/thing in the future. It’s reflexive (“se”) and is typically followed by a noun (often with an article): “se convertirá en médico / en un buen futbolista.”
target_language_example: Con práctica, se convertirá en un gran chef.
native_language_example: With practice, he/she will become a great chef.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a change or transformation into something else. It’s the verb phrase "convertirse en" (to become/turn into) in the 3rd-person singular (él/ella/eso/it). You can also use other persons: "me convierto en" (I become), "se convierten en" (they become).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, el problema se convierte en una oportunidad.
native_language_example: Over time, the problem turns into an opportunity.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of “convertirse en” = “to become.” Used for a completed change at a specific moment in the past. Pattern: “(subject) se convirtió en + noun/adjective” (often a new role/status/identity).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un gran médico.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a great doctor.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "convertirse en" (to become/turn into). "Se" here is part of the verb, not a reflexive pronoun you can omit. Use "en un" with a masculine singular noun ("en una" for feminine, and no article before many jobs/roles: "se convirtió en fotógrafo"). It can describe a literal transformation (a frog turned into a prince) or a change in status/result (a book became a bestseller).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se convirtió en un líder respetado.
native_language_example: Over time, he became a respected leader.

meaning: “(he/she) cut himself/herself” or “it got cut / was cut off.”
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of pronominal "cortarse". Often means someone accidentally cut themselves: "Se cortó con un cuchillo" (He/She cut himself/herself with a knife). With body parts, Spanish commonly uses the definite article: "Se cortó la mano" (not usually *su mano*). It can also be used for things like phone/internet: "La línea se cortó" = the line got cut / the call dropped.
target_language_example: Me asusté porque se cortó la llamada.
native_language_example: I got worried because the call dropped.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun "se" with "cortarse" to mean someone accidentally/inadvertently cut themselves. The person is often implied by context or can be added ("Tom se cortó el dedo"). You can add how it happened with "con" ("con el cuchillo") or a gerund ("abriendo una lata").
target_language_example: Me corté el dedo cocinando.
native_language_example: I cut my finger while cooking.

meaning: "it is believed/thought that"; sometimes "who does (he/she) think (he/she) is...?"
additional_notes: Impersonal/passive "se" construction used to express a general belief or assumption without saying who believes it (common in news and formal writing): "Se cree que..." = "It’s believed/thought that...". In questions like "¿Quién se cree que es...?", it’s a reproach meaning "Who does he/she think he/she is...?".
target_language_example: Se cree que mañana lloverá en el norte.
native_language_example: It’s believed that it will rain in the north tomorrow.

meaning: “he/she thinks he/she is…” (often: “who does he/she think he/she is?”).
additional_notes: From creerse (to believe oneself to be / to think of oneself as). Common in the fixed question “¿Quién se cree que es?” to criticize someone acting important or interfering. Can also be a plain statement about someone’s self-image: “Se cree que es un héroe.”
target_language_example: ¿Quién se cree que es para hablarme así?
native_language_example: Who does he think he is to talk to me like that?

additional_notes: Future tense of the expression "darse cuenta (de)" = "to realize/notice (that/of)." Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive, or "de que" + clause: "Se dará cuenta de que..." (He/She will realize that...). It can refer to suddenly noticing something or understanding it after thinking.
target_language_example: Cuando veas el precio, te darás cuenta de que es demasiado caro.
native_language_example: When you see the price, you'll realize it's too expensive.

meaning: (he/she) decided to; finally made up (his/her) mind to.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb decidirse + a + infinitive to talk about making a decision to do something (often after thinking, hesitation, or difficulty). It changes with the subject: me decidí a, te decidiste a, se decidió a, nos decidimos a, se decidieron a.
target_language_example: Después de pensarlo mucho, me decidí a cambiar de trabajo.
native_language_example: After thinking about it a lot, I decided to change jobs.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb desmayarse (“to faint”). Used to say someone suddenly lost consciousness; often followed by a cause with de (Se desmayó de hambre = “He/She fainted from hunger”) or with al + infinitive to mean “upon/when doing something” (Se desmayó al ver la sangre = “He/She fainted when seeing blood”).
target_language_example: Se desmayó en el metro y llamaron a una ambulancia.
native_language_example: He/She fainted on the subway and they called an ambulance.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb despertarse (“to wake up”). Used for a completed event: se despertó = “he/she woke up.” Often followed by details like con... (“with...”), muy temprano (“very early”), or adjectives describing mood: se despertó malhumorado (“he woke up grumpy”).
target_language_example: Ella se despertó a las seis y no pudo volver a dormir.
native_language_example: She woke up at six and couldn’t go back to sleep.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito) of reflexive verb detenerse (“to stop”). Used for a person, vehicle, or something more abstract: El auto se detuvo (“The car stopped”); Se detuvo y miró… (“He/She stopped and looked…”). Often followed by en/frente a/delante de to say where it stopped, or por/para + infinitive to say why/for what purpose: Se detuvo para mirar el auto.
target_language_example: El tren se detuvo en la estación.
native_language_example: The train stopped at the station.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression used to report rumors, common beliefs, or information from an unknown/general source (no specific subject). Very common in news and storytelling. Often followed by a statement: “Se dice que + [clause]”. Similar in meaning to “dicen que…”, but “se dice que” sounds more neutral/impersonal.
target_language_example: Se dice que este restaurante es el mejor de la ciudad.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is the best in the city.

meaning: "it is said that the..." / "people say that the..."
additional_notes: Impersonal expression used to report a general belief, rumor, or common saying without naming who says it. Uses "se" (impersonal) + "dice" (is said) + "que" (that) + "el" (the, masculine singular). Often followed by a statement in the present tense.
target_language_example: Se dice que el café de Colombia es excelente.
native_language_example: It’s said that Colombian coffee is excellent.

meaning: "it is said that he..." / "people say that he..."
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal "se" to report rumors or general statements without saying who is speaking. Often translates as "they say" or "it’s said". You can replace "él" with another subject (e.g., "se dice que ella...").
target_language_example: Se dice que él vive en otra ciudad ahora.
native_language_example: They say he lives in another city now.

additional_notes: This is the imperfect subjunctive form of **darse cuenta de** (“to realize/notice”). It commonly appears after expressions like **es como si...** (“it’s as if...”) and especially after **sin que...** (“without...”), as in **sin que nadie se diera cuenta** = “without anyone noticing.” It’s often followed by **de** + noun/idea: **darse cuenta del error** (“realize the mistake”), **darse cuenta de que...** (“realize that...” ).
target_language_example: Me fui sin que nadie se diera cuenta.
native_language_example: I left without anyone noticing.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "darse cuenta (de)". Use "se dio cuenta" by itself when the thing is understood (“He realized.”), or add "de" + noun/phrase (“He realized/noticed that…/about…”). Often used with time words like "por fin" (finally) or "en seguida" (right away).
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
native_language_example: I realized that I was wrong.

additional_notes: Past tense of "darse cuenta de". It’s used when someone suddenly understands something or becomes aware of a fact. Very often followed by "que" + clause ("se dio cuenta de que...") or by "lo que" ("se dio cuenta de lo que..."). You can change it for other people: "me di cuenta de" (I realized), "te diste cuenta de" (you realized), "nos dimos cuenta de" (we realized).
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten the keys.

additional_notes: Past tense of darse cuenta de (“to realize/notice”). It’s often followed by que + a clause: se dio cuenta de que estaba perdido (“he realized he was lost”). In plural: se dieron cuenta de que… (“they realized that…”).
target_language_example: Me di cuenta de que había olvidado las llaves.
native_language_example: I realized that I had forgotten the keys.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "disfrazarse de" = to dress up/disguise oneself as someone/something. It’s reflexive ("se"). The pattern is: [person] se disfrazó de + noun (often with an article: de policía / de una niña). For other people: me disfracé de (I), te disfrazaste de (you), se disfrazó de (he/she/you formal), nos disfrazamos de (we), se disfrazaron de (they/you all).
target_language_example: Me disfracé de pirata para la fiesta.
native_language_example: I dressed up as a pirate for the party.

additional_notes: Used with the verb divorciarse (to get divorced) in the past tense: se divorció = “(he/she) got divorced.” It normally takes de to say who the person divorced from: se divorció de su esposa/marido (“got divorced from his wife/husband”). su can mean “his,” “her,” “your (formal),” or “their,” so the context tells you whose spouse it is. Present tense: se divorcia de su … (“gets divorced from his/her …”).
target_language_example: Se divorció de su esposo el año pasado.
native_language_example: She got divorced from her husband last year.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "dormirse" (to fall asleep). Often used when someone drifts off or goes from being awake to asleep: "El bebé se durmió" = "The baby fell asleep." You can add where/when: "Se durmió en el sofá" (He/She fell asleep on the couch).
target_language_example: Me quedé leyendo y al final me dormí.
native_language_example: I stayed reading and in the end I fell asleep.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of enamorarse de. Use it to talk about someone falling in love with a person, or becoming very fond of a place/thing. Structure: [subject] se enamoró de + noun/person (e.g., Se enamoró de ella / de Alemania).
target_language_example: Me enamoré de esta ciudad la primera vez que la visité.
native_language_example: I fell in love with this city the first time I visited it.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb phrase "encogerse de hombros" = "to shrug (one’s) shoulders," often meaning “I don’t know,” “I don’t care,” or “what can you do?” You can swap the subject: "Me encogí de hombros" (I shrugged), "Se encogieron de hombros" (they shrugged).
target_language_example: No sabía la respuesta, así que se encogió de hombros.
native_language_example: He didn’t know the answer, so he shrugged his shoulders.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "encontrarse con". Often means meeting someone unexpectedly/by chance ("run into"), but it can also mean simply "met" in a particular place/time. Structure: [person] se encontró con + [someone].
target_language_example: Me encontré con mi profesora en el supermercado.
native_language_example: I ran into my teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: "is located" / "is found"; also "is" (in a certain condition).
additional_notes: From the verb *encontrarse* (reflexive). Common in formal or neutral speech to say where something/someone is: *¿Dónde se encuentra…?* = “Where is it/he/she?”. It can also describe someone’s state or condition: *se encuentra bien/mal* = “is doing well/badly.” In some contexts it’s closer to “can be found” (availability): *No se encuentra en este momento* = “It’s not available right now.”
target_language_example: El museo se encuentra cerca de la plaza, y mi abuela se encuentra mejor hoy.
native_language_example: The museum is located near the plaza, and my grandma is doing better today.

additional_notes: Used to state where something is (a place, object, institution, or even an abstract idea). It’s a more formal, descriptive alternative to “está en.” The verb is “encontrarse” (to be found/to be located), and it agrees with the subject: “se encuentra” (he/she/it is located), “se encuentran” (they are located).
target_language_example: La farmacia se encuentra en la esquina.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is located on the corner.

additional_notes:
Preterite (completed past action) of the verb "enfadarse" = to get angry. Often used with:
- "enfadarse con + person" (to be mad at someone): "Se enfadó con María."
- "enfadarse por + reason" (to be upset about something): "Se enfadó por lo que dijiste."
target_language_example: Me equivoqué y mi jefe se enfadó conmigo.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, and my boss got angry with me.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb “enojarse” = “to get angry.” Often followed by “con” to say who someone was angry with: “Se enojó con María” = “He got angry with María.” You can add “mucho” to intensify it: “se enojó mucho” = “got very angry.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano se enojó conmigo por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother got angry with me for arriving late.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "escaparse". Used when someone or an animal manages to leave or flee (often unexpectedly), or when a person avoids a danger/problem: "escaparse de" + place/danger; "escaparse con" + something (to get away with it).
target_language_example: El perro se escapó de casa anoche.
native_language_example: The dog ran away from home last night.

additional_notes: Used with a gerund (-ando/-iendo) to talk about an action or process happening right now in a reflexive/impersonal or “se” passive construction (often like English “is being + past participle” or “is …-ing”). It’s very common in descriptions of ongoing changes: “se está calentando” (it’s warming up). With plural subjects, it becomes “se están” (e.g., “Las casas se están vendiendo”).
target_language_example: La cena se está preparando.
native_language_example: Dinner is being prepared.

additional_notes: Present progressive of comerse (to eat up). Used for someone currently eating something (often implies eating it all), or for things like rust/acid that are gradually consuming or eroding something: "El óxido se está comiendo el hierro" = "Rust is eating away at the iron."
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa! El perro se está comiendo mi sándwich.
native_language_example: Hurry up! The dog is eating my sandwich.

meaning: "is getting / is becoming" (with hacerse); sometimes "is getting (something) done".
additional_notes: From the verb hacerse (reflexive). Common uses: (1) change over time: Se está haciendo mayor. / Nuestro mundo se está haciendo más pequeño. / Se está haciendo tarde. (2) with a noun phrase, it can mean "pretend to be": hacerse el tonto = to play dumb. (3) with a service/beauty item, it often means "get it done": hacerse las uñas = get your nails done. It’s usually followed by an adjective (más pequeño, mayor, tarde) or by a noun phrase (el tonto, las uñas).
target_language_example: Se está haciendo más frío.
native_language_example: It’s getting colder.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive: estar + gerund (está moviendo) to talk about an action in progress. With "se" it often refers to something unspecified or already known from context (e.g., "Algo se está moviendo…" = “Something is moving…”). You can add details with phrases like "rápidamente" (quickly) or "hacia…" (toward…).
target_language_example: Algo se está moviendo en la oscuridad.
native_language_example: Something is moving in the dark.

additional_notes: Progressive form: **estar + muriendo** describes something happening right now/these days (“is dying”). **Se** is part of the verb **morirse** (to die), often used to emphasize the process/state. You’ll often see it with causes like **de hambre** (“from hunger”) or **desangrando** (“bleeding out”). It can be literal (a person) or figurative (e.g., **La tierra se está muriendo** = “The Earth is dying”).
target_language_example: El perro se está muriendo y necesitamos un veterinario.
native_language_example: The dog is dying and we need a veterinarian.

meaning: "is becoming / getting"; with the sun, "is setting."
additional_notes: This is the present progressive of "ponerse" (to become/get). It’s used for changes happening right now or developing: "Se está poniendo viejo" (It’s getting old), "Se está poniendo impaciente" (He’s getting impatient). With "el sol", "ponerse" commonly means "to set" (go down): "El sol se está poniendo". The reflexive "se" is part of the verb "ponerse."
target_language_example: La situación se está poniendo difícil.
native_language_example: The situation is getting difficult.

meaning: “is staying” / “is becoming; is getting (into a state)” / “is running out (of something)” / “is falling behind.”
additional_notes: This is the present progressive of quedarse (reflexive): estar + quedando. Common patterns: quedarse en + place = “to stay (somewhere)” (temporary lodging); quedarse + adjective = “to become/get” (e.g., calvo = bald); quedarse sin + noun or quedarse escaso de + noun = “to run out of / be short of”; quedarse atrás = “to fall behind.”
target_language_example: Me estoy quedando sin batería.
native_language_example: I’m running out of battery.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase volverse = “to become, to get” (often a noticeable change of state). Use it with adjectives (más frío, loca, difícil, calvo, descuidado) or with a noun phrase like “una locura.” It’s in the present progressive: se + está + volviendo, meaning the change is happening right now or lately.
target_language_example: La situación se está volviendo peligrosa.
native_language_example: The situation is getting dangerous.

meaning: "they are" / "are being" (used with a gerund to form the present progressive).
additional_notes: Used before a gerund (-ando/-iendo) to say something is happening right now: se están + gerund = “they are ___-ing.” The "se" often marks a reflexive/reciprocal action (e.g., people gathering) or a passive/impersonal idea (something is getting done/occurring). Which meaning it has depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Se están poniendo nerviosos antes del examen.
native_language_example: They’re getting nervous before the exam.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "irse" = "to leave" (to go away). Often used with a time expression: "Se fue hace un rato" (He left a little while ago), "se fue temprano" (left early), "se fue hace tres días" (left three days ago). You can add a place with "de": "Se fue del bar" (He left the bar). "Ya se fue" means "He/She already left."
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, ya se fue.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he/she had already left.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb irse: irse = to leave/go away. Use it with a place (Se fue a París.) or with an infinitive to say someone went to do something (Se fue a acostar. = went to bed). Change the pronoun for other people: me fui a (I), te fuiste a (you), nos fuimos a (we), se fueron a (they).
target_language_example: Anoche se fue a casa temprano.
native_language_example: Last night he/she went home early.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "irse" (to leave/go away): "se fue" = "he/she/it left". Add a subject if needed: "Él se fue a casa" (He went home), "Ella se fue a casa" (She went home). Often implies leaving a place and heading home; you can add time or emotion: "se fue a casa al día siguiente" (went home the next day), "se fue a casa enojado/a" (went home angry).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, se fue a casa.
native_language_example: After work, he/she went home.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb phrase *irse a la cama* (“to go to bed”). The subject is often understood from context, so *Se fue a la cama* can mean “He went to bed” or “She went to bed.” You can add a time: *se fue a la cama a las once* (“went to bed at 11”).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, se fue a la cama temprano.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she went to bed early.

additional_notes: "Se fue" is the past tense (pretérito) of "irse" = to leave/go away. "Al extranjero" means "abroad" (literally, "to the foreign place/country"). The subject is often implied by context (él/ella/ellos/ellas/usted). You can add a reason with "a + infinitive": "se fue al extranjero a estudiar" = went abroad to study.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se fue al extranjero por trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister went abroad for work.

additional_notes: Uses irse (to leave/go away) + gerund (corriendo) to describe leaving while doing the action (running). Often implies quickly/suddenly. With people, it can suggest hurrying away, sometimes because they’re scared, embarrassed, or in a rush.
target_language_example: Cuando sonó la alarma, se fue corriendo del edificio.
native_language_example: When the alarm went off, he ran out of the building.

additional_notes: Preterite of **irse de** (to leave a place). Use **de** for the place you leave: *Se fue de la playa* = “He left the beach.” You can add a destination with **a**: *Se fue de Japón a España* (“He left Japan for Spain”). Often implies leaving/going away (sometimes for good, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ella se fue de la oficina a las seis.
native_language_example: She left the office at six.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (se fue sin decir nada = “left without saying anything”) or with a past infinitive (se fue sin haber sido visto = “left without having been seen”). “Se fue” is the preterite of irse (to leave/go away). Note: Spanish “sin” means “without” (not the English noun “sin”).
target_language_example: Se fue sin avisar a nadie.
native_language_example: He left without telling anyone.

meaning: '(that) he/she leave' / '(that) he/she go away' (past subjunctive).
additional_notes: From irse (“to leave/go away”), in the imperfect subjunctive (se fuera). It’s commonly used after verbs like aconsejar, rogar, dejar, hacer, etc., usually in a clause with que: e.g., “Ella le aconsejó que se fuera” = “She advised him to leave.” Often used when the main verb is in the past.
target_language_example: Mi mamá quería que me fuera a casa.
native_language_example: My mom wanted me to go home.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "irse" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes". Used to say a group departed or went somewhere. Often followed by destination ("se fueron a casa") or manner/time ("se fueron en medio de la noche"). Also used with "por" to mean leaving/taking different routes: "se fueron por caminos separados".
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la fiesta, se fueron temprano.
native_language_example: When the party ended, they left early.

meaning: "they went to" / "they left for" (to a destination).
additional_notes: From the verb irse (to leave/go away) in the preterite: se fueron = “they left/went away.” It’s commonly followed by a + place/event to say where they went. Often implies leaving from where you are/speaking (stronger than just fueron a).
target_language_example: Se fueron a casa temprano porque estaban cansados.
native_language_example: They went home early because they were tired.

meaning: "has/have" in the present perfect (with "se" for passive/impersonal or reflexive actions).
additional_notes: Used as **se + ha + past participle**. Common in: (1) **passive/impersonal "se"** to mean “has been” without naming who did it: *Se ha producido un error* (“An error has occurred / has been made”). (2) **reflexive verbs** in the present perfect: *Tom se ha rendido* (“Tom has given up”), *Un tigre se ha escapado* (“A tiger has escaped”).
target_language_example: Se ha cancelado el vuelo por el mal tiempo.
native_language_example: The flight has been canceled because of bad weather.

meaning: "it’s over" / "it has ended" ("has run out" for supplies, patience, etc.).
additional_notes: Present perfect of acabar(se): something has finished or come to an end. Often used with no subject (Se ha acabado.) meaning “It’s over.” With a subject, it can mean that something has run out: Su paciencia se ha acabado = “His/Her patience has run out.” Common with ya: Ya se ha acabado = “It’s already over.”
target_language_example: Se ha acabado el café.
native_language_example: We’ve run out of coffee.

additional_notes: Present perfect of the reflexive verb "convertirse en" (to become/turn into). It describes a change up to the present: "X se ha convertido en Y". Often used for gradual changes (interests, situations, roles) or transformations. You can change the subject and person: "me he convertido en" (I’ve become), "se han convertido en" (they’ve become).
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, este barrio se ha convertido en una zona muy tranquila.
native_language_example: Over time, this neighborhood has become a very quiet area.

meaning: 'has become' / 'has gotten' (reflexive hacerse), or 'has been done/made' (impersonal/passive se).
additional_notes: Formed with the present perfect: **se + ha + hecho**. With **hacerse** (reflexive), it often means a change in state: *se ha hecho daño* = “he/she has gotten hurt,” *se ha hecho mayor* = “has gotten older,” *se ha hecho a sí mismo* = “has made himself” (self-made). With impersonal/passive **se**, it means something was done in general (who did it isn’t said): *una vez se ha hecho algo* = “once something has been done.” The exact English translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Ya se ha hecho tarde; vámonos.
native_language_example: It’s already gotten late; let’s go.

additional_notes: Used when a dream, wish, plan, or prediction becomes real. It’s the present perfect: "se ha hecho" (has been made/has become) + "realidad" (reality). Often appears after words like "sueño" (dream) or "predicción" (prediction), and can be emphasized with "al fin" (at last).
target_language_example: Después de tantos años, mi sueño se ha hecho realidad.
native_language_example: After so many years, my dream has come true.

additional_notes: Present perfect of the reflexive verb "irse" (to leave/go away). Used when someone has left a place ("Tom se ha ido") or when something has disappeared/ended ("El dolor de cabeza se ha ido"). It often implies the person/thing is no longer here.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, Ana ya se ha ido.
native_language_example: When I arrived, Ana had already left.

additional_notes: Present perfect of "irse" (to leave/go away), used to say someone has left and gone to a destination. Very common with a place after "a" (a Londres, a España). Often implies the person is no longer here now (they’ve left).
target_language_example: María se ha ido a casa.
native_language_example: María has gone home.

meaning: "has gotten/has become" or "has started" (present perfect of ponerse, he/she/it).
additional_notes: This is the present perfect form of the reflexive verb ponerse (3rd person singular): se + ha + puesto. It’s very common in set phrases where ponerse means a change of state or beginning, not literally “to put.” Examples: ponerse en contacto = to get in touch; ponerse a la venta = to go on sale / be put up for sale; ponerse malo = to get sick.
target_language_example: Mi hermano se ha puesto enfermo y no va a venir.
native_language_example: My brother has gotten sick and isn’t going to come.

meaning: 'has stayed/has remained'; often 'has become/ended up (in a state)'.
additional_notes: Present perfect of "quedarse" (to stay/remain), used with "se". It can mean physically staying somewhere or staying with someone ("Se ha quedado conmigo" = "He stayed with me"). Very often it expresses a change into a new state, especially with an adjective or past participle: "se ha quedado ciego" (has gone blind), "se ha quedado antiguo" (has become outdated), "se ha quedado dormido" (has fallen asleep).
target_language_example: Se ha quedado dormido en el sofá.
native_language_example: He fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: From the verb "volverse" (reflexive), used to talk about a change in state. It’s in the present perfect: "se" + "ha" + past participle "vuelto". The "se" is part of the verb (not a direct object). You can also use it impersonally with situations: "Se ha vuelto difícil..." = "It has become difficult..."
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, se ha vuelto más paciente.
native_language_example: Over time, he/she has become more patient.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **volverse loco** (“to go crazy/to go mad”). **Se ha vuelto** is the present perfect (“has become/has turned”), used for a change of state. It can be literal (someone is acting irrationally) or figurative/exaggerated (someone is overreacting). You can change the subject: **Me he vuelto loco** (I’ve gone crazy), **Te has vuelto loco** (you’ve gone crazy), **Se han vuelto locos** (they’ve gone crazy).
target_language_example: ¡Te has vuelto loco si crees que voy a pagar eso!
native_language_example: You’ve gone crazy if you think I’m going to pay that.

additional_notes: Used to say that a language is spoken in a country/region. It’s the passive-style construction with "se" + "habla" (hablar), and it agrees with a singular subject ("el francés se habla..."). Often followed by a place: "se habla en + country/region".
target_language_example: El español se habla en muchos países.
native_language_example: Spanish is spoken in many countries.

additional_notes: Used as **se + había + past participle** to talk about something that **had already happened** before another past event (often with **ya** = “already”). Common with pronominal/reflexive verbs like **irse** (se había ido = had left), **esconderse** (se había escondido = had hidden), **partirse/partir(se)** in contexts where it means “to leave.”
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos, el tren ya se había ido.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the train had already left.

additional_notes: Past perfect of the reflexive verb casarse (“to get married”): se + había + casado. Used to talk about a marriage that happened before another past moment (e.g., “Two days earlier, he/she had gotten married”). The subject can be he/she/you (formal)/they depending on context.
target_language_example: Cuando lo conocí, ya se había casado.
native_language_example: When I met him, he had already gotten married.

additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of irse (to leave/go away): se (reflexive) + había + ido. Used to say someone/something was already gone before another past moment (often with verbs like creí/pensé/me dijeron). Can be literal (someone left) or figurative (e.g., El verano se había ido; Toda esperanza se había ido).
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, él ya se había ido.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already left.

meaning: "they had left" / "they had gone away" (past perfect).
additional_notes: Past perfect (pluscuamperfecto) of "irse" (to leave/go away): "se" + "habían" (they had) + "ido" (gone). Used to say the leaving happened before another past event (often with "cuando", "después que", "antes de que"). Commonly implies they left a place. Contrast: "se fueron" = they left (simple past), not necessarily earlier than another past action.
target_language_example: Cuando llegamos al aeropuerto, el avión ya se había ido.
native_language_example: When we got to the airport, the plane had already left.

additional_notes:
Often uses **se** to avoid saying who does the action.
- **Passive/impersonal se**: *El vino se hace con uvas* = “Wine is made with grapes.” (someone makes it, but not specified).
- **Hacerse = to become**: *Mi sueño se hace realidad* = “My dream becomes reality.”
- With time/experiences, it can mean “to feel/seem”: *Qué larga se hace una hora* = “How long an hour feels/seems.”
target_language_example: El pan se hace en el horno.
native_language_example: Bread is made in the oven.

meaning: 'have' / 'have been' (present perfect, 3rd person plural) used with "se".
additional_notes: "Se han" = "se" + "han" (they have). It’s very common in: (1) "pasiva con se" ("have been" + past participle): "Se han dado órdenes" = "Orders have been given"; (2) pronominal/reflexive verbs in the present perfect: "Se han marchado" = "They’ve left", "Las vacaciones se han acabado" = "The vacation has ended". The subject is often not stated or is something like "orders", "sentences", etc.
target_language_example: Se han cancelado las clases.
native_language_example: Classes have been cancelled.

meaning: “they have left / they’re gone” (present perfect of irse).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb irse (“to leave/go away”). It can mean people/animals have left a place (“Se han ido a Europa.”), or that things like problems or good times are gone/disappeared (“Todos mis problemas se han ido.”). Often implies they are no longer here now. Literally “they have gone (themselves).”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; se han ido sin despedirse.
native_language_example: It’s late already; they left without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect: "se han ido" (they have left / have gone away), with "todos" (all/everyone). Very common with time words like "ya" (already) or with exceptions: "...excepto X" (except X). Refers to a group of people leaving a place.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, se han ido todos.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they’d all left.

meaning: “will take care of” / “will be responsible for”.
additional_notes: Future tense of "hacerse cargo de". Used to say someone (often a person or an institution like "el Estado") will assume responsibility for someone or something, handle a task, or cover what needs to be done. It’s followed by "de" + a noun or pronoun: "se hará cargo de él", "se hará cargo de todo".
target_language_example: Yo me haré cargo de la reserva.
native_language_example: I’ll take care of the reservation.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb hacerse (preterite: me/te/se hizo, nos hicimos, etc.). Common uses: (1) hacerse + noun/adjective = “to become” (Se hizo cristiano. = He became Christian. / Se hizo amigo de… = He became friends with…). (2) hacerse cargo de = “to take charge of / take responsibility for” (Se hizo cargo del negocio…). (3) hacerse + a task/food = “to make/do for oneself” (Se hizo la cena = He made himself dinner).
target_language_example: Después del accidente, se hizo cargo de todo en la casa.
native_language_example: After the accident, he took charge of everything at home.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **hacerse daño** (“to hurt oneself / to get hurt”). **Se** is reflexive and shows the person is the one who got hurt. Often followed by **en + body part**: *se hizo daño en la rodilla* (“hurt his/her knee”). In other tenses you’ll also hear: *me hice daño* (I got hurt), *se hace daño* (he/she gets hurt), *se ha hecho daño* (has gotten hurt).
target_language_example: Me hice daño en la muñeca jugando al fútbol.
native_language_example: I hurt my wrist playing soccer.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “hacerse + adjective” = “to become + adjective.” “Se hizo” is the preterite (completed change in the past). Often followed by “por” (because of: “se hizo famoso por la novela”) or “en” (on/in a place or platform: “se hizo famoso en TikTok”).
target_language_example: Se hizo famoso por sus videos de cocina.
native_language_example: He became famous because of his cooking videos.

meaning: “(it/he/she) sank” or “went down” (ended up under the water/level).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb "hundirse". Used for things that sink in water (un barco se hundió) and also figuratively/visually for something going down below a line or cover, like the sun dipping below the horizon or clouds. Often followed by "en" or "bajo" (se hundió en el mar / se hundió bajo el horizonte).
target_language_example: El barco se hundió en pocos minutos.
native_language_example: The boat sank in a few minutes.

meaning: “(it/he/she) sank all the way to the bottom.”
additional_notes: “Se hundió” is the past tense (preterite) of “hundirse” = to sink. “Hasta el fondo” means “to the bottom / all the way down.” Used for boats and objects in water, and can also describe a person sinking (for example, if they fall into deep water).
target_language_example: La piedra cayó al agua y se hundió hasta el fondo.
native_language_example: The stone fell into the water and sank all the way to the bottom.

additional_notes: Form of **irse a + infinitive** in the **imperfect**: **(él/ella/usted) se iba a + infinitive**. Used to talk about an intention, plan, or something that was imminent **from a past point of view** (often in reported speech: *dijo que se iba a...*).
target_language_example: Pensé que se iba a caer.
native_language_example: I thought he/she was going to fall.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "inclinarse". With "ante" it usually means "to bow before" someone (a sign of respect). Without "ante," it can mean physically leaning or bending down to reach something: "se inclinó y...".
target_language_example: Se inclinó para atarse los zapatos.
native_language_example: He/She bent down to tie their shoes.

additional_notes: Used before a verb when two object pronouns appear together. **se** replaces **le/les** when followed by **lo/la/los/las** (e.g., *le + la* → *se la*). Meaning depends on the verb: *No se la cuentes* = “Don’t tell it to her/him”; *se la tiró* = “threw it at her/him.” In some expressions it can be vulgar or slang depending on the verb (e.g., *tirársela* can be sexual slang).
target_language_example: No se la des a nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t give it to anyone.

additional_notes: This is a combination of object pronouns used before a verb. “las” refers to feminine plural things (“them”), and “se” often replaces “le/les” or marks a reflexive/idiomatic construction. Common set phrases: “arreglárselas” = to manage/get by; “vérselas negras” = to have a hard time. It can also appear with verbs like “robar”: “que se las roben” = “that they steal them (from her/them)”.
target_language_example: No sé cómo se las arreglamos sin coche.
native_language_example: I don’t know how we managed without a car.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb lastimarse (“to get hurt”). Used when someone is injured, often in accidents or falls. Common patterns: “Se lastimó + body part” (Se lastimó la rodilla = He hurt his knee) or “Se lastimó + gerund” to say how it happened (Se lastimó jugando… = He got hurt playing…).
target_language_example: Mi hermano se lastimó el brazo en el gimnasio.
native_language_example: My brother hurt his arm at the gym.

meaning: "to/for him/her" in a "se" construction (often: something happens to them / they can be seen as…).
additional_notes:
This is the combination of two pronouns: **se** + **le**. It’s very common in Spanish when the person is not the direct “doer” of the action.

Common uses:
- **Accidental / unintentional events**: *Se le cayeron los dientes* = “His/Her teeth fell out (on him/her).”
- **Something happening to someone (often with time/feelings)**: *Se le está haciendo tarde* = “It’s getting late for him/her.”
- **Perception / how someone looks**: *Se le ve feliz* = “He/She looks happy” (literally, “he/she is seen happy”).

**le** can refer to **him, her, or you (formal)** depending on context.
target_language_example: Se le nota cansado hoy.
native_language_example: He looks tired today.

additional_notes: Uses the "accidental se" construction: **se** + **indirect object pronoun** (me/te/le/nos/les) + **cayó** (preterite of *caer*, "to fall"). It often emphasizes that it happened by accident, not on purpose. You can add the thing that fell: *Se le cayó la copa* ("She dropped the glass"), and optionally where it fell: *... al suelo / al piso* ("... onto the ground/floor").
target_language_example: Se me cayó el teléfono en el agua.
native_language_example: I dropped my phone in the water.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as the pattern **A [person] se le da bien/mal + infinitive/noun** to talk about someone’s ability: *A Tom se le da bien prever el tiempo* (“Tom is good at predicting the weather”). It literally looks like “it gives itself to him,” so it’s not straightforward word-for-word in English. In other contexts, **se le da** can also be the passive/impersonal of **dar** meaning **“is given to him/her”** (e.g., an award) or **“that’s how you give him/her…”** (*Así se le da una lección…*).
target_language_example: A mí se me da bien aprender idiomas.
native_language_example: I’m good at learning languages.

meaning: "(Someone) is good at (something)" / "(Something) comes easily to (someone)."
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les): se me da bien, se te da bien, se le da bien, etc. It usually appears with the person introduced by "a" (A Tom se le da bien...) and an activity (often an infinitive like "cantar" or a subject like "el francés"). Negative: "no se le da bien".
target_language_example: A mí se me da bien cocinar, pero a mi hermana no se le da bien.
native_language_example: I’m good at cooking, but my sister isn’t.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to say someone is good at an activity or skill: a mí se me da muy bien…, a ti se te da…, a él/ella se le da…, a nosotros/as se nos da…, a ellos/ellas se les da…. Commonly followed by an infinitive (se le da muy bien jugar / imitar / tocar) or a noun (se le da muy bien el ajedrez).
target_language_example: A mí se me da muy bien cocinar.
native_language_example: I’m very good at cooking.

meaning: "it is called" / "you call it" (that’s what it’s named).
additional_notes: Used to say what something/someone is called (its name or label). Often appears with **A + noun/pronoun + se le llama + name**: *A esto se le llama plato* (“This is called a plate”). **Le** refers to the thing/person being named (can change: *se les llama* for plural). Similar to *se llama*, but this pattern often includes the **A...** phrase to highlight what you’re talking about.
target_language_example: A una persona que no come carne se le llama vegetariana.
native_language_example: A person who doesn’t eat meat is called a vegetarian.

additional_notes: Used with the verb olvidarse in a common Spanish pattern: "A + person + se + indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) + olvidó + thing." It emphasizes that the forgetting happened to someone (not as a deliberate action). The forgotten thing can be a noun ("se le olvidó la conferencia") or an infinitive ("se le olvidó pagar"). You can change the pronoun and verb: "se me olvidó" (I forgot), "se te olvidó" (you forgot), "se nos olvidó" (we forgot), "se les olvidó" (they/you all forgot).
target_language_example: A mí se me olvidó tu nombre.
native_language_example: I forgot your name.

additional_notes: This is a common clitic combination: **se** + **les**. It often appears with an explicit group introduced by **a** (e.g., *A los estudiantes se les prohíbe...*) and is used in: (1) **impersonal/passive-style** sentences to say what is done/said/forbidden/ordered **to them** (*se les prohíbe / se les ordenó*), and (2) **accidental/unplanned events** with *se* (*Se les cayó el teléfono* = “Their phone fell / They dropped their phone”). Placement: before a conjugated verb (*se les prohíbe*) or attached to an infinitive/gerund/command (*prohibirseles*, *al prohibírseles*, etc.).
target_language_example: A mis amigos se les olvidó la dirección.
native_language_example: My friends forgot the address. (The address slipped their minds.)

meaning: (he/she/it) gets up; stands up. Also: is adjourned (a meeting/session).
additional_notes: From the verb "levantarse" (reflexive). Most common for waking up/getting out of bed: "Se levanta a las seis" (He/She gets up at six). It can also mean to stand up from a chair: "se levanta y le dice..." (he stands up and says...). In formal contexts, "Se levanta la sesión" means "The session/meeting is adjourned" (it ends for now).
target_language_example: Me levanto temprano, pero mi hermana se levanta tarde.
native_language_example: I get up early, but my sister gets up late.

additional_notes: From the verb "levantarse" (to get up) and the adverb "temprano" (early). "Se" is a reflexive pronoun used with "levantarse". The subject is often mentioned before it (e.g., "Mi mamá se levanta temprano"), but it can also be omitted when it’s clear from context ("Se levanta temprano..."). You can add time expressions like "por la mañana" (in the morning).
target_language_example: Mi hermana se levanta temprano para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: My sister gets up early to go to work.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "levantarse" (to get up / to stand up). Use it for a completed action: getting out of bed ("Se levantó temprano") or rising from a seat/position ("Se levantó de la silla"). Often followed by "de" to say what you stood up from, or "para" + infinitive to say the purpose ("Se levantó para..."), and it can be used without a subject when it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Me oíste entrar y te levantaste enseguida.
native_language_example: You heard me come in and you got up right away.

additional_notes: Used to give a name or label. With things/ideas, it means “it’s called …” (Se llama libertad…). With people, it means “his/her name is …” (Él se llama…). Often followed directly by the name: Se llama Ana. Can also appear in expressions like “lo que se llama …” = “what you call …”.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se llama esta calle?
native_language_example: What is this street called?

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "llamarse" (to be named). Used to ask or say what someone/something’s name was in the past (or at an unspecified time): "¿Cómo se llamaba?" = "What was their name?"/"What were they called?" Commonly refers to people, pets, or things. For plural: "se llamaban".
target_language_example: No recuerdo cómo se llamaba tu profesor.
native_language_example: I don’t remember what your teacher’s name was.

additional_notes: Used with "llevarse" (reflexive) + "bien" + "con" + person/pronoun to say someone has a good relationship with someone else. Conjugate "llevarse" to match the subject: me llevo bien con…, te llevas bien con…, se lleva bien con…, nos llevamos bien con…, se llevan bien con…. Often used with "bien" for emphasis; you can also say "se lleva mal con" = "doesn’t get along with."
target_language_example: ¿Te llevas bien con tus compañeros de trabajo?
native_language_example: Do you get along with your coworkers?

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of llevarse. Often means taking something away from a place: “Alguien se llevó los archivos” = “Someone took the files.” With people (llevarse a + person) it means “to take someone away” (could be simply escorting, or could imply kidnapping depending on context). It can also be used for physical movements like bringing something to a body part: “se llevó el vaso a los labios” = “he brought the glass to his lips.”
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, se llevó mi cuaderno por error.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he took my notebook by mistake.

meaning: 'to him/her/you/them it' (indirect + direct object pronouns together).
additional_notes: Used when an indirect object pronoun (le/les = to him/her/you/them) comes before a direct object pronoun (lo = it/him). Spanish changes le/les to se in this combination: le + lo → se lo, les + lo → se lo. It usually goes before the conjugated verb (Se lo dije) or attached to an infinitive/gerund/affirmative command (Voy a decírselo / Estoy diciéndoselo / Díselo). Meaning depends on context: lo can mean “it” or “him” (masculine).
target_language_example: Se lo doy mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll give it to him/her/them tomorrow.

additional_notes: A polite way to thank someone for something. Literally it’s like “I thank it to you”: **se** = “to you/him/her/them” (often formal “to you”), **lo** = “it/that,” **agradezco** = “I thank/appreciate.” You can add emphasis with **mucho**, **de verdad**, **realmente**.
target_language_example: Se lo agradezco mucho por su ayuda.
native_language_example: I really appreciate your help.

meaning: “I owe it to …” (I have … thanks to …).
additional_notes: Used to give credit to someone for a result, success, or who you are today. The pronouns can change depending on what is owed: se lo debo a él/ella/usted; te lo debo a ti; se la debo a mi madre (la = “the favor/debt” if feminine). Often used in phrases like “Todo se lo debo a…” or “Lo que soy hoy se lo debo a…”.
target_language_example: Este logro se lo debo a mis profesores.
native_language_example: I owe this achievement to my teachers.

additional_notes:
Past tense of decir (“to tell/say”): dije = “I told/I said.”

Pronouns: lo = “it/that” (the thing you told). se here replaces le (“to him/to her/to you (formal)”) when it comes before lo (you don’t say *le lo dije*; you say se lo dije).

You can add who you told: Se lo dije a ella / a él / a usted.
target_language_example: Se lo dije a mi jefe ayer.
native_language_example: I told it to my boss yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of decir: “dije” = “I said/told.” The pronouns se lo mean “to him/to her/to you (formal)/to them” + “it,” and a introduces the person you told. Often the “it” is understood from context, so English may just say “I told him/her.” (se replaces le/les before lo/la/los/las: le + lo → se lo).
target_language_example: Se lo dije a mi hermano ayer.
native_language_example: I told my brother yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you will pass information along. "se" = to him/her/you (usted)/them, and "lo" = it/that. Often said by itself as a quick response meaning “Okay, I’ll let them know.” You can add who you won’t tell: "No se lo diré a nadie" (I won’t tell anyone).
target_language_example: No se preocupe, se lo diré mañana.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll tell him/her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you will tell someone something later. It’s built from pronouns: se = to him/her/you (formal)/them; lo = it; diré = I will say/tell; a = to + the person (Se lo diré a mamá. = I’ll tell her it / I’ll tell it to her). The pronouns can change depending on who you’re telling (e.g., Se la diré a…, Se lo diré a…).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: se lo diré a tu padre esta noche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll tell your father tonight.

additional_notes: Present perfect of decir (“to say/tell”) with two object pronouns. **se** = “to him/to her/to you (formal)” (it often replaces *le/les* before *lo*), and **lo** = “it/that.” Common in complaints or emphasis with phrases like *mil veces* (“a thousand times”).
target_language_example: Se lo he dicho, pero no me escucha.
native_language_example: I’ve told him/her, but he/she doesn’t listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone continued not speaking for a period of time. It’s the past tense (preterite) of "mantenerse" + "en silencio". You can change it by person: "me mantuve" (I stayed silent), "te mantuviste" (you stayed silent), "nos mantuvimos" (we stayed silent).
target_language_example: Durante la reunión, me mantuve en silencio.
native_language_example: During the meeting, I stayed silent.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "marcharse" = "to leave" (often implying going away from a place). Commonly used with "de" (se marchó de la playa = left the beach). You can add how/when: "se marchó de inmediato" (left immediately), "se marchó en avión" (left by plane).
target_language_example: Cuando terminó la reunión, se marchó sin decir nada.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he/she left without saying anything.

meaning: "(it) happened to me" / "(it) got (done) to me" (often for unplanned or accidental things).
additional_notes: Very common structure with an indirect object pronoun (me) plus "se" for accidental/unintended events or changes you experience: "Se me olvidó" (I forgot), "Se me atascó" (it got stuck on me), "Se me pasó" (it slipped my mind / I missed it), "Se me aceleró" (it sped up on me), "Se me pegó" (I picked up [a habit/language] unintentionally), "Se me quitó" (it went away for me). The thing that happens is usually the grammatical subject: "Se me atascó la puerta" = 'The door got stuck (on me)'.
target_language_example: Se me olvidaron las llaves en casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys at home.

meaning: “(something) has happened to me” (often accidental or involuntary).
additional_notes: Used with the “accidental se” to talk about things that happen to you without you intending them. Structure: se + me (to me) + ha + past participle. Common with bodily sensations or mishaps: Se me ha dormido el brazo (My arm fell asleep), Se me ha metido algo en el ojo (Something got in my eye), Se me ha parado el reloj (My watch stopped).
target_language_example: Se me ha olvidado tu nombre.
native_language_example: I forgot your name. (Literally: Your name got forgotten by me.)

meaning: “it occurs to me / I think of (an idea).”
additional_notes: Used when an idea or thought comes to you (often suddenly). Common with algo/nada/una idea: “Se me ocurre algo mejor” (I can think of something better), “No se me ocurre nada” (Nothing comes to mind). Structure: (No) se + indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) + ocurre.
target_language_example: ¿Se te ocurre alguna idea para el regalo?
native_language_example: Can you think of any idea for the gift?

meaning: "It occurred to me" / "I thought of it" (suddenly).
additional_notes: Used when an idea or thought comes to you, often unexpectedly. It’s the past tense (preterite) of "ocurrírsele a alguien" (for something to occur to someone). Structure: "Se + (indirect object pronoun) + ocurrió" → "Se me ocurrió" (to me), "se te ocurrió" (to you), "se le ocurrió" (to him/her). You can add what occurred: "Se me ocurrió una idea" (an idea occurred to me) or "Se me ocurrió que..." (It occurred to me that...).
target_language_example: De repente se me ocurrió llamarte para avisarte.
native_language_example: Suddenly it occurred to me to call you to let you know.

se me ocurrió una buena idea

target_language_multi_word_term: se me ocurrió una buena idea
meaning: “I had a good idea” / “A good idea occurred to me.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "ocurrirse" (to occur to someone). The structure is: "Se + indirect object pronoun (me/te/le/nos/les) + ocurrió + idea". It often refers to an idea that came to you suddenly ("Then it hit me..."). In the past, you’ll usually hear "se me ocurrió" (preterite).
target_language_example: De repente se me ocurrió una buena idea para el proyecto.
native_language_example: Suddenly I had a good idea for the project.

additional_notes: Common way to say you forgot something in Spanish. It uses an indirect-object pronoun (me = to me) and a thing/event as the subject: Se me olvidó tu nombre. / Se me olvidaron las llaves (plural). Often followed by an infinitive to say you forgot to do something: Se me olvidó llamarte.
target_language_example: Lo siento, se me olvidó llamarte ayer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to call you yesterday.

additional_notes: From the verb "merecer" (to deserve), used with a reflexive pronoun: "se merece" = "deserves" (3rd person singular) or formal "you deserve." It’s followed by a noun or phrase: "se merece un trago" (deserves a drink), "no se merece esto" (doesn’t deserve this). Often used to judge whether someone should receive something good (gratitude, a reward) or bad (a punishment).
target_language_example: Después de tanto trabajo, se merece unas vacaciones.
native_language_example: After so much work, he/she deserves a vacation.

meaning: “he/she got into/entered,” “got involved in,” or “put (it) in.”
additional_notes: Preterite (past) of **meterse**/**meter**. With **en/a + place**, it often means **entered/broke into**: *se metió en mi apartamento / se metió a la tienda*. With **en + activity/problem**, it can mean **got involved/got into**: *se metió en una lucha*. With a direct object, it can mean **put something inside**: *se metió el pañuelo en el bolsillo* (“he put the handkerchief in his pocket”).
target_language_example: Cuando oyó el ruido, se metió rápidamente en su habitación.
native_language_example: When he heard the noise, he quickly went into his room.

meaning: he/she got into; he/she got involved in.
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "meterse en". Often means entering a place/vehicle (“got into the car/apartment”), but it can also mean getting involved in something, often trouble or a situation (“got into trouble/a fight”). Typically followed by a noun (en el coche, en problemas).
target_language_example: Se metió en problemas por llegar tarde.
native_language_example: He got into trouble for arriving late.

se miraron el uno al otro

target_language_multi_word_term: se miraron el uno al otro
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb mirar(se) (“to look (at)”) in the past tense (ellos/ellas: se miraron). “El uno al otro” means “each other” (two people). You’ll also see “la una a la otra” (two women) and plural forms for groups: “los unos a los otros / las unas a las otras.”
target_language_example: Cuando escucharon el ruido, se miraron el uno al otro sin decir nada.
native_language_example: When they heard the noise, they looked at each other without saying anything.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "mudarse": "se mudó" = he/she moved (house/apartment). Use "a" before the destination (city/country/neighborhood). You can change the person: "me mudé a" (I moved to), "nos mudamos a" (we moved to), "se mudaron a" (they moved to).
target_language_example: Mi hermano se mudó a Barcelona el año pasado.
native_language_example: My brother moved to Barcelona last year.

additional_notes: From the verb *moverse* (to move). Often describes something that is moving by itself or appears to move (e.g., the ground, a line of people). Used with things and animals; with people it can mean “he/she moves” (as in changing position, going, or shifting).
target_language_example: La puerta se mueve con el viento.
native_language_example: The door moves with the wind.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with no specific subject: it means that something is required. The thing needed usually comes after (Se necesita dinero.) or before with “lo que” (Es lo que se necesita. / Tiene lo que se necesita…). You can also add an indirect object for “who needs it”: Se me necesita (“I’m needed”), Se te necesita (“You’re needed”).
target_language_example: Para entrar, se necesita una identificación.
native_language_example: To get in, you need an ID.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the verb phrase “negarse a” = “to refuse to” + infinitive. It’s used to say someone did not agree to do something (se negó a firmar, se negó a hablar, etc.). Other forms: me negué a (I refused), te negaste a (you refused), nos negamos a (we refused), se negaron a (they refused).
target_language_example: Ella se negó a responder las preguntas.
native_language_example: She refused to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Past tense of "negarse a" + infinitive: "(someone) refused to (do something)." Often implies a firm decision or unwillingness. You can change the pronoun and verb to match the subject: "me negué a aceptar" (I refused), "nos negamos a aceptar" (we refused).
target_language_example: Me negué a aceptar el dinero porque no era mío.
native_language_example: I refused to accept the money because it wasn't mine.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive form of negar (negarse a) + infinitive: me/te/se/nos/os/se niego(a)s(e) a + infinitive. It expresses a firm refusal, often against someone’s request or expectation.
target_language_example: Me niego a esperar más.
native_language_example: I refuse to wait any longer.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with "se" + "notar" (to notice). It’s used to point out something that’s obvious from evidence (someone’s behavior, appearance, tone of voice, etc.). It’s followed by a clause with "que": "Se nota que + [verb]".
target_language_example: Se nota que estás cansado hoy.
native_language_example: You can tell you’re tired today.

additional_notes: Preterite (past) form of "olvidarse de" (to forget). Use it with an infinitive to mean "forgot to do (something)": "Se olvidó de traer...". Use it with a noun/pronoun to mean "forgot about (someone/something)": "Se olvidó de todos sus amigos." You can add who by using "se" + indirect object pronoun: "Se me olvidó..." (I forgot / It slipped my mind), "Se le olvidó..." (he/she forgot).
target_language_example: Se olvidó de llamar a su mamá.
native_language_example: He/She forgot to call his/her mom.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "parecerse" (to resemble). It’s usually followed by "a": "Se parece a su madre" = "He/She looks like his/her mother." You can also use it to compare things: "Tu letra se parece a la de tu padre" = "Your handwriting looks like your father's."
target_language_example: Mi perro se parece a un lobo.
native_language_example: My dog looks like a wolf.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) + parecer + a to say someone or something resembles another person/thing: “Se parece a ti” = “(He/She) looks like you.” You can also specify what kind of resemblance (appearance, handwriting, style, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu casa se parece a la mía.
native_language_example: Your house looks like mine.

meaning: She/He looks like her/his mother; resembles her/his mother.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "parecerse a" = "to look like / resemble" (it takes the reflexive pronoun: me/te/se/ nos/os/se). You can change the person: "Me parezco a mi madre" (I look like my mother), "Se parece a su padre" (He/She looks like his/her father). "A su madre" can also mean "to your mother" or "to their mother" depending on context; to be more specific, use "a su mamá" (mom), "a su madre" (mother, a bit more formal), or "a la mamá de María" (María’s mom).
target_language_example: Dicen que se parece mucho a su madre.
native_language_example: They say she looks a lot like her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone resembles their father (in appearance or sometimes in behavior). The verb is "parecerse a" = "to look like / resemble" and it usually takes an indirect object pronoun: me/te/se/nos/os/se (e.g., "Me parezco a mi madre" = "I look like my mother"). "Su" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: No se parece a su padre; se parece a su madre.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t look like his/her father; he/she looks like his/her mother.
