additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has a similar appearance (and sometimes similar traits) to the person you’re talking to. It comes from the verb phrase “parecerse a” = “to look like / to resemble.” The “se” is required, and “a ti” can change (a mí, a él/ella, a nosotros, etc.).
target_language_example: Tu hija se parece a ti.
native_language_example: Your daughter looks like you.

meaning: looks a lot like; resembles (someone/something) a lot.
additional_notes: Used with a subject + "se parece mucho a" + person/thing. It means strong physical resemblance or that something is very similar in appearance/character. The "a" is required before the person/thing you’re comparing to (a Tom, a mí, a una biblioteca).
target_language_example: Este edificio se parece mucho a un castillo.
native_language_example: This building looks a lot like a castle.

se parece mucho a su madre

target_language_multi_word_term: se parece mucho a su madre
meaning: "(He/She) looks a lot like his/her mother."
additional_notes: "Parecerse a" means "to look like / resemble" someone. It’s reflexive ("se") and uses "a" before the person: "se parece a su madre". "Mucho" intensifies it: "a lot." "Su" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context; you can also specify: "a su mamá" (more casual) or "a su madre" (more formal).
target_language_example: Mi hermano se parece mucho a mi madre.
native_language_example: My brother looks a lot like my mother.

meaning: “they look very similar / they are very alike.”
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb parecerse (“to resemble”). Add “a + person/thing” to say who/what they resemble: “Se parecen mucho a su madre.” You can also use it without “a…” when it’s clear what you mean: “Es que se parecen mucho.”
target_language_example: Mis dos hermanas se parecen mucho, pero tienen personalidades distintas.
native_language_example: My two sisters look very similar, but they have different personalities.

meaning: "(he/she) stood up" or "(he/she) stopped (and stood still)."
additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **pararse**. Often means someone **stands up** or **stands/stays in a certain position**: *Se paró apartado de nosotros* = “He stood apart from us.” With **para + infinitive**, it can mean the person **stopped in order to do something**: *Se paró para fumar* = “He stopped to smoke.” (Related: **parar** = “to stop (something)” vs. **pararse** = “to stop/stand up (oneself)”.)
target_language_example: Se paró frente a la puerta y esperó.
native_language_example: He stood in front of the door and waited.

additional_notes: From ponerse (often reflexive). Common uses: (1) "se pone + adjective" = "it gets/becomes" (Esto se pone interesante. / Se pone mejor/peor.). (2) "se pone a + infinitive" = "starts to" (Se pone a llorar.). (3) Non-reflexive poner: "se pone + noun" = "puts on" clothing (Se pone el uniforme.). (4) "se pone el sol" = "the sun sets" (fixed expression).
target_language_example: Al final de la película, se pone muy interesante.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, it gets really interesting.

additional_notes: From **ponerse** (reflexive). Commonly used for changes of state or appearance: **se ponen amarillas/negras** = “they turn yellow/black”; **se ponen difíciles** = “things get difficult.” With **se ponen a + infinitive**, it means “they start to…”: **se ponen a reír** = “they start laughing.”
target_language_example: Cuando están nerviosos, se ponen a hablar muy rápido.
native_language_example: When they’re nervous, they start talking very fast.

additional_notes: From the verb "preguntarse" (to wonder/ask oneself). "Se preguntaba" is the imperfect tense, used for an ongoing or repeated thought in the past. It’s often followed by a question word (qué, cuánto, por qué, dónde, qué tan...) or by "si" meaning "whether/if."
target_language_example: Me preguntaba si ibas a venir.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you were going to come.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb preocuparse (yo me preocupo, tú te preocupas, él/ella se preocupa) + por + noun/pronoun/infinitive. It can mean being anxious/worried about something (often with a negative feeling) or caring/being concerned for someone’s well-being. Common: “No te preocupes por…” = “Don’t worry about…”.
target_language_example: No te preocupes por mí; voy a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me; I’m going to be fine.

meaning: (that you/he/she) worry; (in “no se preocupe”) don’t worry.
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb “preocuparse” (to worry). You’ll often see it in reassuring phrases like “No se preocupe” (formal, used with usted). It can also appear after “dejar que…”: “Deja que se preocupe” = “Let him/her worry.”
target_language_example: No se preocupe, todo va a salir bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is going to turn out fine.

additional_notes: Very common impersonal structure with "poder" meaning that something is possible or permitted in general (not saying who specifically can do it). Often followed by an infinitive: "Se puede ir" (You can go / It’s possible to go). With a past participle, it means something can be done: "se puede limpiar" (it can be cleaned). In context it can sound like permission (You may...) or possibility (It’s possible...).
target_language_example: Aquí no se puede fumar.
native_language_example: You can’t smoke here. / Smoking isn’t allowed here.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression with "se" meaning "it is possible to do" something (what matters is the action, not who does it). Often used with "lo que" ("what can be done") or to talk about possibilities in general: "Se puede hacer mucho" = "A lot can be done." In conversation it can also mean "We’ll see what’s possible": "Veré lo que se puede hacer."
target_language_example: Aquí se puede hacer todo en línea.
native_language_example: Here you can do everything online.

additional_notes: Impersonal structure with "se" + "poder" + infinitive. It means that going/leaving is possible or permitted in general (not tied to a specific person). Often used to give permission or state a rule: "Se puede ir" (You can go/You may leave) vs. "No se puede ir" (You can’t go/You may not leave). Can also be followed by a destination: "se puede ir al aeropuerto" (you can go to the airport).
target_language_example: Si ya terminaste, se puede ir.
native_language_example: If you’re already finished, you can leave.

additional_notes: Impersonal use of "se" with "poder" + infinitive to talk generally (not about a specific person): "Se puede ver..." = "You can see..." or "It’s possible to see...". Often followed by what can be seen ("se puede ver el Monte Fuji") and sometimes a condition ("con buen clima", "en un día despejado") or a way of seeing ("a simple vista" = "with the naked eye").
target_language_example: Desde este mirador, se puede ver toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: From this viewpoint, you can see the whole city.

additional_notes: Used with a plural verb to talk about what is possible in general, without saying who does it. It often translates as English passive (“can be bought/learned/heard”) or as a general “you can.” Example pattern: se pueden + infinitive (se pueden aprender idiomas) or se pueden + plural noun + past participle implied (se pueden comprar uvas = grapes can be bought). For singular, use “se puede.”
target_language_example: Aquí se pueden hacer fotos, pero sin flash.
native_language_example: You can take photos here, but without flash.

meaning: “they started/began” or “they stood up”; sometimes “were put/laid.”
additional_notes: This is the preterite (simple past) 3rd-person plural form of ponerse/poner with se. Common uses: (1) **se pusieron a + infinitive** = “they started to …” (Se pusieron a trabajar). (2) **se pusieron de pie** = “they stood up.” (3) In an impersonal/passive **se** construction, it can mean “were put/laid” (Se pusieron los cimientos = The foundations were laid).
target_language_example: Cuando sonó la alarma, se pusieron a correr.
native_language_example: When the alarm rang, they started running.

additional_notes: "Se puso" is the preterite (past) of "ponerse" (to get/become; to put on). It often describes a change of state: "El viento se puso más fuerte" (the wind got stronger), "Papá se puso bueno" (Dad got better). It’s also used for putting something on yourself (clothes/accessories): "Se puso los zapatos". With an impersonal "se" and a thing like "atención", it can mean "was given/paid": "Se puso poca atención..." = "Little attention was paid..."
target_language_example: Se puso nerviosa cuando escuchó la noticia.
native_language_example: She got nervous when she heard the news.

additional_notes:
Very common pattern: **ponerse a + infinitive** to show someone begins doing something, often suddenly or as a reaction. 
Examples: *se puso a correr* (started running), *se puso a llorar* (started crying). 
Sometimes **ponerse a + noun/adjective phrase** appears with set expressions like **ponerse a cubierto** = “to take cover” (not followed by an infinitive).
target_language_example: Al oír la noticia, se puso a llorar.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern "ponerse a + infinitive" to mean "to start/begin to do something," often suddenly or in reaction to something. "Se" is reflexive (ponerse). In the past tense you’ll also see: "me puse a..." (I started), "te pusiste a..." (you started), "nos pusimos a..." (we started).
target_language_example: Cuando escuchó la canción, se puso a llorar.
native_language_example: When he/she heard the song, he/she started to cry.

additional_notes: Uses the structure "ponerse a + infinitive" to mean "to begin to (do something)," often implying it started unexpectedly or all of a sudden. "Llover" is "to rain," so "se puso a llover" is a very common way to say that rain began.
target_language_example: Estábamos caminando y se puso a llover, así que buscamos refugio.
native_language_example: We were walking and it started to rain, so we looked for shelter.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ponerse (reflexive) to talk about putting on clothing or accessories: se puso su vestido / su sombrero / su cinturón. "Su" can mean his, her, your (formal), or their—context tells you which. The subject is the person who puts it on (e.g., María se puso su… = Maria put on her…).
target_language_example: Antes de salir, Luis se puso su chaqueta.
native_language_example: Before leaving, Luis put on his jacket.

additional_notes: **Quedarse** is a reflexive verb meaning “to stay” or “to remain.” Use it for staying somewhere or remaining in a state: *Se queda aquí* (“You stay here”), *Ella se queda* (“She stays”). With **con** (**se queda con + noun**), it means “to keep / end up with”: *El ganador se queda con el puesto* (“The winner gets/keeps the position”).
target_language_example: Me quedo en casa hoy.
native_language_example: I’m staying home today.

meaning: “they stayed / they remained,” or “they ended up” (with a result).
additional_notes:
Past tense (preterite) of "quedarse" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes": "they stayed/remained." Very common with:
- "se quedaron + adjective" (they ended up/turned): "se quedaron dormidos" (they fell asleep), "se quedaron abiertos" (were left open).
- "se quedaron sin + noun" (they were left without): "se quedaron sin trabajo" (lost their jobs), "se quedaron sin palabras" (were speechless).
- "se quedaron + time/place" (stayed): "se quedaron hasta el final" (stayed until the end).
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin dinero y tuvimos que volver a casa.
native_language_example: We ran out of money (we were left without money) and had to go back home.

additional_notes: Future tense (él/ella/usted) of quedarse. Used to say someone/something will stay in a place or remain in a state/condition (e.g., quedarse aquí = stay here; quedarse vacío = end up/become empty). Often translated as “will stay,” “will remain,” or sometimes “will end up.”
target_language_example: Si llueve, se quedará en casa.
native_language_example: If it rains, he/she will stay at home.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like deja que / permite que / para que, which often require the subjunctive. "Quedarse" means "to stay" or "to remain," and "se" marks it as reflexive (staying somewhere/remaining). "Se quede" can refer to él/ella/usted; for tú it’s "te quedes" and for yo it’s "me quede."
target_language_example: Deja que se quede un rato más.
native_language_example: Let him/her stay a little longer.

additional_notes: Preterite (past, completed action) of quedarse: se + quedó. Common patterns: quedarse con + noun = “to keep” (El solo se quedó con uno = He only kept one); quedarse pegado/trabado = “to get stuck / freeze” (often for computers/phones); quedarse quieto = “to stay still.”
target_language_example: Me quedé en casa todo el día.
native_language_example: I stayed at home all day.

meaning: he/she stayed silent; he/she stopped talking.
additional_notes: From quedarse (to stay/remain) + callado (quiet). It’s often used when someone becomes silent (sometimes suddenly) and remains that way for a moment or longer. You can add time phrases like “por un momento” (for a moment) or “esta vez” (this time).
target_language_example: Cuando le pregunté, se quedó callado y no respondió.
native_language_example: When I asked him, he stayed silent and didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "quedarse dormido": to fall asleep, often unexpectedly or while doing something else. Uses the reflexive "se". It can be followed by "con + noun/adjective" to describe the situation while falling asleep ("con la ventana abierta", "con la ropa puesta") or with a gerund to show what was happening as they fell asleep ("llorando"). Change the ending for gender/number: "se quedó dormida", "se quedaron dormidos/dormidas".
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido viendo una película.
native_language_example: I fell asleep while watching a movie.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **quedarse dormido/a** = “to fall asleep (often unintentionally).” It changes for the person and gender: **me quedé dormido/a** (I fell asleep), **se quedó dormido/a** (he/she fell asleep), **nos quedamos dormidos/as** (we fell asleep). Use **en** before the place or vehicle: **en clase**, **en el bus**, **en el tren**. Often implies it wasn’t planned and can lead to missing something (e.g., your stop).
target_language_example: Me quedé dormido en el metro y me pasé mi estación.
native_language_example: I fell asleep on the subway and missed my station.

additional_notes: From the verb **quedarse** (to stay/remain). **Se quedó en + lugar** = stayed somewhere (often longer than just “went/was”). You can also use it with a **state/situation**: **se quedó en silencio** = he/she fell/was left silent (remained silent). Commonly followed by a time phrase: **se quedó en X por/durante tres semanas**.
target_language_example: Después del concierto, Ana se quedó en el teatro por una hora.
native_language_example: After the concert, Ana stayed at the theater for an hour.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "quedarse" = "to stay/remain." "Se" is part of the verb (quedarse). Used to say someone did not go out or did not go somewhere and instead remained at home. You can change the subject: "me quedé" (I stayed), "te quedaste" (you stayed), "nos quedamos" (we stayed).
target_language_example: Hoy estoy cansado, así que me quedé en casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m tired, so I stayed at home.

meaning: ran out of; was left without.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive form of quedar (quedarse) + sin + noun to mean you end up with none left (often unexpectedly). Tense changes: me quedé sin, te quedaste sin, se quedó sin, nos quedamos sin, se quedaron sin. Common with supplies like gas, water, time, money, battery, etc.
target_language_example: Nos quedamos sin batería en el teléfono.
native_language_example: We ran out of battery on the phone.

additional_notes: From the verb quejarse (“to complain”). It’s reflexive, so it uses a reflexive pronoun: me quejo, te quejas, se queja, nos quejamos, se quejan. Common patterns: quejarse de + noun (“complain about something”): Se queja de todo. / quejarse con + person/institution (“complain to/with someone”): Se queja con el jefe.
target_language_example: Mi hermano siempre se queja del calor.
native_language_example: My brother always complains about the heat.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb quejarse = “to complain.” Common patterns: quejarse de + thing (“complain about”): Se quejó del ruido. Also quejarse con + person (“complain to/with” someone): Se quejó con el chef.
target_language_example: Se quejó de la comida, pero luego se la comió toda.
native_language_example: He/She complained about the food, but then ate it all.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "quemarse" (to get burned). Use it for accidents like food burning (El chorizo se quemó), a light bulb burning out (Se quemó la ampolleta), or a person getting burned (Tom se quemó). With a body part, it’s very common to say: "se quemó la mano / los dedos" (literally "burned himself the hand/fingers" = "burned his hand/fingers").
target_language_example: Me distraje y se me quemó la comida.
native_language_example: I got distracted and my food burned.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb quitarse. Commonly used for taking off clothing or accessories (boots, hat, socks, etc.). The thing removed is usually a direct object: Se quitó el sombrero / Se quitó las botas.
target_language_example: Después de llegar a casa, se quitó el abrigo.
native_language_example: After getting home, she took off her coat.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb "quitarse" (to take off, remove a piece of clothing). The "se" shows the action is done to oneself. Common pattern: "se quitó + [clothing]" (e.g., "se quitó los zapatos"). Note: Spanish "quitar" is not the same as English "to quit."
target_language_example: Cuando entró en casa, se quitó el abrigo.
native_language_example: When he came into the house, he took off his coat.

meaning: “(he/she) took off the …” or “(he/she) got rid of the …”.
additional_notes: Preterite (past) form of the reflexive verb “quitarse” + the feminine direct object article “la”. Most often used for removing clothing/accessories: “Se quitó la camiseta.” It can also mean getting rid of something unpleasant: “Se quitó la resaca durmiendo.” You normally follow it with a feminine noun (la camisa, la pulsera, la resaca). For a masculine noun, use “se quitó el …”.
target_language_example: Después de la playa, se quitó la ropa mojada.
native_language_example: After the beach, she took off her wet clothes.

meaning: he/she took off their clothes (got undressed).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb "quitarse" = "to take off (something you’re wearing)". The reflexive pronoun (se) shows the action is done to oneself. Often followed by what they did next: "...y se metió a la ducha" (and got in the shower). You can change the pronoun/person: "me quité" (I took off), "te quitaste" (you took off), "nos quitamos" (we took off).
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, se quitó la ropa y se puso el pijama.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, he/she took off their clothes and put on pajamas.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "quitarse" = "to take off (something you’re wearing)." Uses a reflexive pronoun (se) because the action is done to oneself. "Las gafas" means "glasses" (eyeglasses), and Spanish normally uses "the" where English uses "my/your" when it’s obvious from context.
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, se quitó las gafas.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, he/she took off their glasses.

meaning: “(he) took off the …” (a masculine plural item).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb quitarse (“to take off” something you’re wearing). In Spanish, you often use the definite article (los) instead of “his” when it’s clear whose item it is: Se quitó los guantes = “He took off his gloves.” The verb is in the preterite (completed past action) and typically refers to removing clothing/accessories like guantes, lentes, auriculares, zapatos, etc.
target_language_example: Se quitó los zapatos al llegar a casa.
native_language_example: He took off his shoes when he got home.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "quitarse" + clothing item: "se quitó" = "he/she took off". You can swap the item: "se quitó la chaqueta" (took off his/her jacket). With a name: "Tom se quitó los zapatos". To say "I took off my shoes": "Me quité los zapatos".
target_language_example: Cuando llegó a casa, se quitó los zapatos.
native_language_example: When he/she got home, he/she took off his/her shoes.

meaning: 'it refers to' / 'it means' / 'it is talking about'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate what something is about or who someone is talking about. It often follows a subject like eso/esto/él/ella or a general topic: "Esto se refiere a..." = "This refers to...". Can also be used when clarifying a person or thing: "¿Se refiere a mí?" = "Are you referring to me?"
target_language_example: Cuando dice "ellos", se refiere a los estudiantes.
native_language_example: When he says "they," he means the students.

additional_notes: From the verb "rehusarse (a)" = to refuse to do something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive ("se rehusó a pagar", "se rehusó a firmar"). You can use it to show a strong decision not to do something. Similar to "se negó a".
target_language_example: Ella se rehusó a contestar la pregunta.
native_language_example: She refused to answer the question.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of reflexive verb "retrasarse". Used for things (a train, a delivery) or people (someone arriving late). Often followed by a length of time ("diez minutos", "una hora") or a reason with "por / debido a / a causa de". For a schedule delay, "El tren se retrasó" = the train was delayed; for a person, "Se retrasó para la cita" = he/she was late for the appointment.
target_language_example: El vuelo se retrasó dos horas por el mal tiempo.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed two hours because of bad weather.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the pronominal verb "reírse de". Use "de" before the person/thing being laughed at: "Se rieron de él/ella" (They laughed at him/her). Depending on context it can mean simple laughter (e.g., at jokes) or mocking/teasing someone.
target_language_example: Se rieron de mí cuando me equivoqué.
native_language_example: They laughed at me when I made a mistake.

meaning: "they laughed at me" / "they made fun of me."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "reírse de" (to laugh at / make fun of). "Se rieron" is the simple past (preterite) for "they". You can change the person: "me reí de..." (I laughed at...), "se rió de mí" (he/she laughed at me), "nos reímos de..." (we laughed at...).
target_language_example: En la fiesta se rieron de mí por mi acento.
native_language_example: At the party they laughed at me because of my accent.

meaning: “they laughed at him” / “they made fun of him.”
additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of **reírse de** = “to laugh at / to make fun of.” **Se** shows it’s the reflexive verb *reírse* (not *reír*). **De él** means “at him” (literally “of him”); you can also say **de ella** (at her) or **de mí** (at me).
target_language_example: Se rieron de él porque se equivocó.
native_language_example: They laughed at him because he made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb reírse (“to laugh”). It’s the simple past (pretérito) form for él/ella/usted: se rió. You’ll often see it with extra info: se rió de + noun (“laughed at”), se rió al + infinitive (“laughed when/on seeing…”), se rió sin motivo (“laughed for no reason”). Note: it should have an accent: rió.
target_language_example: Se rió de mí, pero luego se disculpó.
native_language_example: He laughed at me, but then he apologized.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the verb phrase “romperse” = “to break.” The “se” is used for things that break by themselves or when the cause isn’t mentioned (similar to English “it broke” rather than “someone broke it”). Used for objects (El espejo se rompió.) and also injuries (Se rompió un hueso; se rompió tres costillas). For people, Spanish often uses an indirect-object pronoun: “Se me rompió el móvil” = “My phone broke (on me).”
target_language_example: Se rompió mi reloj, así que llegué tarde.
native_language_example: My watch broke, so I arrived late.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun (se) with romper to talk about an injury that happened to someone (often by accident). In the examples it’s in the past tense (pretérito): él/ella se rompió. You can add which leg with derecha/izquierda (la pierna derecha/izquierda) or add how it happened: se rompió la pierna esquiando (while skiing).
target_language_example: Me caí y me rompí la pierna.
native_language_example: I fell and broke my leg.

meaning: “is known” / “people know”; also “knows (it) well / by heart” (with saberse).
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) Impersonal/passive with “se” (no clear subject): “Poco se sabe…” = “Little is known…”.
2) With a specific person as the subject, from the verb “saberse” (pronominal): “Ella se sabe el camino” = “She knows the way well / has it learned (by heart).”
target_language_example: Se sabe que mañana lloverá.
native_language_example: It’s known (people know) that it will rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of the reflexive verb **secarse** (“to dry oneself; to dry up”). Used with a body part or object: **se secó las manos** (“he dried his hands”). With places/things, it often means “dried up”: **La laguna se secó** (“The lagoon dried up”). You can also say how: **Se secó con la toalla** (“He dried off with the towel”).
target_language_example: Después de nadar, se secó rápido con una toalla.
native_language_example: After swimming, he dried off quickly with a towel.

additional_notes: Preterite (completed past) of the reflexive verb **sentarse** for **ellos/ellas/ustedes**. Often used with **junto a / al lado de** (“next to”) to say where they sat. You can also use **sentarse a + infinitive** to mean “sit down to do something” (e.g., *se sentaron a cenar* = “they sat down to eat dinner”).
target_language_example: Después de caminar, se sentaron en un banco.
native_language_example: After walking, they sat down on a bench.

additional_notes: Past (imperfect) form of the reflexive verb sentirse (to feel). Use it for states/feelings that were ongoing or repeated in the past: Se sentía solo/a (He/She felt lonely), se sentía atrapado/a (felt trapped), se sentía mal (felt sick/bad), se sentía como… (felt like…). It can also appear in an impersonal/passive-style sentence: Se sentía la energía en el aire = “You could feel the energy in the air.”
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, se sentía muy cansada.
native_language_example: After the party, she felt very tired.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb "sentarse" (to sit down). "Se sentó" is 3rd-person singular: "he sat down / she sat down" (and also "you" formal: "usted sat down"). Often followed by where someone sat: "se sentó en la silla" (on the chair) or "se sentó al lado de..." (next to...).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó en el sofá y encendió la tele.
native_language_example: She sat down on the sofa and turned on the TV.

meaning: "(He/She) sat down next to me" / "sat by my side."
additional_notes: "Se sentó" is the simple past (pretérito) of *sentarse* (to sit down), used for a completed action. "A mi lado" means "next to me" or "beside me". Change "mi" to match the person: *a tu lado* (next to you), *a su lado* (next to him/her/you formal), *a nuestro lado* (next to us).
target_language_example: En el autobús, una señora se sentó a mi lado.
native_language_example: On the bus, a woman sat down next to me.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of sentarse: se sentó = “he/she sat down.” Use it to say where someone sat, followed by en + a place/surface (e.g., en la silla, en la cama, en una mesa). Often implies the action of sitting down (not just being seated).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó en el suelo para descansar.
native_language_example: She sat down on the floor to rest.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of reflexive verb sentarse (“to sit down”). The subject can be stated (El profesor…) or omitted (Se sentó…), and it often takes a description of how/while sitting: con los ojos cerrados (“with eyes closed”), con las piernas colgando (“with legs dangling”).
target_language_example: Después de caminar mucho, se sentó en la silla para descansar.
native_language_example: After walking a lot, he/she sat down on the chair to rest.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of the reflexive verb sentarse (“to sit down”). Use it to say someone sat down on or in something: en un/a + noun (e.g., en un taburete, en una silla). The subject is often understood from context (he/she/you).
target_language_example: Se sentó en un banco para esperar el autobús.
native_language_example: He/She sat down on a bench to wait for the bus.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "sentarse" + "junto a" (“next to”). Use it to say where someone sat. Often followed by a person or place: "Se sentó junto a mí" (next to me), "...junto a su hija" (next to his/her daughter).
target_language_example: Ella se sentó junto a mí en el cine.
native_language_example: She sat next to me at the movie theater.

additional_notes: Often used with adjectives to describe how someone feels: *se siente cómodo/a* (feels comfortable), *se siente mejor* (feels better), *se siente a gusto* (feels at ease). Note: in some contexts, *se siente* can instead come from *sentarse* (“to sit down”), especially after *antes de que...* (before he/she sits down).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se siente hoy?
native_language_example: How do you feel today?

additional_notes: Used with a person to talk about how someone feels physically or emotionally: "Él/Ella se siente bien" (He/She feels good). Used with "esto/eso" to describe a pleasant sensation: "Esto/Eso se siente bien" (This/That feels good). You can also use it as a question: "¿Se siente bien?" (Does it feel good? / Do you feel good?).
target_language_example: Después de descansar un poco, se siente bien.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, he feels good.

additional_notes: Used with sentirse (“to feel,” often about health or mood). The subject is third person (él/ella/usted). For other people: me siento mucho mejor (I feel much better), te sientes mucho mejor (you feel much better). Often used when someone is recovering from being sick or feeling down.
target_language_example: Después de descansar un poco, ella se siente mucho mejor.
native_language_example: After resting a little, she feels much better.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **sentirse + adjective** (“to feel” in terms of health/emotions). **Se** changes with the person: *me siento*, *te sientes*, *se siente*, *nos sentimos*, etc. It can mean being very sick (*Se siente muy mal*) or feeling guilty/upset, often with **sobre** = “about” (*Se siente muy mal sobre lo que pasó*).
target_language_example: Hoy no viene porque se siente muy mal.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t coming today because he/she feels very bad.

meaning: "they feel" / "you (all) feel" (in a physical or emotional state); also "they feel" when talking about how things feel.
additional_notes: Present tense of the verb "sentirse" (to feel). It’s used with adjectives (cómodos, bienvenidos, reales) and can describe people’s emotions/health or how something feels (e.g., caminos, pies). "Se" is part of the verb "sentirse" here (not the passive voice).
target_language_example: Después del viaje, se sienten cansados pero contentos.
native_language_example: After the trip, they feel tired but happy.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of sentirse (“to feel,” especially emotions or how you feel). It often comes before an adjective or phrase: se sintió triste/feliz/usado, se sintió en casa (“felt at home”). Changes with the subject: me sentí (I felt), te sentiste (you felt), nos sentimos (we felt), se sintieron (they felt).
target_language_example: Después del examen, me sentí aliviado.
native_language_example: After the exam, I felt relieved.

meaning: “(he/she) got on / got into the …” (entered a vehicle).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of *subirse a* (“to get on/into”). Used with vehicles and transport: *al tren* (on the train), *al avión* (on the plane), *al ascensor* (into the elevator), *al auto* (into the car). It’s reflexive (*se*), and *al* = *a* + *el*. For “I got on,” use *me subí al…*.
target_language_example: Ella se subió al autobús y se sentó atrás.
native_language_example: She got on the bus and sat in the back.

additional_notes: This is the preterite (completed past) form of the reflexive verb suicidarse. It uses a reflexive pronoun (se) and changes by person: me suicidé (I), te suicidaste (you), se suicidó (he/she/you formal), nos suicidamos (we), se suicidaron (they). You can add details with phrases like a los treinta (at thirty) or tomando veneno (by taking poison).
target_language_example: Dicen que se suicidó en 2010.
native_language_example: They say he/she committed suicide in 2010.

additional_notes: Used to say what is expected, planned, or assumed to be true—often with some doubt, uncertainty, or even mild criticism/irony. Common patterns: “Se supone que + verb” (supposedly…) and “(Person) se supone que + debe/tiene que + infinitive” (is supposed to…).
target_language_example: Se supone que la reunión empieza a las ocho, ¿no?
native_language_example: The meeting is supposed to start at eight, right?

additional_notes: Used to say what was expected, planned, or believed to happen, often implying it didn’t happen or that reality didn’t match the plan. Common with the imperfect tense (se suponía) + que + verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., ayudara, estuviera, hiciera) in more formal/standard Spanish, though many speakers also use the imperfect indicative in everyday speech (se suponía que iba a…).
target_language_example: Se suponía que íbamos a salir a las ocho, pero se hizo tarde.
native_language_example: We were supposed to leave at eight, but it got late.

meaning: "(it) occurs to you" / in warnings: "don’t you dare" or "don’t even think about it."
additional_notes: From the verb "ocurrírsele a alguien" = "to occur to someone" (an idea comes to you). With "lo que...": "Lo que se te ocurra" = "whatever comes to mind." Very commonly used with negation as a strong warning: "No se te ocurra (hacer algo)" or "Ni se te ocurra" = "Don’t even think about (doing something)." Uses the (present) subjunctive because it’s expressing a command/warning.
target_language_example: Ni se te ocurra tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t even think about touching that.

additional_notes: Used to comment on how someone looks (appearance, mood, or how clothes suit them). Literally “it is seen on you,” often followed by an adjective: “Se te ve bien/muy bien” (You look good), “Se te ve desorientado” (You look confused). With clothing: “Ese vestido se te ve bien” (That dress looks good on you).
target_language_example: Con ese corte de pelo nuevo, se te ve genial.
native_language_example: With that new haircut, you look great.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb tomar(se) to talk about consuming a drink. In Spanish, tomar is often used for “to drink” (especially in Latin America), even though it literally means “to take,” so you’ll usually translate it as “had” or “drank” in English. The reflexive pronoun (se) matches the subject: me tomé (I had), te tomaste (you had), se tomó (he/she had).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, se tomó una taza de chocolate caliente.
native_language_example: After dinner, he/she had a cup of hot chocolate.

meaning: “(He/She) ran into” / “came across” (someone or something, often by chance).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the reflexive verb phrase “toparse con.” It’s used for unexpected or accidental encounters—either meeting a person by chance (“ran into Jack”) or encountering something (even dangerous) (“came across a wolf”). Commonly followed by a person/thing: “se topó con + noun/person.”
target_language_example: Ayer me topé con mi profesora en el metro.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into my teacher on the subway.

meaning: "it’s about…" / "it’s a matter of…" (usually: "se trata de").
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **se trata de + noun/infinitive** to explain what something is about: *Se trata de un error* (“It’s a mistake”) or *Se trata de ayudar* (“It’s about helping”). Often appears with **no** explicit subject (impersonal). You’ll also see **No se trata de… sino de…** (“It’s not about… but about…”).
target_language_example: Se trata de encontrar una solución rápida.
native_language_example: It’s about finding a quick solution.

meaning: 'it's about…' / 'it's a matter of…'; also 'it's about (someone)' (= it concerns/it’s about).
additional_notes: Very common in explanations. Use it to say what the main point is: "Se trata de + infinitive" (Se trata de hacer lo correcto = It’s about doing the right thing). With a person/thing, it often means "it’s about/concerning": "Se trata de mi esposa" (It’s about my wife). Not used to identify someone directly (for that, use "Se trata de…" only in the sense of "this is about…", while "Se trata de Juan" is less like "This is Juan" and more like "This concerns Juan").
target_language_example: No se trata de ganar; se trata de aprender.
native_language_example: It’s not about winning; it’s about learning.

meaning: "It’s about the…" / "It’s a matter of the…"
additional_notes: Used with the impersonal verb phrase "tratarse de" to introduce the topic or identify what something is. It often answers “What is this about?” or “What is it?” You’ll also see other forms like "se trata del" (masculine), "se trata de" (before a verb or general idea), and "se trata de un/una" (a/an).
target_language_example: No se trata de la cantidad, sino de la calidad.
native_language_example: It’s not about quantity, but about quality.

meaning: "it’s about you" / "it’s about you (the issue involves you)".
additional_notes: From the expression "(no) se trata de..." meaning "it’s (not) about..." or "it’s (not) a matter of...". Common for clarifying what the real focus is: "No se trata de ti" = "It’s not about you." You can also extend it: "Se trata de ti y de mí" (It’s about you and me).
target_language_example: No se trata de ti; se trata de lo que hiciste.
native_language_example: It’s not about you; it’s about what you did.

meaning: "it’s a" / "it’s about a" (introducing what something is or what it’s about).
additional_notes: Common in more formal or neutral speech to identify something or clarify what the situation is: "Se trata de un Picasso" = “It’s a Picasso.” With things like books/movies, Spanish often uses "trata de" (“is about”), but you may also hear "se trata de" in the sense of “it’s about.” The verb is reflexive: "tratarse de" (to be a matter of / to be).
target_language_example: No es una broma; se trata de un problema serio.
native_language_example: It’s not a joke; it’s a serious problem.

additional_notes: Impersonal phrase from **tratarse de** used to identify or explain what something is, or what a story/situation is about. It’s very common in descriptions: **Se trata de + noun** (or **Se trata de + que...**). The article changes with the noun: **se trata de un/una/unos/unas**.
target_language_example: Se trata de una historia real.
native_language_example: It’s a true story.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about something that is going to happen soon or is planned: "se va a + infinitive". It’s the "ir a" (to be going to) structure, often with "se" because the verb is reflexive (e.g., "irse" = to leave: "se va a ir" = is going to leave). Can be used for scheduled events ("se va a celebrar") or intentions/plans ("se va a sentar").
target_language_example: Se va a acabar la clase en cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Class is going to end in five minutes.

meaning: “is going to get married” / “is going to marry” (soon, in the near future).
additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a planned future action. The verb is **casarse** (“to get married”), so it’s reflexive: **se va a casar** = “he/she is going to get married.” You can add **con + person** (“marry someone”): *se va a casar con un español*; and time expressions: *en junio*, *el próximo mes*.
target_language_example: Mi hermana se va a casar el año que viene.
native_language_example: My sister is going to get married next year.

meaning: "it’s going to get" / "it’s going to become"; also "(someone) is going to put on (clothes)".
additional_notes: From "irse a" (going to) + "poner". Very common with situations: "Esto se va a poner + adjective" = “This is going to get + adjective” (bueno, feo, difícil, interesante). With people and clothing, it means “to put on/wear”: "¿Qué se va a poner María?" = “What is María going to wear/put on?” In the examples, "se" often makes it impersonal (“it will get…”).
target_language_example: Si seguimos así, esto se va a poner difícil.
native_language_example: If we keep going like this, this is going to get difficult.

meaning: “(he/she/it) is going to stay / is going to end up (remaining).”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(él/ella/eso) se va a quedar** = “is going to stay/remain.” With **quedarse**, it can mean: staying in a place (**se va a quedar ahí**), something stopping or getting stuck (**se va a quedar parado el coche** = “the car will stall”), ending up in a situation (**se va a quedar solo** = “will end up alone”), or being left with something (**se va a quedar solo con recuerdos** = “will be left with only memories”).
target_language_example: Si no te apuras, te vas a quedar sin tiempo.
native_language_example: If you don’t hurry, you’re going to run out of time.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "irse" (to leave/go away). "Se va" is 3rd-person singular (él/ella/usted). It can mean leaving a place now or in the near future (often with a time expression): "se va mañana". It can also be used repeatedly for emphasis: "Se va, se va" (“He’s leaving, he’s leaving”). With another verb (often a gerund), it can show the manner of leaving: "se va caminando" (“he walks away / leaves on foot”).
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; se va a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late; he’s going home.

meaning: "they're going to" / "they're about to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: This is the verb phrase "irse a + infinitive" in the 3rd-person plural: "se" (reflexive) + "van" (they go/leave) + "a" + verb. It’s commonly used to talk about something that will happen soon or that someone intends to do: "Se van a enterar" = "They’re going to find out" (often as a warning/threat). In some contexts it can also imply leaving in order to do something ("They’re going to go off to...").
target_language_example: Se van a quedar aquí esta noche.
native_language_example: They’re going to stay here tonight.

additional_notes: From **irse a + infinitive** (here: *van a casar*) to talk about a future plan/near future. **Se casar** = “to get married” (reflexive *casarse*). Often used with a time phrase: *se van a casar en octubre* (“they’re getting married in October”).
target_language_example: Mis amigos se van a casar el año que viene.
native_language_example: My friends are going to get married next year.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "irse" (to leave/go away). Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so "se van" can mean "they leave" depending on context. Very common with a destination: "se van a casa" = "they go home". Also used for leaving an event or place: "termina el trabajo y se van" = "work ends and they leave."
target_language_example: Cuando termina la clase, se van.
native_language_example: When class ends, they leave.

meaning: 'he/she/it leaves' (subjunctive), often after 'que' or in commands like 'let him/her leave' / 'don’t let him/her leave'.
additional_notes: From the verb irse (to leave/go away). "Se vaya" is the present subjunctive (él/ella/usted), commonly used after expressions of desire/need/request (Quiero que…, Debo pedir que…) and in indirect commands with dejar (Deja que…). With "no", it means 'doesn’t leave' in that subjunctive context: Dile que no se vaya = 'Tell him not to leave.'
target_language_example: No quiero que se vaya todavía.
native_language_example: I don’t want him/her to leave yet.

additional_notes: From the verb irse (“to leave/go away”). Used with (ellos/ellas/ustedes) in the present subjunctive: after time expressions like "cuando" referring to the future ("cuando... se vayan" = "when they leave"), and in negative commands for ustedes: "No se vayan" = "Don’t leave".
target_language_example: No se vayan todavía; falta el postre.
native_language_example: Don’t leave yet; dessert is still coming.

meaning: 'you can see' / 'it is seen' / 'it looks' (it appears).
additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see), used with "se" in a few very common ways: (1) visibility: "apenas se ve" = "you can barely see it"; (2) impersonal/passive meaning: "se ve una torre" = "a tower can be seen"; (3) appearance: "se ve diferente/bonita" = "it looks different/pretty". Often the subject is a thing being looked at (scar, tower, photo), and the exact English translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Desde aquí se ve el mar.
native_language_example: From here you can see the sea.

additional_notes: Used to say something appears good based on how it looks (clothes, hair, a house, a plan, etc.). It comes from "verse" (to look/appear) and is common as a quick approval: "Se ve bien." You can clarify the subject with a noun/pronoun: "Tu corbata se ve bien" (your tie looks good).
target_language_example: Este diseño se ve bien; me gusta mucho.
native_language_example: This design looks good; I like it a lot.

additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe how someone or something appears: "(algo/alguien) se ve muy + adjetivo". Literally "it/they look very..." or "he/she looks very...". Common with physical appearance or visible condition (hermosa, enferma, costoso, delicioso). You can add a person or thing before it ("Tom se ve muy...") or use it without mentioning the subject if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Desde aquí, el edificio se ve muy alto.
native_language_example: From here, the building looks very tall.

meaning: "it looks very good" / "you look very good."
additional_notes: From the verb "verse" (to look/appear). Use it to comment on how someone or something looks (appearance), often with "en" + a place/medium: "Se ve muy bien en la foto" (in the photo), "...en televisión" (on TV). "Se" is part of the verb here, not a separate word you translate as "it."
target_language_example: Con ese vestido, te ves muy bien.
native_language_example: With that dress, you look very good.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe how someone or something appears: "[Subject] se ve un poco + adjective". "Se ve" comes from "verse" (to look/seem), and it often means “looks” (appearance) or “seems” (impression).
target_language_example: Hoy te ves un poco preocupado.
native_language_example: Today you look a little worried.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe someone or something’s appearance: “se ven + adjective” = “they/you all look + adjective.” Common with people (Ellos se ven felices) and things (Estas manzanas se ven frescas). It’s from the verb “verse” (to look/seem). Note: “se ven” can also mean “they see each other,” but in these examples it means “look/seem.”
target_language_example: Hoy se ven un poco preocupados.
native_language_example: Today you all look a little worried.

additional_notes: From the verb **verse** (“to look/appear”). It’s often used to describe how something or someone looked in the past. Common patterns: **se veía + adjective** (Todo se veía agradable. = Everything looked nice.) and **se veía como + noun/person** (Se veía como Charles Darwin. = He looked like Charles Darwin.).
target_language_example: Con esa luz, la habitación se veía más grande.
native_language_example: In that light, the room looked bigger.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **volverse** (“to become”), used to talk about a **change of state** (often noticeable or relatively sudden). Common with **adjectives** (se volvió feliz/violento) and sometimes with **roles/status** (se volvió presidente; se volvió famoso/a). Here it’s in the **preterite** (past completed change): **se volvió** = “(he/she/it) became.” Not the same as **volver** = “to return.”
target_language_example: Después del accidente, se volvió muy cauteloso.
native_language_example: After the accident, he became very cautious.

additional_notes: Form of "volverse" meaning “to become” (a change in state). Often used with adjectives: "se vuelve difícil" (it becomes difficult), "se vuelve poco profundo" (it gets shallow). Present tense; other forms include "me vuelvo", "te vuelves", "se volvieron".
target_language_example: Con el tiempo, el trabajo se vuelve más fácil.
native_language_example: With time, the job becomes easier.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive of ser ("sea") when talking about something that may or may not be needed, often after expressions like "espero que", "no creo que", "tal vez", or with time words like "cuando" referring to the future: "cuando sea necesario" = "when it’s necessary / when needed." Often appears in the set phrase "lo que sea necesario" = "whatever is necessary."
target_language_example: Llámame si sea necesario.
native_language_example: Call me if it’s necessary.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive form of ser (sea) after expressions like "como" (as), "tan... como" (as... as), and "en cuanto" (as soon as) to mean "as much/soon/fast as possible." Very common patterns: "tan pronto/rápido como sea posible" (as soon/fast as possible), "en cuanto me/te sea posible" (as soon as it’s possible for me/you), and "todo lo que sea posible" (everything possible).
target_language_example: Haremos el trabajo lo antes posible, en cuanto nos sea posible.
native_language_example: We’ll do the work as soon as possible, as soon as we can.

additional_notes: Used to say that the conclusion or decision stays the same regardless of the circumstances (similar to “in any case” or “anyway”). It often introduces a statement you consider true no matter what, or it can close a discussion: “Sea como sea, mañana toma ese tren.” The verb form “sea” is the present subjunctive of ser (to be), but you can learn the whole phrase as a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Sea como sea, tenemos que terminar hoy.
native_language_example: Either way, we have to finish today.

additional_notes: Uses the subjunctive of ser (sea) to express uncertainty or indifference about the exact thing, or that the result is the same regardless. Common patterns: "Sea lo que sea" (whatever it is), "Sea lo que sea eso" (whatever that is), and "Sea lo que sea que + subjunctive" (whatever + clause): "Sea lo que sea que él juegue..." = "Whatever he plays...".
target_language_example: Sea lo que sea, no voy a cambiar de opinión.
native_language_example: Whatever it is, I’m not going to change my mind.

additional_notes: Built from the subjunctive of **ser** (*sea* = “be”) + **que**. It appears in several very common fixed patterns: **ya sea que... o...** = “whether... or...”; **(cuando/donde/como) sea que...** = “whenever/wherever/however...”; **sea lo que sea (que)...** = “whatever it is (that)...”; **no sea que...** = “lest / in case...” (to avoid something happening). It’s normally followed by a verb in the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Ya sea que vengas o no, te guardaré un asiento.
native_language_example: Whether you come or not, I’ll save you a seat.

meaning: "that you be happy" / "for you to be happy" (subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive after expressions of desire, hope, advice, or doubt about someone being happy (e.g., "quiero/espero/dudo que..."). It usually follows "que": "Quiero que seas feliz" = "I want you to be happy."
target_language_example: Ojalá que seas feliz donde estés.
native_language_example: I hope you’re happy wherever you are.

additional_notes: Used to talk about obeying rules, instructions, or policies. Common with obligation phrases like "tener que" (to have to) and "deber" (must/should). You can change the article/number: "seguir la regla" (a rule) / "seguir estas reglas" (these rules).
target_language_example: En esta clase, tenemos que seguir las reglas.
native_language_example: In this class, we have to follow the rules.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about another chance after a mistake or failure. Often follows verbs like dar (to give) or tener (to have): “Dame una segunda oportunidad” (Give me a second chance), “Tenemos una segunda oportunidad” (We have a second chance).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar una segunda oportunidad?
native_language_example: Can you give me a second chance?

additional_notes: Used to say a place is on the building level above the ground floor. In many Spanish-speaking countries, the "segundo piso" is one level above the "primer piso" (which is usually the ground floor), so numbering may differ from places where the ground floor is called the "first floor."
target_language_example: La oficina está en el segundo piso, a la derecha.
native_language_example: The office is on the second floor, on the right.

additional_notes: Used with "estar" to express certainty about a whole clause: "estar segura de que" + [verb]. "Segura" is feminine; use "seguro de que" for a man, and "seguros/seguras" for plural. You can also say "estar seguro/a de" + infinitive (e.g., "Estoy segura de llegar a tiempo" = I’m sure I’ll arrive on time).
target_language_example: Estoy segura de que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I’m sure it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with estar (or parecer estar) to say someone feels certain about something: estar seguro de + noun/pronoun (Estoy seguro de eso; seguro de sus respuestas) or estar seguro de + infinitive (Estoy seguro de no haberla visto). In questions it often asks for confirmation: ¿Estás seguro de esto/de querer…? Feminine form: segura de.
target_language_example: ¿Estás seguro de que tienes las llaves?
native_language_example: Are you sure you have the keys?

additional_notes: Used after forms of **estar seguro/a** to introduce a clause with **que** (something you’re confident is true or will happen). It agrees with the speaker: **seguro** (masc.), **segura** (fem.). Common patterns: **Estoy seguro/a de que...**, **¿Estás seguro/a de que...?**, **No estoy seguro/a de que...**.
target_language_example: No estoy seguro de que él entienda la pregunta.
native_language_example: I’m not sure that he understands the question.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you feel confident is true (a prediction, assumption, or reassurance). Often followed by the indicative: "Seguro que lo hará." It can also be used encouragingly: "Seguro que eres capaz" = "I’m sure you can do it." In speech it’s common to stress it for emphasis.
target_language_example: Seguro que todo saldrá bien.
native_language_example: I’m sure everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: Used to cite the newspaper as your source of information. Often followed by a clause in the future/past ("Según el periódico, ...") and can be used to distance yourself from the claim (you’re reporting what the paper says, not necessarily confirming it).
target_language_example: Según el periódico, el tren llegará con retraso.
native_language_example: According to the newspaper, the train will arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time (duration) or how long ago something happened. Common patterns: "durante seis años" (for six years), "hace seis años" (six years ago), "por seis años" (for six years, often in Latin America), and "llevo seis años + gerund" (I’ve been doing something for six years).
target_language_example: Hace seis años que vivo aquí.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for six years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or remaining time. With verbs like faltar/quedar it means “there were six hours left / six hours remain.”
target_language_example: Me quedan seis horas para terminar el trabajo.
native_language_example: I have six hours left to finish the work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for six months) or a point in time relative to something else (six months later). You’ll often see it with prepositions like “durante seis meses” (for/during six months) or “seis meses después” (six months later).
target_language_example: Voy a vivir aquí seis meses.
native_language_example: I’m going to live here for six months.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the week after the current one. Very common with "la" (e.g., "la semana que viene") and in farewells like "Hasta la semana que viene" (“See you next week”). Similar to "la próxima semana"; in many contexts they’re interchangeable.
target_language_example: Nos vemos la semana que viene.
native_language_example: See you next week.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns to talk about someone’s ability or instinct in an area: sentido de la música (sense of music), sentido de la orientación (sense of direction). With "perder" it means to lose that ability: Perdí el sentido de la orientación. (I lost my sense of direction.)
target_language_example: Tengo un buen sentido de la responsabilidad.
native_language_example: I have a good sense of responsibility.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se): "me siento mejor" = "I feel better." Often refers to improved health, mood, or comfort, and commonly appears in encouraging statements ("Te vas a sentir mejor") or advice ("Con esta medicina...").
target_language_example: Después de descansar un poco, me siento mejor.
native_language_example: After resting a bit, I feel better.

meaning: to be able to; to be capable of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about having the ability, skill, or possibility to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: ser capaz de + infinitive (e.g., ser capaz de aprender). Often implies having enough skill/strength/resources rather than just permission.
target_language_example: No soy capaz de hacerlo solo, ¿me ayudas?
native_language_example: I’m not able to do it alone—can you help me?

additional_notes: Often used after another verb (quiero/debo/intento/elige/escoge) to express a goal or intention: “to be happy.” You’ll also see it after para (“in order to”): para ser feliz = “to be happy / in order to be happy.”
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio y duermo bien para ser feliz.
native_language_example: I exercise and sleep well to be happy.

additional_notes: Used to say you will tell the truth or give your real opinion. Often appears as "Para ser honesto, ..." meaning "To be honest, ...". It can be followed by "con" + person ("ser honesto contigo" = be honest with you) or "conmigo mismo" (be honest with myself).
target_language_example: Para ser honesto, no me gusta esa idea.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t like that idea.

meaning: to be very (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe a quality or state in a general/lasting way. The adjective agrees with the subject: ser muy eficiente / ser muy cuidadoso(a)(s). In your examples, it’s often used after verbs like esperar (to hope) or phrases like pese a (despite).
target_language_example: Quiero ser muy claro con esto.
native_language_example: I want to be very clear about this.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to compare or to say someone/something should change: “ser más + adj.” (be more polite/independent/fast). In phrases like “nada podía ser más + adj.” it means “nothing could be more + adj.”
target_language_example: Tienes que ser más paciente.
native_language_example: You have to be more patient.

additional_notes: Used to advise or tell someone to pay more attention and avoid mistakes or accidents. Often appears with deberías/tienes que/tenés que (“you should/you have to”) and time phrases like de ahora en adelante (“from now on”) or en el futuro (“in the future”). In Spanish, cuidadoso agrees with the person: ser más cuidadosa (female), ser más cuidadosos/as (plural).
target_language_example: Tienes que ser más cuidadoso con ese cuchillo.
native_language_example: You have to be more careful with that knife.

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to or participates in a group, project, team, event, or someone’s life. You can also use it with other forms of ser: soy parte de… (I’m part of…), somos parte de… (we’re part of…), fue parte de… (was part of…).
target_language_example: Quiero ser parte de tu equipo.
native_language_example: I want to be part of your team.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" + past participle "tratado" to talk about how someone is treated by others. It’s often followed by a noun or description: "como un niño" (like a child), "como cualquiera" (like anyone), or "como tal" (as such). You can change the form to match the subject/tense (e.g., "fui tratado como...", "será tratada como...").
target_language_example: No quiero ser tratado como un extraño.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be treated like a stranger.

meaning: "to be a" (followed by a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe what someone/something is: a job/role (ser un actor), a type of person/thing (ser un impostor), or what something will become (va a ser un éxito). It also appears in expressions like “parecer ser un…” (“to seem to be a…”). For feminine nouns, use “ser una”.
target_language_example: No quiero ser un problema para ti.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be a problem for you.

meaning: to be a good (person/thing), before a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser + un + buen (short form of bueno) + a masculine singular noun: ser un buen padre, ser un buen cantante, ser un buen lugar. For feminine nouns, use “ser una buena …” (ser una buena madre). For plural, use “ser un buen” doesn’t apply; you’d say “ser buenos/buenas …” (Ellos quieren ser buenos padres).
target_language_example: Quiero ser un buen amigo.
native_language_example: I want to be a good friend.

meaning: "to be a little more" (followed by an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to make suggestions or mild requests for a change in behavior or attitude: "be a little more + adjective" (e.g., tolerante, sociable, civilizado, listo). Often appears with advice/softening verbs like "deberías" (you should) or "podrías" (you could).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes ser un poco más paciente, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you be a little more patient, please?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** + the indefinite article **una** before a **feminine** noun (often roles, professions, identities, or descriptions): *ser una estudiante, ser una molestia, ser una buena idea*. With masculine nouns you use **ser un** (*ser un estudiante*).
target_language_example: Quiero ser una doctora cuando sea mayor.
native_language_example: I want to be a doctor when I grow up.

meaning: 'to be like' (to resemble; to want to be similar to).
additional_notes: Used to compare people or things ("X es como Y" = X is like Y) and also to express wanting to imitate or become similar to someone ("quiero ser como él" = I want to be like him). Often followed by a noun/pronoun (como él/ella/yo) or a description (como mi hermano).
target_language_example: No quiero ser como nadie más; quiero ser como soy.
native_language_example: I don't want to be like anyone else; I want to be how I am.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase used to talk about humans in general, often in a neutral or formal tone (e.g., scientific, philosophical, or ethical statements). Singular: "ser humano". Often used with "todos los" (all).
target_language_example: Todos los seres humanos merecen respeto.
native_language_example: All human beings deserve respect.

additional_notes: Literally means “it will be better,” but it’s very often used to give advice or a warning, like “you’d better…”. Common patterns: (1) “Será mejor + infinitive” (Será mejor ir en tren. = It’d be better to go by train.) (2) “Será mejor que + subjunctive” (Será mejor que le cuentes… = You’d better tell her…). Depending on tone, it can sound like a strong suggestion or a threat (“It had better work.”).
target_language_example: Será mejor que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’d better arrive on time.

meaning: “(You) had better…” / “It would be better if…”.
additional_notes: Often used to give strong advice or a warning (sometimes like a threat): “You’d better…”. Very commonly followed by the subjunctive: será mejor que + present subjunctive (e.g., Será mejor que vuelvas.). It can also be used as a comparison meaning “better than” in sentences like “Será mejor que aquí” (“It’ll be better than here”).
target_language_example: Será mejor que llegues a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’d better arrive on time.

meaning: “You’d better…” / “It would be better if you…” (warning or strong advice about ‘it/that’).
additional_notes: Used to warn or strongly advise someone. It’s usually followed by the subjunctive (Será mejor que lo + verb in subjunctive), and “lo” is an object pronoun meaning “it/that” (referring to something already mentioned or understood). Often implies consequences if the person doesn’t do it.
target_language_example: Será mejor que lo hagas ahora.
native_language_example: You’d better do it now.

meaning: "I’d better go / I should probably leave."
additional_notes: Used to say it’s a good idea to leave now (often polite, indirect, or a hint that it’s time to go). It uses the structure "Será mejor que + [present subjunctive]"; here, "me vaya" is the subjunctive of "irme" (to leave/go away). You can add a destination: "Será mejor que me vaya a casa" (I’d better go home).
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; será mejor que me vaya.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’d better go.

additional_notes: Used to advise someone strongly or warn about consequences. It’s followed by the present subjunctive: “Será mejor que te + verb (subjunctive)” (e.g., te vayas, te levantes, te des prisa). Often implies “or else…”.
target_language_example: Será mejor que te vayas ahora.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now.

meaning: "You’d better leave" / "It would be better if you left."
additional_notes: Often used to give strong advice or a warning that someone should leave (now, go to bed, get out of here, etc.). It commonly appears as: "Será mejor que + (subjunctive)". With "te vayas" it’s addressing one person informally (tú). Tone can range from concerned to stern depending on context.
target_language_example: Será mejor que te vayas ahora mismo.
native_language_example: You’d better leave right now.

meaning: “I’d better go” / “it would be better if I go.”
additional_notes: Used to say it’s advisable to leave or to do something right away. Literally “it will be better that I go,” but in everyday English it’s often “I’d better go.” After "será mejor que..." Spanish uses the present subjunctive (vaya). You can swap in other verbs: "Será mejor que hable..." (I’d better talk...), "Será mejor que vaya a ver..." (I’d better go see...).
target_language_example: Será mejor que vaya ahora antes de que se haga tarde.
native_language_example: I’d better go now before it gets late.

additional_notes: Used to say something will become easier in the future, often after a change or with time. It can be general (“Así será más fácil.” = “That way it’ll be easier.”) or specify who it’s easier for: “para ti será más fácil” (for you), “nos será más fácil” (for us).
target_language_example: Si lo hacemos mañana, será más fácil.
native_language_example: If we do it tomorrow, it will be easier.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone/something will be in the future: "Mañana será un gran día" = "Tomorrow will be a great day." It can also express a guess about the present: "Será un experto" can mean "He/She is probably an expert." Change "un" to "una" for feminine nouns ("será una sorpresa").
target_language_example: Creo que será un buen viaje.
native_language_example: I think it will be a good trip.

additional_notes: Uses the future tense of ser (será = 'he/she/it will be') plus un buen + a masculine singular noun (doctor, maestro, marido, lugar, etc.) to predict or judge that someone/something will be good. For feminine nouns, use una buena (e.g., Será una buena doctora).
target_language_example: Creo que será un buen amigo.
native_language_example: I think he will be a good friend.

meaning: “it would be good” (a good idea; it would be nice).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense (sería = “would be”) to talk about a hypothetical situation or to make a gentle suggestion. Often followed by an infinitive: “Sería bueno + infinitive” (e.g., Sería bueno descansar = It would be good to rest).
target_language_example: Sería bueno llamar antes de ir.
native_language_example: It would be good to call before going.

meaning: would be able to; would be capable of.
additional_notes: Conditional form of "ser capaz de" (to be able/capable of). Used to talk about a hypothetical ability or possibility, or to express what you think someone would or wouldn’t do (often with a moral/character judgment, like “he wouldn’t be capable of lying”). Common patterns: "X sería capaz de + infinitive" and "No sería capaz de + infinitive".
target_language_example: No sería capaz de decirte una mentira.
native_language_example: I wouldn't be able to tell you a lie.

meaning: 'it would be better if' (suggesting a preferable action).
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. It’s followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "sería mejor que descanses / no hicieras eso"). You can use it politely with "usted": "Sería mejor que descanse."
target_language_example: Sería mejor que llegáramos temprano para evitar el tráfico.
native_language_example: It would be better if we arrived early to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of ser (sería = “would be”) plus comparative (más fácil = “easier”). Common for suggesting a better option: Sería más fácil + infinitive (“to do something”) or with a subject: Mi vida sería más fácil (“My life would be easier”).
target_language_example: Sería más fácil salir temprano mañana.
native_language_example: It would be easier to leave early tomorrow.

meaning: a “sixth sense”; a strong intuition or gut feeling.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an instinctive feeling that helps you “know” something without clear evidence. Often used with tener (to have): “Tengo un sexto sentido…” or “Ella tiene un sexto sentido…”. It can also be used with para + noun/verb to say what you’re good at sensing: “un sexto sentido para estas cosas.”
target_language_example: Tengo un sexto sentido y sé que algo va a salir mal.
native_language_example: I have a sixth sense and I know something is going to go wrong.

meaning: a sign of; a signal of.
additional_notes: Used to indicate evidence or an indication that something is happening/likely ("Es señal de..."). Also used with nouns to describe an action done as a sign/gesture of something ("en señal de + noun": en señal de respeto/oposición/protesta).
target_language_example: El silencio fue señal de que algo andaba mal.
native_language_example: The silence was a sign that something was wrong.

additional_notes: A very formal way to address a man who is the director/manager (e.g., in a company, school, institution), often used when speaking directly to him: “Señor director, …”. In some workplaces it can function like “sir” when talking to a superior. You can also say “el señor director” when referring to him (“the director”).
target_language_example: Señor director, ¿tiene un minuto para hablar conmigo?
native_language_example: Mr. Director, do you have a minute to talk to me?

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to address a group of people, often at the start of announcements, speeches, or public-address messages (e.g., on planes, at events). It can also be used with phrases like “por favor” or “su atención, por favor” to get everyone’s attention.
target_language_example: Señoras y señores, el espectáculo va a comenzar.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, the show is about to begin.

meaning: whether (with a sense of doubt), or 'if by any chance'.
additional_notes: Used mainly in indirect questions after verbs like preguntar, saber, importar: "No sé si acaso..." It often adds uncertainty or emphasis (similar to "whether... at all" / "if, by any chance"). In many cases you can translate it simply as "whether" (or "if" in indirect questions), but "acaso" makes it sound more doubtful or tentative.
target_language_example: No sé si acaso vendrán mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t know whether they’ll come tomorrow (or if they’ll come at all).

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition about an unspecified person (often followed by a verb): “si alguien + verb…”. It can refer to “anyone” in general or “someone” depending on context.
target_language_example: Llámame si alguien pregunta por mí.
native_language_example: Call me if anyone asks for me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possible situation at any time in the future ("If you ever..."), or to emphasize that something almost never happens ("rarely, if ever"). Often followed by a verb in the present tense for future meaning: "Si alguna vez tienes problemas..." = "If you ever have problems...".
target_language_example: Si alguna vez vienes a Nueva York, avísame.
native_language_example: If you ever come to New York, let me know.

additional_notes: Used to soften a request or express a preference, like “if possible” or “if you can.” It can go at the end of the sentence or at the beginning: “Si es posible, …”.
target_language_example: ¿Podemos reunirnos mañana, si es posible?
native_language_example: Can we meet tomorrow, if possible?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition based on what someone wants/needs/asks for. It often sounds like agreement or acceptance (sometimes reluctant): “Okay, if that’s what it takes / if that’s what you want.” Commonly followed by a verb like deseas (you want), hace falta (is needed), quieren (they want).
target_language_example: Si eso es lo que necesitas, lo haré.
native_language_example: If that’s what you need, I’ll do it.

additional_notes: Used to give hypothetical advice or say what you would do in someone else’s situation. It uses the imperfect subjunctive (estuviera) in an "if" clause: "Si estuviera en tu lugar/situación, ..." Often followed by a conditional verb ("haría", "ayudaría", "tendría"). You can also hear variants like "Si yo estuviera en tu lugar...".
target_language_example: Si estuviera en tu lugar, hablaría con el jefe mañana.
native_language_example: If I were in your place, I’d talk to the boss tomorrow.

meaning: "if you are" (talking about someone’s state, condition, or location).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition with the verb "estar" in the tú form ("estás"). Common before an instruction or suggestion: "Si estás + adjective" (if you’re happy/awake/busy) or "Si estás en + place" (if you’re in Paris). Uses "estar" for temporary states and locations (not "ser").
target_language_example: Si estás cansado, podemos hablar mañana.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, we can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect subjunctive of ser (fuera) after si to talk about unreal or unlikely situations (“if it were…”). Often appears in shortened exclamations like “Si fuera tan fácil…” meaning “If only it were that easy…”.
target_language_example: Si fuera más barato, lo compraría.
native_language_example: If it were cheaper, I would buy it.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or recommendations by imagining yourself in the other person’s situation. It uses the imperfect subjunctive of ser (fuera) after si. Often followed by a conditional verb: “Si fuera tú, haría…” (If I were you, I would do…).
target_language_example: Si fuera tú, hablaría con ella hoy.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would talk to her today.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect subjunctive of ser (fueras) after si to talk about imaginary or unlikely situations. It often pairs with a conditional in the other clause: si fueras…, (yo) haría/sería…. Can also appear in comparisons with como: como si fueras… (“as if you were…”).
target_language_example: Si fueras mi jefe, cambiarías esta regla.
native_language_example: If you were my boss, you would change this rule.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a hypothetical past situation that did NOT happen, often with a result in the conditional: "Si hubiera + past participle..., habría + past participle" (If I had..., I would have...). It can also lead to a present result: "Si hubiera..., ahora sería/estaría..." (If I had..., I would be... now). "Hubiera" is the imperfect subjunctive of "haber" and is commonly followed by a past participle (hubiera ido, hubiera visto, etc.).
target_language_example: Si hubiera estudiado más, habría aprobado el examen.
native_language_example: If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.

meaning: "if I had known that" (talking about an unreal past condition).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical past situation you didn’t know at the time. It commonly pairs with a conditional-result clause, often with "habría" or "hubiera" (e.g., "Si hubiera sabido que..., habría/he hubiera + past participle"). "Hubiera sabido" is past perfect subjunctive of "saber".
target_language_example: Si hubiera sabido que no venías, no habría preparado tanta comida.
native_language_example: If I had known that you weren’t coming, I wouldn’t have made so much food.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical situation in the past that did not happen. It uses the pluperfect subjunctive of ser (haber + sido): si + hubiera/hubiese sido + (noun/adjective). It’s typically paired with a conditional perfect result clause: “..., habría + participle” (would have...).
target_language_example: Si hubiera sido más cuidadoso, no habría tenido ese problema.
native_language_example: If I had been more careful, I wouldn’t have had that problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unreal past condition (something that did not happen). It’s the imperfect subjunctive of "haber" + past participle: "hubiera tenido" = "had had." Often followed by a result in the conditional perfect ("habría..."), e.g., "Si hubiera tenido dinero, habría comprado...".
target_language_example: Si hubiera tenido tiempo, te habría llamado.
native_language_example: If I had had time, I would have called you.
