additional_notes: Used to say you have a scheduled meeting with a person (doctor, friend, etc.), or a romantic date. You can add a time too: "Tengo una cita con el doctor a las 3." In more poetic contexts it can also mean a figurative “appointment” (e.g., "una cita con el destino").
target_language_example: Lo siento, no puedo ir; tengo una cita con mi médico esta tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go; I have an appointment with my doctor this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a (female) child. "Tengo" = "I have" (from *tener*), "una" = "a/one", "hija" = "daughter". You can add details with "de...": "Tengo una hija de tu edad" (a daughter your age) or "Tengo una hija de la misma edad que tu hijo" (the same age as your son).
target_language_example: Tengo una hija de ocho años.
native_language_example: I have an eight-year-old daughter.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a suggestion or plan. Very common in conversation. You can add emphasis or details after it: "Tengo una idea mejor" (I have a better idea), "Tengo una idea para..." (I have an idea for...).
target_language_example: Tengo una idea: vamos al parque después de comer.
native_language_example: I have an idea: let's go to the park after we eat.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb **haber** to form the present perfect: **he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han tenido suerte** = “I/you/he… have been lucky.” It often refers to luck in a specific situation (**¡Has tenido suerte!**) or over time (**hasta ahora**, **toda su vida**). You can also use **tener suerte de + infinitive** (“be lucky to…”) or **tener suerte de que + subjuntivo** (“be lucky that…”): *Ha tenido suerte de que yo pasara por aquí.*
target_language_example: Has tenido suerte; el autobús llegó justo a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’ve been lucky; the bus arrived just in time.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "haber" (he/has/hemos/han tenido) to say someone has reached their limit. Very often used with "ya" to mean "enough already". You can add "de" + noun/pronoun: "He tenido suficiente de esto" = "I’ve had enough of this."
target_language_example: Ya hemos tenido suficiente; vámonos.
native_language_example: We’ve had enough already; let’s go.

meaning: “had a” (past of “to have,” used in perfect tenses).
additional_notes: Used with forms of **haber** (auxiliary verb) + **tenido** (past participle of *tener*) + **un**. Very common in the **present perfect** (e.g., *has/haya/hayan tenido un...* = “have had a...”), **past perfect** (*había tenido un...* = “had had a...”), and with **conditional/subjunctive** structures (*hubiese tenido un...*, *debería haber tenido un...*). In Spanish you usually don’t say *tenido un* alone; it normally needs the auxiliary *haber* before it.
target_language_example: Me alegro de que hayas tenido un buen día.
native_language_example: I’m glad you had a good day.

additional_notes: Used with vosotros/vosotras (Spain) to say that a group must do something. It’s followed by an infinitive: tenéis que + verb (e.g., tenéis que venir). In most of Latin America, people usually say "tienen que" instead.
target_language_example: Tenéis que estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: You (all) have to study for the exam.

additional_notes: Voseo form used in places like Argentina and Uruguay. It’s the same meaning as "tienes que" (tú). Used to express obligation or necessity: "Tenés que + infinitive" (e.g., tenés que trabajar).
target_language_example: Tenés que estudiar hoy para el examen.
native_language_example: You have to study today for the exam.

additional_notes: Imperfect form of **tener ganas de** (“to feel like / to want to”), describing a desire that was ongoing, repeated, or just setting the scene in the past. It’s followed by an **infinitive** (tenía ganas de hablar) or sometimes a **noun** (tenía ganas de helado = “craved ice cream”).
target_language_example: Ayer tenía ganas de salir, pero estaba lloviendo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I felt like going out, but it was raining.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of tener hambre (“to be hungry”). Use it for ongoing/background hunger in the past, or for habitual hunger (“used to be hungry”). Often appears after que: Me dijo que tenía hambre (“He told me he was hungry”). Contrast with tuve hambre (simple past) for a specific moment/instance of being hungry.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué a casa, tenía hambre y comí algo.
native_language_example: When I got home, I was hungry and I ate something.

meaning: I was hoping to / I had hoped to.
additional_notes: Used to express a hope or expectation in the past. Common patterns: (1) "tenía la esperanza de" + infinitive (ahorrar, terminar, poder ver...) and (2) "tenía la esperanza de que" + verb (often in imperfect or past, and sometimes subjunctive depending on context). Similar to "esperaba" but a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Tenía la esperanza de verte antes de irme.
native_language_example: I was hoping to see you before I left.

meaning: I/he/she had intended to; I/he/she meant to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past intention or plan (often one that didn’t happen). It’s the imperfect tense of "tener la intención de" + infinitive. The subject is understood from context (yo/él/ella/usted). For "you (informal) had intended to," say "tenías la intención de"; for "we," "teníamos la intención de."
target_language_example: Tenía la intención de llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
native_language_example: I meant to call you, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "tener miedo" (to be afraid). It often describes a past state/background feeling (something you used to be afraid of, or how someone felt at that time). Common patterns: "tenía miedo de + noun/infinitive" (Tenía miedo de las ranas / de hablar) and "tenía miedo de que + subjunctive" (Tenía miedo de que se perdiera).
target_language_example: De pequeño, tenía miedo de la oscuridad.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of tener miedo: describes an ongoing or habitual fear in the past (“I/he/she was afraid”). Use **de + infinitive** for an action: *Tenía miedo de dormirme* (“I was afraid of falling asleep”). Use **de + noun/person** for what someone feared: *Tenía miedo de Mary* (“He was afraid of Mary”).
target_language_example: Tenía miedo de decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I was afraid to tell the truth.

meaning: was eight years old (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of tener (tenía) to describe someone’s age at a time in the past. The subject is often understood from context: “tenía ocho años” can mean “I/he/she was eight.” Common pattern: “Tenía X años cuando…” = “I was X years old when…”.
target_language_example: Tenía ocho años cuando aprendí a nadar.
native_language_example: I was eight years old when I learned to swim.

additional_notes: Past tense of “tener que” + infinitive, used to talk about a past obligation or necessity. It can be about duty (“I had to tell you”) or practical necessity (“I needed to go home”). With things: “Todo tenía que…” = “Everything had to…”.
target_language_example: Tenía que llamar a mi mamá, pero se me olvidó.
native_language_example: I had to call my mom, but I forgot.

additional_notes: Imperfect of "tener que" (to have to), used to talk about an obligation in the past (often what was necessary or expected). Very common as "lo que tenía que hacer" = "what I/he/she had to do" (or "what ... was supposed to do"). The subject can change: yo tenía, tú tenías, él/ella tenía, etc.
target_language_example: Sabía lo que tenía que hacer, pero tenía miedo.
native_language_example: I knew what I had to do, but I was afraid.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was correct in the past. It comes from the verb tener (to have) + razón (reason/right): tenía razón = '(he/she/you formal) was right.' For other people: yo tenía razón (I was right), tú tenías razón (you were right), nosotros teníamos razón (we were right), ellos/ellas tenían razón (they were right).
target_language_example: Perdón, tenías razón; no era hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, you were right; it wasn’t today.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "tener" (tenía) is used to describe age in the past. Often appears with time expressions like "cuando" (when) or "desde que" (since) to set the scene: "cuando yo tenía siete años" = "when I was seven". You can swap the number: "tenía diez años" (I was ten).
target_language_example: Empecé a tocar el piano cuando tenía siete años.
native_language_example: I started playing the piano when I was seven years old.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of tener (tenía) is commonly used to state someone’s age in the past. It often sets background time (“when I was 13…”). You can replace trece with any number: tenía diez años, tenía veinte años, etc. For emphasis you may hear: tenía trece años de edad.
target_language_example: Cuando tenía trece años, vivía en México.
native_language_example: When I was thirteen years old, I lived in Mexico.

meaning: "I was your age" / "(he/she) was your age."
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of tener to talk about a past time when someone had the same age as the person you’re speaking to. Often used with "cuando" (when): "Cuando yo tenía tu edad..." You can also change the possessive: "tenía mi/su/nuestra edad" (was my/his/her/our age).
target_language_example: Cuando yo tenía tu edad, no tenía celular.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I didn’t have a cell phone.

meaning: 'had a' / 'used to have a' (imperfect of tener).
additional_notes: Used to say someone possessed or had something at a past time, often as background information or a habitual situation. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (tenía un paraguas, un hermano). For feminine nouns, use “tenía una”.
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, tenía un perro.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I had a dog.

additional_notes: Used with an imperfect past form of tener (tenía = “I/he/she had/used to have”) to describe a mild amount of something in the past, often a feeling, symptom, or some time. The noun usually follows: tenía un poco de dolor / tiempo / hambre. You can change the subject: yo tenía, tú tenías, nosotros teníamos, etc.
target_language_example: Ayer tenía un poco de hambre, pero no cené.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was a little hungry, but I didn’t eat dinner.

meaning: “(I/he/she) had a …” or “(I/he/she) used to have a …” (feminine noun).
additional_notes: From **tener** (to have) in the **imperfect past**: **tenía** = “I/he/she had / used to have.” It’s used for describing possession/background in the past, or something that was true over a period of time. **una** is the feminine “a/an,” so it must be followed by a **feminine singular noun** (e.g., *una habitación, una coartada, una camioneta*). For a masculine noun, you’d use **tenía un**.
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, tenía una bicicleta roja.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I had a red bicycle.

meaning: "you had to do" / "you were supposed to do".
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of tener (tenías) + que + infinitive to express obligation in the past. Often means there was a duty/expectation at that time (not necessarily a single completed action). Common pattern: (yo) tenía que..., (tú) tenías que..., (él/ella) tenía que..., (nosotros) teníamos que..., (ellos) tenían que... + infinitive.
target_language_example: Tenías que hacer la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: You had to do your homework before going out.

additional_notes: Past/imperfect form of "tener razón" (to be right). Used to admit or acknowledge that someone’s earlier opinion/guess/advice was correct. Often followed by "en" (about) or "sobre" (about): "Tenías razón en todo" / "Tenías razón sobre eso."
target_language_example: Perdón, tenías razón: el tren sale a las ocho.
native_language_example: Sorry, you were right: the train leaves at eight.

additional_notes: Used for floor numbers in a building. Before masculine singular nouns like "piso," "tercero" shortens to "tercer" (e.g., "el tercer piso"). In many Spanish-speaking countries, floor counting may differ from the U.S./Canada: "planta baja" is the ground floor, and "primer piso" may be one level above it.
target_language_example: La oficina está en el tercer piso, al lado del ascensor.
native_language_example: The office is on the third floor, next to the elevator.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle terminado with el trabajo (“the work/job”). Very common with perfect tenses: ya había terminado el trabajo (“he had already finished the work”), habré terminado el trabajo (“I will have finished the work”). Also appears in a participle clause: Habiendo terminado el trabajo, … (“Having finished the work, …”).
target_language_example: Ya he terminado el trabajo, así que puedo descansar.
native_language_example: I’ve already finished the work, so I can rest.

meaning: to put an end to this; to be done with this.
additional_notes: Used when you want a situation, problem, argument, etc. to stop. Often sounds firm or urgent, especially with "de una vez" (= once and for all). Similar to "acabar con esto". In context it can mean either (1) finish what you’re doing, or (2) stop/take action to end an ongoing issue.
target_language_example: Ya basta; tenemos que terminar con esto hoy.
native_language_example: Enough already; we have to put an end to this today.

meaning: to finish the work/job; to complete the task.
additional_notes: Uses terminar (“to finish”) + el trabajo (“the work/job”). Often followed by a time limit with antes de (“before”): terminar el trabajo antes de las seis. You can also add who does it: terminar el trabajo por mi cuenta (“on my own”).
target_language_example: Tengo que terminar el trabajo hoy.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work today.

meaning: yourself (feminine; for emphasis, after a preposition).
additional_notes: Used with a female "tú" to emphasize that the person is the one affected or doing the action. It commonly appears after prepositions like en/a/de/para (e.g., "confía en ti misma", "mentirte a ti misma"). For a male "tú", use "ti mismo"; for plural, "vosotros/as mismos/as".
target_language_example: Hazlo por ti misma.
native_language_example: Do it for yourself.

additional_notes: Used after a preposition like en/de/para/sobre to emphasize that the action or idea refers to you, not someone else. It often appears in encouragement or self-reflection phrases: confiar en ti mismo (believe in yourself), dudar de ti mismo (doubt yourself). With other prepositions you may see the same pattern: a mí mismo/a mí misma (myself), a sí mismo/a sí misma (himself/herself/themselves).
target_language_example: Hazlo por ti mismo.
native_language_example: Do it yourself.

meaning: the tick-tock (ticking sound) of a clock; also used to mean “in a tick / very soon.”
additional_notes: Literal: describes the rhythmic sound a clock makes in a quiet place (often with oír/escuchar: “to hear”). Figurative: in phrases like “en un tictac del reloj” or “dame un tictac del reloj,” it means “very quickly” or “a moment.”
target_language_example: Qué silencio: se escucha el tictac del reloj.
native_language_example: How quiet: you can hear the tick-tock of the clock.

meaning: plenty of time; more than enough time.
additional_notes: Used to say there’s no hurry because you have extra time beyond what’s needed. Often appears with forms of "tener" (tener tiempo de sobra) or "hay" (hay tiempo de sobra).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, tenemos tiempo de sobra para llegar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we have plenty of time to get there.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has or needs enough time to do an action. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: "tiempo para pensar / hablar / entrenar". Common with verbs like "tener", "necesitar", "dar" (e.g., "Dame tiempo para...").
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo para cocinar hoy.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to cook today.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about having (or not having) time to reflect before deciding or answering. Often appears with verbs like necesitar (to need), dar (to give), tener (to have), querer (to want): “Necesito/Dame/Tengo/Quiero tiempo para pensar (en/al respecto)”. You may also hear “un poco de/ algo de tiempo para pensar” (a little/some time to think).
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de tiempo para pensar antes de responder?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little time to think before I answer?

additional_notes: Common pattern: **[subject] + vende + [thing]**. **Vende** is the **él/ella/usted** form of **vender** (“to sell”) in the present tense. You can swap **tienda** with another subject: *El mercado vende… / Mi amigo vende…*.
target_language_example: La tienda vende ropa y zapatos.
native_language_example: The store sells clothes and shoes.

meaning: "tends to" / "usually" (has a habit or general tendency to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb "tender (a)". It’s followed by an infinitive: "tiende a + infinitive" (e.g., "tiende a exagerar"). Used to talk about a general pattern, not something happening right now. You can use other forms too: "tiendo a" (I tend to), "tienden a" (they tend to), "tendemos a" (we tend to).
target_language_example: Cuando está cansada, tiende a ponerse de mal humor.
native_language_example: When she’s tired, she tends to get in a bad mood.

meaning: "(he/she/it) has something to …" or "has something that …".
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to say someone has something to do/say/hide, etc. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: tiene algo que decir (has something to say), tiene algo que esconder/ocultar (has something to hide). You can change the form of tener: tengo algo que… (I have something to…), tienes algo que… (you have something to…).
target_language_example: Tengo algo que decirte.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone trusts or believes in their own ability/qualities (or someone else’s). After "su", Spanish doesn’t specify gender: it can mean his, her, your (formal), or their. You can add "propia" to emphasize “own” (e.g., "su propia capacidad"). Often followed by words like "capacidad" (ability) or "talento" (talent).
target_language_example: Ella tiene confianza en su experiencia.
native_language_example: She has confidence in her experience.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (“to have”) to say that someone/something has four of something (tiene cuatro hermanos = “has four siblings”; tiene cuatro patas = “has four legs”). It can also be a short answer to a question about quantity (¿Cuántos tiene? — Tiene cuatro.). With measurements, it can mean something measures four units (e.g., Tiene cuatro centímetros de grosor = “It’s four centimeters thick.”).
target_language_example: —¿Cuántas sillas hay? —Tiene cuatro.
native_language_example: —How many chairs are there? —There are four.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled (legally or morally) to do something. Often followed by an infinitive (tiene derecho a consultar) or by a noun phrase (tiene derecho a un abogado). You can change it for other people: tengo derecho a, tienes derecho a, tenemos derecho a; formal/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Todos tenemos derecho a expresar nuestra opinión.
native_language_example: We all have the right to express our opinion.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **tener** (to have) in the **third-person singular**: *él/ella/usted tiene dos...* In Spanish, the subject is often omitted, so **tiene dos** can mean “he/she/you (formal) has two…,” depending on context. It’s usually followed by a plural noun: *tiene dos casas / dos primos / dos clases*.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene dos perros.
native_language_example: My sister has two dogs.

additional_notes: From **tener** (to have) + **dos** (two) + **hijos** (children/sons). **Tiene** can mean **he/she has** or **you (formal) have**, depending on context. In Spanish, **hijos** can sometimes be used in a general sense for “children,” though **hijos** literally means “sons” (for explicitly “children,” you may also hear **dos hijos/dos hijas** or **dos niños** depending on context).
target_language_example: Mi profesor tiene dos hijos y vive cerca de la escuela.
native_language_example: My teacher has two children and lives near the school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or doesn’t have) the necessary age to do an activity. Very common with an infinitive after para: "tiene edad suficiente para votar/decidir/ir". Negative: "no tiene edad suficiente para...".
target_language_example: No tengo edad suficiente para alquilar un coche.
native_language_example: I’m not old enough to rent a car.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone is legally or morally allowed to do something. The pattern is: (person) tiene el derecho a + infinitive (tiene el derecho a votar) or tiene el derecho a + noun (tiene el derecho a un abogado). Also appears formally as: usted tiene el derecho a...
target_language_example: Ella tiene el derecho a saber la verdad.
native_language_example: She has the right to know the truth.

meaning: “has (the) hair…” (used to describe someone’s hair: color, length, condition).
additional_notes: Used with a following adjective or description: tiene el pelo negro/largo/corto/mojado/rizado. In Spanish you typically say “has the hair” (tener + el pelo) rather than “has hair” when describing hair characteristics. You can also use it with “de + color”: tiene el pelo de color azul.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene el pelo castaño y rizado.
native_language_example: My sister has brown, curly hair.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. Spanish commonly says “tener el pelo + color” (“to have + the hair + color”), often with “el” even when talking about a specific person: “Tiene el pelo castaño.” You can change the subject: “Yo/Él/Ella tiene…” and the color: “rubio” (blond), “negro” (black).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene el pelo castaño y los ojos verdes.
native_language_example: My sister has brown hair and green eyes.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s appearance. It’s the 3rd-person singular present of tener: "él/ella/usted tiene..." (he/she/you formal has...). You can change the adjective to describe hair: tiene el pelo corto (short), rizado (curly), liso (straight).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene el pelo largo y negro.
native_language_example: My sister has long, black hair.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. Spanish often says "tener el pelo + adjective" (to have the hair + adjective): e.g., "tiene el pelo castaño" (has brown hair), "tiene el pelo negro" (has black hair). You can add more adjectives with "y": "tiene el pelo rubio y rizado" (blond and curly).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene el pelo rubio y los ojos azules.
native_language_example: My brother has blond hair and blue eyes.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has the skill, power, or possibility to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (verb in the “to do” form): tiene la capacidad de + hablar/entender/hacer. You can change it to match the subject and tense (e.g., tengo la capacidad de…, tenía la capacidad de…, tendrán la capacidad de…).
target_language_example: Ella tiene la capacidad de resolver problemas difíciles.
native_language_example: She has the ability to solve difficult problems.

meaning: “(he/she) has the habit of”; “(he/she) tends to.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a repeated behavior (a habit). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: tiene la costumbre de + hacer/comer/leer… You can change it for other people and tenses: tengo/tienes/tenemos la costumbre de…, tenía la costumbre de…, etc.
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene la costumbre de llegar tarde.
native_language_example: My brother has the habit of arriving late.

tiene la misma edad que yo

target_language_multi_word_term: tiene la misma edad que yo
meaning: “he/she has the same age as me” (is the same age as I am).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the same age as you. You can change the subject and pronoun: “Tengo la misma edad que tú” (I’m the same age as you), “Ella tiene la misma edad que él” (She’s the same age as him). Often appears with a name or pronoun before it.
target_language_example: Mi amiga tiene la misma edad que yo.
native_language_example: My friend is the same age as I am.

meaning: "(he/she) has (the) eyes" (used to describe eye appearance/color).
additional_notes: Used with descriptions of eyes, especially color or size: "Tiene los ojos verdes" = "She has green eyes." Spanish commonly uses the definite article "los" (the) where English uses a possessive ("her/his"). You can also add "de + someone" to show resemblance or inheritance: "Tiene los ojos de su padre" = "He has his father's eyes."
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene los ojos marrones.
native_language_example: My brother has brown eyes.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s eye color. The verb changes with the subject: yo tengo…, tú tienes…, él/ella tiene…, nosotros tenemos…, ellos tienen…. You can swap in other colors: tiene los ojos verdes (green), marrones/cafés (brown), negros (black).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene los ojos azules.
native_language_example: My brother has blue eyes.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tener miedo** (“to be afraid”). **Tiene** is the **él/ella/usted** form of *tener* in the present tense. You often add **de** or **a/al** to say what someone is afraid of: **tiene miedo de** + noun/verb (“afraid of...”), **tiene miedo a/al** + noun (“afraid of...”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: My brother is afraid to speak in public.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **tener miedo (a/de)** = “to be afraid (of).” Here it’s **tiene** (3rd person singular: he/she/it). Add **a** before a specific thing/person you fear: **tener miedo a los perros**. With pronouns, Spanish often adds an indirect object pronoun: **le tiene miedo a los perros** (“he is afraid of dogs”), **les tiene miedo a los perros** (“he is afraid of dogs / of them” depending on context).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene miedo a los perros, pero le encantan los gatos.
native_language_example: My sister is afraid of dogs, but she loves cats.

additional_notes: Used with a subject + tener miedo de + noun or verb (infinitive). With nouns, it’s often followed by de + el/los/la/las (e.g., de la oscuridad, de los perros). With verbs, use de + infinitive (e.g., de caer, de decir la verdad). You can negate it with no: no tiene miedo de…
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene miedo de hablar en público.
native_language_example: My brother is afraid of speaking in public.

meaning: "has a lot of" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "tener" (to have) in the 3rd person singular (él/ella/usted). "Mucha" agrees with a feminine singular noun: tiene mucha paciencia / mucha hambre / mucha experiencia. With masculine nouns, it changes to "tiene mucho" (tiene mucho tiempo).
target_language_example: Ella tiene mucha suerte hoy.
native_language_example: She has a lot of luck today.

meaning: “has many” (used before a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: From the verb **tener** (“to have”): **tiene** = “he/she/you (formal) has”. **Muchas** means “many” and must match a **feminine plural** noun (e.g., *ideas, bolsas*). For masculine plural nouns, use **tiene muchos** (e.g., *tiene muchos amigos*).
target_language_example: Ella tiene muchas preguntas.
native_language_example: She has many questions.

meaning: (he/she) really wants to; is eager to; is really looking forward to.
additional_notes: Used with **de + infinitive** (tiene muchas ganas de ir/practicar/volver) or **de + noun** (tiene muchas ganas de un vestido nuevo). It’s a common way to talk about strong desire or enthusiasm. You can change the subject: **tengo / tienes / tenemos muchas ganas de**.
target_language_example: Tengo muchas ganas de verte este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I’m really looking forward to seeing you this weekend.

meaning: "(he/she/it) has a lot (of)"; often used to mean "(he/she) is very" + noun (e.g., afraid).
additional_notes: "Tiene mucho" is the 3rd-person singular of tener (to have) + mucho (a lot). It’s commonly followed by a noun: tiene mucho miedo (is very afraid / has a lot of fear), tiene mucha hambre (is very hungry), tiene mucho sueño (is very sleepy). With feminine nouns, use mucha (e.g., mucha hambre).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene mucho miedo a las arañas.
native_language_example: My brother is very afraid of spiders.

additional_notes: Uses the verb tener (“to have”). "Tiene" is the third-person singular present tense (“he/she/it has,” also used for formal “you” = usted). You can change the subject: "Tengo mucho dinero" (I have a lot of money), "Tienen mucho dinero" (they have a lot of money).
target_language_example: Mi jefe tiene mucho dinero, pero trabaja todo el tiempo.
native_language_example: My boss has a lot of money, but he works all the time.

meaning: “has a lot to (do/see/lose/etc.)” / “has a lot to do with …” (with **que ver con**).
additional_notes: This is the 3rd-person singular form of **tener**: **tiene**. It’s a common pattern: **tener mucho que + infinitive** = “to have a lot to + verb.” Very often you’ll see **tiene mucho que ver con + noun/pronoun** (“has a lot to do with …”). You can change the subject: **tengo mucho que…** (I), **tenés/tienes mucho que…** (you), **tenemos mucho que…** (we).
target_language_example: Este tema tiene mucho que ver con tu trabajo.
native_language_example: This topic has a lot to do with your job.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (“to have”) in 3rd person singular (él/ella/usted or a thing/place like “la región”). It’s followed by a plural noun: tiene muchos libros / tiene muchas amigas. Many changes to agree with the noun: muchos (masc. plural), muchas (fem. plural). With “more”: tiene muchos más + noun (“has many more … than …”).
target_language_example: Este museo tiene muchas obras famosas.
native_language_example: This museum has many famous works.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **tener** (“to have”) in the **usted/él/ella** form: **tiene**. It can describe someone in general, or you can add details after **amigos** (e.g., **amigos mexicanos**, **amigos en Boston**). With **Usted**, it’s a polite/formal “you.”
target_language_example: Mi profesor tiene muchos amigos en la ciudad.
native_language_example: My teacher has many friends in the city.

additional_notes: "Tiene" is the present tense of "tener" (to have) for él/ella/usted. It’s often used to describe what someone/something possesses (a person, a library, a school, etc.). You can change the subject: "Mi padre tiene muchos libros" (My father has many books).
target_language_example: Esta biblioteca tiene muchos libros en inglés.
native_language_example: This library has many books in English.

meaning: 'has more than' / 'is more than' (age, number, amount).
additional_notes: Used with "tener" to say someone/something is over a certain number. Very common with ages ("tiene más de 30 años" = "is over 30"), but also works for quantities like pages, people, etc. Often followed by a number; with age you usually add "años".
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene más de veinte años, pero parece menor.
native_language_example: My brother is over twenty years old, but he looks younger.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or degrees. Often followed by a noun (“tiene más libros”) or by “que” + what it’s being compared to (“tiene más pan que…”). It can also be figurative: “tiene más clase” = “has more class / is classier.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene más tiempo que yo.
native_language_example: My brother has more time than I do.

additional_notes: Used to compare how much money someone has with another person/thing. Pattern: (él/ella/usted) tiene más + noun + que + person/thing. With a following noun like “cerebro/sesos” (“brains”), it can be an insult meaning someone is rich but not very smart.
target_language_example: Ella tiene más dinero que yo.
native_language_example: She has more money than I do.

meaning: to have nothing to do with; to be unrelated to.
additional_notes: Almost always used with a negative word: "no tiene nada que ver con..." (= "it has nothing to do with..."). You can also use it with people to mean someone is not involved: "Él no tiene nada que ver con el asunto."
target_language_example: Eso no tiene nada que ver con lo que dije.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what I said.

additional_notes: From tener (to have) + problemas (problems). Used to say someone is in a difficult situation or has difficulties (general or specific): personales (personal), financieros (financial), cardíacos (heart problems/heart condition). You can change the subject and tense: tengo problemas, tenía problemas, tiene problemas.
target_language_example: Si necesitas ayuda, dime; sé que tienes problemas.
native_language_example: If you need help, tell me; I know you’re having trouble.

additional_notes: Used to say someone struggles to do an action. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., levantarse, dormir, recordar, concentrarse). You can change the form of tener to match the subject: tengo/ tienes/ tiene/ tenemos/ tienen problemas para…
target_language_example: Tengo problemas para entender este acento.
native_language_example: I have trouble understanding this accent.

additional_notes: Form of **tener que + infinitive** to express obligation or necessity. **Tiene que** is for **él/ella/usted**. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive: *tiene que ir, tiene que salir, tiene que trabajar*.
target_language_example: Ella tiene que estudiar hoy.
native_language_example: She has to study today.

meaning: "it has to be" / "it must be" (it needs to be; it’s supposed to be).
additional_notes: From "tener que" (to have to) + "estar" (to be, in a place/state). It’s used to express necessity/obligation ("It has to be done well") or a strong assumption, often about location: "Tiene que estar en alguna parte" = "It must be somewhere." You can change the subject: "tengo que estar" (I have to be), "tienen que estar" (they have to be).
target_language_example: Si no está aquí, tiene que estar en la oficina.
native_language_example: If it’s not here, it must be in the office.

additional_notes: Uses **tener que + infinitive** (“to have to / must”) to express strong necessity or a logical conclusion. **estar aquí** means “to be here” (temporary/location). Often said when you’re sure someone/something is present: *Tiene que estar aquí en alguna parte/en algún lado* (“It must be here somewhere”). You can change the subject: *tengo que estar aquí* (I have to be here), *tienen que estar aquí* (they have to be here).
target_language_example: Las llaves tienen que estar aquí; las dejé en la mesa.
native_language_example: The keys have to be here; I left them on the table.

additional_notes: Used to express necessity about a location or place where something should be (physical or abstract). It combines: tener que (to have to) + estar (to be, for location/state) + en (in/on/at). You can change it for other subjects: tengo que estar en (I have to be in), tiene que estar en (he/she/it has to be in), tenemos que estar en (we have to be in).
target_language_example: Tu pasaporte tiene que estar en la mochila.
native_language_example: Your passport has to be in the backpack.

additional_notes: Impersonal way to say something is necessary or must exist. It’s built from "tener que" (to have to) + "haber" (there is/are). Often followed by a noun: "Tiene que haber una forma" (There has to be a way). You can change the tense/person: "tenía que haber" (there had to be), "tendrá que haber" (there will have to be).
target_language_example: Tiene que haber una solución.
native_language_example: There has to be a solution.

meaning: "There has to be something." / "There must be something."
additional_notes: Used to say you're sure something exists or is available, often when you're searching or trying to find a solution. You can add details: "tiene que haber algo más (que eso)" (there has to be something more (than that)), "tiene que haber algo aquí/por aquí" (there has to be something here/around here), or "tiene que haber algo que + verb" (there must be something that I/you can do).
target_language_example: Tiene que haber algo que podamos hacer para arreglarlo.
native_language_example: There has to be something we can do to fix it.

additional_notes: Used to express that you strongly believe a solution/option exists. It uses the impersonal phrase “tiene que haber” (there has to be), followed by “algo que” (something that) and usually a verb in the subjunctive: “tiene que haber algo que podamos hacer” = “there has to be something we can do.”
target_language_example: Tiene que haber algo que podamos intentar hoy.
native_language_example: There has to be something we can try today.

additional_notes: Used to insist that an alternative exists. Often followed by a feminine noun (otra explicación/forma/manera/salida). You can also use plural: “Tiene que haber otras opciones.”
target_language_example: Tiene que haber otra manera de hacerlo.
native_language_example: There has to be another way to do it.

meaning: "there has to be a…" / "there must be a…" (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that something must exist or must be true. It’s an impersonal structure: literally “has to be a,” but in English you usually translate it as “there has to be a…”. Use **una** before a feminine noun (e.g., *una manera, una razón*). For masculine nouns, you’d use **un**: *tiene que haber un problema*.
target_language_example: Tiene que haber una solución.
native_language_example: There has to be a solution.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation or necessity. It’s the 3rd-person singular form of "tener que" + infinitive (he/she/it/you formal has to...). You can also see it in questions and in clauses like "lo que tiene que hacer" (“what [someone] has to do”).
target_language_example: Si quiere aprobar, tiene que hacer la tarea.
native_language_example: If you want to pass, you have to do the homework.

meaning: he/she/it has to go; must go.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tener que + infinitive** (“to have to + verb”), used to express obligation or necessity. **Tiene** is 3rd person singular (él/ella/usted). You can add a place or reason: **tiene que ir al banco** (“has to go to the bank”), or use it alone: **tiene que ir** (“has to go”). In sentence 4, **ir en los hombros** means “to go on someone’s shoulders / to be carried on shoulders.”
target_language_example: Lo siento, tiene que irse ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she has to leave now.

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) has to leave” / “must go away.”
additional_notes: Made of "tener que" (to have to/must) + "irse" (to leave/go away). Often followed by a place ("de Boston" = from Boston) or a time expression ("en unos minutos" = in a few minutes, "ya" = right now). You can change the subject: "tengo que irme" (I have to leave), "tienes que irte" (you have to leave), "tenemos que irnos" (we have to leave).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tiene que irse ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Sorry, you have to leave right now.

additional_notes: Form of **tener que + infinitive** to express obligation/necessity. **Tiene** agrees with the subject (él/ella/usted); change it for other subjects: *tengo que pagar, tienes que pagar, tenemos que pagar*, etc. Often used literally (pay money) and also figuratively to mean “to suffer the consequences / pay for it,” especially with **pagar por (algo)**.
target_language_example: Si rompes algo, tienes que pagar por ello.
native_language_example: If you break something, you have to pay for it.

meaning: “has to be / must be” (necessity or strong deduction).
additional_notes: From "tener que" + "ser". Used (1) to express obligation/requirement: "Tiene que ser retirado" = "It has to be removed"; and (2) to express a strong guess or conclusion: "Tiene que ser ella" / "Tom tiene que ser canadiense" = "It must be her" / "Tom must be Canadian." Often you’ll also hear other persons: "tengo que ser", "tienes que ser", "tenemos que ser", etc.
target_language_example: Tiene que ser ahora; después no puedo.
native_language_example: It has to be now; later I can’t.

meaning: 'it has to be a' / 'it must be a' (necessity or strong conclusion).
additional_notes: Used to express either obligation/requirement or a strong guess based on evidence. It’s formed with tener que + infinitive: "tiene que ser" + noun. Change for person/number and gender: "tengo que ser...", "tienen que ser..."; "un" → "una"; plural: "unos/unas".
target_language_example: Con ese acento, tiene que ser un turista.
native_language_example: With that accent, he must be a tourist.

meaning: “has to be / must be” (necessity or strong deduction).
additional_notes: From "tener que" + "ser". Used (1) to express obligation/requirement: "Tiene que ser retirado" = "It has to be removed"; and (2) to express a strong guess or conclusion: "Tiene que ser ella" / "Tom tiene que ser canadiense" = "It must be her" / "Tom must be Canadian." Often you’ll also hear other persons: "tengo que ser", "tienes que ser", "tenemos que ser", etc.
target_language_example: Tiene que ser ahora; después no puedo.
native_language_example: It has to be now; later I can’t.

meaning: “it has to do with…” / “it’s related to…”
additional_notes: Used with **con** to connect two things: **tener que ver con + noun/pronoun**. It can also appear in questions like **¿Qué tiene que ver X con Y?** (“What does X have to do with Y?”). The verb changes by subject: **tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos/tienen que ver**.
target_language_example: Esto no tiene que ver con lo que dijiste.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with what you said.

additional_notes: From tener (“to have”) + razón (“reason/right”). Used to agree that someone is correct. Change the verb to match the subject: tengo razón (I’m right), tienes razón (you’re right), tenemos razón (we’re right), tienen razón (they’re right). Often followed by en + topic: Tiene razón en eso (“You’re right about that”).
target_language_example: Perdón, tienes razón: me equivoqué.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re right: I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical or understandable. You can add "para mí" (to me) or "que" + a clause: "Tiene sentido que...". Other forms: "no tiene sentido" (it doesn’t make sense), "tenía sentido" (it made sense).
target_language_example: Lo que dices tiene sentido.
native_language_example: What you’re saying makes sense.

additional_notes: Used to say something possesses a unique, distinct thing or feature. It agrees with a feminine noun: tiene su propia personalidad/cultura/lengua. For masculine nouns, use “tiene su propio” (e.g., tiene su propio estilo). Often appears with “Cada…” (“Each…”) to emphasize that every person/thing is different.
target_language_example: Cada ciudad tiene su propia historia.
native_language_example: Each city has its own history.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has something that belongs only to them (not shared). The verb changes with the subject: tengo mi propio (I have my own), tienes tu propio (you have your own), tiene su propio (he/she/it has his/her/its own). The noun after it agrees in gender and number: propio/propria/propios/propias (e.g., su propia habitación; sus propios libros).
target_language_example: Cada trabajador tiene su propio escritorio.
native_language_example: Each worker has their own desk.

additional_notes: Used to say someone possesses or has achieved all the things they want/need. It’s the verb phrase “tiene” (has) + “todo lo que” (everything that/that which), usually followed by what the person wants, needs, or could desire. You can change the subject/verb: “tengo todo lo que…” (I have everything that…), “tienes todo lo que…” (you have…), “tenemos…” (we have…).
target_language_example: Ella tiene todo lo que necesita para el viaje.
native_language_example: She has everything that she needs for the trip.

meaning: “has three …” / “there are three …” (said about what someone/something has).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "tener" (to have) to give a count of things someone or something possesses or includes: "X tiene tres + noun (plural)." Often followed by a measurement or unit (e.g., "tiene tres millas de ancho" = it’s three miles wide). The subject can be a person, object, place, or thing.
target_language_example: El apartamento tiene tres ventanas.
native_language_example: The apartment has three windows.

additional_notes: Uses **tener** (to have) in the **él/ella/usted** form: **tiene**. **Hijos** can mean “children” in general, but literally “sons”; for mixed or unspecified gender you can also hear **tres hijos** used to mean “three kids,” or **tres hijos e hijas** for clarity.
target_language_example: Mi vecino tiene tres hijos y una hija.
native_language_example: My neighbor has three sons and a daughter.

meaning: "(he/she/it) has a" (introduces a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (to have) in the él/ella/usted form: tiene. It’s followed by un + a masculine singular noun (e.g., un coche, un problema). For a feminine noun, use tiene una.
target_language_example: Tiene un perro muy simpático.
native_language_example: He/She has a very nice dog.

meaning: "(he/she/it) has a good ..." (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe that someone or something possesses a positive quality: "tiene un buen + [noun]". "Buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" and is used before a masculine singular noun (buen estilo, buen aroma, buen manejo). You can change "tiene" to match the subject: "tengo un buen..." (I have), "tienes un buen..." (you have), "tenemos un buen..." (we have).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un buen sentido del humor.
native_language_example: My sister has a good sense of humor.

additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is the present tense for él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). You can add adjectives after "coche" (e.g., "tiene un coche azul") or add details with "de" (e.g., "tiene un coche de Japón"). In many countries, "car" can also be "auto" or "carro".
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un coche nuevo.
native_language_example: My sister has a new car.

additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is used for he/she/it/you (formal) in the present tense: "Él/Ella/Usted tiene un gato". Often followed by an adjective like a color: "tiene un gato blanco/negro".
target_language_example: Mi vecino tiene un gato negro.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a black cat.

meaning: “has a great/big …” (to describe something as large or important).
additional_notes: Used with a singular masculine noun: tiene un gran + noun (gran is the shortened form of grande before a singular noun). It can describe physical size (un gran dormitorio) or importance/quality (un gran interés, un gran futuro, un gran corazón). For a feminine singular noun, use una gran + noun (e.g., una gran idea).
target_language_example: Esta ciudad tiene un gran problema de tráfico.
native_language_example: This city has a big traffic problem.

additional_notes: From the verb tener (“to have”) in the present tense (tiene = “has”). It’s often followed by details with que (“who/that”): “Tiene un hermano que vive en Tokio.” Can also be used with people’s names (“Tom tiene un hermano…”) and combined with other family members: “Tiene un hermano y dos hermanas.”
target_language_example: Mi amiga tiene un hermano menor.
native_language_example: My friend has a younger brother.

meaning: "(He/She) has a son" / "has a child" (a son).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has a son (male child). It’s the 3rd person singular of tener (“to have”): él/ella/usted tiene un hijo. For other people: tengo un hijo (I have a son), tienes un hijo (you have a son), tenemos un hijo (we have a son).
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene un hijo de cinco años.
native_language_example: My sister has a five-year-old son.

meaning: 'has a lot of' / 'has loads of' (a large quantity of).
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to say someone/something has many of something: tiene un montón de + plural noun. It’s very common in spoken Spanish and sounds informal/colloquial. You can change the subject and the verb: tengo un montón de…, tenemos un montón de…, etc.
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de trabajo hoy.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work today.

additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is used with él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). Often followed by an adjective (e.g., "un perro grande") or combined with other pets ("y seis gatos").
target_language_example: Mi vecino tiene un perro muy amable.
native_language_example: My neighbor has a very friendly dog.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone/something has a small amount of something (food, a quality, a feeling, a condition, etc.). Often interchangeable with "tiene algo de" (has some). You can change the verb for other people: "tengo un poco de" (I have a little), "tienes un poco de" (you have a little), "tienen un poco de" (they have a little).
target_language_example: Hoy tengo un poco de fiebre.
native_language_example: Today I have a little fever.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **tener un problema** (“to have a problem”). **Tiene** is the 3rd-person singular form (he/she/it/you-formal). Use it for a general issue (“Tiene un problema”) or specify what kind: **tiene un problema de** + noun (e.g., *de acné*), **tiene un problema con** + thing/person (e.g., *con la bebida* = with alcohol/drinking), or **tiene un problema en/al** + body part (common in some regions: *al corazón*).
target_language_example: Mi coche tiene un problema, no arranca.
native_language_example: My car has a problem; it won’t start.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something tastes. Often followed by an adjective (extraño, amargo, dulce) or by “a + noun” (a chocolate, a fresa). You can change the verb to match the subject: tengo/tienes/tiene/tenemos/tienen un sabor.
target_language_example: Esta salsa tiene un sabor picante.
native_language_example: This sauce has a spicy flavor.

meaning: 'has a' (he/she/it has a + feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: From the verb **tener** (to have), **tiene** is the 3rd-person singular present tense: *he/she/it has*. **Una** is the feminine singular form of “a/an.” Use **tiene una** before a feminine singular noun (e.g., *una vaca, una frontera, una esposa*). For masculine singular nouns, use **tiene un**.
target_language_example: Mi hermana tiene una bicicleta nueva.
native_language_example: My sister has a new bicycle.

meaning: "(he/she/it) has a good …" (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to say someone has a good chance, opportunity, reputation, collection, etc. It’s from the verb *tener* (to have): *tiene* = “has” (for él/ella/usted). Change it to match the noun: *tiene un buen +* masculine noun (e.g., *tiene un buen trabajo*), or plural: *tiene buenas / buenos +* plural noun.
target_language_example: María tiene una buena oportunidad de estudiar en el extranjero.
native_language_example: María has a good opportunity to study abroad.

additional_notes: From the verb "tener" (to have). "Tiene" is the third-person singular form, used with él/ella/usted or a name (e.g., Tom). Often followed by a location ("en el sur", "en Italia") or by a description introduced by "que" ("una casa que..."). In many contexts it implies ownership, but it can also simply mean someone has access to a house.
target_language_example: María tiene una casa cerca del mar.
native_language_example: María has a house near the sea.

additional_notes: Used to describe where someone’s scar is located. After en, you usually give a body part or place: en la cara (on the face), en el brazo (on the arm). Possession is expressed with tener (“to have”), and articles are common with body parts (el/la). You may also hear en su brazo (“on his/her arm”) for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Ella tiene una cicatriz en la pierna.
native_language_example: She has a scar on her leg.

meaning: “(He/She) has a flower in/on …” (followed by a body part or place).
additional_notes: Used with a location phrase after en (e.g., en su pelo = in her hair, en la mano = in the hand). In Spanish, en can mean “in” or “on” depending on context.
target_language_example: Tiene una flor en el pelo.
native_language_example: She has a flower in her hair.

meaning: "has a great / large" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "tener" (to have) + "una" (a, feminine) + "gran" (short form of "grande" used before a noun). It’s followed by a feminine noun: "una gran prioridad", "una gran carga". With masculine nouns you typically say "un gran ...".
target_language_example: Ella tiene una gran oportunidad para estudiar en el extranjero.
native_language_example: She has a great opportunity to study abroad.

meaning: 'has a personality' (describes someone's character or way of being).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to describe what someone is like as a person: "tiene una personalidad fuerte/dócil/maravillosa". In Spanish, "personalidad" is commonly paired with "tener". You can also say "Tiene personalidad" (without "una") to mean someone has presence/character (often positive).
target_language_example: Mi jefe tiene una personalidad muy tranquila.
native_language_example: My boss has a very calm personality.

meaning: "has a (… ) voice" (used to describe someone’s voice).
additional_notes: Use "tener" + "una voz" + an adjective to describe the quality of someone’s voice (e.g., dulce = sweet, suave = soft, hermosa = beautiful, agradable = pleasant, baja = low, profunda = deep). You can also use "voz" with "de" + noun: "Tiene voz de niño" (He has a childlike voice).
target_language_example: Ella tiene una voz muy tranquila.
native_language_example: She has a very calm voice.

additional_notes: From the verb tener (“to have”) + hambre (“hunger”). Spanish commonly uses tener + hambre to express hunger (literally “to have hunger”). Tienen is the present tense for ellos/ellas/ustedes (“they/you all”).
target_language_example: Mis amigos tienen hambre, así que vamos a comer.
native_language_example: My friends are hungry, so we’re going to eat.

additional_notes: Used to say two people, languages, countries, or things share many similarities (interests, traits, features). The verb changes with the subject: yo tengo / tú tienes / él-ella tiene / nosotros tenemos / ellos-ellas tienen mucho en común. You can add “con …” to say “in common with …”: “Los japoneses tienen mucho en común con los chinos.”
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos mucho en común: nos gusta la misma música.
native_language_example: My sister and I have a lot in common: we like the same music.

additional_notes: Third-person plural of “tener que” + infinitive to express obligation or necessity. Used for rules, requirements, strong advice, or logical necessity: “Tienen que estar en alguna parte” = “They have to be somewhere.” In speech you may also hear it without the subject (as in “Muchachos, tienen que ver esto”).
target_language_example: Si quieren aprobar, tienen que estudiar más.
native_language_example: If they want to pass, they have to study more.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "tener" for "they" (ellos/ellas/ustedes). Used before a feminine singular noun (una + noun): "tienen una casa", "tienen una pista". For a masculine noun, use "tienen un".
target_language_example: Mis vecinos tienen una perra muy tranquila.
native_language_example: My neighbors have a very calm (female) dog.

meaning: “you have the right to” / “you’re entitled to”.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is allowed to do something or is legally/morally entitled to something. Usually followed by an infinitive (tienes derecho a hablar, a estarlo) or a noun (tienes derecho a un abogado, a la verdad). It can also appear in more formal/legal contexts (e.g., police rights: “Tienes derecho a permanecer callado”).
target_language_example: Tienes derecho a pedir una explicación.
native_language_example: You have the right to ask for an explanation.

meaning: You have a lot to learn.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they still need to gain knowledge/experience. It can be neutral or sound critical/condescending depending on tone and context. Often followed by "sobre/acerca de" (about) or "de" (from someone/something): "Tienes mucho que aprender de él" = you can learn a lot from him.
target_language_example: Todavía tienes mucho que aprender sobre este trabajo.
native_language_example: You still have a lot to learn about this job.

additional_notes: From "tener que" + infinitive to express obligation or necessity. "Tienes" is used with "tú" (informal singular "you"). For formal "you," use "tiene que" (usted), and for "you all" use "tienen que" (ustedes).
target_language_example: Tienes que estudiar hoy si quieres aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: You have to study today if you want to pass the exam.

meaning: “you have to endure / put up with it” or “you have to hold on.”
additional_notes: Uses tener que + infinitive to express obligation (“you have to…”). Aguantar often means to tolerate something unpleasant (noise, pain, a situation) or to keep going for a little longer (“hang in there”). You’ll often see it with time expressions like un poco / un poco más.
target_language_example: Lo sé, es difícil, pero tienes que aguantar un poco más.
native_language_example: I know it’s hard, but you have to hang in there a little longer.

meaning: "you have to learn to" / "you need to learn to".
additional_notes: Used to say something is necessary or important to learn. It’s addressed to one person (tú). You can add any verb after a: Tienes que aprender a decir, a hablar, a respetar, etc. (You’ll often hear the same pattern with other people: tienes/tenés que aprender a, tiene que aprender a, tenemos que aprender a…).
target_language_example: Tienes que aprender a pedir ayuda cuando la necesitas.
native_language_example: You need to learn to ask for help when you need it.

meaning: “you have to trust me” / “you must trust me.”
additional_notes:
Used to tell someone it’s necessary they trust you. 
- tienes que = “you have to / you must” (informal singular tú)
- confiar en = “to trust (in)” someone or something: confiar en mí/ti/él/ella
For a more formal “you,” use: "tiene que confiar en mí" (usted).
target_language_example: No puedo explicarlo todo ahora, pero tienes que confiar en mí.
native_language_example: I can’t explain everything right now, but you have to trust me.

meaning: you have to say; you need to tell (me/us).
additional_notes: "Tienes que" expresses obligation/necessity (“you have to / you need to”), and it’s followed by an infinitive like "decir" (to say/tell). It can mean "say" (e.g., give a speech: "tienes que decir tu discurso") or "tell" when there’s an object: "me tienes que decir" (you have to tell me), "nos tienes que decir" (you have to tell us). Often used for instructions, requirements, or urgency (e.g., "de inmediato").
target_language_example: Me tienes que decir la verdad.
native_language_example: You have to tell me the truth.

meaning: you have to tell me / you need to tell me.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone directly that it’s necessary for them to tell you something. It’s formed from "tener que" (to have to) + "decir" (to say/tell) + "me" (to me). You can follow it with a question word ("dónde", "qué", "quién") or with "lo que" to ask for information: "Tienes que decirme dónde está..." / "Tienes que decirme lo que piensas".
target_language_example: Tienes que decirme la verdad.
native_language_example: You have to tell me the truth.

meaning: "You have to leave / stop (doing something) / let (someone/something)".
additional_notes:
tienes que = “you have to” (obligation). dejar is flexible:
- dejar + a alguien/algo: “leave someone/something” (Tienes que dejar Boston.)
- dejar + infinitive: “stop doing” (Tienes que dejar de fumar.)
- dejar atrás: “leave behind” (Tienes que dejar atrás lo más importante.)
- dejar + algo + adjective/place: “leave something” a certain way/place (Tienes que dejar el plato limpio.)
- dejar que + [verb]: “let / allow that…” (Tienes que dejar que yo ayude.)
target_language_example: Tienes que dejar que te explique.
native_language_example: You have to let me explain.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they must stop an action: “tienes que” = “you have to,” and “dejar de + infinitive” = “to stop/quit doing.” Common with habits or repeated actions (apostar, beber, decir, hacer, etc.). Often sounds like advice or a strong warning depending on tone.
target_language_example: Tienes que dejar de fumar; te hace daño.
native_language_example: You have to stop smoking; it’s hurting you.

meaning: "you have to understand" / "you need to understand."
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that understanding something is necessary. It uses the verb phrase "tener que" (to have to) + an infinitive ("entender"). "Tienes" is the tú form, so it’s said to one person you address as "tú." Often followed by "que" + a full idea: "Tienes que entender que..." (You have to understand that...).
target_language_example: Tienes que entender que no puedo ir hoy.
native_language_example: You have to understand that I can’t go today.

meaning: “you have to be” / “you need to be.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required/expected to be in a place or in a certain state/condition. It combines tener que (to have to) + estar (to be, for location/temporary state). You can follow it with a place (en casa), an adjective (listo), or a situation (aquí, allí).
target_language_example: Tienes que estar aquí a las ocho.
native_language_example: You have to be here at eight.

meaning: 'you have to do' / 'you need to do'.
additional_notes: Uses tener que + infinitive to talk about obligation or necessity. "Tienes" is the tú (you) form in the present tense, so it’s used when speaking to one person informally. You can add an object after "hacer" (e.g., "tienes que hacer mil puntos" = you have to score 1,000 points). Often appears in "lo que tienes que hacer" = "what you have to do."
target_language_example: Primero tienes que hacer la tarea y luego puedes salir.
native_language_example: First you have to do your homework, and then you can go out.

meaning: "you have to do this" / "you need to do this".
additional_notes: Uses tener que + infinitive (hacer) to express obligation/necessity. It’s addressed to one person informally (tú): tienes. With no, it means “you don’t have to / you don’t need to” (not that you must not). Ya no tienes que… means “you don’t have to anymore.”
target_language_example: Si quieres aprobar, tienes que hacer esto.
native_language_example: If you want to pass, you have to do this.

meaning: "you have to do it" / "you must do it."
additional_notes: Used to say someone is required or obligated to do something. It’s the phrase "tener que" (to have to) + "hacerlo" (to do it). Often followed by emphasis words like "ya" (right now), "inmediatamente" (immediately), or "tú mismo / tú" (you yourself) to stress urgency or who must do it.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que hacerlo hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you have to do it today.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity. It’s the structure **tener que + infinitive**: *tienes que* (you have to) + *ir* (to go). Depending on context, it can mean going somewhere (*tienes que ir con ellos* = you have to go with them) or leaving (*si te tienes que ir* = if you have to leave). You can add a destination with **a** (*tienes que ir a casa*) or a purpose like **a por** (*tienes que ir a por ella* = you have to go get her).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que ir ahora.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you have to go now.

meaning: “you have to go to …” / “you need to go to …”
additional_notes: Used to tell someone an obligation or requirement: tienes que (you have to) + ir a (to go to) + a place or an action. Common with destinations (la corte, la fábrica, la policía) or an infinitive after "ir a" (e.g., ir a presentar cargos = to go file/press charges).
target_language_example: Tienes que ir a la oficina mañana.
native_language_example: You have to go to the office tomorrow.

meaning: “you have to leave” / “you need to go (away)” (said to one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell or remind one person (tú) that they must leave. It’s very common with places or destinations: “Tienes que irte a casa / a la oficina…”. It can also mean “go to (do something)” with an infinitive phrase: “Tienes que irte a dormir” = “You have to go to sleep.” Often strengthened with time words like “ahora” (now) or “ya” (right away).
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que irte ya.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but you have to leave right now.

meaning: you have to pay (you must pay).
additional_notes: "Tienes que" + infinitive expresses obligation/necessity. "Tienes que pagar" is used when telling one person (tú) they are required to pay, either for a bill/service ("pagar el teléfono") or as a consequence ("pagar por ello" = pay for it / face the consequences).
target_language_example: Lo siento, tienes que pagar antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Sorry, you have to pay before going in.

additional_notes: From tener que (to have to) + quedarse (to stay/remain). Used to tell someone it’s necessary to remain somewhere or not leave. With an extra word like con (quedarte con algo), it can mean 'to keep/hold on to/remember' something: Tienes que quedarte con los detalles = You have to remember/keep the details.
target_language_example: Tienes que quedarte aquí hasta que llegue el médico.
native_language_example: You have to stay here until the doctor arrives.

meaning: "you have to keep (doing something)" / "you have to follow".
additional_notes: "Tienes que" = "you have to" (obligation). "Seguir" can mean (1) "to continue/keep doing" + a gerund: "seguir cantando/comiendo" = "keep singing/eating"; or (2) "to follow" + a noun: "seguir las instrucciones/el guión" = "follow the instructions/the script".
target_language_example: Tienes que seguir estudiando todos los días.
native_language_example: You have to keep studying every day.

meaning: you have to be / you must be.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that it’s necessary to be a certain way. It can be advice, a rule, or an obligation. Uses tener que (to have to) + infinitive ser (to be). For other people: tengo que ser (I have to be), tienes que ser (you), tiene que ser (he/she/you formal), tenemos que ser (we), tienen que ser (they/you all).
target_language_example: Si quieres el trabajo, tienes que ser puntual.
native_language_example: If you want the job, you have to be on time.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they need to improve a quality (often as advice or a mild reprimand). It’s followed by an adjective: Tienes que ser más + educado/específico/paciente. "Tienes que" expresses obligation/necessity (more like "you need to" than "you must" in many contexts).
target_language_example: Tienes que ser más cuidadoso con lo que dices.
native_language_example: You have to be more careful with what you say.

meaning: “you have to have / you need to have”.
additional_notes: Used to express an obligation or requirement: "tienes que" (you have to) + "tener" (to have). It’s often followed by a noun ("tienes que tener público"), an adjective phrase ("tienes que tener bien la espalda"), or a past participle to mean something must be finished by a certain time ("tienes que tener terminado..." = you must have it finished).
target_language_example: Para viajar, tienes que tener pasaporte.
native_language_example: To travel, you have to have a passport.

meaning: you have to come / you need to come.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that coming is necessary or required. "tienes que" expresses obligation/necessity; it can sound like a firm instruction depending on tone. Often followed by a place/person/time (a casa, a verme, ahora mismo).
target_language_example: Tienes que venir conmigo al médico.
native_language_example: You have to come with me to the doctor.

meaning: "you have to come back" / "you must return".
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that returning is required/necessary. Commonly followed by a place or group: volver adentro (go back inside), volver con la familia/con nosotros (come back with the family/with us). In commands, it can sound firm or urgent depending on tone.
target_language_example: Lo siento, pero tienes que volver mañana.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but you have to come back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone or admit they were correct (often after realizing a mistake). It can sound more direct than “sí” and is commonly used with intensifiers like “sí,” “lo siento,” or “claro.” You can change the verb to match the person: “tiene razón” (you formal/he/she), “tengo razón” (I’m right), “tienen razón” (you all/they).
target_language_example: Perdón, tienes razón: me equivoqué.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re right: I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree with someone or admit they’re right. It’s the tú (informal singular) form; for someone you address as usted, say “tiene toda la razón,” and for you all, “tienen toda la razón.” Often said alone as a full response.
target_language_example: Perdón, tienes toda la razón: me equivoqué.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re completely right: I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used with the verb tener (to have) to say someone has/possesses something or has something happening (like a visitor). It’s addressed to “tú” (informal singular “you”). Use **tienes una** before singular feminine nouns (e.g., *Tienes una idea*).
target_language_example: Tienes un problema.
native_language_example: You have a problem.

meaning: 'you have a' (to talk to one person informally, before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with tú (informal 'you') in the present tense of tener: tú tienes. 'Una' is the feminine form of 'a/an' and must match a feminine singular noun (una habitación, una elección, una pluma). For formal 'you', use 'tiene una'.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes una pregunta?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

additional_notes: Used to classify something or someone: “del tipo de…” = “the kind of…”. It can also mean “a type/sort of” in general statements (ningún tipo de = “no kind/type of”), and with “el mismo tipo de” = “the same kind/type of”. It’s sometimes used more loosely like “my kind of … / the kind of … I like” (e.g., mi tipo de éxito = “my kind of success”).
target_language_example: No es mi tipo de música, pero la respeto.
native_language_example: It’s not my kind of music, but I respect it.

meaning: 'kind/type of thing(s)' (often in phrases like 'este tipo de cosas' = 'these kinds of things').
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about categories of things rather than specific items. Very common with demonstratives: este/ese/aquel tipo de cosas = this/that kind of thing. Also appears as 'todo tipo de cosas' meaning 'all kinds of things' (a wide variety). Usually plural 'cosas' even when referring to something in general.
target_language_example: No me gusta hablar de este tipo de cosas en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about these kinds of things at work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a genre or style of music. Often appears with demonstratives like este/ese/aquel ("this/that kind of music") or with todo ("all kinds of music").
target_language_example: ¿Qué tipo de música te gusta?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s typical character or behavior, followed by a verb phrase: “Es del tipo de persona que + verb” (He’s the kind of person who…), or “No es del tipo de persona que + verb” (He’s not the kind of person who…). You’ll also see it with articles: “el tipo de persona que / un tipo de persona que.”
target_language_example: No soy el tipo de persona que se rinde fácilmente.
native_language_example: I’m not the kind of person who gives up easily.

additional_notes: "Tipo" is often used in casual speech to mean "guy" or "dude". "Que" introduces a description (a relative clause): "el tipo que..." = "the guy who..." and "un tipo que..." = "a guy who...". In more neutral/formal Spanish, you might use "hombre" or "señor" instead of "tipo".
target_language_example: Conozco a un tipo que habla inglés muy bien.
native_language_example: I know a guy who speaks English very well.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "tirar" = "to throw". Usually used with "a" for the target ("tiró una piedra al perro" = threw a stone at the dog) or with "en" for the place it lands ("tiró una piedra en el estanque" = threw a stone into the pond).
target_language_example: Tiró una piedra al agua y salpicó.
native_language_example: He threw a stone into the water and it splashed.

additional_notes: From the verb **tocar** (to play an instrument) + **el piano** (the piano). It agrees with the subject: **yo toco**, **tú tocas**, **él/ella/usted toca**, **nosotros tocamos**, **ellos tocan**. Often used with adverbs like **muy bien** (very well).
target_language_example: Mi hermana toca el piano en una banda.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano in a band.

additional_notes: From the verb tocar (“to play” a musical instrument) + la flauta (“the flute”). Change the subject and verb form as needed: yo toco la flauta, tú tocas la flauta, él/ella toca la flauta, nosotros tocamos la flauta. You can also add en + place/group: en la orquesta (“in the orchestra”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana toca la flauta en la banda de la escuela.
native_language_example: My sister plays the flute in the school band.

additional_notes: From the verb "tocar" (to play an instrument). Here it’s conjugated in the present tense for él/ella/usted: "toca". To talk about yourself, use "(yo) toco la guitarra"; for you (informal), "(tú) tocas la guitarra". Spanish uses the article: "la guitarra" (the guitar).
target_language_example: Mi padre toca la guitarra en una banda.
native_language_example: My dad plays the guitar in a band.

meaning: "(he/she) was playing" or "used to play" the piano.
additional_notes: "Tocaba" is the imperfect past of "tocar" (to play an instrument). Use it for ongoing actions in the past (what was happening) or habits/repeated actions in the past (what someone used to do). Often appears with background actions: "mientras" (while), "en ese momento" (at that moment).
target_language_example: Cuando era niño, tocaba el piano todos los días.
native_language_example: When I was a kid, I used to play the piano every day.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (tocando) of "tocar" to describe an action happening now or in the background (often with "estar": "estoy/está/estaba tocando..."). It can also describe someone as "the one who is playing" ("la chica que está tocando...") or something you saw/heard someone doing ("lo/la vi tocando...").
target_language_example: Estamos tocando el piano en la sala.
native_language_example: We’re playing the piano in the living room.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “tocar” (to play an instrument / to touch). With musical instruments in Spanish, you usually say “tocar” + the instrument: “tocar el piano”, “tocar la guitarra”.
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar el piano?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the piano?

additional_notes: Tocar is the verb used for playing musical instruments in Spanish (tocar la guitarra, tocar el piano). It’s often used with saber/poder to talk about ability: saber tocar la flauta = “to know how to play the flute.”
target_language_example: ¿Sabes tocar la flauta?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the flute?

additional_notes: Use "tocar" for playing musical instruments in Spanish (tocar el piano, tocar la batería, etc.). Often used after verbs like "querer", "poder", "aprender a", and "oír" (e.g., "Quiero aprender a tocar la guitarra").
target_language_example: Mi hermana toca la guitarra en una banda.
native_language_example: My sister plays the guitar in a band.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean a wide variety of things. It agrees with the idea of “all” (toda) + “type/kind” (clase) + “of” (de). Often interchangeable with "todo tipo de".
target_language_example: En esta tienda venden toda clase de productos.
native_language_example: In this store they sell all kinds of products.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean "all of the" or "the entire": toda la aldea (the whole village), toda la riqueza (all the wealth). It agrees in gender/number: toda la (fem. sing.), todo el (masc. sing.), todas las (fem. plural), todos los (masc. plural). Common in wishes: toda la suerte del mundo (all the luck in the world).
target_language_example: Pasé toda la noche estudiando.
native_language_example: I spent the whole night studying.

meaning: the whole house; all over the house.
additional_notes: Means the entire house (as a space). Often used with prepositions: "por toda la casa" = "all over/throughout the house" (searching or things scattered everywhere); "en toda la casa" = "in the whole house". "Tener toda la casa para (uno) solo" means having the whole house to yourself.
target_language_example: Busqué mis llaves por toda la casa.
native_language_example: I looked for my keys all over the house.

meaning: the whole city; the entire city.
additional_notes: Means all parts of the city as a single whole. Often appears with "por" ("por toda la ciudad") to mean "all over/throughout the city." "Toda" agrees with the feminine noun "la ciudad."
target_language_example: Hay carteles por toda la ciudad.
native_language_example: There are posters all over the city.

meaning: the whole family; everyone in the family.
additional_notes: Used to include every family member (not just one person). Often appears with a preposition, e.g. “a toda la familia” (to the whole family). It can also be used more emotionally/figuratively: “Eres toda la familia que tengo” = “You’re the only family I have.”
target_language_example: Voy a invitar a toda la familia a la fiesta.
native_language_example: I’m going to invite the whole family to the party.

additional_notes: Means “all the people” in a group or place, often like “everyone.” It’s feminine singular (gente), so it goes with singular verbs: “toda la gente está/anda/quedó…”.
target_language_example: En el concierto, toda la gente cantaba la misma canción.
native_language_example: At the concert, everyone was singing the same song.
