target_language_example: Mi mamá trabaja en un banco cerca de casa.
native_language_example: My mom works at a bank near our house.

meaning: "(he/she) works at/in a …" (a workplace/activity, feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. The verb is from **trabajar** (to work) in the **él/ella/usted** form: *trabaja*. It’s followed by **en** + **una** when the workplace noun is feminine: *una escuela, una tienda, una oficina*. For masculine nouns, you’ll often see *trabaja en un …* (e.g., *un banco*). In English this can be “works at a” or “works in a,” depending on the place.
target_language_example: Mi hermana trabaja en una cafetería del centro.
native_language_example: My sister works at a café downtown.

meaning: working hard in the field (doing farm work).
additional_notes: Uses the gerund "trabajando" (working) plus the adverb "duro" (hard) to describe an ongoing activity. Common with forms of "estar" to express what someone is/was/will be doing: "está/estuvo/estará trabajando...". "En el campo" usually refers to the countryside or farm fields.
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando duro en el campo para terminar antes de que anochezca.
native_language_example: We’re working hard in the field to finish before it gets dark.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (or sometimes seguir) to form the present progressive: estar trabajando en + place/project. With a place, it usually means being employed there or doing work there (e.g., in Africa). With a thing/idea, it means focusing effort on it (working on something).
target_language_example: Estamos trabajando en un proyecto nuevo.
native_language_example: We are working on a new project.

meaning: to work in/at (a place); to work on (a task/project).
additional_notes: Use **trabajar en + place** to say where you work (city, company, building): *trabajar en Osaka / en un hospital*. Use **trabajar en + thing** to mean working on something (improving/preparing it): *trabajar en su discurso / en esto*. Often interchangeable with **trabajar para** (to work for an employer), but **trabajar en** emphasizes location or the thing you’re working on.
target_language_example: Estoy trabajando en un proyecto nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m working on a new project.

meaning: “I work in/at/on …” (to say where you work or what you work on).
additional_notes: Used with places and organizations: “Trabajo en un supermercado” = “I work at a supermarket.” With projects/areas it can mean “work on/in”: “Trabajo en marketing” / “Trabajo en un proyecto.” Note: “Trabajo en equipo” means “teamwork” or “working as a team.”
target_language_example: Trabajo en una oficina cerca del centro.
native_language_example: I work in an office near downtown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about effort that is difficult and requires persistence. Often appears with verbs like "hacer" (to do) or "requerir" (to require), or in set phrases like "con trabajo duro" (with hard work). "Trabajo" is a noun and "duro" is an adjective meaning "hard/tough."
target_language_example: Con trabajo duro, puedes lograr tus metas.
native_language_example: With hard work, you can achieve your goals.

meaning: work to be done; work left to do.
additional_notes: Used to say there is still pending work. Often appears with “hay” (there is/are): “Hay mucho trabajo por hacer.” The pattern “por + infinitive” can express something that remains to be done (pending/unfinished).
target_language_example: Todavía tenemos trabajo por hacer antes de irnos.
native_language_example: We still have work to do before we leave.

meaning: (some) work to do; tasks that need to be done.
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to say you have work to do: "Tengo trabajo que hacer". You can add quantity/degree words like "mucho", "tanto", "un montón de", or adjectives like "importante": "Tengo mucho trabajo que hacer", "Tenemos importante trabajo que hacer". Similar to "cosas que hacer" (things to do).
target_language_example: No puedo salir hoy; tengo trabajo que hacer.
native_language_example: I can’t go out today; I have work to do.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase “hacer trampa (en un examen)” = “to cheat (on an exam).” You may also hear “copiar en el examen” (to copy/cheat) or “hacer trampa en una prueba” (test/quiz).
target_language_example: Si haces trampa en el examen, puedes suspender la clase.
native_language_example: If you cheat on the exam, you might fail the class.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happened following someone’s death. Common in more formal or written Spanish; in everyday speech you might also hear "después de la muerte de". It’s followed by a person (or sometimes an animal) or a noun referring to the deceased (e.g., "su madre").
target_language_example: Tras la muerte de mi abuelo, la familia se reunió en su casa.
native_language_example: After my grandfather’s death, the family met at his house.

additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) **Tratar de + noun** = “to deal with / to be about” (often in definitions or explanations): *La ética... trata de la conducta humana.*
2) **Tratar de + infinitive** = “to try to (do something)”: *Trata de dormir*, *Él trata de ver...*. In commands, **Trata de...** means “Try to...”. (Very common with **no**: *Trata de no preocuparte* = “Try not to worry.”)
target_language_example: Trata de llegar temprano mañana.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (verb in the "to + verb" form): "tratando de + verbo" (e.g., tratando de ahorrar, tratando de averiguar). Often appears with "estar" for an action in progress: "estoy/está/están tratando de..." It can also follow time expressions to show ongoing effort: "Pasé toda la tarde tratando de..."
target_language_example: Estoy tratando de aprender español, pero es difícil.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Spanish, but it's hard.

meaning: 'try to' (usted form); also, in 'se trate de', 'be about / be a'.
additional_notes: From the verb "tratar de". "Trate de + infinitive" is often a polite/formal command to one person (usted): "Trate de comprender" = "Try to understand." It can also appear after expressions like "Es posible que..." with the present subjunctive: "Es posible que trate de hacerlo". With "se trate de + noun", it means "it may be about / it may be a": "Puede que se trate de un bandido" = "It might be a bandit."
target_language_example: Trate de llegar temprano, por favor.
native_language_example: Try to arrive early, please.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (trato de + verb) to talk about making an effort to do something. Often implies the action is difficult or not guaranteed: Trato de no pensar en eso. In many contexts you may also hear "trato" without "de" (Trato de ayudar / Trato ayudar), but "trato de" is very common.
target_language_example: Trato de llegar temprano, pero siempre hay tráfico.
native_language_example: I try to arrive early, but there’s always traffic.

additional_notes: "Trat é de" is the preterite (past) first-person singular of "tratar de" + infinitive. It describes an attempt you made at a specific time in the past; it doesn’t necessarily mean you succeeded. Common pattern: "Trat é de" + infinitive (hacer, conseguir, escribir, no reírme, etc.).
target_language_example: Trat é de llamarte ayer, pero no contestaste.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the phrase “tratar de + infinitive” = “to try to do something.” It’s followed by an infinitive: “trató de convencer”, “trató de consolar”. Often used when you want to say someone made an effort, whether or not they succeeded. Note: “tratar” can look like English “treat,” but “tratar de” usually means “to try to,” not “to treat.”
target_language_example: Ella trató de llamarte, pero no pudo.
native_language_example: She tried to call you, but she couldn’t.

additional_notes: "Trató de" is the preterite (simple past) of "tratar de" (= to try to). "Ocultar" means "to hide/conceal," and "su" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their"—you know which from context. It’s typically followed by a noun, often an emotion or problem (e.g., "su confusión", "su dolor").
target_language_example: Él trató de ocultar su nerviosismo durante la entrevista.
native_language_example: He tried to hide his nervousness during the interview.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made an effort but didn’t succeed. It’s followed by an infinitive: “trató en vano de + infinitive.” Here “trató” is the preterite (past) form of “tratar de” (= to try to). You can change it for other subjects/tenses: “traté en vano de…”, “trataba en vano de…”, “trataron en vano de…”.
target_language_example: Los médicos trataron en vano de salvarlo.
native_language_example: The doctors tried in vain to save him.

additional_notes: Used mainly to talk about someone’s age with the verb "tener": "Tengo trece años" = "I’m thirteen." Also used with "cuando tenía trece años" to mean "when I was thirteen." In Spanish you generally say you "have" years, not "are" years old.
target_language_example: Tengo trece años y estoy en octavo grado.
native_language_example: I’m thirteen years old and I’m in eighth grade.

meaning: "thirty years" (an age or a length of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s age (cumplir treinta años = to turn 30) or a duration (llevar treinta años + gerund = to have been doing something for 30 years; hace treinta años = thirty years ago).
target_language_example: Viví en México durante treinta años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for thirty years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time (how long something takes or how long you wait) or about how late/early someone is. Often appears with phrases like “en treinta minutos” (in thirty minutes), “por treinta minutos” (for thirty minutes), “treinta minutos o menos” (thirty minutes or less), or “treinta minutos atrasado” (thirty minutes late).
target_language_example: La reunión dura treinta minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting lasts thirty minutes.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): “se había ido” (had left) to show the train left before another past action (e.g., arriving at the station). “ya” means “already,” emphasizing it was gone by the time you arrived.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde y el tren ya se había ido.
native_language_example: I arrived late and the train had already left.

additional_notes: Used to count down right before an action begins (starting a game, recording, jumping, etc.). Often said as part of a longer countdown (e.g., cinco, cuatro, tres, dos, uno) or after "en" to mean "in": "En tres, dos, uno" = "In three, two, one."
target_language_example: ¡En tres, dos, uno... acción!
native_language_example: In three, two, one... action!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time (duration) or about time relative to another moment (e.g., “three years later/after”). Often appears with time expressions like “han pasado…” (have passed) and “durante…” (for/during).
target_language_example: Estudié español durante tres años.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three days) or a point in time in the past (about three days ago). With "en tres días," it can mean a deadline/time until something happens (in three days). "Ya van tres días" means three days have already passed.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes terminarlo en tres días?
native_language_example: Can you finish it in three days?

additional_notes: "Tres" = "three" and "hijos" is the plural of "hijo" (son/child). Often used when talking about family size: "tener tres hijos" (to have three children) or "ser padre/madre de tres hijos" (to be the father/mother of three children). If you specifically mean children of any gender, you may also hear "tres hijos" used generically, but "tres hijos y dos hijas" specifies sons and daughters.
target_language_example: Mis padres tienen tres hijos.
native_language_example: My parents have three children.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (lasted three hours), a delay (delayed three hours), a frequency (every three hours), or a time difference (three hours earlier/before). You can also use it with "otras" to mean "another three hours" ("otras tres horas").
target_language_example: Esperamos tres horas en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We waited three hours at the airport.

additional_notes: A time duration or time point measured in months. Common with expressions like: cada tres meses (every three months), en menos de tres meses (in less than three months), tres meses después (three months later), and for how long something lasts: Vivirá aquí tres meses (He’ll live here for three months).
target_language_example: Estudié español durante tres meses.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three months.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a short amount of time (duration) or a point in time (in three minutes / three minutes later). Common patterns: “por tres minutos” = for three minutes; “en tres minutos” = in three minutes (from now); “tres minutos más tarde” = three minutes later; “los últimos tres minutos” = the last three minutes.
target_language_example: Vuelvo en tres minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in three minutes.

meaning: "three or four"; used to mean "about/around a few" (an approximate number).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the exact number and are estimating. It can modify many things: amounts (tres o cuatro mil), time (tres o cuatro días / horas), frequency (tres o cuatro veces), or objects (tres o cuatro libros). You can also say it alone as a short answer: “¿Cuántos?” — “Tres o cuatro.”
target_language_example: Llegaré en tres o cuatro minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in three or four minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three weeks) or a point in the future (in three weeks). With time expressions, Spanish often uses "durante" or "por" to mean "for" (e.g., "durante/por tres semanas"), and "en" to mean "in" (e.g., "en tres semanas").
target_language_example: Estudié español por tres semanas antes del viaje.
native_language_example: I studied Spanish for three weeks before the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens three times (quantity or frequency). Also used in comparisons to mean “three times as much/as old” (e.g., “tres veces tu edad” = “three times your age”). Often appears in phrases like “leerlo tres veces” (read it three times) or “pensárselo tres veces” (think twice/think carefully—literally “think it over three times”).
target_language_example: He visitado Madrid tres veces.
native_language_example: I’ve visited Madrid three times.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). You can swap the number: "dos veces a la semana" (twice a week), "cuatro veces a la semana" (four times a week). It’s often used with phrases like "al menos" (at least) or "unas" (about/around): "al menos tres veces a la semana", "unas tres veces a la semana".
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio tres veces a la semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens in one day, especially routines or instructions (meals, brushing teeth, taking medicine). You can also change the number: "dos veces al día" (twice a day), "cuatro veces al día" (four times a day).
target_language_example: Tengo que tomar esta pastilla tres veces al día.
native_language_example: I have to take this pill three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). You can change the number: “dos veces por semana” (twice a week), “cuatro veces por semana,” etc. You’ll often see it with routines and schedules, sometimes with “al menos / por lo menos” (“at least”).
target_language_example: Voy al gimnasio tres veces por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three consecutive times with no break in between. Often goes after the verb (Ganó tres veces seguidas / Perdimos tres veces seguidas). Similar phrases: dos veces seguidas (twice in a row), cuatro veces seguidas (four times in a row).
target_language_example: He llamado tres veces seguidas, pero no contesta.
native_language_example: I’ve called three times in a row, but they aren’t answering.

additional_notes: A money amount: "trescientos" = 300 and it agrees in gender with the noun ("trescientos dólares"; "trescientas" with feminine nouns). Used with verbs like "recibir" (to receive), "deber" (to owe), and "ganar" (to earn).
target_language_example: Tengo que pagar trescientos dólares por el coche.
native_language_example: I have to pay three hundred dollars for the car.

additional_notes: A literal phrase used when talking about farming or planting. "Trigo" = wheat, "en" = in, "su" = his/her/your/their (formal), and "campo" = field/countryside. "Su" changes depending on who owns the field (e.g., "trigo en mi campo" = wheat in my field).
target_language_example: El agricultor cultivó trigo en su campo este año.
native_language_example: The farmer grew wheat in his field this year.

meaning: a piece of; a chunk of.
additional_notes: Used with nouns to talk about a part cut/broken off or a portion of something (food, material, objects): un trozo de carne (a piece of meat), un trozo de hierro (a piece of iron). Often implies a fairly solid piece (compare: un pedazo de is very similar; una rebanada de = a slice; una porción de = a serving/portion).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres otro trozo de pastel?
native_language_example: Do you want another piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a small piece of paper, often for quick notes or drawing. Very common with verbs like escribir (to write), anotar (to jot down), and dibujar (to draw).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un trozo de papel para apuntar la dirección?
native_language_example: Do you have a piece of paper to write down the address?

additional_notes: "Tu" means "your" (informal singular). "Amigo" is masculine; for a female friend, say "tu amiga". Often used to address someone warmly (e.g., "Soy tu amigo" = "I’m your friend").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, soy tu amigo.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m your friend.

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about the help they give or could give. It often appears after verbs like apreciar (to appreciate), esperar (to hope for/expect), necesitar (to need), and with sin + tu ayuda (“without your help”). Note: 'ayuda' can mean both 'help' (noun) and 'help!' (as a cry), but 'tu ayuda' is the noun phrase.
target_language_example: Gracias por tu ayuda; no podría hacerlo sin ti.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help; I couldn't do it without you.

additional_notes: Literally refers to someone’s head, but in many common expressions it means what someone is thinking or imagining: ¿Qué pasa por tu cabeza? (“What’s going through your head?”), Está en tu cabeza / Todo está en tu cabeza (“It’s all in your head”), Usa tu cabeza (“Use your head” = think). It also appears in physical actions: Inclina tu cabeza (“Tilt/bow your head”).
target_language_example: No sé qué tienes en tu cabeza, pero estás muy preocupado.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s in your mind, but you’re very worried.

additional_notes: Refers to the listener’s face. Often used with prepositions: “en tu cara” = “in your face/on your face” (location) and can also be used as a confrontational expression (“¡En tu cara!” = “In your face!”).
target_language_example: Tienes algo en tu cara.
native_language_example: You have something on your face.

additional_notes: "Tu" is the informal singular "your" (used with friends, family, kids). "Casa" can mean both a house and a home; Spanish often uses "casa" where English would say "home." "Es tu casa" can be literal ("It’s your house") or a welcoming phrase meaning "Make yourself at home."
target_language_example: Cuando quieras, ven a tu casa a cenar.
native_language_example: Whenever you want, come to your place for dinner.

additional_notes: Often used literally for the physical heart (especially with verbs like abrir, mostrar, cuidar), and very commonly figuratively to talk about emotions, love, courage, or what your conscience/desires tell you (e.g., Sigue a tu corazón = “Follow your heart”; Haz lo que te mande tu corazón = “Do what your heart tells you”). As a romantic expression, perder el corazón por alguien means “to fall for someone.”
target_language_example: Escucha a tu corazón antes de tomar una decisión.
native_language_example: Listen to your heart before making a decision.

additional_notes: Most often refers to someone’s bedroom in a home. Common in commands like “Vete a tu cuarto” (“Go to your room”). Note: “cuarto” can also mean “fourth” or “a quarter,” depending on context, but with “tu” it usually means “your room.”
target_language_example: Deja la ropa en tu cuarto, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the clothes in your room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about their physical body (health, injuries, sensations, physical contact). It can also be used figuratively in spiritual/philosophical contexts (body vs. soul). In some contexts it can sound intimate or even threatening depending on tone (e.g., sexual situations or “I’ll take care of your body”).
target_language_example: Escucha a tu cuerpo y descansa si lo necesitas.
native_language_example: Listen to your body and rest if you need to.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a problem or mistake: Es tu culpa. Very common in the phrase No es tu culpa (“It’s not your fault”). You can also contrast with es mía (“it’s mine”) or use past tense: No fue tu culpa (“It wasn’t your fault”).
target_language_example: Lo siento por lo que pasó, pero no es tu culpa.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about what happened, but it’s not your fault.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something good is happening to them now, or that they're about to get a lucky break. Often said as: "(Hoy/Este) es tu día de suerte"; can also be negated: "Hoy no es tu día de suerte" (today isn’t your lucky day).
target_language_example: Tranquilo: hoy es tu día de suerte, todavía quedan entradas.
native_language_example: Relax: today is your lucky day—there are still tickets left.

additional_notes: Literally means "your age" (tu = your, edad = age). It can refer to someone's current age (e.g., comparing ages), and in phrases like "A tu edad" it means "at your age"—often used to talk about what is typical or expected for someone of that age.
target_language_example: A tu edad, yo ya trabajaba.
native_language_example: At your age, I was already working.

additional_notes: Used to address someone and refer to their wife. Commonly appears with verbs like hablar con/de (to talk with/about), estar (to be), and irse (to leave): “Tu esposa está al teléfono” (Your wife is on the phone), “Tu esposa se fue” (Your wife left). Note: when speaking directly to your wife, you’d say “mi esposa” (my wife), not “tu esposa”.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu esposa ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your wife now?

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "tu" (your, informal singular) + "familia" (family). Used when speaking to one person you address as "tú". For formal "you" (usted), use "su familia". In many situations, "familia" can mean immediate family or relatives in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Cómo está tu familia?
native_language_example: How is your family?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tu" (“your,” for one person you address as tú). "Habitación" can mean “room” in general, but in everyday contexts like home it often means “bedroom.” You can use it with verbs of location and movement: "estar en tu habitación" (to be in your room), "ir/volver a tu habitación" (to go back to your room).
target_language_example: Deja tu mochila en tu habitación, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave your backpack in your room, please.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive adjective "tu" (“your”) + "hermana" (“sister”). It agrees with the noun (hermana = feminine singular). For a male sibling, use "tu hermano". With a more formal "you" (usted), you’d usually say "su hermana" (which can also mean “his/her/their sister,” depending on context).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo se llama tu hermana?
native_language_example: What is your sister’s name?

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone about their brother. In Spanish, family words often take a possessive (tu = your) instead of saying the person’s name. It can be either literal (your actual brother) or used casually to refer to someone’s “brother” in conversation.
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hermano ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your brother now?

additional_notes: Used to address someone and refer to their female child. It can appear as the subject ("Tu hija es...") or after prepositions like de/con ("orgullosa de tu hija", "con tu hija"). You’ll also see it with emphasis: "Es tu hija."
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hija ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your daughter now?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive “tu” (you = tú) + “hijo” (son). Use it when talking to one person you’re on tú terms with (friend, family, child). For formal “your,” use “su hijo.”
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu hijo?
native_language_example: Where is your son?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to someone about their mother. "Mamá" is the common, family word (like "mom"); it's more personal than "madre" (mother). Often appears after verbs like "ver" (to see), "llamar" (to call), "llevar" (to take/bring), etc. Accent matters: "mamá" (mom).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes llamar a tu mamá, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you call your mom, please?

additional_notes: Direct way to refer to someone’s hand. Often used with commands/instructions (e.g., abre/extiende/muéstrame/pon tu mano…). In Spanish, body parts are often referred to with the definite article instead (la mano) when it’s obvious whose it is, but "tu mano" adds emphasis or clarity (your hand, not someone else’s).
target_language_example: Toma mi mano y dame tu mano.
native_language_example: Take my hand and give me your hand.

additional_notes: Used to talk directly to someone about their closest friend. The possessive "tu" means "your" (informal singular). "Mejor" means "best". "Amigo" is masculine; for a female friend, say "tu mejor amiga". You can also make it plural: "tus mejores amigos".
target_language_example: ¿Quién es tu mejor amigo?
native_language_example: Who is your best friend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your thoughts, imagination, memory, or mental state. Very common in phrases like "está en tu mente" (it’s in your mind), "leer tu mente" (read your mind), and "dejar tu mente en blanco" (clear your mind / go blank).
target_language_example: No dejes que ese problema ocupe tu mente todo el día.
native_language_example: Don’t let that problem take up your mind all day.

additional_notes: Literally “your woman.” In everyday Spanish, "mi/tu/su mujer" commonly refers to someone’s wife (and sometimes a long-term female partner, depending on region and context). Used to address or refer to the woman associated with “you.”
target_language_example: Tu mujer está en la oficina.
native_language_example: Your wife is at the office.

additional_notes: Used to address one person informally (tú). Common with verbs like anotar (write down), firmar (sign), and when someone says your name (digan tu nombre). For formal situations or with someone you don’t know well, use "su nombre".
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu nombre?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about someone’s phone number. "Tu" is the informal singular "your" (to one person you address as "tú"). In more formal situations or with strangers, you often use "su número de teléfono" (your phone number—formal). You can also shorten it to "tu número" when it’s clear you mean a phone number.
target_language_example: ¿Me das tu número de teléfono?
native_language_example: Can you give me your phone number?

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone informally (tú). Often appears with verbs like expresar (to express), respetar (to respect), or dar (to give/share). For formal address (usted), use “su opinión”.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu opinión sobre esta idea?
native_language_example: What’s your opinion about this idea?

additional_notes: "Tu" means "your" (informal singular), and "padre" means "father." Used to talk directly to someone about their father: "Llama a tu padre" = "Call your dad." In most of Spain, "tu padre" is common; in many parts of Latin America, people may say "tu papá" more often in everyday speech. Note the accent: "tu" (your) vs. "tú" (you).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu padre?
native_language_example: Where is your dad?

additional_notes: Used to say something about the person’s father (identity, profession, nationality, description, etc.). "Tu" means "your" (informal singular). "Padre" is "father" and "es" is the verb "ser" ("to be") for descriptions/identities in the present tense. Often followed by an adjective ("alto"), a noun ("mi jefe"), or a nationality ("japonés").
target_language_example: Tu padre es médico.
native_language_example: Your father is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to address someone about their father. "Papá" is common and slightly more affectionate than "padre" (more formal). The possessive "tu" changes with the person: "mi papá" (my dad), "su papá" (his/her/their/your formal dad), "nuestro papá" (our dad).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde está tu papá ahora?
native_language_example: Where is your dad right now?

meaning: “your part” / “your share”; in “por tu parte,” “on your part.”
additional_notes: Often used to talk about someone’s contribution or responsibility: “Hiciste tu parte” = “You did your part.” With **por tu parte**, it comments on someone’s behavior in a polite way: “Es muy generoso por tu parte” = “That’s very generous of you.” It can also mean someone’s role/section in something: “Tu parte en la historia…” = “Your part in the story…”.
target_language_example: Gracias por ayudar; fue muy amable por tu parte.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping; that was very kind of you.

meaning: "your plan" (your idea or strategy for what to do).
additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to someone’s intended course of action. Often appears with verbs like "funcionar" (to work), "fracasar" (to fail), and comparisons like "mejor que" (better than). "Plan" can mean a specific arrangement (a plan) or a general strategy.
target_language_example: ¿Cuál es tu plan para mañana?
native_language_example: What’s your plan for tomorrow?

meaning: your own (emphasizes that it belongs to you/yourself).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "tu propia cena", "tu propia seguridad", "tu propia vida") to stress that it’s yours personally—often for emphasis or contrast ("your own" vs. someone else’s). For masculine nouns, use "tu propio" (e.g., "tu propio coche").
target_language_example: Quiero tomar mi propia decisión, no la tuya.
native_language_example: I want to make my own decision, not yours.

meaning: your own (emphasizes that it belongs to you / is unique to you).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to stress ownership or independence: tu propio esfuerzo (your own effort), tu propio destino (your own destiny), tu propio ritmo (your own pace). It’s an emphatic form of "tu" + "propio/a" and agrees with the noun: tu propia idea, tus propios planes, tus propias cosas.
target_language_example: Hazlo a tu propio modo.
native_language_example: Do it your own way.

meaning: your point of view; your perspective.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s opinion or perspective on a situation. Often appears with verbs like agradecer (to appreciate), entender (to understand), or phrases like depende de… (it depends on…). You can change the possessive: mi punto de vista (my point of view), su punto de vista (his/her/your formal/their point of view).
target_language_example: Respeto tu punto de vista, pero no estoy de acuerdo.
native_language_example: I respect your point of view, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: "Rostro" is a slightly more formal/literary word for "face" (more neutral: "cara"). Used with possessives like "tu" (your, informal singular). Common in expressions like "ver tu rostro" (see your face) or "borrar esa sonrisa de tu rostro" (wipe that smile off your face).
target_language_example: Me gusta tu rostro cuando sonríes.
native_language_example: I like your face when you smile.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s physical (and sometimes mental) well-being. Often appears in phrases like “cuidar tu salud” (to take care of your health), “tu salud es importante” (your health is important), or “preocupado/a por tu salud” (worried about your health). Note the possessive changes with the person: mi salud (my), tu salud (your), su salud (his/her/your formal/their).
target_language_example: Deberías dormir más para cuidar tu salud.
native_language_example: You should sleep more to take care of your health.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone does for work (their job) or the work/task they did. It uses the informal singular possessive "tu" (you = tú). For formal "your," use "su trabajo."
target_language_example: ¿Te gusta tu trabajo?
native_language_example: Do you like your job?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone it’s their turn in a sequence, game, or responsibility. Common patterns: "Ahora es tu turno" (Now it’s your turn), "Es tu turno de + infinitive" (It’s your turn to + verb), "Espera tu turno" (Wait your turn). In work contexts, "cubrir tu turno" means to cover your shift.
target_language_example: Ya terminé; ahora es tu turno de hablar.
native_language_example: I’m done; now it’s your turn to speak.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to someone’s legal/real identity (not a nickname, username, or alias). Word order: Spanish often places adjectives after the noun too, so you may also hear "tu nombre verdadero" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: No uses tu apodo; dime tu verdadero nombre.
native_language_example: Don’t use your nickname; tell me your real name.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective **tu** (“your”, informal singular) + **vida** (“life”). Don’t confuse **tu** (your) with **tú** (you). Common in serious contexts (value of your life, risking your life, saving your life).
target_language_example: No pongas tu vida en peligro.
native_language_example: Don’t put your life in danger.

additional_notes: Used when talking directly to someone about the sound of their voice (in person, on the phone, in a recording, etc.). It’s a possessive phrase: tu = your (informal singular), voz = voice. With verbs like escuchar (to hear/listen to) or sonar (to sound): "Escuchar tu voz" = "to hear your voice"; "Tu voz me suena familiar" = "Your voice sounds familiar to me."
target_language_example: Me alegra escuchar tu voz otra vez.
native_language_example: I’m happy to hear your voice again.

meaning: your last chance; your final opportunity.
additional_notes: Used to warn that this is the final time you can do something before it’s no longer possible. Often appears in the pattern: “Esta es tu última oportunidad de/para + infinitive” (This is your last chance to + verb). Also: “Puede ser tu última oportunidad…” (This may be your last chance…).
target_language_example: Esta es tu última oportunidad para decir la verdad.
native_language_example: This is your last chance to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Describes someone in a lying position on a bed (often resting, sick, or doing nothing). Uses the verb phrase "estar tumbado" (to be lying down) + location "en la cama" (in bed). In Latin America you may also hear "acostado en la cama" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Estoy tumbado en la cama porque me duele la cabeza.
native_language_example: I’m lying in bed because my head hurts.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the friends of the person you’re speaking to. It uses the informal singular possessive "tus" (for "tú"); with "usted" you’d say "sus amigos". For one friend: "tu amigo / tu amiga".
target_language_example: ¿Vas a salir con tus amigos esta noche?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your friends tonight?

additional_notes: Used for things that concern you (your responsibilities, problems, private life). In commands like “Métete en tus asuntos” or “Ocúpate de tus asuntos,” it means “Mind your own business” and can sound rude or confrontational depending on tone.
target_language_example: No te preocupes por lo mío; ocúpate de tus asuntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about my stuff; mind your own business.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s belongings/possessions in a general way (bags, clothes, items, etc.). Very common in instructions or requests like “Coge/Junta tus cosas” (get your things together).
target_language_example: ¿Ya recogiste tus cosas?
native_language_example: Have you picked up your things yet?

additional_notes: “Tus” means “your” (informal singular: used when speaking to one person you call “tú”). “Hijos” literally means “sons,” but it’s commonly used to mean “children” in general (mixed group). For a more explicitly gender-neutral term, you may also hear “tus hijos e hijas” or “tus hijas” (your daughters).
target_language_example: ¿Cómo están tus hijos?
native_language_example: How are your children?

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "tus" (for someone you address as "tú"). Common in instructions and requests (e.g., "Levanta tus manos", "Mantén tus manos limpias"). In the expression "Estoy en tus manos", it means "I'm in your hands" = "I'm in your care / it's up to you".
target_language_example: Lávate tus manos antes de comer.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **tus** (your, informal singular “you”) + **ojos** (eyes). Used literally (“Let me see your eyes”) and also in poetic/romantic ways (“With your eyes you tell me to come closer,” “Everywhere I look I see your eyes”). For formal singular “your,” use **sus ojos**; for “your eyes” to more than one person, use **vuestros ojos** (Spain) or **sus ojos** (Latin America).
target_language_example: Me encantan tus ojos.
native_language_example: I love your eyes.

additional_notes: Used to talk to someone (tú) about their mother and father. Possessive adjective + plural noun: tus (your) + padres (parents). Often used in questions about where they are or statements about what they should do/feel.
target_language_example: ¿Vienen tus padres a la fiesta?
native_language_example: Are your parents coming to the party?

additional_notes: Literally means “your dreams.” It can refer to dreams you have while sleeping (e.g., “in your dreams”) or, very commonly, to your hopes and life goals (e.g., “pursue/achieve your dreams”). It’s also used in the phrase “la chica/el chico de tus sueños” = “the girl/boy of your dreams” (your ideal partner).
target_language_example: No dejes que nadie destruya tus sueños.
native_language_example: Don’t let anyone destroy your dreams.

meaning: "I had the opportunity to" / "I got the chance to."
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of "tener la oportunidad de". Use it to say you had a chance to do something (often something special, lucky, or possible because of the situation). It’s followed by an infinitive: "tuve la oportunidad de + ver/estudiar/viajar...". You can also use other persons: "tuviste", "tuvo", "tuvimos", "tuvieron".
target_language_example: Tuve la oportunidad de conocer a la autora después de la charla.
native_language_example: I had the chance to meet the author after the talk.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to" (I was required to).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "tener que" + infinitive, used to say you were forced/required to do something at a specific time in the past. Common pattern: "tuve que" + infinitive (e.g., "tuve que ir", "tuve que dejarlo"). With a reflexive verb: "me tuve que" + infinitive (e.g., "me tuve que quedar").
target_language_example: Ayer tuve que levantarme temprano para trabajar.
native_language_example: Yesterday I had to get up early to work.

meaning: I had to do (I was required/forced to do).
additional_notes: "Tuve" is the preterite (finished past) form of "tener" for "yo". "Tener que + infinitive" expresses obligation/necessity in the past; it often implies you didn’t really have a choice. After "que" you use an infinitive: "hacer", "llamar", "trabajar", etc. (e.g., "Tuve que llamar", "Tuve que trabajar").
target_language_example: Tuve que hacer la tarea antes de salir.
native_language_example: I had to do the homework before going out.

additional_notes: Used to say you were obligated to go somewhere in the past. It’s the preterite (completed past) of **tener que**: **tuve que + infinitive**. Here it’s followed by **ir a + place** (e.g., *tuve que ir a Boston / a urgencias*).
target_language_example: Ayer tuve que ir al hospital.
native_language_example: Yesterday I had to go to the hospital.

additional_notes: “Tuve” is the preterite (simple past) of “tener” for “yo,” used for completed events in the past. It’s followed by a noun: “tuve un día…” (I had a day…), “tuve un amigo…” (I had a friend…). Use “tuve una” before feminine nouns (e.g., “tuve una idea”), and “tuve unos/unas” for plural.
target_language_example: Ayer tuve un problema, pero lo resolví.
native_language_example: Yesterday I had a problem, but I solved it.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite tense of tener (tuve) to talk about a dream you had while sleeping, usually referring to a completed event (often with time words like anoche “last night”). You can add an adjective after sueño: Tuve un sueño extraño/triste/espantoso. (SUEÑO can also mean “dream/goal” or “sleepiness,” but in this pattern it commonly means a dream you had while asleep.)
target_language_example: Tuve un sueño raro anoche.
native_language_example: I had a weird dream last night.

meaning: "I had a" (for a completed past event/experience).
additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of "tener" for "yo": "tuve" = "I had" / "I experienced." It’s used for single, finished actions in the past and is typically followed by a feminine noun because of "una" (e.g., "tuve una charla", "tuve una crisis"). For a masculine noun, you’d use "tuve un ...".
target_language_example: Ayer tuve una conversación importante con mi jefe.
native_language_example: Yesterday I had an important conversation with my boss.

meaning: “we had to” / “we needed to” (we were forced/required to do something).
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of the obligation phrase "tener que" + infinitive. It describes a completed situation in the past where you had no real choice: "Tuvimos que + infinitive" (e.g., "tuvimos que irnos" = we had to leave). Common alternatives: "teníamos que" (we had to / were supposed to, ongoing or habitual in the past).
target_language_example: Por el tráfico, tuvimos que tomar otra ruta.
native_language_example: Because of the traffic, we had to take another route.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to say someone did something kind for you. Uses the preterite (tuvo) for a completed action; you can change it for other people/tenses: "tengo la amabilidad de" (I’m kind enough to / I have the kindness to), "tuvo la amabilidad de" (he/she was kind enough to), "tuvieron la amabilidad de" (they were kind enough to). Often followed by an infinitive (ayudar, invitar, mostrar).
target_language_example: El doctor tuvo la amabilidad de explicarme todo con calma.
native_language_example: The doctor was kind enough to explain everything to me calmly.

additional_notes: Past tense of the obligation expression "tener que" + infinitive. "Tuvo que" is the 3rd person singular in the simple past (pretérito): he/she/it had to; you (formal) had to. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., "tuvo que ir", "tuvo que usar"). For plural, use "tuvieron que" (they/you all had to).
target_language_example: Carlos tuvo que quedarse en casa por la lluvia.
native_language_example: Carlos had to stay home because of the rain.

additional_notes: From **tener** (to have). **Tuvo** is the **simple past (preterite)**, **third-person singular** form: *él/ella/usted tuvo...* It’s used for completed past events or results (e.g., *tuvo un final feliz* = “had a happy ending”, *tuvo un problema* = “had a problem”). For feminine nouns, use **tuvo una**.
target_language_example: La reunión tuvo un buen resultado.
native_language_example: The meeting had a good result.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "tener un accidente". "Tuvo" refers to a third person singular (él/ella/usted) or can refer to a named person (e.g., Tom). Often used for car crashes or other mishaps; add a place with "en" ("tuvo un accidente en el restaurante").
target_language_example: Ayer tuvo un accidente en la carretera.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she had an accident on the highway.

additional_notes: Preterite (simple past) of **tener** for **él/ella/usted**: **tuvo**. It’s used for a completed event in the past. **Una** is used because the noun that follows is feminine (e.g., *una idea, una charla, una oportunidad*). Spanish often drops the subject: **Tuvo una...** can mean “He/She had a...” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ayer tuvo una reunión importante.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she had an important meeting.

additional_notes: Used to politely order or request tea, especially in cafés/restaurants. You can also say “Un té, por favor” (“A tea, please”). Often said on its own as a short order; you can add details after it (e.g., “con leche”, “sin azúcar”).
target_language_example: Un té, por favor, sin azúcar.
native_language_example: A tea, please, without sugar.

additional_notes: A common drink order. You’ll often hear it with an article when ordering: "Un té con limón, por favor." You can add preferences like "sin azúcar" (without sugar) or "con azúcar" (with sugar).
target_language_example: ¿Me pones un té con limón, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you get me a tea with lemon, please?

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun tú (“you”, informal singular) plus eres (the tú form of ser, “to be”). Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so eres can mean “you are” by itself; tú eres adds emphasis or contrast (“you, not someone else”). Use with friends/family/people your age; with formal you (usted) say usted es.
target_language_example: Tú eres mi mejor amigo.
native_language_example: You are my best friend.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as “the” one with a certain quality or role. It’s followed by a masculine noun/adjective phrase, often with superlatives like “el más …” (the most …) or with “único” (only). For a feminine person, use “tú eres la”.
target_language_example: Tú eres el mejor jugador del equipo.
native_language_example: You are the best player on the team.

meaning: "you are the" (used before a feminine noun or "la que...").
additional_notes: Use "tú eres la + [feminine noun/adjective]" to identify someone: "Tú eres la doctora" (you’re the doctor). It must match feminine gender and number: "tú eres la" (fem. singular), "tú eres el" (masc. singular), "tú eres la(s)" / "tú eres lo" depending on what follows. You can also say "tú eres la que + verb" to mean "you’re the one who..." (feminine): "Tú eres la que se comporta mal."
target_language_example: Tú eres la persona indicada para ayudarme.
native_language_example: You’re the right person to help me.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone what they are to you, usually followed by a noun phrase: a person (mi chica, mi mejor amigo), a role (mi padrino, mi jefe), or a term of affection (mi ángel, mi amor). Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you’ll also commonly hear/see just “Eres mi…”. Use “mi” before a singular noun; for plural, use “mis” (Eres mis amigos).
target_language_example: Tú eres mi persona favorita.
native_language_example: You are my favorite person.

meaning: "you are a" (talking to one person, with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** (permanent/identity descriptions) to say what someone is: **Tú eres un + [masculine noun/adjective used as a noun]**. If the word is feminine, use **una**: *Tú eres una profesora.* In everyday Spanish, the subject pronoun **tú** is often omitted because **eres** already shows who it is: *Eres un profesor.* For plural: *Ustedes son…* / *Vosotros sois…*.
target_language_example: Tú eres un buen amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: “you + it / him / that” (you with the direct object pronoun “lo”).
additional_notes: Used when the subject “tú” (you) is stated for emphasis or contrast (often Spanish can drop the subject). “Lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “it,” “that,” or “him” (masculine singular, or neutral “that”). It goes before the conjugated verb: “Tú lo necesitas” = “You need it.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: tú lo haces muy bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you do it very well.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the listener already knows a fact or understands something. "Lo" refers to the idea/situation being talked about. Often appears with intensifiers like "bien" or "muy bien" ("you know it well / you know very well").
target_language_example: No hace falta explicarlo; tú lo sabes.
native_language_example: No need to explain it; you know.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the subject is “you” and not someone else, often meaning “by yourself” (without help) or “for yourself” (see/decide personally). It agrees in gender/number: tú mismo (male), tú misma (female), vosotros mismos/vosotras mismas. Common in commands: Sé tú mismo. / Sírvete tú mismo.
target_language_example: Tienes que hacerlo tú mismo, nadie va a hacerlo por ti.
native_language_example: You have to do it yourself; nobody is going to do it for you.

additional_notes: Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so you can say just “no te atreves” or “no estás comiendo.” Adding “tú” makes it more emphatic or contrasting (like “you, on the other hand…”). Common with contrasts: “Si tú no…, yo sí…” (“If you don’t…, I will…”).
target_language_example: Tú no quieres ir, pero yo sí.
native_language_example: You don’t want to go, but I do.

additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) that they are not something, often followed by a noun or adjective: "Tú no eres + noun/adjective" (e.g., "tú no eres médico", "tú no eres tímido"). For a temporary state, Spanish often uses "estar" instead ("tú no estás cansado" = you're not tired).
target_language_example: Tú no eres mi profesor.
native_language_example: You are not my teacher.

meaning: “you don’t … it / you don’t … him” (you + not + direct object “lo”).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to say that “you” do not do/know/understand something. “Lo” is a direct object pronoun that usually means “it” (an idea, a fact, an action) or “him” (a male person). You’ll normally see it right before the verb: “Tú no lo sabes / entiendes / conoces.”
target_language_example: Tú no lo sabes todavía, pero mañana te lo diré.
native_language_example: You don’t know it yet, but tomorrow I’ll tell you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone lacks information or understanding. Often followed by a question word or clause: tú no sabes cuánto... (you don't know how much...), tú no sabes lo que... (you don't know what...), tú no sabes quién... (you don't know who...). Can also be used emphatically, like “you have no idea,” depending on tone and context. Usually written without the subject pronoun in everyday speech: No sabes...
target_language_example: Tú no sabes lo difícil que fue para mí.
native_language_example: You don’t know how hard it was for me.

meaning: "you can" / "you’re able to" (said to one person).
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular subject "tú". Often used to encourage someone: "¡Tú puedes!" = "You can do it!" It can also give permission or state possibility/ability: "Tú puedes elegir..." = "You can choose..." In Spanish the subject pronoun is often optional, so you’ll also hear just "Puedes"; adding "tú" makes it more emphatic (like "You can, YOU.").
target_language_example: No te rindas: tú puedes lograrlo.
native_language_example: Don’t give up: you can do it.

additional_notes: “Quieras” is the present subjunctive of “querer” for “tú.” It commonly appears after words like: **como** (however/as you want), **lo que** (whatever you want), **cuando** (whenever you want), **donde** (wherever you want). It often implies giving the other person freedom to choose.
target_language_example: Nos vemos a la hora que tú quieras.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at whatever time you want.

additional_notes: Literally “you know.” Commonly used to introduce a clause with “lo que…” (“what…/that which…”), e.g., “Tú sabes lo que…” = “You know what…”. It can also be used as a conversational filler like English “you know,” but in these examples it’s used to emphasize that the other person already has the information.
target_language_example: Tú sabes lo que tienes que hacer.
native_language_example: You know what you have to do.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to point out that the other person already knows something: “Tú sabes lo que + verb/clause.” Often followed by a verb like debes/tienes que/quiero/me gusta, etc. In many situations you can also drop the subject pronoun: “Sabes lo que …”
target_language_example: Tú sabes lo que necesitamos para el viaje.
native_language_example: You know what we need for the trip.

meaning: “you know that …” (often like “you know,” to introduce or emphasize what follows).
additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something, stress that something is true/obvious, or add emphasis before a statement. In speech it can sound a bit insistent depending on tone. Often followed by a full clause (e.g., "tú sabes que no puedo...").
target_language_example: Tú sabes que mañana no voy a poder ir.
native_language_example: You know (that) I won’t be able to go tomorrow.

meaning: “you have” (talking to one person, informal tú).
additional_notes: Used with the verb tener to talk about possessing something or having a relationship/status: Tú tienes el anillo. / Tú tienes una esposa. In Spanish, the subject pronoun tú is often omitted (Tienes…), but it can be included for emphasis or contrast (e.g., Tú tienes…, pero yo no).
target_language_example: Tú tienes las llaves, ¿verdad?
native_language_example: You have the keys, right?

meaning: "you and" (talking to one person plus someone else).
additional_notes: Used to link the person you’re speaking to (tú) with another person or group: “Tú y yo…”, “Tú y tu madre…”. It normally appears as the subject of the sentence. Note the accent: “tú” = “you” (pronoun), but “tu” (no accent) = “your”.
target_language_example: Tú y yo tenemos que hablar.
native_language_example: You and I have to talk.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the speaker and the person addressed are included together (often for teamwork, relationships, or shared responsibility). It can be added at the end for emphasis (“…, tú y yo.”) or placed at the start (“Tú y yo…”).
target_language_example: Tú y yo podemos hacerlo.
native_language_example: You and I can do it.

additional_notes: Used to say that you and the other person do NOT belong to a category or relationship. It uses the verb **ser** in the **nosotros** form (**somos**) because the subject is **tú y yo** (= we). It’s typically followed by a noun or adjective: *tú y yo no somos amigos / iguales / hermanos*.
target_language_example: Tú y yo no somos pareja.
native_language_example: You and I are not a couple.

meaning: “you and I are / you and I (we) are” (used to say what you and I are).
additional_notes: Used to talk about you (tú) and me (yo) together with the verb ser (“to be”) in the nosotros/as form: somos. Often used to emphasize the two people specifically ("you and I"). Follow it with a noun, adjective, or description (e.g., amigos, iguales, de la misma edad). In everyday speech you can also just say “somos …” if it’s clear you mean “you and I.”
target_language_example: Tú y yo somos un buen equipo.
native_language_example: You and I are a good team.

additional_notes: Used to say that you and the other person share or possess something. Spanish often states the subjects explicitly (“tú y yo”) for emphasis or contrast, even though “tenemos” already means “we have.”
target_language_example: Tú y yo tenemos que hablar.
native_language_example: You and I need to talk.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a (male) lawyer. For a female lawyer, you’ll often hear "una abogada." After verbs like "necesitar" (to need), "querer" (to want), or "hablar con" (to talk with), it commonly appears as "un abogado" (an/any lawyer).
target_language_example: Si tienes problemas legales, busca un abogado.
native_language_example: If you have legal problems, look for a lawyer.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dar (“to give”): “Dame un abrazo” = “Give me a hug.” By itself (“Un abrazo.”) it can be a friendly goodbye or sign-off in messages, like “Hugs” or “A hug.”
target_language_example: Antes de irme, te doy un abrazo.
native_language_example: Before I leave, I’ll give you a hug.

additional_notes: A common noun for an outer garment worn to keep warm. Often used with adjectives like grueso (thick), caro (expensive), nuevo (new), fino (thin/light), or a color (azul). The article changes with gender/number: un abrigo (a coat), el abrigo (the coat), abrigos (coats).
target_language_example: Hace frío; necesito un abrigo.
native_language_example: It’s cold; I need a coat.

additional_notes: Used for an unplanned harmful event (e.g., a car accident, a fall). You can also use it more broadly to mean something happened “by accident” or “not on purpose” (e.g., “Esto no es un accidente” = “This isn’t an accident,” implying it was intentional). Common collocations: “tener/sufrir un accidente” (to have/get in an accident), “un accidente de coche/tráfico” (a car/traffic accident), “un accidente laboral” (a workplace accident).
target_language_example: Tuvo un accidente de coche, pero está bien.
native_language_example: He had a car accident, but he’s okay.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a traffic accident involving a car. Also common: “accidente de auto” (especially in Latin America). You can use it with verbs like “tener” (to have), “sufrir” (to suffer), “morir en” (to die in), or “perder a alguien en” (to lose someone in).
target_language_example: Hubo un accidente de coche en la autopista y llegué tarde.
native_language_example: There was a car accident on the highway and I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used for accidents on the road involving vehicles (cars, motorcycles, etc.). Also commonly said as "accidente de coche" (car accident) or "accidente de tránsito" (especially in Latin America).
target_language_example: Hubo un accidente de tráfico en la autopista y llegué tarde.
native_language_example: There was a traffic accident on the highway and I arrived late.

meaning: “an act of …” (a deed or action motivated by something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe what kind of act it is, often highlighting the motive, nature, or category: un acto de desesperación (an act of desperation), un acto de fe (an act of faith), un acto de guerra (an act of war). It’s formal/neutral and common in news, law, religion, and serious contexts.
target_language_example: Ayudar a un desconocido fue un acto de bondad.
native_language_example: Helping a stranger was an act of kindness.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a grown person (18+). Often said to emphasize maturity or responsibility: “Eres un adulto” = “You’re an adult.” The feminine form is “una adulta” (less common than “una mujer adulta”).
target_language_example: Ya soy un adulto, puedo tomar mis propias decisiones.
native_language_example: I'm already an adult; I can make my own decisions.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article un (“a”). It can mean (1) one friend in general (“a friend”), or (2) “a friend of [someone]”: un amigo de tu madre = “a friend of your mother.” For a female friend, use una amiga.
target_language_example: Voy a cenar con un amigo esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with a friend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say who someone is friends with: “Soy un amigo de tu madre” = “I’m a friend of your mother.” The “de” shows the connection (“of”). It can also introduce a chain of connections: “un amigo de un amigo” = “a friend of a friend.”
target_language_example: Juan es un amigo de mi hermano.
native_language_example: Juan is a friend of my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say “one of my friends” (not necessarily a specific one). The pattern is: un/una + [noun] + mío/mía (mine), e.g., una amiga mía. You can also use it after the noun without “un/una” when it’s definite: mi amigo (my friend) vs. un amigo mío (a friend of mine).
target_language_example: Un amigo mío vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: A friend of mine lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of a friend with a relative clause: "un amigo que + verb" (e.g., "un amigo que cumple años"). "Que" here usually means “who/that,” not “what.”
target_language_example: Tengo un amigo que vive en México.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Mexico.

meaning: an elderly man; an old man.
additional_notes: Commonly refers to an elderly man, sometimes with a respectful tone. For “an elderly woman,” use “una anciana.” You may also hear “una persona mayor” as a more neutral/polite option for “an older person.”
target_language_example: El anciano necesita ayuda para cruzar la calle.
native_language_example: The elderly man needs help crossing the street.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a non-human animal (a living creature). It can also be used figuratively to compare a person to an animal to emphasize instinct, harsh living conditions, or a lack of dignity (e.g., "vive como un animal"). In insults, Spanish often uses "animal" without the article ("¡Eres un animal!" / "¡Animal!") to mean someone is rude, brutal, or stupid—context and tone matter. Common collocations: "animal de terapia" (therapy animal), "animal hambriento" (hungry animal).
target_language_example: Encontraron un animal herido cerca del río.
native_language_example: They found an injured animal near the river.

additional_notes: "Arma" is feminine, so you say "un arma" (not *una*) because the word starts with a stressed "a" sound. In plural it’s "las armas". Often used for firearms in everyday speech (as in "disparar un arma" = to fire a gun), but it can also mean other weapons depending on context.
target_language_example: La policía encontró un arma en el coche.
native_language_example: The police found a weapon in the car.

meaning: an artist (a person who makes art).
additional_notes: A masculine noun phrase. Use it for someone who creates art (drawing, painting, etc.). Feminine form: una artista (often also used) / una artista or una artista depending on region; plural: artistas. With professions, Spanish often uses the indefinite article (un/una): Es un artista.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es un artista y pinta cuadros increíbles.
native_language_example: My brother is an artist and paints incredible paintings.

additional_notes: Used to label a man as someone who kills people, often intentionally (murderer). Feminine form: una asesina. Common with ser: "Es un asesino" / "No es un asesino". With convertir in: "Eso no te convierte en un asesino" (“That doesn’t make you a murderer”). Can also be used figuratively as a strong exaggeration (e.g., "¡Esa tarea es asesina!" = “That task is killer/brutal”), but the examples here are literal.
target_language_example: No quiero pensar que mi padre era un asesino.
native_language_example: I don’t want to think that my father was a murderer.

meaning: a matter; an issue; a business/affair.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a topic or situation that needs attention or discussion. Common with adjectives like urgente (urgent), familiar (family), serio (serious), and in phrases like un asunto más que discutir (one more matter to discuss).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar contigo sobre un asunto importante.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about an important matter.

meaning: an attack; a (sudden) episode/fit (e.g., asthma attack, heart attack); a burst (of anger).
additional_notes: Often used for a violent/military action (un ataque sobre/contra la ciudad). Also very common for medical episodes: dar/tener un ataque ("Le ha dado un ataque" = "He/She had an attack"), and more specifically un ataque de asma / un ataque al corazón. It can also describe a sudden emotional outburst: en un ataque de rabia ("in a fit of rage").
target_language_example: Le dio un ataque de pánico en el metro.
native_language_example: He/She had a panic attack on the subway.

additional_notes: Used to describe a medical emergency involving the heart. Often appears with verbs like "tener" (to have): "Tuvo un ataque al corazón" and "morir de" (to die of): "Murió de un ataque al corazón."
target_language_example: Mi abuelo tuvo un ataque al corazón el año pasado.
native_language_example: My grandfather had a heart attack last year.

additional_notes: Common word for “car” in many Spanish-speaking countries (especially Latin America). Also said as “un coche” (Spain, and also used elsewhere) or “un carro” (some regions). In your example, “en movimiento” means “in motion / moving.”
target_language_example: No tengo un auto, así que voy en autobús.
native_language_example: I don’t have a car, so I go by bus.

additional_notes: Common phrase made from the indefinite article un (“a”), auto (“car”, common in Latin America), and nuevo (“new”). Use it when talking about buying, selling, or wanting a car that is new (not used). You can also say "un coche nuevo" in many countries (especially Spain).
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un auto nuevo este año.
native_language_example: I want to buy a new car this year.

meaning: a bird (a more general/formal word than "pájaro").
additional_notes: "Ave" is a feminine noun even though it often uses the masculine article in the singular: "un ave" (like "un águila"). In plural it becomes "unas aves". Common in poetic or literary descriptions and comparisons ("como un ave" = "like a bird").
target_language_example: En el parque vi un ave muy colorida.
native_language_example: In the park I saw a very colorful bird.

additional_notes: Refers to an aircraft. Very common with verbs like “tomar/coger un avión” (to take/catch a flight) and in descriptions like “un avión grande” (a big plane). It can also be used for a toy or model, e.g., “un avión de papel” (a paper airplane).
target_language_example: Vamos a tomar un avión mañana por la mañana.
native_language_example: We’re going to take a plane tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of one year in general: un año = one year. Common in time expressions like “hace un año” (a year ago) and “en un año” (in a year / in one year, depending on context).
target_language_example: Voy a estar en España por un año.
native_language_example: I'm going to be in Spain for a year.

meaning: a bank (financial institution); also a bench/seat.
additional_notes: "Banco" is a common word with two everyday meanings: (1) a bank where you keep money, and (2) a bench (a public seat), especially in parks or on the street. Context usually makes it clear (e.g., "robar un banco" = rob a bank; "sentarse en un banco" = sit on a bench).
target_language_example: Voy al banco a sacar dinero.
native_language_example: I’m going to the bank to withdraw money.

additional_notes: Refers to a water vessel used for travel or transport (boat/ship depending on size and context). Often used with prepositions like "a bordo de" (on board) and in expressions like "un barco hundido" (a sunken ship).
target_language_example: Vamos en un barco hasta la isla.
native_language_example: We’re going by boat to the island.

meaning: a bathroom; a bath (the act of bathing).
additional_notes: Usually means “a bathroom/restroom” when talking about rooms or asking where it is (e.g., en mi casa hay un baño; ¿Dónde está el baño?). It can also mean “a bath” with verbs like darse/tomar un baño (“to take a bath”). For a shower, Spanish typically uses una ducha (darse una ducha).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un baño cerca?
native_language_example: Is there a bathroom nearby?

meaning: a baby; (figurative) a crybaby / someone acting childish.
additional_notes: Usually means a baby/infant. In phrases like “No seas un bebé”, it’s used figuratively to call someone a crybaby or say they’re being childish. Gender is masculine: “un bebé”, but you can refer to any baby regardless of gender.
target_language_example: El bebé está durmiendo ahora.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about giving/receiving a kiss (dar un beso, darme un beso, me dio un beso). It can be romantic, friendly, or as a greeting depending on context.
target_language_example: Antes de irme, te doy un beso.
native_language_example: Before I leave, I’ll give you a kiss.

additional_notes: A common, friendly or polite greeting/farewell in many Spanish-speaking cultures (often between friends or family). Uses the verb "dar" (to give): "dar un beso" = "to give a kiss." You can specify who receives it with "a": "Le di un beso en la mejilla a Ana."
target_language_example: Nos saludamos con un beso en la mejilla.
native_language_example: We greeted each other with a kiss on the cheek.

additional_notes: “Buen” is the shortened form of “bueno” used before a singular masculine noun: “un buen restaurante”, “un buen espectáculo”. It can also work as an intensifier meaning “quite a / a good (amount of)”, often with quantities or time: “un buen tanto más viejo” = “quite a bit older”, “un buen rato” = “quite a while.”
target_language_example: Esperamos un buen rato antes de entrar.
native_language_example: We waited quite a while before going in.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a competent lawyer, or to say you have/know a reliable lawyer. In Spanish, adjectives usually go after the noun (un abogado bueno), but common adjectives like buen(o/a) often come before the noun: un buen abogado. Feminine: una buena abogada.
target_language_example: Si tienes un problema legal, habla con un buen abogado.
native_language_example: If you have a legal problem, talk to a good lawyer.

additional_notes: Means a close, loyal, reliable friend. Often used with the verb "ser" (to be): "Es un buen amigo" (He/She is a good friend). You can also use it with "de" to show whose friend someone is: "Soy un buen amigo de tu padre" (I’m a good friend of your father).
target_language_example: Ella es un buen amigo en quien puedo confiar.
native_language_example: She is a good friend I can trust.

meaning: a good boy / a good kid (a well-behaved, nice guy).
additional_notes: Often used as praise or as a gentle (sometimes slightly patronizing) way to tell someone—often a child—to behave or do what you ask: “Sé un buen chico…” (“Be a good boy…”). For adults, “buen chico” can also mean “a good guy/nice guy” (good person, friendly, trustworthy). Feminine: “una buena chica.”
target_language_example: Sé un buen chico y no hagas ruido, por favor.
native_language_example: Be a good boy and don’t make noise, please.

meaning: a good piece of advice; good advice.
additional_notes: Used to refer to helpful advice or a recommendation someone gives you. "Consejo" is countable in Spanish, so you often say "un consejo" (a piece of advice) and can add an adjective like "buen" (good). "Buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" used before a masculine singular noun ("un buen consejo").
target_language_example: Gracias por el buen consejo; lo voy a seguir.
native_language_example: Thanks for the good advice; I'm going to follow it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having a nice day, or as a polite goodbye/wish. Common in expressions like “Que pase/pasen un buen día” (formal: you) and “Ten un buen día” (informal: you).
target_language_example: Espero que tengas un buen día en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day at work.

meaning: a good example (a positive model to follow).
additional_notes: Often used with the verb dar: "dar un buen ejemplo" = to set a good example, especially for children or others who may copy your behavior. It can also introduce an illustration of an idea: "un buen ejemplo de..." = a good example of...
target_language_example: Como hermano mayor, tienes que dar un buen ejemplo.
native_language_example: As the older brother, you have to set a good example.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who studies well or does well in school. "Buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" and is commonly used before a masculine singular noun ("un buen estudiante"). For feminine, say "una buena estudiante"; for plural, "unos buenos estudiantes / unas buenas estudiantes".
target_language_example: Mi hermana es una buena estudiante.
native_language_example: My sister is a good student.

additional_notes: Used in goodbyes to wish someone an enjoyable weekend. Common patterns: "(Que) pases/tengas un buen fin de semana" (informal, to one person), "(Que) pase/tenga un buen fin de semana" (formal), and "Pasen/Tengan un buen fin de semana" (to a group). Often preceded by "que" meaning “(I hope) that…”.
target_language_example: Nos vemos el lunes; que tengas un buen fin de semana.
native_language_example: See you Monday; have a good weekend.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man’s character in a general way (honest, kind, decent). Often appears with the verb ser (more permanent quality: “Es un buen hombre”) or parecer (an impression: “Parece un buen hombre”). You can also change it to match gender/number: una buena mujer, buenos hombres, buenas mujeres.
target_language_example: No lo conozco mucho, pero parece un buen hombre.
native_language_example: I don’t know him very well, but he seems like a good man.

additional_notes: Common phrase to describe a book positively. Uses the masculine singular article and adjective: un (a) + buen (short form of bueno before a masculine singular noun) + libro (book). You can compare books with "mejor" (better): "Este es un buen libro, pero ese es mejor."
target_language_example: ¿Me recomiendas un buen libro para practicar español?
native_language_example: Can you recommend a good book for me to practice Spanish?

additional_notes: Used to recommend or describe a place as suitable for an activity. It’s often followed by an infinitive (para cazar, para visitar, para escondernos) or by “para que + subjunctive” when the subject changes (un buen lugar para que pasemos el feriado).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un buen lugar para comer cerca de aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a good place to eat near here?

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular noun (profesor). For a female teacher, say "una buena profesora". "Buen" is the shortened form of "bueno" used before a masculine singular noun ("un buen libro").
target_language_example: Creo que Marta sería una buena profesora.
native_language_example: I think Marta would be a good teacher.

meaning: for a good while; a good time (enjoyable).
additional_notes: Has two common meanings depending on context: (1) duration: “for quite a while / a long time” (e.g., esperar, quedarse callado, reflexionar), and (2) enjoyment: “a good time” (often with pasar: pasar un buen rato = to have a good time).
target_language_example: Tuvimos que esperar un buen rato, pero al final lo pasamos un buen rato.
native_language_example: We had to wait quite a while, but in the end we had a good time.

meaning: a good place; a good spot (also: a good seat/location).
additional_notes: Means “a good place” in general (restaurant, town, area), but in contexts like events/transport it often means “a good spot/seat” (coger un buen sitio = get a good spot/seat by arriving early). “Sitio” is masculine: un buen sitio.
target_language_example: Vamos temprano para coger un buen sitio cerca del escenario.
native_language_example: Let’s go early to get a good spot near the stage.

meaning: a good guy; a nice person (usually a man).
additional_notes: Common, informal way to describe someone as kind, decent, and likable. Often used with ser/parecer: "Él es un buen tipo" (he’s a good guy), "Parece un buen tipo" (he seems like a good guy). "Tipo" can mean "guy" or "person" depending on context, but "un buen tipo" typically refers to a man.
target_language_example: Tu hermano es un buen tipo; siempre ayuda a los demás.
native_language_example: Your brother is a good guy; he always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s performance or the result of an effort. With the verb "hacer": "Hiciste/Habéis hecho un buen trabajo" = “You did a good job.” Also commonly said as a compliment on its own: "¡Buen trabajo!"
target_language_example: ¡Has hecho un buen trabajo con la presentación!
native_language_example: You did a good job with the presentation!

meaning: a good trip; have a good trip.
additional_notes: Used to describe a trip positively ("It was a good trip") and very commonly as a polite wish to someone who is about to travel. In formal situations you may see it with subjunctive/polite forms: "Que tenga un buen viaje" / "Tenga un buen viaje" (to you, formal). With friends: "¡Que tengas un buen viaje!".
target_language_example: ¡Que tengas un buen viaje!
native_language_example: Have a good trip!

additional_notes: Often a respectful way to refer to a man, especially in formal situations (e.g., on the phone: “un caballero llamó…”). It can also praise someone’s manners or honorable behavior: “Es todo un caballero” = “He’s a true gentleman.” Used with ser to describe character (Es un caballero) or with behavior: “su comportamiento era el de un caballero.”
target_language_example: Aunque no lo conocía, fue muy amable conmigo: es todo un caballero.
native_language_example: Even though I didn’t know him, he was very kind to me: he’s a real gentleman.

additional_notes: "Caballo" is a masculine noun, so it uses "un" (indefinite article = “a”). For a female horse, you can say "una yegua". It can also be used in comparisons ("se asemeja a un caballo" = “he resembles a horse”).
target_language_example: En el campo vi un caballo muy grande.
native_language_example: In the countryside I saw a very big horse.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about a coffee as a drink. With verbs like tomar/tomarse: “tomar(se) un café” = “to have a coffee.” Common in cafés/restaurants: “Tráigame un café…” (more formal) / “Ponme un café…” (more casual).
