You can add details: “un café con hielo” (iced coffee), “un café solo” (black/espresso), “un café con leche” (coffee with milk).
target_language_example: ¿Me pones un café, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you get me a coffee, please?

additional_notes: A very common polite way to order in a café or restaurant. You can replace "un café" with another item (e.g., "una cerveza, por favor"). Often said on its own when ordering; you can also add a verb for extra politeness, like "Quisiera un café, por favor" (I'd like a coffee, please) or "Tráigame un café, por favor" (Bring me a coffee, please).
target_language_example: Para mí, un café con leche, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: Most often means “a change” in a situation, plan, weather, etc. It can also mean “an exchange/swap” (changing one thing for another), especially with verbs like hacer (hacer un cambio) or cambiar. In shops you’ll also hear cambio for “change (money)” in expressions like ¿Tiene cambio? (“Do you have change?”).
target_language_example: Necesito hacer un cambio en mi horario.
native_language_example: I need to make a change to my schedule.

additional_notes: Used to talk about switching or replacing something: un cambio de propietario (a change of owner), un cambio de escenario (a change of scenery/setting), un cambio de actitud (a change of attitude), un cambio de moneda (a currency exchange/change). Often appears with verbs like necesitar (to need) or venir bien (to be good/come in handy).
target_language_example: Me vendría bien un cambio de planes.
native_language_example: A change of plans would come in handy for me.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: el camión / un camión; plural: camiones. Often used for large vehicles that carry goods (e.g., on highways/roads).
target_language_example: Hay un camión estacionado frente a mi casa.
native_language_example: There’s a truck parked in front of my house.

meaning: "a ... field" / "a ... (sports) field"; sometimes "a ... camp" (depending on the noun).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to specify what kind of campo it is: un campo de fútbol (a soccer field), un campo de golf (a golf course), un campo de prisioneros (a prisoner camp). In English it doesn’t always translate literally as “field of”—often it becomes “field,” “course,” or “camp” depending on context.
target_language_example: Hay un campo de golf cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: There’s a golf course near here.

meaning: a car (also: a cart; meaning depends on country).
additional_notes: In much of Latin America, carro commonly means “car” (automobile). In Spain, coche is more common for “car,” and carro may be understood as a cart/wagon in some contexts. Use un carro / una carro? → It’s masculine: un carro; plural: unos carros.
target_language_example: Necesito un carro para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: I need a car to go to work.

meaning: a pig; (as an insult) “a pig” (dirty, gross, rude).
additional_notes: Literally refers to the animal (“a pig”). Used about a person, it’s an insult meaning someone is messy/dirty, disgusting, or behaves in a rude/sexist way (similar to English “You pig!”). Often appears with "Eres un cerdo" / "Qué cerdo".
target_language_example: ¡No seas un cerdo! Limpia la mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t be a pig! Clean the table, please.

additional_notes: "Chico" usually refers to a boy or a young man. It can be neutral ("un chico tímido") or affectionate/complimentary ("un chico increíble"). In some places it can also mean "a kid" or "a guy" in general depending on context.
target_language_example: Hay un chico nuevo en mi clase.
native_language_example: There’s a new boy in my class.

additional_notes: Means one cigarette (singular). Often used with verbs like fumar (to smoke), necesitar (to need), or pedir/dar (to ask for/give). You can also say "un cigarro" in many places; "cigarrillo" can sound a bit more formal or specific.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un cigarrillo?
native_language_example: Do you have a cigarette?

additional_notes: A noun for someone who lacks courage. Used with the verb ser (e.g., “Es un cobarde”) or after como to describe someone’s behavior (“Huyó como un cobarde” = “He ran away like a coward”). Feminine form: una cobarde.
target_language_example: No seas un cobarde y dímelo a la cara.
native_language_example: Don’t be a coward and tell me to my face.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" = "a" (one). Used when talking about any car or introducing a car for the first time. "En un coche" often means "in a car / by car" (traveling in a car).
target_language_example: Voy al trabajo en un coche de mi hermano.
native_language_example: I go to work in my brother’s car.

additional_notes: "Coche" means "car" (common in Spain; in many Latin American countries you’ll also hear "carro" or "auto"). "Nuevo" agrees with the noun: "un coche nuevo" (masculine singular). For feminine nouns: "una casa nueva".
target_language_example: Quiero comprar un coche nuevo este año.
native_language_example: I want to buy a new car this year.

additional_notes: Most often the literal animal (a pet or a wild rabbit). It’s also common in comparisons to describe someone/something as fast, shy, or scared: “corría como un conejo” (“ran like a scared rabbit”). Sometimes it can be used playfully about a person, similar to English “bunny.”
target_language_example: En el jardín vi un conejo blanco.
native_language_example: In the garden I saw a white rabbit.

additional_notes: Common noun for an email message. You’ll often see the shorter form "un email" as well. Typical verbs: "recibir" (to receive) un correo electrónico; "enviar" / "mandar" (to send) un correo electrónico; "escribir" (to write) un correo electrónico (often "a" + person: "escribirle un correo electrónico a mis padres").
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes enviar un correo electrónico con la información?
native_language_example: Can you send me an email with the information?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "necesitar" (to need) or "querer" (to want): "Necesito/Quiero un corte de pelo." Also common with "hacer" in some regions: "Me voy a hacer un corte de pelo" (I’m going to get a haircut).
target_language_example: Mañana tengo cita para un corte de pelo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an appointment for a haircut.

additional_notes: Used for something illegal or punishable by law. Common with verbs like cometer (to commit) and adjectives like violento (violent). It can also be used hyperbolically in casual speech to mean something is very bad or unfair (e.g., Bailar no es un crimen = “Dancing isn’t a crime”).
target_language_example: Robar una bicicleta es un crimen.
native_language_example: Stealing a bicycle is a crime.

additional_notes: Common noun for a knife; used for cutting. Gender: masculine (el cuchillo). Plural: cuchillos. Often followed by "para" + infinitive to say what it’s for: "un cuchillo para cortar...".
target_language_example: Necesito un cuchillo para cortar el pan.
native_language_example: I need a knife to cut the bread.

additional_notes: Used for a positive remark about someone (their appearance, work, personality, etc.). Often appears with the verb "hacer": "hacerle un cumplido a alguien" = to pay/give someone a compliment. Pronoun placement is common: "Te hizo un cumplido" (He/She complimented you), "Él me hizo un cumplido" (He complimented me).
target_language_example: Gracias por el cumplido; me alegra que te guste mi trabajo.
native_language_example: Thanks for the compliment; I'm glad you like my work.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article un (“a”). The plural is demonios (“demons”). Can be used literally (religion/folklore) and sometimes figuratively to describe someone as very evil or cruel.
target_language_example: Dicen que en ese bosque vive un demonio.
native_language_example: They say a demon lives in that forest.

additional_notes: Used both for real disasters (an accident, a catastrophe) and informally to say something is in terrible condition or very disorganized: "Es/está un desastre" (It’s a mess). With places or situations, you’ll often hear "Esto/Esta casa es un desastre".
target_language_example: Mi cuarto es un desastre; tengo que ordenar hoy.
native_language_example: My room is a mess; I have to tidy up today.

additional_notes:
Used with verbs like hacer/tomar/darse un descanso. 
- hacer/tomar un descanso = to take a break (pause an activity)
- darse un descanso = to give yourself a break (rest, or be less hard on yourself).
target_language_example: Voy a tomar un descanso antes de seguir trabajando.
native_language_example: I'm going to take a break before I keep working.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. Use it for a book (or app) that lists words and their meanings/translations. Often followed by “de + language” to say what kind of dictionary it is: “un diccionario de francés/inglés”.
target_language_example: Necesito un diccionario de español-inglés.
native_language_example: I need a Spanish-English dictionary.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular form of “a/an.” In Spanish, "doctor" often refers to a medical doctor; for other meanings, Spanish may use context or phrases like "doctorado" (PhD).
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con un doctor.
native_language_example: I need to talk to a doctor.

meaning: a gift; a talent (a natural ability).
additional_notes: "Don" can mean either a natural talent/ability (often used with "tener un don para..." = "to have a talent for...") or a gift in a more general sense. Don’t confuse it with English "don" (to put on clothes) or "a don" (a university teacher).
target_language_example: Tiene un don para la música.
native_language_example: He/She has a talent for music.

meaning: a nobody; an insignificant person (often insulting).
additional_notes: A common, pejorative way to say someone is unimportant or has no status. Often used with **ser** (e.g., *Soy/Es un don nadie*) or in the phrase **no ser más que un don nadie** (“to be nothing but a nobody”). Can also be used self-deprecatingly, but it usually sounds harsh.
target_language_example: No dejes que te digan que eres un don nadie.
native_language_example: Don’t let anyone tell you that you’re a nobody.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a single day/24-hour period ("I stayed one day"). With a future wish or plan ("Un día quiero..."), it often means "someday." In weather/time-of-day comments, it can mean "a (nice/terrible) day" ("Hace un día magnífico").
target_language_example: Un día volveré a visitarte.
native_language_example: Someday I’ll visit you again.

meaning: “a day of” (a day for a specific purpose or type of day).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe what kind of day it is: un día de trabajo (a workday), un día de descanso (a day off/rest day), un día de enfermedad (a sick day). In expressions like “un día de éstos” it means “one of these days / someday soon.”
target_language_example: Mañana tengo un día de trabajo muy largo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a very long workday.

additional_notes: Used for time when you are not working or studying. Common with verbs like “tomarse” (to take for yourself) and “pedir” (to request): “tomarse un día libre”, “pedir un día libre”.
target_language_example: Mañana voy a tomarme un día libre para descansar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to take a day off to rest.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **un día muy + adjective**. You use **muy** (“very”) to intensify the adjective: *un día muy caluroso* (a very hot day), *un día muy largo* (a very long day). Note the adjective usually comes after the noun in Spanish.
target_language_example: Hoy es un día muy frío.
native_language_example: Today is a very cold day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single dollar (the currency unit). Often appears with amounts and money words like billete(s) (bill), centavo(s) (cent), and in expressions like Tengo un dólar (I have one dollar).
target_language_example: Solo me queda un dólar.
native_language_example: I only have one dollar left.

additional_notes: Refers to paid work or a position at a workplace. Very common with verbs like conseguir (to get/find), tener (to have), buscar (to look for), and obtener (to obtain). You can also specify the type: un empleo fijo (a steady/permanent job), un empleo de tiempo completo (full-time job), un empleo de medio tiempo (part-time job).
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un empleo, pero todavía no encuentro nada.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job, but I still can’t find anything.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: el error / un error. Common with verbs like cometer (to make/commit) and phrases like “Ese es un error común” (That’s a common mistake). Also used in technical contexts (computers/servers): “El servidor encontró un error temporal” (The server encountered a temporary error).
target_language_example: Cometí un error al escribir tu dirección.
native_language_example: I made a mistake when I wrote your address.

meaning: a student (male; or a generic student).
additional_notes: “Un” means “a/an.” “Estudiante” can refer to a male student, and in many contexts it’s also used as a gender-neutral term; for a clearly female student you may also hear “una estudiante.” It’s commonly followed by “de …” to say what kind of student (e.g., “un estudiante de secundaria” = “a high school student”), or an adjective like “aplicado” (hardworking).
target_language_example: Mi hermano es un estudiante de este colegio.
native_language_example: My brother is a student at this school.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to describe something as excellent: un excelente profesor/trabajo/jugador. It agrees with the noun: feminine is "una excelente" (una excelente idea), and plural is "unos/unas excelentes".
target_language_example: Hiciste un excelente trabajo en el examen.
native_language_example: You did an excellent job on the exam.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who knows a lot about a topic or area: un experto en finanzas, un experto en reptiles, etc. After en you typically use a noun (en astronomía) or an infinitive to describe a skill/activity (en resolver problemas). Feminine form: una experta en. Plural: expertos/ expertas en.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un experto en informática para arreglar el sistema.
native_language_example: We need an expert in IT to fix the system.

meaning: a ghost; also used in expressions like “as if you’ve seen a ghost” (very shocked or scared).
additional_notes: Most literally means “a ghost” (a spirit). Common in comparisons: "parecer/lucir como si hubiera visto un fantasma" = to look extremely frightened or surprised. With "ver": "vi un fantasma" = “I saw a ghost.”
target_language_example: Cuando me llamaste a medianoche, parecía como si hubieras visto un fantasma.
native_language_example: When you called me at midnight, you looked like you had seen a ghost.

additional_notes: Refers to Saturday and Sunday (or the time off around those days). Often used with verbs like pasar (to spend): "Pasé un fin de semana..." Also common with libre (free): "un fin de semana libre".
target_language_example: Este fin de semana no trabajo.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m not working.

additional_notes: Used to describe intense pain. Often followed by where it hurts: "un fuerte dolor de cabeza" (a bad headache) or "un fuerte dolor en + body part" (a severe pain in the back/stomach/abdomen). "Fuerte" here means 'strong' = 'severe' (not 'loud').
target_language_example: Tengo un fuerte dolor en el pecho.
native_language_example: I have a severe pain in my chest.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Gato" means “cat” (male cat, or cat in general). Plural: "unos gatos" = “some cats.” Feminine form: "una gata" (a female cat).
target_language_example: Hay un gato en el jardín.
native_language_example: There’s a cat in the garden.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: un (a) + gato (cat) + blanco (white). The adjective usually comes after the noun in Spanish. Use "un" for a male cat or when the gender is unknown; use "una gata blanca" for a female cat.
target_language_example: En mi casa hay un gato blanco muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: In my house there is a very calm white cat.

meaning: a genius; (also) very skilled at something.
additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s intelligence or talent. With "ser" it describes someone as a genius (often in a general sense). With "con" + a thing/activity, it means "to be really good with/at" something. Can also be used jokingly depending on tone.
target_language_example: Mi hermano es un genio con las computadoras.
native_language_example: My brother is a genius with computers.

meaning: a hit/blow; a knock; a bump (injury).
additional_notes: Used for physical impacts: give someone/something a hit (dar un golpe), knock on a door (dar un golpe en la puerta), or a bump/injury someone has (tener un golpe). Often followed by where: en la cara, en la oreja, etc. It can also be used more generally for a hard setback (“recibir un golpe duro”).
target_language_example: Me di un golpe en la cabeza y me duele.
native_language_example: I bumped my head and it hurts.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun. "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" placed before the noun: "un gran día" (= a great day). It can mean physical size (“big”) or importance/quality (“great”). For feminine nouns, use "una gran"; for plural, "unos grandes / unas grandes".
target_language_example: Hoy es un gran día para empezar.
native_language_example: Today is a great day to start.

meaning: a great day; a big/important day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a day that will be especially good, memorable, or important. Very common in greetings and wishes: "Que tengas un gran día" = "Have a great day." You can also use it to describe today, tomorrow, or a past day: "Fue/Ha sido un gran día".
target_language_example: ¡Ojalá tengas un gran día en tu nuevo trabajo!
native_language_example: I hope you have a great day at your new job!

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like cometer (to make/commit) or ser (to be): cometer un gran error = “to make a big mistake.” Gran is a shortened form of grande used before a singular noun (un gran error, una gran idea).
target_language_example: Sería un gran error no estudiar para el examen.
native_language_example: It would be a big mistake not to study for the exam.

meaning: a great man; an important/respected man.
additional_notes: Usually means someone admirable (good character, achievements) or influential. Note that **gran** is the short form of *grande* used before a singular noun: *un gran hombre*. In contexts like *en la empresa*, it often means “a big deal / an important person” rather than literally physically big.
target_language_example: Para mí, mi abuelo fue un gran hombre.
native_language_example: To me, my grandfather was a great man.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say there are a lot of something. It’s fairly formal/neutral and common in writing. Verb agreement is usually plural because the real subject is the plural noun after de: “Un gran número de personas murieron…”.
target_language_example: Un gran número de estudiantes no pudo asistir a clase hoy.
native_language_example: A large number of students couldn’t attend class today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very difficult or has major negative consequences. You’ll often hear it with "tener" (to have): "Tengo un gran problema". "Gran" is a shortened form of "grande" used before a singular noun: "un gran problema".
target_language_example: Si perdemos este documento, vamos a tener un gran problema.
native_language_example: If we lose this document, we’re going to have a big problem.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s performance or effort. You can adjust gender/number: "un gran trabajo" (masc. singular), "un gran trabajo" is fixed because "trabajo" is masculine; add emphasis with "¡" in speech/writing: "¡Un gran trabajo!". Often appears with "hacer": "Hiciste un gran trabajo" = "You did a great job."
target_language_example: ¡Has hecho un gran trabajo con este proyecto!
native_language_example: You did a great job on this project!

meaning: a grain of sand; something very small (often in the idiom “make a mountain out of a grain of sand”).
additional_notes: Literally means “a grain of sand.” It’s most commonly seen in the expression “hacer una montaña de un grano de arena” (= to make a mountain out of a molehill), meaning to exaggerate a small problem. Note: Spanish “arena” means “sand,” not an “arena” (stadium).
target_language_example: No hagas una montaña de un grano de arena; se puede arreglar fácil.
native_language_example: Don’t make a mountain out of a molehill; it can be fixed easily.

additional_notes: Used to talk about several people or things considered together. It’s usually followed by a plural noun: un grupo de estudiantes, un grupo de niños. Note: as a collective noun, it’s common to hear either singular or plural verb agreement depending on whether the speaker focuses on the group as one unit or the individuals (e.g., Un grupo de niños estaba/estaban jugando).
target_language_example: Vi un grupo de turistas frente al museo.
native_language_example: I saw a group of tourists in front of the museum.

additional_notes: A polite, common greeting when you meet someone for the first time. You can also say "Mucho gusto" or "Encantado/a" (use -o if you’re a man, -a if you’re a woman). Often used right after saying "Hola" and/or the person’s name.
target_language_example: Hola, soy Ana. Un gusto conocerte.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Ana. Nice to meet you.

additional_notes: "Hijo" means "son". In a broader sense, it can also mean "child" when the gender is already known or not important. "Un" is the masculine singular form of "a/an" (use "una" with "hija" = daughter).
target_language_example: Tenemos un hijo de cinco años.
native_language_example: We have a five-year-old son.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular indefinite article (un) + hombre (“man”). It can mean “a man” in general, “a certain man” (someone unspecified), or “one man” to emphasize that it’s just a single person (e.g., “Sólo un hombre”). Often followed by descriptions: “un hombre como tú” (a man like you), “un hombre de…” (a man with/of…), “un hombre en…” (a man at/in…).
target_language_example: Hay un hombre esperándote afuera.
native_language_example: There’s a man waiting for you outside.

additional_notes: “Hombre” means “man” and “alto” means “tall.” The adjective usually goes after the noun: “un hombre alto.” If you’re describing a specific person, use “el hombre alto” (“the tall man”). In Spanish, adjectives agree in gender/number: “un hombre alto” (male), “una mujer alta” (female), “hombres altos” (plural).
target_language_example: En la fiesta conocí a un hombre alto con gafas.
native_language_example: At the party I met a tall man with glasses.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man by adding a characteristic or possession after **con** (“with”): *un hombre con ambición* (a man with ambition), *un hombre con iniciativa* (a man with initiative). You can swap **hombre** for other nouns (e.g., *una mujer con…*, *una persona con…*).
target_language_example: Busco un hombre con buen corazón.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a man with a good heart.

meaning: "a man of ..." (used to describe a man by a quality, principle, or characteristic).
additional_notes: You use **un hombre de + noun phrase** to highlight what kind of person someone is (often a personal quality or value): *un hombre de honor* (a man of honor), *un hombre de palabra* (a man who keeps his word), *un hombre de familia* (a family man), *un hombre de carácter* (a man of character). It can also describe a visible trait: *un hombre de pelo blanco* (a white-haired man).
target_language_example: Es un hombre de principios y no cambia de opinión fácilmente.
native_language_example: He’s a man of principles and doesn’t change his mind easily.

meaning: a businessman (a man who works in business).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man's job/role in the business world. Often with ser: "Él es un hombre de negocios." For a gender-neutral option you can say "una persona de negocios" (less common) or more specific roles like "empresario" (business owner/entrepreneur).
target_language_example: Mi padre es un hombre de negocios y viaja mucho por trabajo.
native_language_example: My dad is a businessman and travels a lot for work.

additional_notes: A descriptive noun phrase: "un" (a) + "hombre" (man) + "honesto" (honest). The adjective usually goes after the noun. You can change "un" to "una" for a woman ("una mujer honesta"), or make it plural: "hombres honestos" / "mujeres honestas".
target_language_example: Todos confían en él porque es un hombre honesto.
native_language_example: Everyone trusts him because he is an honest man.

meaning: "a very ... man" (a man who is very [adjective]).
additional_notes: Use this to describe a man with an adjective: **un hombre muy + adjective** (e.g., *rico, feo, amable, modesto, peligroso*). In Spanish, the adjective often comes **after** the noun (*un hombre rico*), and **muy** goes right **before** the adjective (*muy rico*). Adjectives agree in gender/number: *un hombre muy alto* / *una mujer muy alta* / *unos hombres muy altos*.
target_language_example: Es un hombre muy inteligente.
native_language_example: He’s a very intelligent man.

meaning: “a man who …” (used to introduce a description).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to add information about what kind of man someone is (often giving a characteristic, habit, or defining action). Typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “Busco un hombre que sea honesto” = I’m looking for a man who is honest) when the person is unknown/desired, and by the indicative when referring to a specific, known man.
target_language_example: Es un hombre que siempre cumple su palabra.
native_language_example: He’s a man who always keeps his word.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man who has a lot of money. Often appears after verbs like ser/era (to be/was), casarse con (to marry), or trabajar para (to work for). Feminine: una mujer rica (“a rich woman”).
target_language_example: Quiero ser un hombre rico algún día.
native_language_example: I want to be a rich man someday.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man who is intelligent and makes good decisions. Often appears in general statements (e.g., "Un hombre sabio no…" = "A wise man wouldn’t…"). You can swap the article depending on context: "un" (a) vs. "el" (the). For a woman, say "una mujer sabia".
target_language_example: Un hombre sabio escucha antes de hablar.
native_language_example: A wise man listens before speaking.

additional_notes: “Hospital” is a masculine noun in Spanish, so it uses the article “un” (a) or “el” (the): “un hospital”, “el hospital”. Common with prepositions like “en” (in/at) and “a” (to): “trabajar en un hospital”, “ir a un hospital”.
target_language_example: ¿Hay un hospital cerca de aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a hospital near here?

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Hotel" is masculine: un hotel, el hotel. Used to talk about any (not specific) hotel. In sentence 4, "¡iros a un hotel!" can be a blunt/impolite way of telling two people to go somewhere private (similar to “Get a room!”).
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar un hotel cerca de la estación.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a hotel near the station.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for someone admired for bravery or great achievements. Often used with verbs like "ser" (to be) and "volverse" (to become): "Es un héroe" / "Se volvió un héroe". In sentences like "Consideraban a Tom un héroe", it means "They considered Tom a hero" (using "considerar a + person + noun"). Feminine form: "una heroína".
target_language_example: Para mí, mi madre es un héroe.
native_language_example: For me, my mother is a hero.

additional_notes: Use "un idioma" to mean a (spoken) language: "Aprender un idioma" = “to learn a language.” It’s interchangeable with "una lengua" in many contexts, but "idioma" is very common in everyday speech. Plural: "idiomas".
target_language_example: ¿Cuántos idiomas hablas?
native_language_example: How many languages do you speak?

additional_notes: Refers to any language that is not your native language (or not the main language where you live). Often used with verbs like aprender (to learn), estudiar (to study), and hablar (to speak).
target_language_example: Estoy aprendiendo un idioma extranjero este año.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language this year.

additional_notes: A strong, rude label for a person (can be hurtful). Used with ser: “Es un idiota.” Also common in phrases like “tomar a alguien por un idiota” (to take someone for an idiot) and “tratar a alguien como a un idiota” (to treat someone like an idiot). For a softer option, consider “tonto/a” (silly/stupid).
target_language_example: No soy un idiota; sé lo que pasó.
native_language_example: I’m not an idiot; I know what happened.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a very short amount of time. Common patterns: "en un instante" = "in an instant" (very quickly), "por un instante" = "for a moment" (briefly), and as a polite request "Un instante, por favor" = "One moment, please."
target_language_example: Un instante, por favor; ahora te ayudo.
native_language_example: One moment, please; I’ll help you now.

meaning: a game; (figuratively) “just a game” / something not taken seriously.
additional_notes: Common with verbs like "ser" and "ver" ("Sólo era un juego", "Todo lo ven como un juego"). It can also be used figuratively to criticize someone for treating something serious (like war) as if it were just entertainment.
target_language_example: No es un juego: ten cuidado.
native_language_example: It’s not a game—be careful.

meaning: "a set of" (things) or "a game of" (a type of game).
additional_notes: Used before a noun. With objects that come in a group (tools, speakers, dishes, etc.), it often means “a set of.” With activities/sports/board games, it means “a game of” + the game (e.g., un juego de ajedrez, un juego de fútbol americano). The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: ¿Jugamos un juego de cartas esta noche?
native_language_example: Shall we play a card game tonight?

additional_notes: Used for one side of an object/place/person/idea. Often appears in contrasts like “un lado..., otro...” (“one side..., the other...”) and in figurative uses like “un lado oscuro/oculto” (“a dark/hidden side”). With locations it can mean “on one side/at one side of,” e.g., “en un lado de la cama.”
target_language_example: Mira un lado del papel: está en blanco.
native_language_example: Look at one side of the paper: it’s blank.

additional_notes: "Ladrón" is a masculine noun; the feminine form is "una ladrona." It’s often followed by "de" + what they steal ("un ladrón de bancos" = a bank robber). You can also use it more generally as an insult meaning someone is a thief.
target_language_example: ¡Cuidado! Ese hombre es un ladrón.
native_language_example: Careful! That man is a thief.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something that lasts or stretches for a long time or distance (e.g., un largo camino/viaje/día). Often translated simply as “a long …” in English. Feminine form: una larga (e.g., una larga espera).
target_language_example: Va a ser un largo día, pero lo lograremos.
native_language_example: It’s going to be a long day, but we’ll make it.

meaning: a long way; a long journey.
additional_notes: Used literally for a long distance (a long road to travel) and figuratively for a long process or period of effort ("It’s been a long journey"). Common with verbs like ser (Es un largo camino), haber (Ha sido un largo camino), and recorrer (Hemos recorrido un largo camino). You can also say "tener un largo camino por recorrer" = "to have a long way to go."
target_language_example: Todavía nos queda un largo camino por recorrer.
native_language_example: We still have a long way to go.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. Often appears with time expressions like "desde hace un largo tiempo" (for a long time) and "ha pasado un largo tiempo" (a long time has passed).
target_language_example: No te veo desde hace un largo tiempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in a long time.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" = "a/an" (masculine singular). Used to mention a lion in general or one you’re introducing for the first time. Feminine is "una leona" (a lioness).
target_language_example: En el zoológico vimos un león muy grande.
native_language_example: At the zoo we saw a very big lion.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular form of "a/an." "Libro" is a masculine noun, so you say "un libro" (not *una libro*). You’ll often see it after verbs like "leer" (to read), "traer" (to bring), and "tener" (to have).
target_language_example: Necesito un libro para la clase.
native_language_example: I need a book for class.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like coge/cogí/cogió (“(to) take/pick up”) or se cayó (“fell”) to say the book is taken from or falls off a shelf. "De la" = “from the” (feminine), because estantería is feminine.
target_language_example: Voy a coger un libro de la estantería.
native_language_example: I’m going to take a book from the shelf.

additional_notes: Used to say the topic of a book. Common patterns: “un libro sobre + noun” (un libro sobre China) and “un libro sobre + article + noun” (un libro sobre la historia de Australia). “Sobre” here means “about/on.”
target_language_example: Estoy buscando un libro sobre cocina española.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a book about Spanish cooking.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the animal. In stories or dramatic speech it can also suggest a dangerous threat that 'takes' someone away (e.g., being eaten by a wolf), contrasted with other dangers like hunger.
target_language_example: Dicen que anoche vieron un lobo cerca del pueblo.
native_language_example: They say they saw a wolf near the town last night.

meaning: a place; a spot; a location.
additional_notes: Often used with adjectives to describe a place: un lugar sagrado (a sacred place), un lugar pequeño (a small place). In the expression "de un lugar a otro," it means "from one place to another."
target_language_example: Busquemos un lugar tranquilo para hablar.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a quiet place to talk.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing what happens in that place or what the place is for. It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "un lugar donde estudiar" = a place to study) or by a conjugated verb (e.g., "un lugar donde estaríamos solos" = a place where we’d be alone).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un lugar donde podamos hablar tranquilos?
native_language_example: Is there a place where we can talk quietly?

additional_notes: Used to say a place is suitable or intended for an action. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "un lugar para dormir" (a place to sleep). In negative statements it often means “not a place for (something/someone)” by context: "No es un lugar para humanos" (It’s not a place for humans).
target_language_example: ¿Hay un lugar para sentarse aquí?
native_language_example: Is there a place to sit here?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a location where you are protected from danger or trouble. Often used with verbs like ir a (go to), llevar a (take to), llegar a (arrive at), encontrar (find), or llamar desde/de (call from). You can also say: "Este es un lugar seguro" (This is a safe place).
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar un lugar seguro antes de llamar a la policía.
native_language_example: Let’s find a safe place before calling the police.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Lápiz" is masculine: un lápiz, el lápiz. Commonly used with colors (un lápiz rojo) and in requests (Deme un lápiz / ¿Me prestas un lápiz?).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un lápiz para escribir mi número?
native_language_example: Do you have a pencil to write down my number?

additional_notes: Often used before a noun to mean “bad” in a general sense: un mal día (a bad day), un mal olor (a bad smell), un mal sabor (a bad taste), un mal conductor (a bad driver). It can also mean “an evil” or “an illness/ailment” depending on context (un mal terrible = a terrible evil/ill). For feminine nouns, use mala: una mala idea.
target_language_example: Tuve un mal día en el trabajo.
native_language_example: I had a bad day at work.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine indefinite article un (“a”). Often followed by de + place/thing: un mapa de la ciudad (“a map of the city”). In Spanish, mapa is masculine: el mapa, un mapa.
target_language_example: Necesito un mapa de la ciudad para no perderme.
native_language_example: I need a map of the city so I don’t get lost.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken or written message (e.g., voicemail, note, or in an app). Very common with verbs like dejar (to leave) and mandar/enviar (to send). For a text message you can also say "un mensaje de texto".
target_language_example: Si no contesto, déjame un mensaje.
native_language_example: If I don't answer, leave me a message.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like escribir/enviar/dar to say who the message is addressed to. Very often you’ll also see the indirect object pronoun before the verb: “Le escribió un mensaje a su novio” = “She wrote her boyfriend a message.” (Le = to him/her; Les = to them).
target_language_example: Voy a enviar un mensaje a mi mamá.
native_language_example: I’m going to send a message to my mom.

additional_notes: Used to say who the message is addressed to. Often appears with verbs like “tener” (Tengo un mensaje para Ana) or “dejar” (Quisiera dejar un mensaje para el señor García). You can also add who it’s from with “de”: “Tengo un mensaje para Juan de María.”
target_language_example: Tengo un mensaje para ti.
native_language_example: I have a message for you.

additional_notes: A noun for a man/boy who lies. Feminine form: "una mentirosa". Often used with "ser": "Eres un mentiroso" (You’re a liar). Can be insulting depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: No le creas: es un mentiroso.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him: he’s a liar.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration or time period of one month: for how long something lasts (por un mes, durante todo un mes) or how long ago/since something happened (tras casi un mes, lleva… un mes). Can also be part of ranges: “un mes o dos” = “a month or two.”
target_language_example: Voy a quedarme aquí un mes.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for a month.

additional_notes: Used literally for a religious/supernatural miracle, and very commonly in everyday speech to mean something extremely unlikely or surprisingly good (“We need a miracle”). The noun is masculine: un milagro. Similar to English “miracle.”
target_language_example: Llegar a tiempo con este tráfico sería un milagro.
native_language_example: Getting there on time with this traffic would be a miracle.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express the literal number (1,000,000) or, very often, an exaggeration meaning “a ton of / so many.” Common set phrase: "Un millón de gracias" = “Thanks a million.”
target_language_example: Tengo un millón de cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a million things to do today.

additional_notes: A money amount: "un millón" = one million, and "de" is used before the currency or item being counted ("un millón de + [noun]"). It can be used for exact amounts or approximate ones with words like "casi" (almost). Often appears after verbs like "tener" (to have) or "elevarse a" (to rise to).
target_language_example: El premio es de un millón de dólares.
native_language_example: The prize is a million dollars.

additional_notes: Used as an exaggeration to emphasize that something has been done/said/called repeatedly. Common with the present perfect: "He ... un millón de veces" (I’ve ... a million times) and "Te lo he dicho un millón de veces" (I’ve told you a million times).
target_language_example: Ya lo he intentado un millón de veces, pero no funciona.
native_language_example: I’ve tried it a million times already, but it doesn’t work.

additional_notes: Often used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say something won’t take long: Será un minuto / Solo llevará un minuto. Can also mean “for a minute” (duration): Déjame pensar un minuto; ¿puedo hablar contigo un minuto? Variations like Un minuto más / Sólo un minuto (más) mean “one more minute” / “just a minute.”
target_language_example: Espera un minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, please.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to wait briefly. Common on its own (“Un minuto, por favor.”) or after a request (“Espere un minuto, por favor.” / “Dame un minuto, por favor.”). Often means “just a moment,” not literally exactly one minute.
target_language_example: Un minuto, por favor; ya vuelvo.
native_language_example: One moment, please; I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Polite way to ask someone to wait briefly. Often used in customer service and formal situations. You can also hear it as “Un momento, por favor” or “Un momento.”
target_language_example: Un momento, por favor, ahora le atiendo.
native_language_example: One moment, please; I’ll help you now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a scary imaginary creature (in stories, myths, etc.). In Spanish it can also be used about a person who is cruel or very unpleasant, but in these examples it’s literal. Plural: "monstruos."
target_language_example: Dicen que en ese lago vive un monstruo.
native_language_example: They say a monster lives in that lake.

additional_notes: Very common and informal-ish way to intensify quantity or degree. Use it with verbs (e.g., "trabajar un montón" = to work a lot), with "me gusta" ("me gusta un montón" = I like it a lot), or like an adverb meaning "very" in casual speech. Literally "a pile/a heap," but it usually just means "a lot."
target_language_example: Gracias por venir; me ayudaste un montón.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming; you helped me a lot.

additional_notes: Common, slightly informal way to talk about a large quantity or number. Used before a noun (countable or uncountable): "un montón de gente" (lots of people), "un montón de tiempo" (a lot of time). Literally means "a heap/pile of."
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things; lots of stuff.
additional_notes: Very common, informal-ish way to say you have/see/do many things. Often used as an intensifier: “un montón de + noun” (un montón de trabajo = a lot of work). Can also be a short answer by itself: “¿Qué compraste?” — “Un montón de cosas.”
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de cosas que hacer hoy.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of money; a large amount of money.
additional_notes: Common, informal-ish way to emphasize that the amount is big. Often used with verbs like ganar (to earn), pagar (to pay), robar (to steal), dar (to give): "Ganaba/Pagó/Robó/Dio un montón de dinero". You can also say just "un montón" (a lot/tons) when the noun is clear from context.
target_language_example: Gasté un montón de dinero en ese viaje.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of money on that trip.

meaning: a lot of people; lots of people.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say that many people are involved (more casual than "mucha gente"). It can be followed by a verb in singular or plural depending on whether you think of the group as one unit or as individuals: "Un montón de gente estaba..." / "Un montón de gente estaban..." (singular is often preferred in standard Spanish).
target_language_example: Había un montón de gente en la estación, así que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: There were a lot of people at the station, so we arrived late.

meaning: a lot of books; lots of books.
additional_notes: “Un montón de + noun” is a common way to say “a lot of” or “a bunch of.” It’s informal but very frequent in everyday speech. You can swap in other nouns: un montón de trabajo (a lot of work), un montón de gente (lots of people).
target_language_example: Tengo un montón de libros, pero casi no tengo tiempo para leerlos.
native_language_example: I have a lot of books, but I hardly have time to read them.

meaning: a lot of time; lots of time.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you have plenty of time. Often used with tener (to have): Tengo/Tienes/Tenemos un montón de tiempo. You can swap in other nouns too (un montón de dinero = a lot of money).
target_language_example: No te preocupes: todavía tenemos un montón de tiempo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we still have plenty of time.

meaning: 'a very good' (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe a masculine singular noun: un muy buen trabajo / un muy buen profesor. Note that bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun (not *bueno*): un buen día, un muy buen día. For feminine nouns, use una muy buena: una muy buena idea.
target_language_example: Este restaurante tiene un muy buen ambiente.
native_language_example: This restaurant has a very good atmosphere.

additional_notes: A common phrase for a figure made of snow (usually round snowballs stacked). Often used with the verb hacer: hacer un muñeco de nieve (“to make a snowman”).
target_language_example: Después de la nevada, los niños hicieron un muñeco de nieve en el parque.
native_language_example: After the snowfall, the kids made a snowman in the park.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: use **un** for “a/an” with masculine singular nouns. **Un médico** is “a doctor” (not a specific one). For “the doctor,” use **el médico**; for a female doctor you can also say **una médica** (common in many places) or **una mujer médico**.
target_language_example: Necesito hablar con un médico.
native_language_example: I need to speak with a doctor.

additional_notes: "Niño" usually refers to a male child ("boy"), but it can sometimes be used more generally for "child" in context. It’s often contrasted with being grown up (e.g., "ya no eres un niño" = "you’re not a kid anymore"). Feminine: "una niña" (a girl). Plural: "unos niños" / "los niños" (boys/children).
target_language_example: Ese es un niño muy inteligente.
native_language_example: That is a very smart boy.

meaning: a little boy; a young/small child (boy).
additional_notes: Literally “a small boy.” Used to talk about a boy who is very young (often a toddler or young kid). You can say it about someone’s past: "Desde que era un niño pequeño..." = “Ever since he was a little boy...”. For a young girl, say "una niña pequeña"; for a small/young child without specifying gender, you can use "un niño/una niña" or "un niño pequeño/una niña pequeña" depending on the child’s gender.
target_language_example: Cuando era un niño pequeño, me daba miedo la oscuridad.
native_language_example: When I was a little boy, I was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: “Nombre” means “name” (not “number” — that’s “número”), so it’s a common false friend for English speakers. Often used with verbs like “elegir/escoger” (to choose) or “tener” (to have): “Elija un nombre.” You can add “de …” to give extra info about the name (e.g., where it’s from): “un nombre de Cornualles”.
target_language_example: Necesitamos un nombre para el bebé.
native_language_example: We need a name for the baby.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something newly made, recently introduced, or different from the previous one: un nuevo modelo, un nuevo sistema. Adjective agreement matters: feminine is "una nueva" (una nueva idea), plural is "unos nuevos / unas nuevas".
target_language_example: Necesito un nuevo teléfono.
native_language_example: I need a new phone.

meaning: a new beginning; a fresh start.
additional_notes: Used to talk about starting again after a change, mistake, or difficult period. Common with verbs like hacer (hacer un nuevo comienzo = to make a fresh start) or with por (Por un nuevo comienzo = To a new beginning / For a fresh start, like a toast or slogan).
target_language_example: Después de mudarnos, fue un nuevo comienzo para todos.
native_language_example: After we moved, it was a new beginning for everyone.

meaning: a number; a (certain) amount; a phone number.
additional_notes: Most literally it means “a number” (a digit/quantity). In expressions like “un número de + noun” it means “a number of / some / several” (an unspecified amount). In places with waiting turns (like a deli or office), “Coge/Saque un número” means “Take a number” (get a ticket for your turn). In contact contexts, “dejar un número” usually means leaving your phone number.
target_language_example: ¿Me dejas un número y te llamo más tarde?
native_language_example: Can you leave me a number and I’ll call you later?

meaning: an eye; (tener un ojo en...) to keep an eye on.
additional_notes: Most literally means the body part “an eye” (e.g., ciego de un ojo = blind in one eye; perder un ojo = lose an eye; un ojo morado = a black eye). In the common expression “tener un ojo en/en algo o alguien,” it means to watch/monitor someone or something.
target_language_example: Voy a tener un ojo en los niños mientras cocinas.
native_language_example: I’m going to keep an eye on the kids while you cook.

additional_notes: Idiom used with costar (to cost) to complain that something costs way too much. Often appears as costó/costaba/cuesta un ojo de la cara. Literally “an eye from the face,” but it’s not meant literally.
target_language_example: El alquiler aquí cuesta un ojo de la cara.
native_language_example: Rent here costs an arm and a leg.

additional_notes: A common noun for the animal. It can be used literally (talking about an actual bear) and in comparisons like "gordo como un oso" (“as fat as a bear”).
target_language_example: Vi un oso en el bosque.
native_language_example: I saw a bear in the forest.

meaning: “a package/pack of” (a packaged quantity of something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about something sold or grouped as one unit (food, supplies, papers, etc.): un paquete de arroz, un paquete de galletitas. It can also be used more abstractly for a set/bundle, like a software “update package” (paquete de actualización).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes comprar un paquete de café cuando vayas a la tienda?
native_language_example: Can you buy a pack of coffee when you go to the store?

additional_notes: Common when ordering or talking about quantity. Use it with verbs like comprar (to buy), fumar (to smoke), or dejar (to leave/put down): “Me compra un paquete…” “Se fuma un paquete al día.” You can also say just “Un paquete de cigarrillos, por favor.”
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un paquete de cigarrillos?
native_language_example: Do you have a pack of cigarettes?

additional_notes: Literally “a pair of,” but very often used loosely to mean a small number (not necessarily exactly two): un par de horas, un par de llamadas. With countable nouns it means “a couple/few (things),” and with time/amounts it means “a couple (of minutes/hours),” i.e., a short amount.
target_language_example: Dame un par de minutos y vuelvo.
native_language_example: Give me a couple of minutes and I’ll be back.

meaning: a couple of years (about two years).
additional_notes: Often used to mean approximately two years, not always exactly. Common with time expressions like "desde hace un par de años" (for a couple of years) or "hace un par de años" (a couple of years ago).
target_language_example: Viví en México un par de años.
native_language_example: I lived in Mexico for a couple of years.

additional_notes: A common way to say you have a small number of things (usually 2, but often just “a few”). Used in everyday speech with verbs like hablar de (talk about), explicar (explain), decir (say), acabar (finish), or encontrar (find): “Tengo que acabar un par de cosas…”
target_language_example: Antes de salir, tengo que hacer un par de cosas.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I have to do a couple of things.

meaning: a couple of days; a few days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short, approximate amount of time (usually around two days). Often used with verbs like quedarse (to stay), esperar (to wait), or tardar (to take).
target_language_example: Voy a estar fuera un par de días.
native_language_example: I'm going to be away for a couple of days.

additional_notes: Used when you mean two gloves that go together (one for each hand). "Un par de + [plural noun]" is a common way to say “a pair of …” in Spanish.
target_language_example: Necesito un par de guantes para el invierno.
native_language_example: I need a pair of gloves for the winter.

meaning: a couple of hours; a few hours.
additional_notes: Literally “a pair of hours,” but it’s used loosely to mean about two hours or just a short amount of time. Common after time expressions to show an approximate duration or distance: “dormir un par de horas” (sleep for a couple of hours), “un par de horas después” (a couple of hours later), “a un par de horas de distancia” (a couple of hours away).
target_language_example: Voy a descansar un par de horas y luego salimos.
native_language_example: I’m going to rest for a couple of hours and then we’ll go out.

meaning: a couple of months; a few months.
additional_notes: "Un par de" literally means "a pair of," but in everyday Spanish it often means "a couple" or "a few" (an approximate small number, usually around two). It’s used with time expressions to give a rough duration: "un par de meses" = for/about a couple of months.
target_language_example: Voy a estar fuera un par de meses.
native_language_example: I’m going to be away for a couple of months.

additional_notes: Means a small amount of time (usually around two minutes, but often used loosely to mean “a few minutes”). Common in requests and estimates: “Espera un par de minutos” (Wait a couple of minutes), “llego un par de minutos tarde” (I’ll be a couple minutes late). You can add “más” to mean “a couple more minutes.”
target_language_example: Espera un par de minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait a couple of minutes, please.

meaning: a couple of weeks (about two weeks).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate short period of time. It often means “around two weeks,” but in casual speech it can sometimes mean “a few weeks.” You can use it with “hace” (ago) and “después” (later): “hace un par de semanas” = “a couple of weeks ago.”
target_language_example: Me voy de viaje por un par de semanas.
native_language_example: I’m going on a trip for a couple of weeks.

meaning: a couple of times; a few times.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened a small number of times (often around two, but it can also mean “a few”). Common with past tenses like "he" (I have) and "intenté" (I tried).
target_language_example: Lo intenté un par de veces, pero no funcionó.
native_language_example: I tried a couple of times, but it didn’t work.

additional_notes: "Un par de" means "a pair of" (two of something that goes together). Use it when talking about shoes as a set. "Zapatos" are shoes (not boots: "botas"). You can add adjectives after "zapatos" (e.g., "zapatos rojos", "zapatos de fútbol").
target_language_example: Necesito un par de zapatos cómodos para caminar.
native_language_example: I need a comfortable pair of shoes for walking.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. Use "un" (or "el") with it: "un paraguas", "el paraguas". The plural is "unos paraguas / los paraguas" (same form as singular). Commonly used with "con" to say you have one: "con un paraguas".
target_language_example: Está lloviendo; voy a salir con un paraguas.
native_language_example: It’s raining; I’m going out with an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used with a sport to say “a game/match of…”: un partido de tenis, un partido de fútbol. For some sports you might also hear other common nouns (e.g., un juego de béisbol, un encuentro de fútbol), but partido is widely understood.
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ver un partido de baloncesto esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch a basketball game tonight?

meaning: a walk; a stroll; a short outing/ride.
additional_notes: Usually means a leisurely walk (“dar un paseo” = to go for a walk). It can also mean a short trip/ride or route (e.g., “un paseo corto” can refer to a short walk/way to a place). Common verbs: dar un paseo, tomar un paseo.
target_language_example: Después de cenar, vamos a dar un paseo por el barrio.
native_language_example: After dinner, we’re going to go for a walk around the neighborhood.

meaning: one more step; one step further.
additional_notes: Used literally for physical movement ("take one more step") and figuratively for making progress ("one more step toward a goal"). In warnings/threats it often appears as "Ni un paso más" (“Not one more step”) or "Un paso más..." implying consequences if someone advances further.
target_language_example: Solo necesito un paso más para terminar el proyecto.
native_language_example: I only need one more step to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a nation or state. Often paired with adjectives like extranjero (foreign), neutral (neutral), seguro (safe), etc. Note: país is masculine, so it uses un/el; the plural is países.
target_language_example: Quiero vivir en un país tranquilo.
native_language_example: I want to live in a peaceful country.

additional_notes: Often means a small piece of cloth. In everyday contexts it can be a handkerchief (to blow your nose: “sonarse con un pañuelo”) or a small scarf/bandana used as an accessory or as a signal.
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un pañuelo? Me tengo que sonar la nariz.
native_language_example: Do you have a tissue/handkerchief? I need to blow my nose.

meaning: a piece of; a chunk of (a portion of something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean part of a larger whole, especially food or material: un pedazo de pastel (a piece of cake), un pedazo de tierra (a piece/plot of land). It can refer to a fairly big, solid piece (a chunk), but in everyday speech it can also just mean “some” of something.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un pedazo de pan, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of bread, please?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: un pequeño país/regalo/problema/bote. In Spanish, adjectives usually come after the noun (un país pequeño), but with size/quantity words like pequeño you’ll often hear it before the noun, especially in common phrases. Feminine form: una pequeña.
target_language_example: Necesito un pequeño descanso.
native_language_example: I need a short break.

additional_notes: Refers to a small population center; in Spanish, "pueblo" can mean "town" or "village" depending on context. It’s often followed by details with "en" (location) or "de" (type), e.g., "un pequeño pueblo en Cataluña" / "un pequeño pueblo de montaña". The adjective usually agrees in gender/number: "un pequeño pueblo" (masc. singular), "una pequeña ciudad" (fem. singular), "pequeños pueblos" (plural).
target_language_example: Quiero visitar un pequeño pueblo cerca de la costa.
native_language_example: I want to visit a small town near the coast.

additional_notes: Literally “a dog” (un = “a” for a masculine noun; perro = “dog”). In neutral contexts it refers to an actual dog (pet, animal). In some contexts it can be used as an insult about a person (e.g., calling someone “un perro”).
target_language_example: No tengas miedo: es solo un perro.
native_language_example: Don’t be scared: it’s just a dog.

additional_notes: A basic noun phrase: un (a) + perro (dog) + negro (black). Adjective color usually comes after the noun in Spanish. You can change the article depending on context: el perro negro (the black dog), mi perro negro (my black dog).
target_language_example: En mi casa hay un perro negro muy tranquilo.
native_language_example: In my house there is a very calm black dog.

meaning: a weight off (my/your/his/her) shoulders; a big relief.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb quitar: "quitar(se) un peso de encima" = to feel relieved after worrying or feeling responsible for something. It can be reflexive/impersonal: "Se me quitó un peso de encima" (literally "a weight got taken off me"), meaning you suddenly felt relief.
target_language_example: Cuando terminé el examen, se me quitó un peso de encima.
native_language_example: When I finished the exam, it felt like a weight was lifted off my shoulders.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: "pez" = fish; "un" = a/an (masculine singular). Plural: "unos peces" (some fish) or "peces" (fish). Used literally for the animal; can also appear in comparisons ("como un pez...") or humorous/figurative sayings.
target_language_example: En el lago vi un pez muy grande.
native_language_example: In the lake I saw a very big fish.

additional_notes: A polite, common phrase used when greeting or saying goodbye, especially after meeting someone or talking. It’s often shortened to just “Un placer.” You can add an infinitive to specify what was pleasant: “Un placer hablar contigo” (Nice talking to you), “Un placer verte” (Nice to see you).
target_language_example: Un placer conocerte. ¿Nos vemos mañana?
native_language_example: Nice to meet you. See you tomorrow?

meaning: "Nice to meet you" / "It’s a pleasure to meet you."
additional_notes: Polite, common phrase said when you meet someone (often when you’re introduced). Also used at the end of a conversation or when leaving: "Ha sido un placer conocerte" = "It’s been a pleasure meeting you." You can swap in a name: "Un placer conocerte, Judy."
target_language_example: Hola, soy Ana. Un placer conocerte.
native_language_example: Hi, I’m Ana. Nice to meet you.

additional_notes: A polite, friendly phrase used when greeting someone you’re happy to see, or when saying goodbye after seeing them. Often appears as a full sentence (Es/Fue/Ha sido un placer verte) or shortened to just Un placer verte. You can change verte (“to see you”) to verlo/verla/verlos/verlas depending on who you’re addressing (formal usted / them).
target_language_example: ¡Hola, Marta! Un placer verte otra vez.
native_language_example: Hi, Marta! It’s a pleasure to see you again.

meaning: a plan; an idea/arrangement of what to do.
additional_notes: Used for a strategy or intended course of action (Tengo un plan), or an arrangement (Es un plan para cuatro). Common with para + person/goal (un plan para nosotros / para cuatro) and with adjectives like a largo plazo (“long-term”).
target_language_example: Hagamos un plan para mañana.
native_language_example: Let’s make a plan for tomorrow.

meaning: a plate; a dish/serving of food.
additional_notes: Use "un plato" for a physical plate (tableware) or for a dish/portion of food, often followed by "de" + food: "un plato de sopa" (a bowl/serving of soup), "un plato de lentejas" (a serving of lentils). In "por un plato de lentejas," it’s a common expression meaning to give up something valuable for very little (like “for a mess of pottage”).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes un plato de arroz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a serving of rice, please?

meaning: “a little (bit) of” (some, a small amount of).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (usually an uncountable noun or a mass noun) to indicate a small quantity: un poco de agua, un poco de mantequilla. With verbs like comer/beber/ver, it often means “a little” in general: ver un poco de televisión (“watch a bit of TV”). You can also use it with indirect object pronouns to mean “give/leave someone a little of something”: Dale un poco de carne.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a small amount of water. "Un poco de" + noun = "a little/some" with uncountable nouns (like agua). You can also use it politely in requests: "¿Me puede dar un poco de agua?".
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water, please?

meaning: "a little air" / "some fresh air"; also "a little space (breathing room)".
additional_notes: Often literal (air/fresh air): you might open a window or step outside. It can also be figurative, meaning to give someone some space, time, or relief from pressure (e.g., "Denle un poco de aire" = "Give them some breathing room"). Common with verbs like "necesitar" (to need), "tomar" (to take), "dar" (to give), and "dejar entrar" (to let in).
target_language_example: Necesito un poco de aire; voy a salir un momento.
native_language_example: I need some air; I'm going to step out for a moment.

additional_notes: Used literally (going outside to breathe fresh air) and also as a common way to say you need a break, to clear your head, or to feel better. Often appears with verbs like respirar (to breathe), salir (to go out), necesitar (to need), and phrases like me vendrá/me vendría bien (it will/would do me good).
target_language_example: Voy a salir un momento por un poco de aire fresco.
native_language_example: I'm going to step out for a moment for some fresh air.

additional_notes: Used to say you need or received some (not a lot of) help. Common patterns: “Necesito un poco de ayuda” (I need a little help) and “Recibí un poco de ayuda de…” (I got a little help from…).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco de ayuda con esto?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little help with this?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about a small amount of sugar. Common in cooking and drinks. After verbs like añadir/poner/echar it often takes "a/al": "Añade un poco de azúcar al café."
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco de azúcar, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little sugar, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about making, preparing, bringing, or wanting a small amount of coffee. "Un poco de + [noun]" means "a little (of) + [noun]"; with drinks like coffee it often implies a small serving rather than a precise measurement.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de café, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used when you mean a small amount of cash or money in general. Often appears with verbs like pedir (to ask for), llevar (to carry/bring), necesitar (to need), and dar (to give).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un poco de dinero para el autobús?
native_language_example: Do you have a little money for the bus?

additional_notes: Used to say you know/speak/learn a small amount of the French language. Often with verbs like saber (to know), hablar (to speak), and enseñar (to teach). You can swap francés for another language: un poco de español / inglés.
target_language_example: ¿Hablas un poco de francés?
native_language_example: Do you speak a little French?

additional_notes: Used to say you know/understand/speak a small amount of English. Often appears with verbs like hablar (to speak), entender (to understand), saber (to know how), and poder (to be able to): “Hablo un poco de inglés.” “Entiendo un poco de inglés.”
target_language_example: Perdón, solo hablo un poco de inglés.
native_language_example: Sorry, I only speak a little English.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention a small quantity of milk. Common with verbs like querer (to want), agregar (to add), calentar (to heat), comprar (to buy), and in polite requests like "Deme..." (Give me...). "Un poco de" can be used with many foods and drinks: "un poco de agua", "un poco de azúcar".
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes poner un poco de leche en el café?
native_language_example: Can you put a little milk in the coffee?

additional_notes: Used to say there is a small amount of milk inside a container or place. Very common with verbs like "hay" (there is/are) and "queda/quedaba" (there is/was left): "Hay un poco de leche en la botella" / "Queda un poco de leche en la botella." In English you usually say “a little milk in…”, not “a little of milk in…”.
target_language_example: Queda un poco de leche en el vaso.
native_language_example: There’s a little milk left in the glass.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait or not rush. Common in requests and commands: (solo) te pido un poco de paciencia (“I’m just asking for a little patience”), ten/tenga un poco de paciencia (“have a little patience” / “please be patient”).
target_language_example: Un poco de paciencia, por favor; ya casi termino.
native_language_example: A little patience, please; I’m almost done.

additional_notes: Used when talking about adding a small amount of salt to food. Often appears with verbs like poner/añadir (to put/add) or faltar (to be missing): “Le falta un poco de sal” = “It needs a little salt.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes poner un poco de sal en la ensalada?
native_language_example: Can you put a little salt on the salad?

additional_notes: Used to say something takes or needs a short amount of time, or to ask/give someone time (often to wait, think, or be alone). Common with verbs like tomar/llevar (to take), necesitar (to need), and dar (to give): “Dame un poco de tiempo.”
target_language_example: Dame un poco de tiempo para pensarlo.
native_language_example: Give me a little time to think about it.

meaning: a little (bit) of tea; some tea.
additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, make, or drink a small amount of tea. The amount is vague (not a full cup necessarily). You can add details like "sin azúcar" (without sugar) or "con leche" (with milk).
target_language_example: ¿Me das un poco de té, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little tea, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a small amount of wine. Often appears with verbs like tomar/beber (“to drink”), necesitar (“to need”), or quedar (“to be left”). You can also just say un poco de + [drink/food], e.g., un poco de agua (a little water).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres un poco de vino o prefieres agua?
native_language_example: Do you want a little wine, or would you prefer water?

additional_notes: Often used as a polite request to raise your voice or the volume: "Habla/Hablad/Hablen un poco más alto". Literally it means "a little higher," and in other contexts it can also mean "a little taller/higher" (e.g., referring to height or position), but with speaking/volume it usually means "louder."
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar un poco más alto, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little louder, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe an increase in amount or degree. Often followed by a noun (un poco más de pimienta = “a little more pepper”) or an infinitive/noun phrase when talking about doing something more (prestar un poco más de atención = “pay a bit more attention”).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar un poco más de despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or say you need additional time. Common with verbs like necesitar (to need), dar (to give yourself), and pasar (to spend): “Necesito un poco más de tiempo.” / “Date un poco más de tiempo.” / “Pasar un poco más de tiempo en…” means “to spend a little more time on/in …”.
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes dar un poco más de tiempo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little more time, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you want to go or move a small additional distance. Common in directions and encouragement (e.g., “Just a little farther”). It can be used on its own as a short instruction: “Un poco más lejos.”
target_language_example: El baño está un poco más lejos, al final del pasillo.
native_language_example: The bathroom is a little farther down, at the end of the hallway.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after the expected/mentioned time. Common with future tense (llegará un poco más tarde) or as a polite request (¿podemos hablar un poco más tarde?). You can also add a reference point with de + noun: "un poco más tarde de lo habitual" (a little later than usual).
target_language_example: Lo hago un poco más tarde; ahora estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: I'll do it a little later; I'm busy right now.

meaning: a little late; a bit late.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than expected, but not very late. Often comes after a verb ("Llegamos un poco tarde"), can be used with "se está haciendo" to mean "it’s getting a bit late" (time is passing), and can also stand alone as a short comment ("Un poco tarde.").
target_language_example: Lo llamé, pero era un poco tarde.
native_language_example: I called him, but it was a little late.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "un" = "a" (masculine singular) + "poema" = "poem." Used with verbs like escribir (to write) or componer (to compose). Plural: "unos poemas" / "los poemas".
target_language_example: ¿Quieres leer un poema?
native_language_example: Do you want to read a poem?

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to soften a request or indicate “just a bit.” Often used with commands or requests: “Acércate un poquito” (Come a little closer). It’s a diminutive of “un poco,” so it sounds slightly gentler.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar un poquito más despacio?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a small increase in degree, amount, closeness, or time. Common in requests and comparisons: *Acércate un poquito más* (come a bit closer), *Quédate/Duerme un poquito más* (stay/sleep a bit longer), *un poquito más … que* (a little more … than). *Poquito* is a diminutive of *poco*, making it sound softer/politer than *un poco más*.
target_language_example: ¿Puedes hablar un poquito más despacio, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little bit more slowly, please?

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”), and "problema" is masculine in Spanish (el problema). Common patterns: "tener un problema" (to have a problem), "un problema con..." (a problem with...), and you can describe it with adjectives: "un problema grande/difícil".
target_language_example: Tenemos un problema con la reserva.
native_language_example: We have a problem with the reservation.

meaning: a problem with; an issue with (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t work well, goes wrong, or causes trouble, or that you have a complaint/negative feeling about a person or thing. Common pattern: "tener un problema con + [noun/person]". Can refer to a one-time trouble (e.g., a car problem) or an ongoing issue (e.g., a problem with gambling).
target_language_example: ¿Tienes un problema con la computadora?
native_language_example: Do you have a problem with the computer?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or worrying (not minor). Often used with "ser" ("Es un problema serio") or with possibility phrases like "podría ser" ("it could be").
target_language_example: Si no pagas a tiempo, será un problema serio.
native_language_example: If you don’t pay on time, it will be a serious problem.

additional_notes: Most commonly a physical bridge that crosses a river/road and provides access. In some contexts (often with the verb "hacer"), "hacer un puente" can also mean to create a bypass/connection—e.g., to hotwire a car or make an electrical shortcut.
target_language_example: Hay un puente sobre el río.
native_language_example: There is a bridge over the river.

additional_notes: Used to describe hitting someone’s face with a fist. Often appears with verbs like “dar” or “pegar” (to hit): “Le di/pegó un puñetazo en la cara (a alguien).” You can add the person with “a”: “Le dio un puñetazo en la cara a Tom.”
target_language_example: El hombre le dio un puñetazo en la cara al ladrón.
native_language_example: The man punched the thief in the face.

additional_notes: Common noun for a bird; used literally (animals that fly, sing, etc.) and sometimes figuratively in comparisons (e.g., “un pájaro raro” = “a rare bird,” meaning an unusual person/thing). Masculine noun: el pájaro / un pájaro; plural: los pájaros.
target_language_example: Hay un pájaro en la ventana.
native_language_example: There’s a bird at the window.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified amount of time (usually not very long). Common with verbs like caminar, estudiar, descansar, dormir. With time expressions it can mean “in a little while”: dentro de un rato / en un rato = “in a bit.” Also used with llevar: Puede que le lleve un rato = “It might take a while.”
target_language_example: Espera aquí un rato y vuelvo.
native_language_example: Wait here for a bit and I’ll be back.

meaning: a mouse; also a computer mouse.
additional_notes: Most commonly means the animal (mouse). It can also mean a computer mouse (often clear from context or with a brand/model: "un ratón Microsoft"). In comparisons, it can suggest something small/weak versus something big/strong ("un ratón contra un gorila"). Set phrases include "borracho como un ratón" (very drunk).
target_language_example: Necesito comprar un ratón nuevo para mi computadora.
native_language_example: I need to buy a new mouse for my computer.

meaning: a lightning bolt; (also) a ray/beam (of light), or a glimmer (of hope).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “a bolt of lightning” (often with verbs like caer/dar: Un rayo cayó/dio en el árbol). With “de + noun,” it can mean a “ray/beam” (un rayo de sol = a ray of sunshine) or figuratively a small sign of something positive (un rayo de esperanza = a glimmer of hope).
target_language_example: Vimos un rayo y después oímos el trueno.
native_language_example: We saw a lightning bolt and then we heard the thunder.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you give to someone (for a birthday, holidays, a visit, etc.). It’s masculine: el regalo / un regalo. Plural: regalos.
target_language_example: Te compré un regalo para tu cumpleaños.
native_language_example: I bought you a present for your birthday.

meaning: a gift from (someone) / a (type of) gift for (an occasion).
additional_notes: Most often means “a gift from” someone: *un regalo de su hermana* (a gift from her sister). With holidays/occasions, it can mean “a [holiday] gift”: *un regalo de Navidad* (a Christmas gift). The verb commonly used is *dar* (to give) or *recibir* (to receive).
target_language_example: Me dieron un regalo de cumpleaños.
native_language_example: They gave me a birthday gift.
