Common options: en taxi, en coche/en auto/en carro (car), en tren, en autobús. "Va" is the present tense of ir for él/ella/usted; for you: "voy al trabajo en...", for they: "van al trabajo en...".
target_language_example: Yo voy al trabajo en autobús.
native_language_example: I go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used with "ir" to talk about how something is going (El negocio va bien; Me va bien; No va bien). With indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/les) it means someone is doing well. With clothing or style it means something suits someone or fits them well: "Le va bien" (it looks good on them) and "Te va bien" (it fits you/looks good on you). You’ll also hear it alone as a short reply meaning “Okay / Sounds good / All right.”
target_language_example: ¿Cómo te va? — Me va bien, gracias.
native_language_example: How’s it going? — It’s going well for me, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say something is contrary to a rule, law, belief, or what someone wants. It can also mean to oppose someone (e.g., "go against your parents"). The verb changes with the subject/tense: "voy/vas/va/vamos/van en contra de..."; "fue/iba/irá en contra de...".
target_language_example: Eso va en contra de las normas de la empresa.
native_language_example: That goes against the company’s rules.

meaning: (It) is going very well; (someone) is doing very well.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" to talk about how things are going for someone or something (work, life, a project, etc.). Common patterns: "me/te/le/nos/les va muy bien" = "it’s going very well for me/you/him-her/us/them".
target_language_example: Con el nuevo trabajo, me va muy bien.
native_language_example: With the new job, I’m doing very well.

additional_notes: Used to say something exceeds a limit, ability, understanding, expectations, or what’s normal. Very common with nouns like mi comprensión (my understanding), mi poder (my ability/power), lo que puedo imaginar (what I can imagine), or lo absurdo (the absurd). You can also conjugate it: va / van / iba / irá más allá de.
target_language_example: Lo que pasó ayer va más allá de lo que puedo explicar.
native_language_example: What happened yesterday goes beyond what I can explain.

additional_notes: Refers to the vacation period in summer (often the break from school or work). It’s commonly used with possessives (mis/tus/sus vacaciones de verano) and with verbs like pasar (to spend) or acabar(se) (to end): «Mis vacaciones de verano se están acabando».
target_language_example: Este año mis vacaciones de verano son en agosto.
native_language_example: This year my summer vacation is in August.

meaning: “it’s worth it / it’s worth the effort.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is worthwhile (the benefit is worth the time, cost, or effort). Often followed by an infinitive: “Vale la pena + verb” (Vale la pena estudiar). You can also say “No vale la pena” = “It’s not worth it.”
target_language_example: Vale la pena intentarlo otra vez.
native_language_example: It’s worth trying again.

additional_notes: Used to recommend a place or attraction by saying the visit is worth the time/effort. You can swap in other infinitives: vale la pena ver (to see), probar (to try), etc. Often followed by a noun (vale la pena visitar el museo) or a place name (vale la pena visitar Suiza).
target_language_example: Si tienes tiempo, vale la pena visitar el centro histórico.
native_language_example: If you have time, it’s worth visiting the historic center.

additional_notes: Used to compare value or importance. It can mean literal monetary value (e.g., “the frame is worth more than the painting”) or figurative importance (e.g., “health matters more than gold”). Common pattern: [thing] vale más que [other thing].
target_language_example: Tu amistad vale más que cualquier regalo.
native_language_example: Your friendship is worth more than any gift.

additional_notes: Often used with something + “que valga la pena” (“something that’s worth it”). Uses the present subjunctive of valer (“valga”) because it’s commonly in relative clauses or after expressions like “nada/algo” (e.g., “nada que valga la pena”). You can also use it as a set phrase: “Vale la pena + infinitive” (“It’s worth + -ing”): “Vale la pena leerlo.”
target_language_example: No quiero perder tiempo en algo que no valga la pena.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time on something that isn’t worth it.

meaning: 'it was worth it' / 'it was worth the effort.'
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of "valer la pena" = "to be worth it." Used to say that the effort, cost, or waiting was justified by the result. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause with "que": "Valió la pena esperar" (It was worth waiting), "No valió la pena que hiciera cambios" (It wasn’t worth it for him to make changes).
target_language_example: Aunque fue cansado, valió la pena hacerlo.
native_language_example: Even though it was tiring, it was worth doing.

meaning: “it was worth it / it was worth the effort.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **valer la pena** (“to be worth it”). **Valía** is the imperfect past (“was worth”), often used when looking back on something or describing a past situation: *No valía la pena* = “It wasn’t worth it.” Commonly followed by an infinitive: **valía la pena + infinitive** (*valía la pena intentarlo/probar* = “it was worth trying”).
target_language_example: Aunque fue difícil, valía la pena hacerlo.
native_language_example: Even though it was hard, it was worth doing.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive**. Most often it expresses a near-future plan: *Vamos a salvarla* (“We’re going to save her”). It can also be used like an invitation/suggestion, similar to “let’s”: *Vamos a prepararnos* (“Let’s get ready”). The next verb stays in the infinitive (e.g., *vamos a ver*, *vamos a comer*). In questions it can mean “shall we…?” (*¿Vamos a ver?*).
target_language_example: Vamos a comer algo antes de salir.
native_language_example: Let’s eat something before we leave.

meaning: let’s look for / we’re going to look for.
additional_notes: From ir a + infinitive ("to be going to" + verb). "Vamos" can mean either "we go" or "let’s"; in context, "vamos a buscar" is often used to suggest an action together ("Let’s look for...") or to state an immediate plan ("We’re going to look for..."). You can replace what you’re looking for: "Vamos a buscar un restaurante / una salida / mis llaves".
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar tu teléfono; seguro que está aquí.
native_language_example: Let’s look for your phone; I’m sure it’s here.

meaning: “we’re going to look for” / “we’re going to go get (someone).”
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about going to find or pick up a person. The "a" is the personal "a" and is required before a direct object that is a person (e.g., "buscar a Zé", "buscar a las chicas"). In conversation, it often implies going to pick someone up or go meet them.
target_language_example: Vamos a buscar a mi hermana a la estación.
native_language_example: We’re going to pick up my sister at the station.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or announce that it’s time to eat. Literally “we go to eat” = “we’re going to eat,” but in conversation it often works like an invitation: “Let’s eat.” In a different context, it can also be literal (“We’re going to eat couscous / in the kitchen”). Related idiom: “No te vamos a comer” means “We’re not going to hurt you” (literally “We’re not going to eat you”).
target_language_example: Si ya estás listo, vamos a comer.
native_language_example: If you’re ready, let’s eat.

additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive (“vamos a” + verb) to talk about what you’re about to do. Often used as an invitation/suggestion (“Let’s start”), especially with con (“with”), desde (“from”), or por (“by/with”). In “Ya vamos a empezar,” ya can add emphasis like “Here we go again / We’re starting already,” depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Bueno, vamos a empezar con la primera pregunta.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s start with the first question.

additional_notes: Often used to start a conversation or to suggest discussing something. Literally it’s “we’re going to talk,” using **vamos a + infinitive** (near future). Depending on tone and context, it can also feel like “let’s talk (about this).”
target_language_example: Vamos a hablar de lo que pasó ayer.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about what happened yesterday.

meaning: “we’re going to do/make” (we are going to do).
additional_notes: Formed from "vamos a" (we’re going to) + "hacer" (to do/make). Used to talk about a plan or what you and others will do next. In questions like "¿Qué vamos a hacer?" it means “What are we going to do?”
target_language_example: ¿Qué vamos a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are we going to do tomorrow?

meaning: “let’s do it” / “we’re going to do it.”
additional_notes: From "vamos a" (let’s / we’re going to) + "hacerlo" (do it). Often used to suggest starting an action together (“Let’s do it”), but it can also simply state a plan (“We’re going to do it”). Add-ons like "juntos" (together), "otra vez" (again), or "a tu modo" (your way) are very common.
target_language_example: Está bien, vamos a hacerlo ahora.
native_language_example: Okay, let’s do it now.

meaning: "we're going to go" / "we're going to leave".
additional_notes: Formed with **ir (to go)** in the present (**vamos**) + **a** + infinitive (**ir**). It often expresses a near-future plan or intention. Very commonly used to talk about leaving: **Nos vamos a ir** = “We’re going to leave / We’re heading out.” (Even though it’s literally “we’re going to go,” English usually uses “leave/ head out” in this context.)
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; vamos a irnos.
native_language_example: It’s late; we’re going to leave.

meaning: “we’re going to go to … / we’re going to …” (near future plan).
additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive for the near future with nosotros (vamos). With places, it’s often “vamos a ir a + place” (two a’s in a row: one from “ir a” + one introducing the destination). With an action, use “vamos a ir a + infinitive” (e.g., “vamos a ir a hablar…”). In casual speech, people may shorten it to “vamos a…” when the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Mañana vamos a ir a comprar comida.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to go buy food.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure ir a + infinitive: vamos a + morir. It can be meant literally (a real danger) or used dramatically to express that a situation is very bad. Also common as nos vamos a morir (“we’re going to die”).
target_language_example: Si no encontramos agua pronto, vamos a morir.
native_language_example: If we don’t find water soon, we’re going to die.

meaning: "we’re going to have to" (we must / we need to).
additional_notes: Used to express necessity/obligation for “we,” often because circumstances require it. It’s the near-future structure: vamos a + infinitive (tener que + infinitive). After it, use another infinitive: Vamos a tener que esperar / hacer / hablar.
target_language_example: Vamos a tener que salir más temprano para llegar a tiempo.
native_language_example: We’re going to have to leave earlier to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Literally “we’re going to take.” Used to propose a shared plan. With transportation (el autobús, el barco), tomar = “to take/catch.” With drinks (té, una copa, cervezas), tomar = “to have/drink.” Often followed by the thing you’ll take/have: “Vamos a tomar + noun.”
target_language_example: Hace frío; vamos a tomar un café caliente.
native_language_example: It’s cold; let’s have a hot coffee.

meaning: "Come on" / "let’s go" (urging someone to move or continue).
additional_notes: Repetition adds emphasis and impatience/encouragement, like “come on, come on” or “hurry up.” It’s common in speech when pushing someone to act, keep going, or speed things up.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Come on, come on—we’re going to be late.

meaning: “Come on, come on!” (urging someone to hurry up or do something).
additional_notes: Repeated for emphasis, often said impatiently or to encourage someone (like “come on!” or “let’s go!”). You can repeat it more or fewer times depending on how strong you want it to sound. Common in speech and in excited/urgent situations.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos, vamos, que llegamos tarde.
native_language_example: Come on, come on, we’re late.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive**. Most often it expresses a near-future plan: *Vamos a salvarla* (“We’re going to save her”). It can also be used like an invitation/suggestion, similar to “let’s”: *Vamos a prepararnos* (“Let’s get ready”). The next verb stays in the infinitive (e.g., *vamos a ver*, *vamos a comer*). In questions it can mean “shall we…?” (*¿Vamos a ver?*).
target_language_example: Vamos a comer algo antes de salir.
native_language_example: Let’s eat something before we leave.

meaning: “we go to the” / “let’s go to the”.
additional_notes: "Vamos" can mean either (1) "we go/are going" (present tense) or (2) "let’s go" as a suggestion/command. "Al" = "a" (to) + "el" (the), used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., al valle).
target_language_example: Vamos al supermercado después de clase.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the supermarket after class.

meaning: "are going to" (they are about to / will do something).
additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** to talk about a near future or planned action. **van** = "they go" (present of *ir*), **a** = "to". It’s followed by an infinitive: *van a quedarse* (are going to stay), *van a aumentar* (are going to increase). Object or reflexive pronouns often go before *van*: *se van a encontrar* (they’re going to meet), *no te van a sacar* (they’re not going to get you out).
target_language_example: Van a llegar tarde si no salen ya.
native_language_example: They’re going to arrive late if they don’t leave now.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”). **van** is from *ir* (to go) and matches **ellos/ellas/ustedes** (they/you all). **hacer** means “to do/make.” Often used to talk about plans or what will happen soon; in questions it can be **¿Qué van a hacer?** (“What are they/you all going to do?”).
target_language_example: ¿Qué van a hacer este fin de semana?
native_language_example: What are you all going to do this weekend?

additional_notes: This is the near-future construction **ir a + infinitive**. **Van** is the **ellos/ellas/ustedes** form of **ir** (to go), and **ser** is “to be.” It’s used to talk about what something/someone will be like: *Van a ser famosos* (They’re going to be famous).
target_language_example: Van a ser días muy largos.
native_language_example: They’re going to be very long days.

meaning: “you/they are going to see” (and sometimes “you’ll see.”).
additional_notes: Form of the near-future: **ir (van) + a + infinitive (ver)**. **Van** is used with **ustedes** (“you all”) or **ellos/ellas** (“they”). It can also be said on its own (**Van a ver.**) meaning “You’ll see.” to build suspense or as a warning/promise depending on tone.
target_language_example: Si no me crees, van a ver lo que pasa mañana.
native_language_example: If you don’t believe me, you’ll see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of time (more than a couple of hours, but not exact). Often appears with duration phrases like "durante varias horas" (for several hours) or "me llevó varias horas" (it took me several hours).
target_language_example: Estuvimos esperando varias horas en el aeropuerto.
native_language_example: We waited several hours at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future action: present tense of ir (vas) + a + infinitive. Often expresses a plan, intention, or a prediction: Vas a venir, vas a ser, vas a volver. Informal vs formal: 'vas a' (tú) vs 'va a' (usted/él/ella).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a estudiar hoy?
native_language_example: Are you going to study today?

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone (about their health, safety, or a situation). It’s the near future with **ir a + infinitive** (“vas a estar” = “you’re going to be”). Often said with a supportive tone: *Vas a estar bien, tranquilo/a.* As a question, it can check on someone’s condition: *¿Vas a estar bien?*
target_language_example: No te preocupes: vas a estar bien.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—you’ll be fine.

meaning: "you are going to do" / "you will do" (informal singular).
additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **vas a hacer** = **you’re going to do/make**. It’s used with **tú** (informal “you”); formal would be **va a hacer** (usted) and plural **van a hacer** (ustedes). **Hacer** can mean “to do” or “to make,” depending on context.
target_language_example: ¿Qué vas a hacer mañana?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tomorrow?

additional_notes: Formed with **ir (vas) + a + infinitive (ir)** to talk about a planned/near-future action. Very common in conversation (often like English “going to”). In questions/negatives: **¿Vas a ir?** (Are you going to go?) **No vas a ir.** (You’re not going to go.) With **te** it becomes **te vas a ir**, which usually means **“you’re going to leave”** (to go away).
target_language_example: ¿Vas a ir a la fiesta mañana?
native_language_example: Are you going to go to the party tomorrow?

additional_notes: Uses **ir a + infinitive** (“vas a llegar”) to talk about something that will likely happen soon. **Llegar tarde a/al + place/event** = “to arrive late to…”. Often used as a warning or reminder: *Vete… o vas a llegar tarde* (“Leave… or you’ll be late”).
target_language_example: Si no sales ahora, vas a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: If you don’t leave now, you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Literally the near-future form of "morir" (to die): "vas a" + infinitive. Often used as a dramatic statement or a threat ("¡Vas a morir!"), and very commonly in the negative to reassure someone: "No te vas a morir" = "You’re not going to die" / "You’ll be fine."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, no te vas a morir; solo es una inyección.
native_language_example: Relax, you’re not going to die; it’s just a shot.

additional_notes: From **ir a + infinitive** (“to be going to…”) + **necesitar** (“to need”). **Vas** is the *tú* form of **ir**. It often appears with an object: **Vas a necesitar esto** (“You’re going to need this”), or with a pronoun before the verb: **La vas a necesitar** (“You’re going to need it/her”). Can also be used for emphasis like “You’re going to need more than that.”
target_language_example: Vas a necesitar ayuda para terminar a tiempo.
native_language_example: You’re going to need help to finish on time.

meaning: “you’re going to lose” / “you’re going to miss (it)”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **vas a + perder** (you’re going to lose). Often used as a warning about something that will happen soon: **Vas a perder el tren** = “You’re going to miss the train.” With things like **el tren / la oportunidad / el partido**, English often uses “miss” rather than “lose.”
target_language_example: ¡Date prisa o vas a perder el autobús!
native_language_example: Hurry up or you’re going to miss the bus!

meaning: “you are going to be” / “you will be.”
additional_notes: Formed with ir (vas) + a + infinitive (ser) to talk about the future. It can describe a future identity/state (“Vas a ser padre”) or a future event affecting you (“Vas a ser arrestado”). Often translates naturally as “you’ll be…” in English.
target_language_example: Si estudias mucho, vas a ser un gran médico.
native_language_example: If you study a lot, you’re going to be a great doctor.

meaning: 'you're going to have to' / 'you'll have to' (you must).
additional_notes: Common way to express obligation or necessity directed at "tú" (you, informal). It’s the near-future structure "vas a" + "tener que" + infinitive: "Vas a tener que confiar" = "You’ll have to trust." Can sound firm or like a warning depending on tone. For "usted": "va a tener que"; for "ustedes": "van a tener que".
target_language_example: Vas a tener que estudiar si quieres aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: You’re going to have to study if you want to pass the exam.

additional_notes: Commonly used to predict what will happen next or to emphasize a warning, promise, or challenge (often like “just you wait”). It’s the informal (tú) form of the near-future: ir a + infinitive (ver). In context it can mean literally “you’re going to see (something/someone)” (e.g., Me vas a ver = “You’re going to see me”), or idiomatically “you’ll see (what I mean/what happens).”
target_language_example: Vas a ver que todo sale bien.
native_language_example: You’ll see—everything will turn out fine.

meaning: "a glass/cup of" (a serving in a glass/cup).
additional_notes: Used to say what the glass/cup contains: "un vaso de agua" (a glass of water), "un vaso de jugo" (a glass of juice). With a material, it can describe what it’s made of: "un vaso de papel" (a paper cup). "Vaso" can mean a glass or a cup depending on the context.
target_language_example: ¿Me das un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you give me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase: "vaso" is a drinking glass (not a cup), and "de" means "of." You can pluralize it: "dos vasos de agua" (two glasses of water).
target_language_example: ¿Me traes un vaso de agua, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to one serving of milk in a drinking glass. You can modify it with quantities like un/medio/dos vasos de leche. In everyday Spanish, people often drop “de leche” if it’s clear from context: “Dame un vaso, por favor” (when you’re already talking about milk).
target_language_example: ¿Me puedes traer un vaso de leche, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of milk, please?

meaning: “(that) … is going to … / will …” (subjunctive of *ir a* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about something that might happen (a future action) in a clause that requires the subjunctive—often after expressions of doubt, fear, denial, or uncertainty like *dudo que…*, *no creo que…*, *tengo miedo de que…*, *espero que…*. Negative: *no vaya a + infinitive* (“might not / isn’t going to…”). Note: *vaya* can also be a formal command meaning “go” (e.g., *Vaya a casa* = “Go home”), but in your examples it’s the subjunctive future idea.
target_language_example: No creo que vaya a llover mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: “(that) … is going to … / will …” (subjunctive of *ir a* + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to talk about something that might happen (a future action) in a clause that requires the subjunctive—often after expressions of doubt, fear, denial, or uncertainty like *dudo que…*, *no creo que…*, *tengo miedo de que…*, *espero que…*. Negative: *no vaya a + infinitive* (“might not / isn’t going to…”). Note: *vaya* can also be a formal command meaning “go” (e.g., *Vaya a casa* = “Go home”), but in your examples it’s the subjunctive future idea.
target_language_example: No creo que vaya a llover mañana.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Vayamos" is the present subjunctive of "ir" for "nosotros" and is commonly used to propose an action (“Let’s …”) or as a polite command. It’s usually followed by (1) a place: "Vayamos a la cocina" (Let’s go to the kitchen), or (2) an infinitive: "Vayamos a comer" (Let’s go eat / Let’s eat). You’ll also see it in phrases like "Es hora de que nos vayamos a casa" (“It’s time for us to go home”), where "que" triggers the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Vayamos a tomar un café.
native_language_example: Let’s go have a coffee.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **ir** for **ustedes** (you all / you plural). Used to tell a group to go somewhere (**Vayan a la casa**) or to go do something (**Vayan a trabajar**). Often followed by a place (a + el/la/los/las) or an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: Chicos, vayan a dormir; mañana tenemos clase temprano.
native_language_example: Guys, go to sleep; tomorrow we have class early.

meaning: "(that) you go to"; in warnings with "no": "don’t you (go and)… / don’t…"
additional_notes: "Vayas" is the tú present subjunctive of *ir* (to go). It often appears after expressions like *para que* (so that) to express purpose: *para que vayas a…* = “so that you go to…”. With *no* it can be a negative command or a warning/threat: *No le vayas a decir…* = “Don’t you tell him…” / “Don’t go and tell him…”. It can also be literal movement: *No vayas a tu casa* = “Don’t go to your house.”
target_language_example: No vayas a contarle a nadie lo que pasó.
native_language_example: Don’t you tell anyone what happened.

additional_notes: Imperative (tú) form of **ir**: **ve**. Use **ve a + place** (Ve a casa) and often **ve a + infinitive** to tell someone to do something (Ve a lavarte la cara). For a more polite command, use **vaya a**.
target_language_example: Ve a tu cuarto y termina la tarea.
native_language_example: Go to your room and finish your homework.

meaning: “go to the” (addressing one person; feminine singular place/thing).
additional_notes: Command form of **ir** (to go): **ve** = “go” (tú). **a** = “to”. **la** is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., *la enfermería*, *la consola*). Often used to give directions or instructions. (With masculine nouns: **ve al**.)
target_language_example: Ve a la puerta y espera aquí.
native_language_example: Go to the door and wait here.

meaning: "go and see" / "go check"; also "go watch" (TV, a movie).
additional_notes: Imperative (tú) form of **ir a ver**. Use it to tell someone to go look/check something (**Ve a ver quién es** = go see who it is), to go look somewhere (**Ve a ver al otro lado** = go look on the other side), or to go visit someone (**Ve a ver a tu hija** = go see/visit your daughter). With people, you often use **a**: **ver a + person**.
target_language_example: Ve a ver si la puerta está cerrada.
native_language_example: Go check if the door is closed.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of ir (“ve”). It’s followed by a + ver (“to see/visit”) and then the personal a before a person (or pets treated like people): ve a ver a Tom / a mi madre. You can replace the person: ve a ver a María / ve a ver a los niños. More formal: vaya a ver a…; plural: vayan a ver a…
target_language_example: Ve a ver a tu abuela esta tarde.
native_language_example: Go see your grandmother this afternoon.

meaning: Go get… / go for… / go via (a place).
additional_notes: “Ve” is the tú command form of “ir” (to go). With “por”, it often means (1) go to fetch something or someone: “Ve por el libro” = “Go get the book,” or (2) go through/along a route: “Ve por el pasillo” = “Go down/through the hallway.” “Ve por ellos” can mean “Go get them” or “Go after them,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ve por agua, por favor.
native_language_example: Go get some water, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the next step: checking, finding out, or considering options before deciding what to do. It’s the nosotros (we) command form of "ver" (to see), followed by "qué" (what). Often followed by a clause like "podemos hacer" (we can do) or "tienes" (you have).
target_language_example: Veamos qué pasa si lo intentamos otra vez.
native_language_example: Let’s see what happens if we try again.

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes/amounts with a multiplier: [number] + veces más grande que + [thing]. It agrees in gender/number with what’s being described (grande doesn’t change; you can also hear “más grandes que” with plural subjects). Common numbers: dos/tres/cuatro veces…, veinte veces…, etc.
target_language_example: Este país es diez veces más grande que el mío.
native_language_example: This country is ten times bigger than mine.

meaning: 'times per week' (how many times something happens each week).
additional_notes: Used with a number to talk about frequency: "una/dos/tres/cuatro... veces por semana". You can also use ranges like "dos o tres veces por semana" (= two or three times a week). "Vez" is singular; "veces" is plural.
target_language_example: Hago ejercicio tres veces por semana.
native_language_example: I work out three times a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about age (tener veinte años = “to be 20 years old”) or a length of time (hace veinte años = “20 years ago”, en veinte años = “in 20 years / over 20 years”, llevo + gerundio + veinte años = “I’ve been … for 20 years”, han pasado veinte años = “20 years have passed”).
target_language_example: Mi hermano tiene veinte años y yo llevo veinte años viviendo aquí.
native_language_example: My brother is 20 years old, and I’ve been living here for 20 years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration ("for twenty minutes," "twenty minutes ago") or an estimated time/distance ("It’s twenty minutes away" = by car/on foot depending on context). With "hace" it means "twenty minutes ago"; with "en" it means "in twenty minutes" (time needed to do something).
target_language_example: El restaurante está a veinte minutos de aquí.
native_language_example: The restaurant is twenty minutes from here.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the physical constant (how fast light travels, especially in a vacuum). It can also be used figuratively to mean “very fast,” often with the phrase “a la velocidad de la luz” (“at lightning speed”).
target_language_example: Contestó a la velocidad de la luz.
native_language_example: He replied at lightning speed.

meaning: “Come, come!” (calling someone over / urging them to come).
additional_notes: Repeat of the imperative "ven" (from "venir") to sound more insistent, urgent, or encouraging. Often used when calling someone closer: "Ven, ven aquí". You can repeat it more times for emphasis ("Ven, ven, ven").
target_language_example: Ven, ven, no tengas miedo.
native_language_example: Come on, come—don’t be scared.

meaning: "come to" / "come and" (used to invite someone to do something or come somewhere).
additional_notes: Imperative of "venir" (tú): "ven" = "come". With a place/noun: "Ven a nuestra mesa" = "Come to our table." With an infinitive: "Ven a acostarte" / "Ven a jugar" = "Come (and) lie down" / "Come (and) play" (often like an invitation or suggestion).
target_language_example: Ven a cenar con nosotros esta noche.
native_language_example: Come have dinner with us tonight.

additional_notes: Used to invite or tell someone to come and meet a person (often for the first time). It’s an imperative: ven (“come”) + a + conocer (“to meet/get to know”) + a (before a person). You can change the verb form: Ven a conocer a mis amigos. / Venga a conocer a mis amigos. / Vengan a conocer a mis amigos.
target_language_example: Ven a conocer a mi hermana; acaba de llegar.
native_language_example: Come meet my sister; she just arrived.

additional_notes: An invitation/request using the tú command form of **venir** (“ven” = “come”). **A** means “to,” and **mi casa** is “my house/home.” You can add time phrases after it (e.g., *a las ocho*, *esta tarde*, *por la mañana*) or soften it with *por favor*.
target_language_example: Ven a mi casa después de la escuela.
native_language_example: Come to my house after school.

additional_notes: Informal command (tú) using the affirmative imperative of venir (ven) + a + infinitive (ver) + object pronoun (me). Used to invite/ask someone to visit you, often with time phrases like antes de…, antes de que…, or de vez en cuando (from time to time).
target_language_example: Si estás cerca, ven a verme esta tarde.
native_language_example: If you’re nearby, come see me this afternoon.

additional_notes: An informal singular command (imperative) using "venir" (to come): "ven" = “come” (to one person). "Aquí" means “here,” near the speaker. Used to call someone closer or get their attention. For a more polite command, use "venga aquí"; for more than one person, "vengan aquí".
target_language_example: Ven aquí un momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Uses the tú imperative of "venir" ("ven") + "aquí" ("here") + "y" ("and") to tell someone to come to where you are and then do something else. Often followed by another command: "Ven aquí y siéntate." You can also say "ven acá y" in many regions with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ven aquí y explícame qué pasó.
native_language_example: Come here and explain to me what happened.

additional_notes: An invitation/command telling someone to accompany you and your group. Uses the informal (tú) command form of venir: ven. You can soften it with por favor, or turn it into a question: ¿Vienes con nosotros? (Are you coming with us?).
target_language_example: Ven con nosotros al parque esta tarde.
native_language_example: Come with us to the park this afternoon.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using **venir** (tú form): **ven**. Used to invite or tell someone to accompany you. You can add a destination: **Ven conmigo a la tienda.** You may also hear **Ven conmigo y hablamos de...** (“Come with me and we’ll talk about...”).
target_language_example: Ven conmigo al parque.
native_language_example: Come with me to the park.

meaning: would be good for (someone); would come in handy.
additional_notes: Conditional form of "venir bien" (to suit/to be good for someone). Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "me/te/le/nos/les vendría bien" + noun/infinitive. Common for giving advice or making polite suggestions (e.g., "Le vendría bien una taza de té").
target_language_example: Me vendría bien un descanso después de clase.
native_language_example: A break would be good for me after class.

additional_notes: Used with places/origins to say where you are from. It’s the 1st-person singular present of "venir" + "de" (origin). You can also use it to mean "I’m not here as a visitor / I’m not just visiting" depending on context (e.g., "no vengo de visita").
target_language_example: Hola, vengo de México, ¿y tú?
native_language_example: Hi, I’m from Mexico—how about you?

meaning: “(have/has) come to” (a place) or “come to” (do something).
additional_notes: “Venido a” is the past participle of venir (“to come”) used with haber to form the present perfect: he/has/habíamos venido. It’s often followed by either a destination (a + place: “venido a Londres”) or by an infinitive to express purpose (a + infinitive: “venido a ayudar” = “come to help”). Word order with pronouns: “Han venido a verte” = “They’ve come to see you.”
target_language_example: He venido a estudiar español.
native_language_example: I’ve come to study Spanish.

meaning: to come see me / to come to see me.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to visit you. Structure: "venir a" + infinitive expresses coming somewhere in order to do something. "verme" = "to see me" (ver + me). Often said as a request or expectation: "Tienes que venir a verme" (You have to come see me).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir a verme mañana por la tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come see me tomorrow afternoon?

additional_notes: Used to invite, tell, or ask someone to come to the speaker’s location (“here”). Often followed by an infinitive to say the purpose: “venir aquí a + infinitive” (e.g., venir aquí a hablar = come here to talk). In commands, it commonly appears as “ven aquí” (informal tú) or “venga/vengan aquí” (formal usted/ustedes).
target_language_example: ¿Puedes venir aquí un momento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a moment, please?

meaning: 'to come with us' / 'to come along with us'.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join your group or to say they must accompany you. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., ¿Quieres venir con nosotros? / Tienen que venir con nosotros). With other groups, swap the pronoun: venir con ustedes (with you all), venir con ellos/ellas (with them).
target_language_example: ¿Quieres venir con nosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an observation or realization based on what you’ve just seen or learned. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “Veo que + [clause]”. Depending on tone/context, it can sound neutral (“I see that…”) or slightly pointed/ironic (“Oh, I see you…”).
target_language_example: Veo que ya terminaste la tarea.
native_language_example: I see that you already finished the homework.

meaning: to see (a person); to meet with (someone).
additional_notes: Used with people (or personified animals) because Spanish uses the “personal a” after many verbs when the direct object is a specific person: ver a mi amigo, ver a Tom. With things, you usually don’t use “a”: ver la película, ver el coche. Often implies meeting/seeing someone in person.
target_language_example: ¿Vas a ver a tus abuelos este fin de semana?
native_language_example: Are you going to see your grandparents this weekend?

meaning: "to see" / "to meet" (someone who is mine: my…).
additional_notes: Used before a person: **ver a + [person]**. The **a** is the “personal a” and is required with direct-object people (e.g., *ver a mi tía*, *ver a mi profesor*). Often means either literally seeing someone or going to meet/visit them.
target_language_example: Voy a ver a mi amiga después de clase.
native_language_example: I’m going to see my friend after class.

additional_notes: Used when talking about visiting or meeting your son. Spanish uses "ver a" with people (the personal "a"), so it’s "ver a mi hijo" (not *ver mi hijo*). Often appears with needs/obligations like "necesito", "quiero", "tengo que", or "déjame".
target_language_example: ¿Puedo ver a mi hijo un momento?
native_language_example: Can I see my son for a moment?

additional_notes: "Ver a" is used when the direct object is a person (or pet): ver a tu jefe/abuela/esposo. It can mean 'see' (catch sight of) or 'meet/visit' (go to see someone), depending on context. In formal situations like appointments, it often translates as 'meet with' or 'see' (a professional).
target_language_example: Tengo que ver a tu doctor esta tarde.
native_language_example: I have to see your doctor this afternoon.

meaning: to see (a male person); to go see the.
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns that refer to a specific person (or pet). It combines **ver** + the **personal a** + **el** → **al** (e.g., *ver al dentista*, *ver al chef*). With feminine nouns you use **ver a la** (e.g., *ver a la doctora*).
target_language_example: Tengo que ver al doctor hoy.
native_language_example: I have to see the doctor today.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **tener (mucho/poco/nada) que ver con + noun/idea**: *El clima tiene mucho que ver con la salud* (“The weather has a lot to do with health”). You can also use **¿Qué tiene que ver X con Y?** (“What does X have to do with Y?”). In some contexts, **ver con** can be literal (“to see with”), but the very common idiomatic meaning is “to be related to.”
target_language_example: Esto no tiene nada que ver con el trabajo.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with work.

meaning: to have to do with that; to be involved in that.
additional_notes: Used with forms of "tener que ver" to talk about connection or involvement: "¿Qué tenía yo que ver con eso?" = "What did I have to do with that?" It often appears with "algo / nada" (some / nothing): "tener algo que ver" = be involved; "no tener nada que ver" = have nothing to do with. You can also say "tener que ver con" + a thing/topic.
target_language_example: Yo no tengo nada que ver con eso.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with that.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect question ("cómo" = "how") after verbs like "ver" to mean checking the state of something ("go see how the cookies are"), finding out the result ("see how it ended"), or observing how something happens. Often followed by a verb: "ver cómo van/queda/acaba/estás".
target_language_example: Voy a ver cómo está el arroz.
native_language_example: I’m going to see how the rice is doing.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ver" (to see/watch) + "esa" (that, near the listener) + "película" (movie/film). Common after verbs/phrases like "querer" (to want), "poder" (to be able to), "esperar" (to hope), or "merecer la pena" (to be worth it): e.g., "Merece la pena ver esa película."
target_language_example: ¿Te apetece ver esa película esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you feel like watching that movie tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ver" (to see/watch) + "esta" (this) + "película" (movie). Common with expressions like "vale la pena" / "merece la pena" (it’s worth it) and with "tener que" (to have to): "Tienes que ver esta película" = "You have to watch this movie."
target_language_example: ¿Quieres ver esta película conmigo esta noche?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch this movie with me tonight?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they should look at something, often because it’s interesting, surprising, or important. With "tienes que ver esto" it means “you have to see this.” "Ver" can mean “see” (notice with your eyes) or “watch” (a video/show), depending on context.
target_language_example: Tienes que ver esto: acaban de abrir un restaurante nuevo aquí.
native_language_example: You have to see this: they just opened a new restaurant here.

additional_notes: Common, casual way to say “watch television.” It uses the verb "ver" (to watch/see) + "la tele" (short for "la televisión"). You’ll often hear it with "me gusta" / "le gusta" (to like) or "quiero" (to want): "Me gusta ver la tele" (I like watching TV).
target_language_example: Hoy no quiero salir; prefiero ver la tele en casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t want to go out; I’d rather watch TV at home.

meaning: to watch TV / to watch television.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ver" (to see/watch) + "la televisión" (television). Commonly used with time expressions like "cada día" (every day) or after "antes de" + infinitive: "antes de ver la televisión" (before watching TV).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, me gusta ver la televisión.
native_language_example: After dinner, I like to watch TV.

meaning: to see things; to view/think about things (a certain way).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s perspective, attitude, or way of interpreting situations (often followed by "desde..." = "from..." or "tal y como son" = "as they are"). It’s more about how you understand a situation than physically seeing objects.
target_language_example: A veces es difícil ver las cosas con calma cuando estás estresado.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to see things calmly when you’re stressed.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun phrase “lo que” (“what/that which”) to introduce information you’re going to find out or observe: “ver lo que hay” (see what’s there), “ver lo que hará” (see what he/she will do). Often follows verbs like “querer” (to want) or can be used as an infinitive phrase: “Es difícil dejar de ver lo que has visto” (It’s hard to stop seeing what you’ve seen).
target_language_example: Vamos a ver lo que dice el profesor.
native_language_example: Let’s see what the teacher says.

meaning: to see what… / to find out what…
additional_notes: Used when you’re going to check or wait to learn some information or outcome. Very common with "ir a" or "vamos a": "Voy a ver qué pasa" (I’m going to see what happens), "Vamos a ver qué dice" (Let’s see what he/she says). Often implies investigating, checking, or waiting for someone’s response.
target_language_example: Voy a ver qué pasa y te llamo.
native_language_example: I’m going to see what happens and I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the result yet and you’ll wait, check, or go find out. Often implies “let’s wait and see” (we’ll decide later) or “go see what’s going on” (investigate). Common with verbs like tener que (“we’ll have to”), ir (“I’ll go”), and the command ve (“go”).
target_language_example: Vamos a esperar un poco y ver qué pasa.
native_language_example: Let’s wait a bit and see what happens.

meaning: to see if; to check whether.
additional_notes: Used when you’re going to check or find out something, or when you’re about to try something to find out the result. Very common after commands and plans: "vamos a ver si..." (let’s see if...), "ve a ver si..." (go see if...), "quería ver si..." (I wanted to see if...). Often expresses uncertainty or testing a possibility.
target_language_example: Voy a ver si puedo terminarlo hoy.
native_language_example: I’m going to see if I can finish it today.

meaning: "see if I understand (it)" / "let me see if I’ve got it straight."
additional_notes: Used when you’re checking your understanding, often before repeating what you think the other person means. Common with "Déjame ver si lo entiendo" (Let me see if I understand) or "Vamos a ver si lo entiendo" (Let’s see if I understand). The "lo" refers to what was just explained.
target_language_example: Ver si lo entiendo: ¿quieres que te llame mañana por la mañana?
native_language_example: Let me see if I understand: you want me to call you tomorrow morning?

meaning: to watch TV; to watch television.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ver" (to see/watch) + "televisión" (television). Very common with "me gusta" (I like) and after verbs like "disfrutar" (to enjoy): "Me gusta ver televisión", "Disfruta ver televisión". If you’re using it as an activity (as a subject), you can start a sentence with the infinitive: "Ver televisión es divertido". You may also hear "ver la tele" (more informal).
target_language_example: Los fines de semana me gusta ver televisión con mi familia.
native_language_example: On weekends I like to watch TV with my family.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ver" (to see/watch) + "una película" (a movie). Often appears after verbs like "ir a" (to go to) or "llevar a" (to take someone to): "ir a ver una película" = "to go watch a movie" (often at the cinema, but it can also mean at home if the context says so). In questions you may hear "¿Quieres ver una película...?" (Do you want to watch a movie?).
target_language_example: Esta noche podemos ver una película en casa.
native_language_example: Tonight we can watch a movie at home.

additional_notes: Refers to the summer in the previous year. Often used with prepositions like “el” (in the last summer) or “del” (from/of last summer): “en el verano pasado”, “a finales del verano pasado”.
target_language_example: Viajamos a México el verano pasado.
native_language_example: We traveled to Mexico last summer.

additional_notes: Used in the cleft structure **"Lo que + [subject] + verdaderamente quería era + [thing]"** to emphasize the real desire (often contrasting with what others think). *Verdaderamente* = truly/really, *quería* = (he/she) wanted, *era* = was. In everyday speech, people also often use **de verdad** or **en realidad** instead of *verdaderamente*.
target_language_example: Lo que yo verdaderamente quería era descansar un poco.
native_language_example: What I really wanted was to rest a little.

meaning: real/true name (legal name; not a nickname or username).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that it’s someone’s actual identity, not an alias, stage name, or online handle. Often appears with possessives: mi/tu/su verdadero nombre. Common in contexts like privacy, publishing, and anonymity.
target_language_example: En internet casi nadie usa su verdadero nombre.
native_language_example: On the internet, almost nobody uses their real name.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s actual name (often contrasting with a nickname, stage name, or false identity). Normally appears with a possessive: mi/su verdadero nombre es + name. You can also say: Mi verdadero nombre es…, Su verdadero nombre es….
target_language_example: Su verdadero nombre es Alejandro, pero todos le dicen Alex.
native_language_example: His real name is Alejandro, but everyone calls him Alex.

additional_notes: Literally “see-you again” (ver + te + de nuevo). It often appears after another verb that takes an infinitive (e.g., desear, necesitar): “Necesito verte de nuevo.” It’s also used in polite greetings like “(Un) gusto/placer verte de nuevo” (“Nice to see you again”).
target_language_example: Me alegra verte de nuevo.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you again.

meaning: 'to see you again' (talking to someone you know).
additional_notes: Used when you meet someone again or want to meet them again. "Verte" = "to see you" (informal singular tú), and "otra vez" = "again". You can swap in other people: "verlos otra vez" (see you all again), "verte de nuevo" (see you again). Often appears after phrases like "Qué bueno" or "Me alegra": "Qué bueno verte otra vez."
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte otra vez!
native_language_example: It’s great to see you again!

meaning: 'I will see (you/him/her/it) in/at …' (future + time or place).
additional_notes: Used with an object pronoun (lo/la/le) to say you’ll see someone at a place (en el trabajo, en el tribunal) or in a time period (en menos de una semana, en la mañana). The pronoun can change depending on who you’re talking about (te veré…, la veré…, lo veré…).
target_language_example: Te veré en el restaurante a las ocho.
native_language_example: I’ll see you at the restaurant at eight.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person’s clothing. It’s the feminine form: a man would be "vestido de blanco"; a group/mixed gender would be "vestidos de blanco". Common for wedding dresses, nurses’/medical uniforms, etc.
target_language_example: En la boda, ella iba vestida de blanco.
native_language_example: At the wedding, she was dressed in white.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "vestido" (dress) + "azul" (blue). Used to describe which dress you mean or to talk about what someone is wearing. Adjectives usually come after the noun in Spanish (vestido azul). You can add a shade like "azul claro" (light blue) or "azul oscuro" (dark blue).
target_language_example: ¿Dónde compraste el vestido azul?
native_language_example: Where did you buy the blue dress?

additional_notes: Used to describe a dress that is new (recently bought or not worn before). Usually follows the noun: vestido + adjective (nuevo). You can use it with verbs like usar (to wear/use), comprar (to buy), and ponerse (to put on/wear).
target_language_example: Me encanta mi vestido nuevo.
native_language_example: I love my new dress.

additional_notes: "Vete" is the informal (tú) command of "irse" (to leave/go away). Use "vete a" + infinitive to tell someone to go do something ("Vete a dormir" = Go to sleep), or "vete a" + place to send them somewhere ("Vete a tu cuarto" = Go to your room). More formal: "Váyase a…" / "Vaya a…".
target_language_example: Vete a estudiar ahora mismo.
native_language_example: Go study right now.

additional_notes: An informal, direct command telling someone to leave and go home. It uses the tú imperative of "irse" (to leave/go away): "vete". Often sounds firm or even rude depending on tone and context; for a more polite option, use "Vaya a casa" (formal) or "Por favor, vete a casa".
target_language_example: Estoy cansado; vete a casa y descansa.
native_language_example: I'm tired; go home and rest.

meaning: Go to sleep. / Go to bed.
additional_notes: An informal command telling one person (tú) to go to bed/sleep. It uses the affirmative imperative of "irse" (vete) + "a" + infinitive (dormir). Often used with "ahora" (now) or "mañana hablamos" (we’ll talk tomorrow). It can sound caring or firm depending on tone/context (e.g., telling someone who’s tired or drunk).
target_language_example: Es tarde; vete a dormir y mañana lo hablamos.
native_language_example: It’s late; go to bed and we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

meaning: Go away; get out of here.
additional_notes: Command form (tú) of irse: vete = “leave.” Used to tell someone (or something, like pain) to leave the place you’re in. Can sound strong/angry; you can soften it with “por favor.”
target_language_example: No quiero problemas: vete de aquí ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I don’t want trouble: get out of here right now.

meaning: 'time in' (used with una/otra/primera, etc.: 'once in…', 'the first time in…', 'that time in…').
additional_notes: You’ll almost always see it with a word before vez (una, otra, primera, ni una sola, etc.) to count or refer to an occasion, and then en introduces the place or time period: una vez en Inglaterra (once in England), la primera vez en el mes (the first time in the month).
target_language_example: Fue la segunda vez en mi vida que vi la nieve.
native_language_example: It was the second time in my life that I saw snow.

additional_notes: Used with an article or adjective to talk about a specific occasion: la/una vez que… (“the/a time when…”), la última vez que… (“the last time that…”). In the fixed expression a la vez que, it means “at the same time as / while” (doing two things simultaneously).
target_language_example: No olvido la vez que nos perdimos en el metro.
native_language_example: I don’t forget the time we got lost in the subway.

meaning: “I saw …” (preterite of ver), often with the personal “a” before a person.
additional_notes: “Vi” is the past tense (“I saw”) of ver. In Spanish, when the direct object is a specific person (or a pet), you usually add the personal “a”: Vi a Liz. With nobody/anyone: No vi a nadie. You normally don’t use this “a” with things: Vi una película (not *Vi a una película*).
target_language_example: Ayer vi a mi hermano en el centro.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw my brother downtown.

additional_notes: "Vi" is the preterite (past) of "ver" = "to see": "I saw". Spanish often uses the **personal a** before a direct object that is a **person** (and sometimes a pet/animal): "vi a un hombre" (I saw a man), "vi a María" (I saw María). You don’t translate this extra "a" into English; it just marks the person as the object of the verb.
target_language_example: Ayer vi a un médico en la entrada del hospital.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw a doctor at the entrance of the hospital.

additional_notes: Uses the preterite tense of ver (yo vi = “I saw,” a completed past action). The “a” is the personal a, used before a direct object that is a specific person (vi a Juan, vi a un hombre). Word order can vary (Vi a un hombre entrar... / Vi a un hombre cuando salía...).
target_language_example: Ayer vi a un hombre en la calle.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw a man on the street.

meaning: 'I saw it with my own eyes' (I witnessed it personally).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you personally witnessed something and it’s not hearsay. Often appears with an object pronoun: "Lo vi con mis propios ojos" / "Los vi con mis propios ojos." You can change the verb to match the subject/tense: "Lo vimos...", "Lo he visto..."
target_language_example: No es un rumor: lo vi con mis propios ojos.
native_language_example: It’s not a rumor: I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: "Vi" is the simple past (preterite) of **ver** (to see): *yo vi* = "I saw." It’s used to talk about something you saw at a specific moment in the past. **Una** is the feminine form of "a/an"; for masculine nouns you use **vi un** (e.g., *Vi un perro*).
target_language_example: Vi una película muy buena anoche.
native_language_example: I saw a really good movie last night.

meaning: to travel abroad / to travel to a foreign country.
additional_notes: Common phrase with viajar (to travel) + al (to the) + extranjero (foreign countries/abroad). Often used with verbs like poder (can), querer (want), gustar (like), tener la oportunidad de (have the chance to), and with a transport phrase (en avión, en tren, etc.).
target_language_example: Este verano queremos viajar al extranjero por primera vez.
native_language_example: This summer we want to travel abroad for the first time.

additional_notes: Used to say what life (or a life) is like or what it means. In real sentences you usually add an article or quantifier before it: **la vida es** (life is), **una vida es** (a life is), **toda vida es** (every life is), **mi vida es** (my life is).
target_language_example: La vida es corta, pero hermosa.
native_language_example: Life is short, but beautiful.

additional_notes: A warm, friendly way to greet someone you’ve known for a long time. You can say it directly as a greeting (often with “Hola,”) or use it in a longer sentence (e.g., “Mi viejo amigo…”).
target_language_example: ¡Qué gusto verte, viejo amigo!
native_language_example: So nice to see you, old friend!

additional_notes: Used to talk about friends you’ve known for a long time (not necessarily elderly). Often appears with verbs like "ser" (somos viejos amigos) and "ver"/"visitar" (pasó a ver a unos viejos amigos).
target_language_example: Nos reunimos con viejos amigos después de muchos años.
native_language_example: We got together with old friends after many years.

additional_notes: Used to talk nostalgically about the past, often with verbs like recordar (to remember) or phrases like como en viejos tiempos (“like in the old days”). Very commonly appears as los viejos tiempos (“the old times”) and especially los buenos viejos tiempos (“the good old days”).
target_language_example: Cuando nos reunimos, siempre hablamos de los viejos tiempos.
native_language_example: When we get together, we always talk about the old times.

additional_notes: "Viendo" is the gerund of "ver" (to watch/see). It’s commonly used with "estar" to talk about an action in progress: "estoy/está/estaba viendo la tele" = "I am / he is / he was watching TV." "La tele" is a very common informal short form of "la televisión".
target_language_example: Estoy viendo la tele ahora.
native_language_example: I’m watching TV right now.

additional_notes: Used with a form of **estar** to describe what someone is doing right now: **estar viendo la televisión** = “to be watching TV.” In Spanish you usually say **ver la televisión** (literally “to see the television”) to mean “to watch TV.”
target_language_example: Estoy viendo la televisión ahora.
native_language_example: I'm watching TV right now.

additional_notes: "Viendo" is the gerund of "ver" (to see/watch). It’s used to talk about an action in progress (often with "estar": "estaba viendo televisión" = "was watching TV") or to describe what someone was doing when something else happened. It can also describe the activity during which something happened: "se quedó dormido viendo televisión" = "fell asleep while watching TV."
target_language_example: Estoy viendo televisión ahora mismo.
native_language_example: I'm watching TV right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that help, someone, or something has already started traveling and will arrive soon. Often used to reassure someone: "Ya viene en camino" = "It’s already on the way." You may also hear the more common variant "viene en camino" / "va en camino" / "viene de camino."
target_language_example: Tranquilo, la ambulancia ya viene en camino.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the ambulance is already on the way.

meaning: "Are you coming with us?" / "You’re coming with us."
additional_notes: Uses the verb venir (to come) with con nosotros (with us). In questions it often means “Are you coming with us?” (¿Vienes con nosotros?). With tú/te (Tú vienes… / Te vienes…) it can sound more direct, like confirming or inviting someone to join. Te vienes is very common in spoken Spanish; it can feel a bit more casual or persuasive than plain vienes.
target_language_example: ¿Vienes con nosotros al cine?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the night of Friday (typically Friday evening and later). With "el" it often means "on Friday nights" in general (repeated habit): "el viernes por la noche". Without an article it can also refer to this specific Friday night: "Es viernes por la noche."
target_language_example: ¿Qué haces el viernes por la noche?
native_language_example: What are you doing on Friday night?

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **venir** + **a** + infinitive: **vine a + infinitive**. It’s used to say you came somewhere in order to do something (purpose): *Vine a hablar* = “I came to talk.” You can also use it when the place is understood from context (you don’t have to say where you came).
target_language_example: Vine a ayudarte con la tarea.
native_language_example: I came to help you with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say you came somewhere with the purpose of visiting/seeing a person. "Vine" is the preterite (completed past) of "venir" for "yo". The second "a" is the personal "a" used before a direct object that is a specific person: "vine a ver a mi madre". (Without that personal "a" it would sound wrong when referring to people.)
target_language_example: Vine a ver a tu hermana esta tarde.
native_language_example: I came to see your sister this afternoon.

additional_notes: Past tense (third person singular) of "venir a". Use it for someone arriving somewhere ("vino a mi cuarto" = he came to my room) or coming to do something ("vino a visitarnos" = she came to visit us). "Vino" here means "came" (not "wine").
target_language_example: El doctor vino a verme esta mañana.
native_language_example: The doctor came to see me this morning.

additional_notes: "Vino" is the past tense (preterite) of "venir" for él/ella/usted. "A casa" means "to home" (often expressed in English as "home"). You can add a time ("a las nueve") or an adverb ("muy tarde"). For plural, use "vinieron a casa" (they came home).
target_language_example: Anoche mi hermana vino a casa temprano.
native_language_example: Last night my sister came home early.

additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **venir**: **(él/ella/usted) vino** = “he/she/you (formal) came.” You can change the subject: **Yo vine**, **tú viniste**, **nosotros vinimos**, etc. Common with **nadie** (“nobody”): **Nadie vino a la fiesta** = “Nobody came to the party.” Note that **vino** can also mean “wine,” but in this phrase it’s the verb “came.”
target_language_example: ¿Por qué no vino a la fiesta?
native_language_example: Why didn’t he come to the party?

meaning: "(He/She) came to see me" / "(He/She) came to visit me."
additional_notes: Past tense (preterite) of **venir**: **vino** = “came” (3rd person singular: he/she/you-form came). **a verme** literally means “to see me” (a + ver + me). Often used with time expressions: **ayer**, **el domingo**, **hace tres días**. Note: **vino** can also mean “wine” as a noun, but here it’s the verb “came.”
target_language_example: Mi primo vino a verme ayer por la tarde.
native_language_example: My cousin came to see me yesterday afternoon.

meaning: “(He/She) came to see you” / “came to visit you.”
additional_notes: Uses the preterite (completed past) of **venir**: **vino** = “he/she came.” The subject can be a name or implied by context (e.g., *Ella vino a verte*). **verte** = “to see you,” made from **ver** + **te** (informal singular “you,” *tú*). Often used to say someone came by when you weren’t there or at a specific moment.
target_language_example: Tu hermano vino a verte, pero estabas en una reunión.
native_language_example: Your brother came to see you, but you were in a meeting.

additional_notes: Vino is the preterite (simple past) of venir (“to come”) for él/ella/usted. Con means “with.” Su hermano means “his/her/your (formal) brother,” so su can be ambiguous—use context to know whose brother it is. You can also drop the subject (Él/Ella/Usted) because the verb form already shows the person.
target_language_example: ¿Vino con su hermano o vino solo?
native_language_example: Did you come with your brother, or did you come alone?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "venir" (to come) in the preterite: "vino" = "he/she/it came" (also "you" formal, "usted"). Often followed by "a" or "al" + place: "vino por primera vez a Boston" / "vino por primera vez al club". Don’t confuse "vino" (came) with "vino" (wine) — same spelling, different meaning.
target_language_example: Mi hermana vino por primera vez a España el año pasado.
native_language_example: My sister came to Spain for the first time last year.

meaning: '(he/she/you formal) saw' + marks a person/animate object ('saw someone').
additional_notes: “Vio” is the simple past (preterite) of *ver* (“to see”) for él/ella/usted. The “a” is the **personal a**, used before a direct object that is a specific person (and often animals or personified beings): *Vio a María*, *Vio a alguien*, *No vio a nadie*. In English you usually don’t translate this “a”; you just say “saw Maria / saw someone.”
target_language_example: Ayer vi a mi profesor en el supermercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw my teacher at the supermarket.

meaning: “was forced/compelled to” (had no choice but to).
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject: “(Él/Ella) se vio obligado/a a + infinitive.” It’s common in formal/neutral writing and emphasizes that circumstances forced the action. Change the ending for gender/number: obligado (masc.), obligada (fem.), obligados/obligadas (plural).
target_language_example: Por falta de dinero, me vi obligado a vender el coche.
native_language_example: Because I didn’t have enough money, I was forced to sell the car.

additional_notes: Use **a** (the “personal a”) when the direct object is a person or a pet: **visitar a Tom**, **visitar a mi familia**. With places, you normally drop **a**: **visitar el museo** (to visit the museum).
target_language_example: Voy a visitar a mis abuelos este fin de semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my grandparents this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say you have seen someone/something previously. Very commonly appears with the verb **haber** (present perfect): **he/has/hemos/habéis/han visto antes** (“I/you/he/we/you all/they have seen before”). Often used with object pronouns: **la he visto antes** (I’ve seen her before), **lo he visto antes** (I’ve seen it before).
target_language_example: Creo que ya te he visto antes, pero no recuerdo dónde.
native_language_example: I think I’ve seen you before, but I don’t remember where.

additional_notes: Used with **de + place** to say someone lives on the opposite side of a street, river, city, etc.: **Vive al otro lado de la calle / del río / de la ciudad**. You can also say **al otro lado** by itself if the place is clear from context.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo vive al otro lado del parque.
native_language_example: My grandpa lives on the other side of the park.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives relative to a place. Pattern: "[persona] vive cerca de + lugar". With specific places you often add an article: "cerca de la playa / del centro"; with "aquí" you say "cerca de aquí" (no "de el").
target_language_example: Mi abuela vive cerca del parque.
native_language_example: My grandma lives near the park.

additional_notes: "Vive" is the 3rd-person singular of "vivir" (to live). "Con" means "with." "Sus" means "his/her/their" and agrees with the plural noun "padres" (parents). You can change the subject: "Él vive con sus padres" / "Ella vive con sus padres." Common with "todavía" (= still): "Todavía vive con sus padres."
target_language_example: Mi hermano todavía vive con sus padres.
native_language_example: My brother still lives with his parents.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something lives. It’s the present tense of the verb "vivir" for él/ella/usted: "(he/she/you formal) lives" + "en" (in). You can swap the subject: "Vivo en…" (I live in…), "Vives en…" (you live in…), "Viven en…" (they live in…).
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive en Madrid.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. It’s the 3rd-person singular of **vivir** (él/ella/usted **vive**). **En el** = “in the” / “on the” before a masculine singular noun (**el castillo**, **el tercer piso**, **el este**, **el Polo Norte**). For other nouns, you’ll use **vive en la**, **vive en los**, **vive en las**.
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive en el centro de la ciudad.
native_language_example: My sister lives in the city center.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. "vive" is the third-person singular of "vivir" (to live), so it refers to él/ella/usted (he/she/you formal). "en el campo" means “in the countryside” (outside the city). For other people: "vivo en el campo" (I live…), "vives en el campo" (you live…).
target_language_example: Mi tía vive en el campo, cerca de un pueblo pequeño.
native_language_example: My aunt lives in the countryside, near a small town.

additional_notes: "Vive" is the he/she/usted form of "vivir" (to live). "En" means "in/at," and "esa casa" means "that house" (usually a house not right next to you; "esta" = this one near you). You can change the subject: "Él vive en esa casa" (he), "Ella vive..." (she), "Usted vive..." (you formal).
target_language_example: Ella vive en esa casa desde 2020.
native_language_example: She has lived in that house since 2020.

meaning: "(he/she) lives in the" (before a feminine singular place or location).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. "Vive" is the present tense of "vivir" (to live): "él/ella vive" = "he/she lives" (also used for "you" formal: "usted vive"). "En la" is "in the" and is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., "la cabaña", "la calle"). With masculine nouns you use "en el" (e.g., "vive en el centro").
target_language_example: Mi abuela vive en la ciudad.
native_language_example: My grandmother lives in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. "Vive" is the present tense (él/ella/usted) of "vivir". Change "un" to "una" for feminine nouns ("vive en una casa"). With "el/la" you get "vive en el..." / "vive en la...". Common with places like "barrio" (neighborhood), "pueblo" (town), "apartamento" (apartment), "vecindario" (neighborhood).
target_language_example: Mi amiga vive en un apartamento cerca del centro.
native_language_example: My friend lives in an apartment near downtown.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular place/thing after it (una van, una calle, una zona). It’s the verb vivir (“to live”) + en (“in/on/at”) + una (“a/an”). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., vive en una realidad paralela = “lives in a parallel reality”). For other nouns, you change the article: vive en un… (masculine), viven en… (they live).
target_language_example: Mi hermana vive en una ciudad pequeña.
native_language_example: My sister lives in a small city.

additional_notes: From the verb **vivir** (“to live”). **Vive** is the **third-person singular** present tense (él/ella/usted). Often followed by **en** + a place: *vive en una casa / en un apartamento / en el campo*. You can change the subject for other persons: *vivo* (I live), *vives* (you live), *viven* (they live).
target_language_example: Ella vive en una casa pequeña cerca de la escuela.
native_language_example: She lives in a small house near the school.

meaning: “they live in” (they reside in / live in a place or situation).
additional_notes: "Viven" is the present tense (ellos/ellas/ustedes) of "vivir" (to live). Use "viven en" before places ("viven en Egipto", "viven en el mar") and also for broader situations or ways of living ("viven en manada" = they live in herds; "viven en mundos separados" = they live in separate worlds). For one person: "vive en".
target_language_example: Mis abuelos viven en Madrid.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in Madrid.

meaning: "they live in/on the" (before a feminine place word).
additional_notes: Used to say where "they" live. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun (ellos/ellas), so "Viven..." can mean "They live..." from context. Use **en** for locations (cities, buildings, neighborhoods) and also for many streets/avenues. **la** is the feminine form of "the" (e.g., *la casa, la jungla, la avenida*). For masculine nouns, you’d use **viven en el** (e.g., *Viven en el centro*).
target_language_example: Viven en la calle principal.
native_language_example: They live on the main street.

additional_notes: A simple sentence meaning someone’s home is a house. Spanish often drops the subject pronoun, so "Viven en una casa" usually means "They live in a house" (or "You all live in a house" in Spain), depending on context. "Viven" is the present tense of "vivir" for "ellos/ellas/ustedes."
target_language_example: Mis vecinos viven en una casa grande.
native_language_example: My neighbors live in a big house.

additional_notes: Gerund of "vivir" + "en". Used to say someone is currently residing in a place, or (more broadly) experiencing a time/era ("viviendo en la era..."). Often appears with "estar" for a temporary/current situation ("estamos viviendo en...") or with "llevar" to emphasize duration ("lleva mucho tiempo viviendo en...").
target_language_example: Estoy viviendo en Madrid por trabajo.
native_language_example: I’m living in Madrid for work.

additional_notes: A classic fairy-tale ending. Literally “they lived happy forever.” Uses the past tense (vivieron), so it refers to what happened after the story’s events (often after getting married). You’ll also see it with other subjects, e.g., “y vivió feliz para siempre” (and he/she lived happily ever after) or “y vivieron…” (and they lived…).
target_language_example: Y el dragón se fue, y ellos vivieron felices para siempre.
native_language_example: And the dragon went away, and they lived happily ever after.

meaning: “we live in” (we reside in / we are living in).
additional_notes: From the verb vivir (“to live”). Used with en + a place (city, country, neighborhood) or a time/era (“in the information age”). Also used for general statements about where people exist (e.g., “on planet Earth”).
target_language_example: Vivimos en un apartamento pequeño, pero cómodo.
native_language_example: We live in a small apartment, but it’s comfortable.

meaning: “we live in the” (or “we live on the”), before a masculine singular noun/place.
additional_notes: Used to say where “we” live: vivir (to live) + en (in/on) + el (the). Choose “in” for most places (en el sexto piso = on the sixth floor / in the sixth-floor apartment area) and “on” for planets/surfaces (en el planeta Tierra = on planet Earth). It’s specifically for masculine singular nouns; for feminine use “vivimos en la…”, and for plural “vivimos en los/las…”.
target_language_example: Vivimos en el centro de la ciudad.
native_language_example: We live in the city center.

meaning: “we live in a world…” (often used to introduce a general statement).
additional_notes: Common setup for making a broad comment about reality/society, usually followed by an adjective or description (e.g., complejo, complicado, cruel) or a clause. In speech and writing it can sound a bit reflective or serious.
target_language_example: Vivimos en un mundo donde todo cambia muy rápido.
native_language_example: We live in a world where everything changes very fast.

additional_notes: Used with a place (city/country/house): "Vivo en Madrid." It can also be used more figuratively to describe a condition or lifestyle: "vivir en el lujo" = to live in luxury. With an object pronoun like "él/ella" it can refer to a place/thing you can live in (e.g., an apartment): "Voy a vivir en él."
target_language_example: ¿Vives en esta ciudad desde hace mucho?
native_language_example: Have you lived in this city for a long time?

meaning: to live in the countryside (rural area).
additional_notes: Used to talk about living in a rural place (not the city). Often contrasted with "vivir en la ciudad". Here, "campo" means "countryside" rather than an individual "field."
target_language_example: Mis abuelos viven en el campo, cerca de un pueblo pequeño.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in the countryside, near a small town.

meaning: to live without; (often) to not be able to do without.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or a person/pronoun (vivir sin ti / él / ella / eso). It can be literal (survival/necessity: vivir sin agua) or emotional/figurative (vivir sin amor). With "no poder" it strongly means "can’t do without" (dependency/need): No puedo vivir sin él.
target_language_example: No puedo vivir sin mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I can’t live without my phone.

meaning: to live without air; to survive without air.
additional_notes: A literal, common-sense phrase. Used to say that something is impossible or cannot survive without air (often in general statements or explanations). You can swap in other necessities: vivir sin agua (to live without water), vivir sin comida (to live without food).
target_language_example: Nadie puede vivir sin aire por mucho tiempo.
native_language_example: No one can live without air for very long.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s life in the past, often followed by an adjective (larga, tranquila, dura) or details about where/how they lived. It’s the preterite of vivir (vivió = “lived”), typically for a completed life period.
target_language_example: Mi abuelo vivió una vida sencilla, pero feliz.
native_language_example: My grandfather lived a simple but happy life.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live in relation to a place or person. It’s the verb "vivir" (to live) in the 1st person singular present ("vivo") + "cerca de" (near/close to) followed by a noun or pronoun: "Vivo cerca de la escuela" (near the school), "Vivo cerca de ti" (near you).
target_language_example: Vivo cerca de la estación, así que voy caminando.
native_language_example: I live near the station, so I walk.

additional_notes: Use it to say who you live with. "Vivo" is the present tense of "vivir" (to live). After "con" you usually use a possessive + noun (mi madre, mi tío, mi compañero de piso) or you can switch to plural: "Vivo con mis padres" (I live with my parents).
target_language_example: Vivo con mi hermana en Madrid.
native_language_example: I live with my sister in Madrid.

additional_notes: Used with a place you live: a city/country (vivo en Boston / Japón) or a type of home/building (vivo en un piso = I live in an apartment/flat). For an exact street address, Spanish often uses "vivo en" + street name and number (e.g., Vivo en la Calle Mayor 10).
target_language_example: Vivo en Madrid desde 2022.
native_language_example: I live in Madrid since 2022.

meaning: "I/he/she used to live in" (was living in) a place.
additional_notes: "Vivía" is the imperfect past of "vivir" (to live). Use "vivía en + place" to describe where someone lived habitually or for an ongoing period in the past, often as background information (e.g., "cuando era niño" = "when I was a child"). It doesn’t specify a clear start/end the way "viví en" can.
target_language_example: Antes vivía en Madrid, pero ahora vivo en Valencia.
native_language_example: I used to live in Madrid, but now I live in Valencia.
