additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like salir/irse/entrar to describe something moving through a window while flying (often with insects, birds, or even objects that come flying in). Word order can vary (e.g., «salió volando por la ventana»).
target_language_example: El pájaro se fue volando por la ventana.
native_language_example: The bird flew out through the window.

meaning: to go back home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "volver" + "a" + destination (here, "casa"). Often means returning to your home after being out: "volver a casa". You can add how you return with phrases like "andando" (on foot) or time expressions like "por fin" (at last).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, quiero volver a casa temprano.
native_language_example: After work, I want to go back home early.

meaning: to go back/return to the (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to a place/thing: volver a la cabaña, volver a la selva, volver a la consola. It’s the verb volver + a + la (“to the”). With masculine nouns, it becomes volver al (a + el). Also common with an infinitive (volver a + verb) meaning “to do something again” (e.g., Volvió a llamar = He called again).
target_language_example: Después de cenar, voy a volver a la oficina.
native_language_example: After dinner, I’m going to go back to the office.

meaning: to see again; to meet/see someone again.
additional_notes: Used for doing the action of seeing a person or thing another time (again). Often appears in negative statements to mean “never see (someone) again”: “no volver a ver”. You can add time words like “nunca más” (never again) or “más” (again/anymore), especially with people: “no volver a ver más a + person”.
target_language_example: Espero volver a verte pronto.
native_language_example: I hope to see you again soon.

additional_notes: Used when you see a person again after some time. Structure: "volver a" + infinitive (ver) + "a" + person (because "ver" takes the personal "a"): "volver a ver a Tom". You can also use it with a pronoun: "volver a verme" (to see me again), "volver a verte" (to see you again).
target_language_example: Espero volver a ver a mis amigos pronto.
native_language_example: I hope to see my friends again soon.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern “volver a + infinitive” to mean “to do something again.” Here, “verlo” = “ver” (to see) + “lo” (him/it). In real speech you can swap who you’re seeing: “volver a verla” (see her again), “volver a verlos/verl as” (see them again).
target_language_example: Espero volver a verlo mañana.
native_language_example: I hope to see him again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when you meet someone again after some time. Literally “to return to seeing you.” You can swap the pronoun depending on who you’re talking to: volver a verlo (him/you formal), volver a verla (her/you formal), volver a verlos/verlas (them/you all). Common in greetings/farewells: “Es un placer volver a verte” (Nice to see you again). Can also be negative: “No quiero volver a verte” (I don’t want to see you again).
target_language_example: Me alegra volver a verte después de tanto tiempo.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you again after so long.

meaning: to go back to work; to return to work.
additional_notes: Used when resuming work after a break (lunch, vacation, time off, etc.). Often follows a conjugated form of volver (vuelvo, vas a volver, tengo que volver, debería volver) + al trabajo (“to the work/job”).
target_language_example: Después de comer, tengo que volver al trabajo.
native_language_example: After eating, I have to go back to work.

additional_notes: This is the future tense of **volver** (to return) + **a**. It’s used in two common ways: (1) **volverá a + place** = “he/she will return to (a place)” (often **volverá a casa** = “will come back home”); (2) **volverá a + infinitive** = “will (do something) again” (repeat an action), e.g., **volverá a intentar** = “will try again.” Negative: **no volverá a + infinitive** = “will never (do) again.”
target_language_example: Si estudias más, volverás a aprobar el examen.
native_language_example: If you study more, you’ll pass the exam again.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (volveré a + infinitive) to say you will repeat an action in the future. It can also mean "I will return to" (a place), but in many everyday sentences it means "again."
target_language_example: Volveré a llamarte mañana.
native_language_example: I’ll call you again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Conditional of "volver a ver" (to see again). Often used with words like "nunca" or "nunca más" to express that you didn’t expect to meet someone again: "No pensé que te volvería a ver." You can add an object with "a": "volvería a ver a mi amigo".
target_language_example: No creí que te volvería a ver después de tantos años.
native_language_example: I didn’t think I would see you again after so many years.

meaning: "would see you again" / "would go back to seeing you."
additional_notes: "Volver a + infinitive" means "to do something again" (or "to go back to doing it"). Here, "volvería" is the conditional of "volver" and expresses a hypothetical/uncertain future from the past (often after verbs like "creí" or "pensé"): "I thought I would never see you again." "Verte" = "to see you" (informal singular "tú").
target_language_example: Pensé que no volvería a verte nunca más.
native_language_example: I thought I would never see you again.

additional_notes: Comes from the verb phrase "volverse loco" = "to go crazy" (often with "me/te/se estoy/estás/está... volviendo loco"). It can describe your own mental state (sometimes exaggerated: "This is making me crazy") or something/someone causing it: "Las hormonas me están volviendo loco" = "Hormones are driving me crazy." You’ll also hear the feminine form "volviendo loca" when referring to a woman.
target_language_example: Este ruido me está volviendo loco.
native_language_example: This noise is driving me crazy.

additional_notes: Preterite (past) of **volver a**. Used in two common patterns: **volvió a + infinitive** = “did X again” (repeat an action): *volvió a sonar* (“rang again”), *volvió a empacar* (“packed again”). Also **volvió a + place/thing** = “returned (back) to”: *volvió a la biblioteca* (“went back to the library”), *todo volvió a su lugar* (“everything went back to its place”).
target_language_example: Después de perderla, volvió a encontrar su cartera.
native_language_example: After losing it, he found his wallet again.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito) of volver: "volver" = to return/come back. "Volvió a casa" is commonly used to say someone returned home after being out. You can change the subject: "Volví a casa" (I went back home), "volvimos a casa" (we went back home).
target_language_example: Después del trabajo, volvió a casa y se fue a dormir.
native_language_example: After work, he/she went back home and went to sleep.

additional_notes: From the verb **volver** (to return). **Volví a + lugar** = “I went back to + place” (Volví a casa). **Volví a + infinitivo** = “I did + verb again” (Volví a quedarme dormido = I fell asleep again). Often implies something happened a second time (or didn’t happen again: *Nunca volví a hablar con ella* = I never spoke to her again).
target_language_example: Volví a llamar, pero no contestó.
native_language_example: I called again, but he/she didn’t answer.

additional_notes: From the pattern **volver a + infinitive**, meaning “to do something again.” Here **ver** = “to see,” so **volver a ver** = “to see again / to see (someone) again.” In real sentences, an object pronoun is usually included: **la volví a ver** (I saw her again), **lo volví a ver** (I saw him/it again), **los/las volví a ver** (I saw them again). With **le**, many speakers use it for “him” (especially in Spain): **No le volví a ver** = “I didn’t see him again.” Often used with **nunca** to mean “I never saw (them) again.”
target_language_example: Después de la fiesta, no la volví a ver.
native_language_example: After the party, I didn’t see her again.

additional_notes: Uses vosotros (Spain; informal “you all”) + dos to single out exactly two people. It matches verbs and pronouns in the vosotros form (e.g., vosotros sois, debéis, habéis; os). Often used to emphasize or call out the pair, sometimes as a direct address: “Vosotros dos, …”.
target_language_example: Vosotros dos, venid aquí un momento.
native_language_example: You two, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis with the plural informal "vosotros" (common in Spain). It can mean (1) emphasizing the subject: “be proud of yourselves / believe in yourselves,” or (2) “in person / for yourselves”: “go see it yourselves.” Often appears after a preposition with "con" or "en" (e.g., "con vosotros mismos", "en vosotros mismos").
target_language_example: Podéis comprobarlo vosotros mismos.
native_language_example: You can check it yourselves.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about the near future or an intention: "voy a" + infinitive (e.g., "voy a ir", "voy a pensar"). It’s the 1st-person singular form of "ir" (to go) in the "ir a + infinitive" future construction.
target_language_example: Voy a estudiar esta noche.
native_language_example: I’m going to study tonight.

meaning: “I’m going to look for…” / “I’m going to go get…”
additional_notes: Used for a near-future plan: ir a + infinitive (voy a + verb). With buscar it can mean either (1) “look for” something/someone (search) or (2) “go get/pick up” something/someone. Often followed by a noun (voy a buscar agua) or by “a” before a person (“voy a buscar al novio” = I’m going to go get/look for the boyfriend).
target_language_example: Ahora vuelvo: voy a buscar mi teléfono.
native_language_example: I’ll be right back: I’m going to get my phone.

meaning: “I’m going to eat” / “I’m about to eat.”
additional_notes: Uses the common near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a** (I’m going to) + **comer** (to eat). You can add what you’ll eat: **Voy a comer chocolate** (I’m going to eat chocolate). With pronouns like **me/te/lo**, it can mean “eat it all up” (**Me lo voy a comer entero** = I’m going to eat it all/whole). **Te voy a comer** can be literal (“I’m going to eat you”) but is often used as a sexual/very suggestive phrase, so avoid it in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; voy a comer algo rápido.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to eat something quickly.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(yo) voy a contar** = “I’m going to tell.” Often used before sharing information or a story: **Te voy a contar...** (“I’m going to tell you...”). Be careful: **contar** can also mean “to count” (numbers), depending on context.
target_language_example: Te voy a contar algo importante.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you something important.

meaning: “I’m going to give” (near future: ir a + dar).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you’re about to do: **voy a + infinitive** = “I’m going to…”. With pronouns it often becomes **le/te/la/lo voy a dar** (“I’m going to give him/her/you/it…”). In some common reflexive uses, **me voy a dar + noun** can mean “I’m going to have/take…” (e.g., **me voy a dar un baño** = “I’m going to take a bath”). In contexts like **Ya te la voy a dar**, it can sound like a warning/threat: “I’ll show you / I’ll get you.”
target_language_example: Te voy a dar mi número mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to give you my number tomorrow.

additional_notes: From "ir a" + infinitive ("decir"): a very common way to talk about a near future action or intention. Often used to introduce what you’re about to say (e.g., before giving instructions, explaining, or setting a limit like "Es todo lo que voy a decir"). You can change the subject: "vas a decir" (you’re going to say), "va a decir" (he/she is going to say).
target_language_example: Te voy a decir la verdad.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: This is the **near-future**: **ir (voy) + a + infinitive (dejar)**. **Dejar** is very common and its meaning depends on context: **leave/abandon** (No te voy a dejar. = I’m not going to leave you.), **leave something to someone / hand over** (Le voy a dejar todo a él. = I’m going to leave everything to him.), **quit/stop** (No voy a dejar el espectáculo. = I’m not going to quit the show.), **drop it / let it go** (No voy a dejar lo del pollo. = I’m not going to drop the chicken thing.), **leave/drop someone off somewhere** (Te voy a dejar en mi apartamento. = I’ll leave you/drop you off at my apartment.), and in set phrases like **dejar en claro** (“make clear”).
target_language_example: Voy a dejar de fumar este mes.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop smoking this month.

meaning: "I’m going to be" / "I’ll be" (future state or where you’ll be).
additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive (estar) to talk about the near future. Often refers to how you will feel/state (Voy a estar muy bien) or where you will be/your availability (Ahí voy a estar; Voy a estar por aquí un rato; No voy a estar = I won’t be there / I won’t be available).
target_language_example: Mañana voy a estar en casa todo el día.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll be at home all day.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive**: *voy a* (I’m going to) + **hacer** (do/make). Used for plans, intentions, or what you’re about to do. Negative: **no voy a hacer** (“I’m not going to do it”). Often followed by **lo que**: *Voy a hacer lo que quieras* (“I’ll do whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a hacer la cena.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to make dinner.

additional_notes: Form of **ir a + infinitive** (near future): **voy** (I go) + **a** + **ir** (to go). Often used to say you plan/intend to go, or that you’re about to leave soon. It’s commonly followed by a destination or purpose: **voy a ir mañana**, **voy a ir a la función**, **voy a ir con usted**. In speech, it can also be used simply to confirm attendance: **Sí, voy a ir** (“Yes, I’ll go / I’m going”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, voy a ir contigo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going with you.

additional_notes: This is the near-future structure: **ir (conjugated) + a + infinitive**. When you say **voy a ir a + infinitive**, you’re emphasizing that you will **go somewhere in order to** do that action (e.g., go visit, go talk, go pick someone up). Often you can shorten it to **voy a + infinitive** if the “going” part isn’t important.
target_language_example: Voy a ir a comprar pan ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to go buy bread now.

meaning: “I’m going to call” (on the phone) or “I’m going to call/name.”
additional_notes: "Voy a" is the very common near-future: "I’m going to" + infinitive. "Llamar" can mean (1) to call someone (often by phone): "Te voy a llamar en una hora" = “I’m going to call you in an hour,” and object pronouns can attach before the verb phrase: "La voy a llamar" = “I’m going to call her.” It can also mean (2) to call/name someone: "Te voy a llamar Flannery" = “I’m going to call you Flannery.”
target_language_example: Voy a llamarte mañana por la tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used for near-future plans: ir a + infinitive (voy a) + llamar + a + person/organization being called. The personal “a” is required before a person (a mamá, a tu padre) and is also common with groups/services (a seguridad). You can swap “voy” for other forms: vas a llamar a…, va a llamar a…, vamos a llamar a….
target_language_example: Voy a llamar a mi mamá ahora.
native_language_example: I’m going to call my mom now.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **(yo) voy a + llevar**. **Llevar** often means to take something/someone with you (away from where you are now), or to carry/transport it. It can also be used more figuratively, like **llevar esto más lejos** (“take this further”) or **llevar esto hasta el final** (“see this through to the end”). Contrast: **traer** usually means “to bring (toward the speaker).”
target_language_example: Me voy a llevar el libro a casa.
native_language_example: I'm going to take the book home.

additional_notes: Literally the near-future form: "(yo) voy a" + infinitive. Often used as a threat ("te voy a matar" = "I’ll kill you") and can also be exaggerated/joking among friends, but it’s still very strong language. Add the person with "a": "Voy a matar a ese tipo"; with pronouns: "Te voy a matar" (I’m going to kill you).
target_language_example: ¡Si vuelves a mentirme, te voy a matar!
native_language_example: If you lie to me again, I’ll kill you!

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a** (I’m going to) + **necesitar** (to need). Common for stating a requirement or request, often polite but firm depending on tone. You can change the subject: **vas a necesitar** (you’ll need), **vamos a necesitar** (we’ll need).
target_language_example: Para mañana, voy a necesitar tu dirección.
native_language_example: For tomorrow, I’m going to need your address.

meaning: “I’m going to pass / I’m going to go by / I’m going to spend (time).”
additional_notes: "Voy a + infinitive" is the common near-future (“going to”). "Pasar" is very flexible: (1) to hand/pass something to someone: "Te voy a pasar el número"; (2) to pass by / go through: "Voy a pasar por debajo"; (3) to spend time: "Voy a pasar el fin de semana…"; (4) in set phrases like "pasar desapercibido" = to go unnoticed.
target_language_example: Te voy a pasar la sal.
native_language_example: I’m going to pass you the salt.

meaning: I’m going to ask (for) / I’m going to request.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re about to ask someone to do something (often followed by "que" + subjunctive: "Voy a pedir que se vaya") or to request something: "Voy a pedir refuerzos". "Le voy a pedir" is more formal/polite (asking of you), while "te voy a pedir" is to you (informal).
target_language_example: Voy a pedir una cita con el médico.
native_language_example: I’m going to request an appointment with the doctor.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a + pelar** (“I’m going to peel”). **Pelar** means “to peel” (also “to skin”), and **patatas** is the common word for “potatoes” in Spain (in many Latin American countries you’ll often hear **papas**).
target_language_example: No te preocupes, yo voy a pelar las patatas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m going to peel the potatoes.

meaning: "I'm going to put / place / set" (near future with poner).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure ir a + infinitive: (yo) voy a poner = “I’m going to put/set/apply.” The exact meaning depends on context: physical placement (Voy a poner las flores en agua.), starting/applying something (Le voy a poner una multa. = “I’m going to give you a ticket/fine.”), or common expressions like poner fin a… (“to put an end to…”). Object pronouns often go before voy: Te lo voy a poner… (“I’m going to make it/put it for you…”).
target_language_example: Voy a poner la mesa ahora.
native_language_example: I'm going to set the table now.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: *voy a preguntar* = I’m going to ask. Change **voy** depending on the subject: *vas a preguntar* (you), *va a preguntar* (he/she/you formal), *vamos a preguntar* (we), *van a preguntar* (they/you all). With pronouns, they usually go **before** the conjugated verb (*te/lo/le/les voy a preguntar* = I’m going to ask you/it/him-her/them), or they can attach to the infinitive (*voy a preguntarte*, *voy a preguntarlo*). *Le/les* often mark the person being asked; *lo* can refer to “it/that” (the thing being asked).
target_language_example: Voy a preguntarte mañana si puedes venir.
native_language_example: I’m going to ask you tomorrow if you can come.

meaning: "I’m going to stay" / "I’m going to keep (it)."
additional_notes: This is the near-future pattern **ir a + infinitive** (here, **voy a + quedar**). In everyday Spanish you’ll very often hear it as **me voy a quedar** (with *quedarse* = “to stay/remain”). With a direct object pronoun, **quedarse con algo** means “to keep something”: **Me lo voy a quedar** = “I’m going to keep it.” With a place word, it means “to stay”: **Me voy a quedar aquí** = “I’m going to stay here.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: me lo voy a quedar yo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’m going to keep it.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a** = “I’m going to” + **salir** = “go out/leave.” It can mean going out socially (**No voy a salir esta noche**), leaving a place (**Voy a salir ahora**), appearing somewhere (especially in media: **salir en televisión** = “be on TV”), or dating/going out with someone (**Voy a salir con ella** = “I’m going to go out with her”).
target_language_example: Voy a salir ahora, pero vuelvo en una hora.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave now, but I’ll be back in an hour.

additional_notes: Common near-future form: **ir (voy) + a + infinitive (ser)**. Used before adjectives/nouns to say what you will be like or become: *Voy a ser breve* (“I’ll be brief”), *Voy a ser tu esposa* (“I’m going to be your wife”). Often used to introduce honesty: *Te voy a ser sincero/franco* (“I’m going to be honest/frank [with you]”).
target_language_example: Voy a ser honesto: no entiendo la pregunta.
native_language_example: I’ll be honest: I don’t understand the question.

meaning: "I'm going to have" / "I'll have" (and with "que": "I'm going to have to").
additional_notes: Used with a noun to talk about something you will possess or experience soon: "Voy a tener dinero." Very commonly followed by "que" + infinitive to express obligation/necessity: "Voy a tener que irme" = "I'm going to have to leave."
target_language_example: Mañana voy a tener que madrugar para ir al trabajo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to have to wake up early to go to work.

meaning: "I'm going to have to" (I will need to; I’ll be forced to).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to have to do something, often because of a situation or obligation. It’s the near-future form of "tener que" (to have to): "voy a" + "tener que" + infinitive. You can change the subject: "vas a tener que" (you’re going to have to), "va a tener que" (he/she is going to have to), etc.
target_language_example: Lo siento, voy a tener que cancelar la cita.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to have to cancel the appointment.

meaning: “I’m going to take / have” (often: drink, take a seat/flight, get some air).
additional_notes: “Voy a” is the near-future (“I’m going to…”). With “tomar,” it’s very flexible: you can “tomar” food/drinks (take/have), “tomar” un café (have a coffee), “tomar” aire fresco (get some fresh air), “tomar” un vuelo (take a flight), “tomar” asiento (take a seat). In some contexts it’s figurative: “Me lo voy a tomar como venga” = “I’ll take it as it comes.”
target_language_example: Voy a tomar un café antes de salir.
native_language_example: I’m going to have a coffee before leaving.

meaning: "I'm going to see/watch"; also "I'll see" (I'll check/find out).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a + ver**. **Ver** can mean **to watch** (TV, a movie), **to see/visit** a person (**ver a + person**), or **to check/figure out** (**voy a ver qué es** = “I’ll see what it is”). By itself (**Voy a ver, señor.**) it often means “I’ll see / Let me check.”
target_language_example: No estoy seguro, pero voy a ver si puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: I'm not sure, but I'll see if I can help you.

meaning: "I’m going to go back to..." / "I’m going to return to..." or "I’m going to do ... again."
additional_notes: Uses ir a + infinitive (voy a = “I’m going to”) plus volver a. With a place/noun: volver a + lugar = “go back/return to a place” (Voy a volver a la universidad). With an infinitive: volver a + infinitive = “do something again” (Nunca voy a volver a tomar = “I’m never going to drink again”).
target_language_example: Voy a volver a intentarlo mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to try again tomorrow.

meaning: “I’m going to go back home” / “I’m going to return home.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future structure **ir a + infinitive**: **voy a** (I’m going to) + **volver** (to return/go back) + **a casa** (home). Often said to announce a decision or plan to head home; you can add details like **con...** (“with...”) to say what you’ll return with.
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; voy a volver a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going to go back home.

meaning: "I’m going to" (used to talk about a future action).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: **voy a + infinitive** (e.g., *voy a comer*, *voy a estudiar*). It’s the **yo** (I) form of **ir a** to express the near future or an intention. Other common forms: *vas a* (you), *va a* (he/she), *vamos a* (we), *van a* (they).
target_language_example: Voy a llamarte mañana.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir (to go): yo voy = “I go.” With a + casa it usually means “go home” (English drops “to”). Often used for routines or near-future plans, depending on context. You’ll also hear "me voy a casa" to emphasize leaving: “I’m heading home / I’m going home now.”
target_language_example: Ya es tarde; voy a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late; I’m going home.

meaning: "I go to the" (to a feminine singular place).
additional_notes: Used to say you go to a place: ir + a + la + [place]. It agrees with feminine singular nouns (la farmacia, la cafetería, la peluquería). For masculine singular places, use "voy al" (a + el): "voy al supermercado".
target_language_example: Hoy voy a la biblioteca a estudiar.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the library to study.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going/attending school in general. Structure: ir (to go) + a + place. It changes with the subject (voy = I go; vas = you go; va = he/she goes) and with tense (voy = I go / I’m going).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a la escuela temprano.
native_language_example: Today I go to school early.

additional_notes: Uses the verb ir (“to go”) in the present tense: voy (“I go”). a + la = al, but it doesn’t contract here because la is feminine, so you say a la iglesia. Often used for routines/habits (e.g., Los domingos…).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a la iglesia con mi familia.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to church with my family.

additional_notes: “Voy” is the present tense of “ir” (to go) for “yo” (I). “a la” = “to the” (a + la), and “playa” = “beach.” You can swap in other places: “Voy al trabajo” (I go to work), “Voy al parque” (I go to the park).
target_language_example: Hoy voy a la playa con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the beach with my friends.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **ir a por** (very common in Spain): **voy a por + noun/pronoun** means you’re going somewhere in order to bring something/someone back. It can be used for things (*Voy a por agua*) or people (*Voy a por él* = I’m going to get him / go after him, depending on context). Not the same as **voy a + infinitive** (*voy a comprar…* = I’m going to buy…).
target_language_example: Espera aquí; voy a por las llaves.
native_language_example: Wait here; I’m going to get the keys.

meaning: "I go to the" (to a masculine singular place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ir (to go): yo voy = “I go”. "Al" is a contraction of "a" + "el" and is used before masculine singular nouns (voy al trabajo, voy al centro). With feminine singular nouns, you use "a la" (voy a la playa).
target_language_example: Hoy voy al supermercado después del trabajo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the supermarket after work.

meaning: "I go to the movies" / "I'm going to the movie theater."
additional_notes: From ir (to go): yo voy = "I go" / "I’m going." The meaning depends on context: it can describe a habit (often/usually) or a near-future plan (especially with time words like ahora, hoy, esta noche). Al = a + el, and cine refers to the movie theater (or going to see a movie).
target_language_example: Hoy voy al cine con mis amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the movies with my friends.

meaning: 'I go to work by…' / 'I go to work in… (wearing)'
additional_notes: Use this pattern with **en + transportation** to say how you commute: *en tren, en autobús/bus, en bicicleta, en colectivo* (country-dependent). It can also be used with **en + clothing** to say what you’re wearing when you go to work: *en vaqueros* = “in jeans.”
target_language_example: Hoy voy al trabajo en metro.
native_language_example: Today I go to work by subway.

meaning: “I’m going there” / “I’m on my way (over there).”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re heading to a place away from the speaker/listener (“allá” = “over there”). Very common as a reassurance or response to a request: “Tranquilo, voy para allá.” You can add emphasis with “ahora/ahora mismo” (right now) or “ya” (already/coming now): “Ya voy para allá.”
target_language_example: Espérame en la entrada; ya voy para allá.
native_language_example: Wait for me at the entrance; I’m on my way there now.

additional_notes: Used almost always in the phrase “en voz alta” (“out loud”). Common with verbs like pensar (to think), leer (to read), decir (to say), or hablar (to speak): “pensar/leer/decir en voz alta.”
target_language_example: ¿Puedes leerlo en voz alta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you read it out loud, please?

meaning: “returned to” / “(have) done again” (used in the structure "haber vuelto a" or "volver a").
additional_notes: “Vuelto” is the past participle of “volver.” With “haber” it forms the present perfect: “he/has/hemos/han vuelto a…”. It can mean (1) returning to a place: “ha vuelto a EE. UU.” = “has returned to the U.S.”, or (2) doing something again: “he vuelto a perder” = “I’ve lost again.” Very common pattern: “volver a + infinitive” = “to ... again,” and in the negative “no he vuelto a + infinitive” often means “I haven’t ... again/since then.”
target_language_example: He vuelto a llamar, pero no contestan.
native_language_example: I called again, but they aren’t answering.

meaning: (that you/he/she) do something again; return to (doing something).
additional_notes: “Vuelva” is the usted (formal) subjunctive/command form of “volver”. With “a + infinitive” it often means doing an action again (repeat) or returning to a previous state (“vuelva a ser…”). Common after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (quiero que…, no dejes que…, es mejor que…) and also as a formal command: “Vuelva a + infinitive…”. For “you” informal (tú), use “vuelvas a”.
target_language_example: No quiero que vuelva a llegar tarde.
native_language_example: I don’t want him/her to be late again.

additional_notes: A formal/plural command (ustedes) using the verb "volver". It’s typically followed by a plural noun: "vuelvan a sus asientos" (your seats), "vuelvan a sus casas" (your homes), "vuelvan a sus dormitorios" (your dorm rooms). In Spain, you might also hear the informal plural version "volved a vuestros/vuestras".
target_language_example: Por favor, vuelvan a sus mesas y sigan trabajando.
native_language_example: Please go back to your tables and keep working.

additional_notes: From the verb "volver a" + infinitive, used to say someone does something again (repeat an action) or goes back to a place. "Vuelvas" is the present subjunctive "you" form, often triggered by expressions like "No..." (commands/requests) and "Quiero que..." (wanting someone to do something): "No vuelvas a decir eso" = "Don’t say that again"; "Quiero que vuelvas a casa" = "I want you to come back home."
target_language_example: No vuelvas a tocar eso.
native_language_example: Don’t touch that again.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (vuelve a + infinitivo) to tell someone to repeat an action or to resume doing something. It’s the tú (informal singular) command form of volver (to return). In other persons/tones you’ll see: vuelve a, vuelva a (formal), vuelvan a (you all), etc.
target_language_example: Vuelve a intentarlo, por favor.
native_language_example: Try again, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "volver" (to return) addressed to "tú". Often used as a request or command: "Por favor, vuelve a casa". With a time phrase it can mean "go back home" in the sense of returning: "Vuelve a casa mañana" (comes back home tomorrow). You can add "conmigo" = "with me".
target_language_example: Vuelve a casa antes de las diez, por favor.
native_language_example: Come back home before ten, please.

additional_notes: An imperative (command) using the verb volver (to return): vuelve = “(you) go back/return.” Used to tell someone to return to bed, often because it’s still early, they’re sick/tired, or you want them to come back to bed. You can soften it with por favor or make it affectionate with cariño/corazón.
target_language_example: Estás enfermo; vuelve a la cama y descansa.
native_language_example: You’re sick; go back to bed and rest.

meaning: "Go back to your..." (informal command to one person).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tú) to return to their place/location. It’s the tú imperative of volver (vuelve) + a + tu + a noun: vuelve a tu asiento/cama/cuarto/sitio. If the noun is feminine, use "tu" as well (e.g., "vuelve a tu habitación"). For a more formal command to one person, use "vuelva a su...".
target_language_example: Por favor, vuelve a tu asiento.
native_language_example: Please, go back to your seat.

additional_notes: Used when listing people and you are included as an object of the verb. With people, Spanish often uses the personal “a” (e.g., invitar/llamar/ver **a** alguien), and it’s common to repeat **a** before each person: “a Tom **y a mí**”. You may also hear it by itself as a response meaning “What about me?” (¿Y a mí?).
target_language_example: Nos dieron un regalo a Marta y a mí.
native_language_example: They gave Marta and me a gift.

additional_notes: Used to move the action forward or transition to the next point. Very common at the start of a sentence, especially in questions like “¿Y ahora qué…?” meaning “So what now?”
target_language_example: ¿Y ahora qué hacemos?
native_language_example: So what do we do now?

meaning: and that’s how; and that’s the way (it is/was/will be).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or summary, or to explain the result of a story/process: “and that’s how X happened / is done.” It often leads into a verb phrase (e.g., "y así es como se hace" = “and that’s how it’s done”) or is followed by a clause about how things are/should be/will be.
target_language_example: Te lo muestro paso a paso, y así es como se prepara esta salsa.
native_language_example: I’ll show you step by step, and that’s how this sauce is made.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what you might expect with what actually happens. It links to the previous idea and means the second clause is true anyway: "..., y aun así + result." Often followed by a verb phrase: "y aun así me quemé", "y aun así lo intentaste". Also written "y aun así" (aun = even), not to be confused with "aún" (= still/yet in time).
target_language_example: Estaba cansado y aun así salí a correr.
native_language_example: I was tired, and even so I went out for a run.

additional_notes: Used to connect two actions in sequence. The verb is in the preterite (cerró = “closed”), and the subject is often omitted because it’s understood from context (he/she/you formal). You can add details like detrás de él/ella (“behind him/her”).
target_language_example: Entré a casa y cerré la puerta.
native_language_example: I came into the house and closed the door.

additional_notes: Used to link actions in a story or sequence. It normally comes right before an infinitive verb (e.g., "y comenzó a llorar" = "and she began to cry"). "Comenzó" is the past tense (pretérito) for "he/she began."
target_language_example: Escuchó la noticia y comenzó a temblar.
native_language_example: He heard the news and began to tremble.

additional_notes: Used to add your opinion or a guess as you continue speaking. Very common in conversation. Often followed by a verb clause (e.g., “y creo que puede… / y creo que él…”). You can also hear it without “y” (“creo que…”) when starting a sentence.
target_language_example: Y creo que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: And I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when talking about two people or things: you mention the first with "uno/una..." and then refer to the second with "y el otro / y la otra". It agrees in gender: "el otro" (masc.) / "la otra" (fem.).
target_language_example: Tengo dos hermanos: uno vive en Madrid y el otro en Valencia.
native_language_example: I have two brothers: one lives in Madrid and the other in Valencia.

meaning: “and the other is …” (when comparing two things/people).
additional_notes: Used after describing the first of two items with “uno es …” to introduce the second: “uno es X y el otro es Y.” It agrees in gender/number: “y la otra es …” (feminine), “y los otros son … / y las otras son …” (plural). Often used with “dos” (two) to contrast or list differences.
target_language_example: Tengo dos opciones: una es más barata y la otra es más rápida.
native_language_example: I have two options: one is cheaper and the other is faster.

additional_notes: Used to link two actions in sequence: someone does one thing and then begins another. After "empezó a" you use an infinitive (e.g., "empezó a escribir", "empezó a correr"). You can change the subject/tense: "y empecé a…" (I started to), "y empezaron a…" (they started to).
target_language_example: Abrió la ventana y empezó a llover.
native_language_example: He/She opened the window and it started to rain.

meaning: 'and that is…' / 'and that's…' (to explain or emphasize what something is).
additional_notes: Used to add a conclusion, clarification, or emphasis after what was just said. It’s often followed by a noun/adjective ("Y eso es importante" = "And that’s important") or by "lo que + verb" to mean "and that’s what…" ("Y eso es lo que haré" = "And that’s what I’ll do"). In speech, you’ll also hear the contracted form "y eso es" → "y eso’s" is not standard; instead Spanish keeps it as "y eso es" / "y eso es lo que…".
target_language_example: No tengo mucho tiempo, y eso es todo lo que puedo decir.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time, and that’s all I can say.

meaning: "and that's what…" (used to emphasize what follows).
additional_notes: Used to point back to what was just said and then highlight the conclusion, result, or important point: “And that’s what matters / happened / we have to do.” Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., importa, pasó, tenemos que hacer) or a relative clause.
target_language_example: Y eso es lo que necesitamos ahora.
native_language_example: And that's what we need now.

y eso es todo lo que

target_language_multi_word_term: y eso es todo lo que
additional_notes: Used to say that nothing else matters/exists beyond what follows. Very common with verbs like importa (matters), recuerdo (I remember), tengo/voy a decir (I have/am going to say). You can also shorten it to “y eso es todo” (“and that’s all”).
target_language_example: Y eso es todo lo que necesito por ahora.
native_language_example: And that’s all I need for now.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do the same thing as someone else does, or to follow instructions: “y haz lo que yo hago / quieres / te diga / dice.” It’s the imperative of hacer (haz = “do/make”). Often followed by a person or instruction.
target_language_example: Mírame y haz lo que yo hago.
native_language_example: Watch me and do what I do.

meaning: "and it" / "and her" (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Usually, **la** here is a **direct object pronoun** meaning “it” or “her,” referring back to something feminine already mentioned: *la música → y la escucho* (“music → and I listen to it”). It’s very common after another verb to avoid repeating the noun: *se sacó la chaqueta y la colgó* (“he took off the jacket and hung it”). Be careful: **y la** can also literally mean **“and the”** when **la** is the feminine article (*y la casa* = “and the house”), but in your examples it’s the pronoun.
target_language_example: Compré una camisa y la usé ayer.
native_language_example: I bought a shirt and wore it yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to add “the children” to a group (often family members) already mentioned: “con tu mamá y los niños” = “with your mom and the children.” It uses the plural masculine article "los," which is also the default for mixed-gender groups.
target_language_example: Vamos al parque con mi hermana y los niños.
native_language_example: We’re going to the park with my sister and the children.

meaning: and then; afterwards; what next? (as a question).
additional_notes: Used to show the next step in a sequence: *primero... y luego...* (“first... and then...”). At the start of a sentence it can mean “and then…” continuing a story. As a question (*¿Y luego?* / *¿Y luego qué?*) it means “And then?” / “What happened next?” or “So what?” depending on tone.
target_language_example: Terminé el trabajo y luego me fui a casa.
native_language_example: I finished the work and then I went home.

additional_notes: Used after *y* (“and”) to link another action involving **me**. The *me* is a clitic pronoun that comes before the verb: it can be **reflexive** (*me caí* = “I fell”, *me golpeé* = “I hit myself”), or an **indirect/direct object** depending on the verb. Often translates naturally as “and I…” or “and then I…”, not literally as “and me…”.
target_language_example: Llegué tarde y me disculpé con el profesor.
native_language_example: I arrived late and (then) I apologized to the teacher.

additional_notes: Used after a number to add “half.” Most commonly used with time to mean “half past” the hour (e.g., a las siete y media = 7:30). It can also be used with durations or quantities: dos horas y media = 2.5 hours. Feminine because it refers to an implied feminine noun like “hora” (la media hora).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las cuatro y media.
native_language_example: See you at 4:30.

additional_notes: Used after a number to add “half.” Most commonly used with time to mean “half past” the hour (e.g., a las siete y media = 7:30). It can also be used with durations or quantities: dos horas y media = 2.5 hours. Feminine because it refers to an implied feminine noun like “hora” (la media hora).
target_language_example: Nos vemos a las cuatro y media.
native_language_example: See you at 4:30.

additional_notes: Used to add a stronger negative point after something else. It often comes before a verb (y ni siquiera lo sabes) or before a noun/amount (y ni siquiera tenemos dinero). It emphasizes that something expected didn’t happen ("not even").
target_language_example: Le escribí tres veces y ni siquiera me respondió.
native_language_example: I texted him three times and he didn’t even reply.

additional_notes: Used to add a stronger negative point after something else. It often comes before a verb (y ni siquiera lo sabes) or before a noun/amount (y ni siquiera tenemos dinero). It emphasizes that something expected didn’t happen ("not even").
target_language_example: Le escribí tres veces y ni siquiera me respondió.
native_language_example: I texted him three times and he didn’t even reply.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a phrase or clause to continue an idea while adding a negation. Often follows something already mentioned, like English “and I/they don’t…” or “and not…”.
target_language_example: Quería llamarte, y no tenía tu número.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you, and I didn’t have your number.

meaning: "and (he/she/it) doesn’t" / "and (he/she/it) isn’t" (referring back to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **y no lo + verb**. **Lo** is an object pronoun meaning “it/so/that,” and it refers to a previous idea or description. Examples: **y no lo parece** (“and he/she doesn’t seem like it”), **y no lo han pillado** (“and they haven’t caught him yet”), **y no lo logro** (“and I can’t do it”), **y no lo es** (“and he/she/it isn’t”). Often you’ll hear it with **ser** or **parecer** to avoid repeating the same adjective/noun.
target_language_example: Dice que es fácil, y no lo es.
native_language_example: He says it’s easy, and it isn’t.

meaning: “and I don’t / didn’t …” (with “me” before the verb).
additional_notes: Used to add a negative second idea: y = “and”, no = “not”, me = “me” placed before the verb (e.g., y no me escuchas = “and you don’t listen to me”; y no me quedaban fuerzas = “and I had no strength left”; y no me uní = “and I didn’t join”; y no me preocupaba = “and it didn’t worry me”). The subject depends on the verb ending and context.
target_language_example: Quería ayudarte, y no me llamaste.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, and you didn’t call me.

meaning: “and don’t…” / “and you won’t…” (introduces a negative clause with “te”).
additional_notes:
Used to add another point starting with “y” (“and”), then a negation (“no”), plus the object/reflexive pronoun “te” (roughly “you”). It often appears in:
- Negative commands: “Y no te duermas.” = “And don’t fall asleep.”
- Negative future/conditional statements: “Y no te irás…” = “And you won’t leave…”
The exact translation depends on the verb that follows (e.g., irte = “leave”, importarte = “matter to you”).
target_language_example: Y no te preocupes, yo me encargo.
native_language_example: And don’t worry, I’ll take care of it.

meaning: “and we / and us” (linking to an action that involves “nos”).
additional_notes: “Y” means “and” and connects ideas. “Nos” is the pronoun for “us” (object) and is also used as a reflexive pronoun for “we” (like “we … ourselves/each other”), so it often appears right before a verb: “y nos fuimos” (and we left), “y nos presentamos” (and we introduced ourselves), “y nos tomamos una copa” (and we had a drink). The exact English translation depends on the verb (e.g., “nos encontramos” = “we met/found each other”).
target_language_example: Terminamos el trabajo y nos fuimos a casa.
native_language_example: We finished the work and went home.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize repetition, often as part of patterns like “otra vez y otra vez” (“again and again”) or “una y otra vez” (“over and over”). As a standalone sentence (“Y otra vez.”), it means “And again.”
target_language_example: Lo intentó, y otra vez no funcionó.
native_language_example: He tried, and again it didn’t work.

meaning: "and" + "se" (used to link actions, often with reflexive, impersonal, or passive "se").
additional_notes: "Y" means "and". "Se" is very common in Spanish and can mark: (1) reflexive actions ("he left" = "se fue"), (2) accidental/unintentional situations ("se me olvidó" = "I forgot"), (3) impersonal/general statements ("here you eat well" = "aquí se come bien"), or (4) passive-like meaning ("it is said" = "se dice"). "Y se" simply connects two clauses where the second one uses "se".
target_language_example: Terminamos la clase y se fueron todos a casa.
native_language_example: We finished class and everyone went home.

additional_notes: “Y” means “and.” “Se fue” is the past tense (preterite) of “irse” = “to leave/go away.” It often follows another action to show what happened next (“He smiled and left”). It can also be followed by a destination or activity: “se fue a casa” (went home), “se fue arriba” (went upstairs), “se fue a dormir” (went to sleep), “se fue conduciendo” (drove off).
target_language_example: Terminó su café y se fue.
native_language_example: He finished his coffee and left.

meaning: “and … to him/her/them” (with object pronouns), e.g. “and gave it to him/her/them” / “and took it away from him/her/them.”
additional_notes: "y" = “and.” "se lo" is a common pronoun combination that usually means “(to) him/her/them + it/him” depending on context. Important rule: "se" often replaces "le/les" before "lo/la/los/las" (you say "se lo di" not *"le lo di"*). The exact English translation depends on the verb: "se lo llevó" = “took him/it away,” "se lo entregó" = “handed it to him/her,” "se lo dio" = “gave it to him/her.”
target_language_example: Encontré tu libro y se lo devolví a Ana.
native_language_example: I found your book and I gave it back to Ana.

additional_notes: This is the past tense (3rd person singular) of the reflexive verb "ponerse" ("se puso"), often linked with "y" ("and then"). Common uses: (1) "ponerse" + adjective/state = "to become/get" ("se puso enfermo" = he got sick; "se puso oscuro" = it got dark; "se puso sólida" = it became solid). (2) "ponerse" + clothing = "to put on" ("se puso los zapatos" = she put on the shoes). You’ll also see intensifiers like "como loco" ("like crazy").
target_language_example: Oyó un ruido extraño y se puso nervioso.
native_language_example: He heard a strange noise and got nervous.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or surprising fact that goes against what was just said or what you would expect. Often placed at the start of a sentence/clause, and it’s common to add a comma after it: “Y sin embargo, …”. Similar in meaning to “pero / sin embargo” but with an added “and” linking it to the previous idea.
target_language_example: Dijo que no iba a venir, y sin embargo llegó temprano.
native_language_example: He said he wasn’t going to come, and yet he arrived early.

additional_notes: Used after a person (or possessive like mi/tu/su) to add that person’s family as well. The pronoun in “su” depends on context (his/her/your formal/their). Often appears as “X y su familia” = “X and his/her family.”
target_language_example: Carlos y su familia viven cerca de aquí.
native_language_example: Carlos and his family live near here.

additional_notes: Used after a person/character/group to add "and their friends" (often in titles, headings, invitations, or descriptions). "Sus" is a possessive meaning "his," "her," "their," or formal "your" (usted/ustedes); context tells you which one.
target_language_example: Mañana vienen Carlos y sus amigos a cenar.
native_language_example: Tomorrow Carlos and his friends are coming over for dinner.

additional_notes: “Y” links two actions/ideas (“and”). “Te” is the unstressed object pronoun for “you” (informal singular, tú) and usually goes before a conjugated verb: “y te lo digo” = “and I tell you.” It can also appear with reflexive verbs: “y te dejaste llevar” = “and you let yourself go / got carried away.”
target_language_example: Ven mañana y te ayudo con la tarea.
native_language_example: Come tomorrow and I’ll help you with the homework.

meaning: “and I’ll tell you …” / “and I’m going to tell you …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the speaker will say next, often after a condition or request: “Dime X y te diré Y” (“Tell me X and I’ll tell you Y”). It can also start a new point: “Y te diré algo más/otra cosa/una cosa …” (“And I’ll tell you something else/another thing/one thing …”). The verb is future tense of decir: “diré” = “I will say/tell.”
target_language_example: Dime dónde estás y te diré cómo llegar.
native_language_example: Tell me where you are and I’ll tell you how to get there.

additional_notes: Used to add a broad, inclusive idea after something already mentioned. Often introduces a relative clause (y todo lo que + verb), meaning “and anything/everything that (goes with it),” similar to “and everything else” or “and all that has to do with it.” Can also be followed by a subjunctive like in polite offers: “y todo lo que usted quiera” (“and anything/everything you want”).
target_language_example: Trae tus documentos y todo lo que necesites para el viaje.
native_language_example: Bring your documents and everything you need for the trip.

additional_notes: Used to include the other person in a statement ("me and you"), to contrast two people’s actions ("I do X, and you do Y"), or to shift focus to the other person (often like "and you?" or "as for you..."). In speech it can sound neutral or confrontational depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Yo ya terminé; ¿y tú?
native_language_example: I already finished; what about you?

meaning: "and you are..." / "and you’re..." (introducing what someone is, often for emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to add or highlight information about the person you’re speaking to (“tú”). It often comes after talking about someone else (“because he is…, and you are…”) or to point the finger/spotlight at someone (“And you’re next.”). In questions it can sound challenging or confirming: “Y tú eres un héroe, ¿no?”
target_language_example: Él es el jefe, y tú eres su asistente.
native_language_example: He is the boss, and you’re his assistant.

additional_notes: Used to include the listener in what was just said about someone else. It often adds emphasis (sometimes like “you too, you know”). The pronoun is stressed: tú (not tu). You’ll also hear variations like “tú también” (without y) and “y usted también” (formal).
target_language_example: Yo ya terminé, y tú también puedes terminar hoy.
native_language_example: I already finished, and you can finish today too.

additional_notes: Used to show something is finished or decided and there’s nothing more to add. Often closes a conversation or expresses firmness: “I want it, and that’s it.” Similar to “y punto.” It’s common in everyday speech and can sound blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: No voy a discutir más: lo hacemos así y ya está.
native_language_example: I’m not going to argue anymore: we’ll do it this way and that’s it.

additional_notes: Used when you mention yourself together with someone else: “ella y yo” (she and I), “usted y yo” (you and I). In Spanish, it’s common to put the other person first ("Tom y yo..."). After the conjunction "y" (and), the subject pronoun stays "yo" (not *mí*). Spelling note: "y" becomes "e" before words starting with the “i/hi” sound (e.g., "tú e Isabel"), but it stays "y" before "yo".
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo vivimos aquí.
native_language_example: My sister and I live here.

meaning: “and I are” (used with a plural verb like estamos = “we are”).
additional_notes: Used to say that another person + you ("X y yo") are doing/being something together. Even though “yo” is singular, the subject becomes plural (“we”), so you use the plural verb form: “estamos” (not “estoy”). Word order is typically “Tom y yo…”, not “Yo y Tom…”.
target_language_example: Mis amigos y yo estamos listos.
native_language_example: My friends and I are ready.

meaning: “and I don’t / didn’t” or “and not me.”
additional_notes: Used to contrast yourself with someone else. Often the verb is understood from context (ellipsis): *Ellos no preguntan y yo no (pregunto)*. The exact meaning depends on the tense of the omitted verb: *y yo no pensé* = “and I didn’t think,” *y yo no reprobé* = “and I didn’t fail.”
target_language_example: A ellos les gusta el café, y yo no.
native_language_example: They like coffee, and I don’t.

meaning: “and I, we …” (used before a verb with **nos**: ourselves/each other).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression, but a common structure: **[Name/person] y yo + nos + verb**. It’s used with verbs that take **nos** (reflexive or reciprocal), meaning **we (to ourselves)** or **we (to each other)**. Examples: **María y yo nos vimos** = “María and I saw each other / met up.” **Tom y yo nos ayudamos** = “Tom and I helped each other.”
target_language_example: Mi hermano y yo nos conocemos desde niños.
native_language_example: My brother and I have known each other since we were kids.

meaning: “and I are …” (used to say that someone and you are something, using the verb *somos* = “we are”).
additional_notes: Used after another person/people to form a subject with *yo* (“I”): *Tom y yo somos…* = “Tom and I are…”. Because it’s two people (or more), Spanish uses the plural *somos* (“we are”), not *soy* (“I am”). You can also use *tú y yo somos…* (“you and I are…”).
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo somos de Texas.
native_language_example: My sister and I are from Texas.

additional_notes: Used to add information about yourself after someone/something else is mentioned (“X is…, and I am…”). Often gives emphasis or contrast in conversation. Follow with a noun, adjective, or role: “y yo soy el jefe” (and I’m the boss), “y yo soy Julieta” (and I’m Juliet).
target_language_example: Ella es la doctora, y yo soy el enfermero.
native_language_example: She’s the doctor, and I’m the nurse.

additional_notes: Used to say you share the same situation or characteristic someone just mentioned. It often comes after a statement: “Ella sabe…, y yo también.” You can also say it by itself as a short reply: “—Estoy cansado. —Y yo también.”
target_language_example: No tengo tiempo hoy, y yo también estoy ocupado.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today, and I’m busy too.

meaning: "and I" + "you" (te), used to start a clause like: “and I will … you”.
additional_notes: Used to add a second action or response, often in patterns like “(Tú) … y yo te …” (“You … and I’ll …”). Here, **y** = “and”, **yo** = “I” (often for emphasis/contrast), and **te** is the object pronoun for **tú** (“you”), meaning “you” as the person receiving the action (e.g., “I’ll help you,” “I’ll watch you,” “I envy you”). Word order is flexible in Spanish, so you may also see “y te …” without **yo** when the subject is obvious.
target_language_example: Tú me llamas y yo te respondo.
native_language_example: You call me, and I answer you.

meaning: "and I have" / "and we have" (when the subject is "someone + me").
additional_notes: Used after another subject to make a combined subject: “X y yo” = “X and I.” Because it’s plural (“X + I”), the verb is in the “we” form: tenemos (“we have”). Common with names (Tom y yo tenemos…) and also with formal “usted” (Usted y yo tenemos…).
target_language_example: Mi hermana y yo tenemos el mismo problema.
native_language_example: My sister and I have the same problem.

meaning: “and I are going to …” (we’re going to …).
additional_notes: Used after a person (or noun) to make a subject meaning “X and I.” Then **vamos a + infinitive** is the near-future: “we are going to (do something).” The verb is **vamos** (1st person plural) because the subject is “we.”
target_language_example: Carlos y yo vamos a cocinar esta noche.
native_language_example: Carlos and I are going to cook tonight.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something because it’s too much or has gone on too long. Often followed by "con" or "de" + something: "Ya basta con eso" / "Ya basta de eso". Tone can be firm or annoyed; adding "por favor" softens it a bit.
target_language_example: Ya basta, déjame en paz.
native_language_example: Enough already—leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very close to happening or being finished. "Ya" adds a sense of imminence/"now" (we’re at the stage where it’s almost done): "Ya casi está listo" = "It’s almost ready." It often goes before a verb phrase (ya casi + verb), and can also appear with negatives like "ya casi ni..." to mean "I can barely... anymore" or "I almost don’t... anymore," depending on context.
target_language_example: Ya casi terminamos, solo falta un detalle.
native_language_example: We’re almost done; there’s just one detail left.

additional_notes:
Used to say you were beginning to feel worried (often because someone was late, not answering, etc.).

Structure: **ya** (already/by now) + **empezar a** + infinitive → **empezaba a preocuparme** (“I was starting to worry”), and **preocuparse por + someone/something** (“to worry about”).

You can change the person you’re worried about: **por ti** (you, informal), **por usted** (you, formal), **por ustedes** (you all), **por vosotros/vosotras** (you all, Spain).
target_language_example: Ya empezaba a preocuparme por ti porque no contestabas.
native_language_example: I was starting to worry about you because you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Used to say something was expected or overdue (often with a hint of impatience or relief). It’s followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive: ya era hora de que + vinieras / llegaran / alguien lo hiciera. You can also hear the present version: ya es hora de que...
target_language_example: ¡Ya era hora de que me llamaras!
native_language_example: It was about time you called me!

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen now (often implying it’s a little late or overdue). Usually followed by an infinitive (ya es hora de volver, de comprar…) or by “que” + subjunctive (ya es hora de que te vayas).
target_language_example: Ya es hora de empezar la reunión.
native_language_example: It’s time to start the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you want someone to stop (talking, doing something, giving you more, etc.). Often said as a firm boundary or to signal you’ve had enough. You’ll also hear the shortened version “¡Ya basta!”.
target_language_example: Ya es suficiente, por favor. No quiero más.
native_language_example: That’s enough, please. I don’t want any more.

additional_notes: Common with estar + adjective/participle to say a state has already begun or is already true: "Ya está levantado" (He’s already up), "Ya está todo preparado" (Everything is already prepared). In other contexts, "ya" can also mean "now" or "anymore" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: No te preocupes: ya está todo listo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is already ready.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **ha** (from **haber**) to form the **present perfect**: **ya ha + past participle** (e.g., *ya ha comido*). **Ya** usually goes before **ha** to emphasize that something has already happened. The subject can come before or after (*Mary ya ha… / Ya ha…*).
target_language_example: Ya ha terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: He/She has already finished the homework.

meaning: “it has already passed” / “it’s already happened” (or “it’s over already”).
additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ha pasado) with ya (“already”). Common for saying something is finished or in the past: Lo peor ya ha pasado (“The worst is over”); Ya ha pasado una hora (“An hour has already passed”); Ya ha pasado antes (“It’s happened before”). The subject can be an event (todo, lo peor) or a period of time (una hora).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, ya ha pasado el problema.
native_language_example: Relax, the problem is already over.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): **ya había + participle** (e.g., *ya había llegado* = “had already arrived”). It says something happened before another moment in the past.
target_language_example: Cuando llegué, él ya había terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already finished the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say that something had already happened before another action in the past. Very common with time clauses like “cuando llegué…” (“when I arrived…”). Often implies you were too late (the person/train/bus was gone).
target_language_example: Cuando llamé, ella ya había salido de casa.
native_language_example: When I called, she had already left the house.

meaning: "I've already" / "I already have" (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect: ya + he + past participle (bebido, enviado, estado, llegado, pospuesto) to say you have already done something. Common in statements like "Ya he llegado" (I’ve already arrived). You can also hear "Ya he..." as a short, complete answer meaning "I already have."
target_language_example: Ya he terminado la tarea.
native_language_example: I've already finished the homework.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say something is already done or already known. **Ya** = “already,” and **lo** is a direct-object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him,” in some contexts). **Lo** refers to something previously mentioned or understood from context: *Ya lo arreglé* = “I already fixed it.”
target_language_example: No te preocupes: ya lo hice.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I already did it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone already knows a fact or piece of information. **Ya** = “already,” **lo** refers to “it/that” (the thing being talked about), and **sabe** is from *saber* (“to know” facts). Often used as a complete sentence: *Ya lo sabe.* Can also be used with **usted** for polite “you”: *Usted ya lo sabe.*
target_language_example: No hace falta explicarlo otra vez; ya lo sabe.
native_language_example: There’s no need to explain it again; he/she/you (formal) already knows it.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something they’re expected to know, or to emphasize that the information isn’t new. "Ya" = already; "lo" refers to the thing being known ("it"); "sabes" is (tú) "you know." Often comes at the end of a sentence for emphasis, and can be followed by a tag like "¿verdad?" (right?).
target_language_example: No te preocupes; ya lo sabes, siempre estoy aquí para ayudarte.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; you already know it—I’m always here to help you.

additional_notes: Common reply when someone tells you information you already know. "Ya" = already; "lo" refers to "it/that" (the thing you know); "sé" = "I know." Often used alone as a short answer, sometimes with an impatient or dismissive tone depending on context (like "Yeah, I know").
target_language_example: Tranquilo, ya lo sé.
native_language_example: Relax, I already know.

additional_notes: Used before a verb with the pronoun **me** (me/myself). **Ya** often adds a sense of immediacy (“now, right away”) or completion (“already”), and **me** is the object/reflexive pronoun placed before the conjugated verb: **ya me voy** (I’m leaving now), **ya me encargo** (I’ll take care of it now). The exact meaning depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Ya me voy a casa.
native_language_example: I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Used with **ser** to say someone has stopped being something (age/status/identity/quality): **ya no eres + noun/adjective** (e.g., *ya no eres un niño*, *ya no eres joven*). Often contrasted with **ya eres** (“now you are/already you are”): *Ya no eres una niña, ya eres una jovencita.*
target_language_example: Ya no eres estudiante; ahora eres maestro.
native_language_example: You’re not a student anymore; now you’re a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say that something that used to be true is not true now. It’s the present tense of "ya no ser" (no longer to be). You can add a noun/adjective after it: "ya no es mi amigo" (he’s no longer my friend), "ya no es un niño" (he’s not a child anymore).
target_language_example: Este lugar ya no es lo que era.
native_language_example: This place is no longer what it used to be.

meaning: "there is/are no longer"; "there isn’t/aren’t any left".
additional_notes: Used to say something used to exist/be available, but now it doesn’t. Common with plural nouns (Ya no hay autobuses.) or uncountable nouns (Ya no hay arroz.), and with "más" to emphasize that nothing remains: "Ya no hay más." It can also express finality/impossibility in fixed expressions like "Ya no hay vuelta de hoja" (there’s no way around it / no turning back).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ya no hay entradas para hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no tickets left for today.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern **ya no + lo + verb** to say something is no longer true or you no longer do something to/with **it/him/that**. **Ya no** = “not anymore / no longer”, and **lo** refers to a masculine thing or an unknown/abstract idea (“it/that”), or sometimes “him” depending on context. The verb comes after **lo** (e.g., *Ya no lo sé* = “I don’t know it anymore”).
target_language_example: Ya no lo entiendo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand it anymore.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to say something is no longer true for you or doesn’t happen to you anymore. Pattern: "ya no me" + verb (often with an indirect object meaning: "it doesn't ... to me anymore"), e.g., "Ya no me funciona" = "It doesn't work for me anymore."
target_language_example: Ya no me interesa ese tema.
native_language_example: I'm not interested in that topic anymore.

meaning: “I can’t anymore” / “I can’t (do it) now (any longer).”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re no longer able to do something (because of time, rules, exhaustion, etc.) or that you’ve reached your limit emotionally/physically. Often followed by an infinitive (ya no puedo escribir) or used alone when the action is understood (Ya no puedo.).
target_language_example: Lo siento, ya no puedo ayudarte hoy.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t help you anymore today.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of shared knowledge or something that’s obvious, or as a filler like English “you know.” Often comes at the end of a sentence ("Es Italia, ya sabe") and can also introduce something assumed ("Ya sabe lo que tiene que hacer"). It can be formal with "usted" ("ya sabe") or informal with "tú" ("ya sabes").
target_language_example: Es tarde, ya sabe; mañana lo hablamos.
native_language_example: It’s late, you know; we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

meaning: "you know" (used to add emphasis, soften a statement, or introduce an example).
additional_notes: Very common conversational filler. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence to signal shared context or that the listener understands what you mean. Often followed by more detail ("ya sabes, ...").
target_language_example: Ya sabes, no es tan fácil como parece.
native_language_example: You know, it’s not as easy as it seems.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker assumes is already known or understood (shared context). Very common in conversation and can sound like: “you know how it is…”, “you know what I’m like…”, or “you know how this will end…”. Often followed by a clause with ser (cómo soy/es/son) to make a general statement.
target_language_example: Ya sabes cómo es esto: siempre se complica al final.
native_language_example: You know how this is: it always gets complicated at the end.

meaning: "you know how it is" (you understand what it’s like).
additional_notes: Used to appeal to shared experience or understanding, often when something is hard to explain or is just “the way things/people are.” It’s commonly followed by a person or thing: ya sabes cómo es ella/él/la gente/esto/eso. Tone is casual, conversational.
target_language_example: No me contestó en todo el día, pero ya sabes cómo es él.
native_language_example: He didn’t reply to me all day, but you know how he is.

meaning: “you know how they are” / “you know what they’re like.”
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person or a type of situation as predictable or typical (often with a tone of resignation or mild criticism). You can change the subject: “ya sabes cómo es” (he/she/it is), “ya sabes cómo son ellos/ellas,” “ya sabes cómo son las cosas.”
target_language_example: Ya sabes cómo son mis padres: siempre llegan temprano.
native_language_example: You know what my parents are like: they always arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something you assume they already know, or to introduce information as if it’s obvious/shared. Often said conversationally as a lead-in before the main point; the verb after "que" is usually in the indicative (facts, known information).
target_language_example: Ya sabes que mañana no trabajo, así que puedo ayudarte.
native_language_example: You know I’m not working tomorrow, so I can help you.

additional_notes: Used when something has already happened or is now possible. The "se" is usually a pronoun that belongs to the verb (often a reflexive or pronominal verb like "irse" = to leave/go away). Examples: "ya se fueron" = they already left; "ya se pueden ir" = you can leave now.
target_language_example: Ya se acabó la clase.
native_language_example: Class is already over.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "irse" (to leave/go away). "Ya" emphasizes that the departure has already happened—often implying you missed it or it happened sooner than expected. You can replace the implied subject: "Ya me fui" (I already left), "Ya nos fuimos" (we already left).
target_language_example: Lo siento, el taxi ya se fue.
native_language_example: Sorry, the taxi already left.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect of "irse" (to leave/go away) to say someone/something is gone already. Often followed by a destination with "a" (e.g., "ya se ha ido a casa" = has already gone home). In everyday Spanish you may also hear "ya se fue" (simple past) with a very similar meaning, especially in Latin America.
target_language_example: ¿El último autobús ya se ha ido?
native_language_example: Has the last bus already left?

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect (pluscuamperfecto): "había" + past participle ("ido") to say someone left before another past moment. "Ya" emphasizes that it happened already. "Irse" means “to leave” (literally “to go away”), so you’ll often see it with a reflexive pronoun: me/te/se/nos/os/se.
target_language_example: Cuando la llamé, ella ya se había ido del trabajo.
native_language_example: When I called her, she had already left work.

additional_notes: Uses irse (“to leave/go away”) in the present perfect: se han ido = “they have left.” Ya adds “already.” The subject is often implied by context (they), but it can refer to any plural group (los niños, ellos/ellas, etc.). Often followed by a destination with a (a la escuela, a casa).
target_language_example: No los busques: ya se han ido.
native_language_example: Don’t look for them—they’ve already left.

additional_notes: Often used to show you’ve realized or remembered something (“Oh, I know!”). Also used to say you already have the information or are aware of something. Very common in conversation; can sound a bit blunt depending on tone (like “I know, I know”).
target_language_example: Tranquilo, ya sé cómo hacerlo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know how to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you already know/understand something, followed by a clause starting with “what” (lo que + verb). Often used to show certainty or that you’ve figured something out: “Ya sé lo que estás haciendo” = “I know what you’re doing.” You can also use it when you remember something: “Ya sé lo que vamos a hacer.”
target_language_example: Ya sé lo que quieres decir.
native_language_example: I already know what you mean.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to show that something has already happened to/with you (Ya te he dicho… = I’ve already told you…), that the speaker understands/hears you now (Ya te oí / Ya te pillo), or that something will happen soon/inevitably involving you (Ya te llamaré = I’ll call you soon; Ya te va a pagar = He’ll pay you—just wait). Word order: ya te + verb.
target_language_example: Ya te lo expliqué, pero te lo repito.
native_language_example: I already explained it to you, but I’ll repeat it.

meaning: "I already told you that..." (often: "I told you already...").
additional_notes: Used to remind someone you said this before; it can sound impatient or annoyed depending on tone. Follow it with a full clause: "ya te dije que + [statement]". The verb is in the past (dije = "I told"); you can also hear "ya te dije" without "que" when the rest is implied.
target_language_example: Ya te dije que mañana no puedo.
native_language_example: I already told you that I can’t tomorrow.

meaning: "(I’ll) ... it to you" with emphasis like "already / right now / soon".
additional_notes:
This is a common pronoun bundle used before a verb: ya (already/now/soon) + te (to you) + lo (it). The exact meaning depends on the verb and context: 
- Future: "Ya te lo contaré" = "I’ll tell you (about it) later/soon." 
- Present: "Ya te lo explico" = "I’ll explain it to you right now." 
- Past: "Ya te lo expliqué" = "I already explained it to you." 
It’s not usually a complete phrase by itself; it needs a verb after it.
target_language_example: Ya te lo mando por mensaje.
native_language_example: I’ll send it to you by message (right now / in a moment).

additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you have mentioned something before (often with impatience or emphasis). Refers to information already given: ya = already; te = to you; lo = it/that; dije = I said/told (preterite of decir). You can add details after it (e.g., “por teléfono”, “antes”), or use it alone as a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Ya te lo dije: salgo a las ocho.
native_language_example: I already told you: I’m leaving at eight.

additional_notes: Used to stress that you’ve said it before (often with impatience or emphasis). Breakdown: ya = already; te = to you; lo = it/that; he dicho = I have said/told. You can add how many times: "Ya te lo he dicho tres veces."
target_language_example: Ya te lo he dicho: no voy a ir.
native_language_example: I already told you: I'm not going to go.

additional_notes: Used to show you’ve just understood something or figured it out from what someone said or did. Often translates to “I see,” “I get it,” “Now I understand,” or “I see what you mean.” It can also be used to react to an explanation (“Ya veo; …”). In phrases like “Ya veo por dónde vas” or “Ya veo a dónde vas con esto,” it means “I see where you’re going with this.”
target_language_example: Ah, ya veo lo que quieres decir; tiene sentido.
native_language_example: Oh, I see what you mean; that makes sense.

additional_notes: Used as a quick reaction when something surprises you or you want an explanation. Often said alone (Ya-sho!) or as a question (Ya-sho?). It matches the use of «¿Y eso?» in everyday Spanish.
target_language_example: —Me duele la barriga. —¿Ya-sho? ¿Qué comiste?
native_language_example: —My stomach hurts. —How come? What did you eat?

meaning: "I believe in" / "I have faith in" / "I trust in."
additional_notes: Used with a person, thing, or idea you have faith in or trust. It can mean believing something exists (Yo creo en Dios = I believe in God) or trusting someone/something (Yo creo en ti = I believe in you). For opinions, Spanish often uses "yo creo que..." (I think that...).
target_language_example: Yo creo en ti; puedes hacerlo.
native_language_example: I believe in you; you can do it.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or what you believe is true. In everyday Spanish it often sounds softer and less direct than stating something as a fact. The word “que” (“that”) is commonly used, but in casual speech it can sometimes be dropped: “Yo creo que…” / “Yo creo…”.
target_language_example: Yo creo que mañana va a llover.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed in the past, often implying you later found out it wasn’t true or you were mistaken.
